articles.title: Zaporizhzhia RMA head: I feel like someone who has no home
articles.body:
Zaporizhzhia RMA head: I feel like someone who has no home
He made these remarks in an interview with Ukrinform, responding to a question about whether he considers himself an internally displaced person (IDP).
“I definitely feel like someone who has no home. My home was taken from me. What I miss most in the occupied territory is my parents’ house,” he said.
The head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration noted that his family moved into his parents’ house when he was in first grade.
“My father built it himself. We moved there before any renovations had been done; we gradually fixed it up ourselves. Later on, I would visit my parents on Saturdays or Sundays to have lunch with my mom. There’s an expression: ‘my parents’ home.’ That’s exactly what it is. It’s what I miss the most. So, I am definitely someone whose home was taken away, and I definitely have to get my home back. That’s one of the main reasons why I’m in public service today. It’s true. I want to get my home back,” Fedorov added.
As previously reported, Ivan Fedorov is a native of Melitopol. Prior to his appointment as head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional State Administration, he served as mayor of Melitopol.
As reported by Ukrinform, due to intensified Russian shelling in Zaporizhzhia, an exodus of residents is being observed, particularly families with children.

articles.title: Yemen government vows response after Houthi missiles hit Mokha
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen government vows response after Houthi missiles hit Mokha port
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has vowed a "harsh" response intended to deter further attacks after Houthi forces fired ballistic missiles at the Red Sea port of Mokha, in the latest escalation around the strategically important west-coast city near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
One member of port security was killed, while two sailors were reported missing. Eight civilians, including two security personnel, were wounded, according to an initial toll issued by the government.
Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili, spokesman for the Yemeni armed forces, said six ballistic missiles struck Mokha port on Friday evening in what he called an attack on a civilian, economic and maritime facility.
"The armed forces will not allow civilian facilities to be turned into military targets," al-Nuzaili said, pledging a "deterrent and harsh" response to attacks on Yemeni infrastructure and interests.
The Houthi shelling also struck residential areas in Mokha, with Yemeni authorities reporting that four civilians were killed and several fishing boats set on fire. A military source told the state-run Saba News Agency that air defences shot down a Houthi drone during the attack.
Port officials said four ballistic missiles hit a quay where an excavator was deepening the navigation channel. Abdulmalik al-Sharabi, Mokha port’s director, said the strike appeared intended to disable the excavation work and damage its equipment, potentially disrupting shipping activity.
Mokha is a key government-held port on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, located close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a maritime chokepoint linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and a major route for global commerce.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had carried out a large-scale operation using ballistic missiles, claiming it targeted gunboats, weapons stores and military gatherings in Mokha.
Saree said the attack had caused destruction to military equipment and killed and injured "Saudi military mobilisations", without providing evidence, a casualty figure or precise locations. The Houthis have framed the operation as a response to what they describe as Saudi-backed military deployments along Yemen’s western coast.
The government-aligned forces and port authorities, however, said civilian neighbourhoods and critical commercial infrastructure had been struck.
Government and diplomatic warnings
A source in Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council said continued Houthi attacks on ports, civilian facilities, economic sites and international shipping lanes "will not go unpunished".
The council said Mokha was one of the supply arteries relied on by millions of Yemenis for food, medicine, fuel and other essentials, warning that continued attacks could deepen an already severe humanitarian crisis.
Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba also said the targeting of Mokha threatened a Yemeni "lifeline" and jeopardised efforts to safeguard shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab. In a post on X, she accused the Houthis of seeking to undermine government forces’ efforts to curb arms-smuggling routes and secure maritime navigation.
"Bab al-Mandab will not become a tool for pressure in the hands of an armed terrorist group," she said, calling for greater support for government forces, navies and coast guards to protect commercial ports, cargo vessels and freedom of navigation.
Government artillery meanwhile targeted Houthi gatherings and movements west of Jabal Han, west of Taiz city, according to the Yemeni Armed Forces Media Centre, without providing information on casualties or damage.

articles.title: India's Modi announces nationwide AI-skilling program on 80th Independence Day
articles.body:
NEW DELHI, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a series of major initiatives, including a nationwide AI-skilling program, as the country celebrated its 80th Independence Day on Saturday.
The AI-skilling program was designed to benefit 10 million young people nationwide, according to Modi in his address to the nation.
"We organized the AI Impact Summit recently. The expansion of AI is taking place at a very rapid pace ... We have decided that, in the next one year, we will train one crore (10 million) young people in AI skills, so that the youth of our country have the capability to lead in the world of AI as well," Modi said.
The initiatives also included free online coaching for competitive examinations, civil defense reforms, a sports talent hunt for children, expansion of semiconductor manufacturing and new targets for nuclear power generation.
The prime minister highlighted the critical role of semiconductor chips in the digital and technological world and said India was moving towards self-reliance in this sector.
Modi also underlined the importance of energy security and nuclear power.
Ahead of India's Independence Day celebrations, security was beefed up across the country, including the capital city New Delhi. ■

articles.title: World Insights: Haunting nightmares: how medical records become evidence of Japanese wartime atrocities in China
articles.body:
TOKYO, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- As Japan marks the 81st anniversary of its surrender in World War II, thousands of old military medical records preserved in Japan are offering rare documentary evidence of atrocities committed by Japanese soldiers during the war of aggression against China -- records that the Japanese military once ordered destroyed.
Hidden for decades in iron containers beneath the ground and later painstakingly copied by hand, the files contain soldiers' own confessions of killing civilians, burning villages and bayoneting children. Japanese scholars said the records not only document wartime crimes, but also expose how militarist ideology normalized violence while the military sought to erase evidence of its responsibility.
RECORDS THAT SURVIVED
On Aug. 15, 1945, Japan announced the acceptance of the Potsdam Declaration, agreeing to unconditional surrender. In the days surrounding the defeat, the Japanese military ordered the destruction of large quantities of confidential documents, including the medical records of Japanese troops who had invaded China and received treatment at the Kohnodai Army Hospital in Ichikawa City, Chiba Prefecture -- now the Kohnodai Hospital, National Center for Global Health and Medicine.
"The military wanted to burn documents that could reveal war crimes and serve as evidence for future accountability," Tomio Hosobuchi, professor emeritus at Saitama University, told Xinhua.
Fortunately, the hospital's then-director preserved the medical records, citing their value as "precious historical materials," Hosobuchi said. The records were sealed in iron barrels and buried underground, allowing them to survive till now.
The original documents are now housed at a psychiatric medical institution in Chiba City. Their complete photocopied collection is preserved in the archives of Asai Hospital in Togane City, also in Chiba Prefecture.
PATIENTS' CONFESSIONS
Inside the archive, thousands of yellowed photocopies of medical records document the psychological conditions of Japanese soldiers hospitalized during the war.
One medical record reviewed by Xinhua contains the following statement by a former soldier: "I killed six civilians in Shandong Province; the memory frequently haunts my dreams, leaving me unable to find peace."
The soldier continued: "The experience of killing young children, in particular, causes me profound anguish when I think of my own children of the same age."
Before enlistment, this soldier had worked at a post office in Yamagata Prefecture. After Japan launched its full-scale invasion of China, he was deployed to northern China and was admitted to the Kohnodai Army Hospital in August 1938 after developing "mental illness."
Hosobuchi explained that some Japanese soldiers developed numbness in the limbs, tremors and other psychological symptoms after experiencing battlefield terror or severe mental trauma. During the war, such conditions were broadly classified as "war neurosis," and the Kohnodai Army Hospital specialized in treating these patients, admitting approximately 10,000 individuals.
Why did the military want the files erased? Eri Nakamura, associate professor at Sophia University, believes that many cases of "war neurosis" were linked to soldiers' own "use of violence or direct participation in acts of perpetration." "After Japan's defeat, the military feared these records would become evidence of war responsibility, so it ordered them destroyed," she added.
Nakamura showed Xinhua another medical record of a Japanese soldier. It contained a personal account describing how he had bayoneted a 12-year-old child to death: "That child was so pitiful; the scene of the stabbing keeps lingering in my mind, and the image flashes back whenever I have an episode."
Nakamura noted that expressions such as "pitiful" were exceptionally rare in wartime records because Japanese soldiers had generally been conditioned to regard killing as legitimate and to deny the humanity of their victims. Moreover, wartime censorship discouraged any discussion of atrocities committed during the war; consequently, soldiers were not only reluctant to speak of the grim reality of "killing" but also subconsciously rationalized their own acts of perpetration even while seeking psychiatric treatment.
NORMALIZING VIOLENCE
Hosobuchi said numerous files explicitly record atrocities committed by the Japanese military, including accounts such as "burned down the entire village" and "I even killed infants."
More strikingly, Hosobuchi noted, descriptions like "total annihilation" or "the village was burned" were often recorded not as causes of the soldiers' psychological illness but as "military achievements."
The reason, he argues, lies in the militarist education promoted by wartime Japan.
People were intensely indoctrinated with the ideology of "hakko ichiu," or "all the world under one roof," Hosobuchi said, referring to the imperial slogan that envisioned Japanese domination over Asia and eventually the world.
"Under that ideology, ruling and subjugating other peoples was presented as something natural. Many were driven to the battlefield by precisely this way of thinking," Hosobuchi added.
This militarist atmosphere not only distorted soldiers' perceptions of war and killing, but also drove the Japanese military to go to great lengths to cover up the existence of "war neurosis."
According to Nakamura, acknowledging widespread psychological trauma would have made soldiers aware of war's destructive impact on themselves, undermined morale and exposed the vulnerability of the state, so the Japanese military deliberately concealed it from the public; in effect, this was a form of "image management."
As Japanese military deaths mounted during the war, public willingness to continue fighting steadily weakened, Hosobuchi added. "In order to sustain the war, the Japanese military became even more deliberate in concealing the reality."
WARNING FOR FUTURE GENERATIONS
The medical records have acquired profound historical significance precisely because they escaped destruction.
Nakamura said they provide documentary proof that Japanese troops committed numerous atrocities in China while also revealing the institutional mechanisms that made such violence possible.
"These atrocities occurred because the Japanese military carried out training designed to make people capable of perpetrating violence," she said. "Its purpose was to eliminate soldiers' psychological resistance to killing."
For Hosobuchi, the files are more than historical evidence; they are a warning.
"War causes people to lose their humanity," he said. "I hope future generations will understand the cruelty of war through these preserved records, remember the suffering it brought, and prevent such tragedies from ever happening again." ■

articles.title: Economic Watch: U.S. retail sales fall in July, raising concerns over consumer spending
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- U.S. retail sales fell in July, pointing to softer consumer spending amid persistent price pressures and signs of a cooling labor market, according to data released Friday by the U.S. Commerce Department.
Retail sales declined 0.6 percent in July from a revised 0.2-percent increase in June, marking the biggest downtick since May last year. The decline came after stronger spending in April and May, when tax refunds helped support household consumption.
The latest figures fell short of analysts' expectations for a modest increase and prompted concerns among some economists about the underlying strength of consumer demand.
"The biggest fall was with autos, but pulling out autos and gas sales, nominal sales were still down 0.2 percent for the second consecutive month," Dean Baker, a macroeconomist and co-founder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told Xinhua. "And this is even with the boost to restaurant sales from the World Cup."
"That looks (like) some real weakness to me. In a context where job growth has slowed to a crawl and wages have not kept pace with inflation, this should not be surprising," Baker said.
Gasoline prices have also remained elevated compared with a year earlier. The average U.S. retail price for regular gasoline stood at 4.077 U.S. dollars per gallon on Friday, nearly 1 dollar higher than a year earlier, according to the American Automobile Association.
At the same time, consumer sentiment dropped 8 percent from the month prior, according to last week's report from the University of Michigan.
Consumer spending is a key component of the U.S. economy, and economists said a sustained slowdown in household purchases could weigh on overall economic activity.
"Retail sales are a big part of the economy. If consumers slow their purchases, it harms the overall economy," Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told Xinhua. "People have difficulty buying things when the cost of living keeps rising."
Christopher Galdieri, a political science professor at Saint Anselm College in the northeastern state of New Hampshire, said the retail sales report is "particularly notable."
It shows that Americans are "adjusting their purchasing to account for higher prices or in the anticipation of further bad news," Galdieri told Xinhua. ■

articles.title: Houthis report Saudi shelling along Yemen's northern border
articles.body:
SANAA, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Saturday that Saudi forces launched "artillery and missile strikes" on areas along Yemen's northern border in the province of Saada, as tensions between the two sides continue to escalate.
The group's affiliated Al-Masirah TV reported that "Saudi artillery fire" targeted Al-Dhaher district in the northern province of Saada, a Houthi stronghold bordering Saudi Arabia.
Separately, heavy "missile fire" struck the Bani Sayyah area in Saada's border district of Razih, damaging farmland belonging to local residents, the television channel said.
No casualties were immediately reported, nor was there any immediate comment from Saudi authorities.
The reported shelling came a day after the Houthis claimed a drone attack on a facility belonging to Saudi state oil company Aramco in the southern region of Najran, saying the strike was a retaliation for an alleged incursion by Saudi warplanes into Saada's airspace.
Tensions have risen sharply since July 20, when the Houthis announced a maritime ban on Saudi shipping, citing an alleged Saudi blockade of Houthi-held areas, a claim Riyadh rejects.
Since then, the Houthis have claimed a series of attacks on Saudi tankers, energy facilities and airports, while also intensifying missile and drone strikes on government-held areas in Yemen.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.
A United Nations (UN)-brokered truce that took effect in April 2022 expired six months later without a formal extension, but a fragile de facto ceasefire had largely contained direct hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis until the recent escalation. ■

articles.title: Japan's Takaichi worships notorious Yasukuni Shrine from distance
articles.body:
TOKYO, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Saturday performed a remote act of worship toward the notorious Yasukuni Shrine, a symbol of the country's militarism and wartime aggression, from nearby instead of visiting in person, local media reported.
On the 81st anniversary of Japan's unconditional surrender in World War II, upon arriving at Tokyo's Nippon Budokan hall to attend her first war memorial ceremony since taking office last year, Takaichi turned toward Yasukuni Shrine across the road and bowed twice, clapped twice and bowed once in an apparent act of Shinto worship from a distance, Kyodo News reported.
Before her premiership, Takaichi used to visit the war-linked shrine during its seasonal festivals and the Aug. 15 anniversary.
Earlier in the day, Takaichi made a "tamagushi" ritual offering to the controversial shrine in her capacity as president of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, while several cabinet ministers and senior politicians paid visits there, triggering strong criticism from peace advocates in Japan.
Yasukuni Shrine, located in central Tokyo's Chiyoda Ward, honors 14 convicted Class-A Japanese war criminals from World War II. For a long time, visits and ritual offerings made by Japanese officials to the controversial shrine have consistently sparked criticism and opposition both at home and abroad, hurting the feelings of the people of China, South Korea, and other countries and regions brutalized by Japan during the war. ■
