articles.title: Northern Metropolis and AI vital to Hong Kong’s 5-year plan: business chambers
articles.body:
Northern Metropolis and AI vital to Hong Kong’s 5-year plan: business chambers
AmCham and FHKI also highlight the need to reinforce Hong Kong’s position as an international financial centre
Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan should prioritise the Northern Metropolis mega development, strengthen the city’s position as an international financial centre and advance its artificial intelligence (AI) strategy, major business chambers have said.
In submissions for the city’s first five-year plan, groups including the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong (AmCham) and the Federation of Hong Kong Industries (FHKI) identified the Northern Metropolis as a key economic driver.
Their recommendations are among more than 16,000 submissions received by authorities before the public consultation closed on Friday. The blueprint, expected to be published in September, will set the direction for Hong Kong’s development in alignment with China’s 15th five-year plan covering the years between 2026 and 2030.
First announced in 2021, the metropolis aims to transform about 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land along the mainland Chinese border into an engine for growth, a housing hub and a university town.
“Over the next five years, the development of the Northern Metropolis should be guided by industrial development, enterprise presence and employment outcomes,” FHKI said.
AmCham called for a single statutory entity to streamline coordination and facilitate public-private partnerships. It also urged deeper Greater Bay Area wealth integration by expanding Wealth Management Connect quotas and widening eligible product scopes.

articles.title: Scientists solve the mystery of a brain “switch” that can trigger weight loss in opposite ways
articles.body:
Scientists solve the mystery of a brain “switch” that can trigger weight loss in opposite ways
- Date:
- August 15, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cambridge
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered why two seemingly opposite ways of targeting the same brain receptor can both promote weight loss. In mice, activating the GIP receptor in the brainstem reduced appetite, while blocking it in the hypothalamus removed a kind of “brake” on fullness signals. The discovery helps explain why very different obesity drugs can achieve similar results and suggests that carefully combining GIP-targeting treatments with GLP-1 drugs like those related to Wegovy and Ozempic could produce stronger effects.
- Share:
Cambridge researchers have uncovered why both activating and blocking the same brain receptor can promote weight loss. The findings may help scientists develop obesity treatments that are more effective and potentially work better in combination.
The mouse study, published in Nature Metabolism, found that the outcome depends on which part of the brain is targeted. Activating the receptor in the brainstem reduced appetite, while blocking the same receptor in the hypothalamus produced a similar weight loss effect through a different mechanism.
More than a billion people around the world are living with obesity, a condition that raises the risk of diseases including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and cancer. Losing weight can reduce some of these risks, but achieving substantial weight loss through diet and exercise alone can be difficult.
How Modern Weight Loss Drugs Target the Brain
A new generation of weight loss medications has emerged in recent years that act on specific receptors involved in appetite. By influencing these receptors, the drugs can reduce food intake, promote weight loss, and help regulate blood sugar.
Several widely used medications, including Wegovy and Ozempic, activate a protein receptor called the glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor (GLP-1R).
Other obesity treatments act on both GLP-1R and another receptor known as the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor (GIPR). This second target has presented scientists with an unusual puzzle.
Some medications, including Mounjaro and Zepbound, activate GIPR. Others, such as MariTide, block it. Despite producing opposite effects on the same receptor, both approaches can help promote weight loss.
Researchers at the Institute of Metabolic Science, University of Cambridge, set out to understand why. Their experiments in mice revealed that the two types of GIPR drugs work through different regions of the brain. The researchers also found that these approaches can increase weight loss when paired with certain GLP-1-based weight loss medicines.
Tracking GIPR Activity in Different Brain Regions
To identify the brain regions responsible for these effects, the team used genetically engineered mice in which GIPR had been selectively removed from specific areas.
One group lacked GIPR in the brainstem, the region at the base of the brain just above the spinal cord that is involved in appetite and nausea. Another group lacked the receptor in the hypothalamus, an important brain region involved in regulating hunger and body weight. A third group consisted of normal, unmodified mice that served as controls.
The scientists treated the animals with different combinations of a GIPR agonist (which activates the receptor), a GIPR antagonist (which blocks the receptor) and a GLP-1 drug. They then monitored food consumption, body weight, fat mass, blood sugar control and brain activity.
Comparing the different groups allowed the team to pinpoint where each treatment was acting.
The results showed that GIPR agonists primarily work through the brainstem. Activating GIPR in this region reduced appetite and led to lower body weight.
Blocking a Brain Brake on Fullness
GIPR antagonists followed a different route.
Instead of acting primarily through the brainstem, the researchers found that blocking GIPR promoted weight loss through the hypothalamus. In this region, GIPR appears to function as a kind of 'brake' that limits how strongly the brainstem responds to signals indicating that the body is full.
Blocking the receptor effectively releases that 'brake', allowing fullness signals to have a stronger effect.
The researchers also found evidence that blocking GIPR could enhance the effects of emerging medicines that target the amylin receptor. This suggests that GIPR antagonists might eventually be useful for strengthening several different classes of obesity treatments.
Clues to More Powerful Obesity Drug Combinations
The results help explain why treatments such as MariTide can be effective. MariTide, currently in phase 3 clinical trials, combines GIPR antagonism with GLP-1 receptor agonism.
Understanding how these separate pathways interact could also help researchers design more effective combinations of obesity medicines in the future.
Dr. Jo Lewis, the study's first author from the Institute of Metabolic Science at the University of Cambridge, said: "Understanding which brain circuits respond to these medications - and how they do so - could help us design better drugs that produce more weight loss with fewer side effects, and which might work in combination with other obesity medicines to even greater effect.
"Our work also strengthens the idea that the brain is central to obesity treatment. Obesity drugs are not acting simply on the gut or pancreas. Instead, they have important effects on specific, identifiable brain circuits that regulate appetite and food intake."
The research was funded by the Medical Research Council and Wellcome.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Cambridge. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Jo Edward Lewis, Mireia Montaner, Danae Nuzzaci, Paula-Peace James-Okoro, Norio Harada, Nobuya Inagaki, W. Scott Dodson, Patrick J. Knerr, Jonathan D. Douros, Fiona Mary Gribble, Frank Reimann. Distinct brain regions mediate regulation of food intake in response to GIPR agonism or antagonism. Nature Metabolism, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s42255-026-01575-z

articles.title: Russian Strikes Target Pavlohrad and Combine Harvester in Zaporizhzhia
articles.body:
Russian forces struck the city of Pavlohrad in the Dnipropetrovsk region, causing a fire and injuring two people, while a separate drone attack targeted agricultural workers in the Zaporizhzhia region.
Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration Head Oleksandr Hanzha reported on Telegram that the strike on Pavlohrad resulted in damage to several private houses and caused a fire that rescue workers subsequently contained.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Hanzha stated that two men, aged 47 and 54, sustained injuries in the attack and were hospitalized in moderate condition.
In a separate attack, the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration reported that Russian forces used an FPV drone to attack a combine harvester operating in a field within the Zaporizhzhia district.
The attack injured two men, aged 30 and 32, who were involved in harvesting operations. The administration stated that the individuals are receiving necessary medical assistance.
Strikes on Marhanets and Zaporizhzhia
The attack follows earlier Russian drone barrages on the Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions early Saturday morning, Aug. 15.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian forces struck a multi-story residential building in Marhanets, resulting in the death of a three-month-old boy.
Hanzha reported that the attack injured 11 people, seven of whom were hospitalized in severe condition. The injured included a five-year-old boy and a 12-year-old girl.
Concurrently, Russian troops launched a drone attack on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia. The regional administration reported that the strike damaged an industrial enterprise and a shopping center, where a fire broke out.
Russian Drone Kills Baby in Marhanets High-Rise
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service later stated that rescue workers had extinguished two fires caused by the Russian drone strikes on Zaporizhzhia during the night of Aug. 15.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Flamingo Missiles Strike Russia’s Soyuz Rocket Factory Behind Its Starlink Rival
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Flamingo Missiles Strike Russia’s Soyuz Rocket Factory Behind Its Starlink Rival
Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles struck the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara overnight on August 15, hitting the factory that produces Soyuz-2 launch vehicles used to deploy Russian military satellites and the Rassvet low-Earth-orbit network—Moscow’s answer to Starlink.
The apparent confirmation that Flamingo cruise missiles were used in the attack came from Fire Point co-founder Denis Shtilerman, who shortly after the strike posted nighttime footage showing the launch of the Ukrainian-made missile.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Samara regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed that a missile strike had hit an industrial facility in the city but did not identify the target. Samara Mayor Ivan Noskov described the attack as a large-scale missile strike.
Local residents reported explosions shortly after a missile alert was issued in the region. Videos published from Samara showed a large fire and a column of smoke rising from an industrial area occupied by the neighboring Progress Rocket Space Centre and Aviakor aircraft plant.
According to Defense Express on August 15, available imagery indicates that the strike may have hit Progress, one of Russia’s key producers of space launch vehicles. The outlet said satellite imagery would still be required to confirm the precise impact point and determine the extent of the damage.
Progress is one of the central enterprises in Russia’s space-launch industry and manufactures the Soyuz-2 family of launch vehicles, including the Soyuz-2.1b.
The Soyuz-2.1b is used to place Russian government and military spacecraft into orbit and has also been used to deploy satellites for Rassvet, a planned Russian low-Earth-orbit communications constellation often described as Moscow’s counterpart to Starlink. On March 23, 2026, a Soyuz-2.1b launched 16 satellites associated with the Rassvet system.
According to Defense Express, the Samara plant represents a particularly concentrated point in Russia’s Soyuz production chain. The enterprise consists of an interconnected industrial complex roughly one kilometer long where launch vehicles pass through successive stages of assembly.
The outlet assessed that the reported strike may have affected the western section of the complex, where later stages of Soyuz production are believed to take place.
Defense Express reported that Russia has conducted approximately six to eight Soyuz-2.1b launches annually since 2022, with the rockets supporting military, government and other space missions.
Soyuz remains one of Russia’s primary methods for placing military satellites into orbit, meaning disruption at Progress could also affect reconnaissance, communications and other space programs beyond Rassvet.
Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy chief of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, previously said Russia was developing the satellite system faster than initially expected. The constellation is intended to provide broadband communications from low Earth orbit and could support both civilian and military users.
The Progress and Aviakor facilities are located roughly 850–950 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border, placing the industrial complex deep inside Russian territory.
Earlier, Russia’s Rassvet satellite network was reported to face a major launch bottleneck because its satellites rely on Soyuz-2.1b rockets produced at the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara. Russia needs at least 18 Soyuz-2.1b launches to deploy the planned 288-satellite constellation, while only six to eight such rockets are typically launched per year.

articles.title: Lavrov Says the War Will Continue—Russian Stock Plunges
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Lavrov Says the War Will Continue—Russian Stock Plunges
The Russian stock market closed August 14 with its sharpest single-day decline since September 26, 2022, as reported by The Moscow Times.
The MOEX Index fell by 4.29%, dropping to 2,136.3 points and erasing roughly 250 billion rubles ($3.2 billion) in total market capitalization.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Over a three-day period the index fell 8.4%, reversing half of the gains accumulated over the previous month and a half.
Market analysts linked the sudden downturn directly to escalating geopolitical tension. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov explicitly rejected freezing the frontline, claiming such a move would "undermine the achievement of ancestors who defeated Nazism."
Lavrov also threatened "destruction" against Western nations supporting Kyiv and warned of "harsher measures" in response to strikes by Ukrainian forces. Furthermore, the Russian Foreign Ministry rejected a proposed ceasefire in the Black Sea.
Trading began with minor gains before shares fell rapidly midway through the session. By late evening, Sberbank dropped 1.4%, Magnit fell 3.2%, Gazprom lost 4.4%, Lukoil decreased 4.8%, Rosneft declined 5.1%, and Rusal plummeted 6.5%.
The downturn comes after a record 17-week decline between late spring and early summer, the longest streak since 1997. Although the market stabilized in late June, market strategists noted that investors are now closing positions previously opened on expectations of improved diplomatic relations between Russia and the United States.
Market participants had been anticipating a visit to Kyiv and Moscow by American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, an initiative announced nearly two weeks ago that has yet to materialize.
Financial experts highlight that geopolitical risks persist while interest rates remain high and domestic economic growth remains virtually absent.
Analysts suggest that ongoing strikes on Russian infrastructure increase the likelihood of a growing federal budget deficit, which may delay potential interest rate cuts and push the MOEX index further toward its annual low of 1,898 points.
During the week ending July 7, 2026, the Russian stock market extended its decline for a 17th consecutive week, reaching its lowest point in more than three years as the Moscow Exchange Index dropped to 2,117.5 points.
The market downturn accelerated following long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on major energy infrastructure, including the Omsk and Moscow oil refineries, which forced extended operational halts, reduced domestic fuel production, and drove down the equity value of major state-linked enterprises like Gazprom and Gazprom Neft.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,370 Troops, 3 Air Defense Systems, and 62 Artillery Systems
Russian forces suffered an estimated 1,370 personnel casualties and lost five tanks and 62 artillery systems over the past 24 hours, according to Ukraine’s latest battlefield assessment.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s General Staff reported on August 15 that the latest figures bring Russia’s total estimated personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, to approximately 1,465,810.
According to the General Staff, Russian forces also lost three armored combat vehicles, two multiple launch rocket systems, three air defense systems, 12 unmanned ground vehicles, and 1,835 operational-tactical UAVs during the reporting period.
Ukraine additionally reported the destruction of 522 vehicles and fuel tankers and four pieces of special equipment.
Russia’s cumulative equipment losses are now estimated at 12,269 tanks, 25,144 armored combat vehicles, 47,932 artillery systems, 2,026 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,568 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 2,241 unmanned ground vehicles, 461,484 operational-tactical UAVs, 5,007 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, 134,375 vehicles and fuel tankers, and 4,528 pieces of special equipment.
Ukraine’s General Staff recorded 233 combat engagements across the front over the past 24 hours. Russian forces carried out 71 airstrikes during the day, dropping 241 guided aerial bombs on Ukrainian positions and populated areas.
They also deployed 10,626 strike drones and conducted 3,042 attacks against Ukrainian settlements and military positions, including 36 strikes using multiple launch rocket systems.
Over the same period, Ukrainian aviation, missile forces, and artillery struck two Russian command posts, five areas where Russian personnel were concentrated, three artillery systems, and eight UAV control points.
Earlier, Ukrainian SBU drones struck several high-value Russian air defense assets, including a key 92N6 engagement radar from an S-400 system, two Pantsir-S2 systems, and Kasta-2E2 and Sopka-2 radars, with the targeted equipment valued at more than $170 million.

articles.title: Boeing’s presidential jet contract grows to $4.49 billion
articles.body:
- Boeing received a $75 million modification for spare parts on two VC-25B aircraft, bringing the contract's cumulative value to $4.49 billion.
- The VC-25B, originally due in 2024, is now projected for delivery in 2028 and 2029, replacing the VC-25A fleet in service since 1990.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Boeing a $75 million modification to buy initial spare parts for two VC-25B aircraft, the in-development replacement for the current Air Force One fleet. The modification brings the cumulative value of the underlying contract to $4.49 billion, up from $4.42 billion.
The modification, listed as P00187 to contract FA8625-16-C-6599, is separate from the contract’s firm-fixed-price engineering and manufacturing development work. Work will be performed in San Antonio, Texas. The U.S. Air Force obligated $30 million in fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds at the time of award. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, is the contracting activity.
Boeing signed the VC-25B deal in 2018, during President Trump’s first term, as a $3.9 billion fixed-price contract to convert two Boeing 747-8 airframes into replacements for the current VC-25A jets, customized Boeing 747-200B aircraft that entered service in 1990 under President George H.W. Bush. The two 747-8 airframes were originally built for Russia’s Transaero airline, which went bankrupt before taking delivery, allowing the U.S. Air Force to acquire them at a reduced cost.
First delivery was originally set for the end of 2024. The Air Force now projects the first aircraft in mid-2028 and the second in mid-2029, according to a Breaking Defense report citing an Air Force spokesperson, a delay of roughly four years. Boeing has attributed the setbacks to COVID-19 disruptions, workforce shortages, wiring defects, subcontractor bankruptcies and security-clearance delays for personnel working on the aircraft. Boeing lost its original cabin interior supplier, GDC Technics, after terminating that contract in 2021. The company has continued to record cost overruns on the fixed-price deal, including a $280 million charge disclosed this month.
The current fleet’s age has drawn attention this year. In January, one of the VC-25A aircraft carrying Trump toward the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, turned back to Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, after the crew reported a minor electrical issue shortly after takeoff. Trump continued the trip aboard a smaller U.S. Air Force C-32, a modified Boeing 757 normally used for domestic travel to smaller airports.
In May, the Pentagon accepted a Boeing 747 donated by Qatar for use as a presidential aircraft while the VC-25B remains undelivered, an arrangement that drew scrutiny over ethics and security concerns.
In July, following a NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, Trump’s departure involved a similar aircraft switch. Trump boarded the older VC-25A in view of the traveling press. He then left the plane through a catering truck and transferred to a smaller C-32A aircraft, CNN and CBS News reported, citing U.S. officials. The VC-25A, the Qatari-donated 747 and the C-32A then flew separately to the United Kingdom, where Trump boarded the Qatari-donated aircraft to fly home.
White House officials said the security measures were tied to a threat linked to Iran but did not answer questions about whether journalists and staff who remained aboard the VC-25A, unaware Trump was no longer on board, had been placed at risk.

articles.title: Türkiye-Syria border 'security problems disappeared': Turkish envoy
articles.body:
Türkiye's Ambassador to Damascus, Nuh Yilmaz, said the main security threats along the Turkish-Syrian border have been eliminated since Syria's new administration took office.
Yilmaz discussed the diplomatic engagement between Ankara and Damascus and regional developments in an interview with the Qatar-based Al Jazeera channel's "Syria Now" programme.
He said Türkiye's largest diplomatic mission in the world is in Damascus, highlighting the historical roots of bilateral relations, as well as military and economic cooperation and shared determination to fight terrorism.
Pointing to the deep historical and cultural ties between Türkiye and Syria, Yilmaz said Damascus holds a special place in the Turkish national memory.
"Throughout history, this ancient city, known as 'Sham al-Sharif,' has carried a deep-rooted legacy stretching from the Ottoman Empire to the Seljuks.
"From the call to prayer at the Umayyad Mosque to our shared traditions, the most distinctive traces of our culture continue to live on here," he said.
‘Security problems disappeared’
Assessing security conditions and military contacts between the two countries, Yilmaz recalled Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's principle that "Syria's security is Türkiye's security."
He said the main strategic security problems along the border had disappeared following the change in Syria's administration.
"After December 8, 2024, four strategic security problems — human smuggling, drug trafficking, uncontrolled migration and terrorism — suddenly disappeared along our border," Yilmaz said.
He also cited a visit by Turkish naval vessels to Latakia Port as a concrete sign of future military and maritime cooperation.
"The visit of Turkish Navy vessels to Latakia Port is also the most concrete indication of the cooperation we will undertake in the military and maritime fields in the coming period.
"We are ready to stand by the Syrian army in meeting its training, equipment, and logistical needs," he said.
Ankara closely following process
Yilmaz said Türkiye's position on terrorist elements in the region was clear, stressing that the PKK/YPG/SDF must be completely removed from the region.
He said Ankara was closely following the process between the Syrian government and the YPG, adding that the complete elimination of PKK and SDF elements across Türkiye, Syria, and Iraq was necessary to preserve Syria's territorial integrity and sovereignty.
"We envision the dream not only as an environment where terrorism has ended in Türkiye, but across our entire region.
"The complete elimination of SDF and PKK elements throughout Türkiye, Syria, and Iraq is essential for Syria's territorial integrity and sovereignty.
"As (Syrian) President Ahmed al Sharaa has also stated, although the integration process is moving slowly, we support steps aimed at bringing terrorism to an end," Yilmaz said.
Goal of $10B in trade
On economic ties, Yilmaz said the bilateral trade volume had increased 40 percent in a short period to $3.75 billion, with a medium-term target of $10 billion.
He said negotiations were continuing on a free trade agreement and joint industrial zones.
Regarding border crossings, and that Türkiye aimed to reopen all crossings along the more than 900-kilometer (559-mile) border.
"We aim to open all crossings along our border, which stretches for more than 900 kilometers. Under the agreement reached between our Ministry of Trade and the Syrian customs authorities, we expect border crossings, particularly along the Nusaybin-Qamishli route, to become operational gradually within three months.
"In addition, the Free Zone and Dry Port project to be established in Idlib will accelerate transportation and customs procedures," he said.
Yilmaz also stressed the importance of supporting education in Syria. Under an agreement reached between Türkiye's Ministry of National Education and Syrian authorities, an international Turkish school will be opened in Damascus and surrounding areas in the coming period, he said.
Regarding Syrians under temporary protection in Türkiye, Yilmaz said an exemption from work permit requirements had been in place for a long time.
He added that Türkiye's Foreign Ministry and Interior Ministry were working on new visa arrangements to facilitate visits to Türkiye by Syrians who return to their country.
Erdogan's Damascus visit
Asked about a possible visit by President Erdogan to Syria, Yilmaz said such a trip remained an aspiration.
"Mr. President has great affection for Damascus and the Umayyad Mosque. Contacts that had been planned previously were postponed because of developments in the region.
"We hope to see Mr. President in Damascus before the end of this year. That historic image of Mr. Erdogan and Mr. al-Sharaa walking together at the Umayyad Mosque would proclaim to the world the strength of the strategic partnership between the two countries," he said.

articles.title: Trump’s 2024 grocery photo op now haunts Republicans in the midterms
articles.body:
Trump’s 2024 grocery photo op now haunts Republicans in the midterms
- Two years after Trump's 2024 grocery photo op blaming Democrats for inflation, food prices remain high, challenging Republicans ahead of the midterm elections.
- Voters feel the cost of living squeeze deeply, with many Republicans less enthusiastic about voting due to rising grocery and petrol prices.
- Despite some price drops in items like eggs, most staples are more expensive, weakening Trump’s promise to lower costs and benefiting Democratic challengers in key districts.
AI generated
BEDMINSTER, New Jersey - Two years after Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump staged a New Jersey press conference flanked by grocery staples to spotlight inflation under Democrats, food prices are still rising despite his pledge to bring them down.
The gap between promise and reality now looms as a vulnerability for Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Standing between tables piled high with fruit, beef, cereal, milk and other household staples at his Bedminster golf club on Aug 15, 2024, Trump blamed the Biden administration for sharp increases in groceries.
The spectacle, complete with charts showing higher prices, was aimed at undercutting the Democratic nominee, Kamala Harris, and highlighted Trump’s central promise: he alone could tame inflation and lower the cost of living.
Two years on, higher petrol and grocery prices are squeezing household budgets and turning the cost of living into the top issue for American voters.
Voters now give Democrats a slight edge over Republicans in who they view as better stewards of the economy for the first time in nearly a decade, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.
Sheila Carney, a 68-year-old Trump voter, punctuated her frustration with an expletive as she unloaded US$70 (S$89.57) worth of groceries into her car outside a supermarket not far from Trump’s Bedminster club.
The haul was modest: some meat, detergent and a 12-pack of iced tea.
For Carney, the receipt was evidence that the affordability concerns Trump has sometimes dismissed as a Democratic “hoax” remain a daily burden for many Americans.
“This is real. He can say it’s not, but it is,” said Carney, a hospital administration assistant who has delayed retirement while helping pay off her son’s student loans. “He hasn’t brought anything down.”
A Reuters analysis of 26 grocery categories tracked by the Bureau of Labour Statistics and featured in Trump’s Bedminster display found prices have risen 3.4 per cent in the first 19 months of his second term.
That’s less than a quarter of the pace recorded at the same point in former President Joe Biden’s term, but still falls short of Trump’s pledge to lower prices, as surges in coffee, beef and apples have more than offset declines in items including eggs and butter.
A White House official pointed to data on Aug 13 that showed US consumer prices barely increased in July from the month before as evidence that inflation is under control.
“The July CPI report is further proof that President Trump’s long-term agenda is delivering: prescription drug and auto insurance costs continue to fall, real wages are rising, and beef prices have cooled while other household essentials like eggs, poultry, and dairy remain low,” the official said.
Lack of enthusiasm
A registered Republican, Carney said high grocery and petrol prices due to the Iran war were among the reasons she had grown disillusioned enough to consider sitting out the midterms, underscoring recent polling suggesting Republicans are less enthusiastic about voting than Democrats.
Carney was one of 17 Republicans and independents Reuters interviewed in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District, a battleground that includes Bedminster and where swing voters and turnout could prove decisive.
The race pits Republican incumbent Tom Kean against Democrat Rebecca Bennett, who has sought to capitalise on voters’ frustration over the cost of living.
More than half of those interviewed said they were either undecided or leaning toward Bennett.
While grocery prices weighed heavily on many voters, complaints about Kean more often centred on his months-long disappearance from public view earlier in 2026, which he later attributed to depression.
Their views on the economy mirror those of other Trump supporters Reuters has interviewed in recent months who, despite standing by the president, say financial pressures have dampened their enthusiasm for voting in November.
That ambivalence presents another potential challenge for Republicans and raises the stakes for the party’s get-out-the-vote operation.
Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley, recently co-authored research finding that Trump drew stronger support in the 2024 election in counties where inflation outpaced income growth, eroding households’ purchasing power.
With real wages rising only marginally and lagging the pace of broader economic growth, Trebbi said it is likely that pattern will reverse in November.
“I expect the same anti-incumbent shift to happen in 2026, this time possibly weakening Republicans,” he said, describing grocery shopping as a “psychologically salient” reminder of the squeeze on household finances.
“Each time one does it, it is the equivalent of a campaign ad against the incumbent.”
Trump support
To be sure, presidents have limited influence over inflation, which is driven by a range of factors and more directly addressed by the Federal Reserve.
And many Republicans appear willing to give Trump the benefit of the doubt, even as his tariffs and the Iran war have contributed to rising prices.
Bonnie Chandler, 64, plans to vote for Kean, saying she believed some companies were keeping prices elevated to make Trump look bad and that the growing influence of the Democratic Party’s progressive faction left her unwilling to consider its candidates.
“I’m going to vote Republican. I’m not a woke person. I’m not a communist. I’m not a socialist,” she said.
Lauren DeGirolamo, a 34-year-old Trump voter, said issues such as education and border security mattered more to her than grocery prices, which she believes have stabilized under Trump following steep increases during the Biden administration.
“I feel grocery prices are pretty much at level with where they were during Biden. I know some of the key things that I look for - eggs - have gone down,” she said, adding that she intended to vote for Republican candidates in November.
According to BLS data, egg prices have fallen nearly 40 per cent under Trump, reflecting a market correction after avian flu-driven shortages triggered a surge that began during Biden’s presidency.
Eggs are among six of the 26 categories showing falls since 2025, along with butter, bacon, and cooking fats and oils.
Yet most of the items Trump displayed at Bedminster are now pricier, some by a lot. Uncooked beef has jumped 19.2 per cent, fresh fish and seafood 8.6 per cent, apples 14 per cent, and coffee nearly 23 per cent.
Hitting close to home
A Reuters/Ipsos poll that concluded earlier in August found Trump’s net approval rating on his handling of the cost of living was at -47 per cent, down from -6 per cent at the start of his term.
It is his weakest issue by a wide margin, trailing his ratings on the economy (-35 per cent) and immigration (-16 per cent).
Bennett told Reuters that if elected she would seek to undo Trump’s tariffs, rein in the Iran war, and restore food stamp benefits to help families struggling to afford groceries.
The issue hits close to home, said Bennett, a military veteran and married mother of two daughters.
“This is not an abstract concept to me,” she said. “For example, beef is very expensive, so we don’t buy beef anymore.”
Whether Kean, whose campaign did not respond to requests for comment, can hold on to his seat may depend on voters like Margaret Derkach, who typically votes Republican but is now considering switching her vote if economic conditions don’t improve.
“The cost of living, as far as homes, apartments and food - the necessities - they have gone up. It’s shocking, shocking,” said Derkach, 84, after shopping at discount grocer Aldi.
Though she said Trump “inherited a mess” from Biden, Derkach added, “I am undecided right now. I have to see.” REUTERS

articles.title: Struggling families urge return of student grant after textbook prices jump
articles.body:
Struggling families urge return of student grant after textbook prices jump
Prices range from HK$4,000 to HK$6,000 for set of books for 2026-27 school year, the highest since pandemic in 2020, according to Education Bureau
Hong Kong parents and concern groups have urged authorities to reinstate student subsidies after textbook prices recorded their sharpest increase since the Covid-19 pandemic, amid the growing use of digital learning tools.
Prices for a list of textbooks now range from HK$4,000 (US$510) to HK$6,000, representing an average increase of 3.6 per cent for the 2026-27 academic year, the highest since the pandemic began in 2020, according to Education Bureau book list data.
During the pandemic, prices barely rose, averaging 0.1 per cent growth, after the bureau asked publishers to freeze increases to ease financial pressure on families.
In 2020-21, prices of more than 90 per cent of titles were frozen, but the practice has since been wound down and the ratio has now declined to 20 per cent in 2026-27, the lowest on record.
Yeung Chi-lin, assistant general manager at major textbook retailer T.H. Lee Book Company, said the growing shift towards digital teaching materials had squeezed print runs and driven up book prices.
“The publishing business is getting harder to run. More schools are switching to digital materials, and not to mention that more parents are buying second-hand books,” he said.

articles.title: U.S. Army Apache parts contract with Boeing tops $1 billion
articles.body:
- Boeing received a $636.1 million modification to its U.S. Army contract for Apache airframe component repair and supply chain support.
- The modification brings the underlying contract's cumulative value to $1.1 billion, with $506.3 million obligated at award.
Boeing has been awarded a $636.1 million modification to its ongoing contract to repair and supply components for the U.S. Army’s AH-64 Apache helicopter fleet, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
The modification pushes the cumulative value of the underlying contract past $1.1 billion.
The modification, listed as PZ0022 to contract W58RGZ-24-C-0028, covers depot-level repair of complex Apache airframe components, system component support, supply of unique consumable parts, test equipment support, transmission infrastructure repair and retrograde, an obsolescence management program and broader supply chain management. Work will be performed at Boeing’s facility in Mesa, Arizona, with an estimated completion date of April 30, 2029.
While the modification carries a face value of $636.1 million, the U.S. Army obligated $506,314,739 in fiscal 2026 Army working capital funds at the time of award, leaving the remainder unfunded until additional money is committed. Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, is the contracting activity.
The U.S. Army first awarded contract W58RGZ-24-C-0028 to Boeing in April 2024 for $116.7 million to cover performance-based logistics support for Apache airframe components. The U.S. Army modified the contract again in March 2025 for $101.6 million and in March 2026 for $95.9 million, bringing the cumulative value to $489.7 million before this latest addition.
Under a performance-based logistics arrangement, Boeing is paid to guarantee parts availability and repair turnaround for Apache airframe components rather than the U.S. Army separately purchasing and warehousing spare parts itself. The obsolescence management program included in the modification addresses a recurring problem for the Apache fleet: the aircraft has been in continuous production and service since 1984, and some original component suppliers no longer make parts designed decades ago, requiring Boeing to requalify replacement sources or redesign affected parts.
The U.S. Army’s Apache program of record covers 791 attack helicopters, a mix of older AH-64D Longbow aircraft and the newer AH-64E, all built or remanufactured at Boeing’s Mesa facility, which also serves as the U.S. Army’s depot for this repair work, a factor that has kept the contract with Boeing without competition since it was first awarded in 2024.
Boeing’s Mesa site has produced or remanufactured more than 2,700 Apaches since 1984 and remains the aircraft’s sole production and depot-level repair location, supplying not only the U.S. Army but more than a dozen foreign operators, including a 96-aircraft order for Poland signed in 2024.
The contract is separate from a $2.7 billion firm-fixed-price agreement the U.S. Army awarded Boeing in late December 2025 for broader Apache post-production support, also managed by Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal.

articles.title: Ukraine says it has struck Russian 'rocket and space' centre
articles.body:
Additional strikes were carried out on Savasleyka air base - which Ukraine said housed aircraft used for missile attacks - and an oil facility in Ust-Luga, per Zelenskyy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Saturday that Ukrainian forces had struck the Progress Rocket and Space Centre" in Russia's Samara region, a facility involved in the manufacturing and operation of space launch vehicles.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy said Ukraine hit the centre with FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, describing it as one of Russian space agency Roscosmos' "key enterprises" and saying it was involved in "electronics production".
Additional strikes were carried out on Savasleyka air base in the Nizhny Novgorod region - which the Ukrainian leader said housed aircraft used for missile attacks on Ukraine - and an oil facility in Ust-Luga, close to the border with Estonia, per Zelenskyy.
He shared video footage on X appearing to show the aftermath of some of the strikes. Large columns of black smoke and flames can be seen at sites in the distance.
"Our plan of long-range sanctions against Russia for this war is being implemented, and it is important that Russia’s war potential be reduced," Zelenskyy wrote.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has since shared more details on the operation as well as its intelligence on the targets, confirming hits were recorded at both the Progress centre and the air base and that a fire had broken out on the facilities' grounds.
It added that the launch vehicles produced at the Progress centre were used to "place Russian military, reconnaissance, and communications spacecraft into orbit."
The Savasleyka air base, the General Staff added, is used to operate MiG-31K fighter jets, which it said were used to carry Kh-47M2 Kinzhal ballistic missiles.
Ukraine's 'long-range sanctions' and Russian strikes
Ukraine has repeatedly hit targets deep inside Russia in an effort to increase pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin and the country's military capabilities and to squeeze the Russian economy.
Kyiv has in particular sought to home in on energy facilities across Russia as part of this strategy, striking oil refineries, terminals, and depots across the country. The attacks have led to fuel shortages across parts of Russia and Russian-occupied territories.
The Ukrainian air force said on Saturday that Russian forces had launched 152 drones and loitering munitions at Ukraine overnight.
"According to preliminary data, as of 9 am, air defences had shot down or neutralised 124 enemy UAVs," it said, adding that strikes had been recorded in 16 locations.
Russian attacks on the Kherson region in southern Ukraine over the past day injured 28 people, including a child, according to Oleksandr Prokudin, the head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration.
A child was also killed and 11 people were injured in a series of strikes on the Dnipropetrovsk region in southeast Ukraine, per regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha, while four were injured in Sumy Oblast in the country's north.
A further nine people were injured across the regions of Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kharkiv, per local authorities.

articles.title: Heathrow passengers face disruption after flood restricts access
articles.body:
Heathrow airport has warned of disruption after flooding caused by a pipe leak restricted access to terminals 2 and 3.
Water in the central terminal area means anyone trying to travel to or from either terminal is unable enter by road. Passengers are being advised to travel by rail and tube instead. Access to the terminal car parks is also impeded, leaving passengers with parked cars unable to access them.
An airport spokesperson said: “Our teams are working to resolve the situation as quickly as possible. We apologise for any disruption caused. The leak has been isolated and repairs are ongoing.”
The disruption comes during the school holidays, one of the airport’s busiest periods.
Heathrow said 19 July had been its busiest day of the year so far with more than 267,000 passengers passing through as many schools broke up for summer.
The airport was recently affected by disruption to rail services after a water leak prompted the closure of a tunnel.
The airport is one of the busiest in the world, with as many as 1,300 flight movements – takeoffs and landings – every day.
Heathrow announced the latest disruption on X, leading to a stream of queries and complaints from concerned travellers.
“Do we have to meet and greet at T4 or 5?? When will this be resolved?,” one asked.
An official response read: “We recommend heading to T5 M&G and explaining to staff that your booking has been affected by the flooding.”
Another said: “I am collecting my daughter from Terminal 3 shortly; she has special needs. She has travelled via a wheelchair. Please can you advise?”
The airport replied: “You would not be able to park at Terminal 3 currently as there is no access by road; you would need to park at Terminal 4 or 5 and transfer to Terminal 3. We do have assistance teams in the terminal who would be able to advise on the best way of returning to your vehicle with a wheelchair passenger.”
The consumer rights group Which? urged passengers to check airline policies on booked flights, and advised against unnecessary travel.
The editor of Which? Travel, Rory Boland, said: “Passengers heading to Heathrow today will understandably be worried, so it’s important to follow the airport’s advice and avoid travelling by road to Terminals 2 and 3, instead allowing extra time and using public transport where possible.
 “If you’re worried you may miss your flight because of the disruption, contact your airline as soon as possible. Airlines have different policies on missed flights, so it’s worth finding out if you are entitled to a free rebooking or refund if your flight has operated.
 “If you’ve paid for airport parking but can no longer use it because of the road closures, contact the parking provider as soon as possible to see if you can amend your booking or get a refund. You should also check your travel insurance to see whether you’re covered for any costs you incur because of the disruption, such as a missed flight or additional travel expenses.”

articles.title: Iran's envoy slams 168 days of intl. silence over Minab crime

Each day marks a new wound, symbolizing “each of the 168 white-winged doves of the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school” in Minab, whose dreams were turned to ashes by the brutality of Tomahawk missiles, he added.
These 168 days are the silent yet living cry of 168 children, to whom international organizations and governments have closed their eyes on this black day in history, he noted.
The sorrowful grief of those empty seats and the loss of innocent lives will never grow old, Jalali stated.
Raising the question of how the world can remain silent in the face of such an obvious crime, the Iranian ambassador said the Minab school laid bare the story of child-killing in American human rights.
On February 28, in a joint US–Israeli missile attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh School in Minab, southern Iranian province of Hormozgan,168 students, teachers, and staff were martyred.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine trade overnight drone strikes targeting port, industrial facilities
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
- Zelenskyy says key enterprise within Russian space agency Roscosmos in Samara region, air base in Nizhny Novgorod region hit by Ukraine overnight, while Moscow yet to comment
Russia and Ukraine on Saturday renewed accusations against each other concerning overnight drone strikes, which have targeted port infrastructure and industrial facilities.
In Russia, Samara Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said on Telegram that Ukraine launched a missile strike on an unspecified “industrial facility.”
“An emergency response team has been formed. All emergency services are on the ground,” Fedorishchev said, noting that authorities are assessing the situation, including with regard to casualties.
Samara Mayor Ivan Noskov wrote separately on Russian social media platform Max that the city’s industrial infrastructure sustained “localized damage,” adding that medical assistance has been provided to those injured.
“In Russia’s Samara region, one of the key enterprises within (Russian space agency) Roscosmos – the Progress Center, which was involved, among other things, in electronics production – was hit. Flamingo missiles were used,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement shared on US social media platform X.
Zelenskyy further claimed strikes on the Savasleyka air base in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region, adding Kyiv also received confirmation on damage it aimed to inflict at an oil facility in Ust-Luga, situated in the country’s northern Leningrad region.
Russian authorities have not yet commented on Zelenskyy’s remarks, though the country’s Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses shot down 598 Ukrainian drones overnight across 19 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov, and Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
The ministry later claimed that, since Friday evening, the Russian military hit a warehouse in the port of Pivdennyi, a patrol boat and warehouse in the port of Odesa, and infrastructure in the port of Izmail, which it alleged are “involved in supporting the Ukrainian Armed Forces.”
In Ukraine, Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said that strikes in his region hit the grounds of a shoe factory, damaging warehouses and a canteen, as well as causing fires.
“There were also fires on the territory of a non-working enterprise and an abandoned private residential building. Rescuers have now extinguished all fires,” Kiper further said, noting that there are no casualties based on preliminary information.
Zaporizhzhia Governor Ivan Fedorov said that a shopping center and an unspecified industrial facility were targeted overnight by Russian drones. He later reported that five people were injured during morning strikes.
Meanwhile, Dnipropetrovsk Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said that a 3-month-old baby died and 11 others were injured following a drone strike on a multi-story building in the city of Marhanets.
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that the country’s air defenses downed 124 out of 152 drones launched by Russia overnight.
Moscow and Kyiv have increasingly targeted each other's logistics centers, as well as port and energy infrastructure, during the ongoing war.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

articles.title: First warehouses burned, now payment system is down: Ukraine launches dual campaign against Russia’s largest marketplace that reportedly moves drone parts
articles.body:
Ukraine has hit Russia's biggest marketplace in cyberspace as well as with drones. Cyber specialists disrupted Wildberries' operations across Russia, Ukraine's Defense Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) reports.
Ukraine says that Wildberries is not ordinary commerce but a piece of Russia's war logistics. According to the military command, the network moves military-related goods, and President Zelenskyy has said Russia uses the platform to bring in sanctioned drone components, which is why Ukraine has spent weeks burning its warehouses and now strikes its servers.
HUR reports that on 10 and 11 August, specialists from the Cyber Corps community attacked Wildberries' digital infrastructure, causing failures in its payment and customer service systems.
The attack hit payments and support
The disruption struck where customers feel it. Because of the problems with the payment infrastructure, users complained they could not complete certain transactions.
For a platform whose whole value is the frictionless movement of goods and money, a payment system that will not process transactions is a direct hit to the business.
The strain spread to customer service. At the same time, the load on the support service rose, causing failures in the contact centers, so the attack degraded both the ability to pay and the ability to get help across Russia.
It pairs with the warehouse strikes
In July, Ukrainian drones destroyed eight Wildberries warehouses, about 15.4% of the marketplace's storage.
Pairing strikes on physical infrastructure with Ukrainian cyber operations strengthens the pressure on the company, HUR assessed.
The logic is to squeeze the same target from two directions at once: burn the warehouses that store the goods, then disable the systems that move them to customers, so damage in one domain amplifies damage in the other.
Earlier, Ukraine hit the Progress Rocket Space Center in Samara, which builds Soyuz-2 rockets used to launch Rassvet, Russia’s planned alternative to Starlink.

articles.title: U.S. Army awards $10 billion contract to overhaul pilot training
articles.body:
- The Army awarded M1 Support Services a $10 billion, 26-year contract to run pilot training at Fort Rucker, Alabama.
- M1 will train 800 to 1,500 Army pilots annually on Robinson R66 helicopters, replacing the UH-72 Lakota trainer.
The U.S. Army has awarded a $10 billion contract with a potential 26-year term to overhaul how it trains new helicopter pilots, shifting initial flight instruction at Fort Rucker, Alabama, to a contractor-owned, contractor-operated model.
M1 Support Services L.P., based in Denton, Texas, won the firm-fixed-price, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, beating out 10 other bidders after the Army solicited proposals online. Funding will be determined with each individual task order rather than obligated upfront. The estimated completion date is Aug. 12, 2052. Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, is the contracting activity, under contract number W9124P-26-D-A004.
Under the contract, known as Flight School Next, M1 will supply the aircraft, maintenance, simulators, flight instruction and academic instruction for the Army’s Initial Entry Rotary-Wing training program, using commercially available equipment and services rather than government-owned aircraft. The Army will retain oversight of training standards, safety requirements and operational outcomes. The program is set to train between 800 and 1,500 new Army pilots annually.
“We are honored to be entrusted with this vital mission,” said George Krivo, chairman and chief executive officer of M1. “M1 will deliver a fully integrated, innovation rich training solution designed to develop more proficient Army Aviators on time and on budget.”
M1 will fly Robinson R66 helicopters for initial pilot instruction under the program, replacing the UH-72 Lakota the Army has used as its initial-entry trainer since restructuring its aviation fleet in 2013. The R66 is a light, single-engine turbine helicopter that seats up to five people, a smaller and less expensive aircraft than the twin-engine Lakota. M1 calls its training package Flight School First, describing it as a training and simulation system built around an AI-enabled adaptive learning environment, simulation platforms, virtual training and proficiency-based instruction rather than a fixed number of flight hours for every student.
M1 assembled a team of subcontractors for the program, including Robinson Helicopter Company, which builds the R66; flight school operator Quantum Helicopters; General Dynamics Information Technology; and the University of North Dakota Aerospace Foundation.
Initial Entry Rotary-Wing training has run at Fort Rucker’s Army Aviation Center of Excellence for more than 50 years and currently produces about 1,250 new aviators a year. Flight School Next is intended to consolidate training functions previously spread across multiple separate contracts into a single enterprise arrangement.
M1 Support Services already holds a separate, long-running contract to maintain Army flight training aircraft at Fort Rucker, most recently modified in January for $601 million. That contract covers organizational, intermediate and limited depot-level maintenance on more than 500 Army and U.S. Air Force rotary-wing aircraft, including AH-64 Apache, UH-60 Black Hawk, CH-47 Chinook and UH-72 Lakota helicopters, spread across five primary airfields and supported by a staff of more than 3,000 maintenance, aircrew and support personnel.

articles.title: Man jailed after 3D printing gun in Shropshire
articles.body:
A 62-year-old man has been jailed for four and a half years after National Crime Agency investigators discovered him producing a 3D-printed firearm at his home in Telford, the UK Defence Journal understands.
David Boylett was arrested in July 2021 after NCA officers raided his property in Shropshire and recovered a partially completed firearm, firearms components, tools and two 3D printers.
According to a National Crime Agency news update, forensic examination later concluded that Boylett had been approximately 15 minutes away from completing the weapon. Investigators said only excess polymer needed to be removed before the firearm could function.
Officers examining computers and storage devices seized from the property found material relating to firearms conversion, ammunition manufacture and the production of weapons using 3D printers.
One computer folder, titled “naughty stuff”, contained instructional videos relating to the same model of firearm recovered during the search. Investigators also found a video on Boylett’s mobile phone showing one of his 3D printers manufacturing a firearm component of the type subsequently seized.
NCA firearms specialists used files recovered during the investigation to manufacture the remaining components needed to complete the weapon. The resulting firearm was then successfully test-fired by specialists, demonstrating that the design and components recovered from Boylett were capable of producing a functioning weapon.
Officers also recovered a powerful air rifle and ammunition from the property, along with part of a shotgun which had been reported stolen from a vehicle in Herefordshire in April 2012.
Boylett pleaded guilty in January 2026 to attempting to possess a component part of a prohibited firearm, possessing ammunition and possessing an overpowered air rifle without a licence.
He was sentenced at Shrewsbury Crown Court on Monday 10 August to four and a half years in prison.
NCA Senior Investigating Officer Niall Conner said, as quoted in a news update: “Boylett was in the process of creating deadly weapons that could have done untold harm to individuals in our communities.”
He added: “The depth of his research into 3D printed firearms demonstrates his obsession and intent with the tools in his possession.”
Conner continued: “Firearms crime in the UK is among the lowest in the world and we work tirelessly with partners to tackle the threat posed by illegal firearms and to protect the public.”
3D-printed firearms have become an area of growing interest for law enforcement because some components can be produced using commercially available additive-manufacturing equipment and digital design files. The resulting weapons can combine printed parts with conventional metal components, depending on the design being used.
UK firearms legislation applies to prohibited weapons and their component parts regardless of the manufacturing method. The NCA has increasingly treated the online distribution of firearms designs and the domestic manufacture of weapon components as part of its wider work against the supply of illegal firearms.
In Boylett’s case, investigators were able to combine evidence from the physical components recovered at his home with the digital files, instructional material and video stored on his devices. The successful test firing conducted by NCA specialists established that the components and files seized during the investigation could be used to produce an operational firearm, forming part of the evidence that led to Boylett’s eventual guilty pleas and sentence.

articles.title: Instapaper, the Original Read-It-Later App, Just Got a Huge Upgrade
articles.body:
As you've no doubt noticed, there's a lot to read on the internet. Vast numbers of new articles are published every day. There's still quite a lot of it not being written by AI, too.
Trying to keep up with everything can feel exhausting, and that's where read-it-later apps come in. These apps will queue up content that catches your eye as you go to and fro across the web, and keep these articles, videos, blog posts, and social media updates bookmarked until you get a chance to catch up with them. When it’s time to dig in, the apps present the articles in a clean, uncluttered layout.
It's a neat idea, but it needs to be well implemented for it to work—otherwise you can spend more time compiling and organizing your reading than actually catching up on your queue.
Instapaper is one of the oldest read-it-later apps, having launched back in 2008. It's also still one of the best options, even more so now that it's been given a major revamp. Here's what's new, and why it might be worth your while diving back into your Instapaper account (or signing up for the first time).
Instapaper Basics
Instapaper is available for the web, Android, and iOS, and reflows web articles into a tidily arranged, distraction-free format that doesn't feature any ads, menus, or other onscreen furniture. You just get the text and the images, so reading the articles you've saved is a more pleasurable experience than it is on the web.
You can customize the Instapaper interface in a variety of ways. The apps let you change the font style, size, and spacing, and adjust the background color of the “paper” that the text and images are placed on.
Everything is neatly arranged on the screen, too. You get estimates for how long each article will take to read (as well as the option to see summaries of the text). You can use folders and tags to categorize saved posts in a variety of ways. Also, everything syncs seamlessly across all the devices you're using Instapaper on.
Getting articles into Instapaper—a crucial part of the process—is straightforward. On mobile you can pass web links into the app through the standard share tools, while on desktop you can either paste the URLs straight into Instapaper, or use the extensions that are available for the most popular browsers.
You can add and store an unlimited number of articles in Instapaper for free. There's also a premium package available for $6 a month or $60 a year, which removes the ads from the apps, and gives you extras like a search tool, Kindle support, and the option to have your saved articles read out to you.
Instapaper's Big 2026 Update
I've been using Instapaper very happily for years, but not so much recently. That's nothing to do with Instapaper, really. It's more about an increase in work and family commitments, and having less time than I'd like just to read. It also means that my read-it-later list has grown to a scary length.
Now the service has got its biggest update in quite some time, which means I've got a good excuse to log back in and start chipping away at all the articles I've been meaning to read. The web app revamp is actually only the second full rewrite of the Instapaper code since the service launched, and it brings with it an elegant three-column layout that keeps everything in view and works really well on wide displays (like mine).
Other improvements include keyboard shortcuts (which I noticed are shown on screen next to menus when you start clicking around), and a new multi-select feature. You can now select all of the articles in a specific list, as well as using Shift+Click to select a range of articles in the queue.
Over on iOS, the app has been given a full Liquid Glass refresh, and there are several improvements that cover section counts, section sorting, and a wider choice of appearance options (including new fonts). The existing AI Voices feature, which reads out articles in the synthetic AI voice of your choosing, has now made its way to Android, too.
If you're a premium Instapaper user, you can have articles read out by tapping the three dots up in the top right corner when a saved item is open. This can come in handy when you can't read articles but can listen to them—when you're driving or walking, or tackling the endless list of chores that need doing at home.

articles.title: 6 Best Apple Watch Accessories to Upgrade Your Watch (2026)
articles.body:
If you have an iPhone, you've probably considered buying an Apple Watch—and with good reason. It's the best smartwatch and best fitness tracker for iPhone owners, and it allows you to make calls, send texts, pay for purchases, and more without reaching for your phone. That said, I’m a firm believer that your Apple Watch is only as good as the accessories that support it.
The right band can make it comfortable enough to wear all day and night for sleep tracking. A charging stand will remind you to keep it topped up, and a protective case could save you from a shattered screen. To help upgrade your Apple Watch setup, I, along with a few of my WIRED colleagues, tested chargers, bands, cases, and more to find the accessories worth the money. I’d also recommend getting AppleCare, which is the company's extended warranty plan, given that service pricing for watch repairs is exorbitant.
For more smart accessories, check out our guides to the Best Apple 3-in-1 Chargers and Best Apple Watch Bands.
Featured in This Guide
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Apple Watch Band
When you buy your Apple Watch, you get to choose a band at checkout. I find textile and metal (stainless steel or titanium) bands to be more comfortable and fashionable than fluoroelastomer bands, which tend to be rigid and can irritate your skin. I love the Nike Sport Loop so much that it's been my everyday band for six years, and I ended up buying it in two colors: navy blue and black. Made from recycled polyester, Spandex, and nylon, it's soft, breathable, and easy to hand-wash. The Velcro pull tab makes it as adjustable as a band can get, and it's easy to fasten with one hand. Apple doesn't advertise any water resistance, but I've swum with it multiple times; after rinsing it off and letting it air dry, it looked brand new. The yarn is reflective if you're running at night, though it is subtle.
The band comes in five colors and three case sizes, which makes it compatible with most versions of the Apple Watch. If you're shopping for a leather band, Konsu NYC makes a gorgeous strap, too. For more recommendations, check out our Best Apple Watch Bands guide.
Best Charging Stand
The Nomad Stand One Max is a splurge, costing even more than reviewer Simon Hill’s top pick (the Belkin 3-in-1 Qi2 Charging Stand), but its minimalist design is arguably worth the extra spend. It’s compact enough that it doesn’t overcrowd a nightstand, and with the cable tucked away, it looks sleek. It’s also one of our favorites for fast Apple Watch charging, along with Qi2 25-watt charging for iPhones and MagSafe devices. The angled charging pad supports your phone in either portrait or landscape orientation, and the Apple Watch puck allows for Nightstand mode. It comes in three colors and includes a durable, braided 6.6-foot USB-C cable. The only downside is that there’s no included power adapter. Nomad’s 40W Slim Power Adapter ($25) is an easy add-on, but it does increase the cost of an already pricey charger.
Best Portable Charger
A fully charged Apple Watch should last all day, but since I don't always remember to top it up, I always carry a power bank for backup when I'm out. WIRED reviewer Simon Hill—who specializes in smartphone accessories—says the compact Anker MagGo Power Bank is the best portable Apple Watch charger. It can deliver 5 watts and supports Nightstand mode. It has a 10,000-mAh battery capacity, and its built-in USB-C cable and USB-C port offer up to 30 watts to your phone or small device. Plus, it comes in white, black, teal, and pink for whimsy.
Best Apple Watch Case
Unlike a phone, a watch is worn on your wrist, so every millimeter of real estate counts. If all you want is a thin, affordable, and attractive bumper that will protect your watch from bangs and scratches throughout the day, this is my favorite. It's made from a matte thermoplastic urethane (TPU) that is extremely thin and fits a 41-mm watch well. I have and like the dark green color, but reviewers say the lighter colors show dirt very easily, so I would stick with darker shades.
Runner-Up: The Spigen Thin Fit ($15) is also a very nice, minimal case. But it's a bit pricier, and the plastic is not as soft to the touch. —Adrienne So
Best Apple Watch Screen Protector
Like bands, the best screen protector is not always the most expensive one. I tried pricier options from Spigen and Zagg, but when I pushed or pulled a case on over them, the thin films peeled off or bubbled. This screen protector (also made from TPU) was easy to apply and looks invisible once it's on. I particularly like the small rubber installation pad, which held the watch much more securely than other installation plates.
Even if it's reasonably easy to use, I recommend watching the short instructional video before putting it on your watch. Don't worry—if you mess up, it comes with several replacements. —Adrienne So
Best Storage for Apple Watch Bands
Even the most restrained and minimalist among us probably have at least two bands: a nylon sport loop for everyday wear, and a titanium or steel band for dressing up. You could always keep your spare bands in a shoebox on your dresser, but I like this hanger from Twelve South. The wall mount is incredibly easy to install; the bands slot neatly in a compressive groove at the top. Each holder fits up to six bands, but you can easily add more if your collection is bigger than mine. —Adrienne So
More Accessories WIRED Likes
Nomad Universal Cable for Apple Watch for $89: As WIRED reviewer Simon Hill notes in his Best USB-C Cables guide, this Nomad cable is overpriced. However, it’s undeniably handy because it can charge both your iPhone and Apple Watch. It's Kevlar-reinforced, and the braided finish is nice. You can also charge your AirPods on the charging puck as well as your watch. —Adrienne So
Belkin 3-in-1 Qi2 Charging Stand for $90: Even though Apple markedly improved the battery life on the Apple Watch in 2025, it still won't last for longer than 24 hours on a single charge. If you have an iPhone, AirPods, and an Apple Watch, a 3-in-1 charging station keeps everything organized, reduces cable clutter, and ensures your devices are always ready to go. Reviewer Simon Hill says the Belkin 3-in-1 Qi2 Charging Stand is the best money can buy. Thanks to its Qi2 certification, it can fast-charge an Apple Watch Ultra and Series 7 or newer, but it's also compatible with all other Apple Watches. Hill appreciates the chrome aesthetic of this particular stand; its treelike structure suspends two gadgets in midair (MagSafe-compatible), with a spot for an AirPods case on the circular band.
Insta360 X5 360 Camera for $550: Overlay your fitness stats over your video while filming with the Insta360 X series. Simply connect the camera to the Insta360 app and authorize it to connect to Apple Health. The Insta360 X5 also connects to Garmin and GPS devices. Great for any vlogger showing the world their fitness journey. —Adrienne So
Avoid These Accessories
Zagg InvisibleShield GlassFusion Screen Protector for $30: There is no earthly reason why this screen protector should be so expensive. It also bubbled within several days. —Adrienne So
What Am I Testing Next?
I’m testing the Anker Prime Wireless Charging Station and retesting the Anker MagGo Power Bank.

articles.title: Russian world record holder claims European swimming gold (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Russian world record holder claims European swimming gold (VIDEO)
Russian swimmer Evgeniia Chikunova has taken the gold at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris despite continuing restrictions on Russian athletes.
The 21-year-old won the 200-meter breaststroke on Friday in 2 minutes 19.32 seconds, setting a new championship record. Chikunova has held the world record in the event since April of 2023, when she broke the previous mark at the Russian National Championships in Kazan.
Chikunova is competing in France as a neutral athlete under European Aquatics rules, which still prevent Russian swimmers from representing their country at the championships.
Russia was banned from some international events starting in the mid-2010s, and the trend sharply accelerated following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
Evgeniia Chikunova has an emotional reaction to her win in the 200m Breaststroke Final 💙
She proves that hard work pays off 💪
Where to watch #Paris2026 ▶️ https://t.co/Hhlj1DcK88#EuropeanAquatics#Swimmingpic.twitter.com/CZsHRUkILk
Since the International Olympic Committee’s (IOC) decision last month to provisionally lift the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee and withdraw its recommendations restricting Russian athletes’ participation, various sporting bodies have lifted their bans on athletes from the country.
Athletes have already been allowed to return to international competition with the national Russian flag and anthem in rhythmic gymnastics, boxing, synchronized swimming, wrestling, table tennis, fencing, archery, and other disciplines.
In April, World Aquatics moved to restore full participation rights for Russian and Belarusian swimmers, including the use of national flags and anthems. However, European Aquatics has delayed implementing the change until September 1, meaning Russian competitors in Paris remain neutral.
Moscow has repeatedly accused Western countries of politicizing sport, insisting that competitors should be judged solely on sporting merit.
Chikunova’s victory was one of five medals won by Russian swimmers on Friday, including gold in the mixed 4x100m freestyle relay. By the end of the day, Russian athletes had collected 26 medals, including nine golds, at the Paris event.

Lok Sabha LoP Rahul Gandhi interacts with students on the stage during the 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' program, in Prayagraj on Saturday. (ANI Photo)
NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Saturday said that the next edition of "Chhatron ki Goonj" event, highlighting student issues, will be held in Pune on August 22.Rahul launched the campaign from Kota, a coaching hub in Rajasthan, on June 17 to highlight issues in the education sector and problems faced by students. He addressed the second and third segments of the outreach programme in Dehradun and Prayagraj on July 17 and August 8, respectively."The fourth segment of 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' (voice of students) will be held in Pune on August 22 in the presence of Rahul Gandhi, who will address issues which are women-centric," MPCC president Harshwardhan Sapkal said.Rahul urged students to join the "Chhatron ki Goonj" campaign and said that what the girls of the country needed was equality, safety and opportunities, but instead, they got insecurity, discrimination, and a long wait for their real rights."What do the girls of the country need? Equality, safety, opportunities, and the freedom to speak their minds. What have they received? Insecurity, discrimination, and nothing but waiting for their real rights. No more," he said.During the 'Chhatron ki Goonj' event in Prayagraj last week, Rahul described India’s youth as the country’s biggest strength, but said a lack of jobs, expensive education, paper leaks, poor access to credit and the growing use of AI were holding them back.
“You are the power and pride of India; when I say this, I talk about every Indian citizen,” he had said.He said he wanted to speak about “dard (pain), data, and daulat (wealth)”, framing his address around the problems facing young Indians and the economic resources he believes should belong to them.
