articles.title: Europeans Seek Role in Ukraine Peace Talks Amid US Uncertainty
articles.body:
French, German, and British diplomats are developing their own format for negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, aiming to secure a role in the process and avoid being excluded by US President Donald Trump’s administration, The New York Times reported.
European officials stated that the three nations are working together to ensure Europe maintains a position at the negotiating table. Paris and Berlin are taking the lead in formulating a joint European stance, while London is participating cautiously due to considerations regarding its relationship with Washington.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The diplomats indicated that the resolution of the war in Ukraine and future relations with Russia are critical security issues for Europe, precluding total reliance on the United States, which they perceive as increasingly unpredictable.
While European leaders acknowledge that any negotiations with Moscow will be mediated by the US, they are seeking guarantees that a peace agreement will not be finalized without their involvement. The details of the European participation models currently under discussion have not been disclosed.
Vacancy in Washington
The diplomatic maneuvering in Europe coincides with Ukraine’s difficulty in appointing a new ambassador to the US. 
President Volodymyr Zelensky is struggling to find a candidate with sufficient seniority following the dismissal of the previous envoy, Olga Stefanishyna, on Aug. 3.
Russia Delays New Mobilization Wave Despite Rising Troop Losses
Zelensky confirmed he offered the ambassadorship to Yulia Svyrydenko, who served as Prime Minister until July 16. Svyrydenko declined the position.
Ukrainian politicians and former officials indicated that potential candidates are hesitant to accept the role. Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze, an opposition lawmaker, stated that candidates with the requisite experience might fear they lack the presidential trust necessary to operate effectively in Washington.
Pressing issues and political reshuffle
The vacant ambassadorial post occurs as Ukraine attempts to secure further military assistance from Washington, including permission to manufacture Patriot air defense missiles under license. Zelensky has noted a two-thirds decrease in deliveries of air defense missiles from allies compared to 2025.
The next envoy will also be responsible for managing communications regarding any US-led peace initiatives and lobbying Congress for continued support.
The search for an ambassador is complicated by the political environment following Zelensky’s recent government reshuffle. The July dismissal of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov prompted protests and political criticism.
Opposition lawmaker Yaroslav Yurchyshyn suggested that Zelensky might delay appointing a new envoy until after the US midterm elections to better assess the political landscape in Washington.

articles.title: Demand for free Lithuanian language courses far exceeds places in Vilnius
articles.body:
By Goda Malinauskaitė, LRT TV, LRT.lt.
Demand for free Lithuanian language courses in Vilnius is far outstripping the number of available places, leaving some foreigners unable to enrol and instead receiving offers to take paid classes.
About 200 people are currently taking free Lithuanian courses organised by Vytautas Magnus University and the Vilnius municipality. Registration for a new round of courses beginning in September is scheduled to open next week.
But some applicants say they have been told that no free places are available and subsequently received offers for paid courses.
Piotr, a Russian national who has lived in Lithuania for three years, speaks Lithuanian at an advanced level after learning the language independently and paying for his own studies.
“I wanted it simply to be easier, more convenient and more peaceful to live in the country,” he said. “And I managed to do that.”
Read more: LRT.LT

articles.title: Why Chinese youth are turning to an 84-year-old Cambridge professor for support
articles.body:
Why Chinese youth are turning to an 84-year-old Cambridge professor for support
To some of his 2.4 million followers, he is Grandpa Cute. Meet Alan Macfarlane, the gentle academic soothing China’s anxious generation
Wearing a black mariner’s cap and with a wall-to-wall bookshelf as a backdrop, Cambridge University professor Alan Macfarlane greets his social media audience with a soft ni hao – “Hello” in Chinese.
In his latest video, Macfarlane follows this signature opening by thoughtfully answering a question pulled from the comments: why has making genuine friends become so difficult?
Few would have expected an 84-year-old British anthropologist and historian from Cambridge University to become a social media heartthrob in China – yet Macfarlane has done exactly that.
Young Chinese affectionately call him “Grandpa Cute” or “Dumbledore”, after the beloved Harry Potter character, while his gentle, jargon-free reflections on education, purpose, anxiety, relationships, artificial intelligence (AI) and cultural understanding resonate deeply in a fast-paced, high-pressure society.
Through an intimate Q&A format, Macfarlane has amassed more than 2.4 million followers in roughly one year since launching on the Chinese social media platform RedNote in 2025, with videos often gaining millions of views.
His channels on Douyin – China’s version of TikTok – and Bilibili, another major video-sharing platform, have also attracted about 170,000 and 540,000 followers, respectively.

“Flamingo missiles were used. A good achievement. The distance from our border is about 900 kilometers,” Zelenskyy said on X Saturday.
He also reported a strike on the Russian Savasleyka airfield, where missile carriers are based that carry out strikes on Ukrainian cities and villages at a distance of approximately 700 km from Ukraine.

articles.title: Magnitude 7.7 earthquake off Indonesia kills at least five (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Magnitude 7.7 earthquake off Indonesia kills at least five (VIDEOS)
A massive 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia just before 6 AM local time on Saturday, damaging buildings causing a tsunami. At least five people were killed, according to preliminary reports.
The earthquake’s epicenter hit the seafloor around 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) northeast of Mbay in eastern Indonesia, the country’s Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) said.
Tsunami waves up to 0.94 meters tall were reported in several regions, according to the agency.
Three aftershocks of magnitudes 5.6, 6.1 and 5 followed the initial quake, the US Geological Survey (USGS) reported.
At least five people were killed, Melki Laka Lena, governor of the southeastern province of East Nusa Tenggara, said in a statement cited by the media.
Videos circulating on social media, purportedly capturing the earthquake, show building facades crumbling as terrified people flee.
Other footage shows buildings that had entirely collapsed.
Indonesia, a vast archipelago of thousands of islands, sits at the meeting point of several major tectonic plates and lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire, one of the most seismically active regions on Earth.
The country has faced devastating earthquakes in recent decades, including a devastating 9.1 magnitude event in 2004, which killed more than 220,000 people in the broader region.
Most recently, hundreds were killed by a 6.9 magnitude earthquake in Lombok in south-central Indonesia in 2018.

articles.title: U.S. Army awards AM General new $82 million Humvee contract
articles.body:
- AM General won an $82.2 million Army IDIQ contract for HMMWVs, with a ceiling of up to $754.6 million through August 2028.
- The Army had previously directed a shift away from Humvee procurement toward the JLTV, though large HMMWV orders have continued.
AM General has been awarded a new indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract to build High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicles for the Army, with this initial action valued at $82.2 million against a cumulative ceiling of up to $754.6 million, the Department of War announced Aug. 13.
Work locations and funding will be determined with each individual order placed under the agreement, with an estimated completion date of Aug. 31, 2028. Army Contracting Command at Detroit Arsenal, Michigan, is the contracting activity, under contract number W912CH-26-F-A172.
The new award is separate from an existing HMMWV production contract, W912CH-24-F-0229, that the Army has repeatedly modified over the past year, pushing its cumulative value past $3.2 billion. That contract funded a $126.5 million order for M1165A1B3 vehicles in June 2025, a $50.9 million order for more than 200 vehicles across two variants in September 2025, and a $98.7 million modification in July 2026. It was not immediately clear whether the new Aug. 13 contract represents a follow-on vehicle tied to that same production line or a distinct award for a different portion of the Army’s HMMWV requirement.
AM General has built the Humvee for the Army since the 1980s, and the vehicle remains one of the most widely recognized pieces of American military hardware, with the Army’s current inventory numbering roughly 120,000 vehicles across variants including the M1152 and M1165 series. The standard HMMWV runs on a 190-horsepower Detroit Diesel V8 engine paired with a four-speed automatic transmission, with a range of up to 350 miles (563 km) and a top speed exceeding 70 mph (113 km/h). The vehicle has served in combat and humanitarian operations in more than 70 countries, and its light armor left it vulnerable to roadside bombs during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars, driving the Pentagon’s separate MRAP vehicle program in the mid-2000s and later a series of armor and suspension upgrades to the Humvee fleet itself.
The Army’s 2025 Army Transformation Initiative directed the service to cancel further HMMWV procurement in favor of the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle, which AM General also builds after winning the competition to produce the second-generation JLTV A2. The JLTV A2 contract runs for an initial five years with an option for five more, covering a maximum of 20,682 vehicles and 9,883 trailers for the Army and Marine Corps combined. Despite the Army’s stated shift away from the Humvee, it has continued placing sizable HMMWV orders through 2025 and 2026 as JLTV A2 production has worked through delays, with AM General’s president saying in October 2024 that full-rate production was on track to begin in the summer of 2026.
AM General has also continued to sell Humvees abroad through foreign military sales even as the Army moves toward the JLTV; a separate $13.1 million contract modification announced in September 2025 funded M1152 variants for Lebanon.
The Aug. 13 announcement did not specify which HMMWV variants or how many vehicles the Army intends to order under the new contract. As an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity agreement, the Army sets a ceiling value it can draw against through individual task orders rather than committing to a fixed vehicle count upfront.

articles.title: Midnight wasn't the end: What happened in the first few hours of Independent India
articles.body:
Midnight wasn't the end: What happened in the first few hours of Independent India
Kanchan Yadav / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 15, 2026, 16:40 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
As the date changed from August 14 to August 15, 1947, India emerged as an independent nation.
“At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom. A moment comes, which comes but rarely in history, when we step out from the old to the new, when an age ends, and when the soul of a nation, long suppressed, finds utterance. It is fitting that at this solemn moment, we take the pledge of dedication to the service of India and her people and to the still larger cause of humanity.”With those words, the first Prime Minister of Independent India, Jawaharlal Nehru, gave voice to one of the most consequential moments in the country's history.As the date changed from August 14 to August 15, 1947, nearly two centuries of British rule formally came to an end and India emerged as an independent nation.But midnight was not the culmination of the story. The first hours of freedom brought exhilaration, ceremony and celebration, but also the enormous responsibility of running a new country. A government had to begin functioning, the machinery of the state had to be inherited and reorganised, and millions of people were already caught in the upheaval of Partition.The new nation marked its freedom with flags, crowds, prayers and speeches.
Yet beyond the celebrations, refugees were on the move, communal violence was spreading and India's final borders were still unknown.
A midnight that turned into history
The story of India's freedom began before the clock struck 12. On the evening of August 14, members of the Constituent Assembly gathered in New Delhi for the historic session that would mark the transfer of power.The Assembly, which had been working on India's constitutional future, was now poised to become the central political institution of a sovereign country.Just before midnight, the chamber was charged with the knowledge that the date itself was about to change.Then came Nehru.His speech the “Tryst with Destiny”, transformed the formal transfer of power into a moment of history. He spoke of stepping “out from the old to the new”, of an age ending and the “soul of a nation” finding expression after a long period of suppression.
Jawaharlal Nehru delivering the historic 'Tryst with destiny' speech on 15 August, 1947, at the Parliament House. (Photo: Press Information Bureau/AFP)
It was the beginning.In his message to the nation published on August 15, the Prime Minister described India as “awake, vital, free and independent”, but immediately turned to the responsibilities that came with freedom. Poverty, ignorance and disease had to be fought; democratic and social institutions had to be built; and political freedom had to translate into opportunity for ordinary people.That distinction is crucial to understanding India's first day as an independent country. The midnight ceremony was not simply a celebration of Britain's departure. It was the first public act of a government that suddenly had to govern.
The new government
Even before the midnight ceremony, Nehru had announced the Cabinet that would take charge from August 15. As per the announcement Nehru would handle the external affairs and commonwealth relations in addition to the Prime Minister's responsibilities. Vallabhbhai Patel took charge of home, information and broadcasting, and states. Rajendra Prasad handled food and agriculture. Maulana Abul Kalam Azad was given education. Baldev Singh took defence. B R Ambedkar was given law. R.K. Shanmukham Chetty handled finance and Rajkumari Amrit Kaur was given health, among other portfolios.
Why did India get Independence on August 15, 1947?
The choice of August 15 was not part of the original timetable for India's independence. The British government had initially planned to transfer power by June 1948, but Lord Louis Mountbatten, the last Viceroy of British India, brought the date forward by almost a year.One reason, he later explained, was the urgency of preventing further riots, protests and bloodshed amid the worsening political and communal situation. But the date also had a personal significance for Mountbatten. August 15 was the second anniversary of Japan's surrender to the Allied powers in 1945, marking the end of the Second World War. As Supreme Allied Commander of the South-East Asia Command, Mountbatten had accepted the Japanese surrender in Singapore.Years later, in Freedom at Midnight, Mountbatten was quoted as explaining that the date had essentially “come out of the blue”. He said he wanted to demonstrate that he was in control of the transfer of power and, when pressed for a date, settled on August 15 because of its connection with Japan's surrender.But there was a problem: August 15 was considered inauspicious by astrologers consulted at the time. According to the Hindu calendar, the new day traditionally began at sunrise, making the daytime of August 15 unsuitable for such a momentous occasion.The solution was unusual but symbolic. The Constituent Assembly would meet at midnight between August 14 and August 15, allowing India to enter its new era at the precise moment the date changed in the Western calendar.That is why India's independence was ushered in not at dawn on August 15, but at the stroke of midnight.
Delhi turns into a sea of people
As dawn approached on August 15, the mood in Delhi shifted from solemn ceremony to public celebration. Crowds filled streets and public spaces, flags appeared everywhere and people who had spent their lives under British rule suddenly found themselves living in a country that was politically their own.
Crowds gather to celebrate Independence Day in New Delhi.
The Tricolour, formally adopted by the Constituent Assembly only a few weeks earlier, became the most visible symbol of that transformation.But there was no established Independence Day script. There was no decades-old tradition of the Prime Minister appearing at the Red Fort every August 15, no familiar sequence of ceremonies for officials to repeat. India was inventing its Independence Day even as it celebrated the first one.The ceremony Indians now instinctively associate with August 15, the Prime Minister unfurling the national flag from the Red Fort, did not happen on that date in 1947.The first Independence Day was different.
The flag was not first raised at the Red Fort
The Red Fort, now synonymous with India's Independence Day celebrations, was not the setting for the country's first flag-hoisting ceremony.One of the earliest known hoistings of the Tricolour in independent India took place in Madras, now Chennai, at Fort St George at 5:30 am on August 15, 1947, just hours after India formally became independent.The 12ft by 8ft pure-silk flag used for the ceremony is preserved at the Fort St George Museum and remains one of the surviving flags from that historic day. It offers a tangible link to the dawn of freedom, when the Tricolour was being raised across the country for the first time.Later that morning, Nehru hoisted the national flag at Princess Park near India Gate, rather than at the Red Fort. Historical records preserved in the Nehru Archive note that the official Independence Day function was held there.The Red Fort ceremony came the following day. Nehru unfurled the Tricolour there for the first time on August 16, 1947.That ceremony would eventually become the defining ritual of August 15, turning the Mughal-era monument into the enduring backdrop of India's annual Independence Day celebrations.
Jawarharlal Nehru along with Mountbatten and his wife Lady Edwina Mountbatten.
Mountbatten, the British Viceroy who stayed on
There was another striking contradiction at the heart of India's first hours of freedom: Lord Louis Mountbatten, the last Viceroy of British India, did not leave with the British Raj.Instead, he became independent India's first Governor-General. The Indian Independence Act provided for the creation of two new Dominions, India and Pakistan, while Mountbatten continued in Independent India in his new constitutional role.His presence reflected the complicated nature of the transfer of power. Independence did not mean that every British institution, official or administrative arrangement disappeared at the stroke of midnight. Political authority had passed from the British Crown, but the machinery through which the subcontinent had been governed had to be repurposed almost overnight.Railways had to keep moving, communications had to be maintained, food supplies managed, finances administered, armed forces commanded, courts operated and cities policed, all while the same administrative system was being divided between India and Pakistan.Freedom, in other words, had arrived with a long to-do list.
Gandhi away from the celebrations
While Delhi prepared to celebrate independence with flags, speeches and crowds, Mahatma Gandhi chose to spend August 15, 1947, far from the capital, in violence-hit Calcutta.At the Constituent Assembly, his name was invoked, while outside, crowds raised cries of “Mahatma Gandhi ki jai”. But Gandhi himself was in Beliaghata, trying to prevent Hindus and Muslims from turning on each other.On August 14, Gandhi attended a packed prayer meeting and announced that he would undertake a 24-hour fast, prayer and spinning on August 15. The Gandhi Heritage Portal records that he spent Independence Day on a long fast, receiving a constant stream of visitors.
Mahatma Gandhi is joined by Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy (left) during his fast in Calcutta to stop religious violence in 1947 (TOI archives)
Gandhi had left Delhi about two weeks earlier. After spending four days in Kashmir, he travelled to Calcutta, where communal tensions remained dangerously high.Historian Ramachandra Guha, in India After Gandhi, writes that Gandhi arrived in Calcutta on the afternoon of August 13 and took up residence in Beliaghata, at Hyderi Mansion, a building surrounded by a deeply divided neighbourhood.Gandhi deliberately chose to stay in a Muslim-owned house in a predominantly Hindu locality, accompanied by Bengal's former premier Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy, in an attempt to demonstrate that reconciliation was still possible.The building, now known as Gandhi Bhawan, became closely associated with one of the most extraordinary episodes surrounding Independence. Gandhi stayed there from August 13 to September 7, even as the rest of the country celebrated the end of British rule.His presence in Beliaghata was later associated with what came to be known as the “miracle of Calcutta”, after the communal violence subsided.
Freedom and Partition arrived together
For millions, there was no clean separation between August 15 and Partition. The creation of India and Pakistan triggered one of the largest mass migrations in modern history, as Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs who had lived for generations in the same towns and villages suddenly faced the prospect of displacement.Punjab became one of the worst centres of the violence. Lahore, a major city of undivided Punjab with a substantial Hindu and Sikh population and extensive property ownership among these communities, was caught in the upheaval.As communal tensions intensified, many had already begun leaving for Delhi and eastern Punjab, abandoning homes, businesses and belongings.Across Punjab and Bengal, the drawing of new borders turned ordinary questions of homes, farms, shops and neighbourhoods into matters of survival. Trains carrying refugees became symbols of the upheaval, with some journeys ending in massacre, while roads filled with families carrying whatever they could save.The first morning of freedom was therefore also the beginning of a traumatic displacement that would reshape the subcontinent for generations.
September 1947: Refugees crowd onto trains for Pakistan as they leave New Delhi. (TOI archives)
The law came first. Independence came next.The dramatic events of August 15 can sometimes obscure the legal process that made the transfer of power possible. The Indian Independence Bill was introduced in the British House of Commons on July 4, 1947, in a remarkably low-key proceeding.A Times of India report the following day noted that the actual reading took only moments, with Prime Minister Clement Attlee rising and bowing before the Clerk read out the Bill's title.Behind that brief parliamentary ritual was legislation that would end British rule over a subcontinent of nearly 400 million people and create the two independent Dominions of India and Pakistan from August 15.The Bill provided for the partition of Punjab and Bengal, separate governments and Governor-Generals, and boundary commissions to determine territories that had yet to be finalised. It also ended British paramountcy over more than 500 princely states, with treaties and agreements between the Crown and the rulers lapsing and the states left to determine their future.Mountbatten urged the rulers to act quickly, telling them at a July 25 conference, according to The Times of India archives: “Remember that the day of transfer of power is very close at hand.” But the passage of the Act did not complete Partition. The armed forces, civil services, finances, railways, postal systems and government departments still had to be divided, while the Boundary Commissions continued their work and millions were already on the move.At the centre of this unfinished process was Sir Cyril Radcliffe, the British barrister tasked with drawing the boundaries between India and Pakistan. Having never previously travelled to India, he was given roughly five weeks to divide villages, districts, rivers, roads, canals, property and communities between the two new countries.He arrived on July 8 and worked under intense pressure, relying largely on maps and census data as communal tensions deteriorated. Radcliffe handed the Boundary Awards to Mountbatten on August 13, but they were withheld until after independence and ultimately released on August 17.India therefore celebrated its first Independence Day without knowing its complete territorial boundaries.The announcement suddenly gave places such as Lahore, Amritsar, Gurdaspur and Ferozepur new political identities, forcing families to decide whether to stay or flee. The border was not merely a line on a map but it determined who could remain in their homes and who would become a refugee.
1947 file photo, Muslim refugees crowd onto a train bound for Pakistan, as it leaves the New Delhi, India area. (AP/PTI)
What followed was one of the largest forced migrations in history, with an estimated 20 million people uprooted from their ancestral homes. Refugees moved across the new borders as trains, roads and villages became scenes of violence, arson and death.Hundreds of thousands, and possibly close to a million people are estimated to have died in the communal carnage accompanying Partition.Andrew Mellor, in India Since Partition, records attacks on trains carrying people between the two new countries and describes widespread rioting in Punjab in the days after August 15. Killings, arson, abductions, forced conversions and attacks on entire communities turned the journey to freedom into a terrifying ordeal for millions.Years later, journalist Kuldeep Nayar recalled Radcliffe telling him that he had nearly awarded Lahore to India before deciding that Pakistan needed a major city. While the recollection cannot be independently established in every detail, it captures the extraordinary uncertainty surrounding decisions that would reshape millions of lives. For Radcliffe, the task was over. He left India on August 17 and never returned.
That is what makes India's first Independence Day so different from the August 15 that Indians know today. There was no established Red Fort ceremony. There was only a country experiencing its first morning of freedom.Yet, amid all of this, something irreversible had happened.At midnight, authority had changed hands.By morning, the Tricolour was flying.The British Raj was over, and Indians were now responsible for the country they had fought to free.The first Independence Day was therefore not simply the celebration of an ending. It was the first, uncertain and extraordinary day of the much harder task that followed, building India after freedom had been won.
Kanchan Yadav is a writer at The Times of India, where she covers business, politics, international affairs and social issues. Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

articles.title: U.S. Army orders up to 12 more UH-72B Lakota helicopters
articles.body:
- Airbus Helicopters won a $115.4 million Army contract for up to 12 UH-72B Lakota helicopters, with work completing by Dec. 31, 2030.
- The Army received only one bid for the contract, which builds on a Lakota program running since 2006.
Airbus Helicopters Inc. has been awarded a $115.4 million contract to build up to 12 more UH-72B Lakota helicopters for the U.S. Army, the Department of War announced Aug. 14.
The contract covers the helicopters themselves, designated the MBB-BK 117 D3, along with jettisonable cockpit doors, air conditioning system installation, engine inlet barrier filters and program management. The action obligates $115,406,740 now, with a cumulative value of $140,716,352 if the Army exercises additional options. The Army solicited the contract online and received one bid.
Fiscal 2024 and 2025 Army aircraft procurement funds cover the initial obligation. The contract lists Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, as the place of performance, with an estimated completion date of Dec. 31, 2030. Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal is the contracting activity, under contract number W58RGZ-26-C-0020. Airbus builds Lakota helicopters at a separate production facility in Columbus, Mississippi, where the company employs a workforce that includes a significant share of military veterans.
The Army awarded the first Lakota contract in 2006, choosing what was then Eurocopter’s EC145, a commercial twin-engine helicopter, as its new light utility platform under a commercial off-the-shelf acquisition strategy intended to avoid separate research and development costs. Airbus, which acquired Eurocopter, went on to build 463 of the original UH-72A variant for the Army, Army National Guard and, for a time, the U.S. Navy, before production shifted to the newer UH-72B model.
In 2013, the Army restructured its aviation fleet and selected the Lakota as its primary rotary-wing training helicopter, retiring the older TH-67 Creek in the process. AgustaWestland, a Leonardo subsidiary that had hoped to compete for a training helicopter contract, challenged the Army’s sole-source approach to the decision in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims; Airbus retained the training role. The Lakota has since become the initial platform for Army helicopter pilots at Fort Rucker, Alabama, logging more than 800,000 training flight hours there with no fatal mishaps, according to Airbus.
The Army unveiled the UH-72B variant in August 2020 and delivered the first aircraft to the Army National Guard in September 2021, the initial delivery in a batch of 18 aircraft ordered at the time. The UH-72B is based on the commercial H145 helicopter and adds a five-blade main rotor, a Fenestron shrouded tail rotor, Safran Arriel 2E engines and the Airbus Helionix avionics suite, changes the Army has said come without added government research and development costs under the program’s commercial-derivative structure.
Beyond training, the Lakota fleet flies search and rescue, medical evacuation, disaster response, homeland defense and drug interdiction missions across 49 states and territories, and ranks as the Army’s third-largest rotary-wing fleet by aircraft count.
National Guard Lakota crews flew roughly 14,000 hours during a 2023 rotation supporting Southwest border operations, a pace Airbus has said approaches combat deployment tempos for the airframe. Combined Army, Army National Guard and former Navy operations have logged more than 1.6 million total flight hours on the Lakota fleet.

articles.title: Cyber specialists have "taken down" Wildberries — the HUR reports large-scale disruptions
articles.body:
Cyber specialists have "taken down" Wildberries — the HUR reports large-scale disruptions
Kyiv • UNN
HUR cyber specialists, together with Cyber Corps, have "taken down" Wildberries’ digital infrastructure, disrupting the operation of its customer service and payment system. The incident occurred on August 10–11 as part of an operation in Russia’s cyberspace.
Cyber specialists "took down" the digital infrastructure of the company "Wildberries," disrupting the operation of its main remote customer service channel, partially destabilizing its payment infrastructure, and creating additional pressure on contact centers. This was reported by the press service of the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine on Saturday, UNN reports.
On August 10–11, 2026, as part of an operation in Russia’s cyberspace, specialists from the Cyber Corps community attacked the digital infrastructure of the company "Wildberries," which plays an important role in the aggressor’s logistics and the financing of the genocidal war against the Ukrainian people
Details
The Main Intelligence Directorate emphasized that, despite the facility’s high level of protection, the attack caused large-scale disruptions—the operation of the main remote customer service channel was disrupted, the payment infrastructure was partially destabilized, and additional pressure was placed on contact centers.
Mass complaints were recorded, including complaints about the inability to make financial transactions.
We remind you
The damage from Ukrainian Armed Forces attacks on Wildberries warehouses, including more than a dozen mega-hubs that burned almost completely, continues to increase.

articles.title: CJI Surya Kant urges young lawyers to shoulder responsibility of future, says ‘much remains to be done’
articles.body:
CJI Surya Kant urges young lawyers to shoulder responsibility of future, says ‘much remains to be done’
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 15, 2026, 15:47 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
File photo: CJI Surya Kant
Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Saturday said India had overcome several formidable challenges in the eight decades since Independence, but much remained to be done, urging young law graduates and lawyers to prepare themselves to shoulder the responsibilities of the future.Speaking at the national flag-hoisting ceremony organised by the Supreme Court Bar Association at the apex court premises on the occasion of India’s 80th Independence Day, Kant said the country’s achievements also brought with them a renewed sense of responsibility.“The journey of a nation does not end with what it has accomplished. Every achievement also brings with it a renewed sense of responsibility and duty. There is much that remains to be done, and many more miles to travel in our journey ahead,” he said.Several senior judges, lawyers and court staff attended the ceremony.
‘Responsibility of this Bar will soon rest on your shoulders’
Addressing young lawyers, Kant said the responsibility carried by the legal profession since the freedom struggle would soon pass to the next generation.“The responsibility that this Bar has carried since the days of the freedom struggle will, before long, rest on your shoulders.
The institutions of justice that generations before you have built and strengthened are now yours to protect and to carry forward,” he said.He assured young lawyers that the Bar and Bench remained committed to supporting their professional growth through mentorship and opportunities.“The miles that remain are yours to walk, and we walk with you,” he added.Kant said the freedom struggle had a deep and enduring connection with law and that some of the finest legal minds of the period helped establish the idea that law should serve justice, protect liberty and uphold human dignity.He noted that Mahatma Gandhi and BR Ambedkar, whom he described as two of the greatest architects of modern India, along with Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Motilal Nehru, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Lala Lajpat Rai, were lawyers.This, he said, demonstrated that the legal profession was not a bystander to India's freedom struggle but an integral part of it.
CJI highlights changing challenges for young lawyers
Kant said India's legal and judicial institutions had grown and matured alongside the Republic and played an important role in shaping the country's conscience.Turning to young lawyers, he acknowledged the difficulties of starting a legal career, saying the profession had become more competitive, the learning curve steeper and the pressure of building a practice heavier.“I personally remember the anxieties of those early years at the Bar, and I say this not to discourage our young colleagues, but because I want them to know that we see them, and we understand their challenges,” he said.At the same time, he expressed confidence in the younger generation, citing their resilience, intellect and commitment to justice.Kant said young lawyers had also grown up with technology transforming communication and access to knowledge, bringing greater adaptability to courtrooms. He also highlighted their sensitivity towards equality, inclusion and access to justice.
‘Law must remain connected to lives of people’
Reflecting on India's freedom movement, the CJI said it differed from many earlier struggles against colonial rule because it was not primarily an armed insurrection.“Ours was not primarily an armed insurrection; it was instead a sustained challenge to the legitimacy of colonial rule through political movements, petitions, public debates, and, most importantly, through the language of law,” he said.
He said the freedom movement repeatedly challenged the contradiction between colonial claims of governance through law and the denial of liberty, equality and dignity to Indians.According to Kant, that principle remains relevant today as courts provide a forum for people from different backgrounds to assert their constitutional rights, challenge arbitrary action and seek equal treatment under the law.“Courts have continued to serve as a unifying space for the litigants and members of the Bar alike,” he said.Supreme Court Bar Association president Vikas Singh and other members of the bar body also addressed the gathering.
The TOI News Desk comprises a dedicated and tireless team of journalists who operate around the clock to deliver the most current and comprehensive news and updates to the readers of The Times of India worldwide. With an unwavering commitment to excellence in journalism, our team is at the forefront of gathering, verifying, and presenting breaking news, in-depth analysis, and insightful reports on a wide range of topics. The TOI News Desk is your trusted source for staying informed and connected to the ever-evolving global landscape, ensuring that our readers are equipped with the latest developments that matter most."

articles.title: Europe’s race for dual-use technology has a new contender: Vilnius
articles.body:
Europe’s rapid expansion of dual-use technologies is creating a new generation of innovation centers, and Vilnius is quickly becoming one of them. With strengths spanning lasers, AI, autonomous systems, and secure communications, Lithuania’s capital is building an ecosystem where research moves quickly into real-world civilian and defense applications.
From aerial drones to cybersecurity tools, technologies designed for both civilian and military use have seen increased investment and rapid development in Europe lately. Investment in these “dual-use” technologies increased 25 percent between 2024 and 2025, reaching nearly $1.2 trillion, while over 2,300 new dual-use startups launched across NATO allies in the same period. Supporting a wide range of sectors, from transport and energy to defense and communications, dual-use tech is increasingly important to Europe’s security, infrastructure, and economic interests.
In this climate, emerging tech hubs like Vilnius are establishing themselves as centers for developing and testing versatile technologies like autonomous vehicles and secure communications systems. Such initiatives lay promising foundations for the economic, employment, and security outlook of Lithuania and the wider region.
Turning research into practical dual-use solutions
In recent years, Lithuania has moved from a rich but fragmented innovation ecosystem to a tight-knit network of coordinated efforts, focused on scaling up dual-use tech with real-world applications. The capital’s well-established network of university research groups, technology startups, and defense-focused SMEs is working together, fueled by increased investment, to turn technical know-how and academic research into practical solutions for both civil and military challenges.
“Europe’s security increasingly depends on technologies that can move seamlessly between civilian and defense applications. Vilnius has the rare combination of engineering talent, advanced research, and a collaborative ecosystem that allows those technologies to be developed, tested, and deployed much faster than in larger markets,” says Artūras Medeišis, Dean of the Faculty of Electronics at VILNIUS TECH, one of Lithuania’s largest research universities for engineering, technology, and business. “The future of defense innovation won’t be built only inside defense companies. It will come from universities, startups, and deep-tech businesses working together. That’s exactly the ecosystem Vilnius has been building.”
“Dual-use technologies are no longer a niche sector; they’re becoming part of Europe’s industrial future,” says Mangirdas Šapranauskas, Head of Business at Go Vilnius, the city’s official tourism and business development agency. “Vilnius is already home to globally competitive companies developing technologies with both civilian and defense applications – from Brolis Semiconductors and Astrolight in photonics to Granta Autonomy and RSI Europe in autonomous and counter-drone systems. Combined with close collaboration between universities, startups, manufacturers and the public sector, this creates an ecosystem where innovation moves quickly from research to deployment and attracts international investment and strategic partnerships.”
Many of Lithuania’s most active dual-use areas feature technologies in high global demand. This includes lasers and photonics, cybersecurity, small satellites, wireless communications, electro-optical systems, drones, counter-drone solutions, and advanced data processing for AI and machine learning.
These tools have essential civilian functions, in everything from environmental monitoring and infrastructure inspections to supporting energy grids and government networks. But these same technologies also have important defense functions, especially for countries that face the threat of disruption to electronic systems and key infrastructure. “For countries like Lithuania, systems must remain functional under constant risk of electronic warfare, GNSS disruption, cyberattack, or infrastructure degradation,” says Medeišis. “This means that future systems must be modular, repairable, locally adaptable, and suitable for fast improvement cycles.”
Building autonomous systems at Vilnius Tech
One major step forward for Vilnius in this area is the creation of the Competence Center for Autonomous, Remotely Operated and Connected Systems (ComARC), led by VILNIUS TECH, with Kaunas University of Technology as the Lithuanian partner and Fraunhofer FKIE in Germany as the international partner. Supported by an 8 million-euro investment, the center will focus on developing technologies such as drones, ground vehicles, maritime systems, and secure communications. Core areas of development will include AI-powered sensing, autonomous navigation, drone swarm management, and specialized microelectronics for tasks such as aerial surveillance, ground logistics, and infrastructure monitoring.
“ComARC is needed now because the security environment has changed. Autonomy, drones, AI, resilient communications, and critical-infrastructure protection are no longer future topics; they are immediate strategic requirements. Lithuania cannot rely only on buying foreign technologies. It must be able to understand, test, adapt, improve, and create such systems locally,” says Artūras Medeišis.
The center is designed to grow alongside new technology and talent needs. Its plans include expanding its team to about 50 researchers, engineers, and technologists across electronics, AI, telecommunications, robotics, and materials. The center will support hands-on field testing of systems such as drones and unmanned vehicles across several Lithuanian cities, using a shared testing platform. By bringing research, industrial prototyping, and field implementation together in one location, the center will build the capacity to quickly turn experimental ideas into working prototypes and products ready to address real-world challenges.
The next generation of European innovation won’t be defined only by the biggest economies. It will be shaped by places that can quickly turn research into real-world solutions. Vilnius has built exactly that kind of ecosystem, bringing together talent, industry, and public partners to develop technologies that strengthen both economic competitiveness and resilience.
Source: govilnius.lt

articles.title: Between cartel threats and US airstrikes, Ecuador fishermen have nowhere to hide
articles.body:
Between cartel threats and US airstrikes, Ecuador fishermen have nowhere to hide
JARAMIJO/SAN MATEO, Ecuador, August 15 - At first light on Ecuador's Pacific coast, small fishing boats fan out from the villages of San Mateo and Jaramijo, their bows pointed toward deeper waters and the promise of a good catch. Other boats come in from the rolling surf to battered coves, where crews unload baskets of tuna and swordfish and traders rush to inspect the day's haul.
The scene belies the dangers some fishermen face pushing out into these waters. Onshore, drug cartels have turned the small ports of Ecuador's Manabi province into a cocaine-trafficking hub, extorting local fishermen who are prized for their navigation skills. The cartels present an impossible choice: earn more than a year’s legal income smuggling drugs, or face extortion, threats and violence.
Offshore, the violence comes without warning – from U.S. airstrikes on alleged “narco-terrorists.” The U.S. military has destroyed 67 vessels and killed more than 220 people since last September, as part of Operation Southern Spear.
The U.S. government has claimed responsibility for those attacks and deaths. Two others it hasn’t claimed – but that bear all the hallmarks of U.S. strikes – involved fishing vessels from Manabi province, according to Reuters interviews with three survivors from one attack and a dozen survivor accounts gathered by the Permanent Committee on Human Rights, a local advocacy group. The Washington Post reported this week that the boats were struck as part of a covert CIA program.
Fisherman Simon Villacreses was among the 16-person crew of the Negra Francisca Duarte II that launched from Manta, the largest town in the province. At sea on March 17, they heard the buzz of a drone overhead just before a strike hit near the galley, setting the boat ablaze. Some crew dove into the Pacific while others jumped into two smaller motorized boats, according to Villacreses and two other survivors.
The crew headed for what they thought was a nearby tuna vessel. Instead, the men said, they were met by armed English-speaking men in military-style uniforms.
"They started pointing guns at us. They took us aboard, put hoods over our heads and tied our hands behind our backs," said Villacreses, 52, who suffered a head injury in the attack.
The crew was then transferred at sea to a Salvadoran navy vessel, which took them to El Salvador, offered medical treatment, and flew crew members back home on commercial flights, according to the survivors and the rights group.
A similar sequence of events played out nine days later with another drone attack on a boat called the Don Maca, from the same region. At least eight fishermen from a third vessel, the Fiorella, have been missing since January. Two Fiorella crew members who were on a separate, smaller boat told the Permanent Committee they saw smoke coming from the main boat’s last known location.
Three security experts interviewed by Reuters said the United States was almost certainly responsible for the attacks, given the U.S. Southern Command’s ongoing boat-strike campaign in the area.
Since last year, the United States, Ecuador and El Salvador have announced they are stepping up maritime counter-narcotics cooperation in the eastern Pacific, a key cocaine corridor for northbound shipments. The effort includes intelligence-sharing, surveillance and coordinated interdictions.
The U.S. Department of Defense directed questions about the strikes to the U.S. Southern Command, which declined to comment citing “operational security and force protection reasons.”
Ecuador’s President Daniel Noboa did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment and the military said information about drug enforcement was classified. El Salvador’s navy did not respond to comment requests but said in a March 23 Facebook post that it had rescued 16 shipwrecked Ecuadoreans.
Villacreses remains so shaken by the experience he has yet to return to sea.
"Maybe I've given up fishing for good," he said.
EXTORTING $1,200 IN ‘FEES’ TO KEEP FISHING
The Negra Francisca was usually anchored in San Mateo, a port town where most residents live in poverty.
In recent years, two of Ecuador’s most powerful criminal organizations — Los Choneros and Los Lobos — have expanded in coastal areas, forcibly recruiting fishermen for smuggling, according to Ecuadorean anti-narcotics officials, provincial police and residents.
The United States last year designated the two organizations as terrorist groups. Both are connected to Mexican drug-trafficking organizations; Los Choneros is aligned with the Sinaloa cartel while Los Lobos has ties to the Jalisco New Generation cartel.
Police and local people said fishermen who don’t cooperate are often forced to pay 'fees' of $1,200 per fishing trip — three or four times their earnings in an average month, locals say — or risk retaliation against themselves and their families.
If they do transport cocaine, they can earn as much as $40,000 a trip, according to fishermen in San Mateo and Jaramijo, their relatives and police. Asked about the alleged extortion, Ecuador’s national police said: “Some fishermen are forced to take part in these activities, exposing themselves both to law enforcement action and reprisals from the criminal organizations.”
Ecuadorean police estimate about 300 Jaramijo residents have been jailed in U.S. and Salvadoran prisons on drug-trafficking charges over the last five years.
Maria Mero, who is married to a fisherman from the Fiorella, said some men were cutting back on trips because of threats from traffickers and military strikes. “The fishermen don’t even want to go out now,” she said.
Other fishermen told Reuters they fish at night or alter routes to avoid extortion attempts. A San Mateo fisherman said he had paid extortion fees four times. In return, he said the gang provided coordinates of a route he was allowed to sail and urged him to keep his lights on so he wouldn’t be approached for another payment. Smaller boats fishing closer to shore are charged less and given a type of ID to show they’ve paid the extorted fees, he said.
BANANA BOATS AND TUNA TRAWLERS
The joint drug-enforcement efforts of the United States, El Salvador and Ecuador coincide with Southern Spear, the U.S. airstrike campaign, and Operation Pacific Viper, a parallel U.S. Coast Guard crackdown.
While the Southern Command has published night-vision videos of targeted boats bursting into flames, it has generally only disclosed casualty figures and limited information about survivors.
Leonel Pilay, 21, who was injured along with Villacreses in the March 17 attack, said the crew wasn’t running drugs and its boat had been boarded and searched by Ecuador’s Coast Guard hours before the drone strike.
“We are fishermen,” he told Reuters. “The Ecuadorean coast guard boarded us, searched us, found nothing.”
The crew of the Don Maca also reported being struck by a drone in Ecuadorean waters, according to accounts gathered by the Permanent Committee on Human Rights. They told a similar story – being picked up by people they believed to be Americans and turned over to a Salvadoran navy boat before they, too, were repatriated.
Mike Vigil, the former international operations chief of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, said there was “abundant evidence” that the U.S. Southern Command carried out the boat strikes from the survivors’ testimony and what he called a “distinctive military footprint.”
He noted that Ecuador’s Navy doesn’t have the drone technology to conduct strikes.
Renato Rivera, a senior analyst at the Geneva-based Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime, and Wagner Bravo, former head of Ecuador’s army, agreed that it was likely the U.S. conducted the strikes on the two boats because of their location, the ongoing U.S. campaign of attacks on alleged drug boats and the lack of any other actor in the region capable of such airstrikes.
‘EVERYONE IS REPLACEABLE’ IN THE COCAINE TRADE
The United States and Ecuador say high-seas interdictions are critical to fight drug traffickers, and both countries have celebrated major seizures this year. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Southern Spear would "secure our Homeland from the drugs that are killing our people."
The U.S. Coast Guard said its parallel anti-narcotics campaign had resulted in the seizure of 91,000 kg of cocaine and arrests of 160 suspected traffickers through April. A joint operation of the Coast Guard and Ecuadorean navy in March recovered 760 kg of cocaine from an Ecuador-flagged tuna vessel, about 6% of the total seized offshore of Ecuador in the first half of 2026.
But such efforts are unlikely to slow cocaine trafficking as long as the cartels have a large pool of fishermen to recruit and extort, said Vigil, the former DEA official. “Blowing up these boats is not going to stop anything,” he said.
And despite the cartels’ increased use of small fishing vessels, the vast majority of cocaine shipments continue to move through big commercial ports, said Michelle Maffei, an organized-crime expert at the University of Guayaquil in Ecuador.
"The current government, together with the United States, is placing too much emphasis on go-fast boats," she said. “The fact that they are drawing more fishermen, more people living in poverty and more vulnerable people into this activity is not going to stop simply because they are dropping bombs at sea."
The drug traffickers can simply replace those who are killed or arrested.
"Organized crime understands a central reality,” she said. “Everyone is replaceable." REUTERS

articles.title: Summer Campaign Led to Capture of 19 Settlements in Southeast Ukraine – Defense Ministry
articles.body:
Russian troops have taken control of 19 settlements in southeastern Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions over their summer campaign, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Saturday.
In a statement, the ministry cited a report by Pyotr Bolgarev, commander of the eastern group of forces. It did not name the settlements.
Separately, the ministry said its forces had recently taken control of the settlement of Rybalskoye in Zaporizhzhia region, news agency Interfax reported.
Reuters could not independently verify the battlefield reports.
Russian advances on the frontline have slowed this year even as Moscow has intensified its ballistic strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.
On Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said his forces had recaptured 745 square km (288 square miles) of Russian-held land this year across the southeastern front.

articles.title: Profile: Ecuadorian President Daniel Roy-Gilchrist Noboa Azín
articles.body:
BEIJING, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- At the invitation of Chinese President Xi Jinping, President of the Republic of Ecuador Daniel Roy-Gilchrist Noboa Azín will pay a state visit to China from Aug. 16 to 23.
Noboa was born on Nov. 30, 1987. He served as a member of the National Assembly of Ecuador from May 2021 to May 2023.
Noboa first ran for president in October 2023 and won the election, assuming office in November that year. He was re-elected as president in April 2025 and was sworn in on May 24, 2025. ■

articles.title: Researchers in Australia uncover potential source of natural hydrogen
articles.body:
SYDNEY, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have uncovered a potential source of naturally occurring hydrogen in the state of Western Australia's (WA) vast iron ore deposits, a discovery they say could help unlock a new low-emission energy source.
Edith Cowan University (ECU) researchers in WA have found that magnetite, a mineral found beneath the state's red soil, can generate hydrogen gas when it reacts with hot water deep underground, ECU said in a recent statement.
The research provides insights into how natural hydrogen forms underground and the conditions needed to sustain production, the statement said.
Researchers from ECU's School of Engineering found that injecting a solution into banded iron formations could significantly increase hydrogen production, noting that WA has some of the world's largest such formations.
To test the theory, the team exposed magnetite samples to water at temperatures of 200 degrees Celsius and under high pressure for 60 days, replicating the environment deep beneath the Earth's surface.
The study, published in the International Journal of Hydrogen Energy, found that hydrogen production depends not only on the amount of magnetite present, but also on how easily water can access fresh mineral surfaces through fractures, pores and permeable pathways. ■

articles.title: 2 killed, 3 injured in bus accident in central Nepal
articles.body:
KATHMANDU, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- Two people were killed and three others injured on Saturday after a bus rolled forward and plunged down a cliff in Nepal's central Nuwakot district, police said.
The passenger bus suddenly began moving and rammed into an empty electric vehicle van parked along the roadside, sending both vehicles about 40 meters down the cliff, according to police.
"Two people were pronounced dead at a hospital, while three others are receiving treatment in Kathmandu," Iqbal Hawari, spokesperson for the district police, told Xinhua.
Police have arrested the bus driver for further investigation. ■

articles.title: INTERVIEW – ‘I can’t come back’: Pro-Palestine Cornell student calls funding ultimatum ‘manipulation’
articles.body:
Cornell University has told two graduate students, who left the US over fears of immigration detention linked to pro-Palestinian activism, to return to teach or risk losing their funding, a move one described as "politically motivated."
The move has put the students in a difficult position: return to a country where they fear detention, or face the possible loss of financial support for their studies.
One of them, PhD candidate Amandla Thomas-Johnson, told Anadolu that Cornell knew he could not safely return when it offered him a teaching position.
Thomas-Johnson, who left the US in April 2025 amid concerns over Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) scrutiny, said the university's offer was effectively an ultimatum designed to undermine its obligation to fund him and fellow graduate student Momodou Taal.
The university’s demand was first reported by The Intercept on Friday.
Thomas-Johnson is a dual British and Trinidad and Tobago citizen and previously worked as a reporter before becoming a PhD student.
Thomas-Johnson's dispute with Cornell began following a September 2024 student-led protest at a campus career fair featuring Boeing and L3Harris, companies protesters accused of supplying weapons to Israel amid its ongoing war on Gaza. Cornell suspended him in the weeks that followed.
He said the suspension was eventually lifted, but his concerns intensified after President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025.
The Cornell student said he went into hiding for about four months after ICE officers arrived in Ithaca, NY, where Cornell is located.
He said he eventually left the US in April 2025 after “ICE was stationed" outside his house "at one point” on Cornell's campus, and one of his friends was detained at an airport and questioned about his whereabouts.
He subsequently crossed into Canada and later traveled to Switzerland, where he stayed for about three months. He has since lived in Ghana, Senegal, and Egypt, saying he moved between countries largely because of financial constraints and temporary opportunities.
Thomas-Johnson is currently in Cairo, where fellow Cornell graduate student and pro-Palestinian activist Momodou Taal, who was also suspended by Cornell and ordered to report to an ICE office last year, previously lived.
He said they sought safe and affordable places to live, while ruling out the UK over pressure on pro-Palestinian activists.
Thomas-Johnson had previously told Anadolu in March 2025 that he feared deportation or detention over his activism.
“I don't want to be deported or put in Guantanamo,” he said at the time. More than a year later, he said he still cannot safely return to the US.
“I can't come back,” he said, adding that the US government had effectively revoked his visa.
“I don't know if there's a detention order out for me in the US, for example,” he said, adding that for that reason, Cornell's request for him to return to the US to teach was not a realistic option.
Thomas-Johnson is now entering the sixth and final year of his PhD. He said Cornell is contractually obligated, under an agreement with the union representing graduate workers, to fund students for the duration of their doctoral programs.
Cornell University told Anadolu in a statement that “students outside the United States for personal, legal, or visa-related reasons may also receive fellowship support when such funding is available.” However, the university said it is “not permitted to extend assistantship appointments to students residing outside the United States.”
“Because of student privacy obligations, Cornell will not discuss the personal circumstances or educational records of individual students,” the university added.
Cornell also said it remains “deeply committed” to helping international students continue making academic progress when they face visa or travel-related challenges.
After he declined the position, he said, the university argued that he had been offered work but was unwilling to take it, potentially allowing it to stop funding him.
“They're basically trying to get around the obligation to fund myself and to fund Momodou,” he said, referring to fellow Cornell graduate student Momodou Taal.
“Let me be clear, I think that this is politically motivated,” he added.
Thomas-Johnson said he viewed the university's demand as an ultimatum because the choice it presented, return to the US to teach or risk losing his funding, was not, in his view, a genuine choice given his immigration status.
“They've given us an ultimatum, basically,” he said. “And it's an ultimatum that they know isn't really an ultimatum, it's manipulation.”
He said the dispute goes beyond his own case, arguing that other international students who are unable to return to the US because of visa restrictions or changing immigration rules could face similar problems.
“Our struggle is not just about us, it is about those students as well,” he said.
“This is a bigger struggle. It's about labour rights as much as it is about politics.”
Thomas-Johnson also discussed the disclosure of his personal data to US immigration authorities, an episode he detailed in an article published by the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) in April this year.
He said that weeks after arriving in Geneva, Switzerland, he received what initially appeared to be a routine email from Google informing him that the company had already provided his account data to the Department of Homeland Security.
Thomas-Johnson said he initially expected to receive advance notice because fellow Cornell graduate student Momodou Taal had previously been notified by Google and Facebook when authorities sought his data. In Taal's case, law enforcement later withdrew the subpoenas before the companies disclosed the information, according to Thomas-Johnson.
But Google's notification to Thomas-Johnson came after the disclosure had already taken place, he said.
“Google has received and responded to legal process from a law enforcement authority compelling the release of information related to your Google Account,” he recalled the email as saying.
“There was no opportunity to contest it,” he noted.
He said Google's policy generally promises users notice before their data is disclosed in response to legal process, and that none of the stated exceptions applied in Thomas-Johnson's case.
Months later, Thomas-Johnson's lawyer at the EFF obtained the subpoena. According to Thomas-Johnson's account published by the EFF, the request sought subscriber information, including IP addresses, physical addresses, other identifiers, and session times and durations.
Thomas-Johnson said he believed the disclosure could have helped authorities locate him.
“Google gave my data illegally to ICE,” he told Anadolu, clarifying that he had not filed a legal case but was pursuing the issue.
“I feel like Cornell made an example out of me. Google have done so, and so has the US government,” he said.
“These are a few of the most powerful institutions in the world. One in big tech, one in the realm of knowledge and education, and the other, the most powerful government on Earth.”
Thomas-Johnson also pointed to Cornell's ties with Israeli institutions, particularly the Technion, which he described as reflecting “an ideological commitment, a material commitment to Zionism at Cornell.”
“We know that the university has very, very strong ties to Israeli institutions, including Technion,” he said, adding that the institute had “pioneered the use of technology, weapons, weapons of mass destruction on the Palestinian population,” and used that “information and that know-how to then export and sell abroad.”
“And Cornell has been part of that,” he said. “There are academics at Cornell that make weapons for Israel and do research on behalf of the Israeli state.”
Thomas-Johnson said he does not regret participating in pro-Palestinian activism despite the consequences he says he has faced.
“I paid a very little price comparatively to what people in Palestine have paid, and many have paid the ultimate price.”
He said the financial uncertainty may force him to take outside work, but vowed to complete his PhD and continue speaking out.
“I don't plan to give up. I plan to finish my PhD,” he said.

articles.title: Former 80th Air Assault Brigade commander Ishkulov to lead Ukraine’s 11th Corps
articles.body:
Former 80th Air Assault Brigade commander Ishkulov to lead Ukraine’s 11th Corps
Colonel Emil Ishkulov, former commander of the 80th Air Assault Brigade and currently deputy commander of the 7th Air Assault Corps, will shortly take charge of the Ground Forces' 11th Corps, which is currently responsible for defending two key cities in Donetsk Oblast – Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
Source: three Ukrainska Pravda sources within the defence forces, including senior officials
Details: Ishkulov will replace Brigadier General Oleksii Maistrenko, the current commander of the 11th Corps who has held the post for six months. The official reason for the change is not yet known.
However, Ukrainska Pravda sources within the 11th Corps say the decision is linked to the fact that Maistrenko's management approach "did not correspond to modern decision-making realities".
The 11th Corps is responsible for one of the toughest sections of the front – the Sloviansk and Kramatorsk sectors. This is the main front of Russia's advance in Donetsk Oblast.
According to one of Ukrainska Pravda's senior sources, Ishkulov's appointment will "significantly strengthen" these two sectors.
All of Ukrainska Pravda military sources rate Ishkulov's skills and management qualities fairly highly. Service members from the 80th Brigade who fought under his command describe Ishkulov as a very demanding commander.
Ukrainska Pravda has also learned that, in his new post, Ishkulov will need to work closely with the Third Corps, stationed in Lyman (Donetsk Oblast) and Borova (Kharkiv Oblast). The 11th Corps recently handed over two brigades that were under its operational command – the 81st and the 54th – to the 3rd Corps. They were positioned north of Sloviansk, bordering the 3rd Army Corps' sector.
Ishkulov and Biletskyi are believed to have maintained a good relationship since the time of the offensive near Bakhmut in the summer of 2023.
Why this matters: Newly appointed Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi has decided to "rehabilitate" Ishkulov following the Kursk operation, during which he refused to lead his 80th Brigade onto Russian territory – a decision that earned him the disfavour of former Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi and saw him moved to the post of deputy commander of the 7th Air Assault Corps.

articles.title: Most Gaza oxygen stations forced out of service over Israel's total blockade
articles.body:
At least 22 of Gaza’s 34 oxygen stations have been forced out of service, the Palestinian Health Ministry warned on Saturday, saying the remaining facilities also risk shutting down amid the Israeli blockade and a severe shortage of spare parts.
The ministry said in a statement that the 12 stations still operating are working under “extremely complex technical and mechanical conditions,” making it increasingly difficult to meet the oxygen needs of health facilities and medical service providers.
It added that the stations’ operational capacity has been “completely depleted” and that they are running beyond maximum capacity amid increasingly frequent breakdowns.
Only four of the 30 devices used to fill oxygen cylinders remain operational, the ministry said, warning that they “could stop at any moment” because engineering teams cannot carry out emergency maintenance.
“The availability of oxygen is not a medical luxury; it is a lifeline for many vital and life-saving departments,” it stressed.
‘Complete paralysis’
The ministry warned that the remaining stations face “complete paralysis,” threatening oxygen supplies to hospitals and patients receiving treatment at home.
It called for the “immediate and direct opening of channels” to bring in spare parts and technical equipment needed to repair the stations, as well as the urgent delivery of new oxygen stations.
MSF: Israel continues to restrict entry of equipment
The warning came after Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said on August 12 that Israeli authorities continued to restrict the entry of engine oils and spare parts needed to operate hospital generators, ambulances and other vital facilities, putting thousands of lives at risk.
In its latest report on Friday, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said the Kerem Shalom crossing remains the only operational entry point for goods into Gaza, while restrictions continue on several essential supplies and types of equipment.
The latest World Health Organization data, published on August 11 and covering the period through July 31, also showed major gaps in the availability of health resources and services across Gaza’s medical facilities.
A ceasefire has been in place in Gaza since October 10, 2025, following an Israeli war that caused widespread destruction to the enclave’s health system and infrastructure.

articles.title: Hezbollah: 'Lebanon-Israel deal puts undue pressure on army'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Hezbollah's Qassem says Lebanon-Israel deal puts undue pressure on army
Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem on Friday accused Lebanese authorities of subjecting the country's armed forces to undue pressure by implementing a framework deal agreed with Israel to end hostilities.
The June trilateral framework, to which the United States is also a party, involves the disarmament of the Lebanese militant group and a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon's south, where it has occupied several areas.
It also includes the deployment of the Lebanese army to areas where Israel's military has pulled out, starting in test areas known as "pilot zones".
"How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?" Qassem said in a speech.
In talks between Lebanon and Israel in Rome last week, both sides discussed which countries might participate in a committee tasked with verifying the Lebanese army's deployment in the pilot zones and clearance of Hezbollah weapons and infrastructure, a Lebanese presidency source told AFP.
"Israel is attempting to bind Lebanon to an inquiry committee that oversees the army's deployment, operations, and internal details. Where is the patriotism? Where is the dignity of the army that ought to be preserved?" said Qassem.
Hezbollah has repeatedly rejected the direct talks and refuses to surrender its weapons.
Washington on Tuesday announced it would sponsor a new round of negotiations between Israel and Lebanon in Rome in early September.
But Qassem reiterated the group's rejection of the framework deal and called on Lebanese officials to reverse it.

articles.title: Swiss financial regulator warns over rising cyberattacks and AI risks
articles.body:
Swiss financial regulator warns over rising cyberattacks and AI risks
The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) has warned banks and insurers about the growing risks posed by artificial intelligence and cyber threats.
Cyber attacks have risen significantly, according to Marlene Amstad, chair of the FINMA’s board of directors.
“We are seeing a marked increase in cyber attacks – amounting to a third – across all the financial institutions we supervise,” the 58-year-old told Finanz und Wirtschaft in an interview published on Saturday.
Asked whether advanced AI models developed by companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic pose a threat to UBS, given its extensive international exposure, the executive said the risks extend far beyond any single institution.
More
Swiss federal IT office hit by cyberattack
“The threat posed by highly developed AI affects the entire sector,” she said. To reduce the risks of a systemic collapse, FINMA has placed direct responsibility on the banks. They bear the responsibility and must keep their operational risks under control at all times, particularly those linked to third-party providers, said Amstad, who is also a professor at the University of Bern.
The main challenge is speed. “We must be quick enough to keep pace with technological development,” she added, noting that FINMA is enhancing its internal AI applications and stepping up international cooperation.
+ Almost one attack a day reported on critical Swiss infrastructures
Amstad also warned that industry and the authorities must also prepare for emerging technologies such as quantum computers, which, although still in the development phase, could have “major implications for the security” of the financial system.
