articles.title: Flamingo missiles reportedly strike an industrial site beside a factory building rockets for Russia’s Starlink rival
articles.body:
Samara Oblast Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed that a missile struck an unnamed industrial enterprise overnight on 15 August 2026. Andrii Kovalenko, head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, said the Progress Rocket Space Center was burning. He provided no damage details.
Progress would be a significant target because it builds Soyuz-2 rockets used to launch Rassvet, Russia’s planned alternative to Starlink. Its Soyuz-2.1b rockets carried Russia’s first serial-production Rassvet satellites into orbit this year. However, neither the governor’s statement nor available imagery establishes that Progress itself was hit.
Exilenova+ published early footage from Samara and reported that a Flamingo cruise missile had struck the city.
A mature Rassvet network could reduce Russia’s dependence on unauthorized Starlink terminals. For now, neither damage to Progress nor the reported use of a Flamingo missile has been independently confirmed.
Open-source analysts at Falcon Insight Map geolocated the smoke near Aviakor’s Building No. 106. Militarnyi said Aviakor and Progress sit a few hundred meters apart, and available images could not establish which enterprise was hit. The industrial area lies roughly 900 kilometers from Ukraine.
Kyiv pushes strikes deeper into Russia
Ukraine has increasingly attacked factories far behind the front to disrupt the supply chains sustaining Russian weapons production.
Speaking separately to Euromaidan Press, defense scholar Marc DeVore urged Ukraine to disrupt Russian missile production and launches. Retired US Lieutenant General Ben Hodges noted that Ukraine’s interceptor shortage means it is better to “kill the archer” than try to stop every arrow.
In June 2026, Ukrainian cruise missiles hit a Voronezh semiconductor plant supplying components for the Pantsir-S1, Iskander-K, and Kh-101.
A reported Flamingo strike in July also damaged the Avitek defense plant in Kirov, more than 1,200 kilometers from Ukraine.
The deeper strikes come as Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) says Russian factories are producing 110% to 120% of their monthly missile quotas.
How the Samara plant supports Russia’s Starlink alternative
The Progress factory in Samara makes the Soyuz-2.1b rockets used to launch Rassvet satellites developed by Russia’s Bureau 1440. A second batch of 16 entered orbit in July, bringing the serial constellation to 32.
Rassvet’s coverage remains intermittent. However, Moscow plans to deploy 292 satellites by the end of 2027 and 924 by 2035. A Ukrainian defense adviser estimated that continuous service would require 200–250 satellites.

articles.title: Poland-Ukraine High-Stakes Dispute Is Far From Over
articles.body:
The Polish-Ukrainian historical dispute has already passed its hottest stage – at least for now. But it would be premature to say that it has been resolved, and the stakes are high.
Social tensions on both sides of the border remain high. It is difficult to remember a time when issues concerning Poland were discussed so frequently in the Ukrainian media. The historical dispute is being debated, as are continued Polish support for Ukraine and Poland’s position on Ukraine’s path to EU membership.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
More recently, Ukrainian media have also been discussing the absence of Ukrainian military representatives from the parade marking Polish Armed Forces Day.
The holiday is celebrated on August 15, the anniversary of the Battle of Warsaw and Poland’s victory in the war against the Bolsheviks. In reality, the participation of the Ukrainian military would have been largely symbolic, but it could have been used constructively by politicians. In 1920, many Ukrainians from Symon Petliura’s army fought alongside Poland.
On the other hand, gestures of this kind require a favorable political climate. There is also no point in looking for problems where there are none; the parade is not what is at stake. What matters is substantive support for Ukraine. This includes Poland potentially supplying MiG-29 fighter jets in exchange for Ukrainian drone know-how, as well as the transit of Ukrainian grain at a time when Black Sea ports are blocked. Above all, it includes ammunition for Patriot systems, which can effectively intercept the Russian ballistic missiles terrorizing Ukrainian cities.
Polish Pilecki Institute Websites Hacked With Russian Propaganda
Hands tied
The issue is complicated, however, and Polish politicians are, in a sense, being left with their hands tied. One could argue that President Volodymyr Zelensky’s actions made the impossible possible: by naming a military unit after UPA heroes and, in what many in Poland perceived as a dismissive gesture, returning the Order of the White Eagle – one of Poland’s highest state decorations – by mail, he managed to anger Polish society across the political spectrum.
And in a democracy, that inevitably affects politicians, who have to respond to public sentiment and channel it politically. Handing over Patriot missiles in the current circumstances – particularly when Polish society feels increasingly vulnerable following the recent incursion of a Russian missile into Polish territory – may not necessarily meet with public approval.
Many may wonder why history should have such a direct impact on the present, especially during wartime. By naming a military unit after UPA heroes, Zelensky appears to Poles as having put them before an identity-based choice: support Ukraine or defend their own memory.
One particularly deplorable side effect has been attacks on Ukrainians in Poland. There are countless videos of such incidents online. Although police statistics show an increase in attacks motivated by nationality, this is still not an everyday reality on the streets of Polish cities – particularly when one considers the scale and number of Ukrainians living in Poland. Fortunately, the police are also apprehending perpetrators quickly, and a large part of Polish society firmly opposes such trends.
Neither side wanted the dispute
The fact is that the current crisis emerged from inept handling of an extremely sensitive issue, rather than from a deliberate escalation designed to serve political interests.
One indication of this is a report by the Polish daily Dziennik Gazeta Prawna that Ukraine is planning to involve external actors to improve its image in Poland. Further exhumation work is being carried out in Volhynia, while public statements by, among others, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar – who is soon expected to become Ukraine’s deputy foreign minister – have also taken a conciliatory tone.
Poland’s authorities have likewise shown little appetite for a confrontation, as evidenced by the very fact that talks on military support are continuing. However, there is still little sign of a broader strategy for actually ending the dispute. Instead, both sides appear to be focused on putting out fires.
Poland has consistently supported Ukraine since 1991. It was the first country in the world to recognize Ukraine’s independence. Later it supported the Orange Revolution, co-hosted Euro 2012, backed the Revolution of Dignity, and provided enormous assistance after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
Until now, Polish policy toward Ukraine has largely operated on two separate tracks. Strategic and particular national interests were pursued independently, while historical issues followed a separate path.
That may now change as public sentiment grows increasingly shaped by a perception that Kyiv has been dismissive of certain aspects of the relationship.
Alongside its permanent support for Ukraine, the relationship has also been characterized by frequent political crises. As time goes on, it is becoming increasingly difficult to find satisfactory solutions – but also increasingly difficult for either side to back down.
All of this means that the cost of resolving the crisis is rising. The crisis itself is also convenient for some political groups in both countries. Populists benefit from historical resentments. As we can see, the ultimate cost of these conflicts is high. Both sides stand to lose, but it would not be an exaggeration to say that Ukraine is in a much more difficult position.
The coming days will show whether the two countries can resolve their outstanding problems and bring the talks concerning issues of fundamental importance to both sides to a productive conclusion.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Auk Mini 2 Indoor Smart Garden Review: Better Where It Counts
articles.body:
Attractive design, now with more color options. Extremely easy to set up and maintain. Can grow whatever you want. New, less intrusive light with an optional app and vacation mode. Tomato-and-pepper kit with longer dowels available as an add-on.
TIRED
Lack of pump means potentially stagnant water (but also one less failure point).
When Auk’s originalMini 1 herb garden hit the market in 2024, it touched on something that many tabletop gardens had until that point failed to consider: If you’re going to give up that much counter or table space, you don’t want it to be for something ugly.
Aerogardens and similar models look … fine, but you’re probably not going to see one in the background of an Architectural Digest shoot. The Auk Mini filled that marketplace gap with its pairing of sleek Scandinavian design and utility, transforming the run-of-the-mill herb-growing operation into a conversation piece.
When I reviewed the original Auk Mini last fall, I loved that it allowed users to plant their own seeds in widely available coco coir, an alternative to peat moss made from coconut husks. No proprietary pods, no subscriptions, no fussy app.
When I started testing the brand-new Auk 2 earlier this summer, I wondered what new features could possibly justify a new model. Turns out, there was more room for improvement than I thought.
Same but Different
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
For the uninitiated, Auk (pronounced “owk”) is a Norwegian company that released its first garden, the Auk 1, in 2021. Essentially a larger version of the Mini 1, the Auk 1 received mixed reviews online for its tower water reservoir and inconsistent light and watering cycles. (In fact, a former WIRED director tested it and became so frustrated that he threw it in the trash.)
The Mini 1 was a simplified version of the Auk system, with four oval pots set over a 3-liter reservoir. Users could grow the included herb seeds or anything else they wanted in the pots using coco coir. It was simple, stylish, and effective.
The Auk Mini 2 features a handful of updates, but perhaps the most visible is that it comes in new color variations, rather than just black and white. There are still the oak and walnut wood bottoms, but Mini 2 offers beech and ash instead of the Mini 1's cork. Espresso, sage, and terra-cotta colored tops now join the menu of offerings.
The Mini 2 also sports bigger plant pots and a 25 percent larger water capacity, despite its overall footprint being 12 percent smaller than the original.
Auk Mini 1
Photograph: Kat Merck
Auk Mini 2
Photograph: Kat Merck
There is now also—and I admittedly had mixed feelings about this—an app. Using the Auk Connect app isn’t mandatory; you can still control the light schedule manually using a button on the light bar, as with the Auk Mini 1. The app doesn’t add much, but to its credit, it’s easy to set up. You don’t even need to make an account. Just download it; open it; and choose your garden, which the app should already recognize. You’ll access a page where you can turn the light on or off, dim it, set a time schedule, or swap grow mode from “Herbs & Salads” to “Fruits & Veggies.”
Though the stock dowels for the light bar on the Mini 2 are, as on the Mini 1, too low at a maximum of 15 inches to easily accommodate taller fruiting plants like peppers, Auk now offers a $39 Chili & Tomato Kit with longer dowels and a tray with larger pots (two instead of three). I have not tried it, but I’d be surprised if it didn’t result in substantially increased success rates.
The app also allows you to select the Mini 2’s brand-new vacation mode feature, which it calls Slow Mode. On Slow Mode, the Mini 2’s lights dim to slow down growth and water absorption so that, if you need to step away, you’re not left with a mess of overgrown parsley and bolting basil, as happened when I tested the Mini 1.
Let There Be (Better) Light
For comparison purposes, I grew the same herbs in the Mini 2 as I did in the Mini 1: Italian parsley and Genovese basil. I also used only the included nutrients. However, once the parsley and basil got to harvestable size, I noticed something different: These herbs were not leggy. In fact, they were lush and bushy, just like the marketing photos, with almost none of the floppiness that plagued my plants when I tested the earlier model.
Mini 1 on the top, Mini 2 on the bottom
Photograph: Kat Merck
This result was, I learned, due in part to the Mini 2’s new light bar incorporating an optical lens system that allows the light to not only appear less bright, but also focus more light directly on the plants. Because the plants now get enough light, they don’t have to stretch toward it—which caused overly tall, weak stems in the Mini 1.
I also noticed that less of the light spills over into the surrounding area—I kept the Auk Mini 2 on a console table behind the couch in my living room, and unlike the lights on most gardens I test, it wasn’t visually disruptive while I watched TV. In fact, the light was so visibly dim (in a good way) that I nearly forgot it was on.
Auk Mini 1 herbs
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
Another possible contributing factor to the plants’ ability to stay upright was the starter kit’s new addition of a topper: a bag of fine gravel that forms a sort of crust over the top of the coco coir as the substrate absorbs water. None of the herb stems struggled to pop through, though some wore a little gravel hat for quite a while. Once they were big enough to stand upright, they stayed that way. The gravel was a little bit of a mess to apply, but I don’t advise skipping this step.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Best to Buy Now
Otherwise, the Mini Auk 1 and Mini Auk 2 are quite similar. They have an identical tension assembly for the light bar; the same little dot-studded water-level indicator wheel (seen above), where the red dot means the reservoir is empty; and they have the same nutrient schedule. (Two pumps of each bottle, “Grow” and “Flavour," per liter of new water added.) There’s still no pump, meaning the water in the reservoir is stagnant, but it’s absorbed so quickly, within a few days when the plants are full-sized, that there’s not much risk of mold.
The Mini 1 retails for $259, and for now, the Auk Mini 2 is $229 ($249 for the espresso-and-walnut combination I tested). The Mini 2’s current price is a limited-time launch deal not likely to last past the end of the month. If you’ve been in the market for the Auk specifically, or just an easy-to-maintain indoor herb garden, this is too good a deal to pass up.
Kat Merck is a commerce editor for WIRED, where she covers smart bird feeders, indoor gardening systems, kitchen composters, and all things sustainable home tech. As a forestry major at California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, Kat practiced axe throwing on her college logging team and trained as a wildland firefighter ... Read More

articles.title: What AOC gets right – and wrong – about ‘Woke 1.0’ | Francine Prose
articles.body:
Full confession: I am one of those who have come to think that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez can essentially do no wrong. At times when I most fear for the future of our country, I watch her videos and am consoled and cheered by her clarity, her honesty, her intelligence, her simple common sense. So I was a little surprised to hear that on a recent interview on ABC This Week, she quoted a political ally as having remarked: “Woke 1.0 was crazy.”
What surprised me was not that she called for some moderation of the radical positions – the call to defund the police and the military, for example – that have, at times, been an aspect of progressive politics. But I was frankly a little unnerved to hear her use the word “woke”.
The term has its roots in Black slang. “Stay woke” was originally a warning to keep alert to the dangers posed by prejudice and white supremacy. But its meaning has changed to become a synonym for what used to be referred to, also derogatorily, as “PC” – politically correct.
I’ve politely asked my colleagues at the college where I teach to avoid the word because it has so effectively been weaponized by the far right to mock and discredit anyone who supports racial justice, economic equity, universal healthcare, and many of the issues in which I too believe.
In the ABC interview, AOC explained the ways in which, during the Covid lockdown, “There was a huge opening. The doors were really open to entertain any and every policy that was trying to get us to a better place. But the rhetoric we used at that time is not the rhetoric we use today.” She went on to explain that her primary goal – improving the life of every American – has remain unchanged.
Even though I wish she’d used different language for it, I understand her suggestion that Woke 1.0 was crazy. The strict policing of language, the “cancellation” of anyone who had, at any point in their life, made a mistake that was perceived as injurious to women or people of color, the inflexible and frequently impractical notions of what can be said, taught and legislated raised the specter of a dictatorial left that devalued individual liberties and threatened our freedom of speech almost (though not quite) as much as the extreme right.
In the current issue of The Atlantic, there’s an eloquent and terrifying essay by Tyler Austin Harper, explaining why the absurd and damaging policies regarding the need to root our racism in the college curriculum and in the larger society made him decide that he – a Black scholar with a tenure-track appointment to teach interdisciplinary humanities in an environmental-studies program – had no choice but to abandon academia forever.
In 2021, it was decided that every department at Bates College, where Harper worked, must offer two courses that would “identify areas where white supremacy, ‘colonial’ frameworks, and other forms of bias might be lurking in curricula and major requirements”. This would include the science classes, taught by faculty who often had no idea how to address these complex topics.
Such courses might include a math class aimed to help students understand “the role of mathematics as a gatekeeper and driver of injustice”. A colleague suggested that when a student or teacher made a remark perceived to be insensitive, another student should call out “oops” or “ouch” as a helpful corrective.
Though some of the more extreme policies were eventually rescinded, the final effect was to make Harper decide that he no longer felt capable of functioning with any degree of personal freedom and integrity on a college campus.
The policies implemented at Bates were, I assume, typical of the Woke 1.0 ideology to which AOC was referring. Policies like those, which were heavy-handed interventions in curricula and teaching norms – and the headlines they generated – made it all too easy for the far right to ridicule the ideals of the more moderate and left-leaning Americans, and to use that ridicule as a tool to make sure that the old-fashioned, constitutionally-guaranteed aspects of our democracy – including freedom of speech and assembly – could be characterized as “radical” and even “communist”.
The infighting and mutual recrimination that this inspired between progressive and centrist Democrats made it all too easy for the right to dismiss the worthiest of ideals – freely available healthcare, childcare and education, an end to inflation and to the profiteering that has enabled billionaires to widen the income disparity so harmful to average US families – as the kind of folly that allowed the Bates community to describe an argument between white and Black students as a “lynching”.
So once again, I agree with AOC. We need to focus on what’s politically viable, on what is attainable, on what the American people so desperately need. Censorship and repression are not only counterproductive but destructive, regardless of whether those efforts come from the right or the left.
The midterms are approaching. Our country stands on the brink of a brighter or a much, much darker future. Let’s concentrate on coming together to represent the real needs and interests of our citizens and not on the labels – “woke” or ultra-conservative” – that only deepen the problems of a nation in which the average family must so often choose between feeding the children or paying the rent.
- 
  Francine Prose is a former president of PEN American Center and a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Her latest book is Five Weeks in the Country

articles.title: When consumer similarity backfires: Dark Triad personalities punish brands that act like them
articles.body:
A recent paper published in the Journal of Business Research suggests that consumers who possess manipulative or self-centered personality traits are more likely to punish brands that exhibit those same characteristics. Rather than feeling a sense of loyalty toward companies that mirror their own darker tendencies, these consumers tend to act aggressively against them. This research indicates that shared negative traits between a consumer and a brand can amplify hostility instead of building a connection.
In psychology, the Dark Triad refers to three personality traits associated with manipulative and self-serving behavior. Narcissism involves a sense of grandiosity and a need for admiration. Machiavellianism is characterized by a focus on self-interest and strategic manipulation. Psychopathy involves a lack of empathy and a disregard for social norms.
In the business world, companies can also be perceived as possessing these traits. For instance, a brand might seem narcissistic by silencing critics, Machiavellian by exploiting sustainability trends solely for profit, or psychopathic by operating with poor labor conditions.
“One thing we find particularly interesting is that brands can be judged in surprisingly human terms,” explained the researchers — Silvia Blas Riesgo and Andrea Giuffredi-Kähr of the University of Zurich, along with Lucia Malär of the University of Bern. “Consumers do not simply evaluate what brands do, they also form impressions of who brands are. They can see brands as arrogant, manipulative, or lacking empathy, much like they would judge another person.”
A widely accepted idea in marketing, known as self-congruence theory, proposes that consumers prefer brands that match their own personalities. When a person and a brand share similar characteristics, the consumer typically forms a stronger emotional attachment.
“Self-congruence has long been treated as something that is good for a brand,” the researchers noted. “When consumers perceive a brand’s personality as being similar to their own self-concept, that similarity tends to have positive effects, such as stronger attachment and greater loyalty. We wondered what happens when that self-congruence is ‘dark’: when what a brand and a consumer have in common is not a positive trait like sincerity, but traits from the Dark Triad, namely narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy.”
To explore this dynamic, the authors built on their past work measuring how companies are perceived by the public. “In our previous research, we developed and validated the Dark Triad of Brand Personality, which captures the extent to which consumers perceive brands as narcissistic, Machiavellian, or psychopathic,” they stated. “That gave us the tool we needed to test an intriguing question: if consumers and brands share these darker traits, does self-congruence still produce the favorable outcomes predicted by traditional theory, or can it actually backfire?”
The researchers first recruited 284 European consumers, with an average age of 30.5 years and a sample that was 73 percent female. Participants completed a standard psychological survey measuring their Dark Triad traits. They then read a fictional blog post about a fashion brand called ACE.
Half the participants read a version describing the brand as highly narcissistic, Machiavellian, and psychopathic, giving examples such as deleting critical comments and using unfair labor. The other half read a version portraying the brand positively. The researchers controlled for participants’ age, gender, mood, and interest in fashion.
Participants rated their willingness to engage in unethical punishment against the brand, such as lying or stealing to get even, on a scale from 1 to 7. Although overall punishment intentions were low, participants exposed to the dark brand reported higher punishment intentions, scoring an average of 1.52 compared to 1.11 for the positive brand. Participants who scored high on their own Dark Triad traits reported even higher punishment intentions. On the 7-point scale, the intention to punish the brand increased by roughly 8.7 percent among those with the darkest personality traits.
“The main takeaway is that similarity is not always beneficial,” the researchers told PsyPost. “In consumer psychology, it is well-established that people tend to respond more positively to brands that resemble them. Our research shows that this principle has an important exception.”
“Consumers who score higher on Dark Triad traits are not more forgiving of brands that appear narcissistic, Machiavellian, or psychopathic,” they added. “Instead, they are often more likely to punish them, including through unethical means such as lying to get a refund. In other words, when consumers and brands align on socially aversive traits, similarity can amplify rather than reduce negative reactions.”
A second study sought to understand the emotional mechanism behind this behavior. The scientists recruited 600 participants from the United States, with an average age of 41 and a sample that was 62.3 percent female. Using a similar procedure, participants evaluated a fictional outdoor clothing brand called Annapurna, presented as having either high or low Dark Triad traits.
In addition to measuring punishment intentions, the researchers measured reactive moral outrage. Reactive moral outrage is an immediate, spontaneous feeling of anger in response to a perceived moral violation. The researchers controlled for the same variables as the first study, along with the order in which participants took the surveys.
The second study replicated the initial findings, with punishment intentions averaging 1.83 for the dark brand versus 1.26 for the positive brand on a 7-point scale. The scientists found that reactive moral outrage acted as a bridge between the brand’s dark traits and the consumer’s desire to punish.
“The mechanism behind the effect surprised us,” the research team explained. “Consumers high in Dark Triad traits actually experienced less moral outrage, meaning feelings of anger and indignation about perceived wrongdoing, toward dark brands than other consumers. However, when they did experience moral outrage, they were much more likely to act on it. In other words, they seemed less emotionally reactive, but more willing to translate those emotions into punitive behavior.”
During this phase of the research, the scientists also asked participants how similar they felt they were to the brand, finding identical results regardless of how the connection was measured.
“We were also surprised by how robust the effect was,” the authors pointed out. “We found the same pattern even when we did not measure consumers’ Dark Triad traits directly, but instead simply asked how similar they perceived the brand’s personality to be to their own. In other words, consumers seemed to recognize the similarity between themselves and the brand, but that similarity did not make them more forgiving. If anything, it strengthened negative reactions.”
To see if these patterns apply to the real world, the researchers conducted a third study using real companies. They recruited another 600 participants from the United States, with an average age of 44 and a sample that was 49.1 percent female. Participants read adapted business articles about either Ninety Percent, a brand selected to represent low dark traits, or Loro Piana, selected to represent high dark traits.
This study measured unethical punishment intentions alongside other negative reactions, such as the desire for revenge, a motivation to disengage from the brand, and negative word-of-mouth. The scientists included additional controls, such as prior familiarity with the brands and how believable the scenarios were.
The results matched the previous experiments. The real-world dark brand elicited higher punishment intentions, scoring 1.71 compared to 1.21 out of 7. Consumers with high Dark Triad traits again felt less emotional outrage but acted on it more aggressively, with the overall effect increasing by 10 percent on the measurement scale.
This pattern extended to a desire for revenge and a motivation to cut ties with the brand. It did not apply to negative word-of-mouth. This indicates that consumers with dark traits prefer direct, brand-targeted retaliation rather than simply complaining about the company to other people.
“Consumers’ reactions were driven less by a specific transgression and more by the perception that a brand possesses enduring dark personality characteristics,” the researchers noted. “More broadly, our research highlights that not all forms of consumer-brand similarity are beneficial. The consequences of self-congruence depend not only on how similar consumers and brands are, but also on the nature of the traits they share.”
The reliance on controlled, written scenarios to introduce brand personalities presents a limitation. In the real world, consumers form opinions about a brand’s narcissistic or manipulative tendencies over long periods through repeated exposure to advertisements, news events, and personal experiences.
“Two of our three studies used controlled experimental scenarios with a fictional brand, which is a simplification of real brand relationships,” the authors stated. “Our third study replicated the pattern using real, well-known brands, which increases confidence that the findings generalize beyond hypothetical scenarios. However, all three studies capture a single point in time rather than how perceptions of brands develop over months or years of real-world exposure.”
They suggested that future research could track how consumer perceptions of dark brand traits develop naturally over months or years. “For example, a brand initially perceived as bold or disruptive may later be seen as exploitative once consumers observe the long-term consequences of its actions,” they explained.
Relying on self-reported intentions to punish a brand does not guarantee that consumers will follow through with actual behavior. People might state an intention to steal or cheat in a survey setting but act differently in real life. Observing actual marketplace behaviors, such as fraudulent returns or documented online sabotage, would provide stronger evidence for how Dark Triad traits influence consumer actions. Additionally, the studies focused primarily on Western consumers. Cultural differences in how people view manipulative business tactics or express moral outrage remain unexplored.
“There are several exciting directions for future research on Dark Triad brand personalities,” the research team observed. “One area we find particularly interesting is understanding the broader consequences of relationships with dark brands. Our research focused on punishment and retaliation, but consumers may also experience other outcomes.”
Future research could examine how consuming or identifying with dark brands affects consumer well-being, triggering feelings such as embarrassment or discomfort. The authors also plan to investigate if specific traits lead to different consumer reactions.
“While narcissistic, Machiavellian, and psychopathic brands share a common dark core, they are not identical,” they pointed out. “For example, psychopathic brands, which are perceived as lacking empathy and concern for others, may be especially likely to trigger extreme responses such as brand sabotage, where consumers actively seek to harm a brand.”
Finally, this framework could apply to individuals who operate as commercial entities. “We would like to extend this work beyond traditional corporate and product brands,” the researchers noted. “Influencers, celebrities, and online personalities increasingly function as brands in their own right. Future research could examine whether dark personality perceptions operate similarly in these contexts and whether endorsing a dark brand creates negative spillover effects for the people associated with it.”
The study, “When self-congruence backfires: how Dark Triad consumers react to Dark Triad brand personalities,” was authored by Silvia Blas Riesgo, Andrea Giuffredi-Kähr, and Lucia Malär.

articles.title: NATO condemns Russian airspace violations
articles.body:
NATO Allies have condemned recent airspace violations involving Poland and Romania, blaming Russia for the incidents and pledging further measures to strengthen air and missile defences across the eastern flank.
NATO Allies have condemned recent airspace violations involving Poland and Romania and a series of drone incidents, saying Russia bears responsibility for what the Alliance described as dangerous and unacceptable activity, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The North Atlantic Council met on 12 August to discuss the incidents and the security implications for Allied territory. According to a NATO news update, representatives of the Alliance’s member states expressed their full solidarity with Poland and Romania and reiterated their support for Allies affected by the recent activity. NATO said the violations demonstrated what it described as Russia’s increasing tolerance for risk and made clear that responsibility for the incidents rested with Moscow.
In its statement, the Alliance said: “Allies reiterated that Russia bears full responsibility for the airspace violations, which are dangerous and unacceptable, and demonstrate Russia’s increasing tolerance for risk.” The wording places the incidents within NATO’s broader assessment of Russian military activity around Allied territory, while stopping short of setting out additional details about the individual violations considered by the Council.
The statement added: “NATO Allies made clear that they stand united and resolute in the defence of Allied territory.” It added that the Alliance “continues to strengthen its integrated air and missile defences across the Alliance” and said Allies had underlined measures already taken to bolster defensive arrangements along the eastern flank.
The Council’s discussion also linked the recent incidents with the Alliance’s continuing support for Ukraine. NATO said Allies reaffirmed their backing for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and maintained that the incidents would not weaken their commitment to Kyiv. The statement described Ukraine’s security as contributing to the security of the Alliance as a whole.
NATO said: “Allies underscored that they will not be deterred by these and other irresponsible acts by Russia from their enduring commitment to Ukraine, whose security contributes to ours.”

articles.title: In Kyiv, farewell was held for family killed by Russian strike in Pukhivka
articles.body:
In Kyiv, farewell was held for family killed by Russian strike in Pukhivka
Kyiv • UNN
On August 15, a farewell was held in Kyiv for 3-year-old Dmytro and his grandmother and grandfather, who were killed as a result of a Russian drone attack on Pukhivka. The boy's father spoke about the circumstances of the family's death.
On Saturday, August 15, people said farewell to a family that was killed in Pukhivka, Kyiv region, as a result of a Russian strike on the night of August 8. This was reported by a UNN correspondent from the farewell ceremony.
Details
In Kyiv, people said farewell to three members of one family — 3-year-old Dmytro, his grandmother Halyna, and his grandfather Petro. They were killed on the night of August 8 when Russian drones struck a private house in the village of Pukhivka, Brovary district.
As the boy’s father, Oleksandr, said, 3-year-old Dmytro was killed first.
"I saw his mutilated body — the back of his head, back, and spine were missing. He was the sunshine of our family; his warmth and the love he showed to all of us inspired us to keep living in such a difficult time. My mother Halyna was killed by the third drone; she devoted her entire life to teaching children at school. Her body was torn into millions of pieces. At that time, my father Petro was taking off his burned clothes beside my mother, and a huge fragment ended his life, cutting practically his entire body in half," Oleksandr wrote on social media.
Reminder
As a result of the enemy attack on Kyiv and the Kyiv region, 3 people were killed and another 7 were injured.

articles.title: The Most Important Thing AI Can’t Do in Medicine
articles.body:
I was an early medical student at the University of Miami in Florida, seeing a patient in a local primary care clinic. “Abdominal pain with constipation,” I proudly told my supervising physician. “I think it’s irritable bowel syndrome.”
We went to see the patient and I watched with self-satisfaction as he asked the same questions I had. When did the pain start? Where is it? I waited for him to tell her it was likely IBS. But he didn’t. He paused and looked at her face after his last question, and for the first time I noticed she wasn’t making eye contact. She was looking at the ground. “We’ve known each other for a long time,” he told her gently, “and you seem worried. Can you share what you’re thinking?”
She didn’t say anything right away. Finally, she looked up. “My sister was just diagnosed with stage 4 colon cancer. I’m worried I might have it too.”
For the next 15 minutes I watched as they talked about how she was processing her sister’s diagnosis, her fears about the future, what it all meant for her future colon cancer screening, and why at this point we were most concerned about IBS.
By the end of the visit, her expression had cleared; I realized I hadn’t noticed how frightened she was. I felt ashamed of myself. What kind of doctor was I going to be?
My supervising physician and I talked about it. “You learn how to look,” he said. “When you care, you get a feel for it.”
You get a feel for it.
That lesson has stayed at the forefront for me as I’ve watched artificial intelligence sweep through medicine and enter the clinical environment of our internal medicine residency program at the Johns Hopkins Hospital. AI scribes. Chatbots that tell you a differential diagnosis if you put in a patient’s symptoms. Electronic medical record tools that will summarize a patient’s hospital course for you. But they can’t feel.
To be sure, AI can do incredible things in medicine. In this new world, I hear trainees wonder if AI will make doctors obsolete. I also hear some—usually not physicians—make this claim with confidence. They’re right about one thing: medicine is changing, and we in health care need to figure out our place in this new world.
But they’re wrong that physicians will become obsolete as AI becomes better at processing information. As I learned in medical school, truly caring for a patient begins before the first question is asked and the first test is ordered. It begins with looking. Noticing a second of hesitation before a patient responds. Seeing the pits in a nailbed. Hearing a change in heart sounds between visits. It begins when you commit to focusing entirely on the person in front of you, and to creating a relationship—that’s how you get a feel for it.
AI excels at processing information that is presented to it, like symptoms, test results, and even human expressions. It reasons with the input it is given. But it cannot decide what deserves attention before data exist.
Great physicians define the input. They decide which symptoms matter, observe what wasn’t said, and understand what information deserves the most attention. They are curious about the patient in front of them, and that curiosity drives them to dig deeper, discover information an algorithm couldn’t, and direct the flow of information—not just receive it.
Ironically, healthcare systems are already pushing physicians away from careful observation and curiosity toward the kind of medicine AI performs best: documenting, checking boxes, and following protocols. As a result, now many physicians don’t get the chance to experience the “feel” of medicine. Some ask questions (input) and tell the patient the plan (output)—but don’t observe or connect. They don’t have the time to practice the aspects of medicine that distinguish them from software.
Could AI in the coming decades replace these doctors? Probably. If the input is just data, the output would probably be the same. But the patients’ experience will be the one I would have given my patient with abdominal pain: incomplete and ineffective.
We need to embrace what AI can do to make medicine better while at the same time recognizing what it cannot do. We must see it for what it is—an adjunct to elevate physician care. A modern stethoscope.
Healthcare workers need to inform how medical AI is developed and deployed, so it doesn’t propagate checkbox medicine and promote the creation of AI-equivalent physicians who can follow protocols but have no feel for medicine.
We need to reimagine how we train the next generation of physicians, prioritizing the development of the skills and attributes needed to define the input—curiosity, careful observation, expert communication, and mastery of the physical exam—in the context of AI tools.
It also means we need to focus on recruiting people to medicine who have the “soft skills” and attributes that have defined great physicians for centuries: a focus on serving others, forming connections, building trust, and empathizing.
Years later, I remember little about the details of my patient’s abdominal pain. But I distinctly remember the moment she looked up after my supervising physician asked the question I never thought to ask.
AI will become better at recognizing disease. Whether medicine becomes better at recognizing patients depends on whether physicians still learn to look—and learn to feel.

articles.title: Zyzz Was the Original Looksmaxxer. His Rise and Untimely Death Feel More Relevant Than Ever
articles.body:
“We’re all gonna make it, brah!”
That was the aspirational rallying cry of Aziz Shavershian, better known by his online alias, Zyzz. Once the shy and skinny son of Kurdish parents who struggled to find his place in Sydney, Australia, where the family had moved from Russia, he’d thrown himself wholeheartedly into fitness, spending hours at the gym every day and frequenting the infamous Bodybuilding.com and 4chan forums.
In time, the teenager’s chiseled physique gave him the confidence to develop an online persona that had little in common with the gentle and goofy kid that his friends and family knew. This would be Zyzz, a brash raver who strutted, mugged, danced, and flexed shirtless in front of his webcam while asking if viewers were “mirin’” (that is, admiring his body) and exhorting other men to chase their self-improvement goals. By 2010, his videos had made him an Australian celebrity with fans around the globe.
And as of August 2011, he was dead in Thailand, at the age of 22.
Shavershian’s brief and tragic life is the basis of a new documentary, Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzz, now available on Apple TV and Prime Video. But this keenly nuanced film is more than the familiar tale of an ambitious youth who pursued fame at all costs. It also reckons with the digital forces that could produce a person like Zyzz in the first place, and how his preternatural instincts for navigating a brand-new media ecosystem anticipated an entire generation of masculinity influencers.
Depending on your perspective, Zyzz can be regarded as the original “looksmaxxer”—though the term had yet to be coined—or one of the earliest forefathers of the manosphere as we know it today.
“I really see this as a cautionary tale,” Poster Boy’s director, Selina Miles, tells WIRED. She notes that Shavershian’s meteoric rise and untimely death left a huge impression on Australian millennials, and that his legend continues to reverberate today. “He had his transformation, and his story has really resonated with a lot of people,” she says. “We have to stay curious as to why. Why has he had this impact on men?”
Through a mixture of Zyzz’s archival content and interviews with close friends as well as his older brother, Said Shavershian—a professional bodybuilder to this day—the documentary circles the question of his outsized appeal during a key shift in human communications. At that moment, few imagined YouTube (launched in 2005, when he was 16) or Facebook (first available to him the following year) as a means to notoriety, let alone financial success. Indeed, Zyzz’s earliest videos amount to little more than a kid playing around in his bedroom; later, he and his pals experimented with showing off their abs and biceps at music festivals and nightlife hot spots, hoping for reactions of any kind.
While Zyzz promoted values of inclusion and mutual support for men looking to become the best version of themselves, he also began to feed off those who insulted him, online and off: “U mad?” and “Come at me brah” were two of his recurring catchphrases. He understood sooner than most how controversy drove clicks, and even maintained fake social accounts to amplify the war between himself and the haters. “He made this page on Facebook that was, like, ‘10,000 likes and I'll bash Zyzz,’” Miles says, describing an incident that didn’t make it into the documentary’s final cut. “When the page was doing well, he switched the name of it to be promotion for his protein brand.”
His rhetoric turned homophobic and misogynist, contemptuous of anyone who had not optimized their physical form. A 2010 post on his Facebook page read: “id rather be dead than ‘normal.’”
By then, we learn from the film, Zyzz had more followers on the platform than the prime minister of Australia at the time.
Behind the bravado, however, Zyzz seemed psychologically unprepared for the limelight. In addition to using steroids to sculpt his Renaissance-worthy physique (he and the fitness personalities in his orbit were known as the “Aesthetics Crew”), he took Xanax to deal with the stress and paranoia that came with being mobbed in public, where he was also frequently menaced by young men looking for a fight.
And while acolytes copied his basic workout routines, his own methods grew ever more extreme. In one video, he bragged about obtaining clenbuterol, a prescription drug used to treat asthma in horses, prized by bodybuilders as a supposedly performance-enhancing substance despite the likelihood of dangerous cardiovascular side effects in humans.
Today, manosphere streamers and podcasters can make millions hawking supplements and classes to vulnerable young men looking to take charge of their life in one way or another. Zyzz, Miles says, was “right on the cusp” of that economy, reportedly making about $20,000 in the last three months of his life, which would now be considered a drop in the bucket by major creators. “It makes you realize how much has changed, because you look at how it works today, and it's extraordinary, it's just a gigantic pyramid scheme,” she says.
Poster Boy leaves it up to the viewer to decide the extent to which Zyzz served as a template for the likes of misogynist influencer Andrew Tate, who flashes onscreen in one sequence. (He and his brother, Tristan Tate, are currently fighting extradition from the US to the UK on charges of rape and sex trafficking that their attorney has claimed are without merit.) Setting aside some provocative aspects of behavior, Zyzz did not appear to preach from a place of nihilism or cynicism, and he had a genuine community.
“Aziz did have friends, and I think that male friendship is one of the beautiful themes of this story,” Miles says, referring to the members of the Aesthetics Crew who sat for interviews and remain in touch today. She wonders if they collectively make the case that a currently voguish explanation for radicalization among men, the so-called male loneliness epidemic, “might not be the right term for what we're actually seeing.” In the end, she notes, it was Zyzz who isolated himself from this network as they sought to help him.
Zyzz traveled alone to Thailand in July 2011, having told each of his closest friends that he was traveling with another one of them. After his death, Thai authorities revealed that he purchased a wide variety of pharmaceutical drugs and underwent multiple facial surgeries while in the country. Those who went to identify his body upon its return to Australia recount how they could barely recognize him due to those procedures.
The exact cause of Shavershian’s death was never made public until Poster Boy disclosed the findings of his toxicology report: acute respiratory failure brought on by a combination of morphine, cocaine, and benzodiazepines.
Perhaps it was unavoidable that Zyzz would be mythologized as a martyr for the manosphere. The closing credits of the film show a montage of tattoos in his memory. His brother Said, who runs a fitness brand, sells T-shirts with illustrations of both of their faces and a zeitgeisty, looksmaxxing slogan that would have made little sense 15 years ago: “Mog Them All.” (He continues to follow Zyzz’s playbook when it comes to courting controversy, too, and is shown recording a podcast in which he argues that there is “no such thing as toxic masculinity.”)
But Miles would like viewers to take different lessons from what happened to Shavershian as he evolved into Zyzz, fracturing his real identity in the process of building up the kind of facade that is all too common in the influencer age he prefigured.
“This was this persona that he created, and he felt that it was separate from who he really was, that it was OK to take risks,” Miles says. “It was so successful, and it did kind of take over his life.” Whatever good intentions and ideals he may have had, the incentives of the algorithm “corrupted those, and changed him as a person,” she says.
Yet his formula has clearly endured. There are still a lot of young men who want to hear “that you can be the master of your own universe, you can have some control over your fate, and you can be who you wanna be,” Miles says. “More than ever, men are seeking that sense of hope. And Zyzz kind of gave that to them.”

articles.title: Ukraine Has Imposed Sanctions Against 13 Vessels Transporting Grain From Occupied Territories
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Has Imposed Sanctions Against 13 Vessels Transporting Grain From Occupied Territories
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy enacted a decision by the National Security and Defense Council placing sanctions on 13 maritime vessels, 11 Russian citizens, and 28 legal entities linked to the illegal removal of Ukrainian grain from temporarily occupied territories.
The measure was formalized under Presidential Decree No. 725/2026, published on the official website of the head of state on August 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The sanctions target individuals, companies, and cargo ships involved in transporting agricultural products out of areas under occupation during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Among the 13 affected ships, eight sail under the flag of Russia, three under Panama, one under Belize, and one under Saint Kitts and Nevis.
The restrictions apply directly to shipowners, ship captains, and commercial entities participating in the logistics chain. Ukrainian officials stated that information regarding these entities will be shared with international partners to ensure sanctions are mirrored across foreign jurisdictions.
Vladyslav Vlasyiuk, advisor and presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, stated, "The consequences should affect all participants in such schemes — from companies and owners to captains and the vessels themselves."
During the Ukrainian Youth Forum on August 12, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine and its partner nations had established a joint action plan aimed at ending Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
He stressed the necessity of expanding domestic pressure against the invading power, stating, "We need to bring the war back to the territory of Russia," so that Russian society would feel the consequences and exert pressure on its authorities.
At the same time, the Ukrainian leader urged international partners to strengthen defense support, specifically regarding air defense systems, as Moscow was preparing a new wave of autumn mobilization following pseudo-parliamentary elections.

articles.title: NATO Exercises Test Interceptor Drones Against Shahed-Style Threats in Latvia, Video
articles.body:
- Category
- World
NATO Exercises Test Interceptor Drones Against Shahed-Style Threats in Latvia, Video
Latvia tested counter-drone systems, including interceptor drones, at the Sēlija training ground during the NATO Baltic Trust 26 exercise. Footage showing the interception of a target drone was released by the Latvian Ministry of Defense on August 14.
Approximately 650 participants from Latvia, NATO member states, and partner nations—including Ukraine, Australia, and Japan—took part in the maneuvers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Representatives of the technology industry from several European Union countries also joined the military drills.
Military personnel tested these commercial developments and projects under realistic field conditions.“Drone technologies and counter-drone capabilities are developing very rapidly. No less important than the technology itself is the ability of different systems to work effectively together,” the ministry stated.
During the exercise, specialists tested radar units, sensors, camera systems, electronic warfare equipment, and other solutions designed to detect, track, and neutralize unmanned aerial vehicles. The maneuvers also featured a unique operational concept for NATO.
This approach involves the private defense industry not just as an equipment manufacturer, but as a direct provider of services and practical combat capabilities. Under this concept, once a target is identified, military command can transfer the engagement mission directly to industry contractors.
Participating companies then deploy their own equipment, unmanned systems, software, engineers, and pilots to execute the strike. In late July, Ukraine and Latvia signed several memorandums of understanding aimed at broadening cooperation in unmanned aerial systems, according to Militarnyi.
The partnership focuses on attracting investments for drone manufacturing, transferring Ukrainian technological expertise, and building modern dual-use test facilities in Latvia.
The memorandums formalized cooperation between Latvia’s Ministry of Defense, Ministry of Economics, Investment and Development Agency, Baltic Forces Ltd., Ukrainian industry partners, Riga Technical University, and the Latvian Federation of Defense and Security Industries.
Additionally, in late June, Latvia announced plans to set up joint drone production facilities with Ukraine in the border region of Latgale.
Previously, NATO planned to strengthen its eastern flank with a network of thousands of drones, sensors, and satellites linked through artificial intelligence.
Developed under the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative (EFDI), the system was intended to monitor threats along NATO’s borders with Russia and Belarus, stretching from northern Finland to the Black Sea.

articles.title: India marks 80 years of independence
articles.body:
Ahmad Adil
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
India on Saturday marked its 80th Independence Day, with nationwide celebrations and flag-hoisting ceremonies held across the country to commemorate the occasion.
The main event was held in the national capital New Delhi, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the nation from the historic Red Fort.
In his address, during which around 5,000 guests were present, Modi called for accelerating the pace of reforms.
Talking about India’s dream, Modi said that “by the time India completes 100 years of independence in 2047, “we will build a developed India.”
Modi also said that since 2014, India has been entering into free trade agreements with around 40 countries. “This is a huge opportunity, particularly for our MSMEs (Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises). Indian products must reach global markets,” he said.
He also outlined "seven streams of strength" for India, including manufacturing power, technology and innovation and defense power, which will give India the “strength and momentum to accomplish what could not be achieved in the previous five to seven decades.”
“We must become self-reliant in defence and develop next-generation defence technologies. We must aim to become a global supplier. We need to develop drones, counter-drone systems and hypersonic defence technologies and take leadership in these fields,” he said.
Modi also announced that the country will train 10 million young Indians in artificial intelligence skills, provide free online coaching for various examinations, and create a vibrant modern civil-defense network in the country.
He also said that in the coming “seven or eight years,” another five to eight semiconductor plants are expected to begin operations, and by 2047, India is working toward a target of 100 gigawatts of nuclear power.
“In this decade itself, we aim to commission five new nuclear reactors,” he said, adding that India's “global profile is rising.”

articles.title: ‘Let’s see what he can do’: will Burnham bring voters back to Labour heartlands?
articles.body:
Labour marked its worst performance in more than 50 years when voters went to the polls in Barnsley in May, but 100 days on from those seismic local elections, the political landscape has shifted drastically.
Could the South Yorkshire town, where Reform UK reaped the benefits of dissatisfaction with Labour, prove to be a test case for whether the governing party has turned the tide?
Labour had run Barnsley’s council since its inception in 1974, but was left with just 11 councillors after Reform triumphed with 42 seats.
“I knew that it would be the most challenging set of elections that we’ve ever faced in Barnsley’s history,” said the councillor James Higginbottom, the new Labour group opposition leader. “What I didn’t necessarily expect was the scale of the Reform victory.”
Catastrophic results in places such as Barnsley were a catalyst for Keir Starmer’s resignation. He has been replaced as prime minister by the former mayor of Greater Manchester Andy Burnham, who won the Labour leadership uncontested after a landslide byelection victory.
Meanwhile, the Reform leader, Nigel Farage, is facing scrutiny over his financial affairs. While he was decisively re-elected in Clacton on Thursday, after he called a byelection in protest over a parliamentary standards investigation into his financial gifts, the contest was largely viewed as a sideshow after other major parties declined to stand. The parliamentary standards investigation has now resumed.
Labour is now ahead in the polls for the first time since March 2025, with a YouGov poll on Monday giving Labour a two-point lead, at 24 points to Reform’s 22.
Many in Barnsley used their vote in May to punish Starmer’s government, and while almost everyone the Guardian spoke to there this week said it was too early to judge the Reform council on their record, the new national political picture appears to be enticing at least some back to Labour.
In the town of Penistone, Richard Riding, 71, a retired HGV driver, said he was normally a Labour voter but had backed Reform in May “just for a change”.
“The current government were in a total mess,” he said, “and we’ve had a lot of problems.”
But he is no fan of Farage. “If you think the country’s in a mess now with Europe, it’s going to be totally destroyed if he takes over.” he said. “[Burnham] did a very good job in Manchester so let’s see what he can do now,” he added, saying he would vote Labour next time.
Labour’s Barnsley council was not your usual local administration. It had won both the Local Government Chronicle and the Municipal Journal (MJ) council of the year awards in 2023, becoming the first local authority to win both titles in the same year. In February, Barnsley was named in the top 10 most productive councils in the country, coming in seventh in the Impower Index, published by the MJ.
While in many towns people felt as dissatisfied with local administrations as they did with national government, Barnsley had launched a number of pioneering initiatives, including “health on the high street”, making it the first local authority to bring hospital services into the town centre, and free bus travel for under-18s, a version of which Burnham has since adopted nationally.
Barnsley parents also received free school uniforms for their children in a scheme that saved families about £2.5m in a year. It has already been scaled back by Reform. (Reform’s council leader and local party chair did not respond to interview requests.)
Despite this innovative work, voters still punished Labour at the ballot box. “By and large, people were saying to us: ‘I like what the council’s doing’,” Higginbottom said, “but that national stuff, we just couldn’t overcome that.”
Martin Harvey, 75, who worked in engineering, said he “has been Labour all my life”, but concerns about immigration meant he turned to Reform in May, and plans to stick with them.
“I’ve just been watching on TV, GB News, and I don’t know, locally everything around here seems to be fine,” he said, but added: “Politics in general, I’m frightened, I am frightened of what’s happening. It’s just frightening how many boats are coming across.”
Jessica Morgan, 31, a retail worker, was always a Labour voter, but she voted Reform for the first time in May. “I’m still happy with that decision,” she said.
“I just want the roads to be fixed, the potholes to be filled,” she added. “Labour were just cushty, because Barnsley has always been Labour. Even my grandad, he used to be a pit miner and he’s always voted for Labour, but this time … no. He also voted Reform.”
But there are early signs that some voters are thinking of returning to Labour. In the Penistone East ward of Barnsley, a council byelection has been triggered by the resignation of a Reform councillor. In May, Labour won two of the seats that were up for grabs, and Reform won the third. But a Labour source said they were “confident we will win” the third seat on Thursday.
Higginbottom said: “I think that will be a good barometer as to where we are; are we reconnecting with voters who in May didn’t feel able to put their trust in us?”
Labour has spoken to more than 1,000 voters in the ward so far and aims to double that by polling day.
“I’m not saying they’re rushing out to suddenly say: ‘Yeah, we love Labour and we’re going to be voting for you en masse’,” Higginbottom said, “[but] some are willing to give us a fair hearing, and to listen to what we’ve got to say.”
Marie Tidball, the Labour MP for Penistone and Stocksbridge, said she had “definitely” noticed a shift in voter attitudes while campaigning for the byelection, in comparison to May.
“It really does feel like it’s cut through in terms of Andy being boldly and confidently and authentically Labour once again, and I think people do seem to really identify with him as a person in a very powerful way,” she said.
Keith Hibbert, 67, a retired project manager in engineering, voted Labour in May, as he “wasn’t convinced yet” by Reform. His wife, Jill, a former nurse, also 67, switched to Farage’s party based on “just the manifesto”, having always voted Labour in the past. Both are cautiously optimistic about Burnham’s leadership.
“I think they’ve given Labour a new leaf, because there’s a new face, a new personality,” Keith said. Jill added she would probably vote Labour again.
Dan Jarvis, the MP for Barnsley North, said: “Reform did well when people could only judge their promises. Unfortunately for them, their actions will now be judged too.”
Stephanie Peacock, the MP for Barnsley South, said: “It’s still in early days, but I’ve seen already that residents across Barnsley are more open and willing to give the Labour party a hearing.”
She said one woman who had previously been “pretty anti-government, and pro-Reform” had told her she would vote Labour with Burnham as prime minister. “It’s not just the PM’s focus on tacking the cost of living,” she said, “it’s the government’s more hopeful and positive tone that is cutting through.”

articles.title: Russians allowed to compete in archery under their own flag
articles.body:
Russians allowed to compete in archery under their own flag
Kyiv • UNN
The International Archery Federation has lifted restrictions on Russian athletes, allowing them to compete under the country's flag and anthem. The decision was made after a review of the IOC's recommendations.
The International Federation of Archery (World Archery) has allowed Russians to compete in events with their country's identity, including under their own flag and with their own anthem. This was reported by the federation's press service, according to UNN.
Details
"The Executive Board of the International Federation of Archery held an online meeting on Friday, August 14, to consider the decision of the Executive Board of the International Olympic Committee dated July 7, 2026, which confirmed that the previous recommendations restricting the participation of Russian athletes were no longer in effect," the statement said.
The Executive Board lifted restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes, teams, and officials in competitions held directly under the auspices of the International Federation of Archery.
"Russian athletes and teams can now compete under their country's flag at these events, including the Archery World Cup and World Championships. Restrictions on the use of the Russian flag and anthem, introduced in 2022, have also been lifted in accordance with the decision concerning Belarus adopted in May," the federation said.
The federation also stated that the return of Russian athletes to competitions continues to be governed by the standard participation requirements, eligibility rights, and anti-doping requirements set out in the Statutes and Rules of the International Federation of Archery, as well as the requirements of the host country, applicable national legislation, visa restrictions, and instructions from government authorities.
"This decision applies to competitions held directly under the auspices of the International Federation of Archery. Participation in competitions held under the auspices of World Archery Europe remains within the competence of the continental federation, and the International Federation of Archery will continue its dialogue with World Archery Europe regarding the implementation of this decision. The International Federation of Archery remains committed to supporting the Ukrainian archery community and all those affected by the ongoing war," the federation said.
Recall
In 2023, the International Federation of Archery allowed Russians and Belarusians to return to competitions.

articles.title: While Taliban leaders mark 5 years in power in Afghanistan, a UN official warns of a rights crisis
articles.body:
While Taliban leaders mark 5 years in power in Afghanistan, a UN official warns of a rights crisis
KABUL, Afghanistan (AP) — Taliban rulers and other officials gathered at Afghanistan’s traditional Loya Jirga assembly hall on Saturday to celebrate the fifth anniversary of their return to power, touting having brought stability and an end to conflict after decades of upheaval.
A top United Nations official, however, warned of a grave human rights crisis in the country where girls above the age of 12 are denied an education.
The Taliban seized power on Aug. 15, 2021, as the U.S. and other NATO troops withdrew following a costly two-decade war. The U.S. withdrawal led to chaos at Kabul airport as crowds of people tried to flee the country in desperation.
Soon after taking power, the Taliban administration imposed a ban on girls’ education beyond the sixth grade and later also banned higher education for women, despite having pledged before the takeover that women would be allowed access to education, employment and public participation.
Women have also been banned from public spaces such as gyms and parks, from taking part in sports and traveling to distant locations without a male guardian.
At the Loya Jirga, high-ranking officials were joined by some foreign representatives and thousands of ordinary citizens for speeches marking what they said was Afghanistan’s liberation from American forces.
The Taliban government remains isolated internationally, with Russia being the only country to have recognized it formally.
“We pray to Almighty God to forever protect our homeland from occupation, aggression, wars, and insecurity, and to enable our people to enjoy peace, tranquility, and prosperity under the auspices of the Sharia-based government,” the Taliban government’s deputy spokesman, Hamdullah Fitrat, said during the ceremony.
There were no women present.
Celebrations were also held in provinces across Afghanistan, where Taliban flags and posters emblazoned with slogans in praise of the Taliban’s return to power were displayed along major roads and marketplaces.
In a video message, Richard Bennett, the U.N. special rapporteur on the human rights situation in Afghanistan, said the country was undergoing a deep human rights crisis.
“While the era of war has ended, it’s questionable whether there’s real peace, and the human rights situation has steadily deteriorated, most dramatically for women and girls,” Bennett said. “My mandate has concluded that this system amounts to the crime against humanity of gender persecution.”
“The crisis extends well beyond gender discrimination, even beyond gender apartheid,” he continued. “Across Afghanistan we continue to document arbitrary arrests, torture and ill treatment, extrajudicial killings, corporal punishment, enforced disappearances, restrictions on freedom of expression, attacks on journalists and human rights defenders, persecution of ethnic and religious minorities, discrimination against LGBT plus persons, and the reduction of civic space.”
Bennett warned the international community against “normalizing” the Taliban’s policies, saying it would legitimize the discrimination and tell “victims their suffering is negotiable.”
In an interview with The Associated Press this week, Molvi Hayatullah Mahajar Farahi, deputy minister in the Taliban government for broadcasting at the Ministry of Information and Culture, said despite “challenges and difficulties” the administration has in the past five years delivered security, infrastructure and created jobs.
Farahi, when asked, did not address the issue of the education of girls and women but said “the level of investment made in universities surpasses anything seen in the past.”
The U.N. agency on education and culture, UNESCO, estimates that some 2.4 million girls have been excluded from secondary education.
The world body’s agency on women’s rights, U.N. Women, said this week that women and girls are facing the harshest restriction in the world and that the bans are damaging Afghanistan’s future, with the lack of teachers, doctors, nurses and midwives threatening the country’s social and economic foundations.
___
Fraser reported from Ankara, Turkey.
