articles.title: S.Korean president vows to recover assets of past pro-Japanese collaborators, hold them accountable
articles.body:
SEOUL, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Saturday vowed to investigate and recover assets illicitly accumulated by pro-Japanese, anti-national collaborators during Japanese colonial rule and "hold them accountable before history."
Speaking at a ceremony marking the 81st anniversary of the Korean Peninsula's liberation from Japanese colonial rule here, Lee said the government would pursue the recovery of such assets under the Special Act on Asset Confiscation for Pro-Japanese and Anti-National Collaborators to the State, promulgated on June 2.
The government will also take a more responsible approach to managing the confiscated assets, ensuring that all proceeds go toward honoring and supporting decorated independence activists and surviving family members, Lee said.
"We will spare no effort in redressing the lingering vestiges of our painful history and safeguarding the honor and well-being of those who devoted themselves to our independence," he said.
South Korea first enacted a special law in 2005 to allow the state to confiscate assets acquired by pro-Japanese collaborators during Japan's colonial rule. A special investigative committee was established in 2006 but was dissolved in 2010 after its four-year mandate expired.
The government has since moved to revive the legal framework for recovering such assets. The National Assembly passed a revised special law on May 7, which was promulgated on June 2 and is scheduled to take effect on Dec. 2.
Under the new law, the investigative committee will be reestablished and may operate for up to five years. Assets derived from the disposal of pro-Japanese property, including proceeds from sales to third parties, will also be subject to recovery, according to Yonhap News Agency. ■

articles.title: Death toll from Indonesia's Flores earthquake rises to 38
articles.body:
MAUMERE, Indonesia, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- The death toll from a magnitude 7.7 earthquake and several strong aftershocks that struck off the coast of Flores Island in eastern Indonesia has risen to 38, an emergency official said Saturday.
As of 3:00 p.m. local time, two others sustained serious injuries and 11 suffered minor injuries, while around 2,000 people have been evacuated, National Disaster Mitigation Agency chief Suharyanto told a news conference.
Melki Laka Lena, governor of East Nusa Tenggara province, told a press conference in Kupang that several buildings and homes were damaged, and some roads were cut off or blocked by landslides.
The governor said authorities are still compiling data to assess the full extent of the destruction.
Footage shared on social media showed parts of structures collapsing into dust and rubble, with panicked residents screaming and running into the streets for safety.
Following the earthquake, multiple flights to East Nusa Tenggara province were canceled.
The Chinese Consulate General in Denpasar issued a notice on Saturday morning, reminding Chinese citizens in its consular district, especially tourists in Labuan Bajo, to stay on high alert.
The Chinese consulate urged them to closely monitor local earthquake and disaster warnings, guard against risks of aftershocks and tsunamis, and stay away from coastal areas.
The earthquake, centered near Mbay town in Nagekeo Regency, struck early Saturday and triggered a tsunami warning that was later lifted by Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency.
The agency urged residents to remain vigilant against potential aftershocks.
Rescue teams are continuing to assess casualties and damage across affected areas, with further updates expected as emergency operations proceed. ■

articles.title: Public bus fares to increase from September in Myanmar's Yangon
articles.body:
YANGON, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- Public bus fares on the Yangon Bus Service (YBS) routes, the main public bus network in Yangon, will increase from Sept. 1 to address rising costs of vehicle spare parts and maintenance, the state-owned daily The Global New Light of Myanmar reported Saturday.
The announcement was made by the Yangon Region Transport Supervisory Committee (YRTC) at a press conference on Friday.
Under the new fare structure, the current fare of 200 kyats (about 0.09 U.S. dollars) for downtown routes will increase to 300 kyats, while the current fare of 400 kyats for suburban and outlying routes will rise to 600 kyats, the report said, citing the YRTC.
The YRTC said the fare increase was necessary due to rising costs of vehicle spare parts and maintenance, which have created an imbalance between operators' income and expenses.
The YRTC said it would continue efforts to increase the number of buses in service to meet growing passenger demand and reduce congestion. ■

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz to be opened only under Iran's command: deputy FM
articles.body:
TEHRAN, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- A senior Iranian diplomat said Saturday that the Strait of Hormuz will be closed and opened only under Iran's command.
Kazem Gharibabadi, Iranian deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, made the remarks on X in response to a claim by U.S. President Donald Trump, who said on Friday that he would soon declare the strait a U.S. territory.
"The Strait of Hormuz can be captured neither with a tweet and aircraft carriers nor by issuing orders and a stump speech. Iran is neither afraid of threats nor intimidated by displays of power," he said.
"This strait will only be closed and opened under Iran's command," he added.
Iran tightened its grip on the strait on Feb. 28, barring safe passage of vessels belonging to or affiliated with Israel and the United States following their joint strikes on Iranian territory.
"After we finish defeating Iran -- which is being very badly defeated -- pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," Trump said during a rally in New York. ■

articles.title: Feature: Chinese theater artists bring WWII Chongqing story to Edinburgh stage
articles.body:
by Xinhua writer Zhao Jiasong
EDINBURGH, Britain, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- For people living in Chongqing, southwest China, in the late 1930s and early 1940s, fog was more than weather. It could offer precious hours of cover from bombers overhead.
Thick fog made it harder for pilots of Japanese aircraft to see the ground, giving residents some respite from repeated air raids by the invaders. For a city now known for its misty landscape and viral presence on TikTok, fog was once closely tied to safety and survival.
A Chinese-language solo play staged Aug. 7-8 at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, which runs through Aug. 31 this year, offers audiences a glimpse into what life under such circumstances might have been like.
In "The Red Lantern," Shaolun Fan performs alone, shifting between narration and multiple characters. Through voice, movement and sound, he recreates wartime Chongqing through the eyes of a boy named Guang, whose unusually sensitive hearing allows him to detect danger before others.
Starting in 1938, Japanese warplanes bombed Chongqing, then China's provisional capital, killing and injuring more than 32,000 people. On June 5, 1941, about 2,500 people suffocated to death while seeking shelter in a tunnel during an air raid.
The play was created by Fan and Yumin Liang, who studied theater in Beijing before pursuing postgraduate studies in Britain. The idea grew from conversations about Chongqing's wartime experience and the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression.
"When I first heard that a city had been bombed for more than five years, I began to wonder what that meant for everyday life," Fan said. "How did people's lives change? How did they respond to such difficulties, and how did they keep going?"
For Liang, the history was personal.
A native of Chongqing, she recalled hearing air-raid sirens every June 5 from primary school onward, when the city commemorated those killed in the wartime bombings.
She had learned about the history in school, but revisiting it for the play raised new questions.
"When you really look at the history from the perspective of the people who lived through it, you begin to see how they lived and how they managed to get through those years," Liang said.
In May 2026, Fan and Liang traveled to Chongqing for field research, visiting museums and the June 5 tunnel massacre site and watching the stage production "Chongqing 1949."
They studied records of the bombings and the June 5 attack, as well as air-raid sirens, red-lantern signals, shelters and the daily lives of residents and children. They also examined the city's streets, architecture, dialect, customs and wartime theater.
One detail stood out: the fog.
They found that during periods of particularly heavy fog, air raids could become less frequent. What Liang had regarded since childhood as an ordinary feature of her hometown suddenly took on a different meaning.
"For people at that time, fog was connected with survival," she said.
They also found records of people playing mahjong, chatting and carrying on with their daily routines amid the bombing.
Such details shaped the pair's understanding of the city: people lived with fear and loss, but still found ways to carry on.
"That optimistic attitude toward life really moved us," Liang said.
Fan and Liang chose to tell the story through a child.
"We didn't want to put the transformation of an entire city directly onto the stage," Fan said. "We wanted to follow the changes in one child and, through him, show something of the state of mind of the whole city."
But one image from their research stayed with them above all.
After an air raid, four Chinese characters were written on a surviving wall amid the ruins: "Yu zha yu qiang" -- "The more you bomb, the stronger we are." A replica of the slogan is now displayed at a museum commemorating the June 5 bombing.
"Behind that wall was already rubble," Fan said. "Someone still wrote, 'The more you bomb, the stronger we are.' That really moved us."
The play's Edinburgh run also coincides with an important date in the history it depicts. This year's Aug. 15 marks the 81st anniversary of Japan's announcement of its unconditional surrender in World War II.
Dong Ning, chairwoman of Beijing Performance & Arts Group, said the production offers an accessible way into a difficult chapter of history.
"On a limited stage, the work creates a city through sound, making wartime Chongqing something audiences can hear and feel," Dong said.
She added that the production's blend of local character and contemporary theatrical expression gives overseas audiences an emotional entry point into the history, offering "a noteworthy example of Chinese theater reaching the world."
For Fan and Liang, bringing the play to Edinburgh is another way of allowing audiences to encounter that history through the experiences of ordinary people.
"We are not historians," Fan said. "What theater allows us to do is use imagination to get closer to the people who lived at that time, and to ask where their hope came from." ■

articles.title: S. Korea expresses regret over Japanese leaders' offerings, visits to infamous Yasukuni Shrine
articles.body:
SEOUL, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- South Korea on Saturday expressed its deep regret over Japanese leaders' offerings and visits to the notorious war-linked Yasukuni Shrine, a symbol of the militaristic and colonial past of Japan.
South Korea's foreign ministry said in a statement that the government cannot but deplore the fact that responsible leaders of Japan once again forgot history and repeated anachronistic acts by sending offerings to or paying tributes at the Yasukuni Shrine, which glorifies Japan's past wars of aggression and enshrines war criminals.
The ministry strongly urged Japanese leaders to squarely face up to history and demonstrate their humble reflection and sincere remorse for Japan's history through actions, stressing that it will be an important foundation for building a future-oriented relationship between the two countries based on mutual trust.
While refraining from visiting the shrine in person, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi sent a ritual cash offering in her capacity as head of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) to mark the 81st anniversary of Japan's surrender in World War II.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, alongside other cabinet members and LDP lawmakers, proceeded with direct visits to pay homage to the notorious shrine, which honors about 2.5 million war dead, including 14 convicted Class-A Japanese war criminals from World War II.
Visits and ritual offerings made by Japanese officials to the shrine consistently sparked criticism and hurt the feelings of the people of China, South Korea and other countries brutalized by Japan during the war. ■

articles.title: Xinhua Commentary: Japan's rising neo-militarism must not go unchecked
articles.body:
BEIJING, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- Eighty-one years after Japan surrendered on Aug. 15, 1945, the lessons of its disastrous militarism during World War II ought to be well settled. Yet as Tokyo still speaks the language of peace, the country's increasingly audacious pursuit of a neo-militarist agenda tells a different story, a dangerous development that the international community must not allow to go unchecked.
Since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi assumed office, Japan's right-wing forces have, invoking so-called "external threats" and "national defense" as pretexts, steadily pushed the boundaries imposed by its Constitution, domestic laws and international laws.
From an expanding defense budget to looser arms-export restrictions and a growing emphasis on long-range strike capabilities, Tokyo is undertaking a sweeping overhaul of its defense posture.
In the 2026 defense white paper released on Aug. 4, Japan portrayed the regional security environment as "increasingly severe" and described China as the "greatest strategic challenge ever."
Conjuring up this threat, the paper further revealed plans to develop offensive capabilities, paving the way for the planned revision of Japan's three key security documents by year-end.
Such ambitions for increasingly offensive capabilities leave little doubt that Japan's long-standing post-war principle of an "exclusively defense-oriented policy" is being hollowed out.
More alarming still, Japan's nuclear debate is entering a new and perilous phase. By openly challenging the country's long-standing Three Non-Nuclear Principles, its ruling authorities have laid bare their determination to tear down a key principle of the country's post-war security policy.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi recently suggested that Japan should hold "no-taboo" discussions on nuclear-related policies, which has fueled reasonable concerns that what was once considered politically inconceivable is increasingly being presented as a policy option for Japan.
Coming from the country's incumbent defense chief, such remarks are almost without precedent in Japan's post-war history. As the only country to have suffered atomic bombings during wartime, Japan has long portrayed itself internationally as a supporter of nuclear non-proliferation and a world free of nuclear weapons.
Its current political movements, however, have belied its professed commitments and drawn widespread opposition at home and abroad.
In July, tens of thousands of Japanese citizens gathered outside the National Diet building in Tokyo to protest the Takaichi administration's recent push for a series of dangerous policies, while the country's defense white paper triggered immediate condemnation across Asia.
History gives the concerns of Japan's neighbors particular weight. Japanese militarism inflicted immense suffering across Asia during WWII, making any accelerated move toward remilitarization especially sensitive in a region where memories of aggression remain acute.
Japan's persistent failure to squarely face its wartime past, reflected in historical denial and revisionism, becomes all the more troubling on Aug. 15, a day that should serve not merely as an occasion for remembrance, but as a reminder of the consequences of militarism and the importance of learning from history.
If left unchecked, Japan's pursuit of increasingly offensive military capabilities risks reviving the very dangers that its postwar restraints were meant to prevent. ■

articles.title: Mastercard payments face disruptions in Australia
articles.body:
SYDNEY, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- Mastercard, a global payments technology company, is facing a reported disruption affecting card payments for some Australian customers, with Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CommBank) citing a "global Mastercard issue" on Saturday.
Shoppers across several Australian states have reported problems making card payments, including issues with Apple payments, cash withdrawals and Mastercard travel cards, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) reported.
Downdetector, a website that allows users to report service outages, recorded more than 1,700 reports of Mastercard issues at 3 p.m. local time, with the most commonly reported problems involving funds transfers and mobile banking, the ABC reported.
CommBank advised customers whose payments were declined to insert their cards and select "savings" to pay via eftpos, an electronic payment system for debit cards.
The cause and scope of the reported disruption were not immediately clear. ■

articles.title: Palestinian children gasp for air as Israeli forces fire tear gas in occupied West Bank raid
articles.body:
Several Palestinians, including children, suffered from tear gas inhalation on Saturday, when Israeli forces raided the village of Al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah in the central occupied West Bank, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa said.
Illegal Israeli settlers attacked the Shaab al-Lawz neighbourhood northwest of the village and attempted to storm several homes, the report said.
Israeli forces then raided the area and fired tear gas canisters, causing several Palestinians, including children, to suffer from gas inhalation, it added.
Wafa also said villages and towns northeast of Ramallah have been subjected to repeated Israeli military raids and occupier attacks targeting Palestinians and their property.
Unprecendented levels
The UN warned on Wednesday that illegal settler violence in the occupied West Bank had reached unprecedented levels, saying it had documented more than 1,430 attacks targeting around 260 Palestinian communities since the beginning of this year.
Along with demolitions and evictions, the attacks displaced 3,800 Palestinians, nearly half of them children, according to the UN.
Since the Gaza war began in October 2023, Israeli forces and illegal settlers have escalated attacks across the occupied West Bank, killing more than 1,183 Palestinians, injuring around 13,000 and arresting nearly 25,000, according to Palestinian figures.

articles.title: Investors have backed off the housing market. But will you benefit?
articles.body:
In brief
- Investors appear to be pulling back but it may be an early reaction to the tax reforms announced in May.
- A retreat of investors doesn't mean first-home buyers will fill the gap.
Investors are shying away from the housing market — but experts say it might not be the win the government says it is.
New Australian Bureau of Statistics data on loans show investors have pulled back sharply from the housing market in the June quarter.
Declines in investor loans was the highest since September 2022.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers said on Friday the lending figures were an "encouraging sign" that Labor's changes to negative gearing and the capital gains discount were working as intended and the market was "shifting in favour of first-home buyers" — even before the changes have officially taken effect.
But experts said the retreat hasn't necessarily translated into the wave of first-home buyers the federal government's property tax changes were designed to generate.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
'Not surprising' but not the whole picture
The number of investor loans fell 8.6 per cent in the June quarter, while first-home buyer loans fell a comparatively lower 2.9 per cent, according to ABS data released on Friday.
Independent property researcher Cameron Kusher said ABS' latest lending data was not surprising and reflected a typical knee-jerk reaction to policy changes.
“Across both the number and the value, the biggest falls in lending over the quarter were for investors, which is not really a surprise when you consider the tax changes that have happened,” he said.
The pullback lines up with what major banks have been reporting in their own lending figures, with CBA and NAB both reporting a 15 per cent drop in mortgage applications last quarter, while Westpac saw a 20 per cent drop.
The tax changes were announced in the May budget but aren't set to formally take effect until 1 July 2027. So, this quarter's fall was a reaction to the announcement itself, not the policy in action.
Kusher expects a bigger fall in investor lending in the future.
"We may actually see a larger fall when we get to the next quarter, when we see the full impact of a whole quarter of these changes," he said.
Both Kusher and Real Estate Group's economist Luc Redman say investors have not retreated entirely, rather they have changed strategy.
They are still keen on residential property but the type of property they’re chasing has shifted. They are now eyeing properties that have strong rental growth, or yield.
"Early evidence post-budget suggests that investors are enquiring more towards units that tend to have a higher yield and a lower entry point … compared to prior, when investors would be looking at houses that have stronger prospects of capital growth," Redman told SBS News.
Two places, Tasmania and the ACT, didn't see drops in investor interest — which Kusher said could be a sign they're moving toward properties with good rental returns relative to purchase price.
"I think the fall in new investment will potentially have a flow-on effect to the rental market where rental supply will tighten and landlords will have more scope to put up rents," Kusher said, though he noted there wasn't evidence of that happening "just yet".
Both experts hesitate to call this a permanent retreat for investors.
"It is likely that this won't be the case forever," Redman said.
"Once yields return to more attractive levels, we would expect investors to return to the market at a new equilibrium," he said.
"In the short term in particular, there will probably be a higher proportion of owner-occupier purchases in the market until we see yields rebalance and investor sentiment return ... [separately] the structural undersupply of dwellings means prices will continue to increase over the long run, albeit more modestly than recent price growth."
Kusher says at least two to three quarters of data will be needed before drawing any meaningful conclusions, meaning the next quarterly release will be a better indication of investor behaviour as it will be the first to reflect a full three months under the new environment.
A win for first-home buyers?
The policy case for the tax changes rested on the idea that pushing investors out would clear space for first-home buyers.
But the numbers haven't quite shown that yet, Kusher says, adding that two things may be happening.
First-home buyers do not directly replace all the investors who have retreated — first-home buyers do not entirely fill the gap as they are a smaller group of buyers than investors. Secondly, first-home buyers, like investors, are also in a “wait and see” mode.
"There's an assumption that if you don't have an investor, you have a first-home buyer. That's not always the case. Not everyone that's currently renting is in a position to buy a home,” Kusher said.
Investors make up about 40 per cent of the residential market, but first-home buyers have never been that large a group, he added.
"So, if you're discouraging investors and trying to encourage first-time buyers, you're probably going to struggle to see an uplift in first-home buyer lending offset the weakness in investor lending — and that's certainly what we've seen,” Kusher said.
He notes that some first-home buyers may be falling into a "trap" of trying to time a falling market but warns “picking the bottom of the market” is incredibly difficult.
"I think what these [tax] changes have done more than anything else is just damaged sentiment around the housing market," he said.

articles.title: Israeli motorcyclist killed in Thailand crash
articles.body:
An Israeli man riding a motorcycle was killed Wednesday in a collision with a pickup truck in the Kanchanaburi region of western Thailand, according to local reports. Police have opened an investigation into the circumstances of the crash.
Local media reported that police officers arriving at the scene found a pickup truck with extensive damage to its front end and a large motorcycle that had also been badly damaged.
The Israeli rider was found dead near the motorcycle. Authorities are continuing to investigate what led to the collision.
Kanchanaburi, west of Bangkok near Thailand’s border with Myanmar, is a popular tourist destination known for its national parks, waterfalls and World War II sites.
The fatal crash comes several months after another Israeli tourist was killed in a motorcycle accident in Thailand.
In March, Ofer Dahan, 56, a Jerusalem resident and employee of the Jerusalem municipality, was killed while traveling in the country.
Dahan had rented a motorcycle during his trip and, according to available information, lost control and crashed while riding, suffering critical injuries.
Emergency medical teams called to the scene attempted to resuscitate him for about an hour before he was pronounced dead.

articles.title: Putin says Russia, North Korea coordinating efforts to ensure regional security, stability
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
Russia's President Vladimir Putin on Saturday said his country and North Korea are coordinating efforts to ensure regional security and stability.
In a telegram to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on the occasion of the 81st anniversary of Korea's Liberation Day, Putin said that relations between Moscow and Pyongyang have reached an “unprecedented level of comprehensive strategic partnership.”
“Our countries actively cooperate in all areas, coordinating their efforts to ensure regional security and stability,” Putin said in the telegram published by the Kremlin.
He also expressed confidence that they will continue their joint work on pressing issues on the bilateral and international agendas “for the benefit of the Russian and Korean peoples, in the interests of building a more just and truly democratic world order.”
Moscow and Pyongyang have significantly expanded political, military, and economic ties over the past two years following the signing of a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty in June 2024.
The holiday, marking Japan's defeat in World War II and the end of its 35 years of colonial rule on the Korean Peninsula, is also celebrated in South Korea.

articles.title: Russia Delays New Mobilization Wave Despite Rising Troop Losses
articles.body:
The Kremlin currently has no plans to initiate a new mobilization wave despite growing frontline losses and troop shortages, The Guardian reported, citing sources familiar with internal Russian discussions.
There are no indications that Russian President Vladimir Putin has authorized a new large-scale draft. An unnamed Western official confirmed the absence of preparations for a mobilization.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Kremlin is reportedly relying on volunteer recruitment through Ministry of Defense contracts to avoid the political risks associated with forced conscription.
However, human rights advocate Alexei Tabalov stated that finding individuals willing to fight is becoming increasingly difficult, despite significant financial incentives.
An employee of a Russian recruiting agency confirmed this trend, stating that the organization is required to recruit 20 to 30 men per month to avoid financial penalties. The recruiter, speaking anonymously, noted that meeting these quotas has become harder compared to the previous year.
While internal discussions about a potential mobilization occur, the recruiter said there are no official orders or signs of an imminent draft.
Risks of a second mobilization
International analysts suggest that a large-scale mobilization carries significant risks for the Russian government.
Commentary published by the German business daily Handelsblatt indicated that a new draft could negatively impact the Russian economy by removing more workers from the labor force and could lead to public dissatisfaction, similar to the reaction following the initial mobilization in September 2022.
Russia Admits New Petrol Shortages as Ukrainian Strikes Hit Refineries
Reports suggest Moscow is seeking alternative methods to bolster its forces without resorting to a domestic draft.
According to the Polish daily Rzeczpospolita, North Korea has deployed between 30,000 and 50,000 troops to Russia.
Analysts indicate this deployment is intended to provide the Kremlin with additional personnel and delay the necessity of a second mobilization wave.

articles.title: Dvořák’s "Rusalka" under the baton of Pavel Baleff is broadcast worldwide
articles.body:
News
Dvořák’s "Rusalka" under the baton of Pavel Baleff is broadcast worldwide
Saturday 15 August 2026 10:15
Saturday, 15 August 2026, 10:15
PHOTO resonances-lyriques.org
Font size
These days, great Bulgarian conductor Pavel Baleff once again delighted compatriots with an exceptional musical event. The performance of one of the most beautiful and most frequently staged Slavic opera works - "Rusalka" by Antonin Dvořák, realized by the ensembles of Opéra de Limoges under the baton of Baleff, is included in the program of the prestigious classical music television channel Stingray Classica.
After the August 11 premiere, "Rusalka" airs on August 14 and 26, 2026, in various countries on all continents.
Nicola Raab
PHOTO opera.se
The
production is by famous German director Nicola Raab, who has worked
with success in leading world theaters such as the Bavarian State
Opera in Munich, the Vienna State Opera, Zürich Opera, the New
Israeli Opera, Teatro La Fenice in Venice, Salzburg Festival. The
film version by television director Arnaud Lalanne is a more than
worthy interpretation of Dvořák's masterpiece. Among the soloists
are Ruzan Mantashyan, Adam Smith, Rafal Pawnuk, Marie-Adeline Henry,
Marion Lebègue, Alexandra Marcellier. The performance was recorded
in Limoges in February 2021.
Pavel Baleff – the world-renowned conductor of Bulgarian premieres
Pavel Baleff's repertoire includes almost all of Dvořák's
symphonies. Of his operas, he has only conducted "Rusalka"
in its entirety, which was his first production as chief conductor at
the prestigious theater in Limoges. Balev spoke about this in a
special interview with Radio Bulgaria last summer:
Pavel Baleff
PHOTO pavel-baleff.de
"During the Covid pandemic in 2021, the opera theatre in Limoges
was the only one that continued to operate. We had permission to move
around the streets after 6 p.m. All theaters in France were closed
and were waiting for President Macron's decision - whether the
audience would enter the hall or not. But we continued to work behind
closed doors for four weeks and ultimately, after the decision was
made not to open theaters, we had a plan ‘B’. Our director had
invited the French television to make a film. A television crew came
and recorded our production for a week. It was broadcast and today
‘Rusalka’ of the Opéra de Limoges can be found everywhere in the
media space. It is a very good film and I am really proud of it."

articles.title: Massive 7.7 earthquake kills 38, triggers landslides in Indonesia
articles.body:
A powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck off Indonesia’s coast early Saturday, killing at least 38 people, destroying homes and buildings, and sparking panic in a region frequently hit by deadly earthquakes.
Authorities said six people were injured and two others were missing after a landslide triggered by the quake.
A tsunami warning was issued shortly after the earthquake, prompting authorities to urge coastal residents to move to higher ground. The warning was later lifted after Indonesia’s Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency said monitoring showed no significant changes in sea levels that could threaten coastal communities.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the earthquake struck the Flores region at a depth of 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) at 5:58 a.m. local time. The epicenter was 68 kilometers (42 miles) north-northwest of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province. Several aftershocks followed the initial quake.
Fathur Rahman, head of the Maumere Search and Rescue Agency, said rescuers had recovered at least 38 bodies from the three hardest-hit regencies of Sikka, West Manggarai and East Manggarai.
Eight of the victims were found in a landslide in the village of Reok in Manggarai, Rahman said. Six people were taken to nearby hospitals with severe injuries, while rescuers continued searching for two people reported missing after the landslide.
He said rescuers were still searching for two villagers believed to be buried under tons of mud that tumbled down from surrounding hills in a landslide triggered by the quake.
East Nusa Tenggara Police Chief Rudi Darmoko said the earthquake caused severe damage and collapsed buildings. He said power outages in cities and villages had hampered the flow of information and complicated search and rescue efforts.
"We are continuing to collect reports of damage and casualties, but there are communication disruptions," Darmoko said.
He said landslides in Ende Regency triggered by the earthquake also cut off the Trans-Flores highway, a roughly 700-kilometer (435-mile) paved mountain road spanning Flores Island from Labuan Bajo to Larantuka.
Footage on local television showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution following the quake. Hospital staff moved equipment outdoors, including beds, IV stands and oxygen cylinders, and set up temporary treatment areas to adapt to emergency conditions.
The National Disaster Management Agency deployed a helicopter to assist with logistics and support emergency response operations, including possible evacuations if needed, the agency said in a statement.
The air support is considered crucial given East Nusa Tenggara’s geography, which consists of numerous islands and presents significant transportation and access challenges.
The agency said about 2,000 villagers in Nagekeo regency fled their homes to temporary shelters.
The quake was felt across much of Flores Island, with initial reports indicating heavy damage.
Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka regency, said a number of buildings were damaged by the strong shaking and panicked people ran to higher ground.
"Many buildings here were damaged ... I saw that the waiting room at the port terminal in Maumere had collapsed," she said.
Students at St. Peter Major Seminary in Sikka who were attending morning Mass fled in panic when the roof of an assembly hall collapsed, said the Rev. Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of the seminary, which is known locally as Ritapiret Seminary on the predominantly Catholic island of Flores.
"Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof," Tanga said. "At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake."
The quake also reportedly caused panic in Labuan Bajo, a gateway town to eastern Indonesia’s Komodo National Park, one of the country’s best-known attractions. Damage was also reported in Bima, a city in neighboring West Nusa Tenggara province, and in parts of southern Sulawesi Island.
Indonesian authorities initially issued a tsunami warning for parts of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, and urged residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks. The agency located the shallow undersea quake near Flores Island.
Indonesia, a vast archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity because of its location on the "Ring of Fire," an arc of volcanoes and fault lines in the Pacific Basin.
A powerful earthquake caused a tsunami in 1992 that killed about 2,500 people on Flores, part of a group of islands in eastern Indonesia.
In 2018, a magnitude 7.5 quake spawned a large localized tsunami that wiped out coastal areas, while liquefaction caused by the shaking turned entire neighborhoods into rivers of sludge in the eastern Indonesian city of Palu, on the Palu-Koro Fault. The disaster killed more than 4,400 people.
In 2010, a 10-foot (3-meter) wave struck the Mentawai Islands off the western coast of Sumatra, just minutes after a massive offshore earthquake. More than 400 people were killed and hundreds of homes were destroyed.
In December 2004, a massive magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra in western Indonesia triggered a tsunami that killed 230,000 people in a dozen countries.

articles.title: Kremlin Files Reveal Russia’s Strategy to Target Moldova After Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Kremlin Files Reveal Russia’s Strategy to Target Moldova After Ukraine
Russian authorities are executing a long-term operation to destabilize Moldova, positioning the conquest of Ukraine as their top priority and gaining control over Moldova as their second, as reported by The New York Times on August 14.
According to an investigation based on interviews with Moscow-directed operatives, security officials from Moldova, Europe, and the US, and thousands of leaked documents, Russian leader Vladimir Putin intends to capture southern Ukraine to establish a land corridor connecting Russia directly to Moldova.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In the meantime, Sergey Kiriyenko, deputy head of the Russian presidential administration, oversees destabilization efforts alongside Ilan Shor, a fugitive banker sentenced in Moldova to 15 years in prison for organizing a 2014 fraud scheme that stole $1 billion from local banks.
Before the autumn 2025 parliamentary elections, Shor recruited over 150,000 Moldovans—representing roughly 4.5% of the registered electorate—paying them to vote for specific candidates and participate in staged protests.
Prior to that, during four months leading up to the 2024 European Union integration referendum, Shor distributed nearly $20 million to 38,000 recruits to post anti-government content online and vote against President Maia Sandu, her party, and EU accession, according to The New York Times.
The operations extended to physical training camps managed by Russian military intelligence (GRU) in Serbia, Bosnia, and near Moscow. In Serbia, recruits completed 3-4 day courses for $400, practicing how to break police lines and set fire to buildings.
In a facility near Moscow, over 100 young Moldovans received instruction in making explosives, incendiary devices, and operating drones designed for arson and bomb attacks.
Additionally, hundreds of Moldovan priests from the Russian Orthodox Church were flown to Russia starting in summer 2024, signed contracts with the Kremlin-linked Eurasia organization, and received payment cards from Promsvyazbank. In exchange for roughly $1,000 each, the priests campaigned against EU integration among their parishioners.
When covert political action failed to deliver full control, Russia engaged in direct infrastructure strikes. Russian forces shelled a Ukrainian hydroelectric station near the Moldovan border, contaminating regional water supplies, and struck a high-voltage power line in western Ukraine that provided up to 70% of Moldova's electricity, causing widespread blackouts.
As reported by The New York Times, although pro-EU voters secured narrow victories in the 2024 and 2025 votes—largely due to votes cast by the overseas diaspora—Moldovan officials emphasize that Moscow is pursuing a long-term strategy.
Mihai Lupascu, director of Moldova's Cybersecurity Agency, stated, "We won the battle, but not the war."
On April 8, 2026, Moldovan authorities dismantled a Russia-backed cross-border network that trained operatives in secret camps in Bosnia and Serbia for destabilization campaigns targeting France and Germany.
Recruits received between $300 and $500 to complete training in drone operations, handling incendiary devices, and evading law enforcement during staged unrest. Moldovan officials uncovered the scheme after intercepting operatives at the border with specialized equipment, including drone components and radio controllers.
Following the crackdown, Chisinau offered to share its expertise in fighting illicit finance, disinformation, and election interference with European allies facing similar hybrid threats.

articles.title: NATO Plans Thousands of AI Drones Along Russia and Belarus Borders
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
NATO Plans Thousands of AI Drones Along Russia and Belarus Borders
NATO is planning to strengthen its eastern flank with a network of thousands of drones, sensors, and satellites linked through artificial intelligence, according to Politico on August 14.
The system is being developed under the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative (EFDI) and is intended to monitor threats along NATO’s borders with Russia and Belarus, stretching from northern Finland to the Black Sea.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
NATO plans for the network to detect violations of allied airspace and borders and serve as the first line of defense.
The system would combine data from multiple sources in real time. For example, if a drone detects a hostile UAV, AI could compare that information with satellite images, sensor readings, and radar data before sending the information to NATO allies.
Commanders would then be able to choose which forces should respond. NATO refers to the concept as a “kill web,” designed to send information directly to operators instead of moving it through multiple levels of command.
“Previously, information went through many intermediaries. Today, it can come directly from a sensor to a tool of influence,” US Army Captain Ronan Sefton said.
The platform is being developed in Wiesbaden with military personnel from the US, Canada, Lithuania, Poland, Germany, and other countries, according to Bild.
It is designed to connect allied command systems and allow them to exchange data. “The network works in real time. We are moving at high speed,” Canadian Lieutenant Colonel Mike Mendika said.
According to US Army Major Brian Hobek, if Russia attacked a NATO member, information about the attack would reach Wiesbaden and a response could be launched within five minutes.
The system is also intended to automate some of the most routine parts of drone operations. US Army Major Ben Schiff said this could include keeping a drone over a battlefield for long periods while it searches for targets.
The Wiesbaden team is also using 3D printing to develop drones. Schiff said new parts can be produced and tested on the same day, whereas development and testing previously could take months.
NATO believes the system should allow the alliance to adapt to changes on the battlefield faster than an adversary. The project is planned for implementation on a short timeline, as reported by Politico.
On July 7, 2026, NATO launched a new $40 billion initiative called Drone Edge to strengthen the Alliance’s ability to counter unmanned aerial threats.
Announced by Secretary General Mark Rutte during the NATO Defense Industry Forum in Ankara, the five-year program was developed using lessons learned from recent wars, including Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Under the initiative, NATO member states committed to investing in counter-drone technologies, expanding drone pilot training, and increasing the number of drone operators in their armed forces fivefold by the end of 2027.

articles.title: Europe tightens freight wagon rules after Gotthard rail accident
articles.body:
Europe tightens freight wagon rules after Gotthard rail accident
Three years after the Gotthard Base Tunnel accident, European authorities and the rail industry have agreed to tighten safety checks for freight wagons, requiring more frequent inspections. The new rules were prompted by a Swiss initiative.
“This shows that in Switzerland we can also set standards in Europe,” Christa Hostettler, director of the Federal Office of Transport, told Swiss public television on Friday. In future, freight wagons are to be inspected every 50,000 to 300,000 kilometres, depending on the type of wheel. Until now, the inspection interval has been 660,000 kilometres.
Hostettler announced that Switzerland would adopt the new rules. But she expects industry to make the transition immediately, rather than from 2028, as originally planned.
Following an enquiry from the Keystone-SDA news agency, the transport office confirmed that it is clarifying how the European solution can be made binding for Switzerland through an administrative order. This also involves clarifying how to deal with the order regarding the previous measures, which is pending before the Federal Administrative Court following appeals by wagon owners.
More
Gotthard train crash report notes ignored warning signals
The new rules are set out in the European Railway Agency’s (ERA) fifth report on the accident in the Gotthard Tunnel, which was published last week. According to the Federal Office of Transport, these are recommendations: “The supervisory authorities of the individual countries are responsible for implementation.”
According to the SRF news report on Friday, the new European standards stem from pressure exerted by Switzerland. Following the accident in the Gotthard Base Tunnel three years ago caused by a broken wheel, Switzerland was the only country to introduce stricter regulations.
A success for Switzerland
Although this order has been blocked in court following complaints from wagon owners, Switzerland has prevailed on the substance of the matter, said Hostettler. “It is a success that we have prevailed on the substance here. And it was worth our while to remain steadfast when necessary,” she said.
More
Why is the Gotthard Base Tunnel so important?
The Association of Shippers’ reacted positively to the agreement. Josef Dittli, the association’s president who is also a Swiss senator, described the new rules as a “good solution”. The association had always advocated for a European solution. “Switzerland cannot manage this on its own,” he said.
The question of liability remains unresolved, as this is central to rail safety. “Only if we know who bears responsibility can we be sure that the relevant parties will actually implement these measures,” said Hostettler. The transport office is in contact with the relevant parties on this matter, it confirmed.
The accident in August 2023 was caused by a broken wheel. It resulted in damage costing CHF150 million ($184 million) and the closure of one of the tunnel tubes for over a year.

articles.title: Post-Brexit rights for British citizens are being undermined in Sweden
articles.body:
Back in October 2020, the UK immigration minister stood up in parliament to reassure campaigners concerned about EU citizens who weren’t aware they had to ask the Home Office to stay in the country after Brexit.
Using an example of a child in foster care who might not know they were an EU citizen until they applied for their first job, the Conservative Kevin Foster said the UK would take “a generous approach as to what reasonable grounds [for failing to apply] were”.
In other words, the UK/EU Brexit agreement was designed to protect those who had exercised lawful freedom of movement, and they couldn’t just be chucked out of their host state because the UK had decided to leave the EU.
The Home Office is not perfect, and is regularly criticised by campaigners for missteps over the implementation of the EU citizens chapter in the EU-UK withdrawal agreement. But “reasonable grounds” have been outlined in parliament, providing legal arguments to challengers.
Yet thousands of miles away in Sweden, post-Brexit rights are being undermined with an apparent high level of removal orders for law-abiding British citizens, some at the most vulnerable stage of their lives.
One 74-year-old British man, who has been in Sweden for 25 years, is this week facing deportation despite having vascular dementia and parkinsonism, and being so incapacitated that he is in full-time care.
Rejecting a legal request for him to stay using family ties, a Swedish court ruled that immigration interests trumped human rights. “Upon balancing the state’s interest in regulated immigration against what has emerged regarding Horace Mason’s private life and his adaptation to Sweden, the migration court concludes, on balance, that his deportation appears proportionate,” it ruled.
This week, Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old widow who has been in Sweden for 21 years, also lost her appeal to reverse a migration agency decision that she has to leave the country within four weeks.
“It would be difficult to find anyone who would argue that what is happening to Mrs Thomas and others in Sweden was an intended outcome of the [EU-UK] withdrawal agreement,” said David Milstead, of the campaign group British in Sweden. He said he knew of people who, on receiving the removal order, just left, “too embarrassed” to fight it.
The question now is whether the Conservative party failed British citizens during Brexit negotiations by not spotting the difficulties with the “constitutive” system adopted by 13 countries – including the UK – where EU citizens (including, at the time, British citizens living elsewhere in the EU) had to make an application to stay. Others, such as Spain, opted for a “declaratory” system, whereby EU citizens just had to register their presence before Brexit.
Did the government fail to communicate this effectively to the estimated 1 million Britons in the EU? Or has the European Commission failed to enforce the withdrawal agreement to protect citizens in practice?
“Problems will inevitably emerge when a new treaty is put into practice. However, the UK, the EU and Sweden must act to address them. Words and expressions of concern won’t cut it,” said Milstead.
One of the problems is lack of political interest in Sweden. Politicians in Sweden have the perfect get-out clause: legally, they are unable to interfere in any decisions made by the Migrationsverket, the Swedish migration agency.
The UK government has raised the issue of Sweden multiple times, but it is years since the first cases emerged and nothing appears to have changed.
Two years ago, Kathleen Poole, who had Alzheimer’s, faced deportation from a dementia care home because she did not have up-to-date bank statements and a passport. Her case was paused – long enough not to be acted upon, as she died soon after.
One UK government source said it was “concerned that Sweden is taking a considerably stricter approach to this requirement than other member states”, adding that “in practice individuals are not likely to have their reasonable grounds accepted”.
The latest statistics available (2024) show only about 14,000 applications to stay post-Brexit have been made in Sweden. But of those, 27.5% were refused – a refusal rate three times higher than in any other member state, and far higher than the EU average of 3%-4%.
Thomas, like many others who have contacted the British in Sweden group, believes she had “reasonable grounds” for her late application. She and her late husband were told they didn’t have to do anything – a story told over and over by Britons in touch with Milstead.
Felix Andler, a Swedish hospital neurologist and family friend of Thomas, said he had spoken to her husband before 2020 about how Brexit affected him. “I remember talking to Gwynne and asking him, is there anything you have to do? And he said, ‘No, I checked it and we are good’, so I take it he looked it up or contacted someone at the British Foreign Office.”
Joyce says even if the government had communicated the need to make a special application to stay after Brexit, they didn’t do it well enough. “They have our ID cards, our email addresses and contact us with other important information, why not something as critical as this? It is mind-blowing,” she said.
“Simply stating that the person was unaware of the requirement to apply is not, in itself, considered a sufficient explanation,” said a spokesperson for the Swedish migration authority.
In 2022 similar stories were emerging from Denmark of Britons being ordered to leave: in one instance because a man was three weeks too late to apply to stay, and in another, a man was just four days late. The Danish government acknowledged communications shortcomings and changed the law to allow Britons another chance to apply for residency rights.

articles.title: Gen Z flocks to BirdTok as birding takes flight: ‘It’s a craving for something real’
articles.body:
Sorry Elon, but they’re not your kind of tweets. Social media users are flocking to TikTok to join a burgeoning trend for birding videos as the hobby attracts a younger demographic.
With the internet ever more cluttered with polarising, shouty and AI content, evidence is emerging of Britons preferring a gentler, more melodic window on the world in the shape of footage of the nation’s feathered friends.
TikTok says UK posts of #birdwatching and #birdtok videos have risen by a third over the past three months as users flock to feathered friend content. The number of #birding posts has risen by 40% in the UK and the global number of posts carrying one of those three hashtags now stands at 1m. A video of Steven, a relatively tame seagull, being fed raw Tesco salmon fillet has more than 52m views.
Posts by the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds have received nearly 9m views over the past year, with a third of those coming from under-24s. Dedicated birders say the boom is down to the popularity of apps such as Merlin – a kind of Shazam for birdsong – a resurgence in curiosity about the natural world, a desire for analogue hobbies and the power of social media.
“It’s a craving for something ‘real’ and birding is a really nice gateway to that,” says Jack Baddams, 33, a Derbyshire-based bird enthusiast whose videos about tagging birds have had millions of views.
“Anyone can walk outside or look out of their window and see a bird. And there are communities that build off the back of that.”
Baddams, who has 300,000 followers, is a TV researcher and one of 3,000 bird “ringers” for the British Trust for Ornithology, who places identification rings around birds to help monitor phenomena such as population changes or migratory patterns. A video on his account explaining the craft of bird ringing has had 7.5m views
Baddams admits he has been “shocked” by the scale of interest.
“I’m not tagging protected birds. A lot of them are very common birds. It seems like the more common and recognisable the bird, the more interest it gets. People have a relationship to them,” he says.
Birds tagged by Baddams include blackbirds, blue tits and meadow pipits, the latter dubbed a “classic little brown job” – birding jargon for the small, sparrow-like brown birds that tend to be indistinguishable from each other at first glance.
Tim Jones, 35, a professional ornithologist from York, says social media has helped spread the word about a hobby that is not normally associated with younger age groups. As well as 48,000 followers on TikTok for videos such as “learn one birdsong this week”, Jones has 210,00 on Instagram under his Begin Birding handle. Other birding stars on Instagram include Jacob Cobb, who is attempting to find “every bird in the world”, and US birder-singer Bonner Black.
“If you saw a birder under the age of 40 a few decades ago it would be notable. That’s really changing now because you’re seeing twentysomethings and teenagers all the time,” says Jones.
Nomenclature is also shifting, with the catch-all term of “birding” preferable to “birdwatching” for younger people, while “twitcher” refers to the devotees who will drop everything to attend a rare bird sighting and does not reflect the majority of bird hobbyists, says Jones.
“Social media has shown people that it’s interesting and cool to do these hobbies and that there are other young people out there doing them,” he says.
This avenue is due to be cut off, however, as the government prepares a social media ban for under-16s coming in next year. Jones describes “10 to 13” as the age when people typically get into birding, although he believes the dominant demographic among social media followers is thirtysomethings.
The British Trust for Ornithology told the Guardian there has been a surge in interest in events tailored for young birders, including bird camps, walks and talks for 11-25-year-olds.
“It was a struggle getting young people to events but now are seeing huge demand for everything we do,” said Samuel Levy, a member of the BTO’s youth engagement team. “It’s the first time in my life I can call myself trendy.”
Young wildlife and bird photographers are also proving popular on TikTok, under accounts such as @TomSkylark and @TommyMcewan. The RSPB said it was “brilliant” to see interest in birdwatching growing among a younger demographic.
“It’s hugely encouraging to see more young people engaging with birds and wildlife. That interest can be an important first step towards building a lasting connection with the natural world,” said Joshua Edwards, the RSPB’s social media manager.

articles.title: From food to tech to travel: the best student deals and discounts
articles.body:
With rents on the up and food costing more, maintenance loans are stretched thinner than ever. Knowing how, and where, to get a discount can make a real difference.
A golden rule is to register with the big discount websites and apps – UNiDAYS, Student Beans and TOTUM – using your university email address as soon as you have one. Each has a slightly different roster of retailers, so it is worth signing up to all three.
Many of the deals below are only unlocked once you have verified your student status. The sites explain how to do this. If you are unable to verify using email, you may be able to upload, for example, an acceptance letter from your university.
Food and essentials
Boots: an Advantage Card gets you 10% off thousands of products instore and online – handy for weekly toiletries and the odd emergency paracetamol run. You need to apply for a card then go into a shop with a valid student ID to activate your membership and qualify for the discounts.
Marks & Spencer: 25% off in store’s “food on the move” range through UNiDAYS. This range includes sandwiches, wraps, poké bowls and salads, plus a variety of snacks.
Uber One: after a four-week free trial, students get half-price membership (£2.49 a month), for discounted delivery and takeaways – useful on the days when a big supermarket shop feels like one task too many.
The Co-op: 10% off your shop in-store – but now only for some students, such as those with a Young Scot card. Central Co-op and Southern Co-op give Student Beans members 10% off at their participating stores.
Going out
Many pub and restaurant chains – including Greene King, Pizza Express and Zizzi – offer money off. Greene King offers 20% off all food and drinks (show your student ID at the bar to get one of its 20% off student cards).
Tech and subscriptions
Amazon Prime for Students: new sign-ups get six months of Prime free, after which it drops to half price (£4.49 a month).
Link your Amazon and Deliveroo accounts through a site such as UNiDAYS and you will also get a year’s worth of Deliveroo Plus – which gets you free delivery on orders above £15 from restaurants, or above £25 from shops – at no extra cost instead of the usual £3.49 a month.
Kindle Unlimited: claim 30 days free through UNiDAYS – useful for clearing a reading list without buying every set text.
Microsoft 365: many universities give students free access to the full Office suite – Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook – via their institution’s IT department, so check before you pay for anything.
Spotify Premium: one month free, then £5.99 a month – roughly half the standard price.
Apple: offers “education pricing” – a variety of reductions on MacBooks and other items – to students who have a UNiDAYS account.
Microsoft: up to 15% off items such as laptops and accessories bought directly.
Adobe Creative Cloud: If you are on a creative course or just want to develop your skills, Adobe offers a 75% saving on its Pro subscription for students, reducing the cost from £66.49 a month to £16.24.
Gyms and fitness
The Gym Group: up to 25% off via the student discount sites.
Fitness First: up to 25% off via the student discount sites.
Strava: 30 days of its premium plan for free, then 50% off the subscription (taking it down to £27.49 a year).
University gyms are almost always cheaper than commercial ones, and BUCS (British Universities and Colleges Sport) UNIversal Gym scheme means if your own university’s gym is signed up, you can use any other participating gym for free. That’s great if you are visiting friends or family at or near another campus and don’t want to break your routine.
Travel
FlixBus: 20% off fares via UNiDAYS and Student Beans.
National Express: up to 20% off coach tickets via UNiDAYS, Student Beans and TOTUM.
16-25 Railcard: one-third off most rail fares (you can get one for free for four years if you open a Santander Edge student current account). Alternatively, students get 15% off the cost of the card via Student Beans and UNiDAYS – typically it’s £35 a year.
Fashion
Asos and Nike offer 10% off via UNiDAYS, Student Beans and TOTUM, with JD Sports offering 20%.
Urban Outfitters has 10% off all year-round for students.
Always carry proof of student status – a university ID card, or a UNiDAYS, Student Beans or TOTUM card or login.
Also, don’t be afraid to ask if a student discount isn’t advertised. Many independent shops and cafes offer one but don’t always put up a sign.

articles.title: ‘I don’t even drink whisky’: Scotland reels in visitors as much of Europe swelters
articles.body:
For the tourist industry, 2026 has been a rocky year, with war, EU border delays, climate and economic woes gnawing away at holiday plans. But while much of Britain is feeling the loss of visitors from the Middle East and beyond, one part is thriving.
Scotland is reeling in ever more visitors, with strong annual growth and a 15% rise in flight bookings to Scottish airports in June and July, compared with a drop in bookings to London and the rest of England in recent months, according to VisitBritain figures.
With heatwaves gripping much of Europe, the hope of finding cooler climes farther north may have increased Scotland’s allure – although tourism chiefs say dashing Highland warriors and kilted football fans may have more to do with it.
Long-term plans to increase direct flights from North America have come to fruition in the last two years, bolstering the traditional US-led foreign tourist base.
A rise in visitors from continental Europe, possibly looking to escape the heat, has added to the mix. And more Britons have chosen to holiday at home rather than face the border confusion and delays under the EU’s entry-exit system.
In Edinburgh, where August has long been the busiest time of the year, Princes Street was this week particularly teeming with tourists, gathered around bagpipers and being targeted with leaflets by cheery fringe promoters.
Festival sales are up 30%, according to Marc Crothall, the chief executive of the Scottish Tourism Alliance. “Edinburgh is jumping, which is great. And that’s a massive draw for international visitors,” he said.
Not all were here for the world’s biggest arts festival: Zanet Garcia, from Mexico City and on her second day in the country, had no idea it was on. “I was really confused by it all. I had never heard of the fringe and I didn’t know what it was,” she said with a laugh. “But everyone has been so friendly.”
Garcia chose Scotland because of her interest in Scottish mythology, sparked by books and TV shows that were huge UK exports, such as Harry Potter and Outlander, and had visited locations connected with them. She was taking in traditional national attractions too, fresh from the Johnnie Walker Experience – “I don’t even drink whisky” – and with tickets to the military tattoo.
The majority of tourists are from the UK. But it is the big-spending foreigners who are more likely to stay longer, chalk up the visitor attractions and pack in the experiences. An average overseas visitor to Scotland spent just over £900 in a week in 2024, compared with just over £300 in three nights for a British holidaymaker.
According to data from the Moffat Centre for travel and tourism at Glasgow Caledonian University the biggest jump this year has been in visitors touring by campervan rather than staying in hotels.
Numbers are up but spending per head is down, Crothall said, describing the overall picture as “healthy but by no means booming”.
The holidaying Briton is more likely, he said, to be pursuing free visits to museums and walking in the countryside, with the cost of living still a big issue. “Instead of the three course meal, it’s the one. The 5% VAT and free travel helps, but it’s not magic,” Crothall said.
Although Scotland has suffered its own heatwaves, and devastating wildfires in the Cairngorms, it remains cooler than the southern UK. “We hope and suspect that we’ll see more European visitors given the climate conditions,” Crothall added.
Conclusive data linking the heat to changing tourism habits is not yet available, said Vicki Miller, the chief executive of VisitScotland. “But certainly we’ve seen this year strong demand from Europe including Spain and Italy, which is potentially the climate impact,” she added.
What the research does show, however, is just how many visits, such as Garcia’s, were inspired by the screen. Online searches spiked on the back of reality TV hit The Traitors, although Ardross Castle – the main location for the UK and US versions of the show – is not open to visit. Castles that have featured in Outlander – a long-running hit in the US and parts of Europe – have also become big draws.
“We know that 36%-37% of international visitors are inspired by film or TV,” said Miller. “And people’s memories are long: they remember Braveheart or Local Hero as well.”
Sport has also pulled in visitors, from this year’s Commonwealth Games in Glasgow to big golf tournaments, along with the reflected glory from travelling Scottish football fans.
Interest from Germany increased after it hosted Euro 2024, when the Tartan Army were voted the best supporters at the football tournament: a mixture of “friendliness, banter, and donations to local charities – they capture hearts, they’ve been fantastic ambassadors”, Miller said.
At this year’s World Cup, when Scotland played in the US, VisitScotland “painted Boston tartan” to capitalise, she said, prompting local online searches for Scottish holidays to double.
While Scotland hopes to reap the fruits of a long-term strategic approach, including more direct flights – 100,000 more seats annually from the US alone – and promoting visits in all seasons, many are still feeling the pinch from reduced spending.
On the streets of the Scottish capital, Dexter, working at Edinburgh Bus Tours, was rueful. “I’ve been here seven years and the crowd is going down. Tips have gone, big time. I used to be able to go on vacation just on my tips, now that’s not the case,” said the tour guide, who is originally from Nevada, US.
He said the tourist tax – a 5% levy introduced in July on accommodation in Edinburgh – “has hurt”, on top of the cost of living: “People have got no money.”
Leon Thompson, the executive director of the trade body UKHospitality Scotland, concurred. “People are in their cost of living crisis and that is a challenge,” he said.
Thompson added that companies were feeling the impact of business rates, national insurance contributions and VAT, and were anxiously awaiting tourist levies to be introduced by other Scottish local authorities after Edinburgh.
“Scotland will always be a popular destination, but we can’t be complacent. We can’t allow ourselves to be priced out of what is the global visitor market,” he said.
