Racing will host Buenos Aires rival Boca Juniors in its next league outing on August 23, while Banfield will visit Newell's Old Boys. ■

articles.title: Powerful quake off Indonesia kills dozens, sparks mass evacuations
articles.body:
Rescuers combed through debris for survivors on Aug. 15 after a powerful earthquake struck off Flores island in eastern Indonesia, killing at least 20 people and sending thousands fleeing.
As the full scale of the disaster unfolded, rescue official Fathur Rahman told AFP at least 20 people were confirmed dead from four different towns on the island, popular with tourists.
"From the reports we have received, 20 people have died, six are injured, and two are still buried," Fathur said by telephone from a boat on his way to Nagekeo regency, the hardest-hit area.
Two people were known to be trapped alive under rubble in the neighbouring Manggarai regency after the 7.7-magnitude jolt.
"Our focus will be on locating the victims who are buried under the rubble" said Fathur, adding the rescue effort had been complicated by landslides cutting off several roads.
Residents in Nagekeo, the area closest to the epicentre, raced for higher ground as the sea retreated earlier Saturday — a possible sign of an approaching tsunami, AFP journalists witnessed.
A tsunami warning was later lifted but people were warned not to return to damaged buildings for fear that aftershocks may bring them down.
Dozens of aftershocks have already been felt, the strongest measured at a magnitude of 6.1.
Yohanes Babo, 56, a resident of Nagekeo, said he was at a market when the earth started shaking in the early morning hours.
"The shaking was strong. Thankfully, we were already outside the house," he told AFP.
"People were panicking, running here and there. We're evacuating for the time being... and trying to get to the hills," he said, adding: "My family is safe. No one was harmed."
The epicentre of the shallow quake was located just off the north coast of the island, about 68 kilometres (42 miles) northwest of the coastal town of Ende, US and Indonesian authorities said.
Rescuers pull one dead body from the rubble of a building that partly collapsed at the port of Maumere.
Fathur said two people were evacuated alive from the debris and "one was found deceased", according to video footage released by the agency.
The full extent of the damage is still being assessed.
Lukas Lotar, a resident of Maumere about 2,500 kilometres (1,553 miles) east of Jakarta, recounted how the earth "suddenly started to shake and I panicked".
"Patients also fled the hospital, the jolt was big. I saw some walls were cracked," Lotar, a hospital customer service official told AFP.
The stricken area is comprised mostly of towns and villages with few, if any, high-rise buildings.
Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) initially warned of possible tsunami waves following the quake and urged people to get to higher ground.
Long queues of people could be seen evacuating towns on foot, by motorbike and car, some piled into the back of pickup trucks.
"We have ended (the tsunami warning) but we will keep monitoring the sea level," said BMKG earthquake and tsunami director Wijayanto, who like many Indonesians goes by one name.
Indonesia and neighbouring countries experience frequent earthquakes due to their location in the Pacific "Ring of Fire" — an arc of intense seismic activity stretching from Japan through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific basin.
Flores was struck by a 7.7-magnitude earthquake in 1992, which triggered a tsunami and resulted in around 2,500 deaths.
Among Indonesia's history of deadly quakes is a devastating 9.1-magnitude tremor in 2004 that struck off the coast of Sumatra and triggered a tsunami that killed 220,000 throughout the region, about 170,000 of them in Indonesia.
The Boxing Day tragedy was one of the deadliest natural disasters in recorded history.
In 2018, a powerful quake shook the island of Lombok and several more tremors followed over the next couple of weeks, killing more than 550 people on the holiday island and neighbouring Sumbawa.
Later that year, a 7.5-magnitude quake and a subsequent tsunami in Palu on Sulawesi island left more than 4,300 people dead or missing.

articles.title: The women India’s biggest river project forgot
articles.body:
Madhya Pradesh, India - To reach the women of Kupi village, you must first want to find them.
From Chhatarpur railway station in Madhya Pradesh, it is 74km (46 miles) of broken road through hilly terrain. The road narrows as you enter Panna Tiger Reserve, one of central India's most ecologically rich corridors, home to tigers, gharials, and vultures painstakingly brought back from the edge of local extinction.
It is a humid July morning. The monsoon has settled over the reserve, turning the laterite roads to mud and the air thick with the smell of damp earth and forest.
Beneath an unnamed bridge over the Barna River, in the buffer zone of this reserve, the women have gathered.
About 30 women in bright cotton sarees make their way towards the unlit pyres, their husbands and fathers standing a little way behind in white cotton kurtas. There is no ceremony to it. No silence. Some women talk quietly to each other as they settle among the stacked logs, one by one. A few pull their sarees across their faces. Others stare straight ahead, expressions fixed, revealing nothing.
This is the Chita Andolan, or funeral pyre protest. The pyres are not meant to be lit. For the women, they symbolise what displacement without compensation would leave them with: No home, no land and nowhere to go.
Fifty-year-old Gyan Rani Gond moves slowly. Her face carries something between frustration and anger as she lowers herself onto the pyre. She does not look away. She does not speak.
In the background, Amit Bhatnagar, 43, leader of the protest, and other villagers fill the air with slogans. "Inquilab Zindabad" (long live the revolution). "Nyay do ya maar do" (give us justice or kill us). The words rise above the rain.
Their villages lie in the path of the Daudhan Dam, the centrepiece of India's first river-linking project, which will eventually submerge 10 settlements in and around Panna Tiger Reserve. Some 7,000 families face displacement.
Gyan Rani belongs to the Gond tribe, one of central India's oldest Indigenous communities, recognised as a Scheduled Tribe in Madhya Pradesh. Like many families here, hers depends on the forest for its livelihood.
Her face is weathered from years working the fields and collecting forest produce. To get here from her village, she hitchhiked and walked to the nearest bus stop before travelling more than 70km (40 miles) to Kupi, borrowing 200 Indian rupees ($2) for the journey, to lie on an unlit funeral pyre.
She has come because no one is listening, she says. In her eyes, there is sadness, but no tears.
Gyan Rani's family owns 1.2 hectares (three acres) of agricultural land in Pathapur. Her husband, Gayadeen, and elder son, Hardas, have each received 12.5 Indian lakh (about $13,000) in rehabilitation payments, but the family says it has received no separate compensation for its agricultural land.
The adult women received nothing. Not Gyan Rani. Not her 18-year-old daughter, Muliya. Not her elder son's wife. And not Pooja, the 21-year-old widow of Gyan Rani's younger son, who died before receiving compensation himself.
Gayadeen says the money is being treated as a family resource rather than his alone. But he also believes the adult women in his household should have received compensation in their own names. The current payment, he says, is not enough to rebuild the family's life after displacement.
One of the family's two houses has already been demolished. Where it once stood, rubble remains: Broken terracotta roof tiles scattered across the wet ground and brick walls collapsed into a soggy heap, dark with rain. The second house is under threat. Pooja lives there, in a mud hut near a cowshed in Pathapur, waiting.
“Me, my daughter, and my daughter-in-law Pooja should be compensated,” Gyan Rani shares, her voice steady. “They have broken our house. Two houses. One is already broken. One is about to be broken.”
Adjusting her brown-coloured saree to cover her head, she says:
“If the government cannot give us compensation, then they should send us to another country. Because we have voted. We are citizens of this country. We voted for this government. Where is our right?”
On paper, India's land acquisition law appears to protect women such as Gyan Rani and Pooja. In practice, they say, it is doing the opposite.
The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act (LARR), 2013, passed by Parliament to protect displaced communities, contains an explicit provision: The explanation of Section 3(m) states that every adult, regardless of gender, shall be treated as a separate family for compensation purposes.
In simple terms, Pooja, Muliya and Gyan Rani should each be entitled to independent compensation.
None of them has received a single rupee.
In practice, officials apply only the main text of Section 3(m), which defines family conventionally around a person, their spouse and dependent minor children, while failing to apply the explanation that recognises adults of either gender as separate families. Women without land titles or whose names do not appear on government lists can therefore find themselves excluded from compensation.
Ken-Betwa is the first of 30 planned river interlinking projects under India's National Perspective Plan. Campaigners fear that if the same interpretation of the law is applied elsewhere, women displaced by future projects could face the same exclusions.
As of April 2025, according to a Right to Information request filed by the Press Trust of India, India's national news agency, not a single affected family had been fully rehabilitated.
The government says that has since changed. In July 2026, Madhya Pradesh Revenue Minister Karan Singh Verma told the state Legislative Assembly that all eligible families in Panna and Chhatarpur districts had received compensation and rehabilitation benefits.
But the protests prompted the prime minister's office to seek a report from the state government, including over allegations that in some cases compensation had been deposited into the accounts of agents rather than affected families.
Following Bhatnagar's 18-day hunger strike, the Chhatarpur district administration on July 20 ordered a new verification of affected families, acknowledging that eligible households may have been left out.
On August 6, Union Minister of State for Tribal Affairs Durgadas Uikey told Parliament that his ministry had received no complaint explicitly stating that compensation already disbursed had failed to reach beneficiaries.
Construction of the dam, meanwhile, has continued.
Families whose homes have already been demolished have largely been left to fend for themselves. Using compensation, where it has been paid, they are trying to buy land and build new homes independently. None has yet been formally resettled by the state, and many say the compensation they received was insufficient to rebuild their lives.
From the protest site at Kupi, the road runs another 70km (43 miles) into the forest, towards the villages whose disappearance the women have gathered to resist.
The track is unmarked and largely unmaintained. The monsoon has washed out stretches of laterite, leaving behind mud and loose stone. Rain-washed forest lines both sides of the road.
Kupi will be the last village to disappear. When the Daudhan Dam is fully operational, it will be the final settlement swallowed by the rising waters.
Pathapur sits at the end of that road, quieter still. Several houses stand half demolished. Others are intact but marked, their walls bearing the invisible stamp of government orders. The Barna River runs nearby, its waters feeding into the Ken, the river that the Daudhan Dam will one day hold back.
In the village, Gyan Rani’s daughter-in-law Pooja Gond meets a visitor at the door of her home and offers a cup of sweet black tea.
Pooja is 21 years old, slight and soft-spoken, with a swelling on the right side of her face from a bee sting the night before. She speaks in a quiet, flat voice, the kind that comes not from shyness alone but from a deeper exhaustion, the exhaustion of someone who has already lost too much to spend energy on expression.
She was one year into her marriage when her husband Parshuram died. He was a daily wage labourer. He developed severe abdominal swelling. The family sought treatment from a local doctor, but Parshuram's condition worsened. No formal diagnosis or post-mortem was ever carried out. Their one-year-old son later died after what the family believes was typhoid fever, although there was no formal medical confirmation.
Pooja has not received a single rupee in compensation. Neither has her sister-in-law, who has voted but whom officials describe as underage. Pooja herself does not receive a widow's pension. Officials tell her she is too young for that too.
The compensation built two small rooms. That is all the family has to show for the home they are losing.
When Pooja approached officials after Parshuram's death, she was told her name was not on the compensation list. If she wanted it added, the Gram Panchayat secretary told her, she would need to pay 100,000 Indian rupees [$1,050]. She did not have this money.
The secretary sits in Kishangarh, 10km (6 miles) from Pathapur. Pooja walked there. She also travelled by bus to the district headquarters in Chhatarpur, carrying her documents. She spent 800 Indian rupees ($8) of her own money on the journeys.
Each time, officials collected her papers. Each time, nothing happened.
“Bina paise ke koi baat nahi sunta,” she says quietly. Without money, nobody listens.
One of the two houses her family occupied was demolished without notice. Pooja was there as neighbours watched and the family asked officials to stop. Nobody listened.
Officials told her mother-in-law they were demolishing this house first. Nobody told the family where they were expected to go.
They moved into the house that remains.
It is a small mud house with white walls and a hay-and-terracotta-tiled roof. Faded tribal hand-painted art runs along the walls, its colours worn thin by rain and time. A wooden door opens into a small courtyard. Inside, a wood-fired mud oven sits in the kitchen.
This house is next. Pooja knows that, but she does not know where she will go.
If relocation becomes unavoidable, she says she wants to remain close to the forest. She does not want to move to a city.
“It would have been much better if they had given us land in exchange for land,” she adds. “We don’t just want money. We want land.”
Then there is also Muliya, Gyan Rani's 18-year-old daughter. She has a voter ID. She has voted. Officials told her she was too young for compensation.
She has sores inside her mouth that have not healed. Her sister-in-law Pooja speaks for her. If compensation comes, Pooja says, Muliya would use it for treatment. For an 18-year-old fighting to be recognised as an adult by the state, compensation means something immediate: The chance to see a doctor.
Every summer, she collects mahua flowers and chironji from the forest to sell. Mahua also feeds the family, is used in traditional cooking and medicine, and forms part of Gond cultural life. "The forest gives us everything," she says.
What happened to Gyan Rani, Pooja and Muliya is not an administrative oversight, says Bina Agarwal, professor of development economics and environment at the University of Manchester and author of A Field of One's Own. It reflects a contradiction in how the law defines a family.
"Article 3(m) of the LARR Act defines the family conventionally," Agarwal says. "But the explanation that follows treats every adult as a separate family. If the explanation became the main text of the law, it would unambiguously benefit women."
In practice, officials apply only the conventional definition of the family, she says, meaning wives, widows and adult daughters are routinely excluded from compensation lists.
The solution, Agarwal argues, requires no new legislation.
"Financial compensation should go into the bank accounts of all adults in the family separately," she says. "Land should also be registered jointly, with equal rights for women."
Back at the protest site, Amit Bhatnagar, 43, convener of the Jai Kisan Sangathan, a farmers’ rights organisation, sits quietly beside the Barna River as the slogans rise around him.
For nearly four years, he has organised resistance to the Ken-Betwa displacement. During that time, he says, hundreds of protesters have faced criminal cases, while electricity, water and ration supplies have been disrupted in some affected villages.
“Suppose the survey was conducted in 2018 but displacement occurs in 2026,” he shares. “During those eight years, children become adults, daughters get married, and family structures change. Despite those changes, compensation continues to rely on the old survey.”
Bhatnagar says the problems do not end when compensation is paid. He has documented cases where men spent the money on expensive motorcycles and alcohol, leaving nothing for their families. Some, he adds, were later involved in near-fatal accidents on those same bikes. Money intended to secure a family’s future, he says, was gone before replacement land had even been found.
From his experience working in the affected villages, Bhatnagar estimates that 400 to 500 women, particularly widows, have been excluded from compensation because their names never appeared on the original lists. There is no independently verified count of how many women have been excluded.
After two weeks on hunger strike demanding that officials address the issue, Bhatnagar, now even leaner than his usual frame, explains he was arrested by police on July 19 along with hundreds of protesters as officers moved in to end the demonstration. Authorities said the action was taken because of rising water levels and monsoon conditions.
Bhatnagar's arrest brought the latest protest to an end. The questions raised by the protesters, however, extend far beyond Kupi village. Ken-Betwa is not only transforming one river basin. As the first of India's 30 planned river-linking projects, it could set a precedent for how people displaced by the projects that follow are compensated.
Ken-Betwa is India's first river-linking project under the National Perspective Plan. When complete, the Daudhan Dam will submerge 10 villages inside Panna Tiger Reserve and displace thousands of people. Supporters say it will bring irrigation, drinking water and hydropower to drought-prone Bundelkhand.
Critics have challenged the environmental assessment and approval process. But for women in villages such as Pathapur, the more immediate concern is how compensation is distributed, and whether the interpretation being applied here will be repeated as India's river-linking programme expands.
Officials approached by Al Jazeera either referred questions to publicly available government material or did not respond to specific questions about compensation for women affected by the project.
Back in Pathapur, Pooja sits in the verandah of the family's remaining house and points towards the rubble where the first one stood.
If she ever receives compensation in her own name, she says, the first thing she would do is pay for Muliya's treatment.
For now, she waits. She knows the second house will fall. She just does not know where she will go after it does.

articles.title: Earthquake in Indonesia: at least 20 people dead
articles.body:
Earthquake in Indonesia: at least 20 people dead
Kyiv • UNN
At least 20 people have died as a result of a magnitude 7.7 earthquake and aftershocks in eastern Indonesia. Tsunami waves up to 1 meter were recorded; the warning was lifted after three hours.
At least 20 people have already died as a result of a magnitude 7.7 earthquake and dozens of aftershocks that struck eastern Indonesia on Saturday, the rescue agency said, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Tsunami waves less than 1 meter high were recorded in several areas of the Southeast Asian country after the morning earthquake. The tsunami warning was lifted approximately three hours after the earthquake.
Rescuers around the port city of Maumere found 20 dead people, six injured people and two people trapped under the rubble, said Fatur Rachman, head of the city's rescue agency. Maumere is the main city in Sikka Regency on Flores Island in eastern Indonesia's vast archipelago.
Teams have still been unable to reach Nagekeo, the region closest to the epicenter, and communications there have been disrupted, Fatur told Reuters. Attempts to reach Nagekeo by car were blocked by landslides, while another team was trying to get there by ferry, he said.
About 2,000 Nagekeo residents were evacuated, and damage to a number of houses, warehouses and government facilities was reported, the national disaster management agency BNPB said. Authorities also reported traffic jams on roads and power outages affecting some areas of the regency.
The governor of East Nusa Tenggara province, Emanuel Melkiades Laka Lena, said at a press conference that at least five people had died as a result of falling debris while they were sleeping.
BNPB, which put the earthquake's toll at one dead and four injured, said it was still collecting data.
Parts of a building turned to dust and rubble as people screamed and ran into the street, as seen in a Facebook video confirmed by Reuters as having been filmed at the port in Maumere.
The strong tremor was felt in East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara and parts of South Sulawesi, while residents of several areas reported tremors lasting about one minute, according to a BNPB statement.
"Most people felt shocked and ran out of their homes," the statement said.
A hospital in Ende Regency in East Nusa Tenggara province moved patients outside, footage by Kompas TV showed, while Kompas.com reported at least one landslide.
Indonesia's geophysical agency BMKG recorded the first earthquake at 4:58 a.m. (11:58 p.m. Kyiv time) at a depth of 15 km, followed by several aftershocks.
In 1992, the same area was hit by a magnitude 7.5 earthquake that caused significant destruction, the agency said.
The Australian Tsunami Warning Centre said the undersea earthquake "will pose no tsunami threat to mainland Australia, islands or territories".
Indonesia lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire—a seismically active zone where various tectonic plates meet, causing a large number of earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.

articles.title: Mounting public interest seeing teachers brush up on drone knowledge
articles.body:
Mounting public interest seeing teachers brush up on drone knowledge
Over the next five months, 20 science and mathematics teachers will visit various companies to gain practical insights and work together to create teaching materials for the future.
The "Lae end" ("Charge Yourself") education program is aimed at middle school physics and mathematics teachers, helping them bring more practical examples and real-life connections into the teaching of science and mathematics. This year, 72 teachers applied to the program, of whom 20 were selected. Participants include both new and more experienced teachers who began the program at Metrosert's drone and defense technology testing laboratory.
"We have a whole range of laboratories here for testing subsystems. What is important about all of these laboratories is that the tests can be replicated," said Rainer Kivimäe, head of Metrosert's drone unit.
Interest in drones and artificial intelligence is also growing in schools, meaning teachers increasingly need to be able to explain these topics to students.
"Starting this academic year, as far as I know, some schools will begin talking more about drones. An educational program is also being developed in Tallinn where young people will be able to play drone soccer themselves. So young people's interest in the field is gradually beginning to grow and teachers naturally need to be knowledgeable enough to discuss it in the first place," said "Lae end" program manager Valentina Moskaljova.
For teachers, this means getting up to speed on subjects they have not encountered before.
"I knew as much about drones as I'd read in the news, basically, and as much as has recently been said about introducing a drone curriculum in schools," said Getriin Kokk, a mathematics teacher at Lodijärve School.
The program will also produce teaching materials for students in grades seven through nine.
"Young people need to understand which formulas they can use in both mathematics and physics. Right now, we're giving teachers the opportunity to work together in groups to create materials specifically designed to support that learning," Moskaljova said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

articles.title: In South Korea, some savour last season of legal dog meat
articles.body:
In South Korea, some savour last season of legal dog meat
As the country nears a February 2027 nationwide ban on breeding, slaughter and sale of dogs for meat, some diners turn to black goat meat
For decades, the three days of summer considered the hottest of the year were among the busiest for South Korea’s dog meat restaurants, as diners sought traditional stamina-boosting foods to endure the heat.
The third “boknal”, or hot day, of 2026 on Friday carried an added sense of finality. It was the last before a nationwide ban on the breeding, slaughter and sale of dogs for meat takes full effect in February 2027.
At the Moran Market in Seongnam, once the country’s best-known hubs for dog meat, lunchtime crowds filled alleyways lined with restaurants.
Yet many businesses have shifted to black goat stew and other alternatives, while the few customers still ordering “bosintang”, or dog meat stew, were overwhelmingly elderly.
“It’s really desolate now,” said Kim Yong-book, head of the Moran Market Merchants’ Association, who has worked in the area, which is near Seoul, for more than 40 years.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Industrial Facility in Samara Region
articles.body:
Ukraine struck industrial infrastructure in Russia's Samara region on Saturday, local authorities said.
Ivan Noskov, head of the regional capital Samara, said air defences had repelled a "massive attack" but the city's industrial infrastructure sustained localized damage, without giving further details about which facility was affected.
Footage released by the Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point, which manufactures Flamingo missiles, showed two missiles being launched ahead of the attack. An analysis by the Telegram channel ASTRA suggested the struck facility could be Aviakor aircraft manufacturing plant or the Progress Rocket and Space Center. The Moscow Times has not independently confirmed this assessment.
Ukraine has previously targeted the southwestern region's Syzran oil refinery on the Volga River as part of its campaign to strike energy infrastructure and pressure Russia to end the more than four-year conflict.

articles.title: Viennese woman sues city over ‘discriminatory’ toilet fees
articles.body:
Viennese woman sues city over ‘discriminatory’ toilet fees
VIENNA - A Viennese woman is suing the city council for discrimination over access to public toilets, complaining that women must pay to use cubicles while men can use urinals for free.
“I was in a park with a friend and we both needed to use the bathroom. He could go for free, but I had to pay 50 cents. I thought to myself: How is that possible?” Melanie Gradik, 27, told AFP in the Austrian capital’s Augarten park.
“I want everyone to be able to use the bathroom on an equal footing. Either we all pay 50 cents or no one pays 50 cents,” she said.
It’s not about the money, Gradik added: “It’s a small thing, but it’s also an example of how women are treated unequally in everyday life.”
Gradik has filed a legal complaint against the municipality, arguing that exclusively charging women for access to public toilets violates the city’s anti-discrimination laws.
According to her lawyer, Petra Laback, the fact that some public facilities offer free urinals for men creates inequality between the sexes.
“Men have an additional free alternative, women do not,” she said.
If Gradik wins her case, it could set a precedent across Austria, the lawyer said. “This will certainly have an impact on other municipalities.”
‘Objective justification’
Vienna currently has 168 publicly managed toilet facilities, 139 of which are free to use.
According to the city authorities, the 29 facilities that charge a fee do so because they employ toilet attendants.
“In very busy locations with intensive use it is necessary for organisational reasons to ensure supervision in order to guarantee proper use and cleanliness,” Sandra Holzinger, a spokeswoman for the municipality, told AFP.
“In these 29 facilities, a usage fee of 50 cents must be paid for the use of cubicles by people of all genders,” she said, adding that urinals were additionally provided “in order to prevent fouling caused by urinating in public spaces”.
But for law professor Anna Gamper of the University of Innsbruck, this system raises serious questions about equality.
Under Austrian law, “a distinction between men and women may only be made if there is a special, objective justification for it”, she said.
In the case of public toilets, such a justification “does not appear to exist” since the cost of building, maintaining and cleaning cubicles and urinals is basically the same, the professor said.
Even if cubicles were slightly more expensive to maintain or consumed more water, this would not necessarily be enough to justify a price difference compared with urinals, she added.
Free for everyone
The argument that men also have to pay to use a cubicle does not hold up because they still have a free option that is not available to women, she added.
In Gamper’s view, women should not be financially disadvantaged because of their anatomy or because they need cubicles for safety reasons, for example.
Women in Austria face several extra costs compared with men in everyday life, such as having to pay for menstrual products and more expensive cosmetics, according to a spokesman for Elke Hanel-Torsch, the city of Vienna’s representative for women’s issues.
In their coalition agreement for governing the city, the Social Democrats and liberals pledged to expand public toilet provision and examine whether public toilets could be made free for everyone.
In the Augarten park, new public toilets opened in 2025 provide a possible blueprint for the future.
Designed to blend into the historic Baroque park, they are notable for their curved ceramic facades, daylight from skylights, accessibility features, drinking fountains – and free use.
The new facilities replaced older toilets and were intended to provide free, accessible toilets for everyone, regardless of gender. AFP

articles.title: 'Warmest congratulations': World leaders wish India 80th Independence Day, hail growing ties
articles.body:
'Warmest congratulations': World leaders wish India 80th Independence Day, hail growing ties
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 15, 2026, 13:46 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
India celebrates 80th Independence day
NEW DELHI: From Washington and Jerusalem to Singapore and Kathmandu, leaders and institutions across the world extended greetings to India on Saturday as the country marked its 80th Independence Day, highlighting the strength of bilateral ties and the breadth of cooperation with New Delhi.
Israel
Israel’s president Isaac Herzog congratulated President Droupadi Murmu, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the people of India.“On behalf of the State of Israel, I warmly congratulate President Droupadi Murmu, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and the wonderful people of India on your 80th Independence Day! May we continue to strengthen the beautiful friendship between Israel and India,” Herzog wrote on X. He also posted his wishes in Hindi.
The message came after Modi and his Israeli counterpart Benjamin Netanyahu reviewed progress in the India-Israel Special Strategic Partnership and discussed the situation in West Asia during a recent phone call.
United States
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the India-US relationship continues to grow and is “stronger than ever”.“On behalf of the United States of America, I extend warm congratulations to the people of India on their Independence Day.
Thanks to the personal relationship between President Trump and Prime Minister Modi, the U.S.-India relationship continues to grow and is stronger than ever,” Rubio said.He highlighted cooperation in defence, energy security, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, space cooperation and commerce.“From defence and energy security to critical minerals, artificial intelligence, space cooperation, and commerce, our collaboration is making both of our nations, and the broader Indian Ocean region, safer, stronger, and more prosperous,” Rubio said. He added: “The United States looks forward to the future our two countries will build together.”
Singapore
Singapore president Tharman Shanmugaratnam congratulated India on the “joyous occasion” and underscored the countries’ Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.“On behalf of the people of Singapore, I extend my warmest congratulations to Your Excellency and the people of India on the joyous occasion of India's 80th Independence Day,” Tharman wrote in a letter addressed to President Murmu.He also pointed to close people-to-people ties and expanding cooperation in skills development, digitalisation, sustainability and advanced manufacturing.
Nepal
Nepal prime minister Balendra ‘Balen’ Shah extended greetings and best wishes to PM Modi, the Government of India and the people of India.“On the occasion of India's 80th Independence Day, I extend my heartfelt greetings and best wishes to PM Narendra Modi and the friendly people and Government of India,” the Office of the Prime Minister of Nepal said in a post on X.
Maldives
Maldives president Mohamed Muizzu also joined the global chorus of greetings, extending his “warmest greetings” to the President and PM Modi on the country’s 80th Independence Day. Muizzu said eight decades of independence reflected India’s “aspirations, resilience and enduring spirit” and reaffirmed Male’s commitment to advancing the close partnership between the two countries, built on “mutual respect, shared prosperity and enduring friendship”.Additionally, the former president, Ibrahim Mohamed Solih also greeted India, writing, “Warm felicitations to President Murmu, PM Narendra Modi, and our dear friends, the people of India, on the occasion of India's Independence Day." He described India’s journey since 1947 as an inspiration and said, “May the close ties of cooperation and friendship that exist between Maldives-India grow ever stronger.”
Latvia’s ministry of foreign affairs conveyed its greetings, saying: “Happy Independence Day to India from Latvia! Wishing India continued progress, unity, and prosperity.”
Australia
Australia’s high commissioner to India Philip Green joined the celebrations, sharing visuals of the Australian High Commission illuminated in the colours of the Indian Tricolour.“The High Commission is glowing in saffron, white & green, with our team proudly dressing in the colours of the Indian tricolour,” Green said. “From all of us, a very Happy Independence Day to Indians across the globe,” he added.
Ireland
The Irish embassy in India also extended greetings, saying, “Happy 80th Independence Day, India! Warm wishes from the Embassy & CG Mumbai to Indians everywhere.”

The TOI News Desk is your trusted source for staying informed and connected to the ever-evolving global landscape, ensuring that our readers are equipped with the latest developments that matter most."

articles.title: Construction workers find $10 million gold stash in renovations
articles.body:
Construction workers find gold stash estimated to be worth $10 million during renovations in Belgium
Construction workers in Belgium stumbled upon a stash of gold believed to be worth more than $10 million during renovation work on a building.
Police said they were "immediately" contacted by the workers after they discovered "a large quantity of gold" while working on a building in the east Flemish town of Dendermonde. The local police department posted a picture on its Facebook page of around 50 gold bars and piles of gold coins.
Belgian news outlets reported that bars and coins worth an estimated nine million euros ($10.4 million) were found bricked into the cellar walls during the renovation of a house belonging to a local charity, CAW East-Flanders.
One worker interviewed by Belgian news outlet VRT said the crew's "first reaction was actually disbelief, amazement."
"We stumbled across it while carrying out groundwork to lay a pipe for the sewerage system," said the man identified only as Kobe. "We certainly hadn't expected to find gold."
Police said the gold was "inventoried and secured as quickly as possible in a high-security vault belonging to the federal government services."
"Apparently, several treasure hunters would like to pay another visit to the site," read a Facebook post by the police department -- which changed its profile picture to a gold coin in light of the find.
"A golden piece of advice: it is truly pointless," they said -- cautioning the curious to stay away from the fenced-off construction site.
It was not clear who was considered the legal owner of the trove -- and if anyone would get to keep it.
"Let us hope that this treasure ends up in the right hands," said the police post.

articles.title: Romania Reports Fourth Discovery of Drone Debris in 24 Hours
articles.body:
The Romanian Defense Ministry reported the discovery of drone fragments in the village of Plauru, Tulcea County, near the border with Ukraine, on Friday evening, Aug. 14.
Military specialists arrived at the site to identify the object and secure the area, according to the ministry’s press service. Further information regarding the incident is pending.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This marks the fourth such discovery in Romania within a 24-hour period.
Earlier on Friday, the Defense Ministry reported a drone crash near Luncavița, Tulcea County, approximately five kilometers from the Ukrainian border.
Drone wreckage was also located on the beach at the Saturn resort. Furthermore, on the morning of Aug. 14, a fragment of an unidentified drone was found on the beach at the Costinești resort.
Authorities indicated this fragment may be connected to a drone spotted in the water at that location the previous day.
Drones destroyed near Neptun Deep project
On Tuesday, Aug. 11, Romanian military divers conducted controlled explosions to destroy two drifting Gerbera-type drones in the Black Sea, approximately 167 kilometers east of Constanța.
The objects were located near the Neptun Deep offshore gas project. A civilian vessel operating in the area reported the objects to authorities.
Acting Defense Minister Radu Miruță stated that Ukrainian officials confirmed the systems did not belong to their armed forces.
The Gerbera is a Russian-produced platform. The drones were destroyed due to the hazard they presented to maritime traffic and energy operations in the area.
Ukrainian Flamingo Missiles Target Samara Aerospace Plants in Russia
Previous airspace violations

articles.title: US maintains 400-plus aircraft build-up around Iran
articles.body:
More than 200 US aerial refuelling aircraft and upwards of 230 combat jets have been tracked across the Middle East and the wider network supporting American air operations in the region, according to open-source analysis compiled by UK Defence Journal Senior Editor Jon, known as DefenceGeek on X, alongside the Military Air Tracking Alliance.
The assessment draws together aircraft movements, unit deployments and other publicly available information to provide a snapshot of the scale and geographical spread of US air power positioned across the US Central Command area and supporting locations in Europe and the Atlantic.
A fast-jet order of battle published on 10 August placed the deployed force at around 237 aircraft, covering F-15E Strike Eagles, F-35A and F-35C Lightning IIs, F-16 Fighting Falcons, A-10C Thunderbolt IIs, EA-18G Growlers and F/A-18C/D Hornets.
US ORBAT – Fast-Jets – 10/AUG/2026 #IranWar
So as promised, here’s the slightly more detailed US Orders of Battle for fast-jets in CENTCOM available in case of further conflict with Iran. Due to the fact my list of airframes is over 250, I am not going to list individual… pic.twitter.com/59enR8x6m1
— DefenceGeek 🇬🇧 (@DefenceGeek) August 10, 2026
The largest individual contingent listed is the F-15E force, with 64 aircraft associated with deployments from the 4th Fighter Wing, 366th Fighter Wing and the RAF Lakenheath-based 494th Fighter Squadron. The figure includes two aircraft recorded as unidentified combat losses.
A further 55 F-35As are listed, including aircraft from the Vermont Air National Guard’s 158th Fighter Wing, Hill Air Force Base and RAF Lakenheath. Fifteen F-35As from Lakenheath’s 495th Fighter Squadron were recorded as deploying in July.
The F-16C/CM force is placed at 61 aircraft, with deployments involving units associated with South Carolina, Shaw Air Force Base, Spangdahlem, Aviano and Misawa. Eleven additional aircraft were recorded at Spangdahlem but excluded from the forward total because they had not deployed into the CENTCOM area.
Thirty A-10C Thunderbolt IIs are also listed across deployments involving the 107th Fighter Squadron, 124th Fighter Wing and units from Moody Air Force Base. The figure includes one aircraft recorded as an unidentified loss.
Naval and Marine Corps aircraft add another layer to the force. Twelve F/A-18C/D Hornets from VMFA-312 and ten F-35Cs from VMFA-311 are included, alongside six EA-18G Growlers from VAQ-135.
Another six EA-18Gs from VAQ-138 had previously been tracked at Lajes in the Azores and were initially excluded from the forward total. US imagery dated 3 August subsequently showed a VAQ-138 Growler operating in the CENTCOM area carrying an AN/ALQ-249(V)1 Next Generation Jammer Mid-Band pod, indicating continued movement through the wider deployment network.
The scale of that network becomes clearer when the tanker force is considered. A separate assessment dated 13 August records 209 US aerial refuelling aircraft across locations stretching from the United Kingdom and continental Europe to the Gulf and Indian Ocean. The total consists of 33 KC-46A Pegasus aircraft, 152 KC-135Rs, 23 KC-135Ts and a single KC-135RT.
Of the 209 tankers, 107 were placed in the assessment’s red zone closest to the principal area of operations. Another 48 were in the orange zone and 37 in the green zone farther west. Sixteen were recorded as having returned to the United States during the previous two weeks, with one aircraft listed as being at another or unidentified location.
The accompanying map shows tanker locations across a broad chain of bases. RAF Mildenhall is marked in the United Kingdom, with Lajes in the Azores, Avord and Istres in France, Stuttgart in Germany, Bucharest and Mihail Kogălniceanu in Romania, Bezmer in Bulgaria, Sigonella in Sicily and Souda Bay in Crete also forming part of the tracked network.
Farther east, tankers are shown at locations including Ben Gurion, Ovda and Ramon in Israel, Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar and Al Dhafra Air Base in the United Arab Emirates.
Al Udeid and Al Dhafra had both returned to use by the tracked tanker force by 13 August after previously dropping out of the observed deployment pattern. Diego Garcia is also marked on the map as part of the wider support architecture. The British Indian Ocean Territory facility has long been used by the United States to support military operations across the Middle East and Indo-Pacific.
Aerial refuelling is central to sustaining combat air operations over the distances involved. Tankers allow fighters, electronic warfare aircraft, surveillance platforms and other assets to remain airborne for longer, while also supporting the movement of aircraft from bases in the United States and Europe to forward locations.
The numbers are based on open-source tracking rather than an official US military order of battle, and individual aircraft can move between locations without appearing on publicly accessible tracking systems. They therefore represent a snapshot of observable deployments rather than a definitive real-time inventory. The data shows a US combat-air presence numbering well above 200 fast jets backed by a tanker network of more than 200 aircraft distributed from Britain and the Atlantic through Europe and into the Middle East.

articles.title: Human currency: How migrants became pawns in a global standoff
articles.body:
How Europe betrayed Madrid to punish Sanchez
When European officials talk about migration, their lexicon is rich with high-minded platitudes – “humanitarian values,” “human rights,” “rules-based order,” and “shared responsibility.” Yet behind this rhetoric lies a transactional reality: The European Union’s single overarching policy on migration and asylum is keeping people out, regardless of the human cost and despite all the EU common values.
For decades, Brussels has refused to address the root causes of global displacement. To do so would require confronting a persistent colonial mindset – one that views the Global South, and Africa in particular, as a warehouse of raw resources to be extracted, while abandoning its populations to economic destruction and conflict.
As the late Muammar Gaddafi once bluntly observed, the Africans heading toward Europe are simply chasing the wealth that was stolen from them, leaving their own countries impoverished – a simple logic that is hard to argue with. Instead of fostering genuine development or equitable partnerships, Europe’s approach relies on outsourcing its border enforcement to North African buffer states, effectively turning neighboring regimes into outsourced jailers for Fortress Europe.
The July 30-31 border shock in Ceuta exposed the total bankruptcy and fragility of this setup. When tens of thousands of young Moroccans and migrants surged toward the Spanish enclave, Europe was confronted not just with human desperation, but with the logical consequence of its own security dependency. Yet the anomaly of the aftermath only deepened suspicion over what was actually taking place: The next day, the vast majority of those who crossed had returned to Morocco. Under normal conditions, individuals who risk life and limb to reach EU territory do not simply turn back; that thousands did so as quickly as they arrived suggests the wave was less a genuine migration movement than a staged demonstration of force.
Rabat understands precisely how vulnerable Brussels is; whenever diplomatic frictions arise, border controls suddenly soften, demonstrating that North Africa holds the ultimate asymmetric leverage over European security. In the end, we should not lose sight of the fact that both Ceuta and Melilla are historically Moroccan territories occupied by Spain – an unresolved colonial footprint that Rabat can exploit whenever it seeks to pressure Madrid.
However, the Ceuta shock loses its “spontaneous” appearance when viewed alongside shifting diplomatic signals from Washington. Despite the Trump administration’s signature anti-immigration rhetoric, official Washington quietly signaled an unprecedented openness to Rabat’s territorial ambitions weeks before the surge.
In a report accompanying the Fiscal Year 2027 State Department appropriations bill, the House Appropriations Committee explicitly noted that Ceuta and Melilla are “administered by Spain, located on Moroccan territory, and remain subject to Morocco’s longstanding claim.” By reducing centuries of Spanish sovereignty to mere administrative control while encouraging diplomatic talks over the cities’ future, the committee’s language sent Rabat a potentially consequential signal: Challenging Spain over the enclaves might carry less political cost in Washington than previously assumed.
This signal was further compounded by Washington’s growing frustration with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez over his refusal to allow US military bases to be used for operations against Iran, his vocal opposition to Israeli policy in Gaza, and Madrid’s lagging defense spending.
The crisis exposed the hypocrisy of the EU foreign policy establishment and laid bare ideological fractures across Europe. When similar migration spikes occur along Europe’s eastern borders, Brussels officials such as Kaja Kallas immediately decry them as “hybrid warfare” and an existential threat to democracy. Yet when a key Western partner in North Africa utilizes the exact same border pressure mechanisms against a dissenting member state like Spain, the EU’s reaction is a fractured double standard. Madrid’s isolation was engineered not only from Washington and Rabat, but from within Europe itself, led by conservative governments hostile to Sánchez’s unyielding pro-Palestinian stance and defiance of the mainstream Atlanticist consensus.
Capitalizing on the chaos, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government swiftly suspended the Schengen free-movement agreement with Spain, reinstating border checks to punish Madrid politically. Countries as far away as Denmark even called for Spain to be suspended or expelled from Schengen – a reactionary escalation never directed at Germany when it welcomed over a million asylum seekers in 2015. Rather than standing in solidarity with a member state, Europe weaponized the shock, demonstrating that Rabat succeeded in triggering a secondary systemic crisis inside Fortress Europe itself.
Following the outbreak of the post-October 2023 war, Spain emerged as Europe’s most aggressive critic of Israeli military actions. Sanchez moved beyond standard diplomatic pushback by formally recognizing a Palestinian state and repeatedly accusing Israel of committing genocide in Gaza and explicitly labeling Israel a genocidal state. By invoking the term “genocide” multiple times on the international stage, joining South Africa’s case at the International Court of Justice, and cutting off arms transfers, Sanchez isolated Spain from mainstream Western backing. This made Madrid uniquely vulnerable to a tripartite geopolitical retaliation: Tel Aviv provided intelligence backing, Washington offered diplomatic cover and greenlit Morocco’s sovereignty over the enclave, and Rabat unleashed asymmetric migration pressure on Ceuta to bring down an unruly European regime.
The possibility of high-level geopolitical manipulation behind the Ceuta surge was not entirely dismissible. As many observers point out, the sudden border breach served a dual purpose: providing European far-right “vultures” with an immediate anti-immigrant weapon while simultaneously delivering geopolitical punishment to Sanchez’s government for its principled foreign policy. The reaction of Israeli officials – such as UN Ambassador Danny Danon cynically mocking Spain’s state of emergency and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir demanding Madrid “open its doors” to Gazans – exposed an unmistakable appetite for retaliation against Spain’s recognition of Palestinian statehood and accusations of genocide.
Whether through explicit collusion or strategic alignment, the convergence of Moroccan territorial ambitions, American pressure over military bases and trade, and Israeli anger created an asymmetric pincer movement. In this framework, Morocco acted as the operational hammer on the ground, while Washington and Tel Aviv provided the diplomatic cover, turning human desperation in Ceuta into a deliberate, multi-national strike aimed at crippling an unyielding European administration.
This geopolitical pincer movement exposes the fundamental structural flaw at the heart of Europe’s externalized border regime. By converting displaced people into diplomatic currency and neighboring states into indispensable jailers, Fortress Europe has not secured its frontiers; it has rendered them volatile flashpoints for foreign leverage.
On the ground in Ceuta, the immediate casualties of this strategic maneuvering remain the thousands of young Moroccans and migrants trapped between heavy-handed Spanish security forces and a regime in Rabat that views its own youth as disposable bargaining chips. Far from achieving the stability Brussels constantly preaches, this transactional framework leaves European policy vulnerable to external blackmail.
As long as Europe relies on externalized repression rather than addressing the structural roots of global inequality, its southern perimeter will remain an open fault line – ready to be activated whenever its autocratic partners decide to demand a higher price.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Startup led by young Ukrainian engineer demos interceptor for U.S. Air Force
articles.body:
- Thermopylae Aerospace, founded by Ukrainian engineer Yehor Balytskyi, demoed its SPART interceptor at Edwards Air Force Base in July.
- Balytskyi briefed Air Force Test Center commander Brig. Gen. Mark Massaro on the drone during the "Game of Drones 26-2" event.
Thermopylae Aerospace, a California-based interceptor drone startup launched in June 2025 by a young Ukrainian engineer, said it completed a successful end-to-end demonstration of its SPART interceptor at Edwards Air Force Base, briefing senior Air Force Test Center leadership on the system during the “Game of Drones 26-2” event in mid-July.
“At 412th Test Wing, Edwards Air Force Base, during Game of Drones 26-2, our lean team completed a successful end-to-end demonstration of SPART, a novel interceptor platform designed to counter big drones asymmetrically,” said Yehor Balytskyi, founder and chief executive officer of Thermopylae Aerospace.
Balytskyi is a self-taught engineer who left Ukraine at 17 following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. He founded Thermopylae in June 2025, and the company raised $1.6 million in pre-seed funding that November from investors including Naval Ravikant and Ukraine-focused venture firm UA1, growing from a two-person team to roughly five employees.
SPART is a pneumatically launched, foldable quadcopter interceptor built to counter larger drones, including Group 2-class threats such as Shahed-type attack drones, according to the company. It uses thermal guidance, reaches speeds up to 350 km/h (217 mph) and has a target flight time of up to 20 minutes, with a partial-reuse feature that allows recovery if the interceptor misses its target. Balytskyi said the system can be integrated onto UAVs, ground vehicles, maritime vessels and manned vehicles as host platforms, and is designed to be produced in high volumes at low cost.
“We built it from the ground up in a very short period of time,” Balytskyi said. “Proud of the team for getting us here.”
Balytskyi told the trade publication Janes in July that most Western drone interceptors rely on rocket motors and expensive components, making them costly to fire against cheap drones, and that manually piloted interceptor systems used in Ukraine depend heavily on individual operator skill rather than a scalable, integrated system. Thermopylae is building SPART as a lower-cost alternative meant to be produced and deployed at higher volumes than existing interceptor systems, according to Balytskyi.
Game of Drones is a recurring test event hosted by the 412th Test Wing’s Experimental Test Force at Edwards Air Force Base, in partnership with the Defense Contract Management Agency. The inaugural event ran Dec. 8-12, 2025, on the base’s Rogers Dry Lake, bringing together industry partners and Air Force Research Laboratory engineers for live testing of small unmanned aircraft systems and counter-drone hardware. The event supports the Department of War’s Drone Dominance initiative, which calls for accelerating the testing, acquisition and production of unmanned systems, and results can factor into placement on the department’s sUAS Blue List, a mechanism for rapidly vetting small drone systems for military use.
Balytskyi told DroneLife in July that Thermopylae was working within an Air Force evaluation window expected to last three to four months, after which the company hopes the Pentagon will approve a contract to procure SPART.

articles.title: Netanyahu hits London with ‘Islamic Britain’ jibe
articles.body:
Netanyahu hits London with ‘Islamic Britain’ jibe
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has described the UK as the “Islamic Republic of Britain,” as the country’s new Labour government weighs taking measures against Israel.
Speaking on an Israeli Army Radio podcast on Friday, Netanyahu criticized the British media’s coverage of Israel, while comparing it to reporting during the 1967 Six-Day War.
“Go find that in Britain today, which you could call the Islamic Republic of Britain,” he said, as cited by Israeli media.
Netanyahu then echoed a 2024 joke made by US Vice President J.D. Vance, saying Britain could become the first “Islamic republic with nuclear weapons.”
According to the latest census-based figures, Muslims account for around 6% of the UK’s population, while Pakistan, officially the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, has possessed nuclear weapons since the 1990s.
The British Foreign Office called the comments “completely unacceptable,” noting that the issue had been raised with the Israeli government.
Relations between London and Israel have deteriorated since the UK formally recognized the State of Palestine in September of 2025, a move rejected by Netanyahu’s government.
The exchange comes weeks after Andy Burnham became prime minister. Before taking office, Burnham said Labour “didn’t get it right” on Gaza, asserting that Britain needed to put greater pressure on the Israeli government, including through the use of sanctions and measures targeting trade with Israeli settlements.
Nonetheless, Britain has maintained military-export ties with Israel. While London did suspend some arms licenses in 2024 due to concerns that the equipment could be used to commit serious violations of international humanitarian law, it exempted components supplied through the multinational F-35 program.
Britain also provided military support during this year’s conflict with Iran. London deployed aircraft to intercept Iranian attacks and authorized US forces to use British bases for operations against Iranian missile launchers and related sites. British security cooperation with Israel has included surveillance flights over Gaza and intelligence sharing.
The remarks follow reports that there is growing frustration with Netanyahu in the US. Axios reported on Friday that President Donald Trump has declined to endorse Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s October election so far, despite being repeatedly asked about it. Earlier this month, the Israeli PM rejected a 15-point Gaza plan backed by Trump, while insisting that Israeli forces would not withdraw until Hamas was fully disarmed.

articles.title: Stolen Matisse works tied to infamous art thief in Brazil
articles.body:
Stolen Matisse works tied to infamous art thief in Brazil
- Eight stolen Henri Matisse engravings, valued at around US$200,000 (S$256,000), were recovered from a home in Sao Bernardo do Campo after being stolen from a Sao Paulo library exhibition in December 2025.
- Laessio Rodrigues, a notorious Brazilian art thief with a criminal history and former library science scholar, was identified as the mastermind and arrested; investigations used phone logs and surveillance footage.
- The stolen works were returned to the Mario de Andrade library and are being analysed for damage; five other stolen Brazilian artworks remain missing.
AI generated
SAO PAULO – Phone logs of a notorious art and rare-book thief in Brazil proved to be the key for police to recover eight stolen engravings by famed French painter Henri Matisse, after they were pilfered from a library exhibition in Sao Paulo in December 2025.
The pieces from Matisse’s limited-edition 1947 art book Jazz, valued at around US$200,000 (S$256,000), were found at a home in the town of Sao Bernardo do Campo.
Brazilian authorities accused 53-year-old Laessio Rodrigues of masterminding the theft. A former library science scholar, Rodrigues has a criminal history with similar cases.
The works were stolen on Dec 7, 2025, from the Mario de Andrade library in Sao Paulo, where they were part of a rare-book exhibition.
Police say the thieves overpowered a security guard and an elderly couple, grabbed the engravings and other items from a glass dome where they were kept, and fled.
Big reputation
“Laessio has already been convicted in other cases, he keeps going in and out of jail for stealing books and works of art,” Ronald Quene, the Civil Police commissioner in charge of the investigation, told AFP.
Rodrigues was arrested in April and is awaiting trial for multiple crimes, including the Matisse theft.
His notoriety is in part due to a 2017 Brazilian documentary about him, Cartas Para Um Ladrao De Livros (Letters To A Book Thief).
“He’s a narcissist who tells everyone that he’s the biggest art and rare-books thief in Brazil,” Quene added.
Shortly after the theft, police identified the two suspects with the use of surveillance cameras.
One was arrested and the second fled. Further investigation of their communications revealed contacts with Rodrigues.
“We found several audio recordings of Laessio coordinating the thefts with his accomplices,” Quene said.
“There are conversations about everything: dividing the money, how much each person would get.”
The investigation led to the arrests of Rodrigues’s husband and a woman.
Eventually, a forensic analysis of Rodrigues’s phone cracked the case of where the stolen artwork could be found.
Police searched a residence in Sao Bernardo do Campo, near Sao Paulo, and found the eight pieces in a closet.
Officers arrested a man who lived there, who told police he did not know the provenance of the pieces and that Rodrigues had asked him to keep them there.
In addition to the Matisse works, five illustrations by Brazilian artist Candido Portinari were also stolen and have yet to be recovered.
Artwork returned
Quene said Rodrigues “studied library science so he could tell whether a book is valuable or not”, and that he had earlier worked at the library where the theft occurred.
Rodrigues allegedly told his accomplices while preparing for heist that he could not go in person because he was too well known.
AFP was unable to immediately reach a legal representative for Rodrigues.
The stolen engravings have already been returned to the library, according to Jose Silva Parente, Sao Paulo’s municipal secretary for culture.
Although they appear undamaged, the works are undergoing an analysis to ensure they are intact, he told AFP.
It was not the first time an art thief has got their hands on them – police said the works spent several years lost in Argentina before eventually being recovered. AFP

Drone strikes were recorded at 16 locations, while falling debris from downed targets was reported at another location.

In Donetsk Oblast, Russian forces injured one person in Sloviansk and shelled settlements across the region 37 times, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two people were injured in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia district, while Russian forces carried out 971 strikes against 42 settlements over the past day, Governor Ivan Fedorov said.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, three people were injured in Russian attacks, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russian forces used missiles, guided aerial bombs, Lancet and Molniya drones, FPV drones, and other unmanned systems against the region.

articles.title: Faced with historic drought, the Dutch rethink water management
articles.body:
Faced with historic drought, the Dutch rethink water management
Nijmegen, Netherlands - On the banks of the Waal, the Dutch branch of the Rhine, swimmers are sunning themselves on a Nijmegen beach that did not exist before the river level dropped a few months ago.
Like many European countries, the Netherlands has been hit by a historic summer drought caused by a prolonged dry spell, exceptional heat and intense evaporation.
The Dutch – with their dikes, dams and vast waterworks – have long been admired for their tenacity in the face of flood risks.
Now their country, which is lower than sea level, finds itself, in an era of global warming, facing a dilemma: How to retain water while protecting themselves from it?
“I’ve been coming to this river for, what... 25, 35 years?“ said entrepreneur Leon Berkers. “And this is the lowest, the craziest level it’s ever reached.”
Berkers is the captain of a restaurant boat that is now listing heavily after becoming stuck in the riverbank.
“We can’t even fill the coffee cups to the brim or they spill,” his son Linus, 19, added with an air of amused exasperation.
The drought is particularly visible in the southern and eastern provinces, where the grass has turned the colour of straw and the Rhine this summer reached the lowest level ever recorded there.
Maritime transport affected
The shortage of fresh water and a process of salinisation, as seawater pushes inland through the river network, have affected the entire country. And sometimes the effects are devastating.
“It feels like we’re in the south of France” said Marthe Wens, a researcher specialising in water and climate risks at the Institute for Environmental Studies at the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam.
“First of all, there’s nature, of course – there are the trees, the grass,” she said, noting, “the trees already look like autumn”.
Another crisis is unfolding underground, threatening the very foundations of buildings.
“Foundations are sometimes built on peat bogs: if these dry out, they shrink, and cracks can appear in buildings,” she said.
Since mid‑July, Rijkswaterstaat, the national water management agency, has classified the situation as an “actual water shortage”.
The agency has imposed restrictions on irrigation, while limiting how much certain locks can open to reduce the loss of fresh water and to prevent too much salt water from entering the network.
Shipping, both the inland sector, and by extension maritime transport, has been heavily affected.
“Not only are the carriers suffering, but also the industries that depend on the goods they transport,” Wens said.
Need for adaptation
With extreme weather events becoming increasingly frequent as a result of climate change, the Netherlands will have to rethink a strategy that has until now been “waterproof.”
“We have always designed our systems to protect us from flooding and to drain excess water into the sea,” said Micha Werner, a professor specialising in drought resilience at IHE Delft, the world’s largest institute for water education.
“But as we can see today with climate change, we are increasingly often faced with years of water shortage,” he said.
“We therefore truly have to change the way we manage water resources. Instead of trying to get rid of water, we actually need to start trying to retain it within our hydraulic systems, and that really requires adaptation,” Werner said.
For Leon Berkers, whose restaurant boat has been stuck in the mud for more than a month, adaptation has so far meant improvising fixes to keep “pots and pans from flying around.”
Putting out his cigarette before starting the evening service, he sighed: “I think we’ll be without water for at least another two months.” AFP

articles.title: With nearly 40 mentions, ‘Mere pyare deshwasiyon’ dominates PM Modi’s Red Fort speech
articles.body:
With nearly 40 mentions, ‘Mere pyare deshwasiyon’ dominates PM Modi’s Red Fort speech
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 15, 2026, 14:01 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium

With 10 mentions, 'Saathiyon' was the second-most use dphrase
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday addressed the nation from the ramparts of the iconic Red Fort in Delhi as the country celebrated its 80th Independence Day.His 75-minute speech featured nearly 40 mentions of “Mere pyare deshwasiyon” (my beloved fellow citizens), making it the most-used phrase in his address.“Saathiyon” (friends) was the second-most used phrase, featuring 10 times in the speech.
He also used “mere pyare yuva” (my beloved youth) once while calling on young people to join the fight against drugs and other addictions.The prime minister also used “desh sevak” (those who serve the nation) and “bhai beheno” (brothers and sisters) once each.Over the years, “deshwashiyon” (fellow citizens) has remained PM Modi’s go-to term for addressing the nation during his Independence Day speeches. He used the term 50 times last year, around 30 times in 2024, nearly 15 times in 2023 and more than 40 times in 2022. In 2023, however, his preferred form of address was “parivaarjan” (family member), which he used around 50 times.“Saathiyon” has also featured regularly in his Independence Day speeches. Modi used the term around 35 times in 2025, nearly 30 times in 2024, about five times in 2023 and approximately eight times in 2022.
Meanwhile, the prime minister’s 2026 Independence Day speech was the fourth-shortest among his 13 consecutive August 15 addresses since his first in 2014. Saturday’s address was also his shortest in four years.His 2025 speech was his longest at 103 minutes, surpassing his previous record of 98 minutes in 2024. His shortest Independence Day address came in 2017, when he spoke for 56 minutes.PM Modi’s first Independence Day address in 2014 lasted 65 minutes. Since then, his speeches have ranged from under an hour to more than 100 minutes. He spoke for 88 minutes in 2015, 96 minutes in 2016, 83 minutes in 2018 and nearly 92 minutes in 2019.His address lasted 90 minutes in 2020, 88 minutes in 2021, 74 minutes in 2022 and 90 minutes in 2023.(With PTI inputs)

articles.title: Taiwan college entrant population shrinks by 1.1% per year
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of Education estimates that the number of first-year students at university will decline by an average of 11,000 per year over the next 16 years, reports said Saturday.
At the end of the period, in the 2041 academic year, there will be 151,000 college entrants out of a total school population of 667,000, per UDN. The number of first-year university students will shrink by 1.5% each year, the ministry said.
Education activists forecast the student population decline will also cause a reduction in the number of private colleges. By 2030, only 30 to 40 private colleges will survive, the report said.
The number of college entrants started declining in 2015, from 270,000 to 195,000 in 2023, according to the Ministry of Education. The academic years of 2024 and 2025 saw a slight rebound to 200,000.
However, the ministry forecasts the number will fall again to 186,000 in 2028.
The impact of new population policies could help the first-year college population increase to 221,000 in 2030, but the following years will see the number of university entrants fluctuate between 150,000 and 220,000. In 2041, 151,000 people will start university studies, a drop of 54,000 or 26.3% compared to 2025, the ministry said.
The overall student population at all universities in Taiwan totaled 1.1 million in 2016, but in 2025, the number fell below 850,000 for the first time. The ministry forecast 806,000 students in 2029 and 876,000 in 2033 before a gradual decline during the rest of the decade up to 2040.

articles.title: Budanov Says Moscow “Will Pay” as Ukraine Calculates Full Cost of Russian War
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Budanov Says Moscow “Will Pay” as Ukraine Calculates Full Cost of Russian War
The Register of Damage for Ukraine (RD4U) has opened two new categories of claims, allowing the state to bill Russia for humanitarian spending and the cost of demining territory contaminated by the invasion.
Kyrylo Budanov, the head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, announced the measure on August 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new categories allow Ukrainian authorities and public institutions to document budget expenditures caused by Russia’s full-scale invasion.
B4 includes spending on evacuations, temporary accommodation, emergency medical care, rehabilitation, and compensation for damaged or destroyed housing, including payments under the eRecovery program. B5 covers expenses related to demining, explosive ordnance clearance, specialist training, and mine-risk education.
The register serves as an international mechanism for documenting the damage caused by the invasion, allowing Kyiv to assemble a case for eventual compensation. Budanov described the additions as part of a steady effort to compile a full bill for the aggressor state, itemizing every category of expenditure.
“Russia must pay for every crime it has committed and compensate every hryvnia spent on overcoming the consequences of its aggression,” Budanov wrote. “The enemy created these losses—the enemy will pay for them.”
The inclusion of demining costs reflects the scale of that task. Almost 23% of Ukraine's territory remains contaminated by mines and unexploded ordnance, and full clearance is expected to take at least ten years.
Roughly 128,000 square kilometers are considered potentially hazardous, and clearing a single hectare of farmland can cost at least $1,400.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: NT$8.3 billion budget passed to support Taiwan’s drone development
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Legislative Yuan passed an NT$8.3 billion (US$259 million) drone budget for 2026 on Friday, according to a Ministry of Economic Affairs press release.
The economics ministry welcomed the announcement, part of the 2026 central government general budget, saying it provided domestic firms peace of mind to continue research and development. The ministry noted that it is part of the Cabinet-approved six-year, NT$44.2 billion (US$1.34 billion) unmanned carrier development plan.
The ministry has invested in drone firms such as Aerospace Industrial Development Co., Thunder Tiger, Avix, and Calin for whole carriers and key components. Meanwhile, the Civil Aeronautics Administration will add a drone test site at Taichung's Guanghua Industrial High School. It said it will also continue to expand Chiayi's Asia UAV AI Innovation Application R&D Center, which provides space for offices and flight tests.
Taiwan External Trade Development Council Chair C. F. Huang (黃志芳) said budget approval is the long-awaited stimulus the industry needed, per the Commercial Times. He added the council will mobilize its 60-plus locations worldwide to help domestic manufacturers secure partnerships abroad.
The ministry aims to hit its 2030 NT$40 billion output goal for drones and position Taiwan as the Asia-Pacific center for non-China drone production.

articles.title: US Backs Japan Sovereignty Over Disputed Islands After Provocative Putin Visit
articles.body:
- Category
- World
US Backs Japan Sovereignty Over Disputed Islands After Provocative Putin Visit
The United States has expressed full support for Japan regarding the ownership of the Kuril Islands after Russian leader Vladimir Putin made his first visit to the area in his 26-year rule, as reported by The Moscow Times on August 14.
The trip to the four islands—Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan, and the Habomai ridge—prompted an official protest from Tokyo. The islands are administered by Russia as part of the Sakhalin region, but Japan maintains a claim over them under the name Northern Territories.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
US Ambassador to Japan George Glass announced Washington's official position on Friday via social media. Glass stated, “The United States remains steadfast in its support of its key ally and in its recognition of Japan’s sovereignty over the Northern Territories.
At a time when the US-Japan alliance seeks prosperity in the Indo-Pacific region, we strongly oppose any actions that undermine peace and stability in the region.”
In response to the visit, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi stated that Iturup and the other contested islands “are the ancestral territory of Japan, taking into account historical facts and international law.”
The Japanese Prime Minister added that the Russian president's journey “offends the feelings of the Japanese people” and is “absolutely unacceptable.” A formal statement from the Japanese government noted that the visit creates long-term and medium-term obstacles to restoring bilateral relations.
Following the event, the Foreign Ministry of Japan summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolai Nozdrev. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi delivered a firm protest directly to the envoy.
Officials in Moscow dismissed the stance taken by Tokyo. The Russian Foreign Ministry called the statements from Japan “politically irrelevant, offensive, and legally void,” while accusing Tokyo of “revanchism” and “revisionist narratives.”
Dmitry Medvedev, Deputy Chairman of the Security Council of Russia, stated that the Kurils were, are, and will remain Russian territory, warning that those who fail to understand this face “monstrous consequences.”
On July 29, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had lost the strategic initiative in Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, yet remained the primary obstacle to a ceasefire.
Assessing the evolving battlefield dynamics following a series of diplomatic engagements in Washington, D.C.—including a meeting with US President Donald Trump at the White House—Zelenskyy emphasized that Russian forces no longer held the upper hand, noting that Moscow was losing roughly 30,000 soldiers per month while continuing to reject proposals to halt hostilities.

Fires in Zaporizhzhia following enemy drone strikes extinguished

    In Zaporizhzhia, rescue workers extinguished two fires that broke out as a result of Russian drone strikes on the night of August 15.
    According to Ukrinform, the Main Directorate of the State Emergency Service in Zaporizhzhia region reported this on Facebook.
