articles.title: Alaska that failed to bring peace: what has changed in the year since the Trump-Putin summit
articles.body:
Alaska that failed to bring peace: what has changed in the year since the Trump-Putin summit
Kyiv • UNN
The Trump–Putin summit in August 2025 did not lead to a ceasefire or a peace agreement. A year later, the fighting continues, and Ukraine is once again submitting proposals to the United States.
On August 15, 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump and Kremlin head Vladimir Putin met at Elmendorf-Richardson U.S. military base in Anchorage. The Alaska summit was then viewed as a potential turning point in Russia’s war against Ukraine. In Washington, officials discussed the possibility of a ceasefire, Moscow held its first direct high-level talks with the United States in a long time, while Kyiv and European capitals sought to prevent agreements on Ukraine being made without Ukraine.
A year has passed. The war has not ended, there is no ceasefire, and the issues of territory, security guarantees, and the mechanism for ending hostilities remain subject to negotiations. Moreover, in August 2026, Ukraine is once again presenting American mediators with proposals to end the war, while Washington is again trying to persuade Moscow to move from diplomatic contacts to real agreements.
On the anniversary of the meeting in Alaska, UNN recalls what was expected from the Trump–Putin summit, what happened afterward, and why the diplomatic breakthrough never turned into peace.
Alaska as Trump’s bet on personal diplomacy
Before the meeting in Anchorage, U.S. leader Donald Trump repeatedly demonstrated his belief that personal contact with Vladimir Putin could help move peace talks off dead center. The summit was intended to test this concept in practice.
For Putin, the meeting itself was already a political gain. After years of international isolation, sanctions, and a sharp reduction in contacts between the Russian leadership and the West, the Kremlin head secured a full-fledged summit with the U.S. president on American territory.
The symbolism was evident even before the talks began. Trump personally met Putin upon his arrival in Alaska. The Kremlin head received a ceremonial welcome, and footage of the leaders of the two countries shaking hands and walking down the red carpet quickly spread through the world’s media.
However, the diplomatic protocol concealed a far more complicated political architecture.
Donald Trump traveled to Alaska expecting that the talks could bring an end to hostilities closer. Vladimir Putin, meanwhile, sought to discuss both a ceasefire and a broader agreement that would take Russia’s demands regarding territory and Ukraine’s future status into account.
The talks lasted about three hours. Afterward, the presidents addressed journalists, but announced neither a ceasefire nor a peace agreement. Putin called the conversation constructive and said the talks had taken place in an atmosphere of mutual respect.
No agreement, or the first "cold shower" after the summit
After the talks, Trump acknowledged that no final agreement had been reached. The summit ended without a document obliging Russia to cease hostilities.
Nevertheless, the logic of U.S. diplomacy changed after Alaska. Before the meeting, one of Washington’s main objectives was to secure a ceasefire as an interim step toward negotiations. After speaking with Putin, Trump began placing greater emphasis on the need to move immediately toward a comprehensive peace agreement.
Reuters noted at the time that this shift benefited official Moscow. Russia had long opposed an unconditional ceasefire, fearing that it would freeze the front without resolving political and territorial issues on its terms. According to the agency, the Kremlin’s demands included the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from the parts of Donbas under Kyiv’s control in exchange for freezing the front line in other areas. Ukraine rejected these demands.
Therefore, for the Kremlin, the meeting in Alaska nevertheless produced an important diplomatic result even without a signed document. Russia gained the opportunity to discuss with Washington the conditions for a future political settlement.
It was no coincidence that Russian politicians openly called the summit a success for Moscow afterward. At the same time, even within Russia’s pro-war circles, attention was drawn to an obvious problem: the striking footage from Alaska had no impact whatsoever on the emergence of any clear and effective mechanism for ending the war.
How Ukraine and Europe urgently entered the game
For Ukraine, the key risk of the talks in Alaska was the prospect that two major powers would begin determining the parameters for ending the war without Kyiv’s direct participation. That is precisely why Ukraine’s diplomatic activity accelerated sharply after the summit.
As early as August 18, 2025, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Washington. Alongside him, leaders and senior officials from a number of European countries and NATO also came to the White House. The meeting was intended to demonstrate that any future agreement would require the participation of Ukraine and its European allies.
Another major hope emerged at that point: the possibility of a personal meeting between Zelensky and putin, after which Trump was supposed to rejoin the negotiations. This was despite the fact that on August 19 the White House reported that the American president was working to organize a bilateral meeting between Zelensky and putin, followed by a trilateral format involving the United States.
On paper, the diplomatic framework looked logical: Trump opens a negotiating channel with the kremlin, Ukraine and the Europeans coordinate their positions with Washington, after which the parties move on to direct negotiations on ending the war. But it was precisely this part of the framework that failed to work.
Security guarantees as the biggest promise to survive the talks in Alaska
One of the most important consequences of the diplomatic process was the return of the issue of security guarantees for Ukraine to the center of the negotiations. For Kyiv, this is fundamental: a cessation of hostilities without a mechanism that would prevent or significantly complicate a new Russian attack could become merely a pause between two stages of the war.
After the talks in Washington, the United States and its European partners began discussing a model for such guarantees more actively. But even a year later, they remain merely a point in a plan for a future settlement of conflicts.
In June 2026, the European Council once again confirmed the readiness of the EU and its member states to join "reliable and credible" security guarantees for Ukraine, including through the "coalition of the willing" and in cooperation with the United States. Possible elements included long-term support for Ukraine’s defense capabilities and monitoring of a potential ceasefire.
The very fact that in the summer of 2026 the allies are still talking about a future mechanism for monitoring a ceasefire clearly demonstrates the distance between the expectations of August 2025 and reality a year later.
A war that diplomacy did not stop
The simplest way to assess the effectiveness of the summit in Alaska is to look at the map of the fighting. After all, a year after the meeting of the two presidents, hostilities in Ukraine are continuing.
In 2026, the front did not turn into a frozen line of demarcation. Russian forces continue offensive operations, while Ukraine conducts counterattacks and strikes military and fuel-and-energy infrastructure in the russian federation.
According to President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky, during 2026 Ukrainian forces regained control of 745 square kilometers of territory and 26 settlements. The independent DeepState project confirmed that Ukraine had regained control over 19 settlements and pushed Russian forces out of a number of other areas. At the same time, russia continues its pressure in the Donetsk region, control over which remains one of moscow’s central demands.
The war is increasingly extending beyond the immediate front line. Ukraine is systematically attacking Russia’s oil infrastructure. One such strike in August 2026 disabled the Orsk Oil Refinery, repairs to which, according to the Russian side, could take months.
At the same time, the adversary continues drone and missile attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy and port infrastructure.
Despite this, on August 13, 2026, it became known that Kyiv had proposed to moscow a separate truce in the Black Sea and a halt to strikes on civilian facilities. The very emergence of such a proposal on the eve of the anniversary of Alaska is telling: even a limited sectoral truce a year later still requires separate negotiations.
Pressure on russia has also not disappeared
Another hope on the eve of Trump's meeting with putin in Alaska was the assumption that personal talks between the two presidents could create a choice for the kremlin: an agreement or a sharp increase in American economic pressure. However, sanctions pressure on russia has not only failed to disappear but has intensified.
Thus, in August 2026, the U.S. Senate approved, by a vote of 86 to 11, a sweeping sanctions bill targeting russia and Iran. Among other things, the document gives the president the authority to impose high tariffs on countries that continue to make large-scale purchases of Russian energy resources. Its further fate depends on the House of Representatives. At the same time, criticism of the Trump administration is being voiced in Congress over the insufficient use of sanctions against entities helping russia circumvent restrictions already in force.
In other words, economic coercion, which a year ago was viewed as an alternative to a diplomatic agreement, has itself become part of a protracted international process.
What Remains of the Alaska Agreements a Year Later
Calling the summit of August 15, 2025, completely fruitless would be an oversimplification. It restored a direct political channel between the U.S. president and the head of the kremlin; afterward, consultations between Washington and Ukraine and Europe intensified sharply, while the issue of security guarantees for Ukraine became one of the central elements of negotiations on a possible end to the war.
The main criterion was much simpler: Alaska was supposed to bring an end to the war closer, but that never happened.
At present, there is no comprehensive ceasefire in Ukraine. There is no peace agreement. There is no agreed compromise on territories. There is no launched mechanism for postwar security guarantees. And there are no signs that the fundamental disagreement between the positions of Kyiv and moscow has been overcome.
On August 11, 2026, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the state had handed new proposals on ending the war to American negotiators. The president again emphasized that the United States could bring peace closer in two ways: by strengthening Ukraine's air defense and increasing pressure on russia. American representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are preparing for new contacts with Kyiv and moscow.
This was despite the fact that in August 2025, the world was waiting to see whether one personal meeting between Trump and putin could launch the process of ending the largest war in Europe since the Second World War.
In August 2026, American mediators are once again traveling between capitals, Ukraine is once again formulating proposals, russia is once again showing no readiness to abandon its key territorial demands, and allies are once again discussing how to combine diplomacy with military and economic pressure. Alaska turned out to be neither the point at which the war ended nor even the beginning of a rapid peace process. It became the moment when diplomacy returned to the highest level, while at the same time demonstrating the limits of personal diplomacy: a meeting between presidents can open negotiations, but it cannot by itself eliminate the reasons why the parties disagree on the terms of peace.
Reminder
A few days earlier, Deputy U.S. Representative to the UN Dan Negrea stated that Washington would continue supporting negotiations to end the war.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills seven in south Lebanon as attacks intensify
articles.body:
Israeli strikes kill nine in southern Lebanon as attacks intensify
It was deadliest Israeli attack in Lebanon since agreements reached in June led to a significant reduction in hostilities.
Israeli air strikes have killed at least nine people and wounded 12 in southern Lebanon, according to Lebanese authorities, as Israel intensified attacks across several towns and villages overnight.
Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA) said seven people were killed and three wounded when a strike hit a house on the outskirts of Ansar, in the Nabatieh district, early on Saturday, destroying the building.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Lebanese soldiers injured while Israeli troops intrude on southern town
- list 2 of 4Lebanon points to ‘positive progress’ on borders, prisoners in Israel talks
- list 3 of 4‘No red line’: South Lebanon residents outraged as Israel resumes strikes
- list 4 of 4How fragile is Lebanon’s uneasy peace?
Al Jazeera’s Ali Hashem, reporting from Nabatieh, southern Lebanon, said children and members of one family were among those killed.
“This is an area seen by people as safe, but an air attack has now hit,” Hashem said, adding that the attack had increased fear among residents as Israeli strikes and demolitions continued across southern Lebanon.
The Israeli military said it had struck what it described as Hezbollah infrastructure in the areas of Nabatieh and Ansar, saying the attacks came in response to an action against Israeli soldiers at the Ali al-Taher Ridge.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam rejected Israel’s account, calling the escalation in Nabatieh, Ansar, Deir al-Zahrani and surrounding villages “extremely dangerous” and saying it was undermining efforts to consolidate stability in southern Lebanon.
“The seven people killed in the Israeli strike on Ansar are not ‘military infrastructure’, and the children and women killed in it are not military targets,” Salam said.
He said responsibility for dealing with any military infrastructure on Lebanese territory, “if it exists”, rests exclusively with the Lebanese state, through the army and other state institutions.
“Its presence does not give Israel the right to violate Lebanese territory or put civilians at risk,” Salam said, calling on Israel to halt the escalation.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun also condemned the continuing Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon, particularly in Nabatieh and surrounding areas, saying they constituted repeated violations of the framework agreement, the work of the military coordination group and international laws protecting civilians.
Aoun said the attacks had killed an entire family in Ansar and described the violations as “a clear message” to the negotiating process and US efforts to implement the agreement.
Strikes across southern Lebanon
NNA said Israeli attacks intensified early on Saturday, with a series of air strikes on the Ali al-Taher Ridge near Nabatieh al-Fawqa.
Two other strikes hit areas near the teachers’ training centre and the Husseini club in Nabatieh al-Fawqa, while the valley between Ansar and Zarariyeh was also attacked in what NNA described as the first strike to reach this far into southern Lebanon since the ceasefire two months ago.
Lebanon’s Health Ministry later said an Israeli strike on Deir al-Zahrani, also in the Nabatieh district, killed two people and wounded nine others, bringing the overall death toll from the attacks to at least nine.
Closer to the border, Israeli forces destroyed several homes in Bint Jbeil and opened heavy machinegun fire towards houses along the Kounine-Saf al-Hawa road, the agency reported.
An Israeli air attack also hit the al-Mashaa neighbourhood in al-Mansouri shortly before midnight.
Hashem said Israeli demolitions had also continued in border areas, with some villages suffering extensive destruction, including damage to graveyards and historic sites.
“This is escalating day by day,” he said, adding that diplomatic efforts had yet to produce results on the ground.
Violence has decreased since a United States-Iran memorandum of understanding in June and a subsequent US-sponsored framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel, but Israeli attacks and demolitions have continued in the south.
The framework calls for Hezbollah’s disarmament, the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces and the deployment of the Lebanese army in southern Lebanon.
On Friday, Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem criticised the Lebanese authorities over the implementation of the framework, accusing them of pressuring the army while Israeli attacks continued.
“How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?” he said.
On Thursday, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel would not withdraw unless Hezbollah was disarmed and what he called the “threat” posed by the group was removed.
Katz said Israeli forces currently control about 700 square kilometres of Lebanese territory, or roughly 7 percent of the country.
The Ansar attack was the deadliest reported Israeli strike in Lebanon since agreements reached in June led to a significant reduction in hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah.

articles.title: Drone surveillance system starts work on Narva River
articles.body:
Drone surveillance system starts work on Narva River
A new drone surveillance system has been launched on the Narva River. Initially, border guards will be able to monitor aircraft movements along about a third of the river border, with the entire border river to be covered next year.
The first five radar masts were erected along the Narva River in the spring. They have now been equipped with surveillance equipment and for the first time border guards can monitor drone movements at and near the border. Even Russian reconnaissance aircraft flying along the border show up on the radar.
"These systems are now operational. We can see drones — not just small, civilian drones. In principle, if a military drone appears near our border, it will also show up on the radar screen. This is a significant step forward," Interior Minister Igor Taro said.
Just a few years ago, border guards said they could see about 70 percent of what was happening on the Narva River. By next year, the remaining blind spots are expected to disappear.
"We have state-of-the-art radar systems that, in addition to conventional monitoring of the airspace, can now also track different types of drone traffic. Better eyes and better systems give us a clearer picture to respond to," said Veiko Kommusaar, deputy director general of the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA).
While border guards can currently only monitor drone movements, the next step will be to counter drones both along the eastern border and inland.
"We are currently in the final stages of procuring an experimental site. Once the procurement is complete, an experimental site will be built where various counter-drone solutions will also be tested. If these solutions prove successful, they can then be deployed elsewhere across Estonia where they could be useful," Taro said.
Estonian border guards currently have drone surveillance coverage from Narva to Narva-Jõesuu. Construction of radars that will cover the Narva River as far as Lake Peipus is still underway and they are expected to become operational next year.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Aleksander Krjukov

articles.title: Entrenched, embattled and defiant, the Taliban celebrate 5 years in power
articles.body:
News analysis
Entrenched, embattled and defiant, the Taliban celebrate 5 years in power
Elian Peltier
KABUL – The black and white flags of the Taliban were flying high along the streets of Kabul, Afghanistan’s capital, as the group celebrated five years in power on Aug 15.
Shiny Mercedes cars drifted in front of graffiti praising the Taliban fighters’ “sacrifice”, the word painted in crimson, with depictions of drops of blood. Young Afghans chanted independence songs below posters hailing how “the carpet of democracy” had been removed for Islamic rule.

articles.title: 'Suffocating restrictions' shadow five years of Taliban rule in Afghanistan
articles.body:
'Suffocating restrictions' shadow five years of Taliban rule in Afghanistan
Five years after seizing Kabul and returning to power, the Taliban is celebrating what it calls a more secure and "free" Afghanistan. But its anniversary comes amid mounting criticism over sweeping restrictions on women and girls, economic hardship and continued international isolation.

The Taliban government celebrates five years of ruling Afghanistan on Saturday, with the authorities hailing their country's "freedom" and security, while critics decry tightening restrictions in all areas of daily life.
Afghans riding rickshaws and motorbikes decorated with flags were driving around Kabul, where new murals declared: "Independence is a sign of dignity, pride and identity".
The authorities will host a cricket match and other sports events – which girls and women are banned from attending – while their supporters are expected to gather five years to the day since Taliban insurgents entered the city.
They took the capital unopposed after a lightning offensive that swept across Afghanistan, toppling government forces in the wake of the chaotic withdrawal of US-led troops.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Some of the vehicles abandoned by foreign forces, such as Humvees, were driven in convoy early Saturday through Kabul, where there was an increase in the number of checkpoints.
Economic hardship
Beside vendors selling flags earlier this week, university student Pirooz Mirzaie said the government has brought security, infrastructure projects and "plenty of opportunities for entrepreneurs".
"The biggest challenge for young people is that there aren't many jobs," the 20-year-old told AFP.
“Thank God, the past five years have passed in safety,” Mohammad Qasim, 30, told AP. “Our wish and hope from the government is to create job opportunities for the youth."
“We, along with the entire nation, call upon the government to create employment opportunities for the youth and to encourage them to pursue education,” Qasim added.
Zabihullah Mujahid, the government's chief spokesman, said this month that the authorities were laying the "foundations of the economy" and that patience was needed.
Read more'A very different Afghanistan: Violence now linked to socioeconomic pressures'
GDP per capita is in decline, due to more than six million Afghans arriving from neighbouring Iran and Pakistan in three years, while the World Bank estimated real growth reaching 4.8 percent.
The most severe women's rights crisis
Women have been particularly affected by Taliban government measures, being banned from public places including parks and from most jobs, while education for girls beyond age 12 is outlawed.
A 23-year-old woman said she felt a "profound sense of suffocation", speaking to AFP on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
"The five years have been so gruelling that I feel like a 500-year-old woman, one who cannot die."
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Before the takeover, the Taliban stated that, upon assuming power, it would allow women access to education, employment and public participation, albeit in accordance with its interpretation of Islamic principles.
Soon after it seized power, the Taliban imposed an indefinite ban on girls’ education beyond the sixth grade and, a few months later, also banned higher education for women until “further notice".
Read moreFour years after the fall of Kabul, Taliban succeeds in near-total exclusion of women
Mujahid has repeatedly said the Taliban administration is working to establish conditions under which girls and women can attend classrooms or university campuses in line with Islamic Sharia laws. The restrictions, nevertheless, remain in force.
In a statement this week, the UN's agency on women’s rights said Afghan women and girls are living under the world’s most severe restrictions, which not only violate their rights but also threaten the country’s social and economic future.
“Half a decade after the Taliban takeover in August 2021, Afghanistan has systematically dismantled the rights of half its population, making it a global outlier with no parallel in the modern world,” UN Women said.
“In the past year alone, this exclusion of women and girls from education, employment, public life, justice systems and healthcare has only intensified, entrenching what remains the world’s most severe women’s rights crisis,” it said.
Fazila Soroush, a 39-year-old Kabul-based entrepreneur and an advocate for women’s rights, said the government had “demonstrated its worth to the people through its actions in every area".
“We consider it essential that the officials of the Islamic Emirate who had announced the closure of schools and universities until further notice, now make a clear and practical decision regarding this matter,” she said.
'Suffocating restrictions' and diplomatic isolation
While the UN has acknowledged that the country has become more stable since the takeover, it has warned that lasting stability cannot be possible unless the Taliban rulers – who remain isolated internationally – lift restrictions on women and girls, protect basic rights and address terrorism concerns.
“A reduction in conflict has brought tangible benefits for many Afghans and created opportunities to focus on recovery, development and regional economic cooperation,” the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, or UNAMA, said in a statement ahead of the anniversary.
It added, however, that the restrictions on women and girls impede Afghanistan’s recovery and its reintegration with the international community.
Although Taliban officials have forged ties with multiple countries, including in Europe, their government is still only recognised by Russia.
Read moreFive years on, Afghanistan's Taliban build foreign ties despite rights concerns
Relations with neighbouring Pakistan have plummeted and the two countries went to war this year, exacerbating the humanitarian crisis in Afghanistan when people were already hit hard by international aid cuts.
Some countries have opted to limit their relations with the Taliban authorities until there are changes in Afghanistan, where people are suffering "very real harm" according to the UN.
Fiona Frazer, the human rights director for the UN mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA), told AFP that people have endured the "consolidation of suffocating restrictions that intrude on almost every aspect of their daily lives, and their human rights".
The Committee to Protect Journalists criticised the authorities' "brutal repression of the press" which has seen media workers "surveilled, detained, beaten, censored, or driven into exile".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and AP)

articles.title: Demand for specialists remains high as Estonia's unemployment falls slightly
articles.body:
Demand for specialists remains high as Estonia's unemployment falls slightly
The unemployment rate fell slightly in the second quarter, but the overall employment situation did not improve significantly. Employers say the greatest challenge is hiring specialists, for whom competition is fierce.
According to Statistics Estonia, Estonia's unemployment rate was 6.6 percent in the second quarter, slightly lower than a year earlier. The employment rate, at 68.6 percent, was also slightly below last year's level.
SEB economic analyst Mihkel Nestor said the figures are to be expected given the economy's gradual growth.
"Our economic growth is also relatively slow, which means there is no record-fast demand for new workers. I'm afraid unemployment will remain at around 6 percent for quite some time," Nestor said.
Southern Estonia and Harju County were the only regions where employment increased. Paulig is moving an entire production unit from Sweden to Saue, creating nearly 100 new jobs. Plant manager Margo Kuslap said there is no shortage of applicants.
"Our experience in Saue so far shows that people are willing to commute to work in Saue if the workplace is accessible, stable and offers opportunities for development," Kuslap said.
Kuslap added that hiring specialists is more difficult.
"There are roles that require specific expertise and those people are a little harder to find because many companies are competing for the same specialists," Kuslap said.
Martti Kork, CEO of Võru-based wood processing company Barrus, which was recently named Factory of the Year, said low investment has left the sector in a difficult position and forced his company to lay off employees this year as well. According to Kork, most local wood processing companies are in the same situation.
"The unfortunate thing is that all these companies are in rural areas, so jobs in rural areas are taking the hit," Kork said.
Barrus has created new opportunities in the region by shifting some work to computer-based roles. Kork said data specialists are now easier to recruit than machine operators.
"Our most recent recruitment process for a senior data architect position brought in 80 résumés here in Võru, which is quite surprising," Kork said.
The unemployment rate among 15- to 24-year-olds in Estonia was 22.4 percent in the second quarter. That is relatively high, although significantly lower than last year. Nestor sees this as a sign of society's growing prosperity.
"Families today can afford for young people's childhoods to last a little longer," Nestor said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Aleksander Krjukov

articles.title: Lai urges lawmakers to complete 2027 budget review on time
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) on Friday urged lawmakers to complete their review of the central government budget for 2027 on time, after the 2026 budget took 351 days to clear the legislature.
CNA reported that lawmakers passed the 2026 central government budget in a final reading Friday. Lai said the government submitted the spending plan to the legislature in August 2025 and that it should have been approved by the end of that year.
Lai said he regretted that the final budget still contained what he considered unreasonable spending cuts and freezes. These included major cuts to government publicity spending and freezes that affected the normal operation of government agencies and the salaries of senior officials.
The president said overseeing the government and reviewing its budget are important constitutional duties of the legislature. However, he said lawmakers should examine spending proposals using professional judgment and proportionate standards rather than allowing political disagreements to disrupt government operations.
Lai thanked Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) and the Cabinet for keeping the government running while the budget remained under legislative review. He said officials continued responding to rapid changes in the global economy and international politics while addressing domestic issues involving people's livelihoods.
The Cabinet is scheduled to approve the 2027 central government budget on Thursday, Lai said. He said the government plans to use the benefits of economic growth to provide more support for families and invest in the country's future, per Economic Daily News.
The spending plan will include financial support for children and young people from birth to age 18 and expanded assistance for childbirth, child care, and parenting. It will also increase investment in technology, public infrastructure, industrial upgrades and national defense.
Lai said the measures are intended to strengthen the country's ability to respond to international changes while improving its long-term economic competitiveness and security. He added the budget will directly affect the daily lives of families across the country.

articles.title: Ko downplays KMT-TPP rift over euthanasia referendum
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – TPP founder Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) said Saturday that his party is still cooperating with the KMT even though it failed to support the proposal for a referendum about euthanasia.
Only seven TPP legislators voted in favor of the proposal Friday, while all KMT lawmakers abstained and 51 DPP legislators voted against, defeating the referendum plan. Up until Friday, the KMT and TPP voted together on most proposals on a wide range of issues.
Asked about the vote, Ko said the two parties are cooperating, but have not merged, per UDN. The views of the two parties could not be entirely the same, so it was understandable that the KMT disagreed with the euthanasia referendum proposal, according to the former TPP presidential candidate.
Ko said the TPP and the KMT will cooperate when possible but compete when necessary, UDN reported. Cooperation between the two parties is a trend, but it is not possible for the two sides to agree all the time, he said.

articles.title: Florida venue cancels rally with Palestinian-American lawmaker Rashida Tlaib​​
articles.body:
Florida venue cancels rally with Palestinian-American lawmaker Rashida Tlaib
WASHINGTON – A South Florida site backed out of hosting a rally with Democratic US Representative Rashida Tlaib, a vocal critic of Israel’s government, after complaints by a Democratic state lawmaker in the party’s latest flashpoint over its stance on Israel.
Tlaib, the first Palestinian-American member of Congress, was scheduled to appear on Aug 14 at a rally for three candidates in Florida’s upcoming Democratic Party primary.
However, The Venue Fort Lauderdale, which was scheduled to host the event, suddenly cancelled it after State Representative Michael Gottlieb, chairman of the Florida Legislative Jewish Caucus, posted a statement on Aug 13 calling the planned rally an “anti-Jew” gathering.
Tlaib has condemned anti-semitism and says criticism of Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territories and its attacks in Gaza and Lebanon is not anti-semitic.
The Venue in a statement cited “increased security concerns” for its decision and said it is Jewish-owned and “our values and commitment to the Jewish community are deeply important to us”.
Prominent progressive Democrats, including Tlaib and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, have opposed US support for Israel over Israeli attacks in Gaza and Lebanon, the US-Israeli war with Iran, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s close ties to Republicans, leading to an erosion of Democratic backing for Washington’s ally.
The rally was organised by groups such as “Florida Youth Justice Coalition”, “Gen-Z For Change” and a local chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America.
It was meant to support State Representative Angie Nixon, who is running for the US Senate; and Elijah Manley and Oliver Larkin, who are seeking seats in the US House of Representatives.
After The Venue withdrew its support, the event was expected to proceed on the night of Aug 14 at a Fort Lauderdale wine bar, an organiser told The New York Times.
The Florida Democratic Progressive Caucus said the cancellation of the rally was rooted in anti-Muslim sentiment. Florida’s primary elections are scheduled for Aug 18. REUTERS

articles.title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,465,810 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
articles.body:
Russia has lost around 1,465,810 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 14.
The figure includes 1,370 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,269 tanks, 25,144 armored combat vehicles, 134,375 vehicles and fuel tanks, 47,932 artillery systems, 2,026 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,568 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 461,484 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,241 unmanned ground systems, 34 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs). The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

articles.title: Midnight earthquake hits southern Spain, damaging buildings, vehicles
articles.body:
An earthquake of magnitude 5 struck the southern Spanish city of Granada in the early hours of Saturday morning, with the regional government saying houses and cars were damaged, but no injuries had been reported.
The earthquake hit the metropolitan area of Alhendin just after 1 am.
Spanish television channel TVE showed debris strewn on the street and some damage to cars in the popular tourist city.
Andalusian emergency services rescued a number of people from damaged buildings.
Antonio Sanz Cabello, vice-president of the Andalusian regional government, said in a post on X on Saturday that authorities had declared an emergency.
"If you're in Granada, you've felt the earthquake, you're okay, and your home shows no damage, stay calm and avoid entering and exiting buildings unnecessarily," he said.
"On the street, stay away from facades, cornices, balconies, walls, and other elements that could fall."

articles.title: Shoe factory damaged in overnight drone attack on Odesa region
articles.body:
Shoe factory damaged in overnight drone attack on Odesa region
The Odesa regional office of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine reported this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
At one location in the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi district, a shoe factory building was damaged and subsequently the cafeteria, boiler room and a passenger car caught fire. The blast wave and debris damaged the windows and facade of an administrative building.
At another location, a non-residential private building and dry grass nearby caught fire.
Rescuers have dealt with the aftermath of the attack. According to preliminary information, there were no deaths or injuries.
Fifteen emergency workers and five pieces of equipment from the State Emergency Service were involved in the response.
On August 14, rescuers extinguished fires caused by Russian attacks in two districts of the Odesa region, including fires at a grain storage facility and a hotel building.

articles.title: Flamingo Missiles Strike Industrial Facility in Samara—It May Have Been the Manufacturer of Soyuz-2 Launch Vehicles
articles.body:
Flamingo cruise missiles struck an industrial complex in Samara, home to the Aviakor and Progress Rocket Space Center, which manufactures Soyuz-2 launch vehicles.
Video footage of the attack on the facility was published by Exilenova+.
The attack took place on the night of August 15. At approximately 2:51 a.m., a missile alert was issued in the Samara Region, after which local residents reported explosions.
The governor of the Samara Region, Vyacheslav Fedoryshchev, confirmed a strike on one of the region’s industrial facilities but did not specify which facility was targeted.
At this time, it is difficult to pinpoint the exact location of the strike. Aviakor and the Progress Rocket Space Center are located a few hundred meters apart (53.21761147334546, 50.30151107903643) from each other, so based on the published photos and videos, it is impossible to unequivocally determine on which facility’s grounds the missile struck.
OSINT analysis of the Telegram channel Falcon Insight Map indicates that smoke from the strike is rising in the area between AviaKor’s Building No. 106 and the administrative and residential complex (ABK) of Building No. 106.
Building No. 106 is used for large-scale aircraft assembly, docking, and installation of internal systems. Adjacent to it is the A&CS of Building No. 106, which is integrated into the production facility building. It houses the company’s engineering and design departments as well as its administrative services.
We also recommend reading the author’s article “Anatomy of ‘Bureau 1440’: Structure and Vulnerabilities of Russia’s ‘Rassvet’—the Starlink Analog.”
Exilenova+ claims that the missile struck the territory of the Progress Rocket Space Center.
According to OSINT data from Varta, this is one of the key enterprises in the Russian rocket and space industry. The company develops and manufactures launch vehicles, including the Soyuz-2 family, as well as spacecraft.
In particular, Soyuz-2.1b launch vehicles are used to launch Rassvet-3 communications satellites, which are developed by the Russian company Bureau 1440.
On March 23, 2026, a Soyuz-2.1b rocket placed 16 satellites of this system into orbit.
Both enterprises are located approximately 850–950 km from Ukraine’s state border. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, no strikes on such industrial enterprises had previously been recorded in Samara.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that on the morning of July 24, the Ukrainian Defense Forces attacked the Avitek plant in Kirov, Russia, with Flamingo cruise missiles. The facility is located more than 1,200 km from Ukraine.

articles.title: ‘A tax on being thin’: only high earners make overall savings on food bills from weight-loss drugs
articles.body:
The high cost of weight-loss medication is a “regressive tax on being thin” because the outlay outweighs any saving on food costs for all but the highest earners.
Someone needs to have discretionary income of nearly £100,000 a year to actually save money after covering the £1,200 annual cost of GLP-1 medication, according to an analysis by the consultancy Baringa.
“Our analysis shows that GLP-1s risk becoming a driver of inequality,” said Paddy Winters, a partner at Baringa. “Only very high earners will benefit from savings to their groceries whilst taking the GLP-1 pill.”
A regressive tax is one that takes a larger percentage from lower-wage earners’ income compared with those who are more wealthy. Most users buy the drugs with a private prescription.
A GLP-1 user with £39,000 left over after tax and essentials will spend £481 less a year on food. But it is not until someone has £97,500 left to spend after tax and other outgoings that their grocery spend is reduced by £1,200, according to Baringa. The cost is an average for the pill form of the medication.
For “everyone else” the annual cost of the drug outweighs any reduction in spending on groceries, Winters said. “On top of that, users are spending more on vitamin supplements and personal care products like hair care, to manage side effects. In effect, GLP-1s become a regressive tax on being thin.”
“We’re already seeing early signs that some people cancel their prescription after a few months because the cost adds up – but the weight comes back once you stop,” he added. “So the pattern is likely to be start, stop, regain and return, and to fund that cycle, we may well see people turn to debt.”
There are 14.3 million adults living with obesity in England, according to the King’s Fund. In a recent report, the charity said the government “needs to ensure that the people who benefit from [weight-loss medication] most are not priced out of accessing them, and that we don’t end up with wider health inequalities caused by obesity due to affordability and access”.
It is estimated that 5% of adults, or nearly 3 million people, in Britain are on weight-loss medication, while 9% have taken it at some point, according to separate research by accountancy firm PwC. It expects this number to rise to 13% by the end of next year.
About 60% of GLP-1 users are women, according to PwC. Among current users 6% come from households with income of less than £20,000, whereas 20% are from the wealthiest, earning above £100,000.
Dr Leyla Hannbeck, the executive chair of the Independent Pharmacies Association, said that access to GLP-1s on the NHS is “limited only to a small eligible cohort and many people who might benefit are unable to access treatment at all unless they can afford private care”.
“The NHS commissioning currently protects against some of the financial inequity, but access is limited,” Hannbeck said.
The price of weight-loss drugs varies significantly depending on the retailer, drug, dose and whether any discounts or subscription is being used.
Hannbeck said there had been some price volatility – notably in summer 2025 the cost of Mounjaro more than doubled – but the market was becoming more competitive.
“We are seeing a growing pipeline of GLP-1 products, including oral formulations and next-generation therapies,” she said, pointing to the recent launch of the Wegovy pill.
Those working in the industry regularly see a pattern where a patient is losing weight but ends up discontinuing treatment due to cost pressures and so regains it, said Hannbeck said. “This … reinforces the message that weight-loss is a journey and it must go hand in hand with lifestyle changes, such as diet and exercise, to maintain a healthy weight rather than a short-term quick fix.”

articles.title: It’s the SUV tyranny: where have all the normal family cars gone? | Coco Khan
articles.body:
Recently, while traipsing from showroom to showroom in search of a used car for my growing clan, the iconic line from Christopher Nolan’s seminal Batman movie The Dark Knight came to mind: “You either die a hero, or live long enough to see yourself become the villain.” And by villain, of course, I mean an SUV driver.
Because, if you haven’t shopped for a secondhand family car recently, I’ll save you the shock: wherever you look, it’s SUVs.
It’s no surprise when these giant cars now make up 30% of all cars on the road and were 50% of all new car sales in rich countries in 2023. The look has been so popular that traditional body styles have been modified into taller, wider frames. Even Volvo, the defining family car brand, now only offers SUVs in the UK. All of which means that if, like me, you want a car under 10 years old, hoping it lasts another five, your options are “tank” and “tank-ette”.
Driving the same small city car for nearly 10 years has felt, overall, like a net good. Cheap to run and clean-air-zone-compliant, the compact car is the sociable motor. The people pleaser of the road, at this size a tight parking spot is rarely a worry. Even its horn, a pipsqueak of a beep, conveys more “toodles” than threat. Yes, fine, on a windy motorway it can feel like it might become airborne. But this precious little donkey is reliable and humble. Unlike the flashy warhorse, the SUV, with its ever-widening size (0.5cm wider each year) intimidating other drivers and pedestrians, causing chaos on narrow roads and reducing parking spaces when lines are redrawn to accommodate them. Also, a special mention of the branding: so much military language (the Jeep Commander or Land Rover’s Defender, apparently “built to conquer”) – for a vehicle whose main enemy is the roundabout outside Sainsbury’s.
So when it came to buying my first family car I figured I’d find an estate, a saloon or a hatchback: something that was safe, since it would carry the most precious cargo of all, children; fuel efficient; wipe-down seats; and a big boot big enough for strollers and bikes, and all the hopes and dreams for a happy family life. But my dreams would soon be dashed.
One thing’s for sure, it has been a memorable month hunting for a “normal” family car. The experience of saying “I’m not interested in an SUV” and still being shown one … then a small one … and then one that just looks like one, but technically isn’t because it can’t go off-road, is the closest thing I’ve experienced to performance art in some years.
How can I forget the forecourt so dominated by these cars that the best on offer was a black “mid-size” SUV, a Lexus RX450H, so huge that I genuinely mistook it for a hearse. Or the gentle, sympathetic nature of the used-car salesman showing me a grey and dowdy people carrier. “But, but … I’m in my 30s. I’m still young, I can’t drive this,” I protested, as he gave me a smile conveying “this is all that’s left for you, my friend”.
Yet, I’m not sure what it is about this that deflates me. Is it the illusion of consumer choice, and how we are funnelled into the same purchases and lifestyles even when we don’t really want them? Or the corrosive quality of fear: against your neighbour’s SUV, your regular car looks flimsy, so you arm up, too. The car lobby has pushed the message that these vehicles are fortresses to keep your children safe inside, with no care for how unsafe they may be outside. The increased height of these bonnets means a child is three times more likely to be killed if hit by an SUV rather than by a conventional vehicle – and, as transport writer Christian Wolmar observes, more likely to be hit at all, since the driving position is often too high to see a child ahead.
But mostly I suspect it’s to do with our modern parenting culture, where everything – buggies, cars, technology for baby socks to monitor their breathing – has scaled up to capitalise on our need for safety in a precarious world. Yet the best thing to keep us safe will always be one another, collectivism over individualism. But here we are, driving around in Batmobiles, thinking ourselves heroes, blithely unaware we just might be the baddies.
Needless to say, I still haven’t found the right family car. I do (reluctantly) have an SUV test drive booked, though. Perhaps I should embrace the chaos. It could be my Joker moment.
- 
  Coco Khan is a freelance writer and co-host of the politics podcast Pod Save the UK

articles.title: Quarter of combat engagements in two directions - General Staff updated its data on situation at front
articles.body:
Quarter of combat engagements in two directions - General Staff updated its data on situation at front

Over the past day, there were 233 combat engagements at the front, most of them in the Kostiantynivka and Pokrovsk directions. The enemy carried out 71 airstrikes, deployed 10,626 kamikaze drones, and conducted 3,042 shellings.
233 battles took place at the front over the past day, with the most occurring in the Kostiantynivka and Pokrovsk directions, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported in its morning briefing on August 15, UNN writes.
A total of 233 combat engagements were recorded over the past day
Yesterday, the enemy launched 71 airstrikes, dropping 241 guided aerial bombs. In addition, the invaders used 10,626 kamikaze drones and carried out 3,042 attacks on populated areas and the positions of our troops, 36 of them using multiple-launch rocket systems.

The situation by direction
In the North Slobozhanskyi and Kursk directions, our defenders stopped six enemy assaults over the past day. At the same time, the aggressor launched four airstrikes, dropping eight aerial bombs, and carried out 62 attacks on the positions of our troops and populated areas.

articles.title: Ministry moves to save Cold War-era underground printing press near Kaunas
articles.body:
Lithuania’s Ministry of Defence is stepping in to preserve an underground printing press that secretly operated for a decade during Soviet rule, after a military museum decided not to renew an agreement that had allowed the privately owned site to operate as a museum exhibit.
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas called the decision bureaucratic and said the government would ensure the historic site remains open to visitors.
The underground printing press is located beneath a private property in the village of Saliai, in Kaunas district. A concealed entrance beneath a greenhouse leads to the underground facility.
The press was established by Vytautas Andziulis and his associate, Juozas Bacevičius, during the Soviet era. Andziulis’ son, Vykintas, now leads tours of the site.
“This is the only entrance and exit to the printing press. Paper was brought in through here,” he said, showing the site.
For about 30 years, the printing press operated free of charge as a branch of the Vytautas the Great War Museum under a use agreement. Three members of the Andziulis family worked part time as guides.
But the museum decided not to renew the agreement effective August 6 and removed the site from its list of exhibits.
The museum’s director, Rita Malinauskienė, said the decision was prompted primarily by concerns about the condition of the building. Cracks were discovered in the ceiling in May, making tours potentially unsafe.
She said legal restrictions prevent the museum from using public funds to repair privately owned property.
“The biggest problem was the condition of the printing press, and as the head of the institution responsible for fiscal discipline, I could not use money from the printing press’s budget for repairs because it is private property,” Malinauskienė said.
The Andziulis family said it did not expect the museum to finance repairs. Vykintas Andziulis said the damaged ceiling had already been repaired by the family.
The site attracted about 2,200 visitors last year, free of charge. The family says continued operation at that scale would be difficult without state support.
“If we are not suitable as employees, fine, send someone else,” Andziulis said. “We can discuss and negotiate, but there were no negotiations on this issue.”
Minister Kaunas travelled to Kaunas district to discuss the situation and said he did not understand the museum’s decision to terminate the arrangement.
“The underground printing press was never discovered by Soviet authorities, it was never destroyed, even though it was supposed to operate for only two years. It operated for 10,” Kaunas said. “And now we ourselves want to finish what the Russians failed to do – destroy such an object.”
The Defence Ministry currently provides funding through the museum for staff working at the site. About 30,000 euros is allocated annually for the printing press guides’ salaries, while about 13,000 euros has been spent on maintenance services over the past five years.
Kaunas said the government could find a way to support the privately owned site, pointing to other cases in which the government purchases services from private organisations.
“The state can contribute to private entities and does so – it contributes to private pension funds, purchases services from private schools and private clinics,” he said. “There are precedents and mechanisms, and from the Defence Ministry’s perspective, this site must be protected.”
Malinauskienė said the museum was now working with the deputy defence minister to determine what type of use agreement could allow the site to continue operating.
The underground press operated from the 1980s until the restoration of Lithuania’s independence in the early 1990s. During that period, it produced nearly 140,000 publications, most of them patriotic and religious literature that was banned or restricted under Soviet rule.
The press remained hidden from Soviet authorities throughout its operation and became an important part of Lithuania’s history of underground resistance.

articles.title: Kaplin calls for cessation of mobilization of humanitarian workers involved in evacuation of civilians
articles.body:
Yevhen Kaplin, founder and chairman of the Proliska humanitarian mission, called on those responsible for mobilization to cease the practice of calling up humanitarian workers directly involved in the evacuation of civilians from frontline areas after the mobilization of a tow truck driver from the Ukrainian Red Cross rapid response unit.
"I call on those responsible for mobilization to stop this practice. Not after another scandal. Not after another tragedy. Not when people are left on the bus with no one to take them out, but right now!" he wrote on Facebook.
According to Kaplin, after the driver's mobilization, the evacuees remained in the vehicle in the middle of the road. "You can't take a tow truck driver and leave the people he's evacuating in the middle of the road," he wrote.
Kaplin reported that since 2022, the Proliska humanitarian mission has mobilized more than 150 staff, volunteers, and service providers, about two-thirds of whom are rapid response team members and tow trucks.
He also cited examples of tow truck driver mobilization in Mykolaiv region, after which, he said, certain evacuation routes from frontline areas had to be suspended due to a lack of drivers.
"We cannot weaken the humanitarian system where it is literally supporting people's lives today," Kaplin emphasized.
He called for the creation of a clear mechanism to ensure that humanitarian workers directly involved in evacuating and providing assistance to civilians in frontline areas are not recalled from their work unless absolutely necessary.
Kaplin also expressed hope that the Red Cross driver would be released to continue humanitarian work, and that the rapid response team in Kherson region would resume operations as soon as possible.
As reported, on the morning of August 14, police in Mykolaiv region detained a volunteer driver with the Kherson Rapid Response Team of the Ukrainian Red Cross Society, who was evacuating people from a dangerous area in Kherson, specifically, an elderly woman, a cancer patient, and a 3-year-old child, according to the team's Facebook page.

articles.title: Israeli strikes on south Lebanon kill nine in worst toll since June
articles.body:
Nine people have been killed, including three children, and 11 injured in two Israeli airstrikes on south Lebanon, the worst toll since deals in June brought a lull in hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah.
Israeli warplanes bombed a home on the outskirts of the village of Ansar in south Lebanon, killing seven people early on Saturday morning, flattening the home. Rescue services were working at the site to try to find survivors and locate bodies.
Hours later, Israel carried out another airstrike on a home in the town of Deir al-Zahrani, killing two and wounding nine, covering the streets of the village in rubble and smoke. An Israeli drone also targeted a motorcycle in the nearby city of Nabatieh, but it was unclear if the driver was killed.
The escalation came despite a June ceasefire in which most fighting between Israel and Hezbollah ended.
Residents of south Lebanon wondered if the attacks signalled further escalation to come or if it was safe to stay in their homes. Neither village was in Israel’s self-declared “security zone” – a 231-square-mile area of south Lebanon occupied by Israel.
The roads leading out of Nabatieh and the villages around it were choked with traffic after the strikes as people fled north in search of safety.
The Israeli military spokesperson, Ella Waweya, said Israel had attacked “Hezbollah infrastructure” in the Ansar and Nabatieh area in response to Hezbollah fighters attacking their soldiers in the Ali Taher area.
Ali Taher is a hill where the Israeli military says large underground Hezbollah command and control centres are located; it has been shelling the area for months.
The Lebanese prime minister, Nawaf Salam, condemned the Israeli attacks, calling them “extremely dangerous” and said they “undermined efforts to establish stability in the south”.
Salam called on Israel to stop the escalation. “The seven martyrs of the Israeli strike on the town of Ansar were not ‘military infrastructure’ and the children and women killed were not military targets,” he said.
The latest round of fighting in Lebanon started after Hezbollah struck Israel with rockets on 2 March in retaliation for the killing of the late supreme leader of Iran. Israel responded with an aerial campaign and invasion that killed more than 4,300 people and left about 6% of the country’s territory occuped by Israel.
Violence has significantly decreased since the signing of a US-Iran memorandum of understanding in June on the broader Middle East war, and a US-sponsored framework deal between Lebanon and Israel agreed later that month.
But Lebanon still reports intermittent Israeli strikes occasionally causing casualties, and the broad demolitions of civilian buildings in southern villages and towns.
The news agency NNA said “the valley between Ansar and Zarariyeh was also subjected to a strike, the first at this geographical depth since the ceasefire two months ago”.
It also said “Israeli warplanes carried out a series of airstrikes targeting the Ali al-Taher ridge”. The news agency said Israeli forces detonated homes in the town of Bint Jbeil near the border.
The Israel-Lebanon framework deal includes the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from south Lebanon, and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in “pilot zones”.
On Friday, Hezbollah’s chief, Naim Qassem, accused Lebanese authorities of subjecting the country’s armed forces to undue pressure by implementing the deal. “How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?” he said.
This week, Human Rights Watch urged the UN to keep an international force in Lebanon after its peacekeepers’ mandate ends this year, saying “peacekeepers are a crucial deterrent against attacks on civilians and human rights abuses”.

articles.title: Lula holds narrow lead over Flavio Bolsonaro ahead of Brazil election: Poll
articles.body:
Gizem Nisa Demir
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva holds a narrow lead over Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro ahead of October's presidential election, according to a new Quaest poll commissioned by Brazilian media group Globo.
The poll, conducted on Aug. 10-13 among 2,004 people, found Lula leading Bolsonaro 43% to 40% in a simulated runoff, effectively a statistical tie given the two-point margin of error.
Lula led 44% to 39% in a similar poll on Aug. 5.
In a first-round scenario, Lula received 38%, compared with 31% for Bolsonaro. Renan Santos and Ronaldo Caiado each had 4%, while Romeu Zema had 2%.
Under Brazilian electoral rules, the top two candidates advance to a runoff if no one wins more than half of the valid votes.
 
Brazil's election tightens
Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, has become the leading candidate for Brazil's political right after his father was barred from running.
Jair Bolsonaro was declared ineligible by Brazil's top electoral court for abusing his political power and was later convicted over a plot to overturn his 2022 election defeat to Lula.
Lula launched his reelection campaign on Aug. 2 at the Workers' Party convention in Sao Paulo, framing the race around national sovereignty amid pressure from US President Donald Trump's administration.
"I want to be prepared, so that no one invades this country," Lula said, while pledging to protect Brazil's rare earths and other critical minerals from foreign control.
He warned that China, the US, and France would not gain access to Brazil's mineral wealth without respecting its sovereignty.
"In Brazil, we do not accept anyone sticking their nose where it does not belong," he said.
Trump has maintained close ties with the Bolsonaro family. Lula warned him in June against intervening in Brazil's election, saying: "Don't meddle in the Brazilian elections, because the Brazilian elections are a Brazilian problem, just as American elections are their business, not mine."
With the vote roughly two months away, the latest polling points to a tightening contest, although Lula retains a narrow advantage.

articles.title: 'Iran neither fears threats nor cowers': Tehran defies Trump threat to claim Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that he would “soon” declare the Strait of Hormuz U.S. territory, drawing a defiant response from Tehran that only Iran would determine the future of the strategic waterway.
“Iran neither fears threats nor cowers before displays of power,” Iranian officials said as tensions remained high over control of the strait, a critical artery for global energy supplies.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi responded directly to Trump, saying, “This strait will only be closed and opened under Iran's command, and as long as you do not accept the reality of defeat and cease your fanciful delusions, Iran will continue to enforce the blockade.”
Trump had earlier told Fox News that his administration intended to inflict severe economic pressure on Iran.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, meanwhile, said exchanges of messages through Pakistan and Qatar should not be interpreted as negotiations. Tehran, he said, had yet to decide whether to resume talks with the United States.
The comments underscored the central role the Strait of Hormuz has assumed in the confrontation between Washington and Tehran. The narrow waterway between Iran and Oman connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea and is one of the world’s most important routes for oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.
Iranian commander: War could last until Trump leaves office
The dispute over the strait came as Iranian state television broadcast a rare interview with Brig. Gen. Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior adviser to Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander Ahmad Vahidi, to PBS.
Naqdi insisted Iran was prevailing in the war, pointing in particular to what he described as Washington’s failure to topple the Iranian government.
“We saw confusion and bewilderment in America. It became a war without a strategy,” Naqdi said. “Every two or three days, they announced a new objective. For several nights, they said they want to invade Kharg Island. They said they want to open the Strait of Hormuz. They mobilized their battleships. Everything they tried, we can show how we were victorious.”
He argued that the past five months had shown the U.S. military to be weaker than Iranian officials previously believed.
Asked whether one of Iran’s objectives was to prolong the war, potentially until Trump leaves office, Naqdi said Tehran needed to convince its adversaries that attacking Iran carried an unacceptable price.
“We have to attain deterrence so that the enemy never dares to attack us, so we can live with security,” he said. “One way is to prolong this war until we get to the next term of the presidency and cause attrition, so that if anyone else wants to attack Iran, they will know there is a cost.”
Naqdi also defended Iranian attacks on civilian vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, arguing that such ships could be carrying supplies to Iran’s enemies.
Asked about reports concerning Iran’s remaining missile stockpile, Naqdi said U.S. and Israeli officials were preoccupied with determining how many weapons Tehran still possessed.
“The Americans and the Zionists always want to count our missiles,” he said. “The number of missiles we manufacture every day is more than the number we launch. In a country this vast, we can make them wherever we want.
“We do it in different ways. We have various ways to manufacture them securely. Rest assured, even if this war lasts for years, until the last day, Iran's rockets will be launched.”
Naqdi then warned that Iran could remain dangerous even if its missile arsenal were depleted.
“If there comes a day when Iran has no more missiles left, that's when we will be even more dangerous for America,” he said.
Asked what he meant, Naqdi said the United States had economic assets around the world that could be “easily destroyed.”
The interviewer noted that Washington ultimately possessed a weapon Tehran does not — a nuclear bomb.
Naqdi dismissed the possibility of nuclear use, saying circumstances had changed since World War II.
“The people of the world have awakened,” he said. “No one in the world will allow for such a crime to be committed, because the next time it could be themselves.”
Asked about Israel, Naqdi said he would prefer that the country cease to exist and predicted it would ultimately collapse from within, comparing that prospect to the end of apartheid rule in South Africa.
Questions over Khamenei’s absence
Naqdi was also questioned about Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared publicly since an attempt to kill him during the opening strikes of the war.
Naqdi attributed Khamenei’s absence to “security” considerations.
But when asked whether he had personally met with the supreme leader, he declined to answer.
“Let’s leave this matter alone,” Naqdi said.
The White House responded to his remarks by urging Tehran to reach an agreement with Washington.
“It would be wise for Iran to agree to a deal. Otherwise they know what will happen,” the White House said.
Vance: Cheap energy is the No. 1 goal
The escalating rhetoric over Hormuz followed comments Thursday by Vice President JD Vance, who said preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon was not the administration’s first priority in the confrontation. Instead, he said, its top objective was keeping energy affordable for Americans.
“The thing I can say with confidence is I think this ends with the United States in a stronger position, with Iran not having a nuclear weapon, and with the Strait of Hormuz returned to a place where oil and gas prices are stable for the American people,” Vance told Fox News.
He said the administration was using its tools “very selectively, very strategically” to achieve Trump’s objectives, including ensuring Gulf states can continue supplying oil and gas to the global economy.
“That's goal number one: Keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country,” Vance said. “And obviously, goal number two is ensuring that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon.”
Vance said he was confident Washington was making progress toward both goals but acknowledged that the confrontation remained difficult to predict.
“The Iranians themselves are unpredictable,” he said, “and they sometimes don’t honor the commitments they’ve made to us.”

articles.title: Seoul called for dialogue with North Korea on formally ending Korean War
articles.body:
Seoul called for dialogue with North Korea on formally ending Korean War
Kyiv • UNN
Lee Jae-myung called for talks with North Korea, proposing to replace the armistice with a peace regime. He also emphasized the need to prevent conflict and limit Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung called for the resumption of dialogue with North Korea to ensure peaceful coexistence and prevent a new conflict on the Korean Peninsula. The Guardian writes, UNN reports.
Details
"South Korean President Lee Jae-myung called for talks with North Korea aimed at achieving peaceful coexistence, stating that Seoul would seek guarantees to prevent conflict and emphasizing the need to replace the armistice on the peninsula with a 'peace regime,'" the publication writes.
In a speech marking the anniversary of Korea's liberation from Japanese colonial rule, Lee said that the two Koreas should hold talks aimed at coexistence.
He called for dialogue between North Korea and interested parties with the aim of ending the 1950–1953 Korean War, which was halted not by a peace treaty but by an armistice, and noted that measures to limit Pyongyang's nuclear capabilities could also be considered during the discussions.
Lee also said that Seoul would take preventive and consistent measures to ease tensions and create multilayered safeguards to prevent an escalation of the conflict.
As the publication notes, Lee's call is largely based on his pledge last year to respect North Korea's system and seek peaceful coexistence with Pyongyang.
DPRK removes references to unification with South Korea from constitution06.05.26, 11:17 • 4751 view
As the publication points out, relations between North and South Korea remain frozen. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un abandoned Pyongyang's policy of reunification, called South Korea the most hostile state, and ordered the strengthening of defenses along the front line.
North Korea rejected Lee's proposals to establish dialogue, criticized Seoul's plan for nuclear-powered submarines, and condemned joint U.S.–South Korean military exercises as provocations.
Regarding relations with Japan, Lee called for confronting the past while leaving the future open, and expressed hope of beginning a new 60 years of peace and prosperity with Japan as a "close neighbor."
To remind you
On the morning of August 12, North Korea launched a ballistic missile toward the sea, conducting its second missile test in less than a week.

articles.title: South Korea sacks chief trade negotiator amid growing US tariff pressure
articles.body:
South Korea's chief trade negotiator has been dismissed from his post, officials said on Saturday, as Seoul faces mounting tariff pressure from the United States amid a series of unresolved bilateral trade issues.
No reason was given for the removal.
Trade Minister Yeo Han-koo had been South Korea's principal trade envoy, making several trips to Washington this year to meet US administration and congressional officials on tariffs, chip measures and digital policy concerns.
The ministry said personnel decisions involving political appointees were within the president's authority and that it would work to ensure no disruption to pending trade matters.
The dismissal comes at a sensitive time for bilateral trade relations, as Seoul faces growing US pressure to accelerate its investment commitments under a bilateral tariff deal and a dispute over fines against US-listed e-commerce giant Coupang over a customer data breach.
Coupang was hit with a record $403 million dollars in June over a massive data breach affecting millions of South Korean customers.
On Thursday, US President Donald Trump signed a proclamation imposing new tariffs on drones and their components, including a 15 percent levy on imports from Korea.
Yeo previously served as director-general for trade policy and later as chief trade negotiator at the ministry under the Moon Jae-in administration, before being reappointed to the chief negotiator role when the Lee Jae-myung administration took office.
Since returning to the post, he has played a key role in trade negotiations with Washington, including talks over US tariffs and Korea's investment commitments.

Following the explosions in Samara, Denis Shtilerman, chief designer at the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, published footage of an FP-5 “Flamingo” missile launch.

Orenburg Governor Yevgeny Solntsev stated Thursday that the strike damaged key infrastructure, resulting in a complete shutdown of the facility, which is located 1,300 kilometers from Ukraine and processes approximately six million metric tons of crude oil annually.
Solntsev noted that repairs could require up to six months due to international sanctions restricting the import of necessary replacement equipment. Regional authorities are preparing for potential fuel shortages and reconfiguring logistics to rely on imported fuel.
Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed the strike on the Orsk facility. On Thursday night, an additional strike targeted the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat refinery complex in Bashkortostan.

Iran has not yet decided whether to resume talks with the US - minister

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that the country had not made a decision on resuming talks with the US. He noted that exchanging messages through intermediaries does not constitute negotiations.
Iran has not decided whether to resume negotiations with the United States, the country's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said early Saturday morning, UNN reports, citing CNN.

Araghchi said that mediators Qatar and Pakistan had exchanged messages, but that this interaction did not constitute negotiations.
