articles.title: Chiang to lead Asian-Pacific Parliamentarians' Union general assembly delegation
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Deputy Legislative Speaker Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) will lead 13 lawmakers to Tokyo on Aug. 24 for the Asian-Pacific Parliamentarians' Union general assembly, CNA reported Saturday.
This year's meeting will focus on parliamentary cooperation to promote a free and open economy. The program includes five formal sessions and two dinners.
The Legislative Yuan's international affairs office asked the KMT, DPP, and TPP to nominate members for the delegation. It includes six lawmakers each from the KMT and DPP and one from the TPP, per Economic Daily News.
Taiwan hosted the union's 53rd General Assembly last year. Participants adopted eight resolutions, including three proposed by Taiwan.
One of Taiwan's resolutions called on member countries to join an Indo-Pacific platform for cooperation on marine debris. The proposal aimed to strengthen regional cooperation on marine environmental protection and security.
The Asian-Pacific Parliamentarians' Union was founded in 1965 to promote cooperation among lawmakers and support freedom, democracy, peace, and prosperity in the Asia-Pacific. It has 21 national member groups, including South Korea and Thailand, while Vietnam participates as an observer.

articles.title: Small-scale projects offer hope for Gaza farmers rebuilding lives
articles.body:
Small-scale projects offer hope for Gaza farmers rebuilding lives
Greenhouses and rented plots are lifelines for Gaza’s farmers, helping them grow crops despite the extensive destruction.
Nuseirat, Gaza Strip – Mohammad al-Halabi, 50, bends over tomato and eggplant seedlings in a 300-square-metre plot in the middle of central Gaza’s Nuseirat refugee camp, inspecting the leaves, watering the plants and monitoring their growth.
The small plot he is tending is an attempt to reclaim his old profession as a farmer with his father, Marwan, on their land in northern Gaza’s Jabalia.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Palestine weekly: West Bank in flames after Tal killings
- list 2 of 4Who is behind settler violence in the occupied West Bank?
- list 3 of 4Palestinians in occupied West Bank hold firm on Indigenous Peoples’ Day
- list 4 of 4Fear and attacks grip Taybeh, the last all-Christian town in the West Bank
Al-Halabi once owned a much bigger plot of farmland – around 40,000 square metres (about 10 acres) – in northern Gaza, where he grew strawberries, tomatoes, flowers, potatoes and eggplants. His four children – Mahmoud, 30, Reham, 27, Issa, 24, and Omar, 20 – also worked with him and relied on farming as a source of income for the family.
“I have been working in agriculture since I was a child,” al-Halabi said. “The land is my life, and I have spent my whole life farming it.”
Al-Halabi says his entire farmland was bulldozed in February 2024 by Israeli forces, as part of their general destruction of Jabalia. Al-Halabi’s land there is now covered with rubble and remnants of war, including what he described as remnants of missiles and other weapons.
He believes it will require extensive rehabilitation work before it can be farmed again.
So, for now, al-Halabi’s focus is on his small plot in Nuseirat, which he began renting at the start of the war, after his displacement. He began growing whatever he could obtain.
“Agriculture is my profession,” al-Halabi said. “Even after being displaced, I couldn’t leave it. I found a small piece of land and planted whatever I could get.”
The plot produces only a few kilogrammes of each crop he grows, barely enough for his family, and is too small to generate enough produce for sale.
“When I see the plant growing and producing a fruit, I feel that I can still farm,” al-Halabi said. “The land is small, but it has potential, and hopefully it will produce a crop.”
Data from Gaza’s Government Media Office illustrates the scale of the damage to the agricultural sector.
More than 87 percent of Gaza’s agricultural land has been destroyed. About 8,700 agricultural wells have also been destroyed and put out of service, while 7,748 cattle, sheep and poultry farms have been destroyed. More than 87 percent of greenhouses have also been damaged. Annual vegetable and fruit production has fallen from about 524,000 tonnes to approximately 20,000.
Naser Deeb, director-general of the Agricultural Extension at Gaza’s Ministry of Agriculture, says the damage extends beyond crops to farmland, water sources, irrigation networks, wells and agricultural facilities. Deeb says he has visited and assessed several damaged agricultural sites across Gaza, though he did not inspect al-Halabi’s land.
Deeb said damaged farmland would need extensive rehabilitation before production could resume.
“Farmers today are facing several problems at the same time,” Deeb says. “Even if a farmer returns to his land, that does not mean the land is ready for cultivation. The soil needs to be rehabilitated, water sources and irrigation systems repaired, and seeds, fertilisers and equipment provided.”
And the impact of these issues, Deeb says, is affecting farming families and markets across Gaza, reducing the availability of fresh vegetables and making it harder for farmers to restore their livelihoods.
New farm
Some farmers are trying to rebuild through small-scale projects.
Mohammad Abdul Naser Hassan al-Jadba, 40, from Sheikh Ajleen in Gaza City, lost his source of income during the war after his farmland ended up on the wrong side of the “Yellow Line”, the boundary in Gaza behind which Israeli forces operate and control.
Israeli soldiers have killed Palestinians who have strayed too close to the line, and al-Jadba knows that it is too dangerous for him to even try to access his farmland. Instead, he resigned himself to renting a small plot in Deir el-Balah, where he has established a nursery and greenhouse to grow tomatoes, eggplants and peppers.
Al-Jadba received some funding from a Belgian development fund, which he used to build the greenhouse and obtain agricultural supplies.
“Before renting the farm, my income was zero,” al-Jadba said. “Today, I can support my family, and my monthly income has reached around 3,000 shekels [$1,015] a month.”
He has also been able to employ two farmers on a permanent basis inside the greenhouse. Both had previously been unemployed.
“For me, this project was not just agricultural support,” al-Jadba said. “It was a real opportunity to return to work, regain my source of income and become self-reliant again.”

articles.title: 6 killed, suspect dead in shootings in US State of Michigan
articles.body:
Officers responded just before noon to reports of a shooting at a home in Missaukee County, about 170 miles (270 kilometers) northwest of Detroit, and found three people dead and another in critical condition, Michigan State Police said in a statement. The wounded person was taken to a hospital.
Suspect Chad Hickman, 39, fled before they arrived at the home, according to police. As officers conducted a large-scale search for him, they found a fourth person dead at another home.
In a post on the social platform X, police warned that Hickman was armed and dangerous and told community members not to approach him, according to the New York Times.
Hickman’s vehicle was later found in a wooded area near Whitlock Lake, and that led authorities to his body as well as that of another dead person.
“This situation is heartbreaking for the community and challenging for the investigators involved,” Lt. Ashley Miller said in a statement.
She added that investigators would work through the night to process each scene.
Police asked people to avoid the areas where the shootings took place.
MNA

articles.title: Israeli airstrike kills 7, injures 3 in southern Lebanon despite ceasefire
articles.body:
Strike targets house in Ansar in Nabatieh district, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency
Rania Abushamala
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
ISTANBUL
At least seven people were killed and three others injured in an Israeli airstrike on a house in southern Lebanon early Saturday, Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA) reported.
Israeli warplanes struck the house on the outskirts of the town of Ansar, in the Nabatieh district, toward the nearby town of Zrariyeh, destroying the building, the agency said.
Emergency and rescue teams were working to remove rubble and recover the bodies and injured from the site, transferring the casualties to hospitals in Nabatieh.
The attack was the first Israeli airstrike to reach this geographical depth inside Lebanon since a ceasefire took effect two months ago, according to NNA.
Separately, Israeli warplanes carried out a series of airstrikes targeting the Ali al-Taher hills on the outskirts of Nabatieh al-Fawqa, the agency reported.
Later, the Israeli army claimed in a statement that it struck Hezbollah infrastructure in the Nabatieh and Ansar areas of southern Lebanon in response to an action by the group against Israeli soldiers operating on the Ali al-Taher hills.
Despite the signing of a framework agreement between Beirut and Tel Aviv on June 26 under US sponsorship, Israel continues its assault on Lebanon, which began on March 2 and has killed 4,335 people and injured 12,277 others.
The agreement provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from all occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army there, as well as the disarmament of armed groups, with reference to Hezbollah.
Israel occupies areas in southern Lebanon, some for decades and others since the previous war between 2023 and 2024, while during the current assault, it advanced more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) into Lebanese territory.

articles.title: 20 of the best cabins, campsites and hotels in Europe’s mountains, lakes and forests
articles.body:
In the mountains …
A remote refuge in northern Italy
It’s not easy to get to Rifugio Val di Togno, at 1,317 meters (4,320ft). The dirt road from the nearest town winds for 4 miles through 27 hairpins and is best done in a four-wheel drive, or it’s a solid two-hour hike from the tiny hamlet of Carnale. But as managers Luna Lybeer and Wout Allegaert say: “We offer guests nothing so they can get away from everything.” Although you can hardly describe this beautifully renovated mountain hideout as “nothing”. Every room looks down the valley, whether through a porthole-like round window or huge floor-to-ceiling sliding doors. Breakfast, lunch (or a picnic to take on a hike), afternoon snack, aperitivo and a two-course dinner are included too – delicious vegetarian meals made using produce from the couple’s garden, or foraged nearby, along with homemade kombucha, sourdough and gnocchi.
Doubles from £298 all-inclusive (three-night minimum), rifugiovalditogno.com
An Austrian train station turned B&B
Built in 1910, the old station at Lermoos in Austria’s Tirol had stood empty for years before Johann Ehmann and his wife Cleo Weber bought it in 2019. “We were fascinated by it and contacted Austrian Railways regularly for more than five years asking if it was for sale,” says Ehmann. Now the couple have converted the classic Alpine building at the foot of Zugspitze (Germany’s highest peak) into Lermooser, a design B&B. The eight rooms range from a cosy bunk bed “cabin” to the “team XL” with three single beds and a double in a row. There’s a communal kitchen and a kiosk downstairs for coffee, pastries and homemade soups. The train still stops right outside, and hikes up to the Tuftl Alm viewpoint, and to Seebensee and Drachensee, start right from the door.
Doubles from £106 B&B, lermooser.com 
A historic wilderness hotel in Norway
In summer, the sun doesn’t set until 11pm at Røisheim, which sits on the fringes of Jotunheimen national park in southern Norway. That means all the more time to go on blue ice glacier walks and swim in mountain lakes, cycle over the Sognefjellet pass or tackle Galdhøpiggen, Norway’s tallest mountain at 2,469 metres (8,100ft). The first recorded ascent of Galdhøpiggen in 1850 started from Røisheim and the trail still leads from the courtyard of the hotel, although most hikers now choose quicker routes starting from nearby Spiterstulen. Røisheim, a time capsule of a turf-roofed hotel, has been welcoming mountain-lovers since 1858 and many of the rooms are faithfully preserved with timber-clad walls, carved wooden beds and barrel-like tubs.
Doubles from £243 B&B, roisheim.no
Alpine apartments in Bavaria
“We didn’t choose Mittenwald because we wanted to open a hotel, we chose it because we wanted to live somewhere that summer still feels like summer,” says Anne-Sophie Trinkgeld, who recently opened Karls Mittenwald in this pretty small town near the Austrian border with her husband Dario. Mittenwald came out top in their search for the best combination of climate, outdoor activities and accessibility in the Alps – it’s surrounded by mountains but just 40 minutes from Innsbruck. The couple turned the former bakery into 11 thoughtfully designed one- and two-bedroom apartments with a cafe downstairs serving breakfast spreads and homemade cakes. Just the fuel for days spent swimming in the clear waters of Lautersee, cycling to the source of the Isar River through the Karwendel nature park or hiking to Germany’s highest brewery, Karwendelbräu.
Apartments from £145 a night, karls-mittenwald.de 
An eco-campsite in the Austrian Tirol
Nearly 1,000 metres (3,280 ft) above sea level, the wide Mieming Sun Plateau is known for its mild microclimate and looping hikes through pine forests and Alpine meadows. Josef Volgger grew up on a farm here, Gerhardhof, which his parents also ran as a small guesthouse. Now Volgger, along with two business partners, has transformed Gerhardhof into a sustainability-minded campsite with grey water recycling, wood-chip heating and solar energy, as well as a naturally filtered swimming pond. You’ll still see Josef’s mother Edith in the bakery, turning out apple strudel, and there is a restaurant for dinners of wiener schnitzel and Käsespätzle (an Alpine mac and cheese).
Pitches from £38 a night, gerhardhof.com
A 500-year-old inn in the Italian Dolomites
Over its five centuries in the South Tirolean town of Lana, the building that now houses 1477 Reichhalter has had many incarnations, including a butcher, bakery, sawmill, stable and tavern. Since 2018 it has been a restaurant with eight bedrooms dressed in mid-century furniture. Room number 4, Helmsdorf, has a balcony with views of the Vigiljoch mountain and Braunsberg Castle (you can borrow a bike to explore further), while Schönmüller is another favourite for its raw plaster walls and tiled stube stove. Downstairs, tables spill on to the pedestrianised street from the restaurant, which dishes up a delicious beef tartare and house salad made with homemade pickled vegetables and whatever’s in season from the kitchen garden at sister hotel Villa Arnica.
Doubles from £170 B&B, 1477reichhalter.com
A Bauhaus guesthouse in Italy’s South Tirol
For 40 years, Johanna Fink ran her family’s Alpine hotel Briol with simple efficiency: sheets air-drying on the line, guests summoned to dinner by cowbell at precisely 7pm. Recently, her children Victoria and Valentin von Klebelsberg have taken over, but Briol remains charmingly the same. The main house was renovated in 1928 by artist Hubert Lanzinger in modernist Bauhaus style – the bedrooms have no heating (there is a hot-water bottle service), guests share a bathroom and there are no TVs, wifi or pictures on the walls. But with views like this, from a mountain meadow high above Barbiano and the Eisack valley, the lack of distraction is very welcome, and hiking trails fan out from the doorstep.
Doubles from £255 half-board, briol.it 
By the lake …
A houseboat on a Swedish lake
Stugbaat is a collection of five houseboats that bob around the huge Lake Lelång in Dalsland. Each floats on an aluminium or stainless steel pontoon, and comes with a little motorboat for towing the tiny house to a quiet corner or pootling ashore to explore. On dry land, there are mountains to climb (Egersknatten), berries and chanterelles to forage in the forest, a straw museum in Bengtsfors and a microbrewery in Torrskog. But, really, it’s all about the lake: fish from or dive off the wooden deck that surrounds the cabin or take out the paddleboard included with each booking. You can hire a kayak, check out the floating sauna, or simply drop anchor and do nothing.
From £233 a night (two-night minimum), sleeps 4, stugbaat.se
Back-to-nature cabins in Sweden
Thomas Peterson started with just one log cabin, which he handbuilt on a section of pine and spruce forest on the shores of Lake Eldan in Värmland. Then he built another, and one up in the treetops, and one floating on the water. There are now seven at Naturbyn, all off-grid (no wifi or electricity, just wood-burning stoves and paraffin lamps), all with views of the lake and some with grass roofs dotted with tiny wild strawberries. This being Sweden, there’s a sauna on the lakeshore. Beyond that, borrow a canoe, forage in the forest, watch for elk among the trees, catch a pike for supper or count shooting stars across the inky sky.
Cabins from £160 a night, sleeps 2, naturbyn.se
A waterfront hotel in Jutland
In the heart of the Danish Lake District on the Jutland peninsula, the 19th-century mill town of Silkeborg is known as Denmark’s outdoor capital. Just south of Silkeborg, the waterfront hotel Ny Hattenæs has sat on the forested shore of Brassø Lake since 1896 when it opened as a summer boarding house. It is now open year-round, but summer is still the loveliest time to stay, when days are long, the lake is filled with people swimming, paddleboarding and canoeing, and the terrace at Ny Hattenæs is the perfect place to catch the lingering twilight. Revamped in 2022 by the trio of siblings behind Danish design house Society of Lifestyle, the 14 bedrooms are filled with House Doctor furniture and the bathrooms stocked with Meraki natural products. Room number 7 is the plum pick, with a large balcony overlooking the water.
Doubles from £205 B&B, nyhattenaes.com
A new-gen hotel in Bavaria
Less than an hour’s drive south of Munich, Tegernsee is where city folk flock in the summer to drink in leafy beer gardens, tuck into knödel dumplings in farmhouse restaurants and boat on the lake. Lederhosen and dirndls are still a regular sight in some parts here, but the recently opened hotel Blyb, in the quiet village of Gmund am Tegernsee, is as far from the usual Bavarian cliches as you can get. The villa dates back to 1892, and while it still has original stucco paintings and ornate wooden balconies, they’ve been updated with crisp monochrome decor, a restaurant from the team behind the hip Munich spot Mural, an outdoor yoga deck and events that might include a doner kebab and DJ pop-up or intimate unplugged gigs in the library.
Doubles from £112 room-only, blyb.co
Lakeside cabins in a German biosphere reserve
Berlin school friends Julian Trautwein, Johann Ahlers and Christopher Eilers founded Raus in 2021 with the simple idea of getting city-dwellers like themselves out into nature. They started with a handful of sustainably built cabins near German cities and this year have added their 100th. Lodge am See takes the Raus concept and turns it into a little cabin resort, with 17 huts by a lake in the Unesco Elbe River Landscape Biosphere Reserve, between Berlin and Hamburg. The area is known for its quiet cycle paths, but the water is just as attractive, and there are free paddleboards to borrow, canoe hire nearby and sea eagles, storks and cranes to spot above the wetlands.
Cabins from £126 a night, sleep 2, raus.life 
Log cabins in Finland’s vast Lakeland
Finnish Lakeland is Europe’s largest lake district, a watery labyrinth of thousands of lakes, rivers and channels. Its biggest body of water, Lake Saimaa, is like an inland archipelago of nearly 14,000 forest-covered islands. In summer, Finns flock here to lakeside log cabins (known as a mökki), which are an essential part of Finnish culture. On the site of a historic sawmill on Saimaa’s rippling shoreline, Sahanlahti Resort embodies mökki tradition old and new, with timeless red-painted wooden cabins (some with their own saunas) and sleek modern villas that come with wraparound terraces. You may even spot a Saimaa ringed seal, one of the world’s rarest.
Cabins from £93 a night, sleep 4, sahanlahtiresort.fi 
An adults-only hideout in the Austrian Alps
Just outside the medieval town of Kitzbühel, Schwarzsee is known for its mineral-rich peat waters (its name means black lake), which are some of the warmest in the Alps, reaching 27C in summer. On a hillside above the lake, Seebichl is another black beauty, its darkly painted wooden balconies spilling over with flowers. Brothers Max and Sebastian Witzmann, whose grandfather bought Seebichl in the 1950s, have created an artsy take on a traditional Alpine hotel, with bright orange Eames chairs rather than classic carved-wood Tirolean ones and contemporary art on the walls instead of antlers. And if Schwarzsee or the heated pool in the garden at Seebichl get too balmy, hike up to the nearby Sintersbach Waterfall for a chillier dip.
Doubles from £170 B&B, hotel-seebichl.at
In the forest …
A-frame cabins in the Slovenian Alps
Famed for its emerald green water, the Savinja river runs from the Rinka Falls at the head of the pristine Logar valley in northern Slovenia down through forested gorges in the Slovenian Alps. Along its banks, Forest Camping Mozirje is a peaceful base for exploring the surrounding Savinja valley. Tents and campervans pitch up in meadows among the trees. For those allergic to pegging in a ground sheet, there are bell tents and A-frame-shaped wooden “forest beds” built from local timber. Campers swap hiking tips and debate rafting versus canyoning over dinner at communal tables in the well-stocked covered kitchen. Afterwards, gather around one of the campfires or kick back in a hammock next to the little outdoor library.
Pitches from £15 plus £14 per adult. Forest Beds from £84, campingmozirje.com
A design hotel in the Black Forest
Germany’s Black Forest (Schwarzwald) is named for the canopy of conifers so dense it blocks out much of the sunlight. It’s a mysterious place, often linked to the dark fairytales of the Brothers Grimm, although the siblings actually collected and wrote their folktales farther north around the city of Kassel. It is easy to imagine Hansel and Gretel or Little Red Riding Hood trotting down the trails, although you’re more likely to encounter German families or a hilltop castle. In the Black Forest town of Waldkirch, famous for the production of church and fairground organs, Artbau Designhotel is a sharply modern riposte to all that fairytale tweeness, with concrete walls and steel tables softened by Moroccan textiles and balconies that look out to the treetops.
Doubles from £115 room-only, artbau-designhotel.de
A forest sauna in Latvia
Deep in a pine forest near the Gauja national park, Ziedlejas is dedicated to the Latvian tradition of pirts – steamy wood-fired bathhouses heated to about 65C. There are three here: the glass pirts beside the swimming pond, the smoke pirts under the grey fir trees and the wool pirts with walls made from sheep’s wool (which releases skin-soothing lanolin). Sessions last around four hours, guided by a pirts master (pirtnieks), who takes guests through the ritual, which includes “whisking” (tapping and brushing) bodies with bundled sticks, herbal scrubs, massage and alternating hot and cold water. The glass cabin bedrooms are just as restorative, looking out across wildflower meadows by day and up to star-filled skies after dark.
Cabins from £110 a night, sleeps 2, ziedlejas.lv
Family-friendly huts and camping in the French Alps
Huttopia has dozens of nature-immersed campsites all over France (and a handful farther afield). There’s a formula – tree-shaded spots often beside lakes and rivers, pre-pitched safari tents if you don’t fancy BYO, a wood-fired pizza restaurant for the evening – and it works, with families returning year after year. Set among pine and fir trees on the banks of the Doron de Bozel river, Huttopia Bozel en Vanoise is at the gateway to the Vanoise national park near the Italian border, which is criss-crossed with hiking trails and home to ibex, marmots and chamois. Closer still is the lake beach – a five-minute walk – or canyoning on the Doron de Bozel; while back at camp kids can join the forest-school-like Petits Trappeurs or hang with new friends at after-dinner magic shows and open-air film screenings.
Nature pitch from £20, Trappeur wood and canvas tent from £146 a night, huttopia.com 
Tiny houses in a Swedish forest full of wildlife
The only alarm clock at the four off-grid cabins that make up Inforest, 2½ hours north-east of Gothenburg, is the sound of robins, blackbirds and chaffinches, perhaps joined in their dawn chorus by the odd woodpecker or cuckoo. Each solar-powered tiny house here is a kilometre apart, so your only neighbours will be the roe deer, hares and the odd moose roaming among the hectares of pine, spruce and birch trees. Almost 70% of Sweden is covered in forest and the right of public access, or allemansrätten, means you can walk or bike in every direction. For a little more action, head to the perfectly preserved wooden town of Hjo on the edge of Lake Vättern, just 4 miles away, for a sauna on the harbour or to sail on the steamship Trafik before scurrying back into the woods.
Cabins from £155 a night, sleep 2-4, inforest.se
Modernist treehouses on a farm in Sweden
In the summer of 2022, this family farm in Småland opened five striking suites on stilts among the treetops of the surrounding pine forest. This spring, Trakt Forest Hotel added seven bedrooms in its historic Erik’s House farmstead, the design more rattan headboards, crocheted cushions and views of cows grazing than the angular minimalism and secluded stillness of the treehouses. There is a restaurant, Traktköket, in a nearby log cabin and much of the food is grown on the farm or sourced locally. Outside, there’s a little sauna hut beside the farm pond, with a wood-fired bath squirrelled away deeper in the forest. The team can prepare a fika (coffee break) backpack with coffee, cake and a sandwich to take out on a hike further into the wilderness. 
Doubles from £184 B&B, traktforesthotel.com
Some of the areas mentioned above have been affected by wildfires this summer. Please check before booking.

articles.title: Westminster council threatens Charing Cross soup kitchen with closure
articles.body:
Westminster council is making it “impossible” for soup kitchens to operate by complaining about the “crowds of vulnerable people” who turn up to be fed, a charity has said.
Steven Stuart, who founded Friends of Essex & London Homeless (FOELH) with his wife, Cheryl, a decade ago, said constant complaints from the council could force the soup kitchen to shut down.
The council is also facing a licensing battle with the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, who has objected to its restrictive new draft policy that would ban new bars and pubs from opening in Soho and the West End. The council also plans to restrict “vertical drinking” – standing while having a pint – in new bars, pubs and restaurants.
The homeless charity runs a weekly event in Charing Cross, where volunteers hand out hot meals. It also provides new clothes and sleeping bags to rough sleepers, and runs a food bank.
But Westminster council has sent enforcement agents to the soup kitchen, warning that it cannot operate as it currently does and raising concerns about noise and litter.
Phil Jones, a FOELH volunteer, said: “We’ve received notice from the council that they intend to ban us from operating our weekly soup kitchen in Charing Cross. They cite litter issues but we clear away all waste and leave the area spotless, so that’s just an excuse from them.”
Stuart said: “We are facing increasing challenges with Westminster city council surrounding our weekly Charing Cross outreach. Various requirements and obstacles are making it increasingly difficult to provide the consistent support that vulnerable people have come to rely upon.”
These have included a threat of a £500 parking charge for the vehicle used to transport and distribute food, and demands that the charity obtain a costly waste disposal licence.
Stuart said: “We questioned whether this was proportionate or appropriate for a small, entirely volunteer-run charity carrying out a weekly homeless outreach but, nevertheless, we have now obtained the certificate to ensure we are fully compliant.”
The council has also turned up on several occasions with a group of police and security officers to complain about the soup kitchen, Stuart said. “From our perspective, the scale and manner of these visits have at times felt intimidating and disproportionate given the nature of the work we are carrying out.”
He has asked the council to issue permits to charities for specific days and locations, so they know what is expected of them and can carry out their volunteering without being “blind-sided” by new requirements.
A Westminster city council spokesperson said the soup kitchen was not safe at present.
“Soup kitchens can provide a valuable service but need to be carefully managed. Operators must treat vulnerable people with dignity and take care of the surrounding area,” they said.
“At the moment we have several kitchens operating at the same time and place, leading to large crowds of the most vulnerable people gathering in a confined area.”
The spokesperson said this could lead to drug dealers turning up “looking to exploit the situation”, and that the council had received complaints from residents about “antisocial behaviour, littering and crime in Charing Cross while the soup kitchen is operating”
They added: “Currently, the site is not safe for those using the service or the general public.”
The Conservative council has been taking part in a crackdown on homeless people.
The council’s deputy leader, Caroline Sargent, said of homeless sites in Westminster: “Local people and businesses are fed up with rough sleeping sites springing up, and so are we. This is totally unacceptable in the heart of a capital city.”

articles.title: Five years into Taliban rule, Afghanistan plunges into a state of collapse – visualised
articles.body:
‘I married off my daughter so that none of us would die of hunger.” Malika hesitated before saying the words aloud. The 46-year-old lives with her husband and four youngest children (three girls and a boy) in Chihil Dukhtarān, one of Kabul’s poorest neighbourhoods.
Poverty pushed the family to the brink before Malika and her husband made what they describe as the hardest decision of their lives: marrying off their eldest daughter, Maryam, for 200,000 afghanis (£2,270). She was still a teenager.
“God is my witness that during that winter, our food was almost nothing but dry bread and boiled water. Even that was often unavailable, and many nights we went to bed hungry,” she says.
“My poor daughter cried in secret … [but knew] if she refused this marriage, all of us would die from hunger, cold and misery.”
Almost two years on from Maryam’s marriage, crisis again looms for the family. Malika can no longer afford to send her two youngest daughters (aged 12 and nine) to school, so they work alongside their 16-year-old sister in a clothing factory for meagre wages. Her husband’s job is pushing a handcart, but he often returns home empty-handed – one of millions of Afghans out of work in a crippled economy. The dowry money has almost run out. Like many Afghan families, they have one resource left to tap: their girls.
Five years after the Taliban swept back into Kabul, Afghanistan has entered a quieter phase of emergency.
The fighting that once dominated international headlines has largely faded from view, but for millions of Afghans the crisis has only deepened. Nearly half the population requires humanitarian aid and more than 14 million people are expected to face acute food insecurity this year, while rights have been mercilessly restricted, women systematically erased from public life and millions of deportees forced back to an economy unable to absorb them.
An economy collapsing
The economy remains far smaller and more isolated than it was before the Taliban returned to power. Foreign trade has plummeted, and imports have increasingly outpaced exports since 2021, widening the country’s trade deficit.. Government finances have also contracted significantly. The Taliban’s most recent published budget, for the 2023 fiscal year, totalled $2.44bn, less than half the roughly $6bn budget under the previous government in 2021. In 2024, the authorities also abolished Afghanistan’s public pension system as they sought to cope with the country’s fiscal crisis.
Economic output is expanding, yet it is struggling to keep pace with rapid population growth driven by the return of millions of Afghans owing to deportation drives in Pakistan and Iran.
Inflation has added to those pressures. After averaging 3.6% in 2025, it rose to 7.6% by March 2026, driven by increasing food prices, supply disruptions and rising demand, further eroding household purchasing power.
Unemployment has almost doubled since 2021, according to the UN. More than half a million jobs have disappeared and cuts to international aid have hollowed out public spending, while rising food prices have once again squeezed household budgets.
“Five years after the Taliban takeover, Afghanistan is experiencing the world’s worst women’s rights crisis, one of the worst human rights crises and one of the worst humanitarian crises,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
Years of economic hardship, successive droughts and collapsing international aid have left millions unable to afford basic goods. The numbers are staggering. An estimated 21.9 million people – about 45% of the population – will require humanitarian assistance in 2026. About 11.6 million are children, with 3.5 million under-fives already suffering from acute malnutrition.
But that aid is not arriving. The US, once the country’s largest donor, provided more than $3bn in humanitarian and development assistance between October 2021 and December 2024. But in January 2025, President Donald Trump suspended US humanitarian funding for Afghanistan as part of a pause on all foreign aid programmes, removing a source that had accounted for about 45% of humanitarian support.
The consequences have been immediate. More than 440 health clinics have been forced to close or reduce services because of funding shortages, increasing the proportion of Afghans without access to healthcare from 16% in 2024 to 23% in 2025. Earlier this year, the World Food Programme said it now turned away three out of four acutely malnourished children seeking help because it no longer had the funds to buy food for them.
The annihilation of women’s rights
The humanitarian crisis has unfolded alongside a sweeping assault on women’s rights.
Since seizing power in 2021, the Taliban have barred girls from secondary schools, banned women from universities, excluded them from much of the workforce and public life. In 2022, women were barred from public parks and gyms; in 2024, the Taliban prohibited women from speaking audibly in public, and this year a brutal new marriage law has perpetuated domestic violence and child abuse by effectively recognising child marriage and making it much harder for women to seek divorce.
Zarifa Ghafari, formerly mayor of Maidan Shahr, and one of Afghanistan’s few female mayors, who fled the country in August 2021, says Afghan women and girls have experienced one of the “fastest and most systematic reversals of women’s rights in modern history”.
The consequences are visible across almost every measure of equality. Women’s labour force participation has fallen from about one in six women before the Taliban takeover to roughly one in 20 today. Only 18% of midwives are formally employed, while nearly 80% of female journalists have been forced from their jobs. The UN estimates that excluding women and girls from education and work is already costing Afghanistan at least $84m a year. Afghanistan no longer keeps any records of its child marriage rates, and has also prevents NGOs from gathering data.
But as girls are forced from school and parents struggle to feed their children, rights organisations believe more and more are being pushed into child marriage – with the economic and gender rights crises compounding one another.
Last year, Nilofar, a 13-year-old girl from Bamiyan, completed the sixth grade (year 7) – the final year girls are allowed to attend school. Her small frame makes her look even younger than her age. Her parents have engaged her to be married to an older relative she has never met.
“My parents tell me that now your education is over, it’s time to get married. Keeping a grown daughter at home is a heavy burden,” she says.
Afghanistan now ranks at the bottom of the Georgetown Institute’s Women, Peace and Security Index for measures of women’s inclusion, justice and security. The UN and human rights organisations have described the systematic dismantling of women’s rights as gender apartheid.
“Millions of girls have grown up knowing only exclusion instead of opportunity,” Ghafari says. “The Taliban are not only harming individual lives; they are depriving Afghanistan of doctors, teachers, engineers, entrepreneurs and future leaders. The damage will be felt for generations.” The rise of child marriage exposes girls to high rates of violence and abuse, as well as the prospect of pregnancy and childbirth at a very young age.
At the end of a crowded hospital corridor in Kabul, Shamim, 17, cradles a child in her arms as she waits to see a doctor. She looks more like a schoolgirl than a mother bringing her child to a hospital for treatment.
When approached and asked about the baby in her arms, she replies quietly, without looking up: “He’s my son.” She was forced, along with all other Afghan girls, to leave the school system in sixth grade (about 12 years old). By age 15, she was married, and less than a year later she was pregnant with her first child. Her marriage brought her family 200,000 afghanis, she says. A small portion went to buying household items, and “they used the remaining amount to pay off their debts”.
Geopolitical tensions rise
The country’s internal crises have been compounded by the forced return of millions of Afghans, mostly from neighbouring Iran and Pakistan.
Since 2023, almost 6 million people have returned after intensified crackdowns on undocumented migrants. The UN expects another 2.7 million returns between May and December this year, placing further strain on housing, jobs, healthcare and schools.
“No country can absorb that much population increase, especially a country like Afghanistan where half of the country is already in need of assistance,” says Mihyung Park, chief of mission in Afghanistan for International Organization for Migration.
Relations with Pakistan have also deteriorated sharply. Islamabad accuses the Taliban of harbouring militants from the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan group – allegations the Taliban denies. The dispute has spilled into armed clashes along the border, with exchanges of fire and airstrikes killing civilians and forcing families to flee on both sides. Repeated border closures have also disrupted trade and livelihoods in communities that depend on cross-border movement.
Yet even as rights have continued to deteriorate, the Taliban has steadily expanded its international reach.
Russia has formally recognised the government and signed a military cooperation agreement, while China and the United Arab Emirates have accepted Taliban-appointed ambassadors. Taliban officials have also met European Union representatives in Brussels to discuss migration, prompting criticism from human rights groups.
“Recognising the Taliban without meaningful progress on human rights risks legitimising a system built on gender apartheid,” says Ghafari.
As governments reopen diplomatic channels, many Afghans fear the world is learning to live with a regime that they cannot escape.
“Stability cannot be achieved by sacrificing half the population,” Ghafari says. “To Afghan women, it sends the message that geopolitical interests are outweighing their fundamental rights and freedoms.”

articles.title: The 20-year search for a vanishing custard-and-chocolate coloured moth
articles.body:
Dave Wainwright first surveyed Wallington in Northumberland for a rare custard-and-chocolate coloured moth in 2004. He parked two miles from the site, hauled a moth trap across, and was bitten by a million flies.
He did not find a single dark bordered beauty that night. The ground was heavily grazed by sheep, and the creeping willow the caterpillars depend on was “quite well plucked”.
But he was determined not to give up.
Twenty years later, walking the same Northumberland estate with project officer Charlotte Rankin and National Trust rangers, Wainwright finally found what he had been looking for since he started the job: a population of dark bordered beauty moths, the first recorded at the site since 1952.
“It was a pretty amazing feeling,” he says. “That particular site had been recorded before, but 74 years ago. I surveyed the site about 20 years ago and couldn’t find it … actually finding it after that much effort was really fulfilling.”
The dark bordered beauty is a moth with lemon-yellow wings and a deep chestnut border, sometimes described as custard-and-chocolate coloured. It is also one of the rarest moths in England.
Until this summer, Strensall Common in Yorkshire was the only known site where it survived in the country, and even that population has been collapsing. Hundreds of moths were recorded 20 years ago. The numbers record last barely reached double figures, hit by climate breakdown and a wildfire that tore through much of the reserve.
Wainwright, who is head of conservation in England at Butterfly Conservation, has spent years chasing that narrow margin across some of the country’s landscapes.
“I’ve been to a lot of remote places, particularly in Northumberland, Yorkshire and Cumbria,” he says. “I always felt the dark bordered beauty would be there. I had a sneaking suspicion, but whether or not I’d actually find it, I didn’t know.”
Looking back at that fruitless night in 2004, he now thinks the moth may have been there all along, hidden in plain sight in willow scrub too battered by grazing to support it. “It must have been there,” Wainwright says, “which makes it all the more rewarding.”
The site looks very different now to how it did back then. Where the willow was once cropped bare, there is now lush vegetation and wildflowers. This is the result of years of work between the National Trust and Fiona Goodfellow, a tenant farmer who manages the land as part of a nature recovery project spanning the estate’s 20 sq miles (5,200 hectares).
The discovery came out of a £300,000 grant awarded to Butterfly Conservation last year by the Elgol Fund for Nature to study how rare species across the north of England were coping with climate and human pressures.
For Wainwright, what makes the find matter is not just the science. It is what it means for a species he had feared was running out of time.
“Because I thought we were going to lose [dark bordered beauties] as a species,” he says, when asked why he calls this a highlight of his career.
“You don’t want a species to go extinct on your watch … you feel really powerless. It’s gratifying just knowing that the species isn’t as far down the road to extinction as we feared.”
One of the main challenges in conserving the species is that its caterpillar only eats two plants: aspen and creeping willow.
However, Wainwright still remains wary of moving too fast. The moth has survived at Wallington for more than 70 years without anyone intervening on its behalf, and he would rather understand exactly why the habitat works before anyone starts changing it.
“We wouldn’t want to rush into major changes,” he says. “You could do more harm than good by modifying it without knowing what you’re doing.”
Wainwright explains that as of right now, the work is mostly watching.
Butterfly Conservation is also in the early stages of a captive breeding programme, already planned in partnership with Yorkshire Wildlife Trust at Strensall Common. There is a longer-term hope of introducing the moth to new sites once the right conditions can be created.
Wainwright has spent his career doing the work of finding out what is actually out there and “putting dots on maps”, often in places barely anyone visits. He argues that this is important so that conservation money goes where it is needed most.
It is slow, forensic work, chasing eggs and caterpillars to work out what a moth needs to survive. But every so often, it pays off.
-

articles.title: China blasts Japanese officials’ visit to Yasukuni Shrine on WWII anniversary
articles.body:
China blasts Japanese officials’ visit to Yasukuni Shrine on WWII anniversary
Beijing protests after Japanese defence chief pays visit to controversial shrine and Sanae Takaichi sends ritual offering
Japanese Economic and Fiscal Policy Minister Minoru Kiuchi, Economic Security Minister Kimi Onoda and Hitoshi Kikawada, state minister in charge of Okinawa and the Northern Territories, also visited the shrine.
“During World War II, Japan launched wars of external aggression and committed atrocious crimes. The so-called Yasukuni Shrine is a spiritual instrument and symbol of Japanese militarism,” the Chinese foreign ministry said on Saturday.
“The 14 Class-A war criminals enshrined there were the chief culprits of the war of aggression.”
“No matter what pretext Japanese politicians invent, they cannot hide their true intention – to rehabilitate war criminals, cover up war responsibility, distort historical facts and pave the way for accelerated ‘remilitarisation’,” the ministry said in a statement.

articles.title: ‘Watch your spending, use free perks’: an insider’s tips on student money
articles.body:
Over the past two years university student Erin has been giving Martin Lewis a run for his money when it comes to hunting down the best hacks, tips and tricks to save cash and earn money.
The 21-year-old has seen Oasis for free; earned tickets to race days; made money from selling secondhand clothes (£200 in one weekend alone); and enjoyed cut-price treats with friends.
On Thursday, tens of thousands of young people found out if they had achieved the grades for the course of their choice. Now, as they celebrate, or hurriedly activate, their plan B, the day-to-day costs of student life probably aren’t uppermost in their mind. But perhaps they should be: research from Nationwide Building Society reveals that money mistakes dominate students’ list of regrets.
From failing to budget and track spending properly, overspending on nights out and relying too heavily on their overdraft, to blowing their entire student loan payment in the first few weeks, six of the top seven mistakes students have made are related to money.
“Our research shows just how much more financial pressure today’s students feel compared with previous generations,” says Tom Riley, Nationwide’s director of retail products.
Erin, who is about to start the third year of a psychology and cognitive neuroscience degree at the University of Nottingham, says going to university has “taught me loads” about managing money.
“Before I started, I’d worked and saved, but when that student loan lands in your account, it can feel a bit like free money,” she says. “It’s easy to fall into ‘girl math’ logic and justify little extras that quickly add up.”
She says that working before university and during the holidays “definitely gave me a better sense of what things actually cost”.
Erin sets herself a budget and has a rule that if she needs to go over it, she has to dip into the savings earned from her job, which, she says, focuses the mind on whether she needs to spend that money.
Her view is that wherever possible, the money she is saving “is not money I can spend [as] that is undoing all the good work I’ve done”.
To cut spending, she makes the most of discounts and deals, and joins with friends to maximise the benefits. She, and some of her friends, have Nationwide FlexStudent bank accounts, which offers a £10 Just Eat voucher every month for the first 12 months.
In her first year, she says, they pooled their vouchers and had “floor picnics” in their halls of residence, where they would all sit and share their takeaways.
It was, she says, “a life-saver because we didn’t have great cooking facilities and were on really limited budgets … It was a nice way to treat ourselves”.
Saving money has not meant missing out on a social life, as she has found ways to get into gigs and events that do not involve spending.
As a brand rep for a company that organises days out at racecourses around the UK, she gets a free ticket and transport to any events she has promoted. Tickets can be pricey for these “race day” outings, which are popular with students. She had to post a promotional message on her social media and send a link to three group chats, and she earned commission on any ticket bought via her link.
Signing up with an agency for voluntary work at events has also got her into gigs and festivals for nothing. “I got to see Oasis last year for free,” she says. “I think I did an eight-hour shift scanning tickets.” Her shift finished just as the support act ended, so she was able to watch the band’s entire set. “I was front row – that would have cost a lot of money,” she says. Her stint included a staff meal voucher.
Last year, she volunteered at Truck festival in Oxfordshire. Typically, she says, with volunteering at a festival, you may have to do two or three shifts over the weekend, but still get plenty of free time to enjoy the event.
Her savings pay for things she cannot get for free: this year the big thing she was saving for was the college ski trip. “Every bit I saved I put towards that.”
Here are her money-saving tips:
Think in hours, not pounds Before buying something, work out how many hours you would need to work to pay for it. “A couple of cocktails on a night out can easily be the equivalent of more than an hour’s wages from a summer job. It’s a good reality check and makes me think twice about the impulse purchases.”
Volunteer for freebies and perks There are lots of firms that recruit volunteers for festivals and one-day events – Erin signed up with Festaff and Wicked Events.
Turn fashion into a side hustle Erin snaps up quality pieces from charity shops and similar, some of which she upcycles before selling them on platforms such as Vinted, along with her own items that she no longer wants.
Look out for opportunities A lot of universities have brand ambassador programmes. Students often act as brand reps for nightclubs, as well as other events and venues.
Pool rewards with friends You could combine discounts and deals with housemates or friends to get better value and reduce everyday spending.

articles.title: Russia attacked Odesa region: footwear factory destroyed, fires broke out
articles.body:
Russia attacked Odesa region: footwear factory destroyed, fires broke out
Kyiv • UNN
As a result of a drone strike in Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi district, a footwear factory building was destroyed, and the cafeteria, boiler house, and a vehicle caught fire. According to preliminary data, there were no fatalities or injuries.
Russia attacked Odesa region overnight, causing the destruction of a shoe factory building and fires in Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi district, the Main Department of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine in Odesa region reported on Saturday, UNN writes.
In Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi district, drone strikes caused the destruction of a shoe factory building, followed by fires in the cafeteria, boiler room and a passenger car. The blast wave and debris damaged the glazing and façade of the administrative building
At another location, as indicated, an abandoned private residential house and dry grass nearby caught fire.
"According to preliminary information, there were no deaths or injuries," the statement said.
Rescuers dealt with the aftermath of Russia's overnight attack.

articles.title: Trump Plans to Claim Strait of Hormuz as US Territory
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump stated on Friday, Aug. 14, that he intends to declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory following the conclusion of the war with Iran.
Accoding to Clash Report, speaking at the David S. Mack Training and Intelligence Center in Garden City, Trump said the US currently controls the waterway.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“After we finish defeating Iran, which is currently suffering a crushing defeat, I will fairly soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a territory of the United States,” Trump said. “Essentially, that is exactly what it is. We have established a blockade. No ship will pass unless we want it to.”
Reuters reported that commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz nearly halted on Friday following attacks on two additional vessels. The US government indicated it is prepared to maintain the maritime blockade indefinitely.
A senior Iranian source stated that negotiations to extend a June ceasefire agreement yielded no results. Following the breakdown of the ceasefire, Iran resumed attacks on vessels it claims are attempting to navigate the strait without authorization from Tehran.
Trump on Iran:
Pretty soon, I will be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States. pic.twitter.com/ySyIIhvF5V
Iranian demands and prior negotiations
The escalation follows a list of demands issued by Iran for reopening the strait.
Mohammad Bagher Zolqadr, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, stated that Tehran requires the immediate lifting of the US naval blockade, the withdrawal of US military forces, an end to hostilities, financial compensation, and access to frozen assets.
Zelensky Struggles to Find Ukraine’s Next Envoy to Trump
On Aug. 2, Trump announced a temporary suspension of planned US military strikes to allow for diplomatic negotiations. He stipulated the immediate opening of the strait as a primary condition for any agreement.
Impact on US weapons stockpiles
The ongoing conflict has resulted in a depletion of US military stockpiles, affecting security commitments in other regions. The US has utilized over 1,500 Patriot interceptor missiles in the Middle East, reducing its current inventory to fewer than 1,700 units.
The shortage of Patriot systems, along with ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles, has delayed arms shipments to partners in Europe and Asia, affecting Ukraine’s air defense capabilities against Russian attacks. In the Indo-Pacific, the Pentagon redeployed air defense units, naval destroyers, and Tomahawk missiles from allied nations to support the Middle East campaign.
In response, the US Department of Defense directed defense contractors to accelerate production. Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg issued a letter to leading defense companies requiring plans within 21 days to expand manufacturing capacity for critical weapons.

articles.title: Estonian short film earns nod from Hollywood Shortsfest
articles.body:
Estonian short film earns nod from Hollywood Shortsfest
Estonian short film "Death is Harder Than a Broken Heart" received an honorable mention from Hollywood Shortsfest, earning a spot in the festival's official virtual program.
Director Indrek Spungin's 2025 film "Death is Harder Than a Broken Heart" earned an honorable mention from the festival jury, which evaluates entries for originality, directing, screenwriting and production value.
"It's just so incredible that an Estonian short film was noticed and recognized by a festival based in the heart of Hollywood," said producer Anu Veermäe-Kaldra.
Now in its sixth year, Hollywood Shortsfest (HSF) focuses on independent filmmakers and bringing their work to global audiences.
Veermäe-Kaldra said that both the honorable mention and its selection for HSF's official Virtual Screening Program are a major recognition for the film's cast and crew, and confirm the fact that Estonian stories can find audiences with festival programmers around the world.
HSF's next Virtual Screening Program runs October 22–25, with one film set to receive the Best of Virtual Competition Award and a screening slot at the festival's next live event in Hollywood.
"Death is Harder Than a Broken Heart" premiered at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) last year, featuring performances by Rednar Annus, Ingmar Jõela, Liina Vahtrik, Margus Prangel, Kärk Kokkota, Jarmo Reha and Karl Laumets.

articles.title: China Focus: Japanese abandoned WWII chemical weapons continue to threaten public security in China
articles.body:
HARBIN, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- The latest leak involving abandoned Japanese chemical weapons in northeast China's Jilin Province, which contaminated two Japanese personnel during disposal operations, has renewed concerns about the lingering dangers of wartime chemical weapons still buried in China.
As Saturday marks the 81st anniversary of Japan's unconditional surrender in World War II (WWII), the incident has drawn renewed attention to Unit 516, the invading Japanese army's clandestine chemical warfare unit headquartered in Qiqihar, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, during WWII.
Experts noted that Japan has yet to provide China with critical information regarding Unit 516 and the chemical weapons it abandoned at the end of the war. Some high-risk munitions remained undiscovered, and deterioration of their containers increases the risk that toxic agents could seep into soil and water sources.
At a press briefing on June 4, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning disclosed that on May 26, two Japanese personnel had their arms contaminated with toxic agents during a disposal operation in Jilin when the abandoned Japanese chemical weapons ruptured. The Chinese side immediately provided on-site medical treatment before rushing them to a hospital. After receiving treatment, they returned to Japan on May 29.
The incident was far from unprecedented. According to China's position paper submitted to the Fifth Review Conference of the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), abandoned Japanese chemical weapons have caused more than 2,000 casualties in China since the end of WWII.
This year marks the 81st anniversary of the end of WWII and of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression. The 14-year war was the longest and largest fight against foreign aggression for the Chinese people in modern times. It came with great sacrifices -- 35 million casualties among the Chinese military and civilian population -- before Japan ultimately surrendered in 1945.
Scars left by the war have yet to fully heal, and dangerous remnants from the war continue to threaten communities.
In particular, the Japanese military incorporated arsenic into its chemical weapons both to stabilize mustard agents under extremely cold conditions and to enhance their lethality. Arsenic does not naturally break down in the environment. During excavation, investigators have found many shells already corroded or even ruptured. Ongoing deterioration could allow large amounts of toxic liquid to seep into the ground, experts noted.
Such contamination could permanently pollute local soil and groundwater, increasing long-term cancer risks and threatening nearby communities for generations.
Heilongjiang has been one of the provinces most severely affected by abandoned Japanese chemical weapons. Qiqihar City, where Unit 516 was deployed during the war, is considered the epicenter of the problem.
"Unit 516 was responsible for developing a wide range of chemical warfare agents, including mustard gas, Lewisite and chlorine gas, all of which were used in combat," said Wang Tianjiao with the Qiqihar Museum.
"Qiqihar was used as a major base for Japan's chemical warfare program, so virtually every type of abandoned Japanese chemical weapon could potentially still be found here," Wang added.
The city has seen some of the worst toxic exposures over the years. On Aug. 4, 2003, construction workers unearthed five drums containing mustard gas at a building site. The leak resulted in injuries to 44 people. Some victims have since died, while many survivors continue to suffer severe pain and illnesses.
A long-term follow-up medical study published on the website of the U.S. National Center for Biotechnology Information found that severe autonomic failure, such as hyperhidrosis, pollakiuria, diarrhoea, diminished libido, and asthenia, appeared in almost all victims from the incident. Polyneuropathy occurred in 35 percent of the victims and constricted vision in 20 percent of them, among other malfunctions. Many continued to suffer from severe post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression years after exposure.
In the years following the 2003 incident, abandoned Japanese artillery shells were discovered repeatedly at construction sites and disused factories across Qiqihar.
On July 30, 2010, a group of school kids in Qiqihar were found fiddling with three rusted shells, with fuses still attached to two of the shells. The terrifying discovery sent local police into an intense excavation that lasted over eight hours. By the end of the operation, they had recovered 359 artillery shells of various types from a disused factory. The shells were later identified as abandoned by Japanese invaders.
Shortly afterwards, another 63 shells were uncovered at a construction site and later identified as abandoned by Japanese troops. Thanks to the prompt response of local police, the danger was neutralized without any casualties.
Wang estimated that Unit 516 abandoned roughly 200,000 chemical munitions at the end of WWII. Some were buried underground, while others were dumped into the Nenjiang River. "Unlike germ warfare weapons, effectiveness of which diminishes over time, chemical weapons remain highly toxic for a long time," he said.
Japan has continued to withhold information on the locations, quantities and types of these abandoned weapons, as well as details about Unit 516, hampering efforts to recover and destroy them.
Historical records indicate that abandoned chemical weapons are scattered across numerous burial sites in widely varying quantities. Their small size and varying burial depths make them especially difficult to locate.
Under the CWC, Japan was required to complete the destruction of all abandoned chemical weapons in China by the end of 2007. However, the deadline has already been postponed four times.
Furthermore, legal efforts to seek accountability have also met setbacks. On Sept. 21, 2012, the Tokyo High Court rejected an appeal by victims of the 2003 Qiqihar chemical leak incident seeking state compensation from the Japanese government.
While acknowledging that the abandoned Japanese chemical weapons had caused the injuries, the ruling denied the Japanese government's liability for inaction, citing the lack of clarity over the locations where the chemical agents had been abandoned and the inability to prevent the incident from occurring.
Twenty-three years after the 2003 incident, many of the original 44 victims have died. Those who remain continue to suffer debilitating long-term health problems.
Hao Yanzhi, whose wife Niu Haiying was among the victims, said his wife's immune system has steadily weakened over the years. The youngest victim of the incident dropped out of school at an early age and has endured chronic pain and poor immunity for more than two decades.
Many survivors say they do not know whether they will live long enough to hear an official apology from the Japanese government. ■
