articles.title: What’s in it for Gen Z in PM Modi’s Independence Day speech? AI skills, free coaching, sports & jobs
articles.body:
AI, jobs, free coaching & sports: What PM Modi offered Gen Z on Independence Day
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 15, 2026, 16:16 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Prime Minister Narendra Modi interacts with students during the 80th Independence Day celebrations, at Red Fort in New Delhi. (PTI Photo)
NEW DELHI: From artificial intelligence training for one crore young people to free online coaching for competitive examinations, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Independence Day speech had several announcements aimed directly at India's youth, with technology, jobs, entrepreneurship and skills forming a key part of the message.Addressing the nation from the Red Fort on the 80th Independence Day, PM Modi said India's youth would be the biggest beneficiary as well as the biggest enabler of the country's ambition to become a developed nation by 2047. He linked the Viksit Bharat goal to the country's young population and outlined initiatives spanning AI, education, sports, manufacturing and entrepreneurship.PM Modi announced that one crore youth would be trained in artificial intelligence-related skills. The announcement came as he described AI, quantum technology, robotics, space and data centres as defining technologies of the current era and called for India to become a global hub of innovation."When I speak of a developed India, when I speak of propelling the nation forward at a rapid pace, the greatest beneficiary and the greatest enabler of this vision is the youth of my country, the youthful energy of my nation.
Not only that, but the greatest beneficiary of a developed India is also the youth of my country. Therefore, we must advance the goal of a developed India by linking it with our youth," PM Modi said.For students and young people preparing for government and other competitive examinations, PM Modi announced free online coaching. The initiative was among the youth-focused measures announced during the address.The prime minister also announced a nationwide sports talent hunt to identify and nurture children aged five to 15 years across villages and cities, expanding the focus on identifying sporting talent at an early age.
AI training for 1 crore youth
AI was one of the biggest technology-related announcements in PM Modi's speech. He said one crore young people would receive training in AI skills as India seeks to build capabilities in emerging technologies.PM Modi placed the initiative within his broader 'Shakti Ki Saptadhara' framework, under which technology and innovation form the third stream of India's development strategy."The third strength of the Saptadhara is technology and innovation. This is the era of robotics, AI, quantum technology, space and data centres. Emerging technologies are presenting new challenges, and we must become a global hub of innovation," PM Modi said.He also pointed to India's existing digital infrastructure, including UPI and Digital Public Infrastructure, and said the country needed to take the next step in emerging technologies."We have already demonstrated our strength through UPI and Digital Public Infrastructure. Now, we must take the next leap in next-generation communication technology," he added.The AI training plan comes as PM Modi has repeatedly linked India's young workforce with the country's technology ambitions, with the latest announcement putting a specific focus on building AI-related skills at scale.
Free online coaching for competitive exams
For young people preparing for competitive examinations, PM Modi announced free online coaching.The initiative is aimed at making preparation resources available to youth without requiring them to rely exclusively on physical coaching centres.PM Modi said, "The race for coaching classes has become a massive burden for our middle-class families. Every parent feels that if they don't send their child to a coaching class, they aren't considered a 'prestigious' family. We are concerned about the thousands of crores of rupees these poor and middle-class families spend; we want to save them that expense. We have decided to provide free online coaching for various competitive exams for our youth. We have digital public infrastructure, as well as excellent talent and teachers. By leveraging these resources, we are establishing a comprehensive network to provide free coaching to the nation's youth."
The announcement was made alongside the AI skilling plan as part of the government's broader focus on connecting India's youth with opportunities created by the country's development and technology push.PM Modi said the country's development target must be linked directly with young people, describing them as both the principal beneficiaries and enablers of Viksit Bharat.
Sports talent hunt for children aged 5 to 15
PM Modi also announced a nationwide sports talent hunt to identify and nurture children between five and 15 years of age.The programme will cover children in villages as well as cities, with the focus on identifying sporting talent at an early age and developing it further.
The announcement adds sports to the list of areas through which the government plans to connect young Indians with the broader Viksit Bharat vision.PM Modi also referred to the growing role of women in sports, STEM education, aviation and the armed forces during his address.
Jobs, manufacturing and MSMEs
Beyond direct youth-focused announcements, PM Modi's seven-point roadmap placed manufacturing, agriculture, technology, infrastructure, defence, green and blue economy, and soft power at the centre of India's growth strategy.For Gen Z entering the workforce, manufacturing and MSMEs were among the sectors PM Modi highlighted as areas with global opportunities.He urged Indian businesses, particularly MSMEs, to use free trade agreements to take Indian products to international markets."We have to reach the world. Everything that India produces should reach the world market," Modi said.PM Modi said Indian products in sectors such as textiles, machinery, pharmaceuticals, fisheries and seafood should expand their presence in global markets. He also stressed that companies would need to compete on international standards of cost, quality and scale.In manufacturing, PM Modi said India should become a reliable hub in global supply chains."From Design to Manufacturing, India must become a reliable hub in the global supply chain. For this, I want to place special emphasis on 3 things. My brothers and sisters in the field of Manufacturing, do not let this opportunity slip away. For this, we will have to meet global standards on cost, quality, and scale," PM Modi said.
Start-up and technology opportunities
Technology and innovation were central to PM Modi's seven-point roadmap, with AI, quantum technology, robotics, space and data centres identified as areas where India should develop global capabilities."The third strength of the Saptadhara is technology and innovation. This is the era of robotics, AI, quantum technology, space and data centres. Emerging technologies are presenting new challenges, and we must become a global hub of innovation," PM Modi said.The prime minister also called for India to take the lead in next-generation communication technology, including 6G.For young entrepreneurs and technology professionals, PM Modi also spoke about the need for Indian technology companies to build globally recognised brands."India's technology companies should be a scoreboard in the world," he said.
Defence, green economy and creative industries
PM Modi's roadmap also identified defence production, the green economy and India's soft power as areas for future growth.In defence, he called for self-reliance and the development of next-generation defence technologies, with India aiming to become a global supplier."The importance of defence capability is paramount in every sense. My dear citizens, achieving Aatmanirbharta in defence is essential; India and the world have realised that there is no alternative. When the world looks out for itself, India cannot merely remain an arms market for other nations," he said.The sixth stream, the green and blue economy, covers renewable energy, energy storage, green manufacturing, fisheries, coastal tourism and ocean technology."The sixth strength of the Sapta Dhara is the Green economy. We must work in the areas of renewable energy, energy storage, green storage and manufacturing. India has an opportunity in the area of the Blue Economy. "The seventh stream is India's soft power, covering yoga, Ayurveda, handicrafts, culture, films, animation, gaming and digital content."The seventh strength of the Sapta Dhara is India's soft power. Today, Yoga has connected the world to India. Our Ayurveda, holistic healthcare, handicrafts, culture, films, animation, gaming, digital content. The world is recognizing and looking forward to India's WAVES summit. We have more than 100 national parks. We have an opportunity to attract foreign tourists through the power of soft power."
From ‘Fragile Five’ to a growing economy
PM Modi also used his Independence Day address to highlight India's economic transformation over the past 12 years, saying the country had moved from the 'Fragile Five' to becoming the world's fastest-growing major economy.He said India was now aiming for a larger role in global manufacturing, technology and trade and set out a goal of building Viksit Bharat by 2047.PM Modi cited growth in defence production, electronic manufacturing, railway coach production, internet use and digital transactions as indicators of the country's economic and technological expansion.
He also announced that India had begun production at three semiconductor plants, with five to eight more plants expected to come up in the coming years.For Gen Z, the message running through PM Modi's youth-focused announcements was centred on acquiring skills in emerging technologies, accessing education and competitive-exam preparation, identifying sporting talent and participating in sectors that the government has identified as drivers of India's growth.

articles.title: Son of former Mexican president blasts US barring him from entering country
articles.body:
Jorge Antonio Rocha
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
The son of a former Mexican president, also a prominent figure within Mexico’s ruling political sphere, said Friday that the Trump administration has revoked his visa to enter the US, blasting the move as "political" and baseless.
Andres Manuel Lopez Beltran denounced the US State Department's revocation in a fiery letter posted to social media addressed to President Donald Trump.
“I am writing to you with personal respect and respect for your office to inform you that Marco Rubio, Secretary of State, and Christopher Landau, Under Secretary of State — who has dubbed himself the ‘visa revoker’ — have ordered that my authorization to enter the United States of America be revoked,” he wrote on US social media platform Instagram.
The move comes amid allegations against high-profile officials linked to Mexico’s ruling party, Morena.
In addition to being the son of former President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, Beltran is a political leader within Morena. He served as the party’s secretary of organization, a position he left to pursue a seat in the lower house of Congress.
“As is evident, this decision is political — or rather, petty political and propagandistic — in the Hitlerian style, as there is no reason to justify such arrogant conduct. It is worth emphasizing that these officials have no evidence against me concerning any immoral or criminal act,” Lopez Beltran added.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum also called the move political.
“In my opinion, this cancellation of visas that they have carried out … has an essentially political purpose, because it is not applied equally to all countries if the reason were related to criminal activity,” she told a news conference.
The US has sought to expand its influence in Mexico since Trump returned to the White House. Since the start of his second term, Trump has threatened a trade war and airstrikes on Mexican soil, while accusing politicians and governors linked to Morena of being involved in drug trafficking, and demanding their extradition.

articles.title: East Australian coal mine granted 6-year extension
articles.body:
SYDNEY, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- The state government of Australia's New South Wales (NSW) has granted a six-year extension to the operating life of a coal mine north of Sydney.
The NSW Planning Department on Friday granted MACH Energy's application to extend the life of the Mount Pleasant coal mine, located 180 km north of Sydney, to the end of 2032 and to increase its annual extraction rate from 10.5 million tonnes to 12.5 million tonnes.
The decision was made four months before the mine was set to close at the expiry of existing mining approvals in December amid an ongoing court battle over a 22-year extension.
The owner of the mine, MACH Energy, was granted a 22-year extension through to 2048 in 2022, but it was subsequently blocked by the NSW Court of Appeal in 2025 after a local environmental group challenged it.
MACH Energy subsequently challenged the ruling in the High Court of Australia and applied for the shorter six-year extension while awaiting a decision.
The NSW Court of Appeal found that when it blocked the extension, the Independent Planning Commission failed to take into account the mine's impact on the environment and climate.
The High Court heard the appeal in May and is currently deliberating. ■

articles.title: Dried up creeks and missing waterfalls: What I found on a trip to Austria’s most famous gorge
articles.body:
Heatwaves and lack of winter snow and summer rain have dried up the waterfalls in the Bärenschützklamm.
A day out at Austria's most famous gorge, the Bärenschützklamm, usually means climbing over thundering waterfalls and fast-flowing cold creeks. But this year I found the gorge in a very different state. The water, which attracts 40,000 tourists a year, is gone. The waterfalls have dried up and the creeks are so dry that you can walk along their beds like any other trail.
Gerhard Jantscher, chairman of Austrian Alpine Club Österreichischer Alpenverein, Sektion Mixnitz, tells Euronews Earth that the Alps are suffering in the face of global warming, summer heatwaves, drought and the lack of snow and rain. The landscape - formed over hundreds of years - is changing fast.
"By the end of July, the flow of water through the Bärenschützklamm gorge had ceased due to a lack of precipitation. The water source is the Mixnitz Stream, which originates on the Sommeralm and flows via the Teichalm to the Bärenschützklamm. The region relies heavily on natural precipitation so that the Sommeralm and Teichalm areas can absorb the rainfall and gradually feed it into the Mixnitz Stream."
It would take at least a week of steady rain for the Bärenschützklamm's water levels to recover.
Breathtaking gorge even without water
Don't get me wrong - the gorge is wonderful even without the waterfalls. Walking, or more likely scrambling, between or under majestic rock formations and trees reveals the raw power of nature. The trail takes you across free-floating wooden ladders, built over 100 years ago.
After a deadly accident in 2020, the gorge was closed until this year. During this time, authorities spent more than €2 million making the trails safer.
"We began planning the safety measures and the construction of the walkway system in 2021. We, the Mixnitz Section of the Austrian Alpine Club (ÖAV), were able to raise these funds through our own personal efforts in order to make the Bärenschützklamm accessible to tourists," Jantscher explains.
The Bärenschützklamm was declared a natural monument in 1978. Due to the weather, the wooden ladders and even the rocks have to be checked every year.
"Sigi Wentner (deputy chairman and mountain rescue warden) and I are the ones spearheading the Bärenschützklamm project, and we do this work on a voluntary basis.
"What does the future hold? We have to consult geological experts - which we do every spring - to understand the behaviour of the rock faces, trees, and water, and to be able to intervene should any changes occur. Every year, the Bärenschützklamm undergoes a geological and technical inspection by the relevant authorities and is officially approved for public access," says Jantscher.
Climate change and lack of precipitation
Before the impacts of climate change took hold, precipitation (rain or snow) was abundant in the mountains, exceeding 1,000 millimetres per year almost everywhere, and often 1,500 mm. Winter is usually the driest season in the Austrian Alps, while summer is the wettest season because of afternoon thunderstorms.
This year - as in all of Europe - brought long heatwaves and lack of rain. According to GeoSphere Austria from 1 January to 30 June 2026, precipitation in the country was 27 per cent below the long-term average. That in itself would not be particularly unusual. However, in some parts of the country, conditions have not been this dry since 1885.

articles.title: Is the US ready for President Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez?
articles.body:
“They assume that my ambition is positional. They assume that my ambition is a title or a seat. And my ambition is way bigger than that. My ambition is to change this country.”
The words were delivered slowly, deliberately and with some steeliness by Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Her audience, crammed into the pews of Rockefeller Memorial chapel at the University of Chicago, burst into spontaneous applause. That was in May. In the three months since, the speculation around Ocasio-Cortez’s ambitions – for herself and for America – has only grown louder.
Friends and foes alike wonder if the stars are aligning for the New York congresswoman to run for US president in 2028. They point to voters raging against the machine – including the ageing Democratic party establishment – and hungry for change. They note how progressives pushing for economic justice and universal healthcare have won a string of impressive victories in mayoral elections and congressional primaries over the past year.
Then there are the opinion polls. Last month a Granite State Poll from the University of New Hampshire found Ocasio-Cortez leading a potential Democratic field in that crucial state. She has the kind of name recognition that money can’t buy, nearly 10m followers on Instagram alone and fans ranging from the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) to Nancy Pelosi, the former speaker of the House of Representatives.
As Barack Obama, Donald Trump and Joe Biden showed, presidential elections have a habit of finding the right person at the right time in the right place. Ocasio-Cortez, a 36-year-old with a progressive agenda and can’t-be-taught social media smarts, could meet the moment for a nation eager for a fresh start after a decade of Trumpism.
If modern politics is about pendulum swings, it is hard to imagine anyone who better personifies a rebuke of the octogenarian Trump and his nativist “Make America great again” (Maga) movement. This week a Zogby Strategies national poll found that a generic democratic socialist candidate leads generic Maga candidate 45% to 33%.
Ashik Siddique, a co-chair of the DSA, of which Ocasio-Cortez is a member, said: “If she were to throw her hat in the ring, there would be a lot of excitement for it from members of Democratic Socialists of America. We definitely want to see a strong working class voice in the 2028 presidential primary.”
Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out a run for president and her actions have done nothing to quell the notion of a campaign in stealth mode. Last year she joined her mentor, the independent senator Bernie Sanders, on a “Fighting Oligarchy” tour that drew huge crowds. More recently she has crisscrossed the country to support progressive candidates, further enhancing her national profile.
In the past week alone she made two moves that intensified political pundits’ chatter. First Ocasio-Cortez used Instagram to announce that she is freezing her eggs, a decision she described as a move to “feel more in control of my life”. She acknowledged the “political risk” in sharing personal family planning details but stated her goal is to normalise conversations about the professional and personal challenges women face. The internet quickly became awash in speculation that Ocasio-Cortez ended her relationship with and engagement to long-time partner Riley Roberts , driven by reports from Puck News and others noting she had long since stopped appearing with him in public and mentioning his name.
Then, when asked by ABC interviewer Jonathan Karl about the cultural battles of the 2020 pandemic era – including calls from some on the left to defund the police – she laughed and, quoting a New York city council ally, remarked: “Woke One was crazy” – apparently trying to draw a strategic line between hard-fought struggles for racial justice and the performative excesses of lockdown isolation that became an easy target for the right.
Unlike many would-be presidents of the time, Ocasio-Cortez does not appear to be driven by personal ego, according to those who knew her, which may prove to be her political superpower. She was a volunteer organiser for Sanders’ 2016 campaign, his first presidential run and one that built a national movement around his vision of democratic socialism, even as he lost to former secretary of state Hillary Clinton.
When she decided to run for office herself, the former bartender and waitress had virtually no money but was assisted by progressive organisations such as Brand New Congress and Justice Democrats. In 2018 she beat 10-term incumbent congressman Joe Crowley, a member of the Democratic leadership and potential future speaker, in a New York primary.
Corbin Trent, her first communications director in the House of Representatives and the co-founder of Justice Democrats, was there on the night she ousted Crowley. He recalls that the political industrial complex began trying to map her career path before the ink on the ballots was even dry.
“Primary night, she beats Joe Crowley,” he recalled. “I get phone calls from elected officials and other people and their question is, what’s next? What’s the pathway here? What’s she going to run for? What higher office would she seek? This is literally a few hours after the polls close in the primary. That’s the way DC thinks. Not, hey, what can we do with Medicare for all or this or that or any of the other things?”
As Ocasio-Cortez’s national profile exploded – bringing in $15m in her first electoral cycle and attracting unprecedented demands from foreign heads of state – Trent tried to lay out a long-term strategic map. He suggested upstate New York events to prepare for a statewide Senate run. But she resisted the logic of political careerism.
“To my chagrin and frustration that never was a way in which she could plan or operate. She did not have an idea in her head of this ultimate prize of president or governor or senator.”
Instead, Trent argues, her appeal lies in a rare authenticity – an ability to validate the deep-seated economic anxiety of Americans. “Alexandria has two things going for her. She’s genuinely curious about other people. It’s not like she has to pretend to be. I’ve had politicians ask me, ‘How can I be more genuine?’ Well, that’s probably not going to help if you have to fucking ask me that.
“Two, she is genuinely open about herself. Some people believe that nobody cares what they think or who they are and then other people don’t want you to know who they are. She doesn’t suffer from either of those failings.”
Other observers agree that Ocasio-Cortez has that X factor missing from so many professional politicians: relatability. Chris Scott, a political strategist who served as the coalition director for Kamala Harris’s 2024 presidential campaign, said: “When you talk about AOC’s humble beginnings being a bartender that’s a lived experience story that resonates, especially with millennials, with their upbringing.
“What you are starting to see – whether it’s conservative or progressive - is people are leaning more and more towards candidates with lived experience that they feel they relate to as politics gets more polarising.”
That said, Ocasio-Cortez has now been in Washington long enough to draw accusations of going from outsider to insider. The activist who critiqued the establishment and championed the Green New Deal has spent recent years working closely with Democratic leadership. This week she received warm praise from Pelosi, who told a Politico summit in Sacramento, California: “I think that she has been so operational, and it’s just wonderful. I know it’s a joy to work with her.”
The transition has caused some on the far left to wonder if the system has simply co-opted its most dangerous critic. Cenk Uygur, a controversial political commentator and co-founder of the online progressive news show The Young Turks, watches Ocasio-Cortez’s recent evolution with a mixture of policy agreement and tactical despair.
Ocasio-Cortez has described Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “genocide” and last month voted to block US military aid to the country. But Uygur has not forgotten her high-profile appearance at the 2024 Democratic National Convention, where she delivered a rousing speech praising vice-president Harris’s efforts to secure a ceasefire in Gaza — a claim that many leftwing activists viewed as a dishonest whitewashing of the administration’s complicity in the conflict.
“Why did she basically fib on Kamala Harris’s behalf during the DNC and pretend that Kamala Harris cared about Palestinians and was trying to keep the Israelis in check?” he said. “Because she secretly loves Israel? No, it’s because she wanted to prove to mommy and daddy that she’s a good girl. If you’re a good girl you support Kamala Harris and, if you need to, you fudge her record.
“Then you go tell Jonathan Karl that your side is ‘crazy’ and you changed and you can’t explain what you changed into or how you changed or why you changed. But the message is super clear both for the establishment and progressives: ‘I’m not going to challenge the system so establishment, you can rest easy, I’m not a threat.’ And they have rested easy. That’s why she’s getting enormously positive coverage.”
The 2028 Democratic presidential primary election is expected to be crowded and noisy. If Ocasio-Cortez runs, she might face challenges from fellow progressive Congressman Ro Khanna of California along with heavyweights including Harris, Pete Buttigieg, Gavin Newsom and Jon Ossoff. Some Democrats, scarred by Clinton and Harris’s defeats in 2016 and 2024, might be reluctant to nominate Ocasio-Cortez out of perceived expediency if they believe the US is still not ready to elect its first female president, a fear expressed by former first lady Michelle Obama among others.
The congresswoman faces another potentially formidable hurdle. Centrist Democrats have long argued that the democratic socialist wing of the party might succeed with white, college-educated voters but struggles to connect with African American communities, pointing to primary races where progressive insurgents have hit a wall. That could prove decisive in an early primary state such as South Carolina.
Nina Turner, a national co-chair of Sanders’ 2020 campaign, who has just been travelling in South Carolina, said: “There are some rumblings in some segments of the Black community that DSA and progressives in general are not doing what it takes to court Black voters and in some ways are leaving us behind for other people who are of colour but not Black.
“That’s real and so DSA as well as progressives are going to have to do something to say, no, we understand the Black plight and we understand that the survival of working-class people comes through Black liberation. They have not done a good job of doing that. I’m hoping that they will.”
Antjuan Seawright, a Democratic strategist in South Carolina, suggests that Ocasio-Cortez’s national viability depends on her remaining a disciplined team player who addresses universal, kitchen-table concerns. He said: “I would love her to run as far away as she can from being any sort of liability in places where we know we have to win in November where we’ve lost before because people have been used as a weapon of mass political destruction and distraction.
“If she continues to talk about health care in such a way that is accessible and affordable for all Americans without burning down the system, but making some alterations to the system, she will be a positive voice to the conversation.”
If she runs, Ocasio-Cortez can also expect a crude onslaught from Republicans and a rightwing media machine that has spent years demonising her as a radical communist who threatens the essence of America. Her “Woke One was crazy,” comment has been seen as an attempt to assuage the concern.
Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill, said: “That was a very interesting strategic decision to do that and that’s her way of trying to moderate. But she’s palling around with Bernie Sanders and hasn’t completely, as far as I’m aware, repudiated [the influencer] Hasan Piker and some of those leftwing folks. People are not going to forget that and, in this day and age of the internet, it lives forever.”
Setmayer, cofounder of the Seneca Project, a women-led, bipartisan political super political action committee, argues that, instead of campaigning for the White House, Ocasio-Cortez could seek to cement her legislative power by challenging Chuck Schumer for his New York Senate seat.
“If I were advising her, given the failures, unfortunately, of women candidates for the Democrats over the last two election cycles, it would behoove her to run for Senate,” Setmayer said. “She’s almost guaranteed to win that Senate seat.
“It would provide her more gravitas and she’s young enough that she could do a term or two – or a term and a half like Barack Obama – and then run for president. I don’t think that she can go from being a congresswoman to a serious presidential candidate without some time in the Senate.”
History, however, is littered with examples of White House aspirants who waited their turn and missed their moment. There are others, such as Obama, who said “carpe diem” and rode a wave all the way into the Oval Office.
Ocasio-Cortez, who would beat Theodore Roosevelt and John F Kennedy to become the youngest US president in history, has said her ambition is way bigger than that. The calling to change America may prove irresistible.
Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, said: “When you look at the current trajectory of the Democratic party, she is the natural successor to the Bernie Sanders-Elizabeth Warren coalition. She is one of the most gifted communicators in all of politics.
“She is someone who engenders a tremendous amount of passion, either for or against. She does possess the unique quality of: people give a shit. She’s got a lot more going for her than most people. She never has to worry about standing out. The attention vacuum that we live in, and the way that content works, she is in a league of her own.”

articles.title: I feel guilt talking to those left behind in Afghanistan. While I enjoy freedom, they are prisoners | Nelufar Hedayat
articles.body:
There are fewer and fewer stories coming out of the land of my birth. Before, I would open Instagram and see my cousins, lip-syncing to trending videos, posing with flowers at a rose garden or at a trendy cafe in their coolest outfits, keeping a record of their lives. I would hear British-Afghan friends talk about their recent trips to the provinces, towns and cities of their foremothers and the buzz of learning about their heritage. I would eagerly await the latest music video from Afghanistan’s many pop stars, all vying to become the hottest track played at weddings, not just in Afghanistan but all over the world. Afghanistan, its culture, and people felt closer back then.
Five years ago today, the brittle peace of the fragile new democracy was shattered by the withdrawal of western military, diplomatic and charitable groups that had intervened in the country’s fate since 2001. Overnight, on Sunday, 15 August 2021, Afghanistan was undone and abandoned.
I spent the rest of the month glued to my phone, monitoring WhatsApp groups sprouting every day or so, with people asking for information and help, begging me to get them out of the country because we all knew what was coming, though the rest of the world seemed to lag behind.
I was most focused on evacuating one friend from Kabul. She was a headteacher, and it was always her house I would go to first, whenever I went to Afghanistan. I had to have achingly tough phone conversations with her. “You can’t bring your children or your husband. I can only do this for you,” I said. She would agree. “I think I can get you to Albania or Qatar, but you might be in a refugee camp for months or years.” She would agree.
The closest we came to getting her out her came six months later, in February 2022. I finally managed to get her a passport when it was virtually impossible to do so, but by then it was too late. The Taliban were running the airport and had cracked down on Afghans leaving the country.
The last conversation we had on the phone was one of the hardest of my life. I had to tell the woman who had inspired me for so long, a feminist and someone who had advocated for education and self-fulfilment her whole life, that I was going to stop trying to rescue her. “I’ve tried everything I can think of and pushed everyone I know, but I can’t get you on a flight out.” I felt her spirit break as her uncertain fate collapsed into one reality – a life under Taliban rule.
In a higher register than I had ever heard her voice before, she told me that this was going to wreak havoc on her already unmanageable diabetes; that she would never work or be self-sufficient again, and then she asked me a terrible question: surely to end her life now was better than carrying on?
After all, this was the second time in my friend’s life that she would have to live under a Taliban regime. Neither of us spoke in a protracted, painful silence as we both felt the crushing weight of a learned helplessness that she and millions of Afghans would become intimately familiar with. The line went dead.
Since then, our lives have diverged so much we cannot have a proper conversation. We try to speak but it feels as if the phone line is connecting parallel universes. Mine is full of work, family gatherings, gigs and holiday plans and hers of bombs, “morality police” and hand-to-mouth living. We both hesitate to share stories about our lives for fear it will upset the other. We have been rendered speechless.
With the birth of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan ruled de facto by the Taliban regime, life changed immediately for my family and friends. The systemic assault on the female sex has resulted in the UN calling for gender apartheid to be recognised as a distinct crime against humanity.
“During the previous government, my mother forced me to go to school, attend taekwondo classes, and visit the library,” says a friend who was 14 at the time of the western desertion of Afghanistan. “She wanted me to learn and have opportunities. My father agrees with the Taliban’s rules. He believes I should get money from my future husband instead. For me, this feels like being sold, and it is something I cannot accept.”
It’s not just a gender war that has been raging in Afghanistan. In February 2026, Pakistan declared “open war” with its neighbour, unleashing airstrikes that killed hundreds, displacing many thousands more and devastating lives.
A cousin tells me of the unadulterated fear these airstrikes brought on the citizens of Kabul. “It was truly frightening. Pakistani drones were launching rocket attacks, and we could only see the flames and hear the explosions in despair. I kept thinking that perhaps this time a rocket might strike our house.”
Add this to the 6 million refugees forced back to Afghanistan by Iran and Pakistan, the EU meeting with the Taliban in Brussels for closed-door talks, and half the population facing severe food insecurity, and you’d be forgiven for thinking, like me, that even God is merciless when it comes to the land of my birth.
It’s not that similar things hadn’t happened in Afghanistan before August 2021; it’s that I would also hear of other stories. Stories of heroism, a fight for democracy, a burgeoning arts scene, or event skating teenagers rocking the streets of Kabul. Now, there’s so little to do, such little movement possible, that almost everyone I speak to in Afghanistan sounds as though they’re suffocating. There is no distraction nor relief from the abject suffering of everyday Afghan people.
The question now is what does resistance and resilience look like? The Taliban are not an inevitability. In their entire history, they have been in power half as long as UK and US forces were in Afghanistan: 10 years.
Afghan people must keep their stories alive, of who and what we are, to help us rebuild an identity of our own making outside occupation and brutal theocracy for when the day arrives that the Taliban are no more. For me, that will mean calling my friend to learn about her life – to have, for the first time in five years, the impossible conversation.
- 
  Nelufar Hedayat is an Afghan-British journalist, and the presenter and co-director of the documentary In Real Life: the God Thieves

articles.title: Meera Sodha’s recipe for black rice salad with tomatoes, tamarind and green beans | Meera Sodha recipes
articles.body:
Here’s a recipe straight out of the low-effort, high-reward school of cooking, in which you chop the vegetables and nuts, boil the rice and beans, throw over a dressing … and it’s done! It was written in the middle of a heatwave, when cooking felt impossible, but I couldn’t look at another watermelon and feta salad. The trade-off is that this dish relies heavily on a couple of key ingredients: sambal oelek (which gives the salad its sparkle) and black rice, which, unlike other types of rice in a salad, never tastes worthy.
Black rice salad with tomatoes, tamarind and green beans
Black rice is sometimes sold as “venus black rice” or “black pearl rice”, and cooking times vary from 20-40 minutes, depending on whether the rice has been par-cooked (you’ll know only by checking the cooking time listed on the packet). Sambal oelek can be bought from Asian supermarkets or online, while tamarind paste can vary, though branded ones available from supermarkets tend to be good – if yours is from an Asian supermarket, however, I’d suggest adding it half a tablespoon at a time only at the end, until the mix tastes right to you.
Prep 15 min
 Cook Up to 1 hr (depending on the rice)
 Serves 4
5 tbsp neutral oil (eg, groundnut, sunflower or rapeseed)
2 garlic cloves, peeled and minced
4½ tbsp light soy sauce
  1½ tbsp tamarind paste
  1 tbsp dark brown sugar
  ½ tbsp sambal oelek – I like Lucullus
200g fine green beans, topped
350g black venus rice (AKA black pearl rice)
350g cherry tomatoes, halved
100g frozen shelled edamame beans, defrosted
60g roasted unsalted cashews, roughly chopped
40g fresh coriander, chopped
Bring a large pan of water to a boil, then cock a lid over the top. Meanwhile, make the dressing: in a large bowl, mix the oil, garlic, soy, tamarind paste, sugar and sambal oelek.
Once the water is boiling, drop in the beans and cook for six to eight minutes, until tender. Scoop out with a slotted spoon or tongs, shake off the excess water, then tip into the dressing bowl.
Gently pour the rice into the still boiling water, then cook according to the packet instructions, until tender. Drain, rinse under cold water and drain again well.
Tip the rice into the bean bowl, add the tomatoes, edamame, cashews and coriander, toss to combine, then serve.

articles.title: Concerns grow over increased global ties with Taliban in Afghanistan
articles.body:
The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses.
Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare.
Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement in human rights in return for any diplomatic concessions.
The United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression. Afghanistan has become a “graveyard for human rights,” the UN said in March.
India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul.
“There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even with Europe and the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.
“The Taliban see any kind of contact as a diplomatic win and they have been able to capitalise on that as a sign granting legitimacy to the regime.”
A strict policy of isolation imposed after the Taliban seized power in 2021 towards informal or “de facto” recognition is now fragmenting. Some western commentators have suggested more countries recognise the regime. Others want intensified “back channel” engagement.
“We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“There should be a consistent and coherent message from the international community to the Taliban that they will not have any friends if they do not show real progress in terms of the women’s rights and human rights situation … and that is not happening.”
The new contacts stem from a combination of regional security concerns, pressure in the west to reduce illegal immigration and a general recognition that the Taliban are unlikely to be forced from power in the foreseeable future.
The European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towards regularising consular relations with EU countries.
The meeting prompted outrage.
“You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.
This year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have all visited Kabul or other Afghan cities, seeking trade routes and pipeline deals that would allow their landlocked countries access to seaports or third countries beyond.
India too has moved to reinforce relationships that were frosty after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, in part to exploit new tensions between the movement and the Islamist movement’s historic sponsors, Pakistan.
New Delhi secured a sanctions waiver last year so that Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban foreign minister and a veteran official who has spent decades at the heart of the movement, could travel there.
In June, India’s UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions, such as travel bans, asset freezes and arms embargoes, that target dozens of Taliban members.
“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account,” said Harish Parvathaneni.
Afghan authorities’ diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul, including those from China, Japan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Last year, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, made the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister to Kabul for almost a decade.
The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan “seeks relations with all countries”, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said, though “the countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked”.
Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute focusing on Russia’s policy towards the Middle East, said Moscow had multiple reasons for recognising the Taliban regime and seeking closer relations.
“One likely objective is simply having allies … Afghanistan is also very significant for Russia geographically and Russia just wants influence in that part of the world. There was an opening and they were able to take it,” Borshchevskaya said.
“It’s a very cold, cynical calculation. It’s part of a very simple zero-sum view that for Russia to win the US has to lose. From the Kremlin perspective, this is a global battle and whether you are looking at Europe or Afghanistan or wherever, it’s one geopolitical chessboard.”
Britain has said it pursues a policy of “limited and pragmatic” engagement with Taliban officials, largely through the UK Mission to Afghanistan based at the British embassy in Qatar. Discreet meetings with the Taliban have also repeatedly been held by other western countries in Qatar. In Germany and at least four other western European capitals, key consulates are now controlled by the Taliban, not representatives of the former Afghan government.
Taliban officials have also sought cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country’s fragile economy and diplomacy. Natural resources are another lure for overseas powers. Kabul has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.
China, which is worried about Islamic militancy on and around its south-western borders, has welcomed Taliban officials in recent years, and hosted talks when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war earlier this year.
The Taliban are split, with deep disagreements on the ban on women’s education among other issues, but remain dominated by the most conservative factions. Recent laws have further reinforced repression, designating many religious minorities, including Shia Muslims, as heretics and imposing strict punishments to silence dissent.
Other new laws recognise only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women and facilitate the marriage of girls without their consent. 
Analysts do not believe the Taliban are likely to moderate their position in the near future and point to the continuing authority of Hibatullah Akhundzada, the reclusive and authoritarian cleric leader.
Ramin Mansoori, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Endowment who studies Afghan politics, said the Taliban’s priority was its domestic agenda.
“They are not going to make any significant concessions. Most of them don’t have an international perspective,” Mansoori said.

articles.title: The Great Stink of 2026? Hot, dry summer leaves London holding its nose
articles.body:
London was “reeking with ineffable and intolerable horrors” after weeks of temperatures exceeding 30C and minimal rainfall. This was Disraeli’s description of the Great Stink of 1858, but something similarly disgusting has been happening this summer.
Once again, an exceptionally hot and dry spell has exposed the putrid stench of untreated human waste.
“There’s been a bad smell around for weeks,” said Simon Birkett, the founder and director of Clean Air in London. “After campaigning for 20 years my nose is a bit of connoisseur for air pollution, and there really is a stench.
“If you go anywhere near a stormwater drain you can almost feel it wafting up. The general public are not going to forget the summer of 2026 and one of the symptoms is this toxic stench.”
Drainage experts say this summer’s stench should prompt a radical overhaul of an outdated system, just as the Great Stink ushered in a new sanitation in the Victorian era.
Prof Barbara Evans, the chair of public health engineering at Leeds University, likened the current sewer network to a “giant intestine”.
She says: “In our guts we have a massive microbiome designed to break down organic materials. When we put all that plus the carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus that’s in our gut into the sewer, the process just carries on.”
With frequent rain, this foetid mix would get washed through the sewers to water treatment works, where organic waste is broken down into gases, Evans said.
But in a drought, the fermenting sewage stays in the drains. Evans said: “The microbiological decomposition is currently happening more in the pipes, rather than at the treatment works. And that’s what we’re smelling.”
As a result – and like our digestion – the sewage system “farts and burps”, Evans says. “When microbes get excited they give off a load of gas, so it comes in wafts. It’s a cocktail of methane, [and] a little bit of hydrogen sulphide, which gives the rotten egg smell. There’s also nitrous oxide, which you can’t smell, but it will be in the mix.”
Heat accelerates this microbial activity, according to Simon Clarke, professor of cellular microbiology at the University of Reading. “Bacteria and other microorganisms that decompose organic matter often work more quickly at warmer temperatures, increasing the release of gases that we perceive as unpleasant smells.”
The current stench from the drains is the flip side of creaking system that allows raw sewage to pollute seas and rivers during heavy rain. Evans said: “If you couple the stench with the anxiety about sewage spills, it all points to wastewater system that is very old in a world that has changed a lot.”
Unlike sewage spills, the smell, however unpleasant, is not a risk to the public – or at least not yet. Evans said: “If you get a buildup of gas in the sewers, that could be risky, because methane is an inflammable gas. The risk is tiny, so it’s not yet a public health issue; it is more a public wellbeing and pleasantness issue. The reason we’re noticing it is the because we’re at the extreme of what the system can cope with.”
Evans, whose areas of expertise include “faecal sludge management”, said the public and policymakers were squeamish about confronting these issues.
“People don’t want to talk about it, they want to flush it away and forget about it as they have for 150 years. But it’s the foundation of a civilised world – if you don’t manage it, it’s disgusting and dangerous.”
The UK’s drainage system is still based on the work of the pioneering Victorian civil engineer Joseph Bazalgette, who designed London’s new sewers in response to the Great Stink.
Evans hopes the current stench prompts another overhaul. “I hope it triggers a national conversation. We have to rebuild the system to cope with our new reality of both hotter and drier periods and wetter periods.”
She recommends rebuilding the system so that so-called “grey water” from sinks and baths is separated from the “black water” from toilets. Such systems, which are being introduced in Sweden and Germany, stop rainwater entering the sewers by reusing it in homes and recharging aquifers with it to help replenish water supplies. “You have to design the sewers so that even if it’s not raining it will still work hydraulically and you don’t get the stench,” she said.
Only when the rain finally comes will the microbes smell sweet, according to Clarke.
He said: “Bacteria are also responsible for one of the finest and most iconic smells of a British summer: the petrichor smell of summer rain, which occurs when bacteria in the soil are released by the rain and reach our noses. You don’t need to be a microbiologist to appreciate the beauty of that.”

articles.title: Russia’s role in Middle East politics endures, shifts to being ‘secondary power’
articles.body:
Russia’s role in Middle East politics endures, shifts to being ‘secondary power’
Two Russian military bases will remain in Syria as the region continues to recalibrate its relations with major powers amid the Iran war
At the time, Moscow operated about 100 military facilities in the war-torn country, following its intervention in the Syrian civil conflict from 2015 to prop up then president Bashar al-Assad in alliance with Iran and its regional proxies.
According to a deal announced by the Syrian foreign ministry on Sunday, Russia’s only two official military bases outside the former Soviet Union would be turned into “joint training and capacity-building centres, within new arrangements that preserve mutual interests”.
No further details were given, but Russian military contingents would reportedly remain at both facilities under the new arrangement.

articles.title: 'Many forces don't want India to become Vishwaguru’: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat on Independence Day
articles.body:
'Many forces don't want India to become Vishwaguru’: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat on Independence Day
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 15, 2026, 13:56 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat (File photo)
NEW DELHI: Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) Mohan Bhagwat on Saturday called on people tostrengthen India's independence by making the country happy, prosperous, and secure so that the country becomes "Vishwaguru", noting that many people and forces are working against this goal.“We must make the nation happy, prosperous and secure, and ensure that it makes its rightful contribution to the world. However, many people and forces are working against this goal and creating obstacles. Without abandoning our principles, we must face these challenges and work to make India a ‘Vishwaguru’ — a guide to the world,” Bhagwat said at a gathering after hoisting the national flag at the RSS headquarters in Nagpur.Bhagwat emphasised that Independence Day is a matter of pride for all Indians. The Sangh chief stated that if the freedom struggle is traced to 1857, India’s ancestors made sacrifices for nearly 90 years to secure independence.“We feel proud of their (freedom fighters') sacrifices and are happy that their struggle reached a successful conclusion. But along with this, we must also remember that preserving the freedom achieved through so much effort and sacrifice is our responsibility,” he stressed.
Saffron, he noted, represents action, knowledge and sacrifice. “The freedom of a nation is achieved through hard work and sacrifice, and after independence, these qualities help make the nation prosperous and secure.”White represents purity and discipline, while green symbolises prosperity. When sacrifice, commitment, hard work and knowledge become part of people’s lives, society remains peaceful and minds become pure, he added.
Bhagwat also emphasised that individuals may hold different views, but this diversity reflects unity. “The Ashoka Chakra has many spokes, but all of them emerge from a single central point.”The Ashoka Chakra represents individual and social awareness, with its spokes kept within the limits of dharma, or discipline. “That is why we have placed this Dharma Chakra at the centre of our national flag,” he added, urging people to reflect on the flag’s symbols and incorporate their values into their lives.India will remain an independent nation, Bhagwat asserted, but its responsibility extends further: “This is our duty today” to make the country a meaningful contributor to humanity.
The TOI News Desk comprises a dedicated and tireless team of journalists who operate around the clock to deliver the most current and comprehensive news and updates to the readers of The Times of India worldwide. articles.title: From storied St. Moritz stays to boutique Courchevel properties, these are Europe's best ski hotels
articles.body:
If you consider the hotel to be just as important as the slopes, these are the stays you should be booking this winter season.
The winter holidays may still seem far away, but it won’t be long until Europe’s ski resorts begin gearing up for another season on the slopes.
We’ve already shared Trip.com’s roundup of some of the best ski resorts across Europe. Now, it’s time to look at where to stay once you get there.
The online booking platform has also ranked its top 50 European ski resort hotels for 2026 based on a combination of customer reviews, year-round sales data, consistent quality and unique themes, with luxury properties in Switzerland, France, Italy and Austria among the entries from the continent.
From a storied stay in St. Moritz to a boutique property where your skis and gloves are laid out for you daily, here are this year’s top five stays.
Kulm Hotel St. Moritz, Saint Moritz, Switzerland
Having first opened in 1856, Kulm Hotel is one of Saint Moritz’s most storied stays.
There are 150 rooms and suites on offer, with a choice of alpine or classic décor and either village or lakeside views.
The suites vary from one or two bedroom offerings – each featuring a balcony and a separate lounge and dining area, while some also include an open log fire. Guests are treated to sweeping views of Lake St. Moritz and the Engadin valley, while the spacious Corvatsch Suite also offers views of the grand Corvatsch mountain.
While we can understand wanting to spend all of your time inside the hotel, a major perk is that you are within walking distance of sights like the Leaning Tower of St. Moritz and the Vito Schnabel Gallery – a hub for showcasing world-famous American artists, as well as Swiss newcomers.
Best of all, stays include free ski lessons for all levels.
According to Trip.com’s survey of customer reviews, the ski hotel scored 9.5 among visitors across cleanliness, amenities, location and for its service.
Fouquet's Courchevel, Courchevel, France
Situated at the foot of the Bellecôte slope at the heart of the village of Courchevel 1850 ski resort, Fouquet's Courchevel features a total of 42 keys, each of which offers views of the peaks from the comfort of the room's balcony.
One of the benefits that comes from staying in such a boutique property is the ability for staff to add a personal touch throughout, with each guest’s boots and gloves laid out (and pre-warmed!) in the ski room daily, with your skis ready and waiting on the slopes.
After a long day, guests can unwind at the 1,000 square metre spa, which has six treatment cabins, a double suite, a 20-metre pool as well as an outdoor Jacuzzi. Treatments include facials, massages and sensory experiences, and even your tresses can get a pampering with Balmain treatments, exclusive to Courchevel, from L’Atelier Hair Couture.
The three dining concepts include Italian trattoria-style cuisine at Loulou restaurant, Savoyard and Italian cuisine at La Table Savoyarde and an intimate tea time experience at Christophe Adam’s Afternoon Treat.
Trip.com's survey of user reviews found the hotel rank 9.8 across its cleanliness, amenities, location and service.
Six Senses Residences Courchevel, Courchevel, France
For refined mountain living, Six Senses Residences Courchevel has 27 apartments, ranging from two- to five- bedroom stays. Each apartment features spacious living areas plus a private balcony or terrace with panoramic views to take in during aprés-ski moments.
Prior to check-in, guests can pre-book their ski equipment ready for collection from the residence’s on-site ski shop. Meanwhile, during après-ski, the ski concierge will take care of storing equipment, leaving guests free to explore Courchevel or unwind at the property’s spa without the hassle of thinking about where to keep their ski helmet.
Six Senses Residences Courchevel also offers a range of experiences, such as piste basher driving, or seeing the scenic ski resort from above with a helicopter tour. Other experiences on offer include hot air balloon flight, a guided snow shoeing tour along the frozen lakes to learn about local nature, wildlife and history, as well as husky sledding.
Trip.com found it scored 9 across cleanliness, amenities, location and services among users.
Hotel Le K2 Altitude, Courchevel, France
Perched just above the village of Courchevel 1850 at an altitude of 1,900 metres, Le K2 Altitude Luxury Hotel & Spa is home to 14 rooms and 18 suites.
The flagship Altitude Suite is a two-level duplex designed to feel like a private chalet. The upper floor houses the master bedroom, a spacious dressing room, office and lounge, while the ground floor also features bedroom, lounge and office, alongside a dining room and balcony overlooking the mountains.
Hotel guests benefit from direct access to the Pralong slope, opening to Les Trois Vallées, which is the world's largest ski area.
For entertainment off the slopes, the hotel’s Le K'Baret space serves as the hotel's one stop shop, either as a cinema room, performance hall and setting to celebrate private events.
When it comes to dining, guests can choose from French culinary traditions, a menu inspired by travel or Lebanese flavours at the L'Altitude, Le K2 Restaurant or Base Kamo by Aïnata eateries respectively.
Hotel Le K2 Altitude scored 9.4 across cleanliness, amenities, location and service among user reviews.
L'Apogée Courchevel – an Oetker Collection Hotel, Courchevel, France
Tucked away in Courchevel’s Jardin Alpin, this self-styled ”height of alpine glamour” stay offers skiers a choice of 20 rooms, 33 suites, a penthouse with its own cinema room, as well as two five-bedroom private chalets that can accommodate up to 11 guests and features direct ski-in/ski-out facilities.
For a perfect stay, the hotel recommends a three-day itinerary beginning with a ski trip to Les Trois Vallées, followed by dog sledding and hang gliding on day two and rounding up with rest and relaxation on day three at Spa L'Apogée by La Prairie before checkout.
Little skiers are well looked after, too. The hotel’s family friendly approach includes a Young Spa for guests as young as four years old can benefit from relaxation treatments, and even get their hair done. They can also perfect their ski and snowboarding skills with the help of instructors.
L'apogéee Courchevel scored 8.9 across cleanliness, amenities, location and service among user reviews.
Europe’s top 10 ski resort hotels for 2026
Here’s a closer look at the top resort hotels that made the cut this year:
- Kulm Hotel St. Moritz, Saint Moritz, Switzerland
- Fouquet's Courchevel, Courchevel, France

- Aman le Mélézin, Courchevel, France

articles.title: Russia's economy has defied the skeptics. Cracks are getting harder to hide
articles.body:
After four-and-a-half years of full-scale war with Ukraine, Russia has become a two-tier economy.
"If you are lucky and you're employed by a tank production company, then everything's good. Otherwise, you are probably facing problems," Alex Kolyandr, director for Europe at consulting firm Eurasia Group, told CNBC.
Russia's wartime economy has been brought into sharper focus in recent weeks by Ukraine's long-range drone attacks on oil refineries and delivery warehouses.
Though it has defied expectations and is even growing slowly, according to recent data, analysts say this masks problems, such as the Kremlin's reliance on military spending, higher taxes and subsidized bank lending.
But they question whether this will drive Russia to give up its war. Indeed, Kolyandr warned the worsening economy could incentivize President Vladimir Putin to escalate the conflict.
"If I were Putin, God forbid, I would probably decide that it is in my interest to escalate now and try to finish the war on my terms, than wait until the money ends sometime in the future," Kolyandr said.
The Russian Embassy in London and Russia's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Kolyandr said the Kremlin could balance the books with some "bookkeeping acrobatics," but its economic problems "will not go away and are still mounting."
He added: "It has already started, through inflation, through the slowdown in the non-military economy, through higher interest rates."
Two standout metrics for Russia's economy
For the first time since 2023, Russia's economy returned to growth in the April to June period. The country's gross domestic product grew 1.3% year-on-year in the second quarter, according to official data published this week, while GDP expanded by 0.6% through the first half of the year. The second-quarter figures surpassed government and central bank forecasts.
The data suggest that government spending on its industrial-military complex and a recent boost in oil and gas prices have helped prop up Russia's wartime economy.
But Charles Lichfield, director of economic foresight and analysis at the Atlantic Council's GeoEconomics Center, said the best metrics for understanding what's going on are the deficit and inflation.
"They are on course to double the deficit they had in 2025 and that was already double what they had in 2024," Lichfield said, highlighting the country's depressed energy revenues, despite higher fossil fuel prices in recent months.
In the first half of 2026, oil and gas revenues were 64% of their level in the same period two years ago. Sustained Ukrainian drone strikes have hit Russia's refineries, and tougher Western sanctions have started to bite, like the lower European Union oil price cap and measures targeting Russia's shadow-fleet enablers.
"On inflation, they managed to bring it down to basically the target of 4% late last year, which was a big achievement given all the internal and external inflationary pressures, but it looks like that will not last," Lichfield said.
What Russians' cookie buying says about the economy
Earlier in the year, the country's largest retailer said citizens were increasingly switching to low-cost and store-brand food products.
"We recently noticed that cookie consumption has risen — almost two and a half times," X5 Group President Yekaterina Lobacheva told RBC News in April, according to a translation by The Moscow Times. "It's something sweet, a small indulgence, but cheaper than chocolate and other confectionery."
Read more
Asked what levers the Kremlin can pull to mitigate the situation, Lichfield said the Russian government could tax oil and gas companies more than the current tax code suggests, try to borrow money internationally, or potentially mobilize the half of the central bank's reserves that remain beyond Western sanctions.
Alongside roughly $300 billion frozen after the war began, Russia's central bank is estimated to have around $300 billion in reserves, either in Russia or in jurisdictions not under sanctions. The money could technically be used to plug some fiscal gaps, Lichfield said, although this could undermine confidence in the central bank's commitment to fighting inflation.
Lichfield said he doesn't expect Russia to end the war for economic reasons, despite the pressure it faces.
Russia's economy unlikely to determine Ukraine war
Elina Ribakova, senior fellow at Peterson Institute for International Economics, also said Russia's economy was unlikely to force it to end the war when it was getting a boost from higher oil prices.
"It has to get much more dire," Ribakova told CNBC in a phone interview. "If you tell me that we will have oil prices at $35 or $40 for the next year, then it might decide. But at the moment, especially given the war between Israel, the U.S. and Iran, it is unlikely."
Ribakova said the conversation was different when oil prices were much lower in January and February and the Russian government was talking about revising its 2026 budget, even though the year had only just begun, suggesting serious trouble.
She added that Putin had "staked so much" on the war "that he almost feels as like he has to keep on going."

articles.title: Demand for free Lithuanian language courses far exceeds places in Vilnius
articles.body:
Demand for free Lithuanian language courses in Vilnius is far outstripping the number of available places, leaving some foreigners unable to enrol and instead receiving offers to take paid classes.
About 200 people are currently taking free Lithuanian courses organised by Vytautas Magnus University and the Vilnius municipality. Registration for a new round of courses beginning in September is scheduled to open next week.
But some applicants say they have been told that no free places are available and subsequently received offers for paid courses.
Piotr, a Russian national who has lived in Lithuania for three years, speaks Lithuanian at an advanced level after learning the language independently and paying for his own studies.
“I wanted it simply to be easier, more convenient and more peaceful to live in the country,” he said. “And I managed to do that.”
When free Lithuanian courses became available, Piotr said his wife tried to register but was told there were no places left. A friend received a similar response.
“He also got a reply saying there were no places because so many people had applied,” Piotr said. “But then he started receiving emails offering paid courses. He was offered a school for 99 euros per course or per month.”
Vilnius Mayor Valdas Benkunskas said the city had never promised that Lithuanian language courses would always be free.
“There will also be an option of paid courses, because it was never said that these would be exclusively free,” Benkunskas said. “As far as our possibilities allow, and as much funding as we have from European Union funds, there will be free courses, but certainly not for everyone.”
The demand is substantial. When registration for the free courses organised with the Vilnius municipality opened in February, about 6,000 people applied, said Laura Kamandulytė-Merfeldienė, head of Lithuanian language courses at Vytautas Magnus University.
The applicants are not limited to Ukrainians and other Slavic-language speakers. About half come from further countries, including the Philippines and India, she said.
The shortage of places is also being driven by new language requirements in Lithuania’s service sector, where knowledge of Lithuanian has become mandatory this year.
“Maybe some people had not taken it seriously before, but now they have realised that they should learn the language,” said Lithuanian language teacher Elena Pakalnytė.
Piotr said some people who need to learn Lithuanian have limited access to state-funded integration programs.
“There are refugees and people in exile who do not have refugee status and therefore cannot learn through integration funds,” he said. “They have to study independently. But studying independently does not always make it possible to reach the level where you can speak fluently and pass an exam.”
Mayor Benkunskas said Vilnius will soon launch online Lithuanian language courses. More than 2,500 people have expressed interest, he said.
The city also plans to establish language clubs and expand access to a free self-study platform.
Over the next 18 months, the municipality and its partners aim to provide Lithuanian language instruction to more than 1,000 people.

articles.title: Indonesian earthquake death toll rises to five — newspaper
articles.body:
TOKYO, August 15. /TASS/. At least five people have been killed in the latest powerful earthquake that struck Indonesia, The Straits Times newspaper wrote, citing the governor of the East Nusa Tenggara province.
The report says that five bodies have been pulled from the rubble of collapsed buildings.
A powerful earthquake hit off Indonesia’s coast in the early hours of Saturday. The initial tremor was followed by aftershocks, with the most powerful reaching magnitude of 6.1. Residents of coastal areas of Flores Island were advised to evacuate at least 2 kilometers away from the coastline because of a tsunami threat. Governmental offices, residential buildings, schools, hospitals, and places of worship have been damaged or destroyed all over the island, Jakarta Globe wrote.

articles.title: No decision made so far on resuming talks with US
articles.body:
Araghchi said the Islamabad MoU provided for an "end to the war," but the United States had violated it and fighting had resumed. "We did not have a ceasefire to extend; we had an end to the war, which has now entered a new situation," he said.
He said Qatar and Pakistan, as mediators, were exchanging messages and remained in contact with Tehran, "but this does not at all constitute negotiations. No decision has yet been taken to resume talks with America."
On the separate Iran-Oman talks on the Strait of Hormuz, Araghchi said they were proceeding as a technical matter focused on defining maritime routes in the waterway for vessel traffic. "The routes that previously existed no longer work, and a new route must be defined. We are currently designing a temporary route, which will later become the final one," he said. Specialists from both countries and the armed forces, as the main authorities on the issue, were involved, and a result could come soon.
Araghchi stressed that the technical talks on defining the route were separate from any reopening of the strait. "Whether the Strait of Hormuz reopens or not depends on the fulfilment of other conditions to which America must adhere," he said.

articles.title: Thailand requests Russia’s support for free trade zone talks with EAEU — ministry
articles.body:
BANGKOK, August 15. /TASS/. Thailand has requested Russia’s support for launching talks on signing a free trade zone agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), the Thai Foreign Ministry said, commenting on the 9th joint Russian-Thai commission on bilateral cooperation.
"The meeting placed emphasis on promoting economic cooperation, particularly expanding trade and investment. Thailand sought support for the commencement of negotiations on a Thailand - Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) Free Trade Agreement, as well as addressing trade barriers and enhancing market access opportunities for Thai products, including agricultural and food products," the statement reads.
The commission’s co-chairs, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sihasak Phuangketkeow and Minister for the Development of the Russian Far East and the Arctic Alexey Chekunkov, have exchanged documents covering cooperation in various areas, including trade and investment, agriculture, energy, industry, tourism, education, and addressing climate change. It was also noted that Russia is an important tourist source for Thailand with approximately 1 million Russians visiting Thailand in the first half of 2026.
"Both sides discussed opportunities for cooperation in energy security, food security, transport connectivity, and tourism," the ministry said.
The two ministers "also discussed cooperation on trade facilitation and investment promotion with the 2nd Russian - Thai Investment Forum to be held in Bangkok in October 2026."
The Thai Foreign Ministry noted the kingdom’s efforts "to create new opportunities for the Thai business sector, strengthen trade, investment, and connectivity between the two countries."
Executives from the Thai Chamber of Commerce, the Federation of Thai Industries, the Thai - Russian Business Council, and leading Thai companies in the agriculture and food, energy, health products, ICT, automotive and auto parts sectors joined the Thai delegation in Moscow.
