articles.title: Xinhua Commentary: 81 years on, Japan must not turn back the clock
articles.body:
BEIJING, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- On the 81st anniversary of Japan's unconditional surrender in World War II, Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi visited the notorious war-linked Yasukuni Shrine. So did a group of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party's senior officials, the first such collective visit by the party's top leadership. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi sent a ritual offering.
The shrine honors Japan's war dead, including 14 convicted Class-A war criminals, and has long been seen across Asia as a symbol of Japan's wartime militarism.
The timing was telling. On a day that should prompt reflection on how the war ended and why it must never be allowed to happen again, the gestures raised a troubling question: which parts of history are Japan's leaders choosing to remember, and which would they rather forget?
That question matters as some in Tokyo increasingly invoke Japan's suffering from the atomic bombings while glossing over the history that preceded them: the aggression that once brought untold misery across Asia and ultimately led Japan to surrender.
The argument is not only about how Japan remembers its past. It is also about what lessons it chooses to draw from it.
Under Takaichi, Japan has been steadily dismantling the restraints that have shaped its postwar security policy. Defense spending has continued to rise, restrictions on arms exports have been eased, long-range missiles have been deployed, and the government is pushing ahead with plans to acquire greater offensive capabilities.
Now, even the Three Non-Nuclear Principles, a cornerstone of Japan's postwar policy, are being undermined. Koizumi has called for discussions on nuclear policy "without taboos," including whether to revise the principles that prohibit Japan from possessing, producing or allowing the introduction of nuclear weapons.
Taken together, these moves are dangerous signs that Japan has deviated from its postwar security path, stepping away from an exclusively defense-oriented posture and toward becoming a country increasingly equipped to wage war yet again.
As always, the justification is "security." Japan's right-wing politicians have repeatedly portrayed the regional security environment as increasingly dangerous and pointed to so-called external threats. The latest defense white paper goes even further, labeling China the "unprecedented and the greatest strategic challenge which Japan should respond with its comprehensive national power."
This logic should sound familiar.
Before and during World War II, militarist Japan also invoked "national survival," "security" and "self-defense" to justify military expansion and wars of aggression. The result was catastrophic, bringing untold suffering to the people of Asia and the world.
That is precisely why Japan's postwar Constitution, pacifist principles and restrictions on military capabilities were established. They were not shackles placed on Japan, but guardrails built from the ruins of war. Yet those safeguards are now being steadily eroded.
History does not repeat itself automatically. But when the lessons of history are deliberately forgotten, the risk of repeating them grows.
For Japan, remembering the past is not enough. It should reflect on where it is heading, and whether it is once again allowing militarism to masquerade as security.
The real lesson of the war is that militarism can bring catastrophe not only to its neighbors, but ultimately to Japan itself.
Turning back toward military expansion would betray the lessons learned at the cost of enormous human suffering. Japan should choose peace, not repeat the mistakes of its past. ■

articles.title: No one can seize Straif of Hormuz by Tweets, Iran warns Trump
articles.body:
Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran's deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, said that the Strait of Hormuz can only be closed or reopened by Tehran's command, rejecting comments by U.S. President Donald Trump that Washington would soon declare the waterway American territory.
Trump made the remarks at a campaign event in Garden City, New York, telling supporters that after Iran's defeat he would pretty soon declare the strait a U.S. territory. Writing on X, Gharibabadi said the waterway "cannot be seized by tweet, nor by aircraft carrier, nor by issuing an order, nor by an election speech," adding that Iran fears neither threats nor displays of power.
In a separate post, Gharibabadi said the strait "has been Iranian, is Iranian, and will remain Iranian" and warned that Iran would continue enforcing its blockade of the waterway until Washington accepted its "strategic and heavy defeats."
The exchange comes amid a monthslong war between Iran and the United States that began in February with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian military and infrastructure sites. A ceasefire MoU reached with the mediation of Pakistan and Qatar later collapsed, and both sides have continued exchanging strikes, with control of the Strait of Hormuz remaining a central flashpoint.

PM Modi on 33% women's reservation
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday urged political parties to facilitate the implementation of the proposed 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies so that women can “actively contribute to shaping India’s policies.”He made the call while addressing the nation from the iconic Red Fort in Delhi on the 80th Independence Day.“Today, from the ramparts of the Red Fort, standing under the shadow of the Tricolour, I earnestly appeal to and urge all political parties of our nation: Come forward and celebrate the strength and capability of our women. Step forward in honour of our women, and as swiftly as possible, ensure our mothers and sisters receive 33% representation in the State Legislative Assemblies and the Lok Sabha so that they can actively contribute to shaping India’s policies,” the prime minister said.PM Modi also highlighted the contribution of women representatives in various elected bodies and pointed to the passage of the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam in Parliament aimed at strengthening women’s representation in politics.“My dear fellow citizens, today in Panchayats, Municipalities, and Municipal Corporations, our women public representatives are guiding the nation in very large numbers, solving local challenges, and providing exceptionally capable and empowering leadership.
Keeping this in mind, we passed the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam in Parliament,” he added.However, he noted that “for one reason or another”, in the political arena over the last 40 years, the dream of greater representation for women had “persistently fallen victim to political games and political battlegrounds.”The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023, was passed by both Houses of Parliament but has not moved ahead with implementation after the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill fell in the Lok Sabha on April 17, failing to secure the constitutionally required two-thirds majority of members present and voting.The Bill proposed implementing 33% reservation for women in legislatures and delimiting Lok Sabha constituencies.

articles.title: ‘In the heatwaves, it’s crucial’: the fight to save France’s rural swimming pools
articles.body:
Suzy Bernard took a breath and jumped into the deep end of her village swimming pool with a splash.
“There’s a wonderful feeling of wellbeing in the water,” said the former hospital healthcare assistant, who recently learned to swim aged 75 and was now gliding along with her daughter and grandson.
The municipal swimming pool, bordered by shady oak trees in the village of Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, in western France, has been the Bernard family’s daily refuge from the sweltering heatwaves this summer. Bernard is a member of the village collective, Touche Pas à Ma Piscine (Hands Off My Pool), campaigning to defend the Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe facility and calling for more government support for rural swimming pools. “We’ll fight to make sure this pool survives and stays open,” she said.
As a summer of record temperatures parched much of the French countryside, local village swimming pools, with cheap entry tickets, have often been the only shelter from the heatwaves for rural families on low incomes who cannot afford to go on holiday or who live in heat-trap homes. The pools are also crucial for teaching rural communities to swim. A total of 274 people died from drowning in France between 1 May and 15 July this year, with most deaths occurring when people jumped into rivers and waterways to cool down.
But France’s ageing rural swimming pools, many of which were built in 1970s, are in crisis as village mayors with shrinking budgets struggle to pay the high running costs and some pools are forced to close owing to lack of funds.
In Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, a village of 3,200 people in Les Hauts-d’Anjou, a farming area of the Pays de la Loire, the new mayor, Véronique Langlais, said she was determined to keep running the village pool that opened in 1973, despite an annual cost of at least €100,000 (£85,000) to the town hall’s modest budget. Three other rural pools had closed in the surrounding countryside, making this the only pool in a radius of about 20 miles.
“This pool is a treasure that we have to protect,” Langlais said. But any sudden need for a costly new part or major repair could force the pool’s closure owing to lack of funds. “There’s a sword of Damocles hanging over our head.”
In 1969, after France’s poor swimming performance at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, and a series of tragic drownings across the country, the government under Georges Pompidou launched a plan to build 1,000 pools in mainly rural areas to encourage swimming. Over 600 were built, but those still in use – as well as later 1980s pools – are in urgent need of costly renovation.
François Gernigon, a centre-right lawmaker for the Maine-et-Loire, has petitioned the government for a funding plan. He recently surveyed rural mayors, finding more than 75% feared their village pools risked closure in the short-term. He said the heatwaves made it essential to protect pools as “the only place of leisure to relax in rural areas”. He said village pool closures “make residents feel abandoned”.
Emma-Özlem Kaya, 45, is a printmaker whose Turkish father moved to Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe in 1972 when the local tannery recruited artisan leather-workers from Istanbul. “We didn’t go on holiday because my parents didn’t have the budget,” she said. “So every day in summer, I’d grab my swimming bag and walk to the pool with my siblings and friends and we’d spend the afternoons there with our towels laid out.” She now attends water aerobics classes there and campaigns to protect the pool.
Nadine Lemonnier, a local teacher who is also part of the collective, remembered childhood summers at another local village pool: “whole days spent diving for objects and having deep teenage conversations at the edge”. For her, protecting rural pools that offered children swimming lessons was crucial because her three-year-old cousin died from drowning in a private pool.
Across France, there are dozens of rural village collectives mobilising to protect local pools: campaigning, volunteering to help run them and even painting and carrying out maintenance work.
In Rochefort-sur-Loire, a village of 2,400 people near Angers, members of the local pool support group gathered at the water’s edge. In recent years, they had decorated the village with flippers and rubber rings to convince a visiting government minister to secure funds for reopening the indoor teaching pool. They hosted a poet in residence at the pool and run theatre performances there.
“It’s about making our village pool the focus of life in the community,” said Nicolas Robin, a sociologist.
On 18 July 1969, at nearby Juigné-sur-Loire, 19 children drowned in the River Loire on an outing from a school holiday club – one of many tragedies that led the government to improve swimming teaching facilities. Swimming lessons remain key. There are three rivers in the area and the village is often hit by flooding in winter.
“People need to know how to swim to protect themselves in the flooding season too,” said Guillaume Lusteau, the pool’s lifeguard and swim coach.
The pool sits beside the River Louet, a branch of the Loire that is usually a paddling spot. But the summer heatwaves have left the river level too low for a dip, increasing the number of swimmers at the pool.
The mayor, Didier Le Gall, said that in this area, with a large proportion of organic farming, health was a priority and the pool was essential, particularly for families on low incomes. “It’s important for children learning to swim, but also for the social lives of people who don’t go away on holiday,” he said. “The pool is part of our village’s identity, and in the heatwaves it has become a crucial place to cool down. The pool’s impact on mental health and physical health is considerable.”
Le Gall said the town hall wanted to keep the pool open, despite the €100,000 basic running cost. “But we need help in the long-term,” he said.
Bruno Cheminat, 73, a former special educational needs teacher and one-time competitive swimmer, clocks up 2,000 metres every day, and has also helped with painting and maintenance work as a volunteer. “It’s beautiful to be the first in the water in the morning,” he said.
Estelle, a former flight attendant who works on the pool reception, said it boosted her mood to be in the water, looking out at trees towards the church: “It’s like swimming in a picture postcard.”

articles.title: Suspension of navigation in Black Sea to become Ukraine’s slow death — expert
articles.body:
MELITOPOL, August 15. /TASS/. Russia has sufficient resources and logistical alternatives to minimize the impact of a possible suspension of navigation in the Black Sea on its economy, but this scenario will mean a slow death for Ukraine, Alexander Pataman, who heads the secretariat of the Zaporozhye Region office of the World Russian People’s Council, an international public organization, said.
"With enough resources and alternative logistical routes, Russia can survive the possible situation of Black Sea navigation suspension for an unlimited period of time and without noticeable damage," said Pataman. "However, this scenario will mean a slow death for Ukraine."
"We have no need for the moratorium on attacks on ‘civilian ships’ proposed by Vladimir Zelensky," he added.
In his words, ship traffic in Ukraine’s major ports has de-facto stopped. Apart from sustaining economic losses, the Kiev regime has lost an opportunity to transport weapons, ammunition, and other military cargoes for its armed forces by sea.
Bloomberg reported on August 8, citing sources, that Turkey had begun imposing restrictions on commercial shipping in the Black Sea amid increased attacks on its vessels. It is noted that the Coast Guard had denied passage through the straits to some vessels bound for Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk or had requested additional time to process their applications. There is no official confirmation of this information yet.

articles.title: Hong Kong’s biodiversity ‘richer than we know’ but many species lack protection
articles.body:
Hong Kong’s biodiversity ‘richer than we know’ but many species lack protection
Conservationists highlight new species uncovered in city while urging authorities to formulate ‘red list’ to protect existing vulnerable ones
Hong Kong’s lush forests are teeming with more wildlife ranging from birds arriving from neighbouring regions to newly discovered reptile species, experts have found, as they urge authorities to devise a conservation list to protect vulnerable local species.
The call by the city’s conservationists to formulate a “red list” – a long-awaited measure since 2014 – coincided with National Ecology Day on Saturday.
Marking the occasion, Deputy Chief Secretary Warner Cheuk Wing-hing said the government’s first five-year plan would advance measures to protect the environment.
“The government is, for the first time, formulating a five-year plan that aligns with the national 15th five-year plan’s policy direction to cut carbon emissions, reduce pollution, pursue green development, and boost growth so as to improve ecological environment quality, and steadily pursue green transition, build a liveable city, and realise a beautiful Hong Kong,” he said.
“We have gotten the brown wood owl … the Chinese barbet and the black-chinned yuhina, that expanded its range into Hong Kong – a good sign because it shows us that some of these species found our forests mature enough to find places to nest and food to feed on,” Ades said.

articles.title: How Vietnam’s ‘streamlining revolution’ may lead to uneven success
articles.body:
Asian AngleHow Vietnam’s ‘streamlining revolution’ may lead to uneven success
The most sweeping administrative overhaul in decades is expected to encounter hurdles ranging from staff shortages to resource mismatch
Third plenums are ordinarily the quiet part of Vietnam’s political calendar. Between its five-yearly congresses, the Communist Party of Vietnam governs through numbered plenums of its Central Committee (CC): the first two settle personnel decisions, and the third, six months on, usually does no more than ratify the term’s work programme.
This time, the third plenum of the 14th CC, held from July 20 to 24, did more. It set out the next phase of the country’s most sweeping administrative overhaul in decades: the move from streamlining the apparatus to building the capacity to govern.
An unusually crowded agenda of 13 major items includes issues such as the development model, the land law and national security. These were organised around General Secretary To Lam’s “four strategic shifts”: improving the party’s leadership capacity and the state’s operating quality; unifying the governance of development space and national resources; shifting growth towards productivity, technology and human capital; and moving from reactive crisis management towards prevention and resilience.
The four shifts together describe the developmental state To Lam wants to build: one that steers growth through deliberate coordination rather than leaving it to markets alone. But the first shift – improving the party’s leadership – is the hinge on which the others turn. The second, a unified development space, requires local institutions capable of executing plans drawn up in Hanoi. The third, productivity-led growth, requires predictable regulation and quick approvals. The fourth, prevention over reaction, depends on the ability to detect problems early and respond coherently.
This is what makes the plenum a turning point in the “streamlining revolution” to cut the size of the state bureaucracy. In the past 12 months, the reform concentrated on structure: for example, reducing the number of provinces and centrally governed cities from 63 to 34, abolishing the district tier of government and consolidating commune-level units. It also removed people: nearly 210,000 civil servants and public employees took early retirement or severance under the restructuring. That was the first test, and the leadership passed it. The plenum entailed a second, and perhaps harder test: whether the machinery emerging from upheaval would be effective.

articles.title: South Korea’s Lee urges talks with North Korea about finally ending Korean war
articles.body:
South Korean president Lee Jae Myung called on Saturday for talks with North Korea to pursue peaceful coexistence, saying Seoul would seek safeguards to prevent conflict and noting the need to replace the peninsula’s armistice with a “peace regime“.
In a speech marking the anniversary of Korea’s liberation from Japanese colonial rule, Lee said the two Koreas should hold a sit-down for coexistence.
He urged dialogue between North Korea and concerned parties to end the 1950-53 Korean war, which was stopped by a ceasefire, not a peace treaty, and said discussions could also explore measures to curb Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities.
Lee said Seoul would take pre-emptive and sustained steps to ease tensions and build layered safeguards to contain escalation.
Lee’s call largely builds on his pledge last year to respect North Korea’s system and seek peaceful coexistence with Pyongyang.
Ties between North and South Korea remain frozen. North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has abandoned Pyongyang’s reunification policy, has described the South as its most hostile state and ordered stronger frontline defences.
North Korea has rebuffed Lee’s engagement offers, criticised Seoul’s plan for nuclear-powered submarines and denounced joint US-South Korean military drills as provocations.
On relations with Japan, Lee called for confronting the past while leaving open the future, and said he hoped to launch a new 60 years of peace and prosperity with Japan as a “close neighbour”.

articles.title: New ecology rules drive cross-boundary collaboration
articles.body:
An environmental expert says the country’s new Ecological and Environmental Code, which took effect on Saturday to mark National Ecology Day, opens up opportunities for Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area to deepen ecological partnerships.
Passed by the National People's Congress in March, the legal framework is China’s second formal code, following the Civil Code enacted in 2020.
Spanning five chapters with more than 1,200 articles, it covers key areas such as pollution control, ecological conservation, and green, low-carbon development.
In addition, it regulates new types of pollution - such as light, electromagnetic radiation, organic chemicals, and pharmaceuticals - while requiring companies to file annual emissions reports and register pollution-related facilities.
The code also turns the country’s “dual carbon” goals of peaking carbon emissions by 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality by 2060 from policy aspirations into statutory mandates.
Yau Wing-kwong, founder and chief executive officer of the Environmental Association, noted that the code effectively consolidated over 30 existing national environment-related statutes.
"It is really consolidating all these laws and making it easier for businesses and people to understand, and also easier to monitor and enforce,” he explained.
Yau pointed out the code also opens up greater scope for collaboration between Hong Kong and cities in the GBA.
"We have been building butterfly gardens in Hong Kong and also over the border with Shenzhen and even Macao. So the ecological corridor between butterflies or other species like birds and so on. They are already in practice,” he said.
“But again, conservation, study and citizen science - and getting people involved - can be enhanced and go further.”
Further cooperation, Yau noted, could also include research on renewable energy and waste recycling initiatives.
Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: War of NH blockades in Manipur: Kuki women body moves Supreme Court
articles.body:
CJI Kant said the blockade war must stop, groups must sit together, abjure violence, and cooperate with each other so that the supply of essential commodities and medicines are not disrupted.
NEW DELHI: Blockading NHs in Manipur by ethnic groups to inconvenience opponents is common but the Supreme Court on Friday took serious note of the humanitarian crisis such actions unleash after an NGO of Kuki women claimed that blockading of NH-2 and connected supply routes to Kangpokpi has left the population in there without food and healthcare.Senior advocate Anand Grover, appearing for Kuki Women Organisation for Human Rights, told a bench of CJI Surya Kant, and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that the NH-2 and supply routes to Kangpokpi has been blocked by Naga groups creating a crisis for the population and requested the SC to direct the Centre and the state to reopen the NH. “The state just can’t sit and do nothing,” he complained.Intervening in the matter, an Imphal-based NGO – International Meitei Organization – through senior advocate Ngangom Junior Luwang said the Kukis had been “responsible for blocking all major NHs in Manipur since May 2023, after the Kuki-Meitei ethnic clashes began, and now they are playing the ‘victim card' when faced with the consequences of such blockades by another ethnic group.”“It is a matter of record that since May 3, 2023, members of the community, of which the petitioner is a part of, have been blocking all major NHs in Manipur - NH2 (Imphal to Dimapur), NH-37 (Imphal to Silchar), and NH-102 (Imphal to Moreh) and except for intermittent flow of goods vehicles through extortion rackets reportedly perpetuated by Kuki community,” the NGO alleged.
CJI Kant said the blockade war must stop, groups must sit together, abjure violence, and cooperate with each other so that the supply of essential commodities and medicines are not disrupted.
When Luwang welcomed the CJI’s suggestion, Grover immediately offered the petitioner organisation’s cooperation but wondered who would bring the Naga group to the talks.SC issued notices to the Centre, Manipur govt and National Highway Authority of India (NHAI) and said the larger public interest demands removal of blockade of all NHs in the state as well as restoration of supply to Kangpokpi district.It said Grover assured that his client in cooperation with social organisations would work towards the same and recorded similar sentiments expressed by Luwang on behalf of the Meitei NGO. It asked all the parties to suggest modalities for reopening all NHS without engaging in blame games. It posted the matter for further hearing after two weeks.

articles.title: Double disaster in Colombia: Wildfires surge as emergency crews struggle in aftermath of quake
articles.body:
Laura Gamba Fadul
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
Emergency response agencies in Colombia are facing an unprecedented multi-front crisis as dozens of active wildfires spread rapidly, compounding recovery efforts following a 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck earlier this week.
A total of 344 municipalities have been placed under a red alert for wildfire threats, a staggering 93% single-day surge driven by severe heat and dry conditions, according to the Institute of Hydrology, Meteorology and Environmental Studies (IDEAM).
The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management on Friday reported dozens of active conflagrations concentrated primarily in the departments of Tolima, Cesar, Norte de Santander, Antioquia, Narino, and Santander. Authorities have deployed firefighters, military units, emergency personnel, and aerial support in a race to contain the blazes. In regional reports, officials indicated that destroyed vegetation, crops and homes have exceeded 11,000 hectares (27,182 acres) in multiple municipalities.
The environmental forecast offers little relief. IDEAM projections indicate a 90% probability that the El Nino phenomenon will persist through early 2027, with intense heat anomalies expected to peak toward the end of the year.
The surge in wildfires has severely strained emergency crews already deployed at maximum capacity following the Aug. 10 quake. Official disaster unit reports place the death toll at 288, with 4,018 injured, 12,504 homes destroyed, and more than 80,000 structures damaged.
Firefighting crews from various departments, including Risaralda, one of the regions affected by the quake, have been dispatched to tackle the fires, although authorities said they are short-staffed.
Complicating the response, national risk management agencies are also monitoring heightened activity at the Purace volcano in the southern department of Cauca, forcing authorities to simultaneously manage multiple major natural hazards.

articles.title: Foreign Ministry Spokesperson’s Remarks on Japanese Politicians Paying Respects to the Yasukuni War Shrine Which Honors Class-A War Criminals
articles.body:
Q: August 15 marks the day of Japan’s unconditional surrender in the Second World War. Prime Minister of Japan Sanae Takaichi made a monetary offering to the Yasukuni war shrine today, and certain cabinet members also visited the shrine. What’s your comment?
A: China strongly deplores Japan’s negative moves related to the Yasukuni war shrine, and has lodged serious protests against Japan.
During WWII, Japan launched the war of aggression and committed horrendous crimes. The Yasukuni war shrine is a spiritual tool and symbol of Japanese militarism. It is in fact a shrine for war criminals, as it honors 14 convicted Class-A war criminals responsible for the war of aggression. No pretext whatsoever can hide the Japanese politicians’ true intention which is to change the verdict on the war criminals, cover up Japan’s war crimes, distort the historical facts, and pave the way for accelerating remilitarization. This is an affront to historical justice, a challenge to the foundational norms of civilization, and a provocation against the postwar international order. Such behaviors have been firmly rejected by the overwhelming majority of the international community.
This year marks the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials. To view and treat history correctly is an important prerequisite for Japan’s postwar return to the international community, the political foundation for Japan’s ties with neighboring countries, and more importantly, a key measure for Japan’s commitment to peaceful development. We urge the Japanese side to do serious soul-searching on its history of aggression, make a clean break with militarism, and earn trust from its Asian neighbors and the rest of the world with concrete actions.

articles.title: US: FDA recalls 19 million eggs over Salmonella risk
articles.body:
US: 19 million eggs recalled over Salmonella risk
August 15, 2026
Around 19 million eggs have been recalled in the United States over possible Salmonella contamination, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has said.
Midwest Poultry Services (MPS) voluntarily recalled 1,589,577 dozen eggs on July 22 after detecting potential Salmonella Enteritidis contamination at two Texas farms, the FDA said.
MPS Egg Farms said on its website that it had proactively recalled the eggs as a precautionary measure and initiated testing protocols to identify potential sources of Salmonella.
On Wednesday, the FDA said it was a Class 1 recall, indicating a reasonable probability of serious illness or death.
What did the FDA say about the egg recall?
The eggs were produced between June 6 and July 3 and distributed in the states of Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico and Mississippi.
These included both white shell eggs and brown cage-free shell eggs.
They were sold under several brand names, with sell-by or best-by dates from July 20 to August 17.
According to the FDA advisory:
- Consumers should throw away the recalled eggs or return them for a refund
- Restaurants and retailers should not serve or sell the eggs
- Consumers, restaurants, and retailers who purchased or received recalled eggs should carefully clean and sanitize any surfaces or containers that the recalled eggs touched.

articles.title: SC concerned by continuance of derogatory witch-hunting practice
articles.body:
NEW DELHI: More than 75 years of the Constitution coming into force, the derogatory practice of witch-hunting that targets defenceless women due to prejudice, suspicion, superstition and irrational fear, continues in the country, the Supreme Court lamented while upholding life term for two who murdered a woman in a tribal village of Odisha in Feb 1998.A bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and N V Anjaria said the facets of the case had a disturbing impact on the court as a defenceless woman was branded a practitioner of witchcraft and was brutally assaulted in front of her daughter. “What effect it must have had on the daughter of the deceased who had to witness her mother being killed in the most brutal way,” the bench wondered.Writing the judgment, Justice Mishra said the malady of with-hunting continues to plague sections of our society, where prejudice, superstition, and irrational dear supersede the rule of law and constitutional morality.“The brutality associated with witch-hunting extends far beyond the act of killing; where victims mostly women are subjected to torture, beatings, sexual violence and social ostracization. In such a situation, superstitious beliefs or fears are given precedence leading to vulnerable women becoming victims of collective hostility,” he said.IN Feb 1998, in the remote village of tribal inhabited Sundergarh district, one Manobodha Naik’s daughter died, and family members claimed that she died because of witchcraft practice of one Puni Naik.
Hearing this Udai Oram dragged Puni Naik to Naik’s house and with his associate, mercilessly assaulted her with sticks leading to her death. The trial court had convicted the duo in 2002, but the Orissa HC took two decades to uphold the conviction and life sentence.
Justices Mishra and Anjaria said, “Sometimes in the most difficult situations, it often becomes an easy escape to blame a woman for the acts she did not commit, thus reflecting a deeply rooted social prejudice that often seeks scapegoats rather than solutions. In such situations, what can be given an ascendency is ‘reason’ for reason is the only virtue that stands as a bulwark against collective irrationality.”SC said the Constitution guarantees equality, promotes fraternity and envisages citizens to adopt scientific temperament to rid the society of derogatory practices against women. “Despite this, practices such as witch-hunting continue to persist within a few sections of our society. A Constitutional democracy such as ours cannot survive; wherein such derogatory practices continue to elude the principles of rule of law and Constitutional morality,” it said.

articles.title: NASA chief says Artemis moon program to be accelerated
articles.body:
NEW YORK, August 15. /TASS/. US space agency NASA has made the decision to expedite the implementation of its Artemis moon program, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said.
"We are accelerating the Artemis program. In fact, Artemis III rocket is being stacked right now in the Vehicle Assembly Building. And following that flight, we will return American astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028," he said during an event at Cape Canaveral, Florida.
In May, the New Glenn heavy-lift rocket by Blue Origin, expected to take part in the Artemis III program, exploded during propulsion tests at Cape Canaveral. The company said it would deliver a replacement to NASA next year.
According to the plan, the Artemis III crew will be brought into space by the Orion crewed spacecraft atop the SLS carrier rocket. After that, Orion will dock and undock with the Blue Origin spacecraft, and later - with the Starship spacecraft by SpaceX. After that, Orion will return to the Earth, splashing down in the Pacific. The mission is expected to last two weeks.

articles.title: Live: Wallabies set to unleash hulking prop in historic Test against Japan
articles.body:
Wallabies vs Japan: Australia scores 56 points in dominant win over Brave Blossoms
Massimo De Lutiis has enjoyed a dream debut for Australia, as the 1,000th Wallaby scored a try in his country's commanding 56-17 win over Japan in the second Test.
De Lutiis came on in the 50th minute of the Test match in Townsville with the match delicately poised at 21-17, the half-time score.
But the introduction of the hulking 22-year-old began the start of Australia's dominance in the Test match, as fellow prop Angus Bell scored the first of five second-half tries.
De Lutiis, with the descendants of the very first Wallaby Patrick Carew in attendance, scored minutes later to send his teammates, and the crowd, into a frenzy.
"One thousand is awesome. But just to be a Wallaby in general is crazy to me. It's a dream come true," De Lutiis told the Nine Network post-match.
"When I scored, I was just over the moon. I couldn't believe it."
Despite the impressive scoreline, the Wallabies were tested in the opening 50 minutes, with the Japanese taking the lead late in the first half.
At three tries apiece after 40 minutes, the Brave Blossoms had every right to believe a maiden win over the Wallabies was there for the taking.
But Australia showed the polish which eluded them in the first half, and the first Test in Osaka last weekend.
New coach Les Kiss, in his second match in charge, provided the right team talk at half-time to wrestle momentum from Japan.
"We got challenged by Les [Kiss] at half-time," captain Harry Wilson told the Nine Network.
"A team like Japan, if you're not up for it, they really make you pay.
"I was really proud of the group in the second half. We stepped it up and put on a great performance."
The win is Australia's third in a row, the first time the Wallabies have strung together a trio of triumphs since 2024.
The challenge for Australia gets harder, with two Tests in Argentina followed by one Test against South Africa, and two Bledisloe Cup matches against the All Blacks.
Relive all the action from the second Test between Australia and Japan in the blog below.
Submit a comment or question
Live updates
REPORT: Wallabies defeat Japan 56-17 in Townsville
— reporting by AAP
Australia's forward pack have dined out as the Wallabies wriggled out of an awkward spot to streak away from Eddie Jones' Japan in Townsville.
The host's 56-17 triumph was in the balance until midway through the second half, when the 1000th Wallaby, Massimo De Lutiis, subbed on and stormed over for a debut try to create an 18-point lead.
It was one of six tries from Australian front-rowers on Saturday and — after a three-point win in Osaka seven days earlier — was the welcome breathing room coach Les Kiss was searching for in his second game in charge.
Taniela Tupou barged over for two close-range tries in the first half while Angus Bell added one, hooker Josh Nasser opened the scoring and his replacement Brandon Paenga-Amosa finished the job.
Carter Gordon controlled play nicely in his return at flyhalf while halfback Ryan Lonegan (5/5) was perfect off the tee.
Unforced errors kept Japan in it through the first half and the visitors led 17-14 before Tupou snuck in his second try before halftime to trigger a run of 42 consecutive points.
Slowly the hosts turned the screws, Carlo Tizzano pilfering three times and Fraser McReight immediately adding a steal when he came on in the final 15 minutes.
The Reds flanker replaced lock Lachlan Shaw, who held the lineout together in his starting debut, teaming with fellow pilferer Tizzano and shifting Harry Wilson into the second row.
That finally broke the Japanese resistance, with Charlie Cale and Harry Wilson getting on the board before Paenga-Amosa's after-the-buzzer effort.
Isaac Henry was also impressive in his second Test and first start in the No.13, replacing the injured Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii to give Kiss food for thought ahead of a two-Test tour of Argentina.
Henry's straight running busted the line regularly, with his assist for Lonergan waved away due to an earlier forward pass.
It was mission accomplished for Kiss, who avoided two banana-peel clashes against the side that dropped from 10 to 12 in the world last week.
And his selections, explained as "future-proofing" were also validated after in-form lock Josh Canham and prop Allan Alaalatoa were both rested in Townsville.

That is all for the live coverage
This is where the live coverage of the Wallabies vs Japan ends.
Australia has enjoyed a big win, on a historic day.
The Test matches get tougher from here, but the Wallabies are now on a three-match winning streak.
Thank you for joining us throughout the afternoon.

Here are the remaining Test matches for the Wallabies in 2026.

Thoughts on the Wallabies win from ABC Sport readers
Identifying tactical weaknesses that could be addressed , and the Wallabies constantly were slow to move forward in defence, therefore taking the pressure off, allowing the Japanese room that they should never have had.
- martin Doyle
Excellent structure,the backs will have a say in next Test
- Martin Butler
How good is watching forwards score?
6 of 8 tries by the front row for the Wallabies... the backs will be out of the business shortly
- Louise
Watching forwards score tries is my idea of perfect reality TV.
More of it I say.
We don't want to see backs scoring.
Massimo De Lutiis speaks after becoming Wallaby 1,000
Massimo De Lutiis became the 1,000th capped Wallaby today.
He also scored a debut try.
Here are some of his comments, speaking with broadcaster Stan Sport.
1,000 is awesome. But just to be a Wallaby in general is crazy to me. It's a dream come true.
When I scored I was just over the moon. I couldn't believe it.
Wallabies captain Harry Wilson says coach Les Kiss challenged the team
Australia struggled in the first half, despite holding a 21-17 lead at half-time.
Japan was playing with energy and, at times, the Wallabies were struggling to keep up.
Wallabies captain Harry Wilson told Stan Sport the team was challenged at half-time by coach Les Kiss, and they responded well.
We got challenged by Les [Kiss] at half-time.
A team like Japan, if you're not up for it they really make you pay.
I was really proud of the group in the second half. We stepped it up and put on a great performance.
Japan captain Warner Dearns speaks
Japan captain Warner Dearns has spoken to host broadcaster Stan Sport.
Japan were really good in the first half, and held a narrow lead late in the opening 40 minutes.
But that was as good as it got. as the Wallabies dominated the second half to run out handy winners.
Here is Dearns and his thoughts:
It was a good, tough, really hard battle. Credit to the Wallabies, they came out and gave us one in the second half, which we couldn't keep up with.
We knew that the Wallabies were going to come out hard. They had a big, physical pack at the start of the first half, so we put a real emphasis on trying to move them around and play a bit of our fast rugby.
I think we did it well in the first half, but we couldn't keep it going in the second half.
Isaac Henry speaks after Australia's win
Isaac Henry has spoken to host broadcaster Stan Sport following the Wallabies 56-17 win over Japan.
The Wallabies were tested in the first half, where Japan led at one point.
But the Wallabies came out in the second half and were an improved outfit.
Here are some of Henry's thoughts on the win.
I think all the boys worked extreamly hard and I just tried to do my job the best I could.
We weren't happy with some of the possessions we had in the first half and I think we kind of fixed that up a little bit.
Key Event
FULL-TIME: Australia 56 def. Japan 17
The Wallabies have produced a brilliant second half to secure a dominant 56-17 win over Japan in the second Test, as Australian rugby history was made.
Massimo De Lutiis became the 1,000th capped Wallaby ever, when the hulking prop came on after 50 minutes in Townsville and made an impact with a try less than 10 minutes later.
The Wallabies were tested in the first half by Japan, who had never beaten Australia in eight previous attempts, as both teams scored three tries in the opening 40 minutes.
But Japan wilted in the second half as the Wallabies piled on five tries.
80' TRY: Brandon Paenga-Amosa (16) scores for Australia
It is a cherry on top for Australia.
They marched down field, earned a penalty, and just kept hammering the Japanese line.
Ultimately, it was Brandon Paenga-Amosa who crashed over from close range.
Australia 56
Japan 17
Key Event
75' SIN BIN: Mamoru Harada (16) of Japan
Japan's replacement hooker Mamoru Harada was sent to the sin bin after that last Wallaby try.
The Wallabies were playing with advantage for the hooker being offside.
Japan was warned earlier about infringements on the goal-line, and Harada has been given an early shower.
75' TRY: Harry Wilson (8) scores for Australia
The Wallabies are really humming now.
A line break from Tom Wright (15) down the right flank, followed by a pass to Tate McDermott (21) put Japan on the backfoot.
The Wallabies then did what they have done all game when they get inside the Japan 22, they hammer with the forwards.
Pick-and-drives, short passes to big men, the Wallabies hammer and hammer until captain Harry Wilson crashes over.
Australia 49
Japan 17
72' TRY: Charlie Cale (6) scores for Australia
Fabulous from the Australian forwards.
The Wallabies had a scrum 10 metres out. The Wallabies anhilated the Japan scrum, pushing them back six metres before Charlie Cale, in the number 8 posiiton, picked the ball up and had no-one in front of him.
Great try by the big guys.
Australia 42
Japan 17
68' Japan warned for repeated penalties near the goal-line
The Wallabies are on the attack, and Japan has given away a penalty.
Japan has now been warned for too mamy penalties while defending the goal-line.
The Wallabies attacked the Japanese goal-line, with a chance to end this contest.
But a knock-on close to the line has kept the Japanese in this contest.
Australia 35
Japan 17
66' Wallabies dominating in the break down
Japan's attack in this second half has been nullified by a brilliant display from Australia in the ruck.
Four times the Wallabies have forced a penalty with the Brave Blossoms on the attack, getting their hands on the ball and forcing a penalty.
Carlo Tizzano (7) has been responsible for three of the penalties, in a textbook display of openside flanker play.
Australia 35
Japan 17
Key Event
58' TRY: Wallaby 1,000 scores for Australia
What a moment.
Wallaby 1,000, Massimo De Lutiis, has scored on debut.
It came off a line break from fly half Carter Gordon, who was brought down close to the line.
Subsitiution lock Jeremy Williams gave a lovely pass from the ruck, and De Lutiis charged onto the ball to score.
There is a party in Townsville.
Australia 35
Japan 17
51' TRY: Angus Bell (1) scores for Australia
Both starting props have now scored for the Wallabies.
From close range, Angus Bell crashes over.
The Wallabies have a new game plan: box kick high and let winger Max Jorgensen chase and catch it.
It put them in an attacking positon, and then a penalty allowed the home side to kick for touch and have a line out from close range.
The Wallabies played off the line out, attacked the middle of Japan's defence, and muscled their way over.
Ryan Lonergan converts.
Australia 28
Japan 17
Key Event
50': Massimo De Lutiis becomes Wallaby #1000
History has been made in Townsville.
Hulking prop Massimo De Lutiis has run onto the field for his international Test rugby debut.
The 22-year-old, who plays club rugby for the Queensland Reds, is the 1,000th capped Wallaby.
The Wallabies made two changes here.
ON: Massimo De Lutiis (18); OFF: Taniela Tupou (32)
ON: Jeremy Williams (19); OFF: Lukhan Salakaia-Loto (5)
Half-time changes
There have been changes from both teams.
Australia

Japan
ON: Kazuma Ueda (23) OFF: Haruto Kida (14)

articles.title: Hsiao says stronger Taiwan defenses required to deter China
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan must strengthen its defenses and make military action more costly for China, Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) said Friday.
Speaking in an interview with Al Jazeera, Hsiao said China's intention to take control of Taiwan is well known, while its willingness to use military force remains a serious concern. She said Beijing has been steadily building its military capabilities and some assessments suggest it could be ready for a possible attack by 2027.
Taiwan must therefore improve its ability to defend itself and raise the cost of any Chinese military action, Hsiao said. Preventing conflict is important not only for Taiwan's security but also for regional stability and the global economy.
Hsiao said China is using pressure below the level of open warfare, including cyberattacks, interference in domestic affairs, disinformation, legal measures, and psychological operations. She said Taiwan needs stronger social resilience and democratic institutions to respond to these threats.
China has also increased activities that could be used to pressure Taiwan through a maritime blockade. Hsiao said Beijing has used its coast guard and other nonmilitary forces to carry out maritime actions that Taiwan says have no basis in international law.
She added Taiwan must work with other countries to protect freedom of navigation, the rule of law, and peace in the Indo-Pacific. She said similar maritime tensions involving China have emerged in the South China Sea and waters near Japan, making the issue a wider regional concern.
Asked about possible US military involvement if Taiwan were attacked, Hsiao said the question was hypothetical and that the focus was instead on preventing such a situation. She said Taiwan and the US continue to cooperate to strengthen defenses and maintain peace and cross-strait stability.

articles.title: Taiwan tracks 4 Chinese military aircraft and 9 ships
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked four Chinese military aircraft, eight naval vessels, and one ship between 6 a.m. on Friday and the same time Saturday.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems. Three of the People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s northern, central and eastern air defense identification zones, according to the ministry.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese military aircraft 115 times and ships 179 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around Taiwan.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln's supply issues stem from Iran's Bahrain naval base attacks - report
articles.body:
The supply issues plaguing the USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72) aircraft carrier stem from Iranian drone and missile attacks on a naval base in Bahrain early in the US-Iran war, The New York Times reported on Friday.
According to the report, the US Navy initially used the Bahrain base for supply operations in its offensive against Iran, but was forced to change strategies following Iran's attacks on the base.
The US Navy decided to move its supply operations to the UK naval base located on the island of Diego Garcia, which the NYT noted sits over 3,500 km from the two US carrier strike groups operating in the Gulf of Oman.
The NYT attributed the base change to a direct impact on the supply problems currently facing the USS Abraham Lincoln, which, according to US Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut), include shortages, water contamination, and several other issues that have arisen over the past months.
Blumenthal, a US Marine Corps Reserve veteran, sent a letter to Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday demanding a formal inquiry into the conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.
“The Lincoln’s extended deployment raises broader questions about the Navy’s ability to sustainably generate carrier forces while preserving service member well-being, maintenance, schedules, fleet readiness, and the capacity to respond to future contingencies,” Blumenthal wrote.
CENTCOM denies ship crew members attempted to jump off
Further concerns regard the ship's crew amid reports that several have attempted to jump off the aircraft carrier, facing deteriorating mental health, as well as hygiene and safety issues, claims that US Central Command (CENTCOM) denied in an X/Twitter post on Thursday.
US President Donald Trump dismissed the concerns later on Friday, and the NYT quoted him as saying the ship's deployment length is "not nearly long enough."
According to the NYT, a reporter asked Trump whether the crew's families are concerned, and he replied, "No, they’re not," adding that the carrier would soon be relieved by "another very similar ship.”
Miriam Sela-Eitam and Esther Davis contributed to this report.

articles.title: ‘Have to isolate dimaagi Naxals’: PM Modi in Independence Day speech from Red Fort
articles.body:
‘Have to isolate dimaagi Naxals’: PM Modi in Independence Day speech from Red Fort
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 15, 2026, 09:57 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Armed Naxals are gone, but 'intellectual Naxals' still lurking; we must be vigilant: PM Modi
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday said armed Naxalism had been curbed but warned that people with Maoist thinking were still present in different parts of the country and needed to be "identified, and isolated".Addressing the nation from the ramparts of the Red Fort on the 80th Independence Day, PM Modi said the country had successfully weakened armed Naxalism but needed to remain alert against what he called "dimagi Naxals"."We need to identify these dimagi naxal, isolate them, and bring the youth together for a developed country," PM Modi said.PM Modi said Naxalism and Maoism had destroyed the aspirations of young people and kept large parts of the country under the grip of violence for decades. He also paid tribute to security personnel who lost their lives fighting the insurgency.
"Naxalism, Maoism destroyed the dreams of lakhs of youth. It stole the sons of numerous mothers, crushed the dreams of numerous mothers. This naxalism had kept a large part of India and population as a hostage for 4 decades with the barrel of a gun, they had destroyed the Constitution," PM Modi said.He said more than 3,500 security personnel had been killed while protecting citizens from Naxal violence.
"More than 3,500 security personnel were martyred while protecting the people of the country. More police personnel were killed than soldiers in war, police personnel had to put their lives on the line so that people can get security. This naxalism had covered the country in blood. In 2014, when you gave us the opportunity we had decided that we will rid the country of naxalism, and today I am happy to announce that naxalism does not have even the strength for breathing," the Prime Minister added.
PM Modi warns against ‘dimagi Naxals’
PM Modi drew a distinction between armed Naxals and people he described as "dimagi naxal", alleging that the latter continued to look for opportunities to promote violence and push the country in what he called the wrong direction."For years, people with Maoist thinking were there in public life, even in government committees this thinking had affected various institutions and initiatives. My dear countrymen, we have been able to curb and free the country from 'hathariya naxal' (armed naxal). Even if these naxals are gone, but the 'dimagi naxal' (people with naxal thinking), are looking for an opportunity, looking to see ways of violence, and trying to drag the country to a wrong path. We need to identify these dimagi naxal, isolate them, and bring the youth together for a developed country," PM Modi said.PM Modi said areas that were once affected by Naxal violence were now witnessing development, with the Tricolour representing progress and government initiatives flying in regions where armed insurgency had previously held sway."In the 21st century, it is imperative that we eliminate the decades-old challenges that have held the country back. Naxalism and Maoism have destroyed the future of millions of young people. They have snatched away the young sons of countless mothers and shattered the dreams of families across the country. For nearly four decades, Naxalism had held large parts of India and a huge section of its population in its grip, ruling through the barrel of a gun and tearing the Constitution to shreds. More than 3,500 of our police and security personnel sacrificed their lives while protecting ordinary citizens. Naxalism had turned the land red with blood."
‘Naxalism is breathing its last’
PM Modi said the government had decided to eliminate Naxalism after coming to power in 2014 and claimed that armed Maoist violence no longer had the strength to sustain itself."When you gave us the opportunity to serve in 2014, we resolved on that very day to free the country from Naxalism.""Today, I am happy to say that Naxalite and Maoist violence no longer has the strength to sustain itself and is breathing its last. We are moving towards completely eliminating it. In areas where the bullets of Naxalites once rang out, where the soil was once stained with blood, today the same Naxal-affected regions are witnessing the tricolour of development, trust and endeavour flying high as they move towards becoming Naxalism-free."
PM Modi recalls challenges faced by India
During his Independence Day address, PM Modi also referred to challenges India faced over the past several years, including the Covid-19 pandemic and conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia."In the last 20-12 years, we have faced many dangers. As soon as we emerged from Covid, there was news of wars that started to arise from Ukraine side and West Asia. An atmosphere of tension prevailed. God knows what all the predictions the predictors made!," he said.
PM Modi said attempts were also made to create fear among citizens through rumours over the availability of vaccines, petrol, diesel and fertilisers.The remarks formed part of PM Modi's wider Independence Day address, in which he outlined the government's priorities and India's development ambitions as the country moves towards the goal of becoming a developed nation by 2047.

articles.title: Italy striker Immobile retires at age 36
articles.body:
ROME, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- Former Italy international Ciro Immobile announced Friday his retirement at the age of 36 following his departure from Paris FC.
As one of Italy's most prolific strikers in recent years, Immobile has represented numerous clubs including Juventus, Genoa and Borussia Dortmund, winning the Serie A top scorer of the season award on four occasions.
During his spell with Lazio from 2016 to 2024, Immobile won one Italian Cup and two Italian Super Cup titles, and claimed the European Golden Shoe in the 2019-20 season, before becoming the club's all-time best scorer.
Immobile then played for Besiktas and Bologna, before joining Paris FC in January. He had two goals and two assists during his six-month stint with the France capital team.
At international level, Immobile earned 57 caps and scored 17 goals for Italy. He was part of the Azzurri squad that won the UEFA European Championship in 2021. ■

articles.title: UAE state oil company says vessel attacked in Hormuz Strait
articles.body:
ABU DHABI, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- A vessel belonging to Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Friday evening, the company said Saturday.
The company confirmed that no injuries have been reported, according to the official WAM news agency.
The statement came a day after the UAE accused Iran of attacking two vessels linked to ADNOC as they passed through the strait. The UAE foreign ministry condemned the "hostile Iranian attack."
The state-owned ADNOC is one of the world's largest oil and gas producers, serving as the primary driver of the UAE's economy. ■

Why Israeli settlements will never be a success story | Opinion
At a public event I recently attended, representatives of several organizations working on proposals to resolve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict took the stage one after another to persuade the audience to support their respective plans. They answered questions about different aspects of their proposals and made their case to the audience, which then voted for its preferred plan.
The speakers tried to emphasize the differences between the plans, to make things more interesting, but struggled to do so. Although the proposals all had different names, they were, in essence, variations of the same idea: a two-state solution. The reason is simple: there is no other realistic solution.
In a recent article, Haaretz's Matan Golan surveyed in detail the progress of the settlement enterprise under the auspices of the ruling coalition ("103 Nails on the Map"; June 30). The figures are daunting. The government has approved the establishment of more than 100 new settlements, a move that will nearly double their total number. And that doesn't include the hundreds of outposts and farms currently being regularized.
Two killed, several wounded in IDF strikes in Lebanon, health ministry says
Two people were killed and several were wounded in Israeli military strikes in the village of Deir ez-Zahrani, the Lebanese Health Ministry said Saturday, as rescue teams continued searching for people trapped under the rubble, according to local reports.
Earlier Saturday, Lebanon's National News Agency reported that seven people were killed in an Israeli airstrike in Ansar, in the Nabatieh district.
The Israeli military said it struck targets in the Nabatieh district in response to Hezbollah attacks in the Ali al-Taher ridge, which the military described as an area in the Israeli-controlled buffer zone.
NYPD charges man who assaulted congregant in synagogue with hate crime
New York police charged a 46-year-old Bronx man with hate crimes after he disrupted Shabbat services at Manhattan's Central Synagogue, assaulted a congregant and attacked a member of the synagogue's security team.
NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Saturday that Larry Montes was charged with two counts of assault as a hate crime and one count of criminal mischief as a hate crime, among other charges.
The NYPD has arrested Larry Montes, a 46-year-old man from the Bronx, in connection with this incident. Montes has now been charged with two counts of assault as a hate crime and one count of criminal mischief as a hate crime, among other charges.
Earlier this evening, an individual disrupted Shabbat services at Central Synagogue in Manhattan. As synagogue security was escorting him out, he struck a member of the congregation, damaged synagogue property, and then spit at and headbutted a member of the security team. An
Police said Montes struck a member of the congregation, damaged synagogue property, and spit at and headbutted a member of the security team. He was arrested overnight into Saturday.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani denounced the attack on X, saying he could "only imagine the pain and fear an attack like this, during Shabbat services, causes for the congregation and for Jewish New Yorkers across our city."
At least seven killed in overnight IDF strikes in Lebanon, reports say
At least nine people were killed by Israeli strikes in Lebanon overnight into Saturday, according to Lebanese media reports.
Initial reports indicate that seven people were killed in an airstrike in Ansar, in the Nabatieh district, according to Lebanese media; search operations at the site are still ongoing.
Trump rejects reports of mental health crisis among USS Abraham Lincoln crew amid U.S.-Iran naval standoff
President Donald Trump rejected reports of a mental health crisis among U.S. service members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln on Friday, after reports that sailors tried to jump overboard.
Trump was asked by reporters at Joint Base Andrews whether the Lincoln's eight-and-a-half months at sea was too long, to which the president replied, "No, no, no. Not nearly long enough," according to Fox News. The Lincoln has reportedly spent 250 consecutive days at sea without making land, amid a tense naval standoff between Iran and the United States.
Trump also told reporters that relatives of service members were not worried about their family members' conditions.
Washington is sending a new aircraft carrier to the Middle East to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week. On Wednesday, The Guardian reported that the Lincoln is undergoing a mental health crisis, with multiple instances where the carrier's crew members tried to jump overboard. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth denied reports of poor conditions aboard the carrier, saying they were "completely misrepresented."
Florida venue cancels rally with Palestinian American lawmaker Rashida Tlaib
A South Florida site backed out of hosting a rally with Democratic U.S. Representative Rashida Tlaib, a vocal critic of Israel's government, after complaints by a Democratic state lawmaker in the party's latest flashpoint over its stance on Israel.
Tlaib, the first Palestinian American member of Congress, was scheduled to appear on Friday at a rally for three candidates in Florida's upcoming Democratic Party primary.
However, The Venue Fort Lauderdale, which was scheduled to host the event, suddenly canceled it after State Representative Michael Gottlieb, chairman of the Florida Legislative Jewish Caucus, posted a statement on Thursday calling the planned rally an "anti-Jew" gathering.
Tlaib has condemned antisemitism and says criticism of Israel's occupation of Palestinian territories and its attacks in Gaza and Lebanon is not antisemitic.
The Venue in a statement cited "increased security concerns" for its decision and said it is Jewish-owned and "our values and commitment to the Jewish community are deeply important to us."
The Florida Democratic Progressive Caucus said the cancellation of the rally was rooted in anti-Muslim sentiment. Florida's primary elections are scheduled for August 18.
Yemen government says Houthi missiles kill four civilians in port city
Yemen's internationally recognized government said Iran-aligned Houthis fired six ballistic missiles at the Red Sea port of Mocha on Friday, killing at least four civilians.
The escalation in hostilities between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government has come amid heightened regional tensions from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. The Houthis have emerged as a key front in that war, raising the prospect of a return to large-scale conflict in Yemen.
The Yemeni armed forces aligned with the government said in a statement that the Houthi attack on Mocha targeted a civilian facility and economic and maritime installations, killing one port security guard. Two sailors were also missing and eight civilians were wounded, the armed forces said.
JD Vance's 'Communion' gives readers a chronicle of unconvincing conversions
Vance's most recent book, "Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith" (June 2026) ostensibly sets out to detail the story of Vance's 2019 conversion to Catholicism, after he abandoned his evangelical Protestant upbringing for what was, among young men in the 2000s, a common melange of atheism and liberalism. Yet this is actually the story of not one conversion but three: not just his choice to be baptized a Catholic, but also his transformation from Trump critic to Trump's heir apparent, and his turn away from Republican free-market orthodoxy to a kind of "daddy-state" conservatism: pro-natalist, pro-worker and protectionist. "Communion," then, is also a campaign book intended to reintroduce the new, Trumpified Vance to the American public and, as such, an attempt to craft a coherent ideology for the future of the populist right.
In his own telling, Trump's anti-establishment provocations, which previously had alarmed Vance, were what ultimately won him over. For all Trump's mendacity and vulgarity, Vance came to see Trump as an effective vehicle for the rage of middle America's dispossessed. The more coastal elites shuddered each time Trump punctured liberal pieties and shredded progressive orthodoxies, the more Trump appeared to him as a much-needed shock to the system that had failed people like his family and community. The America that produced Trump, Vance writes, was "a country where my friends' and family's life expectancy was actually declining while the media's loudest voices called them racists for being ticked off about it."

articles.title: German sprinter Ansah wins 200m gold after alleged failure to comply with doping test
articles.body:
German sprinter Ansah wins 200m gold after alleged failure to comply with doping test
BIRMINGHAM, England (AP) — German sprinter Owen Ansah won the 200-meter final at the European championships Friday despite facing a potential ban at home for allegedly failing to comply with a doping test.
Ansah crossed the line in 19.95 seconds for the gold medal at Alexander Stadium three nights after taking the bronze in the 100 meters.
“I hope everyone will know my name now,” Ansah said. “This was the goal, to leave the Europeans with two medals. A bronze and gold is amazing for me.”
The 200 was “was always the main goal,” he added. “This race was just more for me. At a championship you never know what can happen.”
Last week, the National Anti Doping Agency of Germany alleged Ansah “committed a violation of Article 2.3 of the National Anti-Doping Code ... (refusal or failure to submit to sample collection).”
There was no provisional suspension, however, so Ansah remains eligible to compete.
NADA Germany’s “letter of charge” calls for a four-year ban. Ansah had 20 days to either accept the findings “or request the initiation of disciplinary proceedings before the German Court of Arbitration for Sport.”
Ansah told German site sport1 that an anti-doping official came to his house for an out-of-competition test last month as he was leaving to travel to Monaco. Ansah reportedly said he couldn’t immediately give a urine sample and wasn’t aware of the consequences.
Athletes across multiple sports have received lengthy bans under such rules. In June, former Wimbledon tennis champion Marketa Vondrousova was given the maximum four-year ban for refusing a test.

articles.title: Truck driver flees after vehicle crashes and bursts into flames on Lantau highway
articles.body:
Truck driver flees after vehicle crashes and bursts into flames on Lantau highway
16-tonne truck skidded and crashed into barriers amid amber rainstorm alert, with debris from collision injuring two people in nearby taxi, police say
A truck driver fled the scene after his vehicle crashed into roadside barriers and burst into flames on Hong Kong’s Lantau Island early on Saturday, with debris from the collision injuring a taxi driver and a passenger travelling behind.
The crash occurred at about 3.15am during an amber rainstorm warning. A 16-tonne truck carrying electronic parts was heading towards the airport when it crashed on the North Lantau Highway near Tung Chung Eastern Interchange.
The vehicle skidded on the wet road, struck eight metres (26.2 feet) of barriers, then slid a further 30 metres before coming to rest on the hard shoulder, police said.
The truck quickly caught fire, with online footage showing fierce flames and thick smoke billowing into the sky. Explosions were also heard at the scene.
Firefighters arrived about 10 minutes after the crash and confirmed that no one was trapped inside.
According to the Fire Services Department, more than 50 rescue personnel, eight fire engines and three ambulances were deployed, with two hoses and two breathing apparatus teams used to extinguish the blaze by 4.23am.

articles.title: HRW says US civil rights enforcement reduced under Trump: What to know
articles.body:
HRW says US civil rights enforcement reduced under Trump: What to know
A new report documents how federal agencies have reduced the number of civil rights cases they pursue as staffing falls.
According to a new report, the United States federal government has taken a massive step back from its role in protecting civil rights across the country.
On Thursday, the nonprofit Human Rights Watch issued a 112-page analysis of the government’s civil rights activities from January 2025 through the start of 2026, a period that captures the opening months of President Donald Trump’s second term.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump appointee probes Nike over claims of bias against white workers
- list 2 of 3ABC ‘fighting back’, urging US public to defend stations amid FCC scrutiny
- list 3 of 3Why the US may stop collecting workplace race and gender data
The report concludes that the federal agencies responsible for stopping discrimination have largely been gutted of their staff.
Additionally, top-down directives by Trump have de-emphasised the federal government’s role in protecting civil rights across the country, according to the group.
“While claiming to protect all Americans, the administration is rolling back systems that communities have long turned to for relief,” Trey Walk, a researcher at Human Rights Watch, said in a statement.
Which agencies did the report analyse?
The report examines four key agencies within the federal government dedicated to civil rights.
They include the Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice, the Office of Civil Rights at the Education Department, the Fair Housing Office at the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.
Human Rights Watch spoke with current and former federal workers, lawyers, complainants and community groups who had been involved in cases alleging discrimination.
It also reviewed court filings and federal agency directives that illustrated the pivot in priorities under the second Trump administration.
What is the history of civil rights enforcement in the federal government?
The federal government’s role in civil rights protections goes back centuries, starting with the US Constitution.
In 1791, Congress ratified an addition to the country’s founding document that established civil protections like the freedom of religion. Those first 10 amendments became known as the Bill of Rights.
Over the decades, more amendments were added, most notably after the US Civil War, to guarantee rights like equal protection under the law.
While the Constitution contains explicit language about religion and race, critics point out that there is no language that confers equal protection based on sex or gender.
The history of the Department of Justice is closely entwined with the need to enforce civil rights law after the Civil War.
Created in 1870, the department addressed several needs, including a push to professionalise and centralise the country’s federal law enforcement. But it also helped prosecute violent white supremacist groups at a time when local authorities, particularly in southern states, sometimes refused to.
The US Civil Rights Movement, starting in the 1950s, also spurred a surge in federal infrastructure. It was the Civil Rights Act of 1957, for instance, that established a dedicated civil rights division within the Justice Department.
How did federal policy change under Trump?
Trump’s second term ushered in a backlash towards policies broadly considered to be part of the “diversity, equity and inclusion” movement, or DEI.
That movement gained popularity in the early 2020s, particularly after the murder of George Floyd, an unarmed Black man, sparked a public reckoning over racial inequality.
Trump, however, has called DEI “racially discriminatory”. During his campaign for a second term, he argued that there was a “definite anti-white feeling in this country”.
Since starting his second term, Trump has sought to undo policies that his administration argues give unfair advantages to demographics like women and minorities.
In addition, federal agencies like the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division suspended certain cases they were pursuing, including some involving sexual harassment and transgender rights.
New investigations were opened instead, including against the footwear giant Nike, which was accused this year of discrimination against white employees.
In May 2025, the Department of Justice also announced it would halt investigations and reform agreements involving police departments accused of racial discrimination.
Such measures had been taken in places like Louisville, Kentucky, and Minneapolis, Minnesota, after public outcry over the police killings of unarmed Black people, including Floyd.
What did the Human Rights Watch report find?
The report chronicled an overall weakening in the federal bodies designed to protect civil rights.
Job cuts and resignations were part of that trend. The Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice, for instance, boasted about 365 lawyers in January 2025, when Trump took office.
By the end of that year, three-quarters of those lawyers had left the agency, an exodus driven by what Human Rights Watch called a “coordinated effort to undermine career staff”.
A spokesperson for the Justice Department told Al Jazeera its Civil Rights Division “remains dedicated to protecting the rights of all Americans”.
The department also said it had added 100 personnel since the 2025 departures.
According to the spokesperson, the Civil Rights Division is currently focused on “protecting religious liberty, Second Amendment rights, and women’s and girls’ spaces, standing against illegal race-based policymaking and DEI, and defending parents’ fundamental right to direct their children’s upbringing and education”.
What other offices were affected?
Other agencies in the Human Rights Watch report likewise saw a decrease in their ranks as well as a reduction in their civil rights work.
The Office of Fair Housing went from 31 staffers to 11 by mid-2025. Some 115 complaints prepared by the office and referred to the Justice Department for possible legal action were quashed, according to the report.
At the Department of Education, the Office for Civil Rights initially had 568 workers across 12 offices when Trump took office in 2025. Within a few months, seven of those offices were shuttered, and half of the civil rights-related workers were gone.
Between May and September 2025, the office dismissed about 90 percent of the nearly 10,000 complaints it received, a higher rate than it would have in the past, the report said.
What has been the impact of these changes?
Human Rights Watch found that many victims and communities grappling with discrimination no longer had the benefit of a federal agency to help them in their cases.
One community housing group told Human Rights Watch that the Department of Housing and Urban Development no longer responds in a timely fashion to reported instances of anti-LGBTQ discrimination.
Some federal agencies also appear to have walked away from their role in monitoring discrimination and overseeing reforms around the country, according to the report.
The Department of Education’s Office of Civil Rights has a long history of investigating discrimination claims and working with school districts to enact change.
But Human Rights Watch observed that the office has largely stopped dealing with complaints under Trump.
While the Office of Civil Rights required policy changes or monitoring in response to 336 cases in the first half of 2024, only 59 cases received such a remedy over a similar period in 2025.
In Springfield, Massachusetts, for instance, parents complained after white students held a mock “slave auction” on the social media platform Snapchat, where they bid for the sale of their fellow Black students. That case is no longer being pursued by the Office of Civil Rights as of last year.
