articles.title: Mark Rydell, the Oscar-nominated director of ‘On Golden Pond,’ dies at 97
articles.body:
Mark Rydell, the Oscar-nominated director of ‘On Golden Pond,’ dies at 97
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Mark Rydell, the Oscar-nominated director of the sentimental blockbuster “On Golden Pond” who worked with such Hollywood heavyweights as Henry Fonda, Katharine Hepburn, Steve McQueen and John Wayne, has died. He was 97.
His daughter, Amy Rydell, told The Hollywood Reporter that her father died Thursday of natural causes at a retirement community for the entertainment industry in the Woodland Hills section of Los Angeles.
“Hard to put into words how much I loved my dad,” she posted Friday on her Instagram account. “He was truly one of a kind. Funniest and most talented person I’ve ever known.”
‘On Golden Pond’ earned 10 Oscar nominations
“On Golden Pond,” which teamed Fonda with Hepburn and his daughter, Jane Fonda, was nominated for 10 Oscars. Henry Fonda and Hepburn won leading acting honors and the film won for screenplay, which Ernest Thompson adapted from his play of the same name. Rydell was nominated for directing but lost to Warren Beatty for “Reds.”
It earned over $119 million at the box office, making it the second-highest grossing film of 1981 behind “Raiders of the Lost Ark.”
“On Golden Pond” was Henry Fonda’s final movie role. He starred as Norman Thayer, an emotionally brittle and distant father who becomes more accessible at the end of his life after his teenage grandson spends the summer with him and his wife, Ethel (played by Hepburn), at their cottage in New England. The film’s story resembled Fonda’s real-life relationship with daughter Jane, who said working on the movie together helped resolve some of their issues. The elder Fonda died at age 77 months after winning his only Oscar.
Rydell’s other Oscar-nominated films were “The Fox” in 1967, “The Reivers” with McQueen in 1969, “Cinderella Liberty” with James Caan and Marsha Mason in 1973, “The Rose” with Bette Midler in 1979, and “The River” with Mel Gibson and Sissy Spacek in 1984.
Born Mortimer Harold Rydell on March 23, 1929, in New York City, he studied with jazz pianist Teddy Wilson at the Julliard School of Music. During a stint in the Army, he spent two years in Japan developing entertainment for military personnel. He majored in English and philosophy at New York University.
Early acting career opposite Steiger, Cassavetes, Mineo
He turned to acting when he won a scholarship to the Neighborhood Playhouse in New York. Among his early roles were on the CBS soap operas “The Edge of Night” and “As the World Turns.”
Rydell made his Broadway debut in “Seagulls Over Sorrento” with Rod Steiger. In 1956, he made his movie acting debut opposite John Cassavetes and Sal Mineo in Don Siegel’s “Crime In The Streets.”
Among his film acting credits were Robert Altman’s “The Long Goodbye” in 1973 and Woody Allen’s “Hollywood Ending” in 2002.
Rydell moved into directing television, helming episodes of “Mr. Novak,” “Ben Casey,” “I Spy,” “The Wild Wild West,” “The Long, Hot Summer,” “The Fugitive” and “Gunsmoke.”
He made his feature-film directorial debut with 1967’s “The Fox” starring Sandy Dennis, and it was a hit.
Two years later, Rydell directed McQueen in the comedy-drama “The Reivers.”
Teaming with Sydney Pollack
Rydell and Sydney Pollack, who became friends during their acting days, formed Sanford Productions in 1971. Among their efforts were the films “Jeremiah Johnson” starring Robert Redford and “Scarecrow” with Al Pacino and Gene Hackman, which won the Cannes Film Festival’s top honor, the Palme d’Or.
Rydell directed Wayne in 1972’s “The Cowboys.” He reunited with Caan for the 1976 flop “Harry and Walter Go to New York.”
He scored a major hit with 1979’s “The Rose,” with Midler in her Oscar-nominated role as a self-destructive rock star loosely based on Janis Joplin.
Rydell re-teamed with Caan and Midler in “For the Boys” in 1991, but it wasn’t successful.
“He was an actor of note before he became a director, and I was so lucky to have met him when I did; he taught me so much on The Rose and later on For The Boys,” Midler posted on Instagram. “Two Oscars nominations both because of him. He was the actor’s whisperer; just a few words was all it took to understand what was needed. Devoted to Meisner. So many happy memories.”
TV movies and series among his credits
Rydell directed the pilot of the hit ABC drama “Family” in 1976.
Among his TV movie directing credits were “McBride and Groom,” “Crime of the Century” with Isabella Rossellini and Stephen Rea, and “James Dean,” which earned actor James Franco a Golden Globe award. Rydell also appeared in the movie as Warner Bros. chief Jack Warner.
He directed the movies “Intersection” in 1994 and “Even Money” in 2006.
In 2009, Rydell, Oscar-winning actor Martin Landau and screenwriter Lyle Kessler taught a film workshop at UCLA. Rydell and Landau were co-artistic directors of The Actors Studio West, teaching and coaching actors, writers and directors.
“All great art rests on telling the truth,” Rydell told UCLA’s student newspaper The Daily Bruin. “The real pursuit of an artist is to tell the truth.”
Besides his daughter, he is survived by son Christopher. The siblings who went into acting were from his first marriage to actor Joanne Linville. He had another son, Alexander, from his second marriage to producer Esther Rydell.

articles.title: UK lawmaker condemns Bezos-linked investment in Liverpool
articles.body:
Berk Kutay Gökmen
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
British lawmaker Zarah Sultana on Friday condemned the sale of a minority stake in Liverpool Football Club to a consortium including billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, urging supporters to denounce the investment.
Liverpool owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG) agreed to sell a roughly one-third stake in the Premier League club to 1892 Holdings, a consortium led by former Queens Park Rangers Chairman Amit Bhatia, and including the Mittal Family Trusts, EE Capital and K5 Sports, where Bezos is the lead investor. FSG will retain majority ownership and operational control, according to an Anadolu report.
“Sickened by the news that Jeff Bezos’ consortium has bought roughly a third of Liverpool Football Club,” Sultana, an independent MP, wrote on US social media company X.
She cited Amazon’s controversial record on workers’ rights and trade unions among her concerns, warning against Liverpool becoming “just another asset in a billionaire’s portfolio.”
Sultana also criticized Amazon’s involvement in Project Nimbus, a cloud computing contract involving Amazon Web Services and Google that provides services to the Israeli government.
She alleged that Amazon’s technology helps underpin Israeli state infrastructure amid Israel’s genocidal war against the Gaza Strip, and questioned whether the investment is compatible with Liverpool’s identity and history of solidarity.
“Liverpool is more than a business, it’s a community,” wrote Sultana.
She urged supporters to mobilize against the investment, pointing to previous fan campaigns against the proposed European Super League and increases in ticket prices.
“Supporters have a voice. We’ve used it before,” she said. “We MUST use it again.”
Spirit of Shankly, Liverpool’s recognized supporters’ union, also said the deal had raised “many questions for supporters.”
The group said it had contacted the UK’s Independent Football Regulator about the next steps and would also seek clarity on the due diligence required by the Premier League.
SoS said it would consult its members and the wider Liverpool fan base about concerns surrounding the transaction.
“Given the commitments by FSG and the previous roles of head of the consortium Amit Bhatia, we will be seeking engagement to understand better what this sale and consequent changes will mean for the future of LFC and its fans,” it said.
The supporters’ union stressed the importance of scrutiny about ownership, saying Liverpool fans needed “zero reminder of the importance of good governance and club ownership.”
Anadolu reported earlier that Liverpool supporters had sought assurances about the proposed investment, including questions about the identity of the investors, their potential influence, and whether their involvement aligns with the club’s values.

articles.title: Japanese defense minister visits notorious Yasukuni Shrine on WWII surrender anniversary
articles.body:
TOKYO, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi visited the notorious war-linked Yasukuni Shrine on Saturday, the anniversary of Japan's unconditional surrender in World War II, public broadcaster NHK reported.
It marked the first visit by an incumbent Japanese defense minister to Yasukuni Shrine on the anniversary of the end of WW II since then Defense Minister Minoru Kihara visited the shrine on the same occasion in 2024.
Several senior lawmakers of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party likewise paid visits to the controversial shrine on the day, the report said.
Yasukuni Shrine, located in central Tokyo's Chiyoda Ward, honors 14 convicted Japanese Class-A war criminals from World War II. It has long been a source of diplomatic friction between Japan and its neighbors.
For a long time, visits and ritual offerings made by Japanese officials to the controversial shrine have consistently sparked criticism and opposition both at home and abroad, hurting the feelings of the people of China, South Korea, and other countries and regions victimized by Japan's wartime aggression. ■

articles.title: Japanese PM sends ritual offering to notorious Yasukuni Shrine
articles.body:
TOKYO, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Saturday sent a ritual offering to the notorious Yasukuni Shrine, a symbol of Japanese militarism and wartime aggression, local media reported.
Takaichi made a "tamagushi" ritual offering to the war-linked shrine through senior officials of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party on the occasion of the anniversary of Japan's unconditional surrender in World War II, Kyodo News reported.
Yasukuni Shrine, located in central Tokyo's Chiyoda Ward, honors 14 convicted Japanese Class-A war criminals from World War II. It has long been a source of diplomatic friction between Japan and its neighbors.
For a long time, visits and ritual offerings made by Japanese officials to the controversial shrine have consistently sparked criticism and opposition both at home and abroad, hurting the feelings of the people of China, South Korea, and other countries and regions victimized by Japan's wartime aggression. ■

Indonesia sits on the Pacific "Ring of Fire" and is home to more than 120 active volcanoes, making it one of the world's most volcanically active countries. ■

articles.title: 7.7 earthquake rocks Indonesia as residents flee homes
articles.body:
A magnitude 7.7 earthquake and several aftershocks struck off the coast of eastern Indonesia early Saturday, prompting a tsunami warning and sending residents rushing from their homes, Indonesia’s geophysics agency BMKG said.
Tsunami waves of less than 1 meter, or about 3 feet, were recorded in several areas following the quake.
There were no initial reports of significant damage, according to Dodi Yuleova, spokesperson for Indonesia’s national disaster mitigation agency. The earthquake was felt strongly for about a minute in areas including Nagekeo and Bima.
Video posted on Facebook and verified by Reuters as having been filmed at a port in Maumere, the main town in Sikka Regency on Flores Island, showed parts of a building collapsing in a cloud of dust and rubble as people screamed and ran through the street.
At a hospital in Ende district in East Nusa Tenggara Province, patients were being moved outside, footage broadcast by Kompas TV showed. BMKG said the main earthquake struck at 4:58 a.m. local time at a depth of 15 kilometers, or about 9 miles, and was followed by several aftershocks.
Australia’s tsunami warning center said the undersea earthquake posed no tsunami threat to the Australian mainland, islands or territories.

articles.title: Zambia's president takes early lead in first vote count
articles.body:
James Kunda
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema took an early lead Friday in the Southern African country’s presidential vote as the electoral commission started to announce the results in Lusaka, the capital.
From the initial four constituencies out of 226 total, Hichilema, of the ruling United Party for National Development (UPND), had 22,476 votes, with his closest rival, Brian Mundubile of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Progress (NRPUP), with 14,388.
The announcement came hours after the Electoral Commission of Zambia suspended counting and announced results for the day, citing violence against poll agents.
Graphel Musamba, the inspector general of police, said nine suspects had been apprehended in connection with the murder of Livermore Chishima, a polling agent.
Commission Chair Mwangala Zaloumis said all security concerns had been addressed, with adequate measures in place to ensure that there are no further disruptions.

articles.title: Bulgaria to get eight F-16 fighter jets from US only in 2030 — Defense Ministry
articles.body:
SOFIA, August 15. /TASS/. The Bulgarian Air Force is expected to receive eight US-made F-16 Block 70 fighter jets no earlier than in 2030, the country’s Defense Ministry said.
"Lockheed Martin informed us of certain difficulties in the manufacturing process, which will cause delays in the delivery until the second quarter of 2030. This is not the final date, but the US company will do its best to expedite the production of the aircraft," the ministry said in a statement.
Earlier, the Bulgarian Air Force reported that new F-16 fighter jets will enter combat duty in the second half of 2026 or in 2027. The second batch of another eight aircraft was expected to arrive until 2027 so that Bulgaria could form a full-scale squadron.
F-16 deliveries are crucial for the Bulgarian Air Force, whose current fleet of MiG-29 fighter jets is nearing the end of its service life.

articles.title: Lula holds slim lead over Flavio Bolsonaro ahead of Brazil election
articles.body:
Lula holds slim lead over Flavio Bolsonaro ahead of Brazil election
A new poll shows Lula leading Bolsonaro, but the gap has closed ahead of Brazil’s high-stakes presidential election.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has retained his lead over right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro ahead of October’s election, according to a new poll.
A Quaest survey published on Friday found Lula would take 43 percent of the vote in a simulated run-off, against 40 percent for Bolsonaro, effectively a statistical tie given the poll’s two-point margin of error.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israeli soldiers accused of supporting ‘terrorist’ settlers in Qusra
- list 2 of 3A US territory? Trump unveils proposal to control Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 3Houthi attack on port kills four eroding truce with Yemen’s government
The result marks a narrowing from an earlier Quaest poll on August 5, which had put Lula ahead by a wider five-point margin, 44 percent to 39 percent.
In a first-round scenario, Lula leads more comfortably with 38 percent, followed by Bolsonaro at 31 percent. Three other candidates trail far behind: Renan Santos and Ronaldo Caiado each polled at 4 percent, and Romeu Zema at 2 percent.
Under Brazilian electoral rules, if no candidate secures more than half the valid votes in the first round, the top two finishers advance to a run-off.
Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, has emerged as the standard-bearer for Brazil’s right after his father was barred from running in the election.
The elder Bolsonaro was ruled ineligible for office after Brazil’s top electoral court found he had abused his power while in office. He was later convicted separately over a plot to overturn his 2022 election loss to Lula.
The poll, conducted by Quaest between August 10 and 13, surveyed 2,004 people and was commissioned by the Brazilian media group Globo.
Lula launched his re-election bid on August 2 at the Workers’ Party convention in Sao Paulo, casting himself as a defender of Brazilian “sovereignty” as pressure from the administration of United States President Donald Trump looms over the race.
He called for increased defence spending and pledged to shield Brazil’s reserves of rare earths and other critical minerals from foreign control. “I want to be prepared, so that no one invades this country,” he said.
He warned that China, the US and France would not get access to Brazil’s mineral wealth without respecting the country’s sovereignty. He also told the convention: “In Brazil, we do not accept anyone sticking their nose where it does not belong.”
Trump has maintained close ties with the Bolsonaros. In June, Lula warned Trump not to interfere in the presidential race.
“Don’t meddle in the Brazilian elections, because the Brazilian elections are a Brazilian problem, just as American elections are their business, not mine,” Lula said.
With the race tightening two months out from the vote, the results so far have shown a competitive presidential race, even as Lula continues to hold a narrow structural advantage heading into the final stretch of the campaign.

Rubio credited the personal relationship between US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi for the continued growth in bilateral ties
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday extended warm wishes to the people of India on the country's 80th Independence Day, saying the relationship between New Delhi and Washington was growing stronger. Rubio credited the personal relationship between US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi for the continued growth in bilateral ties."On behalf of the United States of America, I extend warm congratulations to the people of India on their Independence Day. Thanks to the personal relationship between President Trump and Prime Minister Modi, the U.S.-India relationship continues to grow and is stronger than ever. From defence and energy security to critical minerals, artificial intelligence, space cooperation, and commerce, our collaboration is making both of our nations, and the broader Indian Ocean region, safer, stronger, and more prosperous..."
Russian Ambassador to India Denis Alipov also extended greetings to India, expressing confidence in the country's continued development and reaffirming Moscow's support for New Delhi.
"Dear friends, Happy Independence Day! Looking at India's predetermined path of development, there is no doubt that all your dreams will come true," Alipov said in a post on X."As you walk the path of progress, rest assured that Russia's support remains the same today as it was a hundred years ago, and it will remain so tomorrow," he added.Concluding his message, the Russian envoy said, "Jai Hind. Long live India-Russia friendship."The messages came as Prime Minister Narendra Modi led the 80th Independence Day celebrations at the Red Fort in Delhi, with this year's ceremony marking 150 years of the National Song ‘Vande Mataram’ and focusing on the role of ‘Yuva Shakti’ in India's journey towards Viksit Bharat 2047.For the first time, ‘Vande Mataram’ was rendered during the Independence Day celebrations at the Red Fort. Modi hoisted the National Flag from the ramparts, with Captain Sonia Singh Chauhan assisting him. The flag hoisting was synchronised with a 21-gun salute by the 1721 Field Battery (Ceremonial), using indigenous 105 mm Light Field Guns.Following the Rashtriya Salute, the Army band played ‘Vande Mataram’, which was sung by those present at the Red Fort before the National Anthem. Two Indian Air Force Mi-17 helicopters also showered flower petals over the venue, with one carrying the National Flag and the other a flag depicting ‘Vande Mataram’.Modi subsequently addressed the nation, marking his 13th consecutive Independence Day speech from the Red Fort. Around 2,500 cadets from the Army, Navy and Air Force, along with ‘My Bharat’ volunteers, participated in the celebrations, forming the words ‘Vande Mataram’ along Gyanpath.
Around 5,000 special guests from different walks of life were invited to the ceremony, including women entrepreneurs, sanitation workers, street vendors, youth innovators, scientists, farmers, students and start-up founders. More than 1,500 people from different states and Union Territories also attended in traditional attire.Across the country, patriotic band performances were held at 343 prominent locations, while flag-hoisting ceremonies were also organised by the Indian Navy and local administrations in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep.

articles.title: Iberian orca known for boat ramming seen with suspected gunshot wounds
articles.body:
Berk Kutay Gökmen
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
Spanish officials have opened an investigation after the matriarch of an orca pod known for jostling and ramming boats off the Iberian Peninsula was spotted with wounds suggesting she had been shot with a pellet gun, The Guardian daily reported Friday.
The Environment Ministry said Toni, the pod’s oldest living member, had been seen swimming in the Strait of Gibraltar with markings on her dorsal fin that were “consistent with shots from a pellet gun.”
A ministry source told El Pais daily that some projectiles remained lodged in her fin, creating the risk of infection. The ministry was also in contact with Portuguese officials, said the source, after the markings were discovered following the orcas’ journey from waters off the Portuguese city of Faro.
The Iberian Peninsula’s orcas made headlines in 2020 when sailors reported rudders being rammed and boats spun 180 degrees or tipped sideways. A small group from the pod has since been blamed for damaging dozens of vessels and sinking at least four, leaving scientists searching for an explanation for the puzzling behavior.
Scientists have long rejected the idea that the orcas are attacking vessels, suggesting instead that the behavior may be playful or a way of practicing hunting skills.
Since Toni’s injuries emerged, the WeWhale and Iberian Orca Guardians (IOG) groups have closely monitored the whale for signs of weakness. “We know Toni. We were with her a few weeks ago and these wounds were not there,” said IOG co-founder Janek Andre.

articles.title: UN urges support for Afghan women’s aid five years into Taliban rule
articles.body:
UN urges support for Afghan women’s aid five years into Taliban rule
More than half of women’s organisations still operating in Afghanistan could cease operations within the next year, UN Women warns.
Five years since the Taliban came to power, the United Nations has warned that funding issues mean more than half of women’s organisations still operating in Afghanistan could cease operations within the next year.
Susan Ferguson, UN Women’s special representative in Afghanistan, appealed to donor countries on Friday not to cut funding for women’s programmes, saying to do so would only deepen the suffering of Afghan women.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Deadliest form of malnutrition has reached critical levels in Afghanistan
- list 2 of 3UNESCO says 2.4 million Afghan girls denied access to further education
- list 3 of 3Nearly 4 million Afghan children ‘acutely malnourished’
More than half of 74 women’s organisations surveyed in April are likely to have to suspend operations or close in the next year due to funding problems, Ferguson said.
The UN’s $1.7bn humanitarian appeal for Afghanistan was only 25 percent funded, and nearly three-quarters of the women’s organisations had experienced funding cuts in 2025, while about two-thirds reported that they had six months or less of operational funding remaining, she added.
The UN’s call comes as the Taliban marks five years since US forces withdrew from the country, effectively handing back power to the group in August 2021, after 20 years of war.
Bright white flags of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan have been installed this week across the Afghan capital Kabul, with new murals declaring: “Independence is a sign of dignity, pride and identity”.
The Taliban is also hosting a cricket match as part of the celebrations – but, just like much of public life in Afghanistan, women and girls are barred from attending.
Crippling restrictions for Afghan women
The Taliban has imposed more than 100 decrees restricting women’s rights since returning to power, affecting nearly every aspect of their daily lives, from education and employment to freedom of movement, healthcare and access to justice, Ferguson said.
Despite repeated Taliban promises to find an ideologically compliant way for them to attend school, girls are still banned from secondary schools and women from universities.
More than half of 3,200 women surveyed by UN Women said they now leave their homes only once or twice a month.
Seven in 10 women described their mental health as bad or very bad, Ferguson said.
On Friday, a group of 56 countries, including Britain, France, Germany, Japan, Lebanon, the United States and the United Arab Emirates, issued a joint statement at the UN renewing calls on the Taliban to reverse restrictions on women and girls, saying its “systematic repression of women and girls has become a defining feature of the current system”.
A slew of challenges
Five years of Taliban rule have left wider Afghan society facing a slew of other challenges.
More than half of primary school-aged children are out of school, and child malnutrition has reached critical levels in a third of Afghanistan’s provinces, according to the UN World Food Programme.
Infrastructure in the country has been damaged by a series of deadly earthquakes and floods that have also killed thousands.
While deaths from “terrorism” have fallen precipitously since the Taliban took power, according to data compiled by the South Asia Terrorism Portal, the country has become embroiled in a series of deadly border confrontations with its neighbours in both Iran and Pakistan.
The country also remains relatively diplomatically isolated, with Russia being the only country worldwide to formally recognise Taliban rule.

articles.title: Scottie Scheffler shoots 61 to take 3-shot lead in Memphis in playoff opener
articles.body:
Scottie Scheffler shoots 61 to take 3-shot lead in Memphis in playoff opener
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (AP) — Scottie Scheffler birdied the first five holes and shot a 9-under 61 on Friday to take a three-stroke lead in the FedEx St. Jude Championship.
“Really just a dream start,” Scheffler said. “Probably one of the best starts I’ve had on tour, to be honest with you. I couldn’t tell you a time where I’ve been lower early in the round.”
The top-ranked Scheffler had 11 birdies and two bogeys in 100-degree heat at TPC Southwind in the playoff opener. He had an 11-under 129 total.
“The tournament is halfway over,” Scheffler said. “I had two good rounds to start and hopefully continue that over the weekend.”
Scheffler tied the tournament course record.
“I wouldn’t say golf’s ever easy,” Scheffler. “I did some good things out there. I hit some iron shots in there close and was able to hole a few putts as well.”
He has played the TPC Southwind more times (seven) without winning than any other course on the PGA Tour.
Viktor Hovland and Sungjae Im were tied for second at 8 under. Hovland had a 64, and Im shot his second 66.
“It was really nice, really solid,” Hovland said. “Hit a lot of fairways, and I think that’s a big deal for my game, but also especially at this golf course. I think it’s really difficult to score if you’re missing fairways.”
Ludvig Aberg was 7 under after a 65.
Jordan Spieth shot 69 to get to 6 under. He was part of a four-way tie for the first-round lead. Spieth is outside the top 50 in the FedEx Cup who advance to the BMW Championship next week.
Scheffler entered the week with a 794-point lead over Matt Fitzpatrick in the FedExCup standings. Fitzpatrick was 3 under after a 67.
So much emphasis is on getting into the top 50 because that locks up all the $20 million signature events for next season.
Rory McIlroy played alongside Scheffler the first two days. He followed an opening 74 with a 70, leaving him tied for 60th at 4 over.

articles.title: Iran defiant on strait as Trump tells Americans to accept high petrol prices
articles.body:
Iran defiant on strait as Trump tells Americans to accept high petrol prices
- Iran insists on controlling the Strait of Hormuz and continues its blockade, rejecting US pressure and halting most oil tanker traffic.
- President Trump calls Iran "evil" and urges Americans to accept higher petrol prices amid conflict and rising fuel costs.
- No peace talks are planned, while economic sanctions and regional attacks escalate tensions and economic impacts on both sides.
AI generated
CAIRO/GARDEN CITY, New York - Iran called on the US to accept defeat while President Donald Trump blasted Tehran as “evil” and told Americans to brace for continued high fuel prices as a result of the war.
Progress toward peace talks and oil tanker traffic through the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway remained halted, with no sign the warring parties were moving toward ending the conflict that the US.and Israel launched on Feb 28.
“This strait will be opened and closed only under Iran’s command, and so long as you do not accept the reality of defeat and stop indulging in fantasies, Iran will continue to enforce the blockade,” Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi posted on X early on Aug 15.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran had not decided to resume talks with the US. He told Iranian news outlet Shahrara News in an interview published on Aug 15 that Washington must meet conditions on the strait in order for shipping to resume in the waterway that handled one-fifth of the world’s oil before the war.
Trump urged Americans to accept slightly higher petrol prices while the conflict with Iran continues.
He told a political rally in Garden City, New York, on Aug 14 that paying “a tiny little bit more for your gasoline” is worth the cost of ensuring “a very evil country” could not have a nuclear weapon, one of the president’s stated rationales for the war.
In a trend that has fuelled inflation and disappointed voters, the average US price of a gallon of petrol was about US$4.08 on Aug 14, up 29 per cent from a year earlier, according to the American Automobile Association.
Trump, a Republican, campaigned for reelection on a promise to lower energy costs, and Democrats are seeking to make the war’s fallout an issue in November congressional elections.
Crude oil futures rose US$1 a barrel on Aug 14. Benchmark Brent futures were on track for a weekly rise of 6.0 per cent and West Texas Intermediate 5.4 per cent.
“The Strait of Hormuz cannot be seized by a tweet or an aircraft carrier, by issuing an order or by delivering an election speech,” Gharibabadi said.
Despite Iran’s defiant tone, though, there were signs of an economic toll there too.
President Masoud Pezeshkian, in remarks on state television, blamed high inflation on a US blockade of Iranian ports and sanctions on Iran’s oil exports.
No crude oil vessels transiting strait
Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent each pledged to inflict more financial damage on Iran. Bessent told Newsmax’s Rob Schmitt Tonight programme on Aug 13 that announcements of more measures against Iran were coming next week.
Iran calls its enforcement of strait traffic a blockade – the term Washington uses for its threat against Iranian vessels leaving their ports.
“What we’re doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves... and we’re really doing a great job,” Trump said, adding that a 260-day deployment by a US aircraft carrier supporting the war effort was “not nearly long enough”.
Only two vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Aug 14 with no crude oil shipments visible, according to analysis from ship-tracking firm Kpler.
Some ships may cross the strait undetected with their transponders off, but the figures are nowhere near the more than 130 ships that traversed it daily before the war.
Vessels that dare navigate the strait without Iranian permission risk missile or drone strikes. The United Arab Emirates' Abu Dhabi National Oil Company said two of its vessels were attacked transiting the strait on the evening of Aug 13, and the Emirati state news agency WAM reported another vessel came under attack on Aug 14.
With a tentative June deal to end the war in tatters.
“We did not have a ceasefire in the first place that we would now want to extend,” Araghchi said. “We had ‘the end of the war,’ and now there is a new situation.”
Attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis renewed concerns about a widening regional war. Yemen’s internationally recognised government said the Houthis fired six ballistic missiles at the Red Sea port of Mocha on Aug 14, killing four civilians.
The Houthi-run SABA news agency cited a military source as saying the group had targeted an Aramco facility in the Saudi city of Najran with a drone. REUTERS

articles.title: Inside Russia’s new gulag: what The New Yorker found in a Rostov cell of Ukrainian women
articles.body:
Inside Russia’s new gulag: what The New Yorker found in a Rostov cell of Ukrainian women
Since 2014 — and especially since 2022 — Russia has seized and still holds at least 1,878 Ukrainian civilians. These are only the confirmed cases; the real number is likely far higher. At least 223 of them are women. Like Ukrainian prisoners of war, many civilian hostages from Ukraine have been tortured and are held in inhumane conditions. But unlike military prisoners, they have little hope of going free in an exchange. Ukraine, citing the Geneva Conventions, insists they should never have been detained at all. Russia points to rulings from its own courts and says they are serving sentences for terrorism, treason, and other serious crimes. The two sides do not trade military prisoners for civilians, which leaves the return of these detainees unresolved.
The New Yorker has published a long piece about Ukrainian women who ended up sharing a cell at Rostov pretrial detention center No. 1. For the story, the magazine’s Joshua Yaffa spoke with former inmates and exchanged letters with several of the women still held there. Some had served in Ukraine’s armed forces; others had no ties to the military. The first group has been exchanged; the second is still in custody. Meduza retells the stories of two of them.
Warning: This article contains descriptions of torture.
Valentina Zayarnaya, 66
Zayarnaya taught English in Amvrosiivka, a small city near Donetsk. Two months into the full-scale war, she got a call from an old acquaintance, a former Ukrainian border guard whom she knew only as Dima. They had met in 2018 at the Hnutove crossing, on the de facto border between the self-proclaimed Donetsk People’s Republic (“DNR”) and the Ukrainian-controlled parts of the Donetsk region. They struck up a conversation, exchanged phone numbers, and stayed in regular touch over the following years. Zayarnaya had once lost a child she had wanted to name Dima, and she came to think of this second Dima not simply as an acquaintance but as family.
Dima was not his real name. The man who introduced himself to Zayarnaya that way is Denys Storozhuk. At the start of the full-scale war, his border-guard unit was sent to defend Mariupol. Storozhuk spent three weeks hidden in a utility shaft deep inside the Azovstal plant, then made it out of the city and called Zayarnaya. When she told him she had gotten her son Kostya out of the embattled city, Storozhuk asked her to get him out, too. He lied, telling her he had taken no part in the war. She drove down the very next day and brought him from Mariupol to Amvrosiivka. They got lucky at the checkpoints: no one searched the car or asked for their documents.
Storozhuk lived with Zayarnaya for nearly a year. One day, he asked her to pick up a package for him at an address in Donetsk. Inside was a forged passport that would have let him leave occupied territory. When she arrived, FSB officers were waiting and quickly arrested her. Under questioning, Zayarnaya learned the truth about him: He was a lieutenant colonel in the Ukrainian military and had fought at Azovstal, escaping before Ukrainian forces surrendered. He had also stayed in touch with fellow servicemen, and investigators said he had hidden weapons and explosives at her house. Zayarnaya was accused of helping Storozhuk plan an assassination attempt on a “DNR” lawmaker and was sentenced to 12 years. Storozhuk was detained as well, but he was exchanged in the fall of 2024, before the trial; he was later sentenced in absentia to 22 years.
Zayarnaya’s cellmates were frustrated that Storozhuk had concealed his identity. But by their account, she always defended him — even though, during the investigation, FSB officers had beaten her son and threatened to send him to a mental hospital unless she gave them the testimony they wanted. She signed a confession, then tried to kill herself.
In a letter to The New Yorker, Zayarnaya called Storozhuk a second son and wrote: “The most important thing is that my boys are alive and free.” She said she considers prison “a school of survival, a test of the humanity and decency in each of us.” In custody, she has gone on teaching English — now to her cellmates.
Natalia Vlasova, 44
Vlasova has been in detention for more than seven years. In court, she said it all began in 2018, when an acquaintance who worked for the SBU, Ukraine’s security service, asked her to go to Donetsk and fill in for Serhii Hruzinov, an agent working at a chandelier shop who needed to travel to Kyiv. Vlasova agreed because, in return, she was promised help with a criminal drug-possession case against her. Soon after that trip came another: this time, she was asked to check whether Hruzinov had switched sides. She was detained trying to enter the “DNR” on a forged passport.
Vlasova was taken to Izolyatsia, a former insulation-materials plant in Donetsk that was turned into a secret prison in 2014. There, she was tortured for months. Her captors stripped her, bound her with tape, and shocked her with electricity. A doctor was present at many of these sessions; when she lost consciousness, he revived her by shoving a cotton ball doused in ammonia up her nose, and the torture started again. She said that one of her torturers was Vasily Yevdokimov, an official in the “DNR” state security ministry who is believed to have created Izolyatsia. “He personally filed my teeth with a metal file, twisted my nipples, and tried to force a bottle into my vagina,” Vlasova said in court.
A person who heard her testimony told The New Yorker that when Vlasova finished describing the torture, a judge asked whether she wanted to enter her written notes into the court record. “We were in shock,” that person said. The judge’s reaction seemed to be a quiet signal: “It was a gesture on the scale he was allowed.” But despite the gesture — and despite the fact that Vlasova recanted her earlier statements in court, saying they had been extracted under torture — she was sentenced to 18 years. Her conviction included the attempted assassination of Yevdokimov, the man she said had tortured her.
Over her seven years in custody, Vlasova has watched countless times as other women were freed and she was left behind. At the Rostov detention center, she kept a bag of clean clothes at the ready, in case she, too, was one day told, “Pack your things — you’re leaving.” So far, that has not happened.
Her daughter, Yulia, who lives with her father in Kyiv, is now 11. Her father and other relatives tried to keep Yulia from seeing news of her mother’s torture, but within days of the testimony she had read the coverage. She had only one question, The New Yorker reported: “What are nipples?” Last year, Yulia took part in a rally in Kyiv’s Independence Square to call attention to Ukrainian women held prisoner in Russia. She brought a sign that referred to one of her last memories of her mother: “Mom, remember you promised me a kitten?”

articles.title: Canadian plasma clinics halt collections after 2 donor deaths
articles.body:
Berk Kutay Gökmen
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
A for-profit plasma donation company said it is temporarily suspending collections at all Canadian clinics amid public scrutiny following the deaths of two donors, public outlet CBC News said Friday.
Grifols said it is pausing operations due to "unfounded attention" around paid plasma collection and plans to resume as soon as practicable, in coordination with Health Canada and Canadian Blood Services.
The move follows demands for government action after CBC News reported two people died following adverse reactions while donating plasma at separate Grifols clinics in Winnipeg. A recent Health Canada inspection also identified problems with donor screening and supervision, with federal data showing 25 serious adverse reactions at Grifols-operated centers since 2018.
The pause begins Friday. Grifols notified Health Canada on Wednesday, the same day the agency gave a Winnipeg clinic a non-compliance rating. Health Canada said the clinic "did not carry out sufficient corrective and preventive actions when required."
It also found that some procedures were not consistently followed and records of "staff qualifications, training or evaluation of their competency" were sometimes inadequate.
"We see this pattern of poor practices," said Noah Schulz of the Manitoba Health Coalition, which has joined demands to ban paid plasma collection.
Schulz said Grifols' for-profit model encourages it to operate "as cheaply" as possible.
"It's not just media attention with no evidence, no basis," he said. "The Health Canada inspection reports are there. We know that there are serious problems at Grifols."
Grifols said donor safety and the quality of its plasma have never been compromised.

articles.title: Reliance to partner Rolls-Royce to develop fighter jet engines
articles.body:
NEW DELHI: In a boost to India's fifth gen fighter programme, 
Mukesh Ambani
's Reliance Industries Ltd and Rolls-Royce Friday announced they plan to jointly develop a sovereign indigenous combat engine for India's Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA).
As part of the partnership to design, develop, manufacture and deliver the same, Reliance and Rolls-Royce will explore formation of a dedicated aerospace gas turbine complex that will be a centre for power and propulsion technology in India.
The aero gas turbine complex will build sovereign, end-to-end Indian capability across design, development, manufacturing, testing, production and through-life support, while unlocking wider collaborations across defence, civil aerospace, and new power and propulsion systems.Aeronautical Development Agency under DRDO is officially designing and managing the AMCA project. As per initial planning, ADA is progressing with imported US GE F414 engines for the initial five AMCA prototypes under the Rs 15,000-crore programme. TNN

articles.title: Türkiye resolving decades-long terrorism problem through national unity, says president
articles.body:
Seyit Şamil Kurt
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Friday that Türkiye is resolving its decades-long terrorism problem through national unity, parliamentary support, and the sacrifices of security forces, as he reaffirmed his commitment to the "Terror-Free Türkiye" initiative.
Speaking at a program in the capital Ankara marking the 25th anniversary of the ruling Justice and Development (AK) Party, Erdogan said that for more than four decades terrorism cost Türkiye lives, resources, morale, and opportunities.
"We said: 'We will solve it. We will free Türkiye from this 40-year problem'," said Erdogan. "We are solving it with the support of our parliament and the prayers of our beloved nation.”
He said the process is being carried out through the "heroism of our martyrs," the sacrifices of veterans, and a broad national consensus bringing together different sectors of society.
The government's objective goes beyond ending terrorism itself, said the president.
"We are not only ending the problem of terrorism. Together with terrorism, we are also thwarting that imperialist plan aimed at stirring up Türkiye from within," he said.
He stressed that the steps in the process are aimed at ensuring the security and prosperity of future generations.
"We are doing it to resolve this issue completely and leave our children a Terror-Free Türkiye and a terror-free region,” he said. 
AK Party unveils vision for next 25 years
At the anniversary program, the AK Party also unveiled its 25th anniversary vision document, with a foreword written by Erdogan.
Erdogan said the party's second quarter-century is beginning as Türkiye entered the new century of the republic, after a first 25 years in which the country built the capacity to "solve its problems, trust its own strength, make its own decisions, and chart its own course."
"The next quarter-century will be a period in which the capacity we have built turns into a formative influence," he said.
Erdogan added that Türkiye's goal is not merely to keep pace with global change but to help shape it and leave its mark on the creation of a "fairer world."

articles.title: Live: Australia in need of big improvements on day three against Bangladesh
articles.body:
Bangladesh remain on top, leading Australia by 67 runs on day three of the first Test at Darwin's Marrara Stadium
Australia has closed day three of the first Test against Bangladesh on 4-161, still 67 runs behind the tourists on another chastening day in Darwin.
Alex Carey (19) and Cameron Green (43) are the not out batters, combining for a valuable 39-run partnership late in the day that will prove crucial for Australia's chances of saving, or perhaps even winning the Test.
Australia will back itself to make Bangladesh bat again but, on an increasingly placid pitch, will have to bat very well to set a challenging target to the tourists, a scenario almost inconceivable for supporters of the world's number one side prior to the match getting underway.
With Bangladesh resuming on 6-351, Australia once again struggled to make inroads, extending their already gruelling labours in the field.
Josh Hazlewood thought he had made the breakthrough when umpire Richard Illingworth fired out Mehidy Hasan LBW, only for the DRS to show the ball was missing the leg stump.
The veteran quick was frustrated then, but soon was celebrating when Hasan Mahmud was trapped bang in front to depart for 14.
Hazlewood then claimed another, having Taijul Islam caught sharply by Cam Green, whose self-preservation instincts came to the fore to stop the ball flying into his face at gully.
If those two wickets had Australia thinking they'd soon be batting, the discipline of the Bangladeshi batters made sure they had to stay out even longer, coupled with a shocking drop from Steve Smith.
Taskin Ahmed top edged a pull shot out to Smith, who settled under the ball and let it through his finger tips.
A few balls later, Travis Head dropped a far harder chance, racing around from close to the wicket as Bangladesh reached 8-417 at lunch.
The mounting frustration eased somewhat by two more Hazlewood wickets, as he claimed Mehidy Hasan Miraz and Ebadot Hossain, both caught behind, to secure a 14th Test five-fa and his 300th Test wicket, becoming the ninth Australian to reach that particular milestone.
Australia needed a good start, but under-pressure home-town favourite Jake Weatherald departed second over for a duck, chopping on after playing with an angled bat to Hasan Mahmud.
Failing to learn from his first innings dismissal and that of his opening partner, Travis Head followed in near identical fashion to leave Australia 2-37 and in desperate trouble.
Marnus Labuschagne and Steve Smith came to the crease and both survived big Bangladeshi appeals, with Smith forced to review a caught behind decision when he was on three, the replay showing that he hit the ground with his bat instead of the ball.
That pair looked set, with Labuschagne seemingly playing with am encouragingly positive intent that was desperately lacking in his first innings effort.
However, the Queenslander was next to depart, playing all around a Taijul Islam fuller ball and yorking himself against the spinner to be out for 31.
Smith and Cameron Green rebuilt with a patient and untroubled 49-run partnership on an increasingly docile pitch, right up until Smith flat-batted a return catch to Bangladesh's other spinner, Mehidy Hasan for 44.
Australia still trailed by over 100 runs at that stage, with Alex Carey joining Green, who incredibly survived an inside edge that clipped his leg stump without dislodging the bail early in the evening session.
They batted out the remainder of the day without too much alarm, but know they will have to fight just as hard to save this Test match over the next two days.
Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog below.
Submit a comment or question
Live updates
Live updates: Australia vs Bangladesh
New: Filters
Choose what information you see below by using filters
We'll leave it there
Received wisdom says that the third day of a Test match is often its "moving day."
And today, only one side was doing the moving, with Bangladesh continuing their path towards a famous, famous victory.
The Australians, once again, listless in the Darwin heat, and will begin day four needing a further 67 runs to make Bangladesh bat again.
Thank you for joining me and Simon today. We hope to see you again tomorrow, with play beginning at 10:30am AEST.
Key Event
STUMPS: Australia 4-161 (trailing Bangladesh by 67 runs)
Well, another day of Bangladeshi domination comes to an end in Darwin.
The Tigers have been so, so impressive at Marrara Stadium, playing with all the discipline, commitment and skill their much-vaunted hosts have lacked.
Taking an enormous 228-run lead into the second innings and then ripping through the Australian top order, they have a gone a long, long way towards securing a famous victory.
Travis Head (17) and Jake Weatherald (0) both chopped on meekly, before Marnus Labuschagne (31) and Steve Smith (44) were careless with their dismissals — Labuschagne being yorked by spinner Taijul and Smith chipping one back to Mehidy.
Australia end the day with just six wickets in hand and still requiring 67 more runs to make Bangladesh bat again.
Bangladesh captain Shanto is speaking to Fox Cricket at the close of play, and is full of praise for his team's all-round effort.
"As a team we need to play all together, we don't have any individual players to win the match for us," Shanto said.
"We have some experienced guys, but we need to perform as a team."
And perform as a team they certainly have.
53rd over - Mehidy to finish day three
The off-spinner is back from the other end, bowling what will be the final over of day three.
There's a slip and a bat pad in place for Cam Green, who is defending the first couple balls.
That's a nice shot from Green, working one off his hip for a single.
Alex Carey has three balls to survive.
And it's a boundary! Carey lashes one through point and that's a lovely square drive. Four runs.
Carey chases another one but doesn't make contact.
And he's defending the final ball of the day.
52nd over - Taijul swung around
So left-arm off-spinner Taijul is back after a couple over's absence.
He's bowling to Cam Green, who has a man underneath his helmet as well as a slip behind his right shoulder.
Green is defending stoutly and then working a single straight.
Lovely shot! There had been some pressure building on Alex Carey, who had been struggling to find timing against the Bangladeshi spin twins. But that's a great shot, firm and down the ground, past the bowler, and to the fence.
He defends to end the over.
Yep, it certainly does
No pressure, but this partnership needs to last a looooong time and score a lot of runs…..
- Tanya
51st over - Taskin goes again
Taskin is coming over the wicket, with only one man in the cordon for Cam Green, who is defending back to the bowler.
Green then slashes through a gap between gully and point for a single.
There's a second slip as well as a gully in place for Alex Carey, who's tapping one into a packed off-side field.
Plenty of catchers in there.
Carey is pushing into the on-side for no run.
A dot to end the over.
50th over - Mehidy with another set
He continues around the wicket to Alex Carey, who has looked a little uncomfortable against the right-arm off-spinner.
A man next to the Australian at bat pad and another behind him at slip.
Carey's defending.
Another maiden for Mehidy.
49th over - Pace returns for Bangladesh
We're entering the final 15 minutes of play, and Shanto decides it's time for some pace.
Hard to argue with the Bangladeshi captain, considering he's got just about everything right so far in the Top End.
It's Taskin tasked with prising his side a final wicket for the day.
Shot! Green strides forward to a full one, and that's a glorious, full-blooded drive through the covers. Four runs.
The big man is defending.
He's looking pretty good, Cam Green.
Best he's looked for quite some time.
He's defending to end the over.
Another stunning afternoon in Darwin
48th over - Mehidy keeps going
Mehidy is bowing to Cameron Green, with two men around the bat.
Green is keeping out a couple probing deliveries pitching outside off, before flicking into the on-side for a single.
Carey is defending.
47th over - Taijul again
Full and straight from Taijul, and Green is able to do what Labuschagne couldn't — keep it from castling him. A single brings Carey onto strike.
Reverse! Carey brings out the reverse sweep for the first time today, and it isn't entirely convincing. He looks slightly unbalanced in getting the ball away, but Ebadot is even more awkward in the infield, completely losing the ball and letting it bobble past him. Four runs.
46th over - Mehidy to Carey
Bat pad and a slip in place for Alex Carey, who is defending the first ball of the over.
Carey is then stepping away and manufacturing some room, he gets his shot away, but only just.
That one was almost through him. No run.
Carey is looking increasingly antsy as the over nears its conclusion, trying to create a scoring opportunity.
He can't, and that's a maiden.
45th over - Taijul continues
Carey works a single of the first ball of the over, and Bangladesh won't mind that one bit.
Taijul, bowling his left arm offies, has been brought on to target Cam Green, with the ball spinning away from the big man from around the wicket.
There are a couple catchers on the off-side and a slip in place.
Green is defending and sees out the over.
44th over - Carey needs to hurry
Run-out chance! Carey dabs the ball into the off-side and sets off rather nonchalantly for a single. Halfway down the track, he realises he needs to hurry and decides to pick up the pace.
It would've been touch and go, but the shy at the stumps flies into an unaware Bangladesh body.
The Australians manage to see out the over.
43rd over - Taijul is back
So, spin from both ends as shadows continue to lengthen on Marrara Stadium.
Taijul is coming around the wicket to Green, angling in and spinning away, with only a slip to play with.
Green defends the first couple and then gives himself some room, swatting out towards the point boundary.
It's collected by the sweeper and only a single.
Oh Alex, you're killing me here. Carey decides to bring out the little paddle sweep and would've been plumb in front if he didn't brush the ball with his glove on its way through.
Over.
42nd over - Mehidy to spin six more
Green works another single down the ground, with Mehidy unable to get to the ball in time.
There's some serious field fiddling going on as Carey returns to strike.
There's a off-side bat pad and a slip in place for the left-hander, who defends one that slides straight.
Carey is defending to end the over.
41st over - Hasan continues with Australia requiring 99 to make Bangladesh bat again
Green works a single, and Australia now require 99 more runs to make Bangladesh bat again.
There is not much to suggest they'll get there.
Green reaches forward to a full one, he looks pretty awkward, but does enough to steer the ball past the bowler for a single.
That's a better shot from Green, who once again plays through wide mid-on.
It's timed well enough for the batters to run three.
40th over - Mehidy continues after wicket
And Cam Green is swatting him straight. It's a single for the Australians, who are looking shellshocked in the dying Darwin sun.
Carey is leaning back and just about keeping a couple cute Mehidy deliveries out.
He survives the over.
39th over - Hasan keeps going
He's getting a first look at Alex Carey, who is forward and defending against the paceman.
And again.
Just over 45 minutes remain in the day's play.
Bangladesh require six more wickets for an innings victory.
Carey is defending once more.
Carey earns a couple courtesy of a cute push forward of point.

articles.title: Zelensky Signals More Deep Strikes as Ukraine ‘Blocks Off Russia’s South’
articles.body:
Ukraine has “succeeded in blocking off Russia’s south” and is expanding its operations in response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports and cities, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and other facilities, alongside military operations in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, are aimed at limiting Moscow’s capacity to continue the war.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The long-range sanctions plan is being implemented, and there are more and more of our mid-range strikes as well,” Zelensky said in his evening address on Aug. 14.
Kyiv describes the campaign as “long-range sanctions” – combining deep military strikes with economic and legal pressure on the infrastructure and networks sustaining Russia’s war.
On Friday, Zelensky signed sanctions targeting individuals and companies involved in the illegal export of Ukrainian grain from Russian-occupied territories, as well as vessels used in those operations.
Ukraine has also prepared new sanctions packages targeting Russia’s military-industrial sector, financial networks and intermediaries helping Moscow sustain its war.
Zelensky called for Ukraine’s measures to be replicated by major international jurisdictions, arguing that Russian companies, individuals and those assisting them should face broader restrictions.
The president also renewed calls for frozen Russian assets to produce tangible benefits for Ukraine.
Zelensky: Ukraine Expects 30,000 Russian Occupiers to Be ‘Eliminated’ in August
Zelensky has repeatedly described Ukrainian deep strikes as a tool for forcing Moscow toward peace.
The message behind “long-range sanctions” is straightforward: as long as Russia continues its occupation and attacks on Ukraine, the infrastructure supporting Moscow’s war will remain under pressure.

articles.title: Pocso on online companies for child sex abuse content? SC to examine
articles.body:
A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran issued notice to Union govt through MeitY and law ministry
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Friday agreed to examine a plea seeking prosecution of social media and online platforms under the stringent Pocso Act for showing child sexual abuse content and not reporting it to police, reports AmitAnand Choudhary. A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran issued notice to the Union govt, through the ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY) and the ministry of law and justice. It asked the petitioner NGO, 'Just Rights for Children Alliance (JRCA)', to implead intermediaries in the case to ensure compliance with the court's 2024 judgment.
Sections 19 and 20 of Pocso Act make it mandatory for anyone who knows about a child sexual offence to report it to local police and the petitioner said the provision was also applicable to intermediaries and they too were liable to be prosecuted for non-compliance.JRCA, described as India's largest civil society network with over 250 NGOs working against child sexual exploitation, child trafficking and child marriage, filed the application following a BBC report alleging that Instagram had carried paid advertisements promoting CSAM (Child Sexual Abuse Material).

articles.title: Women globally place higher importance on moral identity than men
articles.body:
People all over the world consider morality a part of who they are, but how they express it depends heavily on their age, gender, and cultural background. A large new study maps out these differences, revealing that women generally value moral traits more than men do and that younger people in highly competitive societies care deeply about showing their morals to others. These results were recently published in the Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology.
Morality involves caring about fairness, justice, and the welfare of others. It acts as a core psychological need for many people, giving them a sense of being a good person. Yet individuals differ in how strongly they tie moral characteristics to their personal identity.
Psychologists divide this moral identity into two related concepts. Internalization measures the extent to which a person views moral traits as a private, central part of their self-concept. Symbolization measures how much a person values expressing their morality in ways that other people can see, such as through observable actions or group affiliations.
Both aspects predict real-world prosocial behavior, like volunteering and donating to charity. Most previous research on moral identity relied on samples from Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic nations.
Researchers Mariola Paruzel-Czachura and Cillian McHugh wanted to understand how these two aspects of moral identity vary across the globe. By looking at a broader range of countries, the researchers hoped to figure out whether existing assumptions about the moral self are universally human or culturally specific.
The researchers analyzed an existing dataset containing survey responses from 46,490 adults across 67 countries. This qualifies as a large study. Participants filled out a questionnaire assessing how much they valued having nine specific moral traits: caring, compassionate, fair, friendly, generous, helpful, hardworking, honest, and kind.
Participants rated their agreement with statements about these traits on an 11-point scale. The researchers then calculated separate scores for internalization and symbolization.
The researchers also gathered country-level data on several cultural dimensions. These included established metrics assessing a society’s acceptance of hierarchy, its focus on community versus the individual, its emphasis on competition, and its comfort with ambiguity. They also included indices of cultural tightness, which measure the strictness of social norms and a society’s tolerance for people breaking those rules.
Using statistical models that accounted for individuals nested within specific nations, the researchers examined how age, gender, and cultural environment related to participants’ moral identity scores.
The analysis revealed that women scored higher than men on both the private and public components of moral identity. This difference was particularly consistent for internalization. In 41 countries, women scored higher than men on internalization, while men scored higher in only two countries. Women scored higher on symbolization in 21 countries, while men scored higher in only one country.
The researchers predicted this gender outcome based on the idea that moral identity is closely linked to the ethical domain of care. Broad cross-cultural evidence indicates that women, on average, place greater emphasis on caring for others than men do. This stronger commitment to care likely contributes to the self-definitional importance of being a moral person.
The relationship between age and moral identity was also nuanced. When looking at the global population as a single group, older age seemed associated with slightly lower moral identity scores. But when the researchers accounted for the specific country each participant lived in, they found the opposite pattern. Within individual countries, older adults tended to place slightly more importance on having moral traits and on being recognized for them than younger adults did.
Cultural environment also shaped how people viewed their morality, especially regarding public expression. Participants reported higher symbolization in societies that are more collectivistic, meaning social life is tightly structured around community and relationships. Publicly displaying moral traits might help people maintain harmony and social acceptance in these environments where interpersonal reputation carries heavy consequences.
Symbolization was also higher in countries with greater acceptance of unequal power and hierarchy. In these societies, demonstrating socially valued qualities might help individuals navigate status differences and signal their reliability to others.
In cultures that prioritize competition and visible success, younger participants showed higher symbolization. For younger adults focused on establishing their social networks and standing, building a visible moral reputation acts as another form of social achievement. Older adults in these same cultures did not show this pattern, perhaps because their social standing is already established through stable roles.
The private side of moral identity showed a different pattern regarding culture. Internalization was higher in societies that focus on community over the individual. It was also higher in countries with lower acceptance of power inequalities, and in places with lower uncertainty avoidance, which are societies more comfortable with ambiguity.
The strictness of a society’s norms also played a role. In cultures with broad, strictly enforced social rules, people generally reported higher levels of both internalization and symbolization. When community expectations are rigid and closely monitored across many areas of life, internalizing those norms and displaying them to others becomes a central part of everyday functioning.
The results were not statistically significant for other cultural dimensions, such as a society’s focus on long-term future goals or its indulgence of personal desires. These factors did not meaningfully alter how strongly people valued having moral traits.
The study relied on older cultural indices that might not perfectly capture modern societal values. Social norms shift over time, and a country’s historical ranking on a cultural dimension might not reflect its current state. The associations between culture and moral identity found in this data were generally modest in size.
The questionnaire used to measure moral identity was originally developed in the United States. It relies on a specific list of moral traits focused on care and fairness. This list might not fully capture the moral ideals of non-Western cultures, where duty, loyalty, or religious devotion might be considered more central to being a good person. Differences between countries might partly reflect how well these specific traits align with local moral priorities.
Future research could address these limitations by developing measurement tools tailored to diverse cultural perspectives. Assessing cultural values directly from the participants at the exact same time as moral identity would also provide a more precise picture of how societies shape the way people view themselves.
The study, “Who Cares More About Having Moral Traits? Evidence From 67 Countries,” was authored by Mariola Paruzel-Czachura and Cillian McHugh.

articles.title: Wear now, pay later: the new rules of Southeast Asia’s indulgence economy
articles.body:
Wear now, pay later: the new rules of Southeast Asia’s indulgence economy
Instalments and resales are helping customers from Bangkok to Jakarta bridge the gap between aspiration and affordability
With its padded leather and gold “CC” lock, Coco Chanel’s instantly recognisable bag is practically part of the uniform for any self-respecting Bangkok property agent – an apt accessory for a city that recently edged into the top 10 anywhere for luxury spending.
But in chastened economic times liquidity and luxury are no longer in lockstep, challenging many of those with expensive tastes to find new ways to keep up appearances while balancing their books.
Jirapun Ngam, 42, works in the fast-paced business of buying and selling the Thai capital’s skyline.
She pays for her designer goods on instalments, keeping cash to buy, renovate and flip homes as they hit the market.
“I need cash to invest in my business, but I also want luxury items,” she said. “With instalment plans, I get the product immediately and pay it off monthly with only a small amount of interest.”
Instead, an alternative luxury economy is evolving.

articles.title: SC clears way for Tamil Nadu to give Karur victims’ kin jobs
articles.body:
NEW DELHI: Paving the way for Tamil Nadu govt to grant jobs to family members of those who died in the Karur stampede last year, SC Friday stayed operation of Madras HC’s verdict that had quashed the govt decision.
Asking what was wrong if a govt provided succour to a deceased’s family, an SC bench agreed to hear an appeal filed by the state govt against the HC order.
