articles.title: Trump dismisses mental health concerns on USS Lincoln aircraft carrier
articles.body:
Trump dismisses mental health concerns on USS Lincoln aircraft carrier
Members of the US Congress have called for a probe into conditions amid reports of sailors attempting to jump ship.
United States President Donald Trump has dismissed concerns about conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln during its lengthy deployment as part of the US-Israel war with Iran.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump rejected the assertion that the families of those on board the aircraft carrier are worried about their loved ones. “No, they’re not,” Trump said.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US-Iran talks in deadlock – what’s the latest?
- list 2 of 3Will all-out war in Yemen reignite as the Houthis escalate attacks?
- list 3 of 3Norway’s FM tells Al Jazeera the US war on Iran was not ‘smart’
When asked if the aircraft carrier had been deployed too long, Trump replied: “No, no, no, not nearly enough.”
His remarks follow a series of reports this week, documenting supply shortages and mental health strain on the USS Abraham Lincoln. That includes accounts of individuals attempting to jump from the ship.
The aircraft carrier left in November from a base in San Diego, California, and it has since been involved in January’s military operation against Venezuela and, more recently, the war against Iran.
Its deployment was expected to end in May, but that timeframe has been extended. It has spent more than 250 days at sea without a port stop, setting a record for the US Navy. More than 5,000 sailors and Marines are housed on board.
Several US lawmakers have since called for an inquiry into conditions on board the ship. One Democratic senator, Ruben Gallego, has also called on the Navy to allow a bipartisan delegation to visit the ship to assess the state of affairs.
Still, the Trump administration has repeatedly denied worsening conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln.
On Friday, a US official told Al Jazeera the Navy had “not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship”.
The official added that there were five chaplains, one psychologist, one social worker, three “behavioral health technicians”, and one “embedded integrated prevention coordination (EIPC) counselor” on board the vessel. There is also an emotional support dog on board.
‘What military objective?’
While Trump downplayed the length of the deployment, he did confirm reports that the aircraft carrier will be swapped out in the near future.
“That ship is moving right now or very shortly, and it’s being replaced with another very similar ship,” Trump said on Friday.
In a letter to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth earlier this week, Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, asked for information on conditions on the boat, including what metrics the Navy was using to measure the mental health of the crew.
“What military objective is the continued deployment of the Lincoln intended to achieve in Iran, and how does the Department assess whether the carrier’s continued presence is necessary to accomplish that objective?” he asked.
The focus on conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln come as diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israeli war in Iran show no signs of breakthrough. The war began with a US and Israel-led offensive on February 28.
In June, the US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) that called for an immediate pause to the fighting.
But last month, the memorandum collapsed amid a dispute over the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for trade.
The subsequent escalation saw the US re-impose its naval blockade on Iranian ports and Iran constrict traffic through the strait once more.
Iran has since focused its diplomatic efforts on reaching an agreement with Oman over travel routes in the waterway, which is a key artery for oil, natural gas, fertiliser and other goods.

articles.title: US judge clears way for Trump to end Somalis' deportation protections
articles.body:
US judge clears way for Trump to end Somalis' deportation protections
Aug 14 - A federal judge on Friday cleared the way for U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to strip nearly 1,100 Somalis of legal protections against deportation that have allowed them to live and work in the United States.
U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs in Boston allowed the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to terminate the Temporary Protected Status designation for Somalia after the U.S. Supreme Court in June allowed the administration to end similar protections for thousands of people from Haiti and Syria.
The Supreme Court's ruling, powered by its 6-3 conservative majority, curtailed the ability of judges to review DHS efforts under Trump to end TPS designations for 13 countries that provided humanitarian immigration protection to eligible migrants from those nations.
Lawyers for the plaintiffs and DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Two other judges last week allowed the administration to similarly end TPS for South Sudan and Myanmar. Only the end of TPS for Ethiopia remains blocked by a judge.
Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in January announced plans to end TPS for Somalis, arguing Somalia's conditions had improved, despite ongoing fighting between Somali forces and al-Shabaab militants.
Burroughs, an appointee of Democratic President Barack Obama, in March blocked Noem's decision from taking effect in a lawsuit brought by four Somalis and two advocacy groups including African Communities Together.
The plaintiffs argued the administration sought to end TPS for Somalia due to bias against non-white immigrants, pointing to Trump's past descriptions of Somalis as "garbage" and "low IQ people."
After the Supreme Court ruled, Burroughs issued a new order that continued to temporarily block the end of the Somalis' TPS while she considered whether to allow the plaintiffs to try to challenge DHS action on grounds the Supreme Court's ruling did not address. REUTERS

articles.title: Trump threatens to declare strait of Hormuz ‘territory of the United States’
articles.body:
Donald Trump has threatened to declare the strait of Hormuz as “a territory of the United States” as his administration struggles to conclude the war with Iran.
During a speech at a police academy on Long Island, New York, on Friday, the US president said he would “pretty soon” designate the waterway – a crucial chokepoint for global trade, through which about a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil supplies typically pass – a US territory.
The comment came as peace talks with Iran remain at an impasse following failed negotiations, with Tehran refusing to reopen the strait, which has been all but closed since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February.
Almost six months into the war, there is little indication that negotiations will soon yield peace, as Iranian officials continue to defy Trump’s demands. The US has been blockading Iranian shipping and ports in recent months in an effort to pile economic pressure on Tehran.
“After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz strait a territory of the United States,” Trump said on Friday. “Essentially, that’s what it is. We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to.”
The seriousness of Trump’s remark, and whether it signaled a new policy position for his administration, was not immediately clear.
Responding on X, formerly Twitter, Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, said Tehran would not be intimidated by threats, or a show of force, by the US – and added that the strait of Hormuz would only be opened, or closed, under Iran’s authority.
In an interview published on Saturday, Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said that Iran had not decided to resume talks with the US, and messages being exchanged via Qatar and Pakistan did not amount to negotiations, Reuters reported.
Araqchi told Iranian news outlet Shahrara News that separate talks with Oman were focused on defining a sea route through the strait of Hormuz, while the US would have to meet conditions for shipping to resume through the waterway.
Earlier this week, Trump claimed that the US had “total control” over the strait and said “I think we will keep it” on Truth Social, despite the waterway being an internationally navigable strait bordered by Iran and Oman.
Fuel prices have risen sharply since the start of the war, forcing working Americans to pay significantly more at the pump.
Nevertheless, on Friday, Trump said that Americans who have had to “pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline” should remember that they are “doing it so that a very evil country cannot have a – really, it’s the No 1 state sponsor of terror in the world – we don’t want them to have a nuclear weapon.
“When you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK, I mean, it’s not. I’ll never apologize. I did the right thing,” he added.
Over the past six months, the Trump administration has repeatedly claimed victory in the war, saying Iran’s regime has been pleading for a deal.
Tehran has remained steadfast in its demands, saying as recently as last Saturday that it will not reopen the strait of Hormuz unless the US “corrects its behavior”, “completely compensate[s]” Iran for war damage, lifts sanctions and “unconditionally” releases frozen assets.

articles.title: French Constitutional Council strikes down social media ban for children under 15
articles.body:
PARIS, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- France's Constitutional Council on Friday struck down a law banning social media access for children under 15, ruling that the measure constituted a disproportionate infringement on freedom of expression.
The constitutional authority stated that the blanket ban would apply to online communication services whose risks to minors' health and safety have not been established, reported Franceinfo.
It also noted that the law failed to account for minors' age, family situation or maturity level, nor did it specify conditions under which parents could authorize access or lift restrictions.
Following the ruling, the Elysee Palace announced that President Emmanuel Macron directed Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to work on a legally robust revision of the bill as soon as possible, taking into account the Council's decision and European regulations.
The president's office added that Macron remains fully committed to delivering the reform before spring 2027.
The legislation, initially set to take effect in September, was a flagship proposal backed by Macron to protect the health and safety of minors. The bill was passed by the French Parliament on July 21. ■

articles.title: Mbappe looking forward to winning titles with Mourinho
articles.body:
MADRID, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe said he is looking forward to working with Jose Mourinho this season and set his sights on winning silverware after two seasons without major titles.
Speaking to Real Madrid TV, Mbappe said he had been in constant contact with the Portuguese coach who arrived at the start of the summer for a second spell at the club, with the task of turning fortunes around at the Spanish giants.
"We spoke a lot during the World Cup, and he explained a lot of things to me," said Mbappe in an interview published on Friday.
"I think it's very positive to have a coach like that, who knows how to win and knows how to give the direction on how to win. I think every player is delighted to have a coach who knows where he's going, and that's positive for us," he added.
Mbappe admitted there was pressure on the squad after two seasons with little to celebrate.
"We have to win," he admitted, although he was confident that "this year we're going to win titles again. That's what we want, and that's what's going to happen."
"I feel that the team is motivated and we're going to be focused all year, because there's nothing more important than winning titles with the team, feeling that joy, and bringing joy to the fans," commented the French striker.
The top scorer in this summer's World Cup also highlighted the importance of a short, but intense pre-season before Real Madrid kicks off the new season away to Espanyol on August 22.
"Now is the time when we can work the hardest. Later, when the matches start, we have to manage the workload more. It's time to go all out and get a feel for things so I'm ready for the first league match," concluded Mbappe. ■

articles.title: Ex-Cambridge professor dies week after resigning amid plagiarism allegations
articles.body:
Jason Arday, former Cambridge professor, dies week after resigning amid plagiarism allegations
Jason Arday, who was Cambridge's youngest Black professor, died in London on Friday, a week after he resigned from the university amid plagiarism allegations, his family said. He was 41 years old.
"Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for the more than three years since he accepted the role of Professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him," his family said in a statement.
"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone. We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son."
London's Metropolitan Police did not identify Arday, but said in a statement that officers responded to a report of a 41-year-old man found unresponsive inside a property at 3:12 p.m. local time Friday. Police said the man was pronounced dead at the scene and his next of kin have been notified.  
His death is "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," police said. The case is under investigation.
U.K. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said in a social media post that she was "deeply shocked & saddened" to hear about Arday's death.
"My heartfelt condolences are with his friends and family at this very sad time," Powell said in the post. "I urge people to give them privacy through this incredibly difficult period & to remember there are real people with loved ones involved."
Arday resigned from Cambridge Aug. 5 following allegations of plagiarism and fabrications in his biography, saying in a statement, "The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."
He said his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."
"We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time," Vice-Chancellor Professor at Cambridge Deborah Prentice said in a statement.
Arday joined the University of Cambridge in 2023 at age 37, becoming one of Britain's most high-profile academics after sharing an extraordinary account of his life. He said he was autistic and dyslexic, did not speak until age 11 and was unable to read or write until he was 18.
Born and raised in south London, he went to college to earn a degree in education and physical education, and then went on to earn two master's degrees before qualifying as a teacher. He then earned his PhD at Liverpool John Moores University.
"Not many teachers at school had any belief in me," he told CBS News in 2023. "Educational psychologists and behavioral therapists were … very robust in their assessment that I would struggle in later life and I would need assisted living."
Allegations of plagiarism were raised last month by Nathan Cofnas, a philosopher of biology and former Cambridge researcher who has publicly criticized diversity, equity and inclusion policies. Cofnas previously wrote that in a meritocracy, "Blacks would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment."
Arday previously denied any intentional wrongdoing, saying errors in his academic work were inadvertent and arguing that much of the criticism against him was an ideologically and racially motivated campaign against him.
Supporters of Arday also argued the scrutiny went far beyond legitimate academic criticism and said he became the target of an ideological campaign because of his work on race, inequality and diversity.
Liverpool John Moores University previously investigated allegations relating to his doctoral thesis and said it found no evidence of academic misconduct, according to The Times of London.
Articles by The Times of London and The Telegraph reported last month on possible embellishments in Arday's personal history, including claims that he raised millions for charity through endurance challenges, which he later amended. The Telegraph questioned his claim to have published a book, "Being Young, Black and Male: Challenging the Dominant Discourse," saying it could not find evidence it was ever published.
Criticism mounted ahead of this week's release of Arday's memoir, "Great and Unfortunate Things," which chronicles his life from childhood through his appointment at Cambridge.
In his resignation statement, Arday did not address the specific allegations against him, but said his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."
"It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure," he said.

articles.title: Trump says USS Abraham Lincoln deployment 'not nearly long enough' amid outcry from families
articles.body:
Trump says USS Abraham Lincoln deployment ‘not nearly long enough’ amid outcry from families
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln have reportedly tried to jump overboard during the lengthy deployment in the Middle East.
- The U.S. military has announced plans to send the USS George Washington, a Pacific-based aircraft carrier, to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln.
Democratic lawmakers and military families are pressing the Pentagon for answers after reports emerged that thousands of sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln have endured food shortages, plumbing failures and severe fatigue during deployment that has stretched more than 260 days.
The roughly 5,000-person crew, which left San Diego in November and has been stationed in the Middle East to support the U.S. war against Iran, has spent a record amount of time at sea without a port visit, according to Stars and Stripes. Now, families of those on board have begun speaking out publicly, describing concerns about mental health and supply issues aboard the aircraft carrier.
Since those reports — which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth characterized as “completely misrepresented” — the U.S. military announced plans to send the USS George Washington, a Pacific-based aircraft carrier, to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln.
But when asked Friday for a reaction, Trump downplayed families’ concerns and characterized the length of the deployment as “not nearly long enough.”
The president’s remarks stand in contrast to the concerns raised by lawmakers and military families, including reports by the Military Times and the Stars and Stripes that sailors tried to jump overboard as the deployment kept going.
This comes as reports have emerged of mental health and supply problems aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose long deployment to the Middle East in support of the Iran war includes a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days.
“The plans in the works to relieve the USS Lincoln are not enough,” Rep. Mike Levin (D-San Diego) wrote in a letter to Hegseth on Thursday. “We need clear and honest information from the Department of Defense about the operational failures that led to the problems aboard the USS Lincoln to ensure this never happens again.”
Morale aboard a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier already is difficult to maintain without a record-breaking stint, said Julie Roland, a retired veteran Navy lieutenant commander who worked briefly on the USS Lincoln.
Between the lack of sun below deck for some nonpilot personnel and rooms packed with triple-bunk beds, the conditions on vessels like the Lincoln can be difficult to bear. Although service members expect such difficulties, the situation on the USS Lincoln raises additional concern among sailors, Roland said.
“I know what months at sea does to a person even when the ship has hot chow and working plumbing,” Roland said. “The warrior ethos shouldn’t have to include bravely facing water contamination. ... Even warfighters need basic care.”
Roland added that she was not surprised to hear complaints of poor living conditions from sailors on board, given that their few days of reprieve for port call constantly were being delayed. She said she received videos showing trash being tossed overboard because of broken incinerators, heard stories of a lack of proper medical supplies and kept in touch with one sailor who detailed his mental health deterioration as days dragged on aboard the Lincoln.
“The magnitude of difference between official information from the Department of Defense and firsthand reports from the crew should be troubling, and may have serious implications about what else the Pentagon may be withholding regarding the conflict in Iran,” Roland added.
In his letter to Hegseth, Levin said the Trump administration needs to answer concerns from military families and loved ones about the conditions aboard. He said he heard concerns about moldy showers, broken toilets, lack of hot water, lack of access to fresh produce and supply shortages.
Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-San Diego), who serves on the House Armed Services Committee, also demanded answers from U.S. military leaders on what she called “horrific” reports of the conditions aboard the ship.
Tensions over the situation also prompted military leaders to hold in-person and virtual meetings last week with the families of the sailors and Marines. Both meetings were combative, according to a recording obtained by MS NOW.
During the in-person meeting at the Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, Navy leaders were unable to tell families when their loved ones would be relieved from duty. Spouses, in turn, asked what was being done to address issues of mental health and exhaustion, MS NOW reported.
Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. set a deadline of Tuesday for a response by plaintiffs challenging the ballroom project.
Concerns about mental health deteriorating on these types of deployments are well-founded.
A study of nearly 1,000 sailors published in the journal Military Medicine in January 2025 found that service members aboard Navy ships suffer the highest rates of “serious psychological distress” compared to other branches of the U.S. military. Among the reasons are “unique stressors, such as poor habitability, noise and demanding schedules that leave inadequate time for sleep and rest,” the study found.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said the USS Abraham Lincoln was not an “isolated case” and demanded an inquiry.
“Recent carrier deployments have repeatedly stretched beyond their original anticipated duration, suggesting that extended deployments may be becoming a feature rather than an exception of the Navy’s force-generation model,” Blumenthal wrote.
Hegseth told reporters on Thursday that “some deployments are longer than others.”
“What they do in those high seas and those austere conditions with less port calls, it’s incredible. And Americans don’t understand what it’s like to do that,” he said, while adding that he wants “folks rotated as quickly as possible.”
In a message to the crew aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, Hegseth said: “We’re going to do everything we can for you. We are so grateful for the dedication of that crew and others.”

articles.title: Should Australia copy New Zealand's 83-page building code?
articles.body:
Should Australia copy New Zealand's 83-page building code?
In short:
The Albanese government is pushing ahead with its plan to modernise the National Construction Code.
Andrew Bragg, the shadow minister for housing, says Australia should follow the example of New Zealand and adopt a radically-slimmed down and simplified code.
What's next?
Federal, state and territory treasurers agreed on Friday to review the barriers to wider adoption of Modern Methods of Construction in Australia.
Cross-party support for prefabricated and modular homes is building in Canberra as an answer to Australia's housing crisis.
The Albanese government is pouring millions of dollars into the idea. Building industry groups, think tanks, and major banks support it. And Liberal senator Andrew Bragg, the shadow minister for housing, loudly supports the idea.
With such momentum building for the policy, what does it mean for the future of Australian housing?
At Friday's meeting of federal, state and territory treasurers, participants were briefed on the Albanese government's plans to promote Modern Methods of Construction (MCC) to lift productivity in the construction and housing industries.
They were also given an update on the government's efforts to modernise the National Construction Code which has been long in the making.
At the end of the meeting they agreed to review the barriers to wider adoption of MMC in Australia to support manufacturing.
But earlier in the week a Senate committee also released its interim report on Australia's housing industry. The committee, chaired by Senator Bragg, is comprised of Liberal, Nationals and Labor members.
In a speech to the National Press Club on Wednesday, Senator Bragg talked about the recommendations in that interim report.
He used the report as a springboard to promote his own plan to slash the number of pages in the National Construction Code (NCC) and adopt "an 80-page Basic Australian Standard".
But what would Bragg's plan actually look like? Would it help or hinder reforms that are already underway?
And what does it have to do with Modern Methods of Construction and prefab housing?
What does Senator Bragg's plan look like?
The original Building Code of Australia, from 1988, was 209 pages, including a title page.
At the Press Club, Senator Bragg said the Coalition had committed to reducing the size of the modern NCC, which has grown to more than 2,200 pages, back to the size of the original BCA.
The Housing Industry Association (HIA) has been calling for such a policy.
In the HIA's submission to the Senate inquiry on housing it said Australia's government should:
"Undertake a code overhaul and regulatory reform and simplification program, setting a goal to return the code to the 208 pages that reflected the first edition of the BCA (NCC) in 1988."
And in his speech to the Press Club on Wednesday, Senator Bragg made this announcement about his committee's interim report:
"We have met the ambition of industry to get back to an NCC closer to the original 200 pages, when first created in 1988. Our new framework for an 80-page Basic Australian Standard is some 2,000 pages shorter than Labor's NCC."
That second sentence from Senator Bragg about an 80-page Basic Australian Standard led to some confusion.
In response to questions from the ABC later in the week, Senator Bragg's office clarified what his plan was.
It said Senator Bragg wanted to introduce a new framework that would have an "80 to 90-page Basic Australian Standard" sitting within a slimmed down and simplified construction code.
So, his Basic Australian Standard would be the mandatory core requirements for building.
In the current NCC the only mandatory requirements in the code are performance requirements, and they total 200 pages, according to testimony from Simon Croft, chief executive of industry and policy at the HIA.
For Senator Bragg's plan, broader elements for building "optional extras" on a basic house would then come on top of his 80 to 90-page Basic Australian Standard.
It means you would have to familiarise yourself with 80 to 90 pages of his proposed new building code at a minimum because they would cover the essential structural, fire safety, health and basic amenity requirements, including basic energy efficiency.
If you wanted to build something more sophisticated than a basic structure you would have to read additional material to ensure that you were building everything to code.
Those "optional extras" would include things like Graduated Liveable Housing Standards, and Extended Energy Efficiency options.
The interim report from the Senate committee, which Senator Bragg chairs, has suggested that the new framework could look like this:
The interim report also says the Basic Australian Standard would be supported by a federal "pattern book" to fast-track approvals and enable innovation, including for prefabricated housing and Modern Methods of Construction (MMC).
The federal pattern book would contain pre-approved standard housing designs and allow for MMC.
The New Zealand model
After his speech to the Press Club on Wednesday, Senator Bragg was criticised by some groups for suggesting that low-income earners should accept substandard housing built to the most basic code.
On the ABC's Radio National he was asked: "Are you suggesting that to afford housing, some low-income Australians will have to accept housing that is substandard?"
Senator Bragg replied: "Yes, definitely. And I think we've got to be clear there are trade-offs here … if it's more important to have a house than to not have a house.
"So given the affordability crisis we have in the housing system we need to just build more houses," he said.
Loading...
But on Friday afternoon, Senator Bragg said he had misheard the question about housing standards and he did not mean to suggest that houses built to his Basic Australian Standard would be "substandard".
"Houses built to this standard would be strong, safe and sound homes with all the basic amenity, such as insulation, plumbing, sewerage etc. This position has been strongly backed by the industry," he posted on X (formerly Twitter).
His ideas were inspired by the HIA, which has been arguing that Australia should adopt New Zealand's slimmed-down building code model, and the HIA has not said that low-income earners should accept substandard housing.
The HIA says New Zealand's Building Code is 83 pages long but it is underpinned by a broad range of compliance solutions that are attached to the mandatory code.
The HIA imagines that a new NCC compliance structure for Australia could look like the graphic below.
Its proposed model begins at the top of the graphic with an 83-page mandatory building code, and then you read your way through various "pathways" to suit the type of structure you want to build:
The HIA's graphic looks very similar to the dashboard for New Zealand's building code.
How to use Modern Methods of Construction
On the specific topic of Modern Methods of Construction (MMC), the Senate committee's interim report said the federal government should embrace MMC, prefabricated housing and modular homes to build houses more cheaply and quickly.
It puts Senator Bragg and his Coalition colleagues on the same page as the Albanese government and building industry groups which are already investigating MMC as a potential way to boost productivity in the building industry.
This is how the Australian Building Codes Board explains what MMC is:
Modern methods of construction (MMC) refers to a range of construction methods that are different to traditional onsite construction. This includes prefabrication, off-site manufacturing, and modular or volumetric dwellings, as well as new technologies such as 3D printing, robotics, and artificial intelligence.
MMC have the potential to support the delivery of higher quality buildings and increase productivity in the construction sector.
The Productivity Commission reported that prefabricated and modular construction can reduce the cost of homes by up to 20 per cent. Prefabricated and modular homes can be up to 50 per cent faster to construct than homes built using traditional methods of construction.
MMC technologies encourage increased productivity and efficient building processes, resulting from greater speed and accuracy. Prefabricated and modular construction can also offer improved certainty, safety, quality and environmental sustainability benefits.
But the Coalition and Labor may have different visions for what MMC could be used for.
The John Curtin Research Centre, a Labor-aligned think tank, says the federal government could use MMC and prefab homes to rebuild and revitalise Australia's broader manufacturing sector.
It says MMC could be part of an ambitious national strategy that would help Australia to rebuild its industrial base in a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reverse decades of deindustrialisation and underwrite a housing construction boom.
It released a report on the topic recently that explained how that ambition could be realised.
Federal Housing Minister Clare O'Neil launched that report at Labor's National Conference last month.
Growing support for MMC
There is also growing support from industry and building groups for wider adoption of MMC and prefab housing, which suggests that the future of housing in Australia may look quite different from today.
Urban Taskforce Australia wants the government to support the adoption of modular and prefabricated housing, and to remove regulatory barriers to help the building industry make the transition.
Engineers Australia says the government should promote MMC to support off-site manufacturing for faster, cleaner, and more resilient construction, with clear guidance and approval processes.
Treasury says the Albanese government's National Competition Policy agenda is focused on "streamlining and aligning regulation, in areas including Modern Methods of Construction".
The Australian Building Codes Board (ABCB) has been asked by the federal government to develop a national voluntary certification scheme for manufacturers of prefabricated construction.

articles.title: Russia won’t accept a new Black Sea truce, saying the West already broke its word once
articles.body:
Russia won’t accept a new Black Sea truce, saying the West already broke its word once
Moscow has not received a formal proposal for a moratorium on Black Sea strikes, Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said on Friday. A day earlier, Reuters reported that Kyiv had used an intermediary to deliver a proposal to Moscow for a mutual halt to strikes on civilian targets in the Black Sea. Reuters did not name the intermediary directly, but it was likely Turkey — Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan had already said on August 8 that Ankara had sent a moratorium proposal to both sides in the conflict.
“The Russian side has not received, through official channels, any formal communication from Turkey setting out the terms of this initiative,” Zakharova said.
Moscow does not see “grounds for half-measures that only give the Kyiv regime a temporary reprieve,” she said. Russia agreed to a moratorium in 2022–2023 in exchange for access to global markets for its agricultural products, she said, but “the West acted in bad faith” and did not lift sanctions.
Talk of a Black Sea truce has resumed as both sides sharply escalate attacks on merchant vessels and ports. Russia has been striking ports in the Odesa region in recent weeks, and no grain vessel has entered those ports since late July.
On August 12, Ukraine carried out a large-scale strike on Novorossiysk — Russia’s largest Black Sea port and one of its most important grain export hubs. Work stopped at all of Novorossiysk’s terminals as a result: the Novorossiysk Grain Terminal, the Novorossiysk Grain Products Plant, and the KSK Grain Terminal. They have a combined capacity of 26.1 million metric tons.
Ukraine is one of the world’s largest grain producers, and 90% of its grain exports move by sea. Shipments fell in August to about a third of the usual volume, or 463,000 metric tons, Ukrainian Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said.
If the situation does not change, he said, Ukraine could run out of storage space for its new harvest by November, and global food prices could rise by at least 25–30%. Kyiv is negotiating overland routes with Romania, Poland, Hungary, Slovakia, and Moldova, but overland shipping costs more than sea transport and is barely profitable.
Russia, in turn, is the world’s largest wheat exporter, so disruptions at the Novorossiysk terminals could ripple through the entire global market.
Even before the strikes, the Russian Union of Grain Exporters and Producers had warned that the shortfall in Russian wheat deliveries this season could reach 30–35 million metric tons, or about 15% of global wheat trade. Making up the lost volumes with supplies from other exporters would be virtually impossible, the union said. Wheat futures in Chicago rose about 3% on August 12 after the attack on the Novorossiysk terminals.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1633: July was Ukraine’s deadliest month for civilians since 2022, as Russia’s war grinds through another summer
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Russia drops eight FAB-250 bombs on Kramatorsk, killing one and injuring 18. Prosecutors opened a war crimes investigation into the glide-bomb strike, the latest in a series that has hit residential blocks across Donetsk Oblast.
Russia's defense ministry threatens to "freeze" Ukraine this winter. Moscow posted photos of attack drones captioned "like snow on your head," tying the taunt to its strikes on Ukraine's ports.
Poland was ready to scrap these MiG-29s. Bulgaria's interest just revived the Ukraine deal.. Warsaw was ready to let the jets go to the scrapyard, until a rival buyer showed up.
745 km² recaptured in Ukraine's eight-month Oleksandrivka counteroffensive, Kyiv says. The eight-month operation retook 26 villages across three oblasts, halting Russia's push toward Dnipropetrovsk and turning it back on Ukrainian soil, per the report.
Ukrainian drones hit Wildberries warehouse in Tver for the third time in two weeks. Wall damaged again, no injuries reported, marketplace says goods intact.
Ukrainian drones hit Russia's Ust-Luga oil port for the 6th time this year. Fire breaks out at Baltic terminal handling nearly half of Russia's regional exports.
Intelligence and technology
Captured Akhmat fighter says he chose Ukraine and a drone guided him away from Russia's ranks. Magomed said earlier Chechen defections prompted Russian commanders to check fighters' phones and tighten surveillance.
Armor can barely reach Ukraine's front now—so robots drive and soldiers walk. Ukraine's frontline logistics are under strain from drone pressure, forcing soldiers to walk while ground robots take over the most dangerous runs.
They find a sword, we find a shield: Ukrainian soldier on why drones will never replace infantry. He went from mortarman to drone operator, and says neither role can absorb the other.
Ukraine's drones crushed a US armored brigade in a war game in Germany. Ukrainian crews knocked out US units so fast the drill had to revive them, years and billions after America bet big on beating drones.
International
More than 100 drones detected near Romania in four days, NATO jets scrambled seven times. The latest figures underscore how Russia's drone war is increasingly reaching NATO's eastern flank, with Romania already forced to destroy several drones this summer.
Ukraine: 18 of 26 Russian oil and stolen-grain ships face no sanctions. HUR says the oil tankers run for firms like Lukoil and Rosneft, while the dry-cargo ships load stolen grain at occupied ports such as Sevastopol.
Military training from age 15: Belarus splits 10th-graders into drone pilots and battlefield medics. The move deepens a years-long militarization of Belarusian schooling that now reaches from kindergarten military-patriotic groups to mandatory field camps.
Russia's state statisticians report the growth Putin demanded—economists doubt it will hold. The rebound leaned on war spending and one-off boosts, it barely moved the flat first-half trend, and it landed just after Putin ordered his officials to turn the economy around.
Reuters: Russia dismisses Black Sea ceasefire idea after Ukraine's offer. Reuters says Kyiv passed the proposal through a third party after attacks pushed carriers from Odesa and choked routes that move Ukrainian grain.
Russia allegedly sent a hitman after a US-Ukrainian citizen in Warsaw. Poland caught the suspect. Polish services detained the Russian suspect earlier this month after working with US counterparts.
NATO fighter, one drone, one district: a jammed intercept lands over Latvia. A NATO fighter shot down a drone over Latvia's Balvi district after Russian jamming pushed it off course, officials say.
NASA shows Crimea as Russian on a map during its eclipse broadcast. It's the latest in a run of Western maps quietly erasing the line international law still draws around occupied Crimea, this time from the US space agency.
Japan weighs sanctions after Putin's first visit to disputed Kuril Islands. Tokyo says Moscow's move is "totally unacceptable".
Humanitarian and social impact
A stray goat named Borka has become the Spartan Brigade's mascot after 18 months on the front lines in Donetsk Oblast. The soldiers once pulled on body armor and helmets and drove back into drone range to bring him out.
437 killed, over 2,600 injured: Ukraine's deadliest month for civilians since 2022, UN says. 437 killed, 2,610 wounded, the worst toll since May 2022, UN monitors say.
Political and legal developments
Russia plans to remove border zones separating Russia from occupied Ukrainian territories. Russia plans to remove special border zones along its boundaries with occupied parts of Ukraine, further integrating the occupied territories into its legal and administrative system.
A Russian soldier kept a Ukrainian woman in a basement and raped her for two months – Ukrainian court sentences him to 12 years. The abuse ended only when Ukrainian troops captured the Russian soldier during fighting in December 2025, freeing the woman from the basement where she had been held.
“Responsibility is inevitable”: Zelenskyy warns Russian collaborators in occupied territories after explosion kills defector. Zelenskyy said collaborators helping Russia attack Ukrainians will be held accountable as Ukrainian special services continue targeted operations in occupied territories.
Russian agent who set fires in Kyiv receives 15-year prison sentence. He was one more disposable recruit in Russia's Telegram sabotage campaign, hired for two arson jobs, then left to face the court alone.

articles.title: Russian E-Commerce Giants Beg Kremlin for Bailout After Devastating Drone Strikes
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russian E-Commerce Giants Beg Kremlin for Bailout After Devastating Drone Strikes
Russia’s largest e-commerce companies have appealed to the government for non-refundable federal financial aid to compensate sellers for catastrophic losses caused by Ukrainian drone attacks, The Moscow Times reported on August 14.
The appeal follows a Ukrainian drone campaign that destroyed all of industry giant Wildberries' major warehouses, eliminating roughly one-third of the company’s total storage capacity. A recent report estimates the total financial impact could approach 1 trillion rubles ($11.87 billion), comprising up to 700 billion rubles ($8.31 billion) in lost seller merchandise and 278 billion rubles ($3.30 billion) in direct damages and site restoration costs for Wildberries.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Citing the Russian business daily Vedomosti, The Moscow Times noted that an official letter was sent to Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin by the Association of Digital Platforms (ACP), which includes industry giants like Ozon, Yandex, Avito, Kuper, and Wildberries.
According to the publication, the ACP is requesting that the size of budget payouts be determined based on the actual damage and the scale of the affected company’s operations.
Furthermore, the association is asking the cabinet to grant affected entrepreneurs at least a six-month deferral or installment plan for taxes and mandatory payments, as well as the cancellation of all penalties and fines accrued during the period when their normal business operations were disrupted.
The financial aid requested by the ACP is estimated in the hundreds of billions of rubles. The Moscow Times highlighted data from Data Insight showing that after the series of Ukrainian strikes, goods worth between 445 and 507 billion rubles ($5.28 billion and $6.02 billion) burned in Wildberries warehouses.
The Association of Suppliers of Goods for Electronic Marketplaces (APTEP) estimates the losses for sellers to be even higher, reaching between 600 and 700 billion rubles ($7.12 billion and $8.31 billion).
Meanwhile, Wildberries itself, having lost about a third of its warehouse capacity, suffered direct losses ranging from 147 to 223 billion rubles ($1.74 billion to $2.65 billion), according to Data Insight. The Moscow Times pointed out that this sum climbs to 278 billion rubles ($3.30 billion) when factoring in the demolition, waste removal, and land rehabilitation of the affected territories.
Although Wildberries founder Tatyana Kim promised to assist affected sellers, the report states that the company realistically lacks the funds for such expenses. Its own losses easily swallow its entire annual profit—which stood at 175 billion rubles ($2.08 billion) last year—and the sellers' losses exceed that sum several times over.
According to APTEP data cited by the outlet, Wildberries has only paid entrepreneurs between 2,000 and 30,000 rubles ($23.74 and $356.08), failing to cover even 20 percent of their actual losses.
Despite this massive financial hole, the government is unlikely to step in. The Moscow Times referenced a previous statement from a source close to the Kremlin, originally reported by Reuters, stating that Russia simply does not have enough funds to save the affected Wildberries sellers.
Describing the disaster at the marketplace—which controls half of the country’s e-commerce market—as a “serious blow to the economy,” the source delivered a grim outlook. “There will be a wave of bankruptcies. No one has that kind of money to support the sellers,” the source told the publication.
The targeting of Wildberries warehouses follows its role in supporting the Russian army by allowing military equipment to be sold and delivered through its logistics network. Although the company recently disabled its dedicated “Everything for the SMO” product tag following the drone strikes, independent outlets report that tactical gear, body armor, and drone components remain readily available for purchase under other active war-themed categories on the platform.

articles.title: Russia’s Anti-Ukrainian Disinformation Surges in Poland by More Than 250% Using Warsaw-Kyiv Dispute
articles.body:
- Category

Russia’s Anti-Ukrainian Disinformation Surges in Poland by More Than 250% Using Warsaw-Kyiv Dispute
Russia has stepped up a large-scale disinformation campaign in Poland, seeking to deepen divisions between Warsaw and Kyiv by using historical disputes and criticism of Ukrainian refugees, according to Reuters on August 14.
After a public Polish-Ukrainian dispute emerged, the amount of anti-Ukrainian content in Polish on social media rose by more than 250%.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Polish Deputy Minister of Digital Affairs Paweł Olszewski said Russian disinformation literally "exploded" on social media and official Russian media platforms after the dispute began. Some of the narratives were later picked up by Polish media outlets.
Russia’s campaign has focused on sensitive historical issues dating back to World War II, as well as public anger over Ukrainian refugees. According to the Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM), the increase in anti-Ukrainian content was recorded across X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube.
Experts say Russia has changed its approach. A significant share of the content is produced by bot farms to create the impression of widespread anger among Poles.
Instead of inventing completely false stories, Russian actors often distort and amplify real controversial issues. This makes the manipulation harder to identify and remove because the narratives are based on events that actually happened.
Olszewski said the flow of disinformation surrounding the dispute "fell on receptive ground."
Moscow has traditionally denied carrying out information attacks. The Russian Embassy in Warsaw called the allegations "unfounded" and said Russia supposedly "does not interfere in relations between other states."
Tensions between Ukraine and Poland emerged in late May after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave an honorary name, "Heroes of the UPA," to one of the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ special units.
The decision drew criticism in Warsaw. Poland considers the Ukrainian Insurgent Army responsible for the 1943–1945 Volyn tragedy, which Poland recognizes as genocide against the Polish population.
Amid the debate over historical memory and assessments of the UPA’s activities, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Volodymyr Zelenskyy of the Order of the White Eagle. Former Ukrainian presidents later also declined the state honor.

articles.title: US hospitals billed $120mn for sex-change procedures on minors – report
articles.body:
US hospitals billed $120mn for sex-change procedures on minors – report
US hospitals have billed tens of millions of dollars for sex-changing interventions on minors, according to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
The ‘Wolves in White Coats’ report, released this week and citing watchdog research, said hospitals and clinics have billed nearly $120 million for more than 5,500 surgeries and 8,500 courses of hormones or puberty blockers for minors since 2019.
Some providers may have used misleading or potentially fraudulent billing codes to get insurers to cover the interventions, according to HHS. The department identified nearly $50 million in claims for puberty blockers given to children aged nine to 17 under a general hormone-disorder code without a gender-related or early-puberty diagnosis on the same claim.
Hospitals and clinics identified in the report have been referred to the Department of Justice and investigators from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for potential violations of federal law. According to HHS, the observed billing patterns require additional investigation.
Another nearly $11 million was billed for puberty blockers for hundreds of patients aged 13 to 17 under a diagnosis for unusually early puberty. HHS said that diagnosis does not apply at those ages.
The report said the procedures offered hospitals a long-term source of revenue, as minors who begin hormone drugs can remain in medical care for years. Citing outside estimates, it put lifetime costs at up to $75,000 without surgery and as much as $170,000 when operations are included.
“The Biden Administration ... contributed to the expansion and normalization of sex-rejecting interventions through nondiscrimination policies ... and other federal programs,” the report stated.
This week, President Donald Trump moved to end federal Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) funding for sex-change procedures for minors. The restrictions, due to take effect on October 13, cover puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and surgeries, although states can continue funding them themselves.
The move is part of a broader rollback of transgender-related policies since Trump returned to office. His administration has moved to restrict medical transition procedures for minors, bar transgender athletes from competing in women’s sports, and restrict people with gender dysphoria from serving in the US military.
At least 27 US states have enacted restrictions on gender-transition procedures for minors, while several major hospitals have stopped offering some services amid legal challenges, funding pressure and changing medical guidance.

articles.title: Trump: strait of Hormuz will soon be "American Territory"
articles.body:
ALBAWABA - U.S. President Donald Trump has stepped up his rhetoric against Iran, saying he will “very soon” declare the Strait of Hormuz “American territory” and pledging to ramp up military and economic pressure on Tehran.
Trump stated at a law enforcement event that he told senior officials of his administration to plan for a trip to the Middle East to prevent what he called a potential regional catastrophe. He did not offer details of the scheduled visit.
The president again called Iran the world’s greatest state sponsor of terrorism, defended past U.S. military interventions and insisted that continuous pressure is needed to keep Tehran from getting a nuclear weapon.
Trump also reiterated his administration’s promise to ramp up economic penalties, saying that Washington will “hit Iran economically with great force.” "The U.S. naval blockade of Iran is still fully in place," he said, adding, "no ships would get thru without the U.S. allowing it, which he called "a wall of steel."
The president also warned that any Iranian attack on U.S. interests would be met with a response "100 times stronger," hinting that Washington is still ready to respond forcefully to any military escalation.
Trump's comments come a day after U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent indicated the government was poised to unleash unprecedented steps against Iran, with a fresh package of sanctions or economic penalties perhaps released as soon as next week.
The recent pronouncements underline the continuing escalation of U.S.-Iran relations, with Washington relying more on economic pressure and military deterrence while the fate of the strategically critical Strait of Hormuz remains central to regional security concerns.

articles.title: 10-man Super Lig debutant Corum hold champions Galatasaray to 2-2 draw in league opener
articles.body:
Halis Sünnetci
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
Ten-man Corum FK held four-time defending champions Galatasaray to a 2-2 draw in Istanbul in the opening match Friday of the 2026-27 Turkish Super Lig season.
Galatasaray created several chances during a goalless first half, with Victor Osimhen twice coming close and Yunus Akgun having a goal ruled out for offside.
Nigerian striker Osimhen broke the deadlock in the 53rd minute, collecting Lucas Torreira’s looping pass before finishing into the bottom corner from a difficult angle.
Corum responded six minutes later when Alexandros Kiziridis unleashed a spectacular long-range strike from well outside the penalty area into the top-right corner, scoring the club’s first-ever Super Lig goal.
The visitors completed a rapid turnaround one minute later when Ramirez intercepted Davinson Sanchez’s underhit back pass and lobbed goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir to make it 2-1.
Corum were reduced to 10 men in the 70th minute when Kiziridis was sent off for a foul on Yunus Akgun.
Despite being a player down, Corum nearly extended their lead in the 80th minute, but Cakir denied Ramirez in a one-on-one situation.
Galatasaray increased the pressure and equalized in minute 90 when Osimhen headed Gabriel Sara’s corner into the bottom corner for his second goal.
Cakir then prevented Corum from retaking the lead in stoppage time by saving Mame Thiam’s header.
Galatasaray were unable to find a winner in the remaining minutes as the visitors secured a point in their Super Lig debut.
The result extended Galatasaray’s unbeaten home league run to 36 matches. Their last home league defeat came against Fenerbahce on May 19, 2024.

articles.title: A Russian court disqualifies a sitting Communist deputy over the copyright to Microsoft fonts in his campaign ads
articles.body:
A Russian court disqualifies a sitting Communist deputy over the copyright to Microsoft fonts in his campaign ads
The Samara Regional Court has stripped Mikhail Matveyev, an incumbent deputy from Russia’s Communist Party (KPRF), of his registration as a candidate for the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament.
The lawsuit was filed by Anna Sarantseva, a Party of Pensioners candidate running against Matveyev in the single-mandate district. She said his campaign materials used photographs — including some of his own — without permission from the copyright holders. They also used Microsoft fonts whose licenses the company restricted in Russia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The regional election commission backed the lawsuit, and Matveyev plans to appeal the ruling.
Matveyev is considered one of the KPRF’s strongest single-mandate candidates. He won the Krasnoglinsky district in 2021, and ahead of the current campaign, he and Komi deputy Oleg Mikhailov received the most votes among 230 participants in the party’s internal “People’s Candidate KPRF” project, political analyst Konstantin Kalachev said. “Though some might see letting him win the same district twice in a row as overkill,’” Kalachev told the Russian business daily Kommersant in May.
Meduza sources reported in June that the KPRF planned to avoid nominating candidates who had defeated United Russia rivals in 2021. The tactic would hand United Russia a supermajority in the Duma large enough to amend the constitution unilaterally and to push through any measure on the votes of its own faction alone.
In the end, the KPRF itself declined to nominate two strong single-mandate candidates. In Altai Krai, the party replaced Maria Prusakova with Lyudmila Klyushnikova, who has been under criminal investigation for fraud on an especially large scale since November 2025. In Yakutia, the party chose not to nominate Pyotr Ammosov at its congress.
A source told Meduza that similar copyright complaints have begun surfacing against Oleg Mikhailov.
Copyright claims have also been used during the current campaign to remove opposition candidates from other parties. On August 12, Russia’s Supreme Court revoked the registration of Yabloko’s federal list after a lawsuit from the Rodina Party. The court cited several violations, including unauthorized use of the lyrics to Pust vsegda budet solntse (“May There Always Be Sunshine”) and Lish by ne bylo voiny (“As Long As There’s No War”), survey data from the Levada Center, and an image generated by ChatGPT.

articles.title: US Backs Japan After Putin’s Visit to Disputed Kuril Islands
articles.body:
The US has condemned Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, saying it recognizes Japan’s sovereignty over the Northern Territories.
Putin visited the Kuril Islands for the first time in his 26-year tenure on Thursday, Aug. 13, drawing fresh attention to the decades-long territorial dispute with Japan that traces back to the Soviet Union and World War II.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“As Japan and the United States work together through their alliance to promote prosperity across the entire Indo-Pacific region, we strongly oppose any actions that would undermine peace and stability in the region,” George Glass, the US ambassador to Japan, said in a statement on Friday, Aug. 14.
US joins Kyiv in condemning the strike, Russia rejects objections
On Thursday, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Moscow of using the same tactics of occupation it has been using in its war against Ukraine.
“Putin’s provocative visit to Japan’s Etorofu island demonstrates utter disrespect to Japan,” Sybiha said in a statement, adding that the visit “represents a deliberate attempt to intimidate, escalate tensions, and normalize illegal occupation.”
Japan has since summoned Russia’s ambassador over the matter, according to AFP.
“The Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan’s territory, both historically and under international law,” Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said.
Ukraine Sanctions 13 Vessels, 39 Entities Over Stolen Grain Exports
However, the Russian embassy rejected Japan’s objections, with their authorities saying that the islands were “an integral part of the Russian Federation,” and that Putin’s travel there was not “a matter for discussion with foreign states.”
Dispute rooted in World War II
The Moscow-Tokyo dispute dates back to Empress Catherine II’s 1786 declaration that Russian explorers had discovered the islands.
“Japan’s PM Takaichi can prattle on all she likes about the Kuril Islands being ‘historically Japanese,’ but this chatter won’t change a thing,” former President Dmitry Medvedev said on Thursday, adding that “they were, are, and will remain Russian land.”
Stretching from Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula to Japan’s Hokkaido, the Kuril islands remain under Russian control, despite Japan claiming the four southernmost islands in the chain – Etorofu (Russian Iturup), Kunashiri, Shikotan, and Habomai – arguing they were “illegally occupied.”
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Ukraine in 2022, Japan joined Western sanctions against Moscow, straining the relationship further.
In response, Moscow withdrew from formally signing a peace treaty ending World War II. Russia had also frozen joint economic projects involving the islands.
Simultaneously, Glass’s statement reflects a further hardening in the US stance toward Russia.
Over the past few years of the war, President Donald Trump declined to label Russia an aggressor and predicted that Russia would prevail over Ukraine.
In recent months, however, he has begun shifting his diplomatic posture.
In July, he expressed newfound respect for Ukraine following its battlefield gains, and even floating the possibility of allowing Ukraine to domestically produce its own Patriot missiles – a weapon Ukraine urgently needs to defend itself against Russian ballistic missiles.
Ukraine-Japan ties deepen
As Moscow’s dispute with Tokyo grows, Ukraine-Japan ties have deepened.
In 2022, President Volodymyr Zelensky signed a decree formally recognizing the islands as Japanese territory under temporary Russian occupation.
During the week of Aug. 10-16, Ukrainian authorities held a series of meetings throughout the week with Japan’s outgoing Ambassador to Ukraine, Masashi Nakagome, discussing Japan’s possible role in the Drone Deal initiative, further cooperation and broader security measures as winter approaches.
Cooperation between Ukraine and Japan currently operates under the fifth phase of the Emergency Recovery Programme – which has a budget of roughly $38.5 million and covers infrastructure, water systems, the maritime sector, healthcare, and agriculture.
“Ukraine today may be East Asia tomorrow,” Japan’s outgoing Ambassador to Ukraine, Masashi Nakagome said in his official statement, adding that Japan strongly supports Ukraine, and will continue to do so, aiming to “achieve a just and lasting peace as soon as possible.”

articles.title: BBC seeks to subpoena Trump’s eldest children and son-in-law over defamation lawsuit
articles.body:
The BBC is trying to subpoena Donald Trump’s children as it builds its defense against the president’s defamation lawsuit centered on a documentary on the January 6 insurrection.
In a motion filed on Friday, the BBC sought authorization to serve Trump’s two eldest children, Donald Trump Jr and Ivanka Trump, and son-in-law Jared Kushner, with subpoenas for testimony and their records on the events of 6 January 2021.
The BBC, its lawyers wrote in court documents, is entitled to discover Trump’s “intention behind the speech and anything that bears on the impression his audience could have reasonably obtained in listening to the speech”, which includes whether Trump “gave it intentionally or otherwise; the breadth of the audience of the message and impression; and the extent of any resulting injury or harm”.
Trump filed the lawsuit against the BBC in December over scenes in the 2024 BBC documentary Trump, A Second Chance?. It argued that the BBC spliced scenes from Trump’s 6 January 2021 speech so that it appeared Trump directly urged his supporters to attack the US Capitol building.
Trump’s children and son-in-law have, “without question”, knowledge of several incidents that day, BBC’s lawyers wrote, , including when Trump sought to convince former vice-president Mike Pence to refuse certifying the results of the 2020 election. The BBC also said that Kushner allegedly helped to draft a statement for Trump that would have condemned the use of violence at the Capitol.
The British broadcaster had been unable to previously serve Trump’s children and son-in-law with subpoenas because they are protected by the US Secret Service as members of the sitting president’s immediate family, according to the court documents. The BBC had tried previously to serve Ivanka Trump and her husband, Kushner, at their home in Florida but were blocked by law enforcement officials.
Trump’s legal team did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Last week, a federal judge granted Trump’s request to block the BBC from accessing financial records after Trump’s lawyers said they would amend the lawsuit to focus specifically on the reputational damages rather than business impacts. Another judge had previously ruled that Trump would have to start handing over records that would have provided details on the hundreds of businesses owned by Trump’s family trust.
Trump recently claimed that the BBC used artificial intelligence to alter his speech, which the network has denied. While the BBC has apologized for the editing, it has maintained that Trump lacks the grounds for a defamation lawsuit.
The BBC is being represented by the law firm Ballard Spahr, which has also defended several publications facing lawsuits from Trump and his allies, including the New York Times and the Associated Press. It is one of several media organizations that Trump has targeted after they published critical reporting of him. The Wall Street Journal is also facing a $10bn lawsuit for its reporting on Trump’s alleged contributions to Jeffrey Epstein’s birthday book, and several journalists at the New York Times were subpoenaed over an article detailing security concerns with the Air Force One presidential jet.

articles.title: Ontario free to axe Toronto bike lanes, region’s top court rules
articles.body:
The Ontario government is now free to rip out Toronto’s bike lanes on its busiest streets after the region’s top court ruled in favour of the province on Friday, overturning a lower court’s decision that decreed removal would violate constitutional rights.
The win is significant for Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, and his government, who have long railed against Toronto’s bike lanes, blaming the protected zones for the city’s traffic ills.
In 2024, the Ford government passed legislation that would allow Ontario to axe Toronto’s lanes, despite the recent installation of the infrastructure by the municipality.
But the effort to tear up the lanes covering 19km (12 miles) of road was paused after cycling advocacy organisations levelled a legal challenge against the province.
Their challenge was supported in July 2025, when a superior court judge ruled removing the lanes was unconstitutional, as it would create a heightened risk of death or injury, in turn violating the right to life and security of the person. Those rights are protected under Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Friday’s decision from the Ontario court of appeal reverses that ruling. Michael Longfield, executive director of Cycle Toronto, one of the groups that launched the legal challenge, said he is disappointed in the decision.
“This isn’t just about keeping people on bikes safe. It helps pedestrians. It helps other drivers. It has a very strong traffic calming effect that we need in major cities,” he said.
The court of appeal judges in their decision wrote that there is no charter right to bike lanes and the government is free to change legislation on the lanes if it wishes. They explained that courts cannot find legislation unconstitutional because experts predict the government’s policies will fail.
“Neither the government nor the legislature is under any obligation to accept policy advice,” wrote Justice Huscroft in the decision.
In reaction to the ruling, Toronto’s mayor, Olivia Chow, said she has been working with the province to negotiate a path forward “that keeps every road user safe”. There’s hope the municipality will negotiate an alternative with the Ford government that still makes room for cyclists, said Longfield.
Ontario’s transportation minister, Prabmeet Sarkaria, said in a statement the top court’s decision is a “victory for common sense”. The government has not yet announced when or if they plan to remove the lanes.
It was estimated by a city report in 2024 that ripping up the lanes would cost taxpayers an additional C$48m (£26m). Internal briefings obtained by the Trillium also found the province’s own staff reported that bike lane removal would not reduce congestion and could make it worse. Those staff members also warned Ontario may be seen as encroaching on municipal decision-making.
Fundamentally, Ford targeting bike lanes is a gross overreach of the provincial government into city affairs, said Longfield. It is “frankly ridiculous”, he said, to believe the key to solving urban congestion is barring bike lanes.
“The more we can focus on real, evidence-based solutions … the better it will be,” he said.

articles.title: Mount Etna eruption and volcanic ash shut Sicily’s busiest airport
articles.body:
Mount Etna eruption and volcanic ash shut Sicily’s busiest airport
Flights will be suspended until at least 2pm local time (1200 GMT), as hundreds of travellers remain stranded.
Continuing volcanic activity from Mount Etna has forced the closure of Sicily’s busiest airport.
Authorities at Vincenzo Bellini Airport said on Friday that flights will remain suspended until at least 2pm local time (12:00 GMT) on Saturday, with ash from the volcano causing the greatest disruption the airport has seen in more than two decades.

Mount Etna’s eruption led to the cancellation of more than a third of the 1,974 flights between Thursday of last week and Wednesday of this week. Another 600 flights were diverted during the same period.
The volcano is Europe’s tallest and most active and has renewed questions about whether having a key airport nearby makes sense. Catania is located 30 kilometres (20 miles) south of the volcano.
Hundreds of passengers are waiting for flights that have been cancelled or delayed during the busiest travel week of the year. People planning to travel through Catania on Saturday have been contacting airlines to see whether their flights will still be running.
“We were due to leave on Wednesday, but our flight was cancelled; then they rescheduled it for Friday. Now that one’s been cancelled too,” Antonella Thirande Warnakulasuriya Costa, who is travelling to Sri Lanka via Dubai, told Reuters.
Catania airport usually handles at least 40,000 passengers a day. According to local media, about 300 passengers were waiting on Thursday evening to be transferred to another airport.
The ash from Mount Etna has not only affected Europeans; it has reached as far as North Africa.
The pause in flights has led the Italian train company Trenitalia to add six additional trains to the Palermo-Messina-Catania route.
Passengers can usually claim compensation if their travel plans are severely disrupted, but volcanic eruptions tend to come under what is known as extraordinary circumstances, meaning airlines are not legally obliged to compensate.

articles.title: Trump vows to declare Strait of Hormuz as US territory; Iran dismisses threats as empty
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said that he would soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory, while the Iranian government responded by stating that it would not be intimidated by US threats.
"After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," Trump said on Friday at the new Nassau County Police Academy in Garden City, New York.
Trump also said the US blockade of the strategic waterway remains in place, adding that "no ships get through unless we want them to."
He said that Iran's leadership has been decimated by the war, adding: "That's one of my problems: is nobody to negotiate with."
"It is a problem. I said, 'Are you sure this guy's okay?' It's the only country in the world where nobody wants to be president," Trump said.
On rising gas prices tied to the war, Trump said: "So for you to pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline, just remember you're doing it so that a very evil country cannot have — the number one state sponsor of terror in the world, we don't want to have them have a nuclear weapon."
Iranian military officials, however, disputed US control over the waterway, with Iran’s central military command on Thursday calling the claims "baseless lies and fabrications."
Iran responds to Trump's statement
Responding to Trump's Friday remarks, Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said that Tehran would not be intimidated by threats or a show of force by Washington.
Gharibabadi said in a post on X that the strategic waterway of Hormuz would only be opened or closed under Iran's authority.
As of August 12, in the 166 days since the war began, 3,371 vessels have crossed the strait, around 20 percent of pre-war traffic volumes, according to data from Kpler, a commodities and shipping data analytics firm, cited by CNN.
The US and Iran agreed to a Pakistan-brokered ceasefire in April and later signed a deal on June 17, launching negotiations toward a final agreement.
But the talks later stalled over disagreements on security guarantees and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategic routes for global energy supplies and trade.
From July 8 to 24, the US and Iran exchanged more military strikes, with Washington launching attacks inside Iran.
Tehran responded by striking what it described as US military facilities and equipment in several Arab countries, including Jordan, Bahrain and Kuwait.
