articles.title: What to Know About the Growing Concerns Over Conditions on the Long-Deployed USS Abraham Lincoln
articles.body:
The USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea in the Middle East for months, and with no clear end in sight for the war in Iran, concerns for those aboard the aircraft carrier—and for the vessel itself—have mounted amid a series of troubling reports.
Another aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, had begun making its way towards the Middle East as of Thursday to replace the Lincoln, multiple news outlets reported. President Donald Trump appeared to confirm the reported ship swap on Friday, saying that the Lincoln "is moving right now, or very shortly and is being replaced with another very similar ship.”
The Washington’s deployment comes as reports have emerged in recent months recounting worsening living conditions, mental health concerns, and supply shortages on board the Lincoln.
Trump seemed to deny the reports on the state of the Lincoln and its crew on Friday, responding “No, they’re not,” in response to a reporter saying that families of the crew members are worried about conditions on board. He also said, when asked if the carrier has been deployed for too long, that it has been deployed “not nearly long enough.”
Defense Secretary Pete Hegeseth on Thursday called the reports of dire conditions on the Lincoln “completely misrepresented.”
“We make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment. Some deployments are longer than others. I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody,” Hegseth, with a hand to his heart, told reporters. “I want them home as soon as everybody else, too.”
The Defense Department did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for comment.
Here’s what to know about the USS Abraham Lincoln, the concerns that have been raised over conditions on board, and the burgeoning calls for its crew to return home.
What is the USS Abraham Lincoln, and how long has it been deployed?
The Lincoln is in its ninth month at sea and has been deployed for more than 260 days.
The vessel works as a mobile airbase and command center with its own defense systems. It’s the length of more than three football fields and has a crew of roughly 5,000 when fully deployed.
It departed from San Diego in November on an alternate deployment, but was redirected towards the Middle East in January to provide tactical support to U.S. forces ahead of the war in Iran, which began with an initial wave of American-Israeli strikes at the end of February.
The Lincoln has played a key defensive role in the war against Iran, having shot down “hundreds and hundreds of missiles” and drone attacks that targeted the vessel, according to Hegseth.
“Every single one of those shots, easily shot down miles and miles away from the Abe Lincoln,” he said in April. “They were blowing ammo into fantasy land.”
The ship has also had a part in enforcing the U.S.’s blockade of Iranian ports.
The Lincoln’s deployment was expected to end in May, but was extended indefinitely.
The reported ship swap with the Washington comes as Trump has reinstated a blockade against Iran in the Strait of Hormuz and peace talks have stalled between the countries.
Reports of issues on board the carrier
Several reports have detailed poor conditions aboard the Lincoln. According to MS Now, which interviewed a dozen family members of crew members, those aboard the ship have been dealing with moldy showers and running out of key toiletries, such as toothpaste, deodorant, and soap. The outlet was also told that crew members are working grueling shifts with limited days off and that there are holes on the Lincoln’s flight deck, where pilots take off and land.
A spouse of a service member on the Lincoln also told CBS News that sailors had previously experienced food shortages. Another report from USA Today contained photos of rationed meals served to crew on board the carrier.
Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, pushed back against reports of food shortages back in April. “In no way, shape or form, has there been a time where in, at least in this deployment, where they’ve not met the nutritional requirements of our menu,” Caudle said.
As the deployment has stretched on and living conditions on board have allegedly deteriorated, the crew of the Lincoln has also reportedly struggled with increasing mental health concerns. The Navy Times and Stars and Stripes reported several instances of crew members on the vessel attempting to jump overboard.
An unnamed U.S. official confirmed to CNN that a crew member went overboard and was rescued last month, an event that was viewed as a mental health incident by the Navy, according to the outlet.
More than 200 families of crew members attended a meeting in San Diego last week with acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao. Many of the families raised a litany of concerns at a later virtual meeting, including about the crew’s mental health, safety, a lack of supplies and food, and water contamination, according to MS Now, which reviewed recordings of the meeting.
Cao was unable to specify during the meeting when the crew on the Lincoln would return home, according to the outlet.
The U.S. military has strongly pushed back against reporting about mental health concerns regarding the Lincoln’s crew.
“We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship,” a U.S. official tells TIME. “Adapting to life at sea can be difficult, so we've learned how to provide resources and help Sailors with these transitions. We are not experiencing an uptick in mental health issues aboard Abraham Lincoln.”
The official says that “religious, medical and mental health professionals” are aboard the Lincoln, including five chaplains, a psychologist, a social worker, three "behavioral health technicians,” and a service dog “to support crew morale and emotional welfare.”
The official did not provide information regarding the ongoing deployment of those aboard the Lincoln “due to operations security.”
“The Sailors and Marines of the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group remain resilient and resolved after more than 260 days at sea, 10,000 aircraft flights, and 1.5 million pounds of ordnance expended,” U.S. Central Command posted on X on Thursday. “No service members aboard the aircraft carrier have died, and the one Sailor who fell overboard Aug. 3 was quickly and safely recovered.”
Democrats push for answers
The reports about conditions on board the Lincoln have sparked calls from several Democrats urging the Defense Department to remedy the situation.
In a letter to Hegseth and Cao, Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, noted that the vessel’s crew members have not been to a port in a record-setting 200-plus days and demanded answers to a series of questions about the crew and the state of the ship.
“There have been widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system,” Blumenthal wrote. “These reports warrant immediate attention, but they also raise a broader question: whether the Navy can sustain the operational tempo now being demanded of its carrier force, particularly as this Administration repeatedly commits U.S. forces to conflicts of its own choosing and increasingly relies on aircraft carriers to sustain those operations.”
He also noted that the long deployment of the Lincoln is not an isolated incident, “suggesting that extended deployments may be becoming a feature rather than an exception of the Navy's force-generation model.” The USS Gerald R. Ford, used for the U.S.’s military operation in Venezuela, spent 326 days at sea before its return in May, Blumenthal wrote, which he noted was “nearly twice the length of a traditional six-month carrier deployment and the longest modern U.S. carrier deployment since the Vietnam era.”
Sen. Ruben Gallego requested an oversight visit to investigate the reports.
“Unlike Donald Trump, I've seen active duty,” Gallego wrote on X. “The way he's treating our service members as he carries out this illegal war is not just disgusting; it’s dangerous. These sailors are owed a sense of when they will go home.”
Gallego referenced the reports of crew members threatening to jump overboard, shifts lasting as long as 16 hours, rationed meals, and moldy showers, which he called “a frightening alarm bell.”
Rep. Sara Jacobs of California, who has introduced a War Powers Resolution to restrict Trump’s authority to continue the conflict in Iran without congressional approval, said that the Lincoln’s crew was “going through hell” and called for an end to the war. She described the reported poor conditions on the carrier as “a personnel issue and a national security risk.”
Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, a Navy veteran, has also taken to social media to call for accountability.
“Our servicemembers deserve better than this,” he said in a video posted to Bluesky. “There needs to be an investigation.” Kelly also blamed Trump having “no way out” of the war with Iran for the extended deployment of those aboard the Lincoln.
Rep. Mike Levin, who represents part of the San Diego region where the Lincoln was deployed from in November, took jabs at Hegseth’s comments downplaying the reports about the carrier.
“When families first raised the alarm back in April, Pete Hegseth called it fake news,” he wrote on X. “These men and women signed up to serve their country. The least their country owes them is hot water, a working toilet, and a real meal. Hegseth cannot even manage that, and he has the nerve to look their families in the eye and call them liars.”
A number of other Democrats have also joined the chorus of concerned voices over the Lincoln, including Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado; Rep. Seth Moulton of Massachusetts; and Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, the top Democrat on the Senate Defense Appropriations subcommittee.

articles.title: DPR business ombudsman reports losses suffered by entrepreneurs due to Galaktika attacks
articles.body:
DONETSK, August 14. /TASS/. Many entrepreneurs have suffered losses due to the Ukrainian army’s attacks on hypermarkets of the Galaktika chain in Makeyevka and Yenakiyevo, Yaroslav Berezhko, business ombudsman of the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR), told TASS.
"A great many entrepreneurs suffered losses. Galaktika did not own all its merchandise outright, a significant portion was held on consignment, it is a retail business after all. While they did have substantial inventory of their own, a vast amount was also held under deferred payment terms, they don’t purchase everything using their own funds. A good half of that value represents the entrepreneurs’ money," he said.
On the night of August 10, Ukrainian UAVs attacked the Galaktika hypermarket covering an area of 30,000 square meters in Makeyevka. The building burned down almost completely. On the night of August 14, the Armed Forces of Ukraine struck the Galaktika hypermarket covering an area of 8,000 square meters in Yenakiyevo. There were no casualties in the first instance, while two security guards were wounded in the second.
According to data from the Rusprofile counterparty verification service, Namestnik, the company operating the Galaktika retail chain, ranked first in the region within its sector last year in terms of revenue. In 2025, revenue grew by more than 4% to 16.67 bln rubles ($198 mln).

articles.title: Russian kids keep getting bused to the same movie (not ‘Spider-Man’), and the institutions taking them are posting eerily similar praise for it online
articles.body:
Russian kids keep getting bused to the same movie (not ‘Spider-Man’), and the institutions taking them are posting eerily similar praise for it online
School camps and municipal children’s centers across Russia are reporting in large numbers that they took children to see The Last Warrior: Kolobok. Verstka, an independent Russian news outlet, found more than 20 such posts on social media in recent days.
The posts describe how the institutions organized trips to movie theaters for the children, and they include photos from the screenings. Verstka said the posts “actively praise” the film and that the wording in some of them is similar.
Alongside these reports, claims surfaced that the Education Ministry had ordered mandatory screenings of the Kolobok film for students in grades one through nine. The ministry called the claim fake, saying the film “is successfully attracting viewers’ attention even without additional support.”
The Last Warrior: Kolobok opened in Russian theaters in early August. Because of the film, distributors reportedly asked movie theaters to postpone screenings of the blockbuster Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which was due for a gray-market release in Russia at the same time. Theaters were threatened with sanctions if they refused.
After the Spider-Man film was postponed, the creators of Kolobok faced criticism, and viewers drove down the Russian film’s rating on review aggregator sites.
The television channel Rossiya 24 complained to the prosecutor’s office and the Investigative Committee about online critics of the film, saying they had sent threats to its creators. Investigators opened a criminal case.

articles.title: Gemini’s VPN workaround stops working for some users in Russia
articles.body:
Google’s Gemini AI has stopped working for some users in Russia, according to complaints on the Downdetector website. Kod.ru, a Russian tech outlet, flagged the outage.
Gemini was already unreachable from Russian IP addresses, but the disruption has now spread to users accessing it via a VPN. The outage coincided with the release of Gemini 3.7 Flash, a new version of the AI model.
Experts consulted by Kod.ru said the problem may stem from how VPN services operate or how Google determines users’ locations.
“Many VPN services exclude google.com and some other Google services from the tunnel by default, so search and email work faster. But that means traffic to those services goes directly from the user’s real IP address, and Google sees that the person is in Russia, not in the VPN’s home country,” one of the sources said.
“Google has increasingly been determining a user’s location not just by IP address, but by a combination of behavioral signals, including location data from Google Maps. If users from Russia systematically connect through a particular VPN server, over time Google’s algorithms begin to associate that address with Russian jurisdiction, even though the server is physically located in another country,” another source said.

articles.title: Washington quizzes NATO allies on support for Trump – Bloomberg
articles.body:
US issues NATO members ‘loyalty test’ – Bloomberg
The US is making military support for NATO members contingent on how closely they align with President Donald Trump’s foreign policy, Bloomberg has reported.
Washington has recently sent NATO members a document containing a series of questions aimed at gauging their alignment with the Trump administration, the agency said.
Governments were asked whether they had “been publicly supportive” of US foreign-policy initiatives, including those in the Middle East and Western Hemisphere, the outlet reported, citing a copy it had reviewed. Washington also wanted to know what “restrictions” individual countries have imposed on US forces operating from military bases on their territory.
The answers could factor into decisions about how US military capabilities are distributed among NATO members, according to Bloomberg.
The apparent loyalty test comes amid widening tensions between Washington and its traditional European allies, with Trump repeatedly accusing NATO members of relying on US protection while failing to contribute enough to their own defense.
Trump has long been a fierce critic of NATO countries’ defense spending, repeatedly accusing European members of underfunding their militaries and effectively relying on Washington to bankroll their defense.
Earlier this summer, he renewed his criticism ahead of the NATO summit in Ankara, arguing that the US “spends more money on NATO than any other country, by far, to protect them, without getting any benefit.” He contrasted nearly $1 trillion in annual US defense spending with significantly smaller expenditures by individual European allies.
NATO members agreed at last year’s summit in The Hague to raise defense and security-related spending to 5% of GDP by 2035. Trump hailed the pledge as a victory for Washington but has since questioned whether all members are on track to meet the target.
Defense spending is not the only source of friction, however. Tensions have intensified further over the US war with Iran, with Trump criticizing European allies for refusing to become more directly involved and complaining that “they were not there for us.”
Several NATO members also refused to allow Washington to use jointly operated military bases for offensive operations against Iran. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth branded the restrictions “shameful,” arguing that they had put American troops “at risk.”
The US, however, still maintains an extensive military presence across Europe, including tens of thousands of personnel in Germany. Ramstein Air Base is one of Washington’s most important military hubs outside the US and a key logistical center for operations in Europe, Africa, and the Middle East.
The growing disagreements have, in turn, fueled debate in Europe about reducing its reliance on Washington for security. European officials have increasingly discussed “strategic autonomy” and the need to develop greater capacity to defend the continent should US priorities diverge from the rest of NATO.

articles.title: UK criticises Israel’s Netanyahu over ‘Islamic republic of Britain’ comment
articles.body:
UK criticises Israel’s Netanyahu over ‘Islamic republic of Britain’ comment
- UK condemned Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu's comment calling Britain an "Islamic republic," calling it "completely unacceptable" and raising the issue with Israel.
- Netanyahu quoted a far-right claim linking Britain to Islamic rule and nuclear weapons, which UK officials and Israeli spokespeople dismissed as a quote from US Vice-President J.D. Vance.
- Tensions remain high as Britain recognises Palestinian statehood, considers banning goods from Israeli settlements, and distances itself from US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – Britain on Aug 14 hit back at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu derisively calling the country an “Islamic republic” in an interview, branding the remarks “completely unacceptable”.
The diplomatic tit-for-tat came after the right-wing leader made the reference in an army radio podcast interview the previous day, in which he criticised the UK’s stance on Israel.
It echoed the language of far-right politicians and commentators in the Western world who have made baseless claims that parts of Britain have come under Islamic law due to immigration, drawing accusations of Islamophobia.
“These comments are completely unacceptable and we have raised them with the Israeli government,” a UK government spokesman said on Aug 14.
In the podcast interview, Netanyahu spoke of how Winston Churchill’s grandson and namesake vocally supported Israel during the 1967 Arab-Israeli war.
“Would you find that now?” Netanyahu asked.
“Someone once said that the first Islamic republic with nuclear weapons would be the Islamic republic of Britain,” he added with a smile.
“We’re making sure there’s not another one here in Iran.”
In a BBC radio interview earlier on Aug 14, Israeli government spokesman David Mencer appeared to downplay Netanyahu’s comments.
“He (Netanyahu) was making a quote that someone else had given,” Mencer said, noting that US Vice-President J.D. Vance had “made those comments” previously.
“He was quoting what the Vice-President had said.”
Vance had said in 2024 that the UK could become “the first truly Islamist country that will get a nuclear weapon”, drawing a rebuke from senior UK politicians at the time.
Britain was one of a number of European countries that recognised Palestinian statehood in 2025, infuriating Israel.
More recently, its new prime minister Andy Burnham has said his predecessor Keir Starmer did not put enough pressure on Israel to halt its offensive in Gaza.
In an interview with The Guardian shortly before taking office, Burnham said Britain would consider banning trade in goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967.
Britain, usually closely aligned with Washington, has also kept its distance from the US-Israeli war launched in February against Iran.
Netanyahu has long vowed to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, a goal that Tehran denies pursuing.
Britain and the US are nuclear powers, and Israel is widely known to have atomic weapons, although it has never publicly acknowledged its arsenal.
In 1998, Pakistan became the first Islamic nuclear power when it tested an atom bomb in response to parallel tests by its historical rival India. AFP

articles.title: Iran war: Trump dismisses concerns over conditions on USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier
articles.body:
Iran war: Trump dismisses concerns over conditions on USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier
There have been reports of sailors jumping overboard, raising questions about their mental health during the nine-month-long deployment
President Donald Trump dismissed concerns on Friday over living conditions and the mental health of service members on a US aircraft carrier deployed against Iran, while confirming the ship would soon rotate out.
Asked by reporters whether family members were worried about the situation on the USS Abraham Lincoln, Trump said “no, they’re not”.
Trump also rejected the idea that the ship – now at sea for nine months – had been deployed for too long. “No, no, no, not nearly enough,” he said.
The president confirmed reports that the ship was due to be swapped out with another aircraft carrier, as the United States remains locked in a stalemate with Iran over control of the Strait of Hormuz and the country’s nuclear programme.
“That ship is moving right now or very shortly and it’s being replaced with another very similar ship,” Trump said.
US media, including specialist military publications, have quoted multiple relatives of crew members saying living conditions have deteriorated on the Lincoln. There have also been reports of several suicide attempts.

articles.title: Starlink won’t remove Poland from Europe after all, days after Warsaw threatened to drop Ukraine’s funding
articles.body:
Starlink won’t remove Poland from Europe after all, days after Warsaw threatened to drop Ukraine’s funding
Starlink will not remove Poland from the European region of its satellite communications network. Janusz Cieszyński, a former Polish digital affairs minister, was the first to report the reversal.
Poland’s current digital affairs minister, Krzysztof Gawkowski, and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski later confirmed the report. In a post on X, Sikorski thanked Elon Musk, who owns Starlink, for acknowledging that Poland is part of the European Union.
Meduza reported earlier this week that Starlink planned to drop Poland from its European region on August 17. The reasons for the change were not made public. The change would have driven up service costs for Polish customers. In response, Sikorski threatened to stop Poland’s payments for Starlink’s services in Ukraine.
Ukraine uses Starlink’s network in its war with Russia. Poland’s Ministry of Digital Affairs finances satellite communications for Ukraine’s armed forces at a cost of about $50 million a year.
Russian troops also used Starlink terminals, but large numbers of the devices went offline along the front line early this year.

articles.title: Ukraine’s quiet counteroffensive took 745 square km. Russia’s dead Starlink is how
articles.body:
- In six months of unheralded advances, Ukrainian forces liberated a wide stretch of the southeast
- The collapse of Russian communications turned a local push into a six-month advance
- Now the Russians may mobilize yet again, so the Ukrainians are digging in and consolidating their gains
The scale of Ukrainian forces' counteroffensive in southeastern Ukraine early this year is finally becoming clear. In six months of maneuver starting on 29 January, a clutch of Ukrainian units, including the 78th, 79th, 80th, 82nd, and 95th Air Assault Brigades and the 1st and 425th Assault Regiments—tens of thousands of troops, in all—marched through gaps in Russian defenses and, according to Ukrainian officials, liberated around 745 square km and 26 settlements. Mostly in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast but also in neighboring Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk Oblasts.
That is Kyiv's own accounting, and it is the high end. The Institute for the Study of War, which maps control from geolocated imagery, put the figure at roughly 627 square km across the Oleksandrivka direction and the northern Hulyaipole direction—while noting its own conservative method probably undercounts. Either number describes the largest Ukrainian territorial gain since 2023.
The Ukrainian gains helped to offset Russian gains around the last few free cities in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast. Between the start of February and the end of July, Russian regiments captured a net total of just 260 square km of Ukrainian soil, according to a tally by the Black Bird Group. It would've been more than 1,000 square km if those air assault and assault units hadn't been busy clearing the Russians from a wide swathe of the southeast.
The Ukrainian counteroffensive kicked off on 29 January. Three days later, Elon Musk's Starlink bricked Russia's thousands of smuggled and stolen satellite terminals. Practically overnight, the Russians lost their best method for controlling small drones and guiding assault units across the disputed gray zone. Drones couldn't fly. Troops couldn't navigate.
Ukrainian commanders surely knew their communications advantage wouldn't last: the Russians would eventually adapt with new methods of command and control. Seizing the opportunity, Ukrainian paratroopers and assault troops pressed the attack. And in stark contrast to the usual assault tactics for both sides, the Ukrainians attacked in tanks and other armored vehicles, counting on the Russians' connectivity problems to clear a path for heavy forces.
The blackout was not the only thing working in Ukraine's favor. ISW credits the gains to five reinforcing factors: better operational planning, a campaign to suppress and destroy Russian air defenses, deeper strikes on Russian logistics, Ukrainian drone superiority at the tactical level—and the Starlink cutoff. But the cutoff is the one that arrived all at once, and it arrived just as Ukrainian armor was starting to move.
Mechanized assaults
Not all the vehicles got through. The assault troops lost one up-armored M-1 Abrams tank in early February. But by March, other assault forces M-1s were engaging Russian troops at point-blank range with their 120-mm main guns. After clearing a few disputed villages along a 45-km front between Dobropillya and Zelenyi Hai, the Ukrainians focused their maneuver and firepower on Komar, 12 km southeast of Zelenyi Hai.
The Ukrainians "started a slow and quiet offensive, with very few videos and small teams, during April and May," mapper Clément Molin recalled. The strict information security obscured the Ukrainian moves for all but the closest observers, allowing Ukrainian commanders to press their attacks without drawing too much attention—and risking a Russian countercounteroffensive.
By summer, the Ukrainians were within mortar range of Komar. Embarrassed Russian commanders resorted to sending out small teams on virtual suicide missions to plant Russian flags in disputed territory. The flags could create the impression of Russian control on terrain that, in fact, neither side controlled. "Russia is trying to intoxicate us with flag videos, which are meant to hide the real situation to both us and their command," Molin wrote.
The reality was that the Ukrainians had gained ground. A lot of it.
Trending Now
Announcing the results on 12 August, Ukrainian officials also claimed 9,550 Russian troops killed and more than 6,600 wounded—figures no independent body has verified. Former commander in chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, who planned the operation, said it proved the Ukrainian army "is capable not only of steadfastly holding its defences, but also of launching offensives, seizing the initiative, and liberating Ukrainian land."
But the momentum was unsustainable. As the Russians gradually restored command and control through the summer, the Ukrainians encountered more resistance. Now the gray zone is stabilizing again. Observer Moklasen predicted new Ukrainian commander in chief Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi will order his corps and brigade commanders "to dig in positions, consolidate and strengthen more army corps" instead of continuing to attack.
After all, the Russians are pushing hard in Donetsk, and the resources the Ukrainians had devoted to the southeastern counteroffensive could boost the defensive effort in the east. Moreover, there are worrying signs the Kremlin may attempt another mobilization soon, potentially surging hundreds of thousands of fresh troops into Ukraine.
The Ukrainians may soon prioritize holding over attacking.

articles.title: Migrant charity SOS Méditerranée says 11 bodies spotted in sea off Libya's coast
articles.body:
The EU border agency Frontex said the total number of irregular border crossings into the European Union fell by 26% in 2025 from the previous year to almost 178,000.
A plane operated by non-governmental organisations assisting migrants in the Mediterranean spotted 11 decomposing bodies in the sea off the coast of Libya on Friday.
The SOS Méditerranée NGO called it a "harrowing scene" in a statement, saying "some of the bodies still had clothes on, others were kept afloat by tire inner tubes".
It said the bodies were "in an advanced state of decomposition."
"This sighting is a stark reminder of the human consequences of Europe's deadly policies of indifference and deterrence-at-all-costs," the organisation said in a statement.
The Italian coast guard said it had been notified and had informed Libyan authorities since the bodies were in Libya's search and rescue zone.
It said the bodies were around 57 nautical miles (105 kilometres) from the Libyan coastal city of Zuwarah.
The monitoring plane was operated by SOS Méditerranée and the Humanitarian Pilots Initiative.
Every year, tens of thousands of migrants attempt to cross the sea from north Africa to southern member states of the European Union.
The International Organisation for Migration said this week that the number of known migrant deaths in the central Mediterranean has increased drastically, even as migrant numbers fall because of harsher European policies.
It said 821 people died or went missing in the first four months of 2026, a 111% increase from 2025. More than half of the deaths were caused by severe weather in January.
Over the same period, migrant arrivals on that route fell by 46% to 8,577.
The EU border agency Frontex said the total number of irregular border crossings into the European Union fell by 26% in 2025 from the previous year to almost 178,000.

articles.title: Constitutional Council of France lifts ban on social media for children under 15
articles.body:
PARIS, August 14. /TASS/. The ban on the use of social networks by children under the age of 15, supposed to come into force in September after the adoption of the law by parliament, was declared unconstitutional, the Constitutional Council ruled.
In justifying its decision in 23 paragraphs, the Council explains that the ban violates children's right to freedom of expression and communication. The Council agreed that the ban may be constitutional when it comes to protecting the interests of the child and preventing violations of public order. However, in its current form, it covers absolutely all online resources, with the exception of online encyclopedias and educational platforms that allow information exchange without taking into account the specifics of resources, without a risk assessment for minors, and without allowing parents or guardians to allow children to use these resources with their own responsibility.
The Constitutional Council also said that the ban implies that even adults must confirm their age. "Without defining the conditions and limits within which such confirmation should be provided, the legislator did not provide for legal guarantees capable of ensuring compliance with the requirements of the constitution. It follows from all of the above that without the need to consider the remaining complaints, article 1 of the submitted law contradicts the constitution," the decision reads.
Banning social media for children
Earlier, the National Assembly (lower house of parliament) and the Senate (upper house of parliament) of France supported the bill "on the protection of minors from the threats of social networks," which bans the use of social networks for children under 15 years of age. This measure obliged social networks to implement mechanisms for verifying the age of their users to prevent their use by children. It also ordered social networks to delete the accounts of the users under 15. The bill also introduced a "digital curfew" for the users between the ages of 15 and 18, limiting their time using Internet resources.
According to French President Emmanuel Macron, who advocated the ban, the law was supposed to come into force in September. At the first stage, it was only meant to prohibit the creation of new accounts for people under the age of 15. The deletion of existing accounts was supposed to take place before January 1, 2027.

articles.title: Jason Arday: Ex-Cambridge professor found dead — reports
articles.body:
Jason Arday: Ex-Cambridge professor found dead
August 14, 2026
Jason Arday, the former University of Cambridge professor who resigned amid allegations of plagiarism, was found dead on Friday.
Without naming him directly, the Metropolitan Police said he was found "unresponsive" in Battersea, south London, and pronounced dead at the scene.
"At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," a spokesperson said. "His next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by officers."
Arday, a professor of sociology of education at Cambridge, one of the world's top universities, resigned just over a week ago amid mounting allegations that he plagiarized parts of his PhD thesis and overstated his personal achievements.
He had denied wrongdoing, saying in a resignation letter last week that he did not accept "the narratives that have surrounded me."
Questions mounted over thesis and fundraising claims
British newspapers and commentators have seized on the allegations, arguing that he gained an unfair advantage through diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies.
Scrutiny of Arday's credentials intensified last month after criticism from former Cambridge researcher Nathan Cofnas.
The Times of London later reported similarities between passages in Arday's 2015 PhD thesis and an earlier paper by another researcher.
Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated and cleared by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.
But last week, Cambridge launched an investigation following "new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments."
British media also questioned Arday's claims of having raised £5.5 million (€6.4 million, $7.4 million) for charity through endurance challenges. Arday told The Guardian the funds were raised collectively over two decades.
Supporters reject claims, cite racial bias
Supporters, including over two dozen academics and politicians, characterized the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to discredit Arday and other Black people in influential positions.
In his resignation letter, Arday said that "the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."
His family issued a statement denouncing the "campaign of sustained abuse" Arday had faced since he took the role at Cambridge University more than three years ago.
"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," Arday's family said.
"We won't comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long," the statement added.
Cambridge's Vice-Chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice said, "We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time."
Edited by: Rob Turner and Karl Sexton

Arday, a professor of sociology of education at Cambridge, one of the world's top universities, resigned just over a week ago amid mounting allegations that he plagiarized parts of his PhD thesis and overstated his personal achievements.
He had denied wrongdoing, saying in a resignation letter last week that he did not accept "the narratives that have surrounded me."
Questions mounted over thesis and fundraising claims
British newspapers and commentators have seized on the allegations, arguing that he gained an unfair advantage through diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies.
Scrutiny of Arday's credentials intensified last month after criticism from former Cambridge researcher Nathan Cofnas.
The Times of London later reported similarities between passages in Arday's 2015 PhD thesis and an earlier paper by another researcher.
Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated and cleared by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.
But last week, Cambridge launched an investigation following "new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments."
British media also questioned Arday's claims of having raised £5.5 million (€6.4 million, $7.4 million) for charity through endurance challenges. Arday told The Guardian the funds were raised collectively over two decades.
Supporters reject claims, cite racial bias
Supporters, including over two dozen academics and politicians, characterized the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to discredit Arday and other Black people in influential positions.
In his resignation letter, Arday said that "the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."
His family issued a statement denouncing the "campaign of sustained abuse" Arday had faced since he took the role at Cambridge University more than three years ago.
"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," Arday's family said.
"We won't comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long," the statement added.
Cambridge's Vice-Chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice said, "We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time."

articles.title: Peru Plans to Purchase 12 F-16 Block 70 Fighter Jets
articles.body:
Peru is planning to purchase a second batch of 12 F-16 Block 70 fighter jets. The Peruvian Air Force’s rearmament program calls for the acquisition of a total of 24 fighter jets.
This was reported by Infodefensa, citing a statement by Defense Minister Rafael Belaunde Llosa.
According to the minister, the previous interim government did not leave any funds, so the new administration needs some time to ensure the signing of the second contract.
The minister confirmed that the Peruvian Air Force needs to acquire 24 fighter jets to ensure a minimum deterrence capability. Therefore, in his opinion, even despite financial difficulties, it makes no sense to limit the procurement to an initial batch of 12 aircraft.
“My task is to do everything possible, everything in my power, to meet the needs of the Armed Forces,” he said.
The Peruvian Air Force and Lockheed Martin signed a contract for the purchase of the first batch of F-16C/D Block 70 fighter jets in April 2026.
Prior to this, Lockheed Martin reduced the price of the fighter jets offered to Peru to stay within the budget set by the country’s government. While the initial proposal called for the sale of 12 F-16C/D Block 70s for $3.42 billion, the new proposal includes 24 aircraft of the same model for $3.5 billion.
French company Dassault Aviation, with its Rafale F4, and Swedish company Saab, with its Gripen E/F, also participated in the selection process for Peru’s new fighter jets. It is likely that this significant price reduction was the reason Peru chose the F-16 over the Swedish JAS 39 Gripen, which had won the tender.

articles.title: Scientists found a subtle social cue that reveals your choices
articles.body:
An experimental study in Israel found that participants were more likely to prefer a movie synopsis when their positive facial expressions mimicked the facial expressions of the person they were interacting with. This facial mimicry predicted participants’ choices better than the participants’ own facial expressions alone. The paper was published in Communications Psychology.
Facial mimicry is the tendency to spontaneously and often unconsciously reproduce the facial expressions we observe in other people. When someone smiles, frowns, or shows another emotion, our own facial muscles may respond with a subtle version of the same expression.
This behavior appears very early in life and has been linked to empathy, emotional understanding, social bonding, and affiliation. Mimicry may help us understand other people by partially recreating their emotional state in our own facial muscles and brain systems.
At the same time, it is not simply an automatic reflex, because people mimic others more or less depending on social context, relationships, goals, and whether an emotional expression seems appropriate to the situation. People are also generally more likely to mimic individuals they like, identify with, cooperate with, or regard as socially important.
Study author Liron Amihai and colleagues conducted a study in which they explored whether facial mimicry can predict preferences in a situation when people choose between two options during natural, two-person interactions. They hypothesized that facial mimicry would predict participants’ choices and that it would be a more accurate predictor of these choices than facial expressions alone.
Study participants were 120 women. Their average age was 23 years. They were grouped into pairs, and the researchers made sure that members of a pair did not know each other previously.
The study authors selected 16 book synopses from GoodReads.com as stimuli to be used in the study. They were selected from a wider set of 25 books that were released around the time of selection, for which there was no previous Hebrew translation, and that did not have notable popularity in Israel.
The synopses of these books were rated by a different group of 30 participants, and the study authors selected a set of 16 synopses that received similar ratings. Although the synopses were derived from books, the study authors presented them as movie synopses to the study participants. Of the 16 synopses, they chose 8 and recorded an actress reading them.
At the start of the experiment, the study authors fitted electromyography (EMG) electrodes—small sensors used to measure the electrical activity of muscles—on participants’ faces, allowing them to track participants’ facial movements. They then calibrated the system by asking participants to imitate the facial expressions of an actor in a video.
After that, they proceeded to the reading phase of the experiment. In this phase, one participant in the pair read two selected synopses to the other member of the pair, while that member was seated opposite and was able to view the reader’s face. After reading the synopses, each participant indicated which movie they would prefer.
In the listening phase, participants in a pair remained seated face to face, but listened to two synopses read by an actress (the one the study authors previously recorded, audio only). In two of the four trials, they were instructed to indicate which of the two movies they preferred, and in the other two, they indicated which of the two movies their partner would prefer.
Results showed that participants were more likely to choose a synopsis when they showed higher levels of facial mimicry of muscles associated with positive emotions. As the study authors hypothesized, the listener’s choice was better predicted by the speaker-listener’s facial mimicry than by the listener’s own facial expressions alone. The results remained the same even when only smiling mimicry was measured in the listening situation (i.e., in the part of the experiment where they listened to the audio recording of the actress reading the synopses).
“Our findings suggest that facial mimicry is a powerful non-verbal cue that is correlated to and might influence agreement, interpersonal judgments and preferences, offering important implications for understanding the mechanisms behind social cognition and interaction,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to scientific knowledge of the role of facial mimicry in interpersonal interactions. However, it should be noted that the study focused exclusively on women. Results on men might differ.
The paper, “Facial mimicry predicts preference,” was authored by Liron Amihai, Elinor Sharvit, Hila Man, Yael Hanein, and Yaara Yeshurun.

articles.title: Trump says US will hit Iran hard economically after Bessent issues warning
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said Friday that he would soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory, following a Truth Social post on Wednesday in which he said of the waterway, "I think we will keep it."
"Pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," Trump told a crowd at a Garden City, New York, event honoring police.
Trump said the declaration would come "after we [the US] finish defeating Iran," which he described as being "very badly defeated."
He described the US naval blockade in the strait as "unstoppable" and a "wall of steel," saying, "No ships get through unless we want them to."
Trump added that he "built [up]" the US military, which he said he used "a little more than I wanted to, frankly, but that's okay."
"We cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he emphasized. "Do we agree? Can't let them."
The US president described Iran as a "very evil country" and the "number one state sponsor of terrorism in the world."
"Remember that when you have to pay a little bit more [for gasoline]," Trump added.
Trump: Operation Midnight Hammer prevented Iranian nuclear weapons
Trump credited the US military's Operation Midnight Hammer for preventing Tehran from acquiring such weapons.
"If we didn't hit them, you would have had a nuclear weapon," he said, noting it as an outcome that would have been a "very sad day for this country and the entire world."
Trump's comments came a day after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US would impose measures on Tehran that have "never been seen" as soon as next week.
Iran responds, says the regime does not fear threats
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi responded to Trump's comments in an X/Twitter post later on Friday, saying that the Strait of Hormuz "cannot be seized by tweet, nor by aircraft carrier, nor by issuing an order, nor by an election speech."
"Iran neither fears threats nor cowers before displays of power," Gharibabadi added.
On Saturday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iranian news outlet Shahrara News that while Iran has decided not to resume talks with the US, separate talks with Oman were focused on defining a sea route through the Strait of Hormuz.
Araghchi reiterated previous assertions from Tehran that the US would have to meet specific conditions for shipping to resume through the waterway.
He added that messages being exchanged with Washington via Qatar and Pakistan do not amount to negotiations.
Reuters and Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

articles.title: Libyan commander Haftar helped secure release of US hostage in Sahel
articles.body:
A deal to free an American hostage held by an Islamic State affiliate in West Africa's Sahel region was brokered with the help of the eastern Libyan military commander Khalifa Haftar, four sources told Reuters.
The hostage, a pilot working for a Christian missionary organization in Niger, was handed over to eastern Libyan authorities late Thursday, one of the sources said. Libya's role in the deal has not previously been reported.
Haftar's involvement in the freeing of a US hostage reflects how he has carved out a position as a major security broker in the Sahel region, and has used it as leverage to curry favor with the Trump administration.
The missionary, Kevin Rideout, worked for the evangelical agency Serving in Mission and was kidnapped in Niger in October. It was not clear what, if anything, was traded in exchange for his release. One of the four sources said the Libyan side had paid a ransom, without providing further details.
Officials thought Rideout had been moved to Mali
The State Department declined to comment. The White House did not respond to a request for comment about Haftar's involvement. In a social media post, Trump said the US looks forward to welcoming Rideout home.
The authorities in eastern Libya were not immediately available for comment.
Reuters reported last year that Rideout was seized by three unidentified men on his way to the airport in Niamey and taken to the western Tillaberi region of Niger, where Islamist militants linked to Islamic State and al Qaeda operate.
The US has made recovering Rideout one of its top priorities in the Sahel. The Trump administration lifted sanctions on top Malian government officials earlier this year in an effort to secure overflight access to the country's airspace to hunt for the pilot.
For months, officials believed Rideout may have been moved to Malian territory.
The details of Rideout's handover to Libyan authorities and his journey to Libya were not immediately clear.
Two sources said the recent effort to secure his release from the Islamic State affiliate was led by Cherif Ould Tahar, a Malian Arab businessman with connections to regional armed groups and smuggling networks. Tahar could not immediately be reached for comment.

Details

articles.title: Public exams to become more transparent, secure and trustworthy: President Murmu
articles.body:
Noting that 65% of India’s population is below the age of 35, Murmu said, “This young population is our most valuable asset.”
NEW DELHI: Referring to students as “architects of India’s future”, President Droupadi Murmu Friday said govt is undertaking comprehensive steps to reform the public examination system to “completely curb” the use of unfair means, make it more transparent, secure and trustworthy for the youth.“Just as govt and society must remain united to ensure national security, everyone must contribute through joint and concerted efforts to safeguard the present and future of our students. Public exams become gateways to opportunities for our students,” Murmu said in her address to the nation on Independence Day eve.Noting that 65% of India’s population is below the age of 35, she said, “This young population is our most valuable asset.”In a first, the full version of national song Vande Mataram — recently accorded the same legal status as national anthem — was played ahead of and at the conclusion of Murmu’s address. It was followed by the national anthem. The President recalled the pivotal role played by the national song during India’s freedom struggle.In her address, the President highlighted that “the youth of our country are talented, committed, and skilled”.
“I have seen the innovative and practical solutions that young people are developing to address various challenges at the grassroots level. This reflects the dedication of our youth to society and the nation. A new phase of space exploration has been ushered in through the recent successful rocket launch by a young team with an average age of just 28 years,” the Murmu said. “Our younger generations strengthen my faith in India’s bright and prosperous future,” she added.The President also emphasised that physical and mental wellbeing of our youth forms the cornerstone of our country’s future. “Families and society also share the responsibility to motivate our youth to move ahead with enthusiasm,” she said.
Reflecting on various issued during her address, the President, while noting that warfare and instability prevailing in several parts of the world are affecting every country, said that even in such trying circumstances, “according to economic projections, the growth rate of the Indian economy is expected to be more than twice the average global growth rate.”Mentioning that May 7 marked the completion of one year since the launch of Operation Sindoor, Murmu said, “That historic operation against terrorism sent a clear and firm message to terrorists and those who support them, that no matter where they hide, they will have to face the consequences of their actions.”Speaking in the context of Pakistan, the President said that the suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty with "the country that harbours terrorism" is a decisive step in the interest of India, especially the farmers.

articles.title: Russia plans to remove border zones separating Russia from occupied Ukrainian territories
articles.body:
Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) plans to abolish special border zones along several boundaries with Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia, according to draft orders reviewed by the Russian outlet Agentstvo.
The proposed changes would remove restrictions that currently treat movement between Russia and occupied parts of Ukraine much like crossing an international border. The FSB says the move follows Russia’s claimed incorporation of the occupied Ukrainian territories into Russia.
FSB seeks to remove border zones
The draft orders, as reported by Ukrainska Pravda, would invalidate previous FSB orders establishing border zones along the boundaries between Russia’s Rostov and Voronezh oblasts and the occupied territories of Ukraine.
A similar change is planned for occupied Crimea, where the current border zone along the boundary with occupied Kherson Oblast would be abolished.
The existing rules effectively impose additional controls on people entering and leaving the occupied territories, making movement subject to procedures similar to those used at Russia’s state border.
In the draft orders, the FSB justifies the changes by referring to the alleged “admission into the Russian Federation” of the occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, and Kherson oblasts.
Russia illegally claimed to annex those territories, along with Zaporizhzhia Oblast, in September 2022. The move has been rejected by Ukraine and the international community, and Russia does not control all of the territory it claims to have annexed.
Border zone would remain around Crimea's islands
The FSB proposal would not completely eliminate the border zone in occupied Crimea.
A restricted zone would remain “within the boundaries of the Black Sea islands belonging to the Russian Federation,” according to the draft. The FSB’s regional directorate would determine where and when people could enter the zone and would install warning signs.
The proposed changes would remove the existing border zones along Russia’s boundaries with occupied Ukrainian territories, while retaining a border zone around certain Black Sea islands in occupied Crimea.
Russia treats occupied territory as part of its territory
The planned changes reflect Moscow’s effort to incorporate occupied Ukrainian territories into Russia’s administrative and legal system.
In September 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed so-called “accession treaties” claiming to incorporate Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts into Russia. Russia’s parliament subsequently approved the claims.
The treaties purported to define the boundaries of the annexed territories according to the borders they had on the day Russia claimed to admit them into the Russian Federation, despite Russia not controlling the entirety of those regions.
Russia previously used similar measures to formalize its control over occupied Crimea after illegally annexing the peninsula in 2014.

articles.title: Houthis say they attacked Saudi forces’ positions in Yemen
articles.body:
DOHA, August 14. /TASS/. The Houthis from the Yemeni rebel movement Ansar Allah say they have struck positions of the Saudi-led coalition near the city of Mokha.
"The Yemeni armed forces (the Houthis - TASS) attacked the Saudi enemy forces and weapons deployment sites, as well as military boats of its mercenaries near Mokha with the use of a great number of ballistic missiles," Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said, adding that tens of enemy soldiers were killed, and their boats and weapons were wiped out.
The Al Arabiya television channel reported earlier in the day that the rebels had delivered a massive strike on the Red Sea port of Mokha. The attack was followed by fire. According to its source, the attack was carried out with the use of missiles, drones, and boats. Government forces intercepted 15 out of 44 drones.

articles.title: Jason Arday found dead after resigning from Cambridge over plagiarism claims
articles.body:
Jason Arday, the academic who resigned last week as a professor at the University of Cambridge, has been found dead at his home in south London.
The Metropolitan police said officers were called to Arday’s address by the London ambulance service after 3pm on Friday.
A spokesperson for the Met said: “A 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next of kin have been informed and are being supported by officers.
“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious. The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s central south command unit. A file will be prepared for the coroner.”
The body was believed to be that of Arday. At this stage, police are understood not to believe anyone else was involved in the death.
London ambulance service was the first emergency service at the scene. The person discovered inside the home was found unresponsive.
Arday’s family said in a statement: “Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him.
“The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.
“We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son.
“We won’t comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long.”
The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said: “I’m devastated for the family and friends of Jason Arday. He faced an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse. I know many Londoners will be angry and upset this evening.
“Jason Arday was the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn’t have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake-up call for all of us.”
Arday was appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, and was the university’s youngest-ever black professor. But he resigned last week after accusations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements.
In a statement announcing his resignation, Arday said: “It is with profound sadness that I write to resign, with immediate effect, from my position at the University of Cambridge and Jesus College.
“When I accepted the extraordinary honour of becoming professor of sociology at Cambridge, it was, without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life.”
Arday said he had been driven to resign because the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.
Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said in a statement: “We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”
Durham University, where Arday worked between 2019 and 2021, said: “We are shocked and terribly sad to learn of the death of Jason Arday.
“He is remembered at Durham as a kind and warm person who actively sought to promote opportunities for PhD students. We want to express our deepest sympathy to his family who are in our thoughts.”
Arday’s rise to a prestigious professorial chair was remarkable. Arday said he had been nonverbal until the age of 11, requiring extensive speech and language therapy, as well as being illiterate until 18.
That life story contributed to him being made a torchbearer for the 2012 London Olympics flame.
After leaving school, Arday went on to further study before completing a doctorate in education at Liverpool John Moores University in 2015. That was followed by a string of academic posts culminating in a professorship at the University of Glasgow and a professorial chair at Cambridge.
Arday was initially accused of plagiarising another academic’s work for his PhD thesis. But he denied the accusations, and an investigation by Liverpool John Moores University earlier this year upheld its decision to award him a PhD.
But other elements of his life story were increasingly questioned, including claims of prodigious money-raising for charity and feats of long-distance running.
He was also challenged about whether he was nonverbal as a child.
However those claims meant little in the world of academia. After initially defending Arday as the victim of a smear campaign, as further questions arose about his academic career, the university began to temper its support.
On 5 August Cambridge announced it would hold an internal inquiry after it said it received “new information” about his academic qualifications and honorary appointments, as well as what it described as “a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct”. Jesus College, of which he was a member, said it would also hold an inquiry.
But while Cambridge said Arday would remain in post and continue to receive support, Arday immediately announced his resignation.
At the end of last week Glasgow University said it would also investigate Arday’s academic credentials.
The controversy has stirred considerable anger within Cambridge’s academic community, both between Arday’s supporters and those who said the university had erred in appointing him to such a prestigious position.
After resisting calls from senior staff for an independent inquiry, earlier this week Prentice backed down, saying she recognised the “anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case”.
She described it as an aberration that should not be used to cast aspersions on the abilities of its staff of colour.
Arday’s memoir, entitled Great and Unfortunate Things, was published this week in the US by an imprint of Simon & Schuster, with UK publication scheduled for later this month.
A spokesperson for the publisher said: “Simon & Schuster is deeply saddened by the news of Jason Arday’s tragic death, and we send our condolences to his family during this devastating time.”

articles.title: Ukraine’s International Register of Damage Opens 2 New Damage Claim Categories
articles.body:
The Register of Damage Caused by the Aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine (RD4U) has opened two new categories of claims, allowing the country to bill Russia for war-related costs, particularly territory demining and humanitarian spending.
The new categories, B4 and B5, cover “Humanitarian Public Expenditures to Support the Affected Population” and “Demining and Clearance of Unexploded Ordnance,” according to the presidential office on Thursday, Aug. 13.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We must document not only what Russia has destroyed, but also how much it costs Ukraine to overcome the consequences of its aggression,” Iryna Mudra, deputy head of the Presidential Office said.
Categories covering evacuation, housing and medical care
“Evacuating people, providing temporary housing, treatment and rehabilitation, and demining Ukrainian territories – these are enormous expenditures our state bears because of Russia’s war,” she added.
Central, regional and local authorities and institutions can now submit claims tied to these categories.
Rehabilitation programs and compensation for damaged or destroyed housing are also covered under the state’s eRecovery program, according to the presidential website.
“The opening of categories B4 and B5 makes it possible to include these expenditures in the overall body of claims against the aggressor state,” Mudra said.
Budanov: “Russia will pay for every hryvnia spent”
Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Presidential Office, said that Ukraine is consistently documenting the costs of Russian aggression while compiling the bill.
Ukraine Sanctions 13 Vessels, 39 Entities Over Stolen Grain Exports
“Russia must pay for every one of its crimes and compensate for every hryvnia spent on overcoming the consequences of aggression,” he said in a statement on Friday, Aug. 14.
According to United24Media, almost 23% of Ukraine’s territory remains contaminated by mines, with full clearance expected to take at least 10 years and cost at least $1,400 per a hectare (approximately 2,5 acres).
Register now covers 23 categories
Currently, the RD4U includes 23 categories of claims in total, covering issues such as involuntary internal displacement, displacement outside of Ukraine, death or disappearance of immediate family members, sexual violence, torture, forced labor, and the unlawful transfer of children and adults.
According to the presidential website, another 20 categories are planned for future rollout.
Based in The Hague, the register has served as an international compensation mechanism since 2025, uniting 44 states and the European Union and allowing Kyiv to assemble a case for compensation.
The register’s expansion builds on a wider international push to hold Russia financially accountable for the war.
In December 2025, European countries launched an International Claims Commission for Ukraine at a summit in The Hague, aiming to ensure compensation for the extensive damage caused by Russian war crimes.

articles.title: No clear early front-runner in the Steelers backup QB derby as Rudolph, Howard and Allar all shine
articles.body:
No clear early front-runner in the Steelers backup QB derby as Rudolph, Howard and Allar all shine
PITTSBURGH (AP) — If only Mike McCarthy graded on production, then Drew Allar would be in for smooth sailing when the Pittsburgh Steelers sit down to dissect their preseason-opening win over Green Bay.
The rookie quarterback, however, is already well-versed in how his head coach’s mind works. Yes, McCarthy was pleased after watching Allar throw for a pair of scores and run for another.
Yet the final product on a given play is only a piece of the puzzle. McCarthy is just as fixated on the process it takes to get there, which is why the 22-year-old Allar couldn’t help but grin when asked about how his fundamentals are coming along, perhaps knowing the feedback he was going to receive in the aftermath.
“I’ll probably get a minus grade on some of my footwork,” Allar said. “It was kind of a crazy reverse out under center exchange. Other than that, I felt pretty good.”
Just as importantly, he looked pretty good while leading three long scoring drives. The third-round pick was accurate while completing 10 of 13 passes. He frequently made the right decision on where to go with the ball and showcased his athleticism while diving over for a 3-yard touchdown run.
Not bad for his first game action since last fall, when his final year at Penn State ended prematurely with a left ankle injury.
“I feel like the first rushing touchdown I had was the first hit I’ve had in, I don’t know how long, but since mid-October,” Allar said. “I feel like that kind of got the physical part out of the way. I feel like going against our defense every day in practice really helped me mentally prepare for the game.”
Allar wasn’t the only student of McCarthy’s “quarterback school” who aced their first test. Will Howard, playing for the first time since leading Ohio State to the College Football Playoff championship in early 2025, had no issues running the two-minute offense. He connected with tight end Robert Tonyan frequently and didn’t panic during a fourth down call near midfield that required him to roll to his left, where he flipped the ball to wide receiver Ben Skowronek for a first down.
The result was great, sure. So was the jolt of confidence felt when Howard heard the play call.
“You’re, like, man, ‘Coach is throwing the ball on fourth-and-1, and he’s putting the ball in my hands,’” he said. “That feels great. I knew they were going to really trigger on that run. I think Aaron (Rodgers) had a little input on getting that play out there, and I appreciate him for that.”
Rodgers, watching from the sideline with a headset on, promised to crack some dad jokes to keep the mood light. The reality is he spent most of the night serving as an experienced resource for Allar, Howard, and Mason Rudolph, as no clear front-runner to win the quarterback derby to serve as Rodgers’ backup emerged.
McCarthy appears to be in no hurry to make any sort of decision. Rudolph got the start and settled in after some shaky play by the first-team offensive line early. He consistently found rookie wide receiver Germie Bernard and did his best to keep plays alive to give the young playmakers around him time to get open.
“Not to be a broken record, I’ve been talking about it pretty much since the spring ... I really like the room,” McCarthy said. “I think it’s a really good quarterback room, and I thought they played that way tonight.”
The guys behind center weren’t the only ones who stood out. Tonyan, who caught 11 touchdown passes from Rodgers when both were in Green Bay in 2020, finished with four receptions for 61 yards. Bernard caught four passes for 51 yards, and rookie Kaden Wetjen showed his elusiveness on a 74-yard catch-and-run and later pulled in a touchdown pass from Allar.
Sure, it was just an exhibition game, and both sides were more focused on getting through it healthy than on coming up with some elaborate game plan. The scheming will come later.
The preseason opener was mostly just a progress report. Plenty of work remains, but for a first-year coaching staff trying to lay a foundation and for three quarterbacks trying to prove their worth, it was a promising start.
“We have a lot to clean up, but the passing game ... I know the numbers were pretty good,” McCarthy said. “I liked the way our quarterbacks ran the offense, and that’s a big thing.”
