articles.title: Yemen's Houthis claim drone attack on Saudi Aramco site
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthi group said Friday it launched a drone attack on a Saudi Aramco site in Najran, southern Saudi Arabia.
The group’s Saba news agency, citing an unnamed military source, said Houthi forces "successfully targeted Aramco Najran with a drone.”
The source claimed the operation had "successfully achieved its objective” but did not provide further details on the alleged strike or any resulting damage.
According to the source, the attack was launched in response to what it described as a Saudi military aircraft violating Yemen’s sovereignty by entering the northeastern airspace of Saada province.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities or Saudi Aramco on the Houthi claim.
The claim came more than a week after another attack targeting Najran. On Aug. 6, the Saudi-led Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen said 11 civilians, including seven Saudi nationals, were injured in an attack on the city.
Tensions in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden have intensified since early July after the Houthis expanded their attacks to include vessels linked to Saudi Arabia. In response, Riyadh has stepped up airstrikes on Houthi positions in Yemen’s western Hodeidah province, saying the sites were being used to threaten maritime navigation.
Saudi Arabia recently announced the formation of a multinational maritime defense coalition to safeguard freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab Strait. The coalition includes the United States, Yemen, Kuwait, Oman, Jordan, Sudan, Morocco, the Maldives, Bangladesh and New Zealand.
Saudi Arabia backs Yemen’s internationally recognized government through the Coalition to Restore Legitimacy, while regional and Western countries accuse Iran of supporting the Houthis, an allegation Tehran denies.

articles.title: Korean people showed iron will by expelling Japanese in 1945 — Russian defense minister
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 14. /TASS/. The Korean working people demonstrated fortitude, courage and indomitable will by driving out the Japanese invaders 81 years ago, said Russian Defense Minister Andrey Belousov.
"I congratulate you on the 81st anniversary of the liberation of Korea from Japanese occupation. The Korean working people, having shown fortitude, courage and indomitable will, under the leadership of Comrade Kim Il Sung, drove the Japanese invaders from their native land. The victory in the struggle for Korean independence made a significant contribution to the end of World War II. Our common successes on the battlefields laid a solid foundation for a strategic partnership," he said at the reception on the occasion of liberation of Korea from Japanese occupation.

articles.title: CJI, Nalsar students have one query for BCI: ‘Who are you?’
articles.body:
The apex court bench sought BCI’s explanation on the process it adopted before passing the resolutions
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Friday castigated the Bar Council of India (BCI) for threatening to deny licence to practice to Hyderabad-based NALSAR university students who opposed CJI Surya Kant as their convocation chief guest, shielded them against coercive action, and offered the law graduates a start as legal aid counsel in SC.Taking cognisance of the controversy created late Thursday evening by BCI through an unprecedented letter which had to be hastily retracted, a three-judge bench led by CJI Surya Kant said, “This is absolutely uncalled for. BCI has nothing to do with it. The students might have written a letter to me. It is a dialogue between me and students. Who are they (BCI) to unnecessarily create an issue? This action is totally uncalled for.”Senior advocate K Parameshwar sought SC’s urgent intervention in quashing the illegal and arbitrary action of the BCI in seeking to coerce VC of NALSAR University, one of the top law schools, to conduct an investigation and identify students who had opposed CJI’s participation in the convocation as chief guest and issuing the now-withdrawn threat that those identified would be denied registration for licence to practice by all state bar councils.
SC asks bar council to explain process behind resolutions against studentsTrashing Bar Council of India’s threat to blackball protesting Nalsar students, CJI Surya Kant told senior advocate K Parameshwar to convey to the students, who are completing their graduation in law from Nalsar this year, “to get licences to practice at the earliest and begin their careers in Supreme Court”.The apex court bench sought BCI’s explanation on the process it adopted before passing the resolutions prior to issuing a letter to bar licences to protesters, and another shortly after, retracting it.Urging the students to join the SC bar at the earliest, the CJI said, “We will empanel them and give them legal aid cases. This will be our response to all those who intend to create impediments in their professional career.”
The students have a right to protest peacefully, and no one can stop them. They have a fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression
CJI Surya Kant
He added, “We should be largehearted. Even if someone makes a wrong statement at a young age, let it rest there. That does not mean they do not have a right to speak.”“During my student days, I was actively involved in many student activities. Indulging in activities or protests does not mean the students are wrong. The students have a right to protest peacefully, and no one can stop them. They have a fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. So long as they are lawfully and peacefully raising their voice over an issue, it must be heard, not opposed. Unnecessarily, Bar Council of India meddled in it.
Neither BCI nor any other body has any business to interfere with this,” said the CJI.Earlier, the advocate had raised the now-withdrawn threat that those identified would be denied registration for licence to practise by all state bar councils.The CJI-led bench, also comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, without even going through the petition by two formerstudents of Nalsar, restrained BCI and all state bar councils from taking any coercive or punitive action against the students and faculty.Accepting the notice on behalf of BCI, advocate Radhika Gautam said the objectionable circular had been withdrawn. In its order, the Supreme Court asked Bar Council of India to file its counter-affidavit in two weeks.

articles.title: The True Story Behind The Brink of War
articles.body:
The Reykjavik Summit—when U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet Union President Mikhail Gorbachev talked in person in 1986—is not known as an iconic bit of American history. But the face-to-face conversation between the leaders, held over Oct. 11 and 12 in the Icelandic capital, proved to be an important step toward the end of the Cold War.
The summit (or meeting, depending on who you ask) came after “an unexpected invitation from Gorbachev,” says Pete Souza, the former Presidential photographer for Reagan. At the time the Reagan administration refused to call it a summit.
“Before two leaders like that have a summit meeting, there's lots of prep work that goes into it,” recalls Souza. “But this was very last minute. The Reagan administration went to great effort leading up to Reykjavik, to not call it a summit. They’d say, ‘It’s just a meeting, and we’re not characterizing it as a summit.’”
The summit’s purpose was to discuss the arms controls between the two nations, in hopes of bringing an end to the long-lasting threat of nuclear war hanging over both countries, and the world as a whole. Over 30 hours, Reagan and Gorbachev fiercely debated in an effort to bring peace and the end of the Cold War. Now, a new film from writer-director Michael Russell Gunn, The Brink of War, gives this historical moment a worthy spotlight. The film stars Jeff Daniels as Reagan, Jared Harris as Gorbachev, and J.K. Simmons as Secretary of State George Shultz.
For Gunn, the idea for The Brink of War came from a meeting he had with the real George Shultz, to whom the film is dedicated. Shultz told him all about the Reykjavik Summit. “I had never heard of this summit before,” says Gunn, “but once I found out I couldn’t stop thinking of it.”
There was one particular detail from their conversation that made Gunn realize the Reykjavik Summit was a pivotal moment in world history. “Schultz told me he asked Gorbachev years later—and I included this in the movie—what changed to bring an end to the Cold War,” says Gunn. “Gorbachev responded with one word: ‘Reykjavik.’” From that moment, Gunn knew he had a movie.
Shultz detailed a memory to Gunn about how he’d stand outside the meeting room when Gorbachev and Reagan went in, and these two military officers would be standing there, each of them holding a nuclear football. “If things had gone badly, Reagan and Gorbachev could walk out, press the buttons, and end it all,” says Gunn. “The idea of these two military officers with all the power in the world literally in their hands, was an extraordinary memory to share, and an extraordinary thing for us to film.”
Gunn was struck by how generous Shultz was with his time, and he gave the filmmaker something that would allow for an exceptionally realistic approach: the declassified transcripts of the meeting. The transcripts allowed Gunn another first-hand account of the summit, as well as the opportunity to lift dialogue directly from the real conversations into the script. A number of conversations are nearly verbatim to what the transcripts show, though Gunn admits to finessing certain moments for cinematic purposes. “I tried to make it as close as I possibly could,” says Gunn.
The only points Gunn really departed from the transcripts were things they didn’t reveal. “I didn’t have transcripts of what was going on with the advisors, or what was happening with the first ladies,” he says. For that, he researched several books, pointing to Dutch: A Memoir of Ronald Reagan by Edmund Morris and Gorbachev by Willaim Taubman to help gather a fuller sense of the people surrounding the leaders.
Gunn calls himself a lifelong fan of Souza’s photography, and he pulled the original proofs from Souza’s summit photography at the National Security Archives. On a whim, he cold emailed Souza to see if he was available to join them on the film shoot to produce the film’s still photography. To Gunn’s delight, Souza accepted. The veteran photographer provided Gunn great assistance in faithfully recreating the summit, and the photos Souza took have a striking resemblance to the original photos from ‘86.
The summit itself was an incredibly tense showdown that occurred over a brief 30 hours. The discussions of arms controls with a view to bring an end to the Cold War came tantalizingly close to fruition. At one point during the summit, Reagan and Gorbachev were close to agreeing on a deal that would remove every single nuclear missile from the planet, a moment in the transcript that Gunn was particularly stunned by. “Gorbachev proposed eliminating all these different classes of weapons that the Americans weren’t expecting,” recalls Souza. “There was a moment when Reagan and his team thought ‘This can be historic.’ There was a real excitement about it.”
That excitement was all too brief. As a condition of eliminating these weapons, Gorbachev demanded an end to the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), nicknamed “Star Wars,” a missile defense system proposed to protect the United States from attack. “The whole SDI thing doomed that hope. Gorbachev wanted Reagan to not go any further with the SDI. That was the sticking point, and the mood changed to disappointment,” says Souza.
“My main takeaway of President Reagan behind the scenes was he had such an even keeled disposition,” says Souza. “It would take so much to get him angry or pissed off. One of the few times where he got pissed off was at the end of Reykjavik.”
The summit was considered a failure at the time, with no agreement struck at the end. However, it ultimately provided a breakthrough between Reagan and Gorbachev. The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty was signed on December 8, 1987, which was an enormous step forward to the end of the Cold War, which ultimately concluded with the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. If it wasn’t for the Reykjavik summit, it’s likely that treaty never would have been signed.
Gunn hopes the film can show audiences that if we work with people who disagree with us, we can forge a better future.
“For one, I want the audience to walk out of the cinema with hope. That as divided as we are, it's been worse,” Gunn says. “We were literally about to blow up the world with enemies, and we found a way out of that. The second thing I want people to walk out with is courage. It takes courage to engage with people you disagree with. We've decided that listening means we agree, and that's not true.”
Adds Gunn: “They didn't agree, but they listened to one another, and they found a way to make a better, safer world.”

articles.title: Trump asks US Supreme Court to allow $400m ballroom project to proceed
articles.body:
Trump asks US Supreme Court to allow $400m ballroom project to proceed
Appeals court previously ruled that Trump administration must seek authorisation from Congress to continue with project.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has asked the Supreme Court to allow construction of his $400m ballroom to move forward.
On Friday, the Department of Justice (DOJ) asked the country’s highest court for a stay on a lower court’s injunction that paused Trump’s building efforts while litigation proceeds.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3White House construction project to cost almost $1bn
- list 2 of 3US appeals court upholds injunction pausing Trump’s White House ballroom
- list 3 of 3Workers remove Trump’s name from Kennedy Center after court ruling
The DOJ argued that construction on the ballroom, a topic of persistent focus for Trump, is necessary for security reasons.
“This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security,” the DOJ wrote.
Trump’s appeal to the Supreme Court was expected. On August 7, a majority on the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ordered construction of the controversial ballroom halted unless the government gains congressional approval.
It set a deadline of August 21 for the construction to be stopped. But the injunction itself was stayed for 14 days, to allow the DOJ to appeal to the Supreme Court.
The appeals court’s ruling upheld a previous order issued by District Court Judge Richard Leon in April.
Like the April ruling, the appeals court’s ruling specifically related to above-ground construction that changes the visible characteristics of the White House.
“Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help,” the panel wrote in the decision.
Ongoing legal battle
The National Trust for Historic Preservation had filed a lawsuit in December, after the Trump administration tore down the East Wing of the White House and began work on a 90,000sq ft (8,360sq m) ballroom last year.
But Trump has repeatedly defied court rulings and insisted that work on the ballroom will continue.
Meanwhile, the price of the project to US taxpayers has ballooned, contradicting Trump’s earlier claims that it would be funded solely through outside donations.
Trump and his allies have argued that the new ballroom is needed to host secure events following a series of failed assassination attempts.
Critics have noted the ballroom plans come amid a wider push by the president to transform the US capital in his image, including through the construction of a massive triumphal arch.
After last week’s injunction, Trump decried the appeals court ruling on the ballroom construction.
“This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety,” Trump wrote in response.
He added that the ballroom would include bomb shelters, medical facilities, protection from drones and missiles and other security features that are “all tied together as one big, expensive, and very complex unit”.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the UAE are looking to Africa
articles.body:
analysis
Africa is proving strategically vital for Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the UAE
The European official smiled intently and asked a rather surprising question: "Have you been thinking about Djibouti?"
It was 2017 and there was a certain frisson of alarm going around the world about China and its ambitions for global power.
There was certainly alarm in Australia at a regional level: the South China Sea; China's massive 'Belt and Road' Investment spending initiative across the Pacific and the wider region.
And there was alarm across Europe too, where the Poles found themselves at the junction point for a Chinese-funded railway across Central Asia; where the Germans pointed out that Berlin is closer to Beijing than Sydney; and where a newly elected French president, Emmanuel Macron, was attempting to lift and expand French ambitions in foreign policy.
All reasons why all roads led to Djibouti. Or, more correctly, why all undersea cables led to the small kingdom on the north-east coast of the Horn of Africa.
Between 10 and 12 international cables land in Djibouti, making it a critical digital hub connecting Asia, Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
From about 2013 onwards, Chinese state-owned enterprises began making huge investments in local ports and infrastructure in the tiny Republic. By 2017 it had opened a significant military base there — following the French (the former colonial power) and then, post 9/11, the Americans.
It's not just the submarine cables that make Djibouti such a crucial location. It sits on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — the narrow stretch of water linking the Suez Canal, Red Sea and Indian Ocean — which daily threatens to come more into play as the deadlock over the Strait of Hormuz continues.
The Iran-backed Houthis, who live on the other side of the strait in Yemen, announced on July 20 that they were imposing a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, and there is anxiety that they might try to impose a total blockade on Bab el-Mandeb.
Which is why the rapidly changing geopolitics of the region have to be seen in a wider context than just the conflict between the US and Israel and Iran.
A new maritime alliance
Another party that had spoken recently of building a military facility in Djibouti is Saudi Arabia. Given it has been getting around the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz by shipping oil to its western coastline on the Red Sea, it has a particular current interest in that shipping route staying open.
But rather than proceed with the military base, Saudi has now pivoted to establishing a 13-country maritime alliance to safeguard security in the Red Sea which includes Pakistan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Comoros, Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Somalia and Yemen.
Turkiye this week confirmed it was also joining the alliance — a move which follows the announcement of the collective security obligations agreed to earlier this month in the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi, Pakistan and Turkiye.
While early analysis of the Mecca deal focused very much on what it meant for conflict with Iran, the collective actions of this group in keeping shipping moving in and out of the Red Sea will be the first real test of the arrangement.
But the testing of the new alliances in the Red Sea also shifts the focus of all these countries' interests — and those of others in the region — to Africa more broadly.
We don't hear much about Africa in Australia, unless its humanitarian crisis or a civil war.
But even in states which are seemingly failures, there has been the most extraordinary surge of investment and commitment by Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Turkiye. It is no longer just a battleground for influence between China and Russia.
A new 'Scramble for Africa'
There is a new Scramble for Africa of sorts going on: not like the period of invasion and colonisation of its earlier namesake in the lead up to World War I but a tussle for footprints in infrastructure which is at least in part driven by estimates that Africa could be home to around 15 per cent of the world's rare earths.
What makes this particularly fascinating is that African nations are getting better at extracting outcomes from all this investment — for example, in the form of higher revenues, or commitments to manufacturing.
Global Policy Institute analyst Bob Savic notes that "nations like the Democratic Republic of the Congo which controls more than 70 per cent of global cobalt production, have instituted 'super-profit' taxes, while Zambia has repeatedly raised its mining levies".
"Zimbabwe has rapidly followed suit, banning exports of raw lithium — a mineral critical for electric vehicle (EV) batteries — in a bid to end the export of wealth in unprocessed form," he says.
"Across the continent more broadly, governments have increasingly embraced resource-nationalist measures."
Saudi Arabia has pledged over $41 billion in investments in industrial zones, development finance and export credits with African nations.
While it is heavily focused on the Red Sea and Horn of Africa, it has also been buying arable land for food production across East and West Africa as well as contracts for copper, cobalt and lithium.
Turkiye, meanwhile has also dramatically expanded its footprint across Africa, both through a massively expanded diplomatic footprint, new air routes, an eight fold increase in trade, (particularly driven by defence exports) and in infrastructure investments. It has also intervened in the past six years in conflicts in Libya; in confronting piracy off the coast of Somalia and to secure mining infrastructure in Niger.
But both these countries' investments, and interests, are dwarfed by the effort put into Africa by the United Arab Emirates.
Loading
UAE's massive African investment
The Financial Times reported last week that by since 2017, the UAE has announced "investments worth upwards of $US168bn [$237bn]" in Africa.
"The UAE's projection of power spans the continent, ranging from ports to green energy projects to industrial-scale farms," the FT wrote.
The massive state-owned logistical company DP World now operates or is developing ports, inland terminals and free zones in 13 African countries.
The FT says the UAE "has leased millions of hectares of agricultural land to bolster food security".
"It has acquired mining rights from DR Congo to Guinea to secure critical minerals for the energy transition and for its burgeoning defence sector. "
However, it notes "that engagement also comes at a price".
"The UAE is creating a complex system of commercial, industrial and military entanglements that sometimes reinforce but also undermine the sovereignty of fragile states — most notably in war-torn Sudan," the paper reported.
While Saudi Arabia is enmeshed in the conflict with the Houthis in its southern neighbour Yemen, the UAE's presence in the horrific war in Sudan is particularly troublesome.
The Emiratis categorically deny all claims of providing military, financial, or operational support to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan — one of the two militia groups that have been fighting a civil war for control of Sudan.
But it is regularly accused of doing so, backed by analysis from intelligence agencies and human rights groups, and the RSF is also accused of committing documented war crimes on a vast scale.
The expansion of strategic ambitions by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the UAE into Africa, with the added factor of competition for rare earths, gives us another example of just how quickly global forces are shifting.
Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

articles.title: What dozens of empty chairs revealed about Australia's racism inquiry
articles.body:
analysis
Empty chairs spoke loudest, months into racism inquiry testimony
A family who are alive only because a bomb that landed at their feet didn't explode.
An Olympian forced out of the sport that changed her life after being belittled and bullied.
A mother questioning whether sending her children to school is doing them more harm than good.
An elder who is too scared to gather with community in public after another attempt on their lives.
This is just some of the harrowing testimony given at the inquiry into racism, hate and violence directed at First Nations people.
Day after day, witnesses relived some of the darkest moments of their lives. Some spoke of violence. Others of fear, humiliation, and grief. Many did so publicly, knowing the personal cost, like former Olympic boxer Marissa Williamson-Pohlman.
"Institutions celebrate Blak excellence when it is convenient, but abandon us when it matters most," Williamson-Pohlman told the inquiry.
"I wonder where my energy would go … if not so much time was spent with me fighting the very system that was created to 'support' me and make my dreams come true."
Her story was one of many detailing personal and systemic harm through racism, but many of those invited to listen, explain, or respond never appeared.
The inquiry drew heavy hitters, including a former federal minister, lawyers, professors, land councils, and policy advocates, but in many places the absences were just as notable as those who attended.
Dozens of politicians, government officials, and national powerbrokers were asked to attend each hearing.
Most didn't show up.
Inquiries are not just for fact-finding
"It's disappointing. I think the public expectation would be if you are a big organisation, if you are a government service, that you front up to inquiries like this and you are accountable," Senator Jana Stewart told me in between sessions in Melbourne.
"I think the least they could do is show up."
As the senator put it, attendance matters because parliamentary inquiries are not merely fact-finding exercises. They are one of the few opportunities for people with little institutional power to speak directly to those who hold it.
The hearings make for hard listening, with First Nations people speaking plainly about the racism, violence, and abuse they suffer on a daily basis.
Now that the hearings have wrapped up, the weight of expectation is palpable, but the reality of repeated disappointments looms large, as Arrernte woman and chief executive of the peak body for Aboriginal and Islander childcare Catherine Liddle put it.
"I'm here because the story of racism is one of harm. It's a story of hate, it's a story of unfathomable damage — and it's a story that we can change," Liddle told the inquiry.
"Racism is pervasive and it always will be until we front up to reality."
Hanging over the inquiry is a thorny question: how can this process make change, when so many change makers didn't turn up?
A tale of two inquiries
Running in parallel to the national parliamentary inquiry has been the royal commission into antisemitism, stood up in the wake of the Bondi terror attack.
Like the royal commission, the First Nations racism inquiry came on the heels of an alleged terror attack.
A fragment bomb, filled with ball bearings and screws, was lobbed into a crowd of Indigenous people on January 26th.
It is not hard to imagine what would have happened had it exploded as intended, something Noongar and Yamatji woman Renae Isaacs-Guthridge has thought about often.
"We should be dead because it landed right in front of us," Isaacs-Guthridge told the hearing in Perth.
The trauma of a near death experience, was compounded by what she described as antipathy from leaders, police, and the media.
"In the days and weeks that followed, as we found out it was a confirmed terrorist attack on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and our allies … there was a distinct pattern of people who said absolutely nothing," Isaacs-Guthridge said.
"I believe because we were an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander crowd, there is an underlying hate against us and so we're not taken as seriously."
Those sentiments have been echoed across the country as the inquiry travelled, with little acknowledgement outside the hearings themselves.
"We are First Peoples, where is the love and respect for us?" Aunty Muriel Bamblett asked in Melbourne.
Comparisons with the reach and scale of the antisemitism royal commission were unavoidable, despite warnings that measuring the pain of one community against another does little to address the root cause of racism.
"Why is antisemitism put on a pedestal compared to racial discrimination?" Biboolmirn Yorga woman Corina Abraham asked the inquiry in Perth.
"What about what First Nations people of our country go through? Why are we still down below?"
Failed referendum raises new problems
The silence that surrounds the Indigenous experience of racism and hatred from the broader community was noted by many, including inquiry chair Jana Stewart.
"We've certainly heard through lots of the evidence… the experiences of First Nations people aren't elevated or aren't talked about with the same level of importance as other parts of our community," Stewart told me.
"You can see that playing out probably in the experience of this inquiry as well."
But there are those who see the simultaneous inquiries as a built-in accountability system, like former federal minister Ken Wyatt.
"I suspect out of [the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion] will come a number of recommendations to do with changing attitudes and racist behaviour towards the Jewish community of Australia," he told me after he gave evidence in Perth.
"If we're prepared to do that, then we need to put just as much effort and energy into addressing racism that is faced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in this country. They are the First Peoples of the nation."
The existence of two separate inquiries into hatred directed at minority communities has prompted broader questions about the state of social cohesion in Australia, and what has led the nation to this point.
Some have pointed to the example set by politicians, with many years of culture wars and populist politics souring national discourse.
The referendum on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament was described by many as "lifting the lid" on racism directed at First Nations people, as Apunipima Cape York Health Council Chief Executive Deborah Malthouse told the inquiry in Cairns.
"The outcome of the Voice to Parliament appears to have given mainstream Australians permission to be overtly racist," Malthouse said.
"Those who would otherwise stay hidden now have the courage to share their racist views openly and widely under the belief that their actions are unlikely to be challenged by wider society."
Loading
Great expectations
A Wemba Wemba and Mutthi Mutthi woman, senator Stewart is acutely aware of where the inquiry she is leading may go.
"I do not want to see another report gather dust on a shelf," Stewart told me during one of the hearings in Darwin.
"I think that it absolutely should be acted on with a sense of urgency that people have asked us to in this process."
Many previous inquiries, including a national report on racist violence, the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody, and the Bringing Them Home report, all laid out plans to make Australia a better, safer, more reconciled place for First Nations people.
But after three decades, most of the recommendations put forward have been ignored, or in some cases explicitly acted against.
Outcomes are also on the minds of those who gave evidence, like Minang-Goreng Noongar elder Dr Jim Morrison.
"This committees recommendations risk becoming another report that acknowledges harm without addressing it," Morrison said.
"We urge the committee to ensure its recommendations translate into funded, practical action, direct investment in community-controlled truth-telling and healing infrastructures, not another report that sits alongside the many that have come before it."
Last week, in one of the final sessions, Yorta Yorta elder Monica Morgan gave detailed evidence on her landmark case that proved she had been racially vilified — the first Indigenous person to win such a case in Victoria.
She then had a question for the committee.
"What is going to happen as a result of your inquiry? Will there be change?" Morgan asked.
"We hope so, absolutely," Stewart replied.
"We hope that recommendations and evidence given to this process and through this committee is honoured with action."
The survivors who gave evidence have now gone home, but their stories sit in the parliamentary records, proof that we cannot say we didn't know.
The question is whether those empty chairs will remain a symbol of indifference, or whether those who left them vacant will act on the inquiry's final report.

articles.title: US likely to opt for sanctions instead of military action against Cuba — agency
articles.body:
NEW YORK, August 14. /TASS/. The US administration has apparently opted to move forward with tougher economic and sanction pressure on Cuba instead of using military force to change its government, Bloomberg said.
According to the agency, Washington’s plan is to cut off Cuba’s revenue sources and add to internal strife in the country to create conditions for talks with the Cuban leadership that have to this point been met with great resistance.
Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth said earlier that the Washington administration is considering all scenarios for further steps against Cuba, including military action.

articles.title: Houthis claim drone attack on Saudi Aramco facility in Najran
articles.body:
Sahin Demir and Mohammed Sameai
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
Yemen’s Houthis claimed Friday that they carried out a drone strike targeting a Saudi Aramco facility in the southern Saudi city of Najran.
The group’s Saba news agency, citing an unnamed military source, said Houthi forces “successfully targeted Aramco Najran with a drone.”
The source claimed the operation had “successfully achieved its objective” but did not provide further details on the alleged strike or any resulting damage.
According to the source, the attack was launched in response to what it described as a Saudi military aircraft violating Yemen’s sovereignty by entering the northeastern airspace of Saada province.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities or Saudi Aramco on the Houthi claim.
The claim came more than a week after another attack targeting Najran. On Aug. 6, the Saudi-led Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen said 11 civilians, including seven Saudi nationals, were injured in an attack on the city.
Tensions in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden have intensified since early July after the Houthis expanded their attacks to include vessels linked to Saudi Arabia. In response, Riyadh has stepped up airstrikes on Houthi positions in Yemen’s western Hodeidah province, saying the sites were being used to threaten maritime navigation.
Saudi Arabia recently announced the formation of a multinational maritime defense coalition to safeguard freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab Strait. The coalition includes the United States, Yemen, Kuwait, Oman, Jordan, Sudan, Morocco, the Maldives, Bangladesh and New Zealand.
Saudi Arabia backs Yemen’s internationally recognized government through the Coalition to Restore Legitimacy, while regional and Western countries accuse Iran of supporting the Houthis, an allegation Tehran denies.

articles.title: Paris court rejects appeal against expulsion of former RT France chief
articles.body:
Aysu Bicer
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
The Paris Administrative Court has rejected an application for interim relief against the expulsion of former RT France chief Xenia Fedorova, who is currently abroad.
The court said the legal challenge had failed to demonstrate the urgency required for an interim suspension. The judges did not rule on the legality of the expulsion order, according to French public broadcaster RFI.
Fedorova, 45, has been a regular commentator on media outlets owned by conservative French billionaire Vincent Bollore, including CNews and Europe 1.
The court previously said she had failed to show that being ordered to leave France would have "serious personal consequences."
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has previously accused Fedorova of relaying "Russian propaganda" intended to undermine "the fundamental interests of the nation."
Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot has described her as an "agent of influence."
Fedorova, a former journalist with Russia's state-run RT television network, headed its French operation until RT France was banned following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
French authorities have raised concerns about her influence as political parties prepare for next year's presidential election, with the far right seeking to take power.

articles.title: 3 Palestinians injured in Israeli settler attacks in southern West Bank
articles.body:
Hosni Nedim and Lina Altawell
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
Three Palestinians were injured Friday in Israeli settler attacks in Hebron province in the southern occupied West Bank, while the Israeli army arrested one of the wounded, sources said.
The Palestinian Red Crescent said in a statement that its teams in Hebron treated two people shot with live ammunition during a settler attack in the Al-Adissa area of Sa’ir town, north of the province.
One Palestinian was shot in the head and back, while another was shot in the back, without providing further details on their conditions, it said.
In the Al-Qarn area near Beit Ummar, north of Hebron, settlers ran over Palestinian youth Hamada Kawamleh with a motorcycle and assaulted him while he was on his land with his children, local sources told Anadolu.
Israeli soldiers arrested Kawamleh after the assault, the sources said.
Also in Sa’ir, settlers blocked the road leading to the Al-Adissa area amid attacks in the area.
Attacks, raids
In Nablus province in the northern West Bank, settlers redeployed around Palestinian homes in Qusra town as the siege of several families continued, preventing them from moving freely and accessing basic needs.
Since Sunday, settlers have besieged three families by closing roads leading to their homes and preventing them from entering or leaving, amid fears they may be forced out and their homes seized.
The developments come amid a heavy Israeli military deployment in Qusra in recent days, with hundreds of soldiers sent to the area under the pretext of dismantling a settlement outpost established by settlers near the town.
In Qalqilya province in the northern West Bank, Israeli forces raided Jayyus town, with no immediate reports of arrests or injuries.
Recent months have seen a sharp increase in settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank, drawing international and domestic Israeli criticism of the army over its failure to stop the attacks.
On Wednesday, the UN warned that settler violence in the West Bank had reached unprecedented levels, saying it had documented more than 1,430 attacks since the start of 2026 targeting around 260 Palestinian communities.
The attacks, along with demolitions and evictions, have displaced 3,800 Palestinians, about half of them children, according to the UN.

articles.title: Woman charged over vandalism of World War II Memorial in Washington, DC
articles.body:
Woman charged over vandalism of World War II Memorial in Washington, DC
The arrest comes weeks after Trump criticised Jeanine Pirro for dropping charges over damage to the Reflecting Pool.
A woman has been arrested and charged with two felonies over the vandalism of the World War II Memorial in Washington, DC, weeks after President Donald Trump publicly rebuked his own US attorney over a separate vandalism case at the nearby Reflecting Pool.
US Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said on Friday that Melissa Farris, 41, had been taken into custody and charged with depredation of US property and destruction of veterans’ memorials.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump administration to dismiss Reflecting Pool charges against David Hearn
- list 2 of 4US drops charges against Olympian for damage to Reflecting Pool
- list 3 of 4Trump denounces Justice Department decision to drop Reflecting Pool charges
- list 4 of 4Why did Trump attack Jeanine Pirro over US reflecting pool ‘vandalism’?
The charges carry penalties of up to 10 years in prison.
The arrest comes a day after the memorial was vandalised with soap and graffiti. Bubbles filled its fountain, while the words “Clean hands dirty $” were painted in red and green on its surface.
“Vandalising our World War II Memorial is a despicable attack on a sacred monument honouring the Americans who fought and died for our freedom,” Pirro wrote on the social media platform X, adding that her father and grandfather were among those who served in the US armed forces.
Pirro also posted photographs of a woman who appeared to be holding a spray-paint can near red graffiti on the memorial. She did not say where the images came from.
Farris is expected to be arraigned on Friday. The Public Defender’s Office said earlier in the day that she had not yet been assigned a lawyer.
Trump-Pirro clash over Reflecting Pool
The charges come weeks after Pirro dropped vandalism charges against several people accused of damaging the nearby Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. The decision angered Trump and exposed a rare public disagreement between the president and one of his political appointees.
Trump had claimed the pool was deliberately vandalised after renovations he had ordered and overseen. But its condition deteriorated within days of the work being completed, with blue sealant peeling and algae appearing in the water.
Pirro held a news conference in early July to charge former Olympic athlete David Hearn with the alleged Reflecting Pool vandalism. He was one of at least seven people who faced criminal charges over the pool’s peeling sealant.
While Pirro had initially said the government’s case was built on “tremendous evidence”, she issued a court motion less than a month later, on August 1, dropping the charges against Hearn.
Pirro asserted that the Interior Department had provided her office “less than fulsome information at the outset of the case”, and she blamed the damage on faulty repairs to the Reflecting Pool.
Trump responded by sharply criticising Pirro and doubling down on his allegations of vandalism, though he has yet to provide definitive proof.
“I was disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed with Jeanine Pirro. She folded like an umbrella,” he told reporters on 3 August.
Trump appeared to connect that dispute with the latest vandalism at the World War II Memorial on Friday.
“Our beautiful World War II Memorial was just hit by Spray Painting Vandals,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
“First the Reflecting Pool, now this,” he continued. “We are on their trail! Where do these animals come from???”
The Interior Department said US Park Police were investigating the vandalism and pledged to find whoever was responsible.
“The public should know we will find the person responsible for this disgusting act,” the department said.
Trump has made renovations to Washington, DC, a major facet of his second term, and he and his allies have initiated controversial renovations to the White House and the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among other landmarks.
This month also marks the anniversary of Trump’s deployment of the National Guard to Washington, DC, in an effort to crack down on crime.
Critics, however, have criticised Trump for a heavy-handed approach to law enforcement and have questioned the basis for some of the charges brought under his anti-crime campaign.

articles.title: Russia admits new petrol shortages amid ongoing long-range Ukrainian strikes
articles.body:
Ukraine has been targeting Russia's energy sites with drones and missiles for months, hoping to hit a vital source of revenue for the Russian army.
Russian authorities acknowledged on Friday that some regions face new petrol shortages, as Ukraine steps up attacks on the country's oil refineries.
Ukraine has been targeting Russia's energy sites with drones and missiles for months, hoping to hit a vital source of revenue for the Russian army.
Russia has shut down one major refinery at Orsk, around 1,300 kilometres from the front line, for six months after it was attacked this week.
"The situation remains tense in several regions of the country regarding fuel supplies to service stations," the government said in a social media post.
Oil companies are "taking the necessary measures to increase deliveries to the most vulnerable regions," according to the statement.
It said a government meeting had been held on the shortages and the Deputy Prime Minister responsible for energy, Alexander Novak, has ordered that fuel prices be monitored.
Companies and car drivers have suffered repeat shortages in recent months because of the conflict.
Nearly every Russian region has at some point had to limit fuel sales or impose other kinds of rationing, such as banning the filling of jerry cans.
The Krasnodar region on the Black Sea, known for its tourist beaches, has been one of the worst hit.
"The situation regarding petrol supplies at service stations has become complicated," regional governor Venyamin Kondratyev said.
Oil companies "have again started imposing restrictions on the amount of fuel supplied and reduced service station opening hours," he added.
"This is causing concern among the region's residents and visitors," the governor added, stating that he had asked the authorities to send more fuel.
The governor of the Orenburg region, where the Orsk refinery is located, said on Thursday it had been shut down and repairs would take months.
Rare admission
Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged for the first time in June that his country was facing a “certain deficit” of fuel.
Speaking at a meeting with officials that focused on the fuel situation, Putin admitted that the country was “going through a difficult period,” but insisted that Moscow would “honour all its social obligations.”
Shortly after, he told state TV that the country's arms industries will quickly ramp up production of air defence systems to fend off Ukrainian attacks.
Claiming the issues that arise are not critical, Putin also said that Russia will import more fuel and speed up repair works at oil facilities to end the “temporary deficit.”
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has referred to strikes on Russian energy sites deep inside Russia as “long-range sanctions.”

articles.title: Ohio city fires police officer who shot and killed 15-year-old, settles lawsuit with family
articles.body:
Ohio city fires police officer who shot and killed 15-year-old, settles lawsuit with family
AKRON, Ohio (AP) — Officials in Akron, Ohio, have fired a police officer who shot and killed 15-year-old boy while also announcing Friday that the city has agreed to pay $4.75 million to the teen’s family.
The settlement, which still needs a judge’s approval, came after the family filed a lawsuit against the city.
Police have said that Jazmir Tucker was carrying a loaded weapon when he was shot in November 2024. They said two officers heard gunshots, later spotted Tucker and ran after him before one fired multiple times.
Akron Mayor Shammas Malik said Officer Davon Fields was fired for multiple policy violations, including failing to properly provide medical aid and violating the department’s policy for body-worn cameras. The mayor also cited other issues related to a separate criminal allegation involving Fields.
“The loss of life and the circumstances in this case were absolutely tragic, with enormous human and financial costs,” Malik said in a statement. “We have a responsibility to make policy changes that reduce the likelihood of cases like this happening in the future.”
The head of Akron’s police union called the firing unjust and said the officer was being used as a “political scapegoat.” The union plans to fight the firing, said Brian Lucey, president of the local Fraternal Order of Police.
A grand jury decided against indicting the officer nearly a year ago.
Weeks after the shooting, Akron’s mayor said the bodycam video of the shooting raised questions, including why officers didn’t immediately turn on their cameras and why it took so long to provide first aid.
In the video, the shooting officer’s arms and long gun block his camera’s view, obscuring Tucker in the moments before he was shot. Another officer’s camera recorded police unzipping the jacket pocket of the wounded teenager and pulling out a handgun.

articles.title: Pull up to the window, please, for a glimpse of an American icon: The drive-thru
articles.body:
Pull up to the window, please, for a glimpse of an American icon: The drive-thru
WASHINGTON (AP) — Full disclosure: this should really be two tales. How better to pay tribute to the natural and perhaps inevitable combination of two distinctly American icons: fast food and cars?
Those two massive sociological forces had already joined up, Voltron-style, early in the 20th century with the development of the drive-in restaurant – that classic scene evocative of “Happy Days” where customers sat in their cars while servers (ideally on skates) brought out food that was consumed on site from window trays.
But the real innovation dates to the late 1940s and is the brainchild of either (depending on which source you trust) an In-N-Out Burger in California in 1948 or Red’s Giant Hamburg in Springfield, Missouri in 1947. (In comparison, the first reported drive-thru in Europe didn’t open until 1985 in Dublin.)
By the mid 1960s, this had mushroomed into a robust American market, spawning imitators and innovators. Jack in the Box pioneered the drive-thru exclusive restaurant with no indoor seats and no parking — and a talking mechanical clown to take your order. In Western states, residents of a certain age will recall the Wienershnitzel chain with its distinctive A-frame structures specially built with a tunnel down the middle for cars.
The innovation sparked unexpected knock-on developments. Restaurant menus shifted heavily toward sandwiches, fries, chicken strips and other portables that could be consumed on the go. The cars themselves adjusted over the years to accommodate larger and larger drink holders. What sociological (and nutritional) impact this has all had on the actual consumers would be the subject of a much longer essay.
The innovation hasn’t stopped. Modern drive-thrus have evolved into tightly coordinated multi-lane affairs. At Chick-fil-As around the country, actual humans with electronic tablets now stand – breathing in exhaust fumes all day – to ensure a seamless ordering process with no mechanical speaker garbles.
The drive-thru, with its distinctly American creative spelling, has become woven into the fabric of the culture. It has been enshrined in the Smithsonian Museum of American History and has played a memorable role in recent and successful Presidential campaigns.
As one historian put it, somewhat pointedly: “The drive-in was less a pure novelty than an expression of great American passions that go hand in hand: speed, efficiency and, sometimes, laziness.”
Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. For more American objects, click here. For more stories on the anniversary, click here.

articles.title: House Democrats PAC adds $6 million to Cleveland spending after Ohio’s Miller opts to stay in race
articles.body:
House Democrats PAC adds $6 million to Cleveland spending after Ohio’s Miller opts to stay in race
A super PAC affiliated with U.S. House Democrats plans to increase its campaign advertising reservations in Cleveland, Ohio, by roughly $6 million on Friday, in response to Republican Rep. Max Miller’s decision to proceed with his reelection campaign despite allegations of abuse by his ex-wife Emily Moreno.
House Majority PAC’s move is expected to raise the group’s campaign advertising in the Cleveland area to roughly $7 million, the group announced in an email obtained by The Associated Press.
Miller’s decision to press on even after calls from within his own party to step aside also prompted the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, House Democrats’ main campaign arm, this week to move Democratic challenger Brian Poindexter on to the group’s list of priority candidates.
The House Ethics Committee said last week it had opened an investigation into domestic abuse allegations against Miller. The embattled Ohio congressman also last week spoke with Trump, who did not suggest he exit the race but suggested it would be difficult.
President Donald Trump won Ohio’s 7th District in 2024 by 11 percentage points, though Democrats see the swath of suburban Cleveland and rural northeast Ohio as within reach in light of the renewed accusations from Moreno, the daughter of Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno.
Miller, whose deadline to drop from the race passed Monday, has denied the abuse claims and said he would inject $1 million of his own into his campaign.
Officials with the National Republican Congressional Committee, the GOP’s House campaign arm, said Friday they would support Miller’s reelection campaign.

articles.title: Trump says record-setting Navy deployment to support Iran operations ‘not nearly long enough’
articles.body:
Trump says USS Lincoln’s record time at sea during Iran operations ‘not nearly long enough’
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday downplayed the toll on American sailors enduring nearly nine months at sea on the USS Abraham Lincoln as concerns escalated about mental health and supply issues aboard the aircraft carrier supporting U.S. operations against Iran.
In a brief exchange with reporters before flying to New York for an event to highlight falling violent crime rates across the U.S., Trump refuted that family members have raised concerns about the deployment’s length and even said that the deployment — which includes a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days — is “not nearly long enough.”
“That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it’s being replaced with another very similar ship,” Trump said when asked about the lengthy deployment. The acting navy secretary, Hung Cao, said the Lincoln “will return home soon” in a social media post on Friday.
Trump strode into office for a second term vowing to avoid lengthy and expensive military entanglements. And after launching the Iran war, alongside Israel, Trump and his advisers said the conflict would last a matter of weeks. The war is now more than five months old.
But on Friday, during his crime address in Garden City, New York, he acknowledged that he’s used the U.S. military “a little bit more than I wanted to,” while asserting anew that the U.S. operation against Iran is going well. He even said, seemingly in jest, that “pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.”
“I’ll never apologize,” Trump added about the war and its impact on oil prices. “I did the right thing.”
Democrats demand Pentagon briefing on USS Lincoln
Extended deployments of carriers during the Iran conflict have raised concerns about the impact on service members who are away from home for long periods as well as the increasing strain on the ships and their equipment.
Several Democratic lawmakers, including Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ruben Gallego of Arizona, are pressing for accountability from the Pentagon over conditions aboard the Lincoln, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday said were “completely misrepresented.”
Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., who served three tours in Iraq and Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division and 75th Ranger Regiment before being elected, took to social media to criticize Trump’s comments, saying on X that “President Trump does not care about our servicemembers or their families.”
Top Democrats on the House Oversight Committee have requested a classified briefing on the ship’s food inventory, sanitation issues and healthcare availability, as well as an assessment of how much longer it would be deployed before relief arrives.
Republicans have been less outspoken about the situation on the Lincoln. The GOP chairmen of the House and Senate armed services committees did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
While hostilities between the U.S. and Iran have calmed in recent weeks, the Navy has reimposed a blockade on Iranian ports in the crucial Strait of Hormuz, and the Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war. Hegseth said the U.S. military can maintain the blockage of Iranian ports “indefinitely.”
Another aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, left port in Da Nang, Vietnam, last week, and is expected to replace the USS Lincoln, one of two aircraft carriers currently deployed in the Middle East.
After reports emerged that sailors on the Lincoln are struggling with mental health concerns, the Navy said it has “not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship,” though officials have declined to provide data, citing operational security and patient privacy concerns.
A Navy official said a sailor aboard the Lincoln went overboard in early August but the person was quickly recovered, treated by the ship’s medical department and transferred off ship for follow-on care. The official would not say whether it was being considered a suicide attempt.
U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, has also pushed back on reports about poor conditions.
___
AP writers Collin Binkley in Garden City, New York, and Michelle L. Price and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report.
——
This story has been corrected to show that the USS Abraham Lincoln has spent more than 240 days of uninterrupted time at sea and its overall deployment has exceeded 260 days.

articles.title: With US-Iran talks stalled, diplomatic efforts expand to unlikely European players
articles.body:
With US-Iran talks stalled, diplomatic efforts expand to unlikely European players
WASHINGTON (AP) — Faced with an increasingly bellicose Iran as talks to end the war have stalled, the Trump administration appears to be reaching out to a broader swath of countries that might be able to help pressure Tehran or ease its hardline position where traditional mediators have not succeeded so far.
While discussions between Iran and Oman, as well as between Iran and Pakistan, Turkey and Qatar, persist at an uneven and unpredictable pace, the U.S. administration quietly has expanded its outreach to include perhaps unlikely interlocutors in Europe.
Just this week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio met in person in Washington with the foreign minister of Austria on Tuesday and held a call with the foreign minister of Greece on Wednesday.
Those interactions were not notable beyond the normal course of relations between the U.S. and two close European allies. The official State Department readouts of the discussions were bland and vague and did not mention Iran by name as a topic of conversation.
But it then emerged that both foreign ministers — almost immediately after their talks with Rubio — spoke Thursday with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The apparent new tack to break the negotiation logjam comes as the U.S. and Iran are both pushing for control of the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial oil shipping corridor. President Donald Trump faces little wiggle room in his next steps as the economic fallout from the war and dwindling stockpiles of key weapons pose political problems for Republicans ahead of November’s midterm congressional elections.
A desperate push is on to break the diplomatic logjam between the US and Iran
The entry by Austria and Greece is likely less of a formal mediation attempt, analysts say, and more reflective of a desperate push to halt the conflict because of the impact it has on an increasing number of countries, beyond those in the Middle East.
“Everyone is just urging both sides to stop this reckless game of chicken,” said Ali Vaez, Iran project director at the International Crisis Group.
It also shows how much Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has forced countries, which otherwise were neutral bystanders to the larger conflict, to exercise any diplomatic sway they may have on their Iranian and American counterparts to kick-start a lasting resolution.
Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, warned that any efforts by Greece, Austria or any other non-mediating country could prove to be futile.
“While the calls to both sides may entail encouraging both Iran and the U.S. back to the negotiating table, such efforts fall short of mediation, which is a very complex endeavor and requires trust to be built by the mediator with both sides,” Yacoubian said.
She added that it’s not something that any country can “just jump into.”
Rubio discussed Iran with his Austrian and Greek counterparts
The State Department said Friday that it could not comment on the timing of calls by other countries’ foreign ministers and maintained that Rubio had made no requests of either to get in touch with Iran or pass messages to Araghchi.
One European diplomat, who was briefed on the matter and spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive diplomatic conversations, said the timing of the calls was not an accident.
The State Department did allow, however, that Iran had been a topic of conversation in Rubio’s discussions, which occurred as Trump is facing serious political headwinds over a war for which he has offered shifting objectives.
No longer purely about making Iran incapable of producing a nuclear weapon, the immediate goal has become reopening the Strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil usually passes through and which was open before the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.
“That’s goal number one: keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country,” Vice President JD Vance said in an interview Thursday on Fox News Channel. But he did not say anything about the strait being open and toll-free for transiting ships, as he had in the past.
The second goal, Vance said, is to ensure that Iran will never get a nuclear weapon.
The two European countries have key connections to the war’s fallout
Austria and Greece may not be obvious choices to assist on the Iran portfolio, but Vienna is home to the International Atomic Energy Agency, which will play a key role in any resolution to the Iran’s nuclear program, and hosted the final negotiations that resulted in the 2015 Iran nuclear deal. Greece is a major maritime nation in the Mediterranean and has significant shipping interests in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
In statements from the Austrian, Greek and Iranian foreign ministries, it was clear that Iran had been a top topic in all of the conversations this week.
The Greek foreign ministry said Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis had been briefed by Araghchi on “regional developments, and in particular on the ongoing talks regarding the Strait of Hormuz.” It said Gerapetritis “underlined the importance of freedom of navigation and maritime security.”
The Austrian foreign ministry offered Austria’s services as a venue for further potential talks with Iran and said Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger had stressed to Araghchi “the urgency of restoring stability in the region through serious diplomatic efforts.”
“There can be no military solution,” it said. “A diplomatic solution remains possible. Our priority is to safeguard freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.”
Iran’s foreign ministry, expectedly, took a different tack in explaining the calls.
It said Friday that in Araghchi’s calls with his European counterparts they discussed “mechanisms for the future management of the Strait of Hormuz,” which he said had been disrupted by the “unlawful aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran.”
In both calls, he accused the U.S. of violating the interim deal signed by both sides in June to end the immediate hostilities and begin broader talks to end the war.
___
Amiri reported from New York. Associated Press writers Derek Gatopolous in Athens and Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland, contributed to this report.

articles.title: Latvia Tested Drone Interceptors Against Shahed-Like UAVs
articles.body:
During the NATO Baltic Trust 26 exercises at the “Selija” training ground in Latvia, counter-drone systems, including interceptor drones, were tested.
A video showing the interception of a target drone was published by the Latvian Ministry of Defense.
Approximately 650 personnel from Latvia, NATO member states, and partner nations, including Ukraine, Australia, and Japan, participated in the exercises.
In addition, representatives of the technology industry from several European Union countries joined the maneuvers. Armed forces specialists tested their developments and projects under real-world conditions.
“Drone technology and countermeasures are evolving very rapidly. Just as important as the technology itself is the ability of different systems to work together effectively,” the ministry stated.
During the exercises, radars, sensors, cameras, electronic warfare systems, and other solutions designed to detect, track, and neutralize drones were tested.
In addition, the exercises tested a format unique to NATO that involves the private sector not only as an equipment supplier but also as a direct provider of necessary services and capabilities.
Under this concept, once a target is detected, military personnel can delegate the task of engaging it to industry representatives. To do so, companies will use their own equipment and unmanned systems, as well as deploy their own pilots and engineers.
In late July, Ukraine and Latvia signed a series of memoranda of understanding that expand cooperation in the development of unmanned systems.
The goal of this cooperation is to attract investment in UAV production, transfer Ukrainian technologies, and establish modern dual-use infrastructure in Latvia for testing these systems.
The memorandums formalized cooperation in this area between the Ministry of Defense, the Ministry of Economy, the Latvian Investment and Development Agency, Baltic Forces Ltd., Ukrainian partners, as well as Riga Technical University and the Latvian Association of Military Technologies, Drones, and Robotics.
And in late June, it was reported that Latvia, together with Ukraine, plans to establish a joint drone production facility in the border region of Latgale.

articles.title: Russia increases electricity exports to Kazakhstan by 20.3% in 1H
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 14. /TASS/. Inter RAO (Russia’s sole electricity export-import operator) increased electricity supplies to Kazakhstan by 20.3% to 1.68 bln kWh in January-June, which accounts for 53% of the group’s total exports, according to company materials.
Supplies to Mongolia in the first half of the year fell by 6% to 450 mln kWh. The country accounts for 14% of operations. Exports to other countries totaled 1.07 bln kWh, which is 11% lower than in the same period last year.
Kazakhstan accounted for 94% of Russia’s electricity imports in the reporting period. Supplies decreased by 4.7% to 1.13 bln kWh.
Overall, Inter RAO increased exports by 4% to 3.2 bln kWh in the first half of the year and reduced electricity imports by 5.3% to 1.2 bln kWh.

articles.title: Ukrainian ore exports fall 27% in seven months — publication
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 14. /TASS/. Ukraine’s mining industry experienced a 27.3% year-on-year contraction in iron ore exports to 13.9 mln tons in January-July, according to calculations based on data from the State Customs Service of Ukraine conducted by the Ukrainian industry publication GMK Center.
Ore export revenue fell to $1.08 bln in seven months (-14.5%), and to $148 mln in July (-22% compared to July 2025).
China is traditionally the largest consumer of Ukrainian iron ore, with shipments there totaling 6.42 mln tons (down 36% year-on-year) in the reporting period. Exports to Slovakia amounted to 2.44 mln tons (down 12% year-on-year), while shipments to Poland totaled 1.74 mln tons (down 36% year-on-year).

articles.title: IRGC shoots down US MQ-9 drone over Hormozgan
articles.body:
The Islamic Revolution Guards Corps' Public Relations Department said in a brief statement on Friday that the IRGC's new advanced defense system intercepted and destroyed an MQ-9 Reaper drone in the skies of Hormozgan, under the control of the country's integrated air defense network.
This came a day after the Washington Post reported that the United States has lost 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones since launching its war of aggression against Iran, with Iranian air defenses bringing down roughly a quarter of the US fleet and exposing the vulnerability of one of Washington’s key surveillance and strike platforms.
When the war began on February 28, the US had approximately 185 Reapers, including 165 operated by the Air Force and 20 by the Marine Corps.
Iranian air defenses accounted for a substantial share of the losses, highlighting the difficulty faced by the US military in protecting its costly drones while operating over Iranian territory.

articles.title: In response to Pak PM Sharif, J&K CM Omar says IWT sucked ‘our blood’, calls for its cancellation
articles.body:
India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack
SRINAGAR: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif warned at an event in Islamabad on Friday that Pakistan would take any step to protect its water rights under the Indus Waters Treaty, saying “every single drop” of Pakistan’s water is a “red line” and “India must come to the right path” or it would “be given a direct response”. His comments drew a reaction from Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah who said the treaty has been kept in abeyance and should remain so.“Yes, our blood. We have been saying this only, that our blood has been sucked. Thankfully Shehbaz Sharif came to his senses. This (IWT) has sucked the blood out of us. These are our rivers. We have the first right on them,” Omar told reporters here. “For the sake of saying, Pakistanis say that they are great sympathisers of Kashmiris. But when it comes to water, their sympathy disappears. Where was his sympathy when our permission to use our rivers was taken away from us,” the CM said.“Out of the six rivers, three which belonged to Punjab were kept by India and our three rivers were handed over to Pakistan. From then till today we are suffering the consequences of this Indus Waters Treaty,” Omar said, adding that under the treaty J&K could neither extract drinking water from the Chenab nor use the Jhelum for irrigation or building a barrage at Tulbul. “Our blood has been sucked and now the IWT has been cancelled.
This should remain cancelled so that we can use this water properly,” Omar added.The IWT was signed between India and Pakistan in 1960. Under the treaty, India received full rights to use the waters of the three eastern rivers, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, while Pakistan received rights over the three western rivers, Indus, Chenab and Jhelum.
India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack. In May last year, after the treaty was placed in abeyance, Omar called for restarting the Tulbul Navigation Project on Wular Lake in north Kashmir. The project is located on Wular Lake in the Sopore area of Baramulla district. Pakistan has opposed construction of a 439-foot-long, 40-foot-wide barrage, also known as the Wular barrage or Tulbul Navigation Project, with a navigation lock on the lake.The Union govt began work on the project in 1984 to regulate water levels and facilitate navigation. However, work was halted a year later after Pakistan objected. Pakistan raised the issue with the Indus Waters Commission in 1986 and work was stopped in 1987.The governing National Conference in J&K has opposed the IWT all along, calling it detrimental to the interests of the people of Jammu and Kashmir.

articles.title: Farewell ceremony for Colonel Yevhen Konovalets held in Kyiv
articles.body:
Farewell ceremony for Colonel Yevhen Konovalets held in Kyiv
According to an Ukrinform correspondent, the ceremony, held on the first night after Konovalets' ashes were returned to Ukraine, was attended by soldiers and Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, commander of the Third Army Corps.
According to the Third Army Corps, Konovalets' urn was brought to the cathedral in an original Austin armored vehicle dating back to the Ukrainian Revolution, which was restored by servicemen of the corps' repair and restoration battalion.
A torch-lit honor guard of soldiers from the Third Army Corps and the Yevhen Konovalets Military School welcomed Konovalets outside the cathedral.
An artillery carriage was attached to the Austin armored vehicle, which, in Ukrainian and European military traditions, is a sign of the highest honor for a serviceman. A three-inch gun was also attached to the armored vehicle. It is an original 1917 artillery piece that was in service with the Army of the Ukrainian People's Republic, specifically with the Sich Riflemen Division commanded by Colonel Konovalets.
During the ceremony, servicemen paid tribute to Colonel Konovalets. Beams of light were projected into the sky.
On August 13, 2026, the ashes of Colonel Yevhen Konovalets were brought to Ukraine, where they were received with full state and military honors.
A monument from Konovalets' grave was also brought from Rotterdam to the Lviv region. It will be preserved at the colonel's museum-estate in Zashkiv.
In July, the Cabinet of Ministers approved a decision to rebury in Ukraine the remains of Colonel Yevhen Konovalets, an officer of the Army of the Ukrainian People's Republic and the first head of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists.
On August 11, Konovalets' remains were exhumed at Crooswijk General Cemetery in Rotterdam.
On May 25, a ceremony to rebury the remains of OUN leader Andriy Melnyk and his wife, Sofia, was held at the National Military Memorial Cemetery, attended by President Volodymyr Zelensky.
On July 1, the Verkhovna Rada passed a law on the Ukrainian National Pantheon, providing for the creation of a special memorial complex to honor people who made outstanding contributions to the establishment and development of the Ukrainian state, the defense of its independence, and the development of culture, science, art, sports, the Ukrainian language and civil society. The Pantheon is planned to be located in Kyiv.
Photo: Third Army Corps
