articles.body:
Traffic restrictions will be imposed around Tamsui Fisherman’s Wharf and the Danjiang Bridge during fireworks displays on the next three Sundays, the New Taipei Transportation Department said yesterday.
The Tamsui Fisherman’s Wharf Midsummer Festival will stage fireworks shows at 8 pm tomorrow as well as on Aug. 23 and 30 at the wharf’s main waterfront square.

articles.title: KMT, TPP approve full drone budget
articles.body:
In a dramatic reversal, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) yesterday approved the government’s NT$44.2 billion (US$1.38 billion) budget for the development and procurement of uncrewed vehicles until 2030.
The KMT caucus had earlier proposed cutting the entire budget and later said it was considering a freeze.
After negotiations, the KMT and TPP caucuses submitted a joint resolution instead.
Photo courtesy of the Penghu Defense Command via CNA
To bolster Taiwan’s drone industry and supply chain resilience, and establish the nation as an Asia-Pacific hub for democratic supply chains, the Executive Yuan’s six-year, NT$44.2 billion Unmanned Vehicle Industry Development Program would be approved, the opposition caucuses said in a resolution issued shortly before the budget vote.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs would coordinate efforts across government agencies to establish and implement the program, they added.
Building a complete industry supply chain requires establishing a framework covering research and development, production, procurement, talent development and a comprehensive legal system, the opposition said, adding that annual funding should not fluctuate significantly.
They called on the Cabinet to instruct the ministry to distribute the budget evenly over six years, with annual allocations not exceeding the average amount.
All related procurement must also comply with the Government Procurement Act (政府採購法) and other regulations, the caucuses added.
Except for uncrewed systems procured for military purposes, the government’s drone purchases may be conducted under by the Regulation for the Implementation of Inter-entity Supply Contracts (共同供應契約實施辦法), the resolution said.
That would avoid duplicate budgets and improper subcontracting, as well as additional drone purchases without Executive Yuan approval, it said.
Democratic Progressive Party spokesman Lee Kun-cheng (李坤城) said the budget that the KMT caucus claimed to have approved was already intended by the Executive Yuan for military use and to support industrial upgrades, and should not have been cut in the first place.
He accused the KMT and the TPP of staging a political farce by proposing cuts and then hastily withdrawing them, saying they were misleading the public.
Lee called on the opposition to abandon political maneuvering and their “scripted performance,” and instead return to professional oversight.
He also urged them not to hold up urgently needed military equipment procurement during negotiations.
Taiwan’s critical defense industry and national security should not become casualties of partisan interests, Lee said.

articles.title: SMIC lifts prices due to AI demand
articles.body:
China’s top foundry, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (SMIC, 中芯), yesterday said that artificial intelligence (AI)-related demand would continue to underpin orders for its production and that it had raised prices for its most sought-after capacity.
SMIC co-chief executive officer Zhao Haijun (趙海軍) said on an earnings call that the firm raised prices following negotiations with customers in the first quarter and that it would charge more for wafers processed in the third quarter.
“We believe we’ve reached top-tier industry standards in these areas,” Zhao said. “Since there’s still a big gap between industry-leading wafer prices and SMIC’s current prices, we need to negotiate with customers for fairer pricing.”
Photo: Reuters
Silicon wafers serve as the base material onto which chip patterns are printed by SMIC through the fabrication process.
SMIC, the only Chinese foundry able to mass-produce logic chips such as CPUs and GPUs on a 7-nanometer process, posted revenue above US$3 billion for the first time in the second quarter, driven by strong AI demand.
Profit attributable to shareholders tripled to US$479.2 million, with both figures beating average analyst estimates compiled by LSEG.
The company shipped 2.9 million 8-inch-equivalent wafers in the second quarter, up 14 percent from the previous quarter, while the average selling price of wafers rose 5.7 percent, as AI demand drives tightness in semiconductor supply chains around the world.
Zhao said that the rise in shipments was driven mainly by surging AI-fueled demand for chips other than CPUs and GPUs, mostly from China-based customers, as well as earlier-than-expected orders.
SMIC chief financial officer Wu Junfeng (吳俊峰) said the jump in net profit was also boosted by a one-time gain from a subsidiary in the second quarter.
AI would continue to drive robust chip demand for foundry services in the second half of the year, Zhao said, adding that SMIC would adjust its capacity and accelerate the ramp-up of new production lines to help ease industry-wide supply constraints.
SMIC shares were up 5 percent after the earnings call, although they are down 0.21 percent this year.
The company’s monthly production capacity rose 1.7 percent quarter-on-quarter to 1.1 million 8-inch-equivalent wafers, with utilization — a measure of a foundry’s production intensity — reaching 93.7 percent, slightly up from the first quarter.
SMIC added 8,000 wafers of monthly 12-inch capacity during the second quarter.
The company said that first-half amortization totaled US$2.3 billion and it expects full-year amortization of about US$5 billion, up 30 percent year-on-year.
China remained SMIC’s largest market, accounting for 90 percent of second-quarter revenue, while the US contributed 8 percent.
Capital spending in the first half reached US$3.4 billion, up from US$3.3 billion a year earlier.
SMIC expects third-quarter revenue to rise 2 to 4 percent from the second quarter, with wafer shipments continuing to increase.

articles.title: Agency budget cuts pass third reading
articles.body:
The Legislative Yuan yesterday passed the third reading of across-the-board budget cuts for central government agencies in this fiscal year, reducing overall spending by NT$48 billion (US$1.5 billion), or about 1.689 percent.
The Executive Yuan submitted this fiscal year’s central government budget proposal to the legislature on Aug. 29 last year, projecting NT$2.8623 trillion in revenue and NT$3.035 trillion in expenditure.
Budget deliberations have been delayed for 350 days.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
Under the approved cuts, special allowance funds are to be reduced by 60 percent across government agencies, while the special allowance budgets of 20 agencies and institutions, including the Executive Yuan, Judicial Yuan and Control Yuan, are to be eliminated entirely and may not be reallocated.
Spending on media policy promotion and public information campaigns is to be cut by half, while overseas travel budgets face reductions of up to 70 percent.
For overseas travel and training expenses, budgets mandated by law, as well as those of Academia Sinica and the National Audit Office, are exempt from cuts.
The National Development Council, National Communications Commission (NCC), Overseas Community Affairs Council, Mainland Affairs Council and Control Yuan are to face 70 percent reductions.
Overseas travel budgets for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Bureau of Consular Affairs, National Security Council, Executive Yuan Office of Trade Negotiations, agencies under the Ministry of National Defense, Taiwan Transportation Safety Board, National Police Agency (NPA), National Fire Agency, Ministry of Sports, National Immigration Agency (NIA), Coast Guard Administration, National Science and Technology Council (NSTC), Centers for Disease Control, Food and Drug Administration and Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau are to be cut by 10 percent.
The NCC and Control Yuan are to see their China travel budgets eliminated entirely, while Academia Sinica, the NSTC, NPA and NIA are to face 15 percent cuts.
All other agencies are subject to 30 percent reductions.
Domestic travel budgets are to be cut by 15 percent across the board, except for branch courts of the High Court, Academia Sinica and the National Audit Office.
The proposed general budget cuts jointly endorsed by the caucuses of all three major parties are to exclude NT$71.8 billion allocated to 38 newly proposed projects backed by the opposition parties, as well as an additional NT$120 billion earmarked to bolster the Labor Insurance Fund.
The legislature had previously approved the early release of funds for designated new capital expenditure and projects, citing their “urgency and significant impact on public livelihood.”

articles.title: Top Geneva envoy ordered home after misconduct claims
articles.body:
Taiwan’s top envoy in Geneva has been ordered to return home to respond to allegations of workplace bullying, misuse of public funds and other misconduct, Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) said yesterday.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs launched a formal investigation into the behavior of Greg Lee (李冠德), director-general of the Taipei Cultural and Economic Office in Geneva, after receiving a signed complaint from employees at its Geneva office late last month, Lin said.
Because the allegations cover numerous issues and cannot be adequately addressed through written correspondence, the ministry formally instructed Lee to return to Taiwan and provide a detailed explanation, Lin said.
Photo: Taipei Times
A special investigative task force has been formed and includes people from outside the ministry who have legal expertise, he said.
The investigation must be free from interference and any attempt to obstruct it would also be examined by the task force, Lin said.
Asked whether Lee would explain the situation to him personally, Lin said he would respect the task force’s procedures.
The ministry on Sunday last week announced that it was opening an investigation after several Taiwanese news outlets reported on a 134-page complaint signed by “all affected colleagues” that detailed seven categories of alleged misconduct.
Among the allegations was that Lee asked the Geneva office to use public funds to purchase bedding costing more than 2,500 Swiss francs (US$3,074) for his residence.
He was also accused of spending about NT$130,000 in public funds on high-end chocolates for Taiwanese guests attending events held alongside last year’s World Health Assembly, and later asking subordinates to submit false expense claims.
The complaint also alleged that Lee verbally humiliated subordinates and that his management style caused some employees to seek medical help.
Taiwan’s overseas missions represent the country and should provide work environments that allow diplomats to perform effectively, Lin said.

articles.title: EDITORIAL: Young people need AI literacy
articles.body:
Minister of Education Cheng Ying-yao (鄭英耀) said in an interview on Monday that Taiwanese students should learn how to use artificial intelligence (AI) responsibly and think independently, adding that education must place greater emphasis on problem solving, judgement and knowledge application, rather than simply acquiring information.
Two days later, student group EdYouth released its fifth curriculum observation report, a survey that aimed to understand students’ views on curriculum implementation for science and social science subjects. Nearly half of the survey’s respondents said they “did not understand” or were “very confused” about rules and ethics regarding the use of generative AI.
While that figure is jarring on its own, it is even more concerning when placed into context.
AI is already deeply embedded in the daily lives of Taiwanese children. According to a survey by the online educational material vendor Parenting.com.tw, about 92 percent of children aged six to 15 who regularly use technology also use AI. Another poll conducted by National Academy of Educational Research and Academia Sinica found that 69 percent of ninth-graders reported using the technology, most commonly for homework, creating images or videos and chatting.
Students are under considerable academic pressure — thus, from a young person’s perspective, the appeal of AI is obvious. It can be used for anything from answering simple questions, solving math problems and summarizing text to drafting multi-page essays within seconds. Any one of these features might seem like a lifesaver for a student juggling homework assignments, exam preparation and extracurricular activities.
However, a problem arises when occasional use of the technology evolves into daily use, and eventually overdependence.
If students grow accustomed to outsourcing complex and mundane tasks to AI, they risk losing the ability to perform those tasks themselves. And now that a new generation of children has been born into the AI era, some are beginning to rely on it before learning essential skills such as critical thinking, drawing inferences, conducting research, reflecting on information and articulating original arguments.
What is worse is that students can become dependent on the technology without first understanding its imperfections. AI can cite unreliable sources and produce blatantly false or unsupported information — known as hallucinations. It has even been known to cite other AI-generated content, creating a potentially endless cycle of misinformation.
Children who grow accustomed to treating answers provided by AI chatbots as undisputed fact could never develop the skepticism and media literacy necessary for identifying misinformation. This would be particularly detrimental in a democracy already targeted by foreign disinformation campaigns and election interference.
Even if AI were to be banned from schools altogether, there would be no way to prevent students from using it for non-academic purposes.
A survey found that 73 percent of girls in junior-high school had talked to AI chatbots when feeling depressed, nearly three times the proportion who said they would seek help from teachers. That is particularly concerning given documented cases overseas in which AI chatbots have been accused of encouraging suicidal behavior or reinforcing delusions among vulnerable users.
At the same time, AI is becoming increasingly crucial to Taiwan’s economy, and the government is seeking to develop a workforce capable of using the technology effectively. Given these realities, the only practical path forward is to teach students how to use AI safely, responsibly and intelligently, rather than attempting to keep them away from it.
EdYouth urged the government to standardize curricula surrounding AI and introduce courses that teach about the limitations of the technology into the national curriculum. Given the trajectory of AI use among Taiwanese, these steps are essential.
AI can undoubtedly be a valuable tool, but it should remain just that — a tool. It must not be allowed to become a substitute for learning or face-to-face interaction. Young people cannot make the most of this tool without first understanding where it falls short and recognizing the irreplaceable value of human thought and creativity.
Academic integrity is part of that. Students must understand not only what constitutes inappropriate use of AI, but why relying on a machine to produce work that is supposed to be a reflection of their own knowledge and ideas undermines the very purpose of education.
As AI continues to develop, it would undoubtedly play a greater role in the economy and everyday life, but there is still time to define what that role should be. That process can begin in the classroom.

Taiwanese pair advance
Taiwan’s Lin Yun-ju and Cheng I-ching on Thursday upset the world’s top-ranked mixed doubles pair to reach the semi-finals at the WTT Europe Smash in Malmo, Sweden. The Taiwanese duo, ranked 11th in the world, defeated South Korea’s Lim Jong-hoon and Shin Yu-bin 11-3, 11-2, 4-11, 11-9 in the quarter-finals at Malmo Arena. The victory was Lin and Cheng’s first over the South Korean pair after losing their previous two meetings. It secured Lin and Cheng a place in the final four, equaling their best mixed doubles result at a WTT Grand Smash event. They were scheduled to play world No. 5 and third-seeded Chinese pair Lin Shidong and Kuai Man after press time last night for a place in the final. SOCCER
S Africa, Ghana progress
South Africa and Ghana kept alive hopes of competing at next year’s FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil after play-off victories in Morocco on Thursday. Ghana edged Ivory Coast 2-1 in Casablanca, while South Africa held on after conceding in added-time and having captain Refiloe Jane sent off to beat Nigeria 2-1 at another venue in the city. The two winners join Taiwan, Uzbekistan, Papua New Guinea and Venezuela or Ecuador in a six-nation tournament in November and December, with the top two finishers progressing to join two representatives from the North, Central and Caribbean region and one each from South America and Europe. The winners of those three match-ups qualify for Brazil.

Promising teen dies
Promising teenage Australian Jessica Bang died after a brain hemorrhage while preparing for a tournament in Thailand, her family and tour officials said. She was 18. Bang, who won her first professional event in just her fifth start earlier this year, collapsed on Aug. 1 and was rushed to a hospital in Bangkok, where she underwent emergency brain surgery. She did not recover and died on Thursday. “We are truly heartbroken by this news,” family members said on a GoFundMe page set up after she fell ill. “However, we would like to continue to remember Jessica and celebrate her achievements, passion and dedication to golf. The WPGA Tour of Australasia called her an “outstanding young talent” who turned professional at the end of last year following a stellar amateur career. “The WPGA Tour of Australasia and the broader Australian golf community is deeply saddened by the passing of young Tour member Jessica Bang in Thailand,” the WPGA said in a statement. “The thoughts and prayers of everyone at the WPGA Tour of Australasia and the broader Australian golf community are with Jessica’s family, friends and all those who knew and loved her at this incredibly difficult time.”

articles.title: China’s spicy strips take a bite of the global snack market
articles.body:
At a gleaming new factory in China’s central hinterland, masked workers in white uniform season and sift through mounds of latiao, a longtime popular snack that has found hungry fans overseas.
Spicy, sweet and curiously chewy, Chinese latiao — literally “spicy strips” — are made by cooking wheat flour dough at a high temperature and pressure.
Despite their reputation as junk food, the snacks originally developed as emergency supplies have grown into an industry worth more than 60 billion yuan (US$8.9 billion).
Photo: AFP
The Mala Wangzi factory in Hunan Province’s Pingjiang turns out nearly 700 tonnes per day of the spongy, red-colored strips, which look like squashed French fries covered in oil.
The company sells all of that domestically, but latiao have acquired new legions of foreign fans spurred by online enthusiasm for Chinese culture, or “Chinamaxxing.”
“Latiao are now exported to more than 160 countries worldwide, showing that the market is moving increasingly toward internationalization,” Mala Wangzi vice president Li Manliang said.
Some brands have expanded into East and Southeast Asia, where they are growing rapidly, while consumers from the US to Australia are snapping up the snacks in specialist grocery stores, e-commerce platforms and via TikTok.
The country’s largest latiao producer, Hong Kong-listed Weilong, made 117 million yuan from overseas sales last year, up nearly 50 percent from 2024.
TikTok and Instagram are awash with videos of foreigners trying the fiery snacks.
One influencer gained 1.5 million views by chowing down on a model house made entirely of the glutinous strips.
In another TikTok video with 2.6 million views, an Australian reviewer tucked into a giant latiao.
Latiao were created in Pingjiang in 1998 as an emergency staple food, after devastating floods wiped out the local soybean crop. They became ubiquitous in supermarkets across China, but gained a reputation as unhealthy and unsanitary — an image latiao brands have spent years trying to counter.
At the Mala Wangzi facility, an employee livestreamed the factory floor to showcase its hygienic conditions.
Li said these were based on standards used in the pharmaceutical industry.
The recipe has also changed to make the snack healthier, he said.
“We’re reducing the use of oil, salt, sugar and additives, and using more natural raw ingredients,” he added.
Mala Wangzi has opened pop-up museums around the country, held more than 4,000 latiao-themed weddings for superfan couples, and sponsored e-sport events, music festivals, and animation conventions.

articles.title: Colombia quake rescue efforts continue
articles.body:
Colombia’s disaster relief chief vowed to find the hundreds of people still missing after a massive earthquake, as rescuers dug through rubble early yesterday following the end of a critical lifesaving period.
The strongest quake to hit Colombia this century devastated the western cities of Cali and Pereira, and destroyed nearly 13,000 homes across the coffee-growing region and along the coast.
The magnitude 7.4 tremor struck on Monday, killing 281 people and injuring almost 4,000, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella said, adding that 379 others remained missing.
Photo: Bloomberg
Rescuers had little hope of finding more survivors, who are typically saved in the first 72 hours after an earthquake.
David Tamayo, head of Colombia’s disaster relief agency, acknowledged that the “likelihood of finding survivors is going to diminish.”
“But our commitment is to never stop searching... The order is to not rest until we find all the missing persons,” he added.
In Cali, many families that lost their homes sought refuge in makeshift camps set up in streets and parks.
Maria del Carmen Rodriguez lost the apartment she had saved for her entire life.
“We wonder what aid we’re entitled to, whether they’re going to relocate us somewhere else, because this is going to last a long time,” she said.
De la Espriella has declared the disaster an “economic emergency” and announced three days of national mourning.
“We will do what is necessary,” the newly appointed leader said, vowing to “emerge again as a country and as a society.”
Psychologist Javier Alzate was trying to remove tiles and chunks of debris that were obstructing access to his damaged home in Pereira.
“It’s very distressing. Very sad. You work 40 or 50 years to buy a little house, struggling all that time to get it. I finally got it, and a few days later it’s gone,” Alzate said. “I lost my home and my car.”
The impoverished Choco region on the Pacific coast also suffered immensely, with some of its remote communities yet to be surveyed.
In the Valle del Cauca region, Governor Dilian Francisca Toro said officials were conducting a census of damaged and destroyed homes to determine which buildings could still be occupied.
“We have to begin working, because people simply cannot bear staying out on the streets any longer,” she said. “People are telling us: ‘If you give us the materials, we’ll do the work ourselves.’”
Many Colombians have mobilized to help, bringing water, food and supplies to affected neighborhoods, while long lines have formed outside blood donation centers.
“[Quake victims] are not alone, that is a message we want to convey,” said Laura Mendoza, a volunteer organizing donations in Bogota. “We are here giving what we can so that they at least have the most basic things.”
Musician Andres Solomon took to offering hugs to anyone who needed emotional support.
“We are going through a collective trauma, and I think the best way I could help was by giving away the energy I have and the vitality I have left,” he said.
Colombia was preparing to receive international urban search-and-rescue teams from the US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel, disaster authorities said.
De la Espriella’s administration is facing criticism over allegedly blocking rescue teams from countries with leftist leadership, but it has denied the accusation.

articles.title: Nigel Farage wins UK by-election as Count Binface claims ‘moral victory’
articles.body:
Hard-right British politician Nigel Farage was re-elected to his parliamentary seat yesterday in a by-election shunned by the major parties — handing his main rival, joke candidate Count Binface, a larger than expected share of the vote.
Farage, who triggered Thursday’s polls by resigning from the parliamentary seat he had held since 2024 over an investigation into his finances, swept 63 percent of the ballots in Clacton, results showed.
While votes were still being counted, Farage had declared victory,and refused to attend the official count.
Photo: AFP
“The verdict is in and it is a convincing and overwhelming win,” he said.
Meanwhile, Count Binface — the alter ego of comedian Jon Harvey — exceeded expectations, taking 9,455 votes, or 27 percent of the total.
Analysts had anticipated a win for Farage, but underestimated the appeal of the self-styled “intergalactic space warrior” from planet Sigma IX, who campaigns wearing a rubbish bin on his head.
The vote had been snubbed by the UK’s main political parties, including the governing Labour Party, as a stunt by the Reform UK leader to dodge scrutiny of his financial dealings.
That gave dozens of fringe candidates including Binface a chance to seize the spotlight.
“The moral victory is already mine,” Binface said.
If the other parties “choose not to stand, somebody has to stand up and be the opposition. And so it’s my humble duty to actually be His Majesty’s official opposition,” he added.
“If a majority of the voters of Clacton say they would like [Farage] to be returned as their MP, that is to be respected,” Binface said.
Farage said Essex Police had warned him that an “organized campaign to disrupt and degrade the result” was planned.
Turnout reached about 44 percent, down from 59 percent in the 2024 general election, but not unusual for a by-election.
In the seaside resort, many voters appeared unenthusiastic about the vote, with even some Reform party volunteers describing the contest as a joke.
“It’s a bit ridiculous,” party campaigner Jane Embleton said. “It’s all to make Nigel Farage look like an idiot, basically. But he doesn’t look like an idiot to me or his supporters.”
A record 34 candidates — most of them independents and fringe candidates, including Binface — stood in the vote, with some of the longest ballot papers in UK history seen at the Clacton Leisure Centre, where the count was held.

articles.title: Ennoconn expects second-half revenue increase
articles.body:
Industrial computer maker Ennoconn Corp (樺漢科技) yesterday said revenue in the second half of this year is expected to exceed first-half levels driven by rising demand for smart factory and facility management solutions from semiconductor makers investing in high-tech and automation systems.
Ennoconn’s revenue in the first half grew 23.62 percent from a year earlier to NT$85.49 billion (US$2.67 billion).
Capacity expansion by semiconductor customers would remain a key growth driver for Ennoconn’s smart factory and facility management business in the second half, Ennoconn chairman Steve Chu (朱復銓) told an earnings conference in Taipei.
Photo courtesy of Ennoconn Corp
The company since last quarter has benefited significantly from the second-phase expansion of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (台積電) US fabs through its 37.88 percent-held subsidiary Marketech International Corp (帆宣), Chu said.
Growth is also expected to be supported by Ennoconn’s project with Atlanta, Georgia-based retail solutions provider NCR Voyix Corp, he said.
The Atlanta project is expected to generate NT$14 billion to NT$16 billion for the full year, with significant revenue contribution starting last quarter, he said.
Based on a strategic partnership agreement signed by the companies in August 2024, Ennoconn took over NCR Voyix’s design and manufacturing, as well as supply of NCR Voyix’s self-checkout, point-of-sale hardware and other financial end devices, he said.
The hardware products entered volume production in April, Chu said.
Products for NCR Voyix have evolved from traditional boards and box PCs into autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems integrating sensors, cameras, AI computing and software, lifting gross margin to more than 35 percent, Ennoconn president Nelson Tsay (蔡能吉) said.
Collaboration with NCR Voyix is expected to lift Ennoconn’s overall margin, Tsay said.
Meanwhile, Ennoconn expects to complete its tender offer for German embedded computing subsidiary Kontron AG on Thursday next week, raising its stake to about 49.4 percent.
Kontron has high-margin businesses in Europe, including rail transportation, aerospace and software, with combined revenue exceeding NT$10 billion, Chu said.
Ennoconn plans to leverage its supply chain and market presence in Asia to expand Kontron’s products across the Asia-Pacific region, while the two companies would jointly develop the North American market, the company said.
Ennoconn also plans to introduce its centralized procurement, enterprise resource planning and manufacturing management systems to Kontron, it said.
The deeper integration could generate at least 40 million euros (US$46.27 million) in additional revenue, it said.
The firm holds orders totaling NT$255 billion, up from NT$215 billion last quarter, indicating robust shipment momentum this year, it said.
Ennoconn’s business consists of three main segments: industrial Internet of Things (IoT), which accounted for 46 percent of total revenue in the first half; intelligent software and solutions (12 percent); and smart factory and facility management (42 percent), it said.
Among the three segments, growth from IoT, and smart factory and facility management is expected to be the greatest in the second half, Chu said.
Ennoconn on Thursday reported that first-half net profit rose 21.6 percent year-on-year to NT$1.8 billion. Earnings per share rose to NT$12.31 from NT$10.13 a year earlier.
Gross margin fell to 19.66 percent from 19.86 percent a year earlier as higher component costs weighed on profitability, but is expected to improve as memory-related price rises are passed on to customers starting this quarter, Chu said.

The company, a key supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips to Nvidia Corp, is speaking with prospective advisers to help review the business, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. articles.title: At least five dead as rain floods Chiba Prefecture
articles.body:
Record-breaking rainfall flooded cities east of Tokyo overnight, killing at least five people, injuring more than two dozen others and stranding thousands, authorities said yesterday.
As the deluge subsided, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) downgraded its most severe heavy-rain warning in more than a dozen municipalities in Chiba Prefecture while forecasting more rain later yesterday.
The prefecture saw unprecedented rainfall levels on Thursday, with 1.5cm in just one hour in Chiba City and 9.7cm in one hour in Sakura City, JMA said.
Photo: AFP
Photos and TV footage showed widespread damage, with homes, cars and parts of railway tracks filled with muddy water. Roads and dozens of homes were also flooded and some areas remained without power.
Chiba Prefecture officials said the five deaths included a man found floating on a flooded road in Ichikawa City and a woman who had been stuck in a flooded car in Sakura.
Two others were presumed dead after being pulled from flooded cars in the cities of Kashiwa and Chiba.
One person remained missing, and more than 30 people were injured, including five seriously, they said.
Meanwhile, the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force said it dispatched buses to pick up about 4,000 stranded people who stayed overnight at the Soga train station, which did not report any damage.
About 170 homes were flooded in the prefecture and more than 300 people were sheltering at public facilities as of yesterday afternoon, Chiba officials said.
The number of homes that had lost power due to the torrential rain and flooding fell to 18,000 yesterday from 68,000 the day before, according to the TEPCO Power Grid.
Thousands of people stuck overnight at Narita Airport gradually left as train service partially resumed yesterday.
Flights in and out of Narita were operating normally.
In Taiwan, the Tourism Administration yesterday said it had received no reports of Taiwanese tour groups being affected by the rain in Japan.
The Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office in Japan and major Taiwanese travel industry associations also said they had received no reports of Taiwanese travelers requiring assistance.

articles.title: Poland, Baltic states fear a Russian false-flag strike
articles.body:
Russia’s northern NATO neighbors are tightening security around dams, power plants and natural gas infrastructure in a sign of mounting concern that Moscow will stage a “false flag” attack on them using Ukrainian drones.
Lithuania last week said that Moscow is considering such a staged attack; Poland, Latvia and Estonia have also warned of acts of sabotage to test NATO’s response at a time when US commitment to the Western military alliance is in question.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov last month said warnings of Russian clandestine attacks are “scare stories” used to justify militarization against Russia.
Illustration: Louise Ting
Poland and the three Baltic states, which all border Russia and have already found Ukrainian drones on their territory, are taking no chances.
“We are not naive, we see the information, we read between the lines and we are doing our homework,” Lithuanian Minister of National Defense Robertas Kaunas said.
Kaunas, the prime minister of Latvia, and four intelligence and company officials from across the region shared new details of intelligence assessments with Reuters and described measures that are being taken to protect infrastructure in response.
“We are increasing the security of our critical infrastructure, we constantly exchange information with our intelligence on what to do next,” Kaunas said.
Last month, Lithuania dispatched the military to back up riot police in securing its liquefied natural gas (LNG) import terminal, the oil products terminal, a key power link with Poland and the Kruonis Pumped Storage hydro plant.
“We are clearly signaling that, if needed, we will be defending ourselves,” Kaunas said.
Latvia has increased security around all critical infrastructure, including the dam on the Daugava River near Riga and the Incukalns underground gas storage facility, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs told Reuters in an interview.
“A potential hybrid threat is more likely than it was before,” he said.
Russia in May accused the Baltic states of planning to let Ukrainian drones attack Russia from their territory and pledged to retaliate, prompting denials and protest along with concern that Moscow might stage such an attack to justify a response.
A Baltic intelligence official said assessments indicated Russian military and domestic intelligence agencies are planning a possible false-flag attack on infrastructure in Russia or the Baltics and Poland, with Ukrainian-made drones, to be carried out within days of approval from leaders, including Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The main concern cited in the assessments was not so much the immediate impact of such an attack as the “political chaos” it could trigger at NATO headquarters in Brussels, as its European members and the US debate how, and whether, to respond, the official said.
Another source, an official from the region, was less definitive, saying a spate of warnings from “allied intelligence” about Russian activity had made an “overwhelming impression” on the Baltic states, but attacks could take place “between today and never.”
Moscow says the West, out of “Russophobia,” routinely accuses it of malign acts without providing evidence. NATO and the Russian embassy in Vilnius did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
In Poland, the top oil and gas firm Orlen is analyzing alternative gas import routes in case the usual ones are compromised, a person familiar with its operations said.
Orlen imports 80 percent of the country’s gas through the Swinoujscie LNG terminal on the Baltic Sea and an undersea pipeline from Norway that lands nearby. Gaz-System, which owns the infrastructure, is operating under “increased vigilance” there, another person with direct knowledge said.
Orlen declined to comment on the specifics of any preventive measures. A Gaz-System spokesperson said the firm is monitoring the geopolitical situation and responding appropriately.
The state-owned developer of Poland’s first nuclear power plant, Polskie Elektrownie Jadrowe, said forged company documents aimed at confusing stakeholders had appeared and could be traced to somewhere “east of Poland.”
The company is investigating with special services and law enforcement and monitoring for sabotage or other threats at the planned construction site, spokesman Marcin Skolimowski said.
Poland’s power grid operator and an arm of the military last month began increasing security around a power link with Ukraine that helps to stabilize the war-hit country’s grid, which has long been attacked by Russia.
“This is an area where heightened vigilance is required, so we are using all available resources,” the grid operator’s spokesperson Maciej Wapinski said.
It expects the military to eventually help secure its critical infrastructure in other eastern parts of the country.
Mysterious drones have also appeared across Europe. Last week, in Germany, officials found a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport. German Minister of the Interior Alexander Dobrindt called it a hybrid attack, but did not assign blame. Russia has dismissed suggestions by German politicians and media that it is responsible.
Wojciech Kononczuk, director of the Polish state-funded OSW Centre for Eastern Studies, said that a spate of allegations from Russia that the Baltics are working for Ukraine might be paving the way for Russian attacks there.
He said that with Russian forces bogged down in Ukraine, and Ukrainian strikes on Russia’s energy and other facilities hurting its economy, the aim would be to regain the upper hand.
The message to Europe would be that if it does not accept Moscow’s demands, then it will spread destabilization — a risky move based on the calculation that there would be a lack of will to respond, Kononczuk said.

articles.title: ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)
articles.body:
Most prescriptions come with a list of side effects. The Swedish Prescription, however, offers pine-scented air, the slow rhythm of Nordic life, and the idea that recovery can happen in a forest rather than a clinic.
Launched by Visit Sweden, this initiative was created in cooperation with medical professionals willing to prescribe a stay in Sweden if they consider it helpful for a patient’s well-being. This has made Sweden the first country to be offered on prescription. For global reach, the official website provides a downloadable document, allowing patients everywhere to discuss the possibility of a Swedish retreat with their doctors.
With forests covering nearly 70% of Sweden, nature is the program’s primary clinic. Its plentiful forests and clean air can offer relief to people suffering from stress and anxiety. Spending time in green spaces has been linked to reduced blood pressure and improved concentration. This healing effect extends to urban environments, where many cities are built for walking and cycling. Engaging in these activities can benefit both cardiovascular and mental health.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片：AdobeStock
Swedish social customs and cultural life offer another path to managing stress. A prominent part of this is “fika,” a coffee-and-cake ritual where people get together for a communal break and share pleasant conversation. This tradition allows people to connect with others without pressure. The program also encourages patients to find peace in taking in art, whether in a renowned museum or through public installations scattered across the country. These brief cultural encounters have been proven to lower stress and lift patients’ moods. From lush forests to cozy cafes and grand museums, Sweden aims to care for the mind as well as the body.
大多數處方藥都會附上一張條列副作用的清單。但瑞典處方提供的是松香瀰漫的空氣、北歐生活緩慢的步調，以及療癒不是在診所，而是能在森林裡進行的概念。
這項新計畫由 Visit Sweden（編按：瑞典觀光局）發起，是在與醫療專業人士的合作下所創，若他們認為瑞典處方有益於患者健康，便會樂意開給患者瑞典之行的處方。瑞典也因此成為醫師可開立處方箋建議旅遊的首個國家。為了觸及全球患者，官方網站提供可下載的文件，讓各地患者都能與醫師探討在瑞典靜養的可能性。
瑞典近七成國土有森林覆蓋，大自然是該企劃的主要診所。豐富的森林資源和清新空氣能讓飽受壓力和焦慮折磨的人們得到舒緩。花時間在綠地徜徉已被證實與血壓降低和專注力提升有關。這種療癒效果也適用於城市環境，許多城市都設計成適合步行和自行車騎乘。從事這些活動對心血管和心理健康都有益。
瑞典的社會習俗和文化生活也為應對壓力提供了另一種途徑。其中一個重要部分是「fika」，這是一種享用咖啡和蛋糕的儀式，人們聚在一起共度休息時光、進行愉快的交談。這項傳統讓人們能在無壓力的氛圍中與他人聯繫感情。該計畫還鼓勵患者欣賞藝術來獲得平靜，無論是在知名博物館或是透過遍布全國的公共藝術裝置都可以。這些短暫的文化體驗已被證實可以減輕壓力、提振患者的心情。從鬱鬱蔥蔥的森林到舒適的咖啡館和宏偉的博物館，瑞典致力於照顧人們的身體與心理健康。
To be continued tomorrow（明日待續）
https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/lang
Words In Use
1. initiative n. 新計畫，新措施
The city government started an initiative to reduce plastic waste.
市政府發起了一項減少塑膠垃圾的新計畫。
2. professional n. 專業人士
The brand hired professionals to design the website.
該品牌聘請專業人士來設計網站。
3. document n. 文件
David sent a document to his boss by email this morning.
大衛今天早上用電子郵件寄了文件給他的老闆。
4. retreat n. 靜養，靜修（可數或不可數）；僻靜地（可數）
My sister went on a weekend retreat in the mountains to relax and recharge.
我妹週末去山上靜養，好好放鬆充電。
The writer rented a lakeside retreat to work on her novel.
這位作家租了一個湖邊的僻靜處來專心寫小說。
5. plentiful a. 豐富的，大量的
The island has plentiful sunlight, which is great for solar power.
這座島嶼日照充足，利於太陽能發電。
Practical Phrases
1. in cooperation with. . . 與……合作
cooperation n. 合作
We organized the event in cooperation with the local community.
我們與當地社區合作舉辦了這項活動。
2. engage in. . . 從事∕進行……（活動等）
Students are encouraged to engage in sports after school.
學生被鼓勵在課後從事運動。
3. take in... / take. . . in 欣賞∕觀覽……
We sat on the beach to take in the sunset.
我們坐在沙灘上欣賞日落。
4. lift sb’s mood 提振某人的心情
A kind word from a friend can often lift your mood.
朋友的一句溫柔話語往往能讓你心情好轉。
What Did You Learn?
1. Why does the author mention “side effects” in the first paragraph of the Day 1 passage?
(A) To list the official risks of the tourism initiative.
(B) To report the official results of the recovery process.
(C) To explain why some patients struggle with a slow pace of life.
(D) To contrast the pleasant Swedish experience with typical drug reactions.
2. Which of the following is true about the Swedish Prescription?
(A) It depends primarily on physical training like cycling.
(B) It is only available to patients currently living in Sweden.
(C) It allows doctors to recommend travel as a healing method.
(D) It was developed by a group of private hospitals in Sweden.
參考答案 :
1. D 2. C

articles.title: KMT’s Fu should return or resign
articles.body:
The Legislative Yuan on Tuesday continued cross-caucus negotiations to discuss this fiscal year’s general budget, but Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (傅?萁) was once again absent. KMT caucus secretary-general Lin Pei-hsiang (林沛祥) said that he could not represent the caucus if Fu did not sign, highlighting uncertainty over who had the authority to do so. Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), unusually angered by the situation, demanded that Fu appear in person and authorize Lin to act on his behalf or resign as caucus whip.
Although KMT caucus representatives ultimately signed the negotiated conclusions that afternoon, the imbalance of authority exposed by Fu’s absence and confusion over authorization cannot simply be brushed aside.
Article 69 of the Act Governing the Legislative Yuan’s Power (立法院職權行使法) stipulates that cross-caucus negotiations are attended by the legislative speaker, deputy speaker and the leaders or whips of each caucus. Article 71 states that once a consensus is reached, a negotiation conclusion shall be signed, and that the caucus leaders must also sign it.
The Legislators’ Conduct Act (立法委員行為法) requires legislators to meet public expectations, conduct proceedings impartially and properly fulfill their duties. Although the law does not require the caucus whip to personally attend every negotiation, the caucus leaders or whips are central to the negotiation process. If another caucus official is to serve as a representative, the authority to make decisions and sign agreements should be clarified in advance.
During the discussion of the general budget proposal for drones that day, Han asked for the KMT caucus’ position, and Lin responded that it would “reserve its position.” When the negotiations concluded, the KMT caucus initially withheld its signature, only doing so after Han called on it to sign. Fu has the right to oppose the proposal or call for his caucus to reserve its position. However, as the person responsible for negotiations, he should either be present to make decisions or fully authorize a representative to act on his behalf, rather than allowing blurred lines of authority to add unnecessary costs to the deliberation process.
Fu later explained that his absence was a soft protest against the executive branch’s disregard for the legislature, saying he “could not bear to see Han subjected to various indignities by the Executive Yuan.” However, if he truly believes that the Executive Yuan disrespects the legislature, he should have taken a seat at the negotiating table to demand explanations and address each case individually. How could his absence possibly demonstrate a defense of the legislature’s authority? Protesting the executive branch’s actions cannot be done by neglecting the legislative branch, and defending the dignity of the legislature cannot begin by undermining the legislature’s own ability to function.
The ancient Chinese philosopher Confucius (孔子) said that scholar-officials should “act with a sense of shame.” In his Doctrine of the Mean (中庸), he said that “knowing shame is close to courage.” Ming Dynasty academic Gu Yanwu (顧炎武) wrote in his work Honesty and Morality (廉恥) that “the shamelessness of scholar-officials is a national disgrace.” Knowing shame is not about humiliating others, but about understanding one’s duties and reflecting on one’s own shortcomings when they occur.
In questioning the caucus whip’s responsibilities that day, Han also emphasized the Confucian principle that “a gentleman attends to the fundamentals.” The fundamental duty of a caucus whip is not influence or power, but sitting at the negotiating table, making decisions and bearing the consequences.
During the negotiations, Han did not refrain from criticism just because Fu belongs to the same political party. Rather, in keeping with the requirement that the legislative speaker exercise his authority on the basis of fairness and neutrality, he publicly demanded that Fu attend the meeting, grant authorization to a representative, or resign. This deserves recognition.
The general budget is not any political party’s private property — it encompasses national defense, public infrastructure, social welfare and administrative policy. As a legislature and KMT caucus whip, Fu should be held to a higher standard of accountability by the public.
If Fu still believes he is fit for the position, he should return to the negotiating table. If he cannot bother to even attend or designate an authorized representative, then he should accept the third option put forth by Han, and resign. True courage is not finding excuses for one’s absence, but accepting responsibility for the consequences of one’s own choices. If Fu still has a sense of shame, he should resign as caucus whip and hand over the responsibility to someone who is willing to show up, make decisions and be accountable to the public.
Su Wei-cheng is a lecturer and a former secretary of the president of the Legislative Yuan.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

articles.body:

Chen Hsing-yu on Thursday wrote in a post online that she had purchased a property and gifted it to her then-husband Chao Chien-ming (趙建銘), but she was the one who paid the mortgage.
A day before, she had left a “one-star” negative review on a Google review of an orthopedic clinic run by Chao, criticizing his medical practice and accusing him of having an affair while showing no regard for her or their children.

The clinic wrote a reply to the comment, saying: “What she wrote is completely untrue.”
“I will continue to serve my patients through my own abilities and hard work,” it said.
It was unclear whether the comment was posted by Chao or by a social media administrator.
In the post on Wednesday, Chen Hsing-yu referred to herself as Chao’s ex-wife. Until then, the public had not known the couple had divorced.
Chen Hsing-yu on Thursday wrote that she gifted the property to Chao, but had kept the NT$60 million (US$1.87 million) mortgage in her name.
Gifts of property between spouses are not included in the division of marital assets after divorce, she wrote, urging others not to make the same mistake.
Commenting on the case, Chen Ciou-jyun (陳秋君), a lawyer who previously worked as a judge in civil, criminal and family courts, said that many Taiwanese give property to their spouses for tax reasons.
When a marriage dissolves, such arrangements often leave the gifting party without recourse, as the law has specific requirements for a giver to claim a property or asset they gave away, she said.
Chen Hsing-yu could not prove that her ex-husband breached a contractual condition in keeping the clinic because no contract was signed, Chen Ciou-jyun said, adding that she had not claimed Chao was abusive, which would have entitled injured parties to compensation if proven in court.
Chen Hsing-yu can request alimony to support herself or her children, but her economic circumstances and medical license make it unlikely that a court would accept the claim, the lawyer said.
She could attempt to prove that the clinic was intended to be jointly owned or wholly owned by her, which would require witnesses or records such as text messages, Chen Ciou-jyun said.
Couples entering into marriage should agree to a separation of property regardless of their income level to ensure both parties receive an equal share if they divorce, she said.
That legal protection applies to rent generated by jointly owned properties, she added.

articles.title: Prosecutors indict three more suspects in espionage case
articles.body:
The Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office has indicted three additional suspects in a case involving the alleged leaking of military information, which was apprently spearheaded by former TV producer Lee Neng-chien (李能謙), the office said yesterday.
Lee, who was indicted in April on espionage-related charges, is accused of leaking the personal data of intelligence agents and sensitive military information to Chinese intelligence operatives in 2024 and last year, prosecutors said.
The latest indictment named Hung Chia-pei (洪嘉培), Chen Wei-shuo (陳偉碩) and Cheng Chao-an (鄭兆安) as participants in the scheme.
Photo: Taipei Times
Hung allegedly attempted to sell a large database of personal information to Chinese intelligence operatives for profit, they said.
Hung allegedly obtained a dataset in March last year containing the names, months of birth, national identification numbers, job positions and contact information of a large number of Taiwanese, the indictment said.
After meeting Lee in April the same year, Hung allegedly filtered the database using keywords such as “Ministry of Foreign Affairs,” “Ministry of National Defense,” “army,” “navy,” “air force” and “reserves,” and extracted 3,674 records, it said.
Lee was allegedly expected to pass the data on to Chinese intelligence operatives, but the deal fell through after the two sides failed to agree on payment, prosecutors said.
Chen and Cheng were indicted on suspicion of helping Lee collect personal information on military personnel in April 2024.
Lee allegedly instructed Chen to gather information on active-duty military personnel, who then contacted Cheng, who worked in the loan business, prosecutors said.
Using former loan customers, Cheng allegedly compiled the names, IDs and phone numbers of people who had military backgrounds into a file and sent it to Chen, they said.
Chen then allegedly forwarded the information to one of Lee’s associates in exchange for NT$5,000, they added.
Hung was indicted on charges of contravening the National Security Act (國家安全法), the National Intelligence Services Act (國家情報工作法) and the Personal Data Protection Act (個人資料保護法).
Prosecutors said Hung repeatedly denied wrongdoing and justified his actions, even though he put national security at risk. They recommended that he be handed a prison sentence of more than seven years and six months.
Chen and Cheng were indicted on charges of contravening the Personal Data Protection Act, but prosecutors did not recommend prison sentences for either defendant.
Lee allegedly began working with a Chinese military intelligence operative known by the code name “Small Blue” in May 2024 to collect personal information on active-duty military personnel and sensitive defense-related information, the April indictment said.
He was allegedly recruited last year by another Chinese intelligence contact, known as “Fuzhou Hotspring,” while in Fuzhou, China, it said.
Prosecutors alleged he obtained more than 3,000 personal records, including those of intelligence agents and active-duty military personnel, and sent six files to the contact.

articles.title: Carbon fees should aid disadvantaged: advocates
articles.body:
Environmental advocates on Wednesday urged the government to raise corporate carbon reduction targets and prioritize utilization of carbon revenue to support vulnerable groups rather than to subsidize businesses.
Civic groups and experts were invited to a public hearing held by the Legislative Yuan’s Social Welfare and Environmental Hygiene Committee on the Ministry of Environment’s plans to revise carbon regulations to ensure procedural fairness, facilitate industrial transformation and reduce carbon emissions.
As of May, the government had collected NT$4.97 billion (US$155.1 million) in carbon fees from the 461 factories (240 companies) since the scheme was introduced last year.
Photo: Wu Po-hsuan, Taipei Times
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Lin Yueh-chin (林月琴) said a system should be created to ensure the carbon proceeds would be used for groups most affected by pollution and climate change.
Newborns, pregnant women, people with chronic respiratory illnesses and elderly people should benefit from government revenue generated by the fees, she said.
DPP Legislator Wang Cheng-hsu (王正旭) urged the Ministry of Environment and the Ministry of Labor to collaborate on using the funds to help workers whose livelihoods were negatively impacted by the carbon fees.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Wang Yu-min (王育敏) said that regulators might need to strengthen the mechanisms utilized to verify commercial entities’ claimed reductions in their carbon footprint.
Businesses that did not follow through on their sustainability programs should not be allowed to benefit from carbon fee deductibles, she said.
In 2024, the Earth’s average temperature increased by more than 1.5°C compared with pre-industrial levels, crossing the projected inflection point for a global climate catastrophe, said Wei Kuo-yen (魏國彥), former minister of the Environmental Protection Administration, the predecessor of the environment ministry.
Taiwan is situated on the edge of the Western Pacific Warm Pool, the warmest oceanic body of water in the world, which would give rise to increasingly frequent super El Nino events, he said.
This means the nation would face extreme weather in its severest forms, Wei said.
The difficulties involved in achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 are dwarfed by the next global target of negative emissions, Academia Sinica Institute of Economics researcher Hsiao Tai-chi (蕭代基) said.
Reducing emissions and removing greenhouse gases from the atmosphere would likely require the government to impose taxes on energy use and carbon instead of the current fee scheme, he said.
The revenue collected from these policy measures should ideally be allocated to disadvantaged groups, society in general or some form of national development fund, he said.
Mom Loves Taiwan Association secretary-general Huang Pin-han (黃品涵) said the state-run Greenhouse Gas Management Fund used less than 80 percent of its operational budget.
The central government should utilize carbon fees to develop and guide local governments and the private sector in deploying technologies that mitigate green house emissions, she said.
The fund should incorporate measures that encourage local adaptability to sustainability-related challenges on a permanent institutional level, she said.
Carbon Dividend Alliance cofounder Pan Han-shen (潘翰聲) said Taiwan should embrace a true carbon tax that enables the government to fully control the tax revenues.
The current carbon fee scheme imposes significant limits on the subsidies the government could fund, he said.
Citing an example, Pan said there is a subsidy for buying new air control units, but no funds for environmentally friendly screens, eaves, softscaping or fans, he said.
Deputy Minister of Environment Hsieh Yein-rui (謝燕儒) said the government would take into consideration the opinions presented by experts and lawmakers in revising regulations governing carbon fees.
The ministry’s purpose in instituting carbon fees is to encourage compliance with sustainability goals, not increase government income, he said.

articles.title: Lai calls for development of uncrewed systems
articles.body:
President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday called for faster development of uncrewed systems as the Han Kuang Exercises concluded, vowing to bolster defense supply chains.
“Over the 10-day, nine-night drills, military personnel worked around the clock, from carrying out missions on the front lines to handling command, communications, logistics and medical support in the rear,” he said on Facebook, adding that “every role was an indispensable part of safeguarding national security.”
Lai thanked everyone who took part in the drills, adding that “the cooperation and mutual support between the military and civilians represented the best expression of ‘National Unity Month.’”
Photo: Screen grab from President William Lai’s Facebook page
The drills this year incorporated more advanced equipment and uncrewed systems, while testing the latest training programs, he said.
The government will continue to bolster national defense and accelerate the development, production and deployment of advanced equipment, including uncrewed systems, he said.
Leveraging Taiwan’s strengths in ICT, semiconductors and precision manufacturing, the government aims to build a comprehensive and resilient defense supply chain, provide the military with better equipment, bolster the country’s defense capabilities and drive growth in Taiwan’s defense industry, he added.
“This year’s Han Kuang drills had come to an end, but efforts to strengthen national defense and build resilience across society will continue,” he said.
The government will work with the military and the public to prepare for every contingency, he said, adding that Taiwan would protect its democratic way of life through strength, and safeguard peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait through unity, making Taiwan safer and more resilient.

articles.title: Moldova's economy declines as Chisinau funds military goals — MFA
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 14. /TASS/. Chisinau always finds money for military needs to integrate into EU defense structures, despite a rapidly deteriorating economy and an energy crisis, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
"Today, the Chisinau regime can boast only a rapidly deteriorating socioeconomic situation and growing crises in the environmental and energy sectors. In an effort to stay afloat, the authorities have been forced to abandon announced wage increases for public-sector employees and raise VAT rates on grains and oilseeds from 8% to 12%, which will primarily hit small and medium-sized farms. Local farmers are barely surviving during the peak harvest season because diesel prices have risen by up to 70% and fertilizer prices by 35%-40%. Even massive financial injections from the European Union cannot improve the situation," Zakharova said in a comment.
"At the same time, Maia Sandu's regime always finds money for military goals. On August 5, the Moldovan government approved a program for implementing the National Defense Strategy for 2026-2030. It provides for strengthening the country's defense capability by increasing military spending to 1% of GDP and gradually integrating into the European Union's security and defense structures," she added.

articles.title: The first proxy war against Russia? Britain in the Caucasus
articles.body:
Britain’s forgotten proxy war against Russia
What is there in common between Ukrainians and the highlanders of the Caucasus, and what parallels can be drawn between Russia and Great Britain in the 19th century, and these same countries in the 21st century? In the 19th century, the British Empire fought against the Russian Empire using the highlanders in the Caucasus in a way that’s very similar to how Britain is now using Ukrainians.
In the 19th century, the Russian and British empires clashed fiercely over spheres of influence in the Caucasus. This geopolitical rivalry made use of all the means available at the time: wars between spies and diplomats, covert operations, arms smuggling, ideological battles, and active media propaganda. Read more about the confrontation between Russia and Britain, the secret operations in the Caucasus, and the lessons that those who now place their trust in Britain should draw from history.
To India via the Caucasus
“Britain will defend the freedom-loving nation from Russian aggression,” “British military advisers supplied fighters with weapons to resist the Russian army,” “British diplomats organized elites to combat Russian influence” – such headlines have become commonplace in Western media during the Ukraine conflict. Yet these same phrases could very well describe another historical conflict where British and Russian interests collided: the covert war waged by the British Empire against Russia in the 19th century, aimed at undermining Russian influence in the Caucasus.
At first glance, it might seem odd that events in the Caucasus, occurring far from Britain, could threaten London’s interests. But it only appears so.
After the Napoleonic Wars, the Russian Empire was at the height of its power. It led the “Holy Alliance” – a coalition of European great powers that shaped continental politics. Additionally, during the late 18th and early 19th centuries, Russia achieved significant victories over the Ottoman Empire in several wars, acquiring territories such as New Russia, Crimea, and parts of the eastern Black Sea coast.
Naturally, Russia also paid attention to what was happening in the Caucasus. The peoples of the North and West Caucasus, the Circassians, carried out frequent raids on Russian settlers, whom they robbed and enslaved, which caused great concern in Russia. To protect its interests and secure the safety of its people, Russia advanced further into this mountainous territory.
Britain, however, perceived this as a direct threat to its interests in India. London believed that Russia wouldn’t stop in the Caucasus but would advance further, potentially threatening Persia. And through Persia, and then Afghanistan, there lay a direct path to India, which was then referred to as the “jewel in the crown” of the British Empire. Although there was no concrete evidence that Russia intended to seize distant India, British elites firmly held this belief. In order to safeguard India against the mythical “Russian threat,” Britain encouraged tensions in the Caucasus.
In service of the Crown
Britain’s active intervention in Russian affairs in the Caucasus was preceded by two wars: the Russo-Persian War of 1826-1828 and the Russo-Turkish War of 1828-1829. As a result of these military triumphs, Russia solidified its position in Transcaucasia and gained control over much of the eastern coastline of the Black Sea.
Fearing Russia’s growing power in the region, Britain started supplying the Circassians with weapons and ammunition as early as 1830. For instance, in December of that year, six weapon-laden vessels were intercepted off the coast of what is now Abkhazia. However, for a time, these arms shipments remained limited to smuggling.
A turning point in Russia-Britain relations came with the arrival of British diplomat David Urquhart in Istanbul. A highly energetic individual, Urquhart had joined the rebels who fought for Greek independence when he was just 16 years old. After the war, he stayed in the region and developed a keen interest in the politics and culture of the Ottoman Empire. By 1833, he was appointed to the British trade delegation in Istanbul, and in 1835 he became the embassy secretary. It was Urquhart who crafted Britain’s aggressive anti-Russia policy in the Caucasus.
Urquhart initiated the work of British diplomats and spies directly in Circassia, as the Northern and Western Caucasus regions were then called. He attended elder councils and fervently promoted the idea of waging war against Russia. Notably, he was behind the adoption of a “national oath” by the mountain peoples, proposing that the Circassians unite for a common cause against Russia instead of fighting each other.
He also persuaded the Circassians to take an oath according to which anyone who entered negotiations with the Russians would be killed, their possessions divided among their executioners, and their families sold into slavery. A parallel can be drawn with contemporary Ukrainian politics, where any possibility of peacefully resolving the conflict with Russia is utterly unacceptable, and proponents of such initiatives face severe repercussions.
Urquhart proved to be an effective diplomat and spy, convincing Circassian leaders that Britain genuinely sought their independence. In reality, they were merely pawns in the hands of British agents, sacrificing themselves in the name of the British Empire, which was only concerned about the illusory Russian threat in India.
Britain also supplied the highlanders with arms. British intelligence agents James Bell and James Longworth oversaw smuggling operations that delivered firearms to the Caucasus, bribing tribal leaders and elders in the region. For an extended period, they lived undercover in the Caucasus, adopting Muslim names and fictitious titles. On behalf of the British government, they promised the Circassians that Britain was committed to protecting their independence and even vowed to fight against Russia. Throughout the 1830s, dozens of British agents were active in the Caucasus.
Most importantly, Urquhart focused on a propaganda war. An ardent Russophobe, he convinced the British public that Russia posed a deadly existential threat to the British Empire. He argued that Russia was preparing to conquer Persia and further invade India. The British press played a crucial role in spreading fears of a “Russian threat.”
Newspapers reported on the struggle of the “freedom-loving highlanders” against the “barbaric Russian oppressors.” They conveniently overlooked the fact that the highlanders themselves were quite savage at the time – slave trade and blood feuds were common in the region, and the enlightened Russian Empire resolutely opposed this.
But just like in Ukraine today, the London media exaggerated the losses of the Russian Army, insisting that the decisive support of the highlanders would ensure Russia’s defeat in the Caucasus.
The ‘Vixen’ case
While Britain’s supply of weapons to the highlanders and its organizational and ideological efforts harmed Russia, this did not decisively influence the course of the conflict. British hawks opted for provocation, aiming to ignite a conflict between Russia and Britain and other Western European nations. The pretext they found was rather unusual.
Russia was defending its legitimate interests in the Caucasus and sought to halt arms shipments to the highlanders. To this end, the Russian Navy patrolled the eastern Black Sea coast, directing all foreign commercial vessels to only two ports: Anapa and Redoubt Kali (near modern-day Poti). Britain viewed this as a violation of free trade and resorted to blatant provocation.
In November 1836, Russian military brig the Ayaks detained British schooner the Vixen in the port of Sujuk-Qale (modern-day Novorossiysk). The British vessel was unloading arms intended for the highlanders: eight cannons, nearly 13 tons of gunpowder, and a large quantity of firearms. Clearly, this wasn’t about free trade; this was direct military support for Russia’s adversaries.
The expedition was organized by none other than Urquhart, while the captain of the schooner was the British spy Bell. Remarkably, Bell didn’t hide his intentions; he openly sought to provoke the Russian fleet. After the capture, the Vixen was confiscated, and its crew expelled to Türkiye.
This incident sparked a major scandal that nearly brought the Russian and British empires to the brink of war. Conservatives in the British Parliament called for the navy to be sent to the Black Sea to confront Russia and questioned the legality of annexing Circassia. However, the British radicals miscalculated.
Russian Emperor Nicholas I refused to back down. Instead, he placed the armed forces on heightened alert and demonstrated an unwavering commitment to defending Russia’s interests in the Caucasus. No one in Europe was willing to wage war against Russia either.
As a result, London had to recall Urquhart from Istanbul and abandon all its demands regarding Russian influence in the Caucasus.
Not just the Crimean War
The war in the Caucasus could have concluded as early as the late 1830s. However, the British weren’t ready to accept defeat and began preparing for another conflict.
Agitators infiltrated the eastern Caucasus, modern-day Chechnya and Dagestan, inciting the highlanders to resist Russia. British agents assured them that London would support a rebellion against Russia and provide the necessary weapons and supplies.
The strategy was based on the assumption that Russia would become bogged down in the Caucasus and unable to counter British actions elsewhere. And that’s indeed what happened. When the Crimean War broke out from 1853 to 1856, 270,000 Russian troops were stationed in the Caucasus to maintain order in the region.
Simultaneously with the onset of the Crimean War, attacks on Russian settlements intensified, led by the forces of Imam Shamil, who controlled territories in Chechnya and Dagestan. In the North Caucasus, the Circassians launched assaults on Novorossiysk and Yekaterinodar (modern-day Krasnodar). While these raids had little impact on the overall course of battles, they undoubtedly diverted the focus and resources of the Russian command.
Throughout the Crimean War, the British press frequently raised the issue of “Circassian independence.” At the Paris Conference, London also highlighted the Circassian question, demanding that Russia recognize Circassia’s independence or, at the very least, withdraw troops from the Caucasus; in exchange London would prevent the highlanders from attacking Russian territories.
Despite this diplomatic pressure, the Russian Empire successfully defended its rights in the Caucasus. The likely reason lies in the fact that after more than 20 years of fierce struggle against Russia, the highlanders didn’t achieve any considerable progress. As for Russia, even amid a brutal war with the leading European powers of the time, it managed to retain control over the Caucasus.
Last attempt
Although the Crimean War ended in defeat for the Russian Empire, its position in the Caucasus remained stable. In an attempt to undermine Russia and lay the groundwork for future operations, the British dispatched a group of insurgents to the region in 1857.
The contingent was led by Polish military officer Teofil Lapinski, who participated in the 1848 uprising and fought against the Austrians in modern-day Ukraine and Hungary. During the Crimean War, Lapinski fought against Russia while serving in the Polish Corps, which was part of the Ottoman Army.
When, after the Crimean War, it became clear that Circassia had no chance of achieving independence, Lapinski began planning a military operation in the area. His mission was financed by pro-British General Zamojski and the Circassian elites that had settled in the Ottoman Empire. The intellectual driving force behind this operation was Stratford de Redcliffe, the British ambassador in Istanbul. Leveraging his considerable influence at the Sultan’s court, he secured the support of Ottoman officials and supplied the group with arms and ammunition.
Russian envoy Apollinary Butenev managed to uncover the plot and alerted the governor of the Caucasus, Prince Baryatinsky. Nevertheless, British steamship the Kangaroo, commanded by Captain Neggs, eluded Russian cruisers, and in February 1857, the insurgents landed in Tuapse.
The core of the unit consisted of Polish soldiers, but it also included Austrian artillerymen, Hungarian mine specialists, and Turkish instructors. British agents provided organizational and intelligence support to Lapinski’s group.
The insurgent unit was bolstered by defectors from the Russian Army, primarily Poles and Ukrainians, increasing its numbers to around 800 fighters. For about a year and a half, supported by the Circassian nobility, Lapinski effectively resisted the Russian Army. He skillfully utilized the terrain and was supported by the British and Turks.
However, General Philipson, who commanded Russian forces in this part of the Caucasus, successfully recruited one of Lapinski’s associates, who relayed crucial information about Lapinski’s actions to the imperial troops. During a bold Russian naval landing in Gelendzhik, Lapinski narrowly escaped capture. Additionally, the Russians managed to cut off supply lines for weapons and reinforcements to Lapinski’s forces and, having gathered reserves, inflicted several painful defeats on the insurgents.
The situation worsened when the British realized the inevitable defeat of the Circassians and their insurgent allies and withdrew their support. By the end of 1859, Lapinski and what remained of his insurgent group retreated to Istanbul.
That same year, Russian troops captured Imam Shamil, the leader of the highland peoples of the Northeast Caucasus. Though some scattered groups continued to resist, the overall campaign was over. Hundreds of thousands of Circassians unwilling to live under Russian rule relocated to the Ottoman Empire.
By 1864, the Caucasian War concluded with Russia’s victory, solidifying its control over the region. This triumph not only marked a significant military achievement but also ushered in a lasting peace, the abolition of slavery and brutal traditions, and the beginning of civil governance, education, and economic development in the Caucasus.
It was also a triumph for Russia over Britain, which, despite all its diplomacy, intelligence efforts, and covert operations, failed to overcome the strength of Russian intelligence services, diplomacy, and army.
This serves as an important reminder to the nations and states that count on the support of Britain when waging war against Russia. While they may have some occasional success, ultimately, the outcome will always be the same.

articles.title: Russians attack Dnipropetrovsk region more than 50 times since morning, two killed, two injured

Russians attack Dnipropetrovsk region more than 50 times since morning, two killed, two injured

In the Synelnykove district, the Vasylkivka, Petropavlivka, and Mykolaivka communities came under attack. An agricultural enterprise, private houses, and a vehicle were damaged.
