articles.title: Colombia grapples with rebuilding a shattered nation after a deadly earthquake
articles.body:
Hope reborn in Colombia as signs of life emerge under earthquake debris
CALI, Colombia (AP) — Rescuers reported apparent signs of life under the rubble in two of the Colombian cities hit hardest by a massive earthquake, rekindling hopes Friday that more people could be found alive.
Search and rescue teams from Venezuela, Argentina and Israel joined the search for survivors following the 7.4 magnitude quake that struck the South American nation on Monday, killing at least 287 people. At 96 hours since the temblor hit, the window for survival was narrowing Friday afternoon.
The mayor of Pereira, Mauricio Salazar, told radio station FM on Friday that “contact was made with a woman who was asking for help amid the rubble” of a collapsed hotel at around 4 a.m. He suggested other people may have survived but were still trapped.
Authorities in Cali also reported apparent signs of life, saying at least three people were trapped under collapsed buildings. The search and rescue effort has been extended through Saturday.
Residents who lost their homes must start over again
With the overall search for survivors winding down, Colombia faced another challenge: rebuilding a nation shattered by a disaster that affected more than 100,000 people.
Tens of thousands of houses were damaged or destroyed, according to the government. Authorities have also reported damage to thousands of schools, medical facilities and community centers in more than 400 cities.
“There is no place to live, we lost everything,” Ebert Jonathan Morales, 38, said Friday in a shelter in Cali.
Morales is one of the 102,263 people whose lives were upended by the quake. The government says nearly 4,000 people were injured and hundreds remain missing. Private groups estimate the number of missing is in the thousands.
Morales said he, his wife and four children are trying to rebuild from scratch.
“The earthquake destroyed several neighborhoods in the city. Many houses were damaged, and buildings collapsed,” he said. “We are going to stay here until the government gives us some help, some support.”
The government focuses on providing shelter
The devastation has tested Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella, who was inaugurated just days before the earthquake shook the country’s west. De la Espriella acknowledged Thursday night that “the situation is complex” and announced a plan to partner with private companies to rebuild, as well as subsidies for families who are homeless.
“We will not overcome this tragedy alone as a government,” he said. “We need the private sector to rebuild Colombia together.”
Monday’s earthquake was the most powerful to hit Colombia this century. Government aid has yet to arrive in some areas, where many people are relying on volunteers and neighbors for help.
“A neighbor is giving me shelter,” Olga Castro, a mother of five in Cali, said. “At least we survived, but right now we are practically on the street because we don’t have a home anymore.”
De la Espriella said national and international funds raised in response to the disaster will focus on the reconstruction of hospitals, schools, homes, roads and airports.
Rebuilding the country requires a “serious technical assessment” to determine which buildings can be used, which can be repaired and which must be demolished and rebuilt, said Yezid Alvarado Vargas, a professor in construction engineering at Javeriana University, in Bogota, Colombia.
“Before even discussing reconstruction, we must guarantee temporary housing, food, healthcare, continuity of basic services and economic support for families who lost their homes or livelihoods,” Alvarado said.
In Bogota, Colombia’s capital, around 500 volunteers gathered at a reception center to sort food, toiletries and pet food before distributing the supplies in the most affected areas. From youngsters to the elderly, everyone diligently participated in the challenging relief efforts.
“We all have to help. Today is for you, tomorrow might be for me,” volunteer Jorge Muñoz, 85, said. One of the oldest helpers at Bogota’s Vive Claro aid collection, Muñoz has witnessed the devastation caused by other earthquakes, including one in 1999 that killed more than 1,180 people.
National and international aid keeps coming
Authorities have converted schools, parks and public buildings into shelters, providing tents, mattresses and food to the displaced. In other hard-hit cities, residents improvised shelters in the streets, while hundreds of volunteers rush to help those in need in hard-to-reach areas.
“These are isolated, neglected territories, historically lacking in institutional support, already plagued by violence, and now they are hit by an earthquake of this magnitude,” said María Mercedes Liévano, director of Save the Children in Colombia.
“It’s a crisis on top of a crisis, leaving the population in a situation of extreme vulnerability,” she added, citing communities including Buenaventura, the country’s main port, and Choco, the earthquake’s epicenter.
Many buildings in Pereira have limited or no access to electricity and water, and volunteers have been delivering hygiene kits to displaced families in the city’s shelters, said Pamela Londoño, a technical adviser with Project HOPE. Of the five or six shelters in the city, at least one is already full and no longer accepting new residents. The nonprofit is also assessing medical supply needs.
Other areas are also suffering, such as the town of Roldanillo, where approximately 60% of residents do not have access to clean water.
“The main concern is the lack of basic services for multiple communities,” Londoño said. “This is a really critical situation.”
De la Espriella visited several cities to track relief efforts and aid distribution, including Quibdo, in the Choco region, and Pereira. Authorities are still waiting for tons of supplies and humanitarian aid from countries that have pledged their support, including Peru, China, the United States and the United Arab Emirates.
“My heart, my strength and my spirit are with all the victims and with all these territories that have been forgotten and now devastated by nature,” he said. “We must rebuild them. There is a great task ahead and I am committed to it.”
The Trump administration announced Friday an additional $11 million in humanitarian aid — including food, health, protection and shelter assistance — bringing the total U.S. assistance following the earthquake to $26.5 million.
The U.S. “continues to coordinate with Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella and the Colombian government to assess and respond to earthquake-related needs,” the State Department said in a statement.
___
Suarez reported from Bogota, Colombia and Batschke reported from Santiago, Chile.

articles.title: Russia’s current account surplus up to $21 bln in Q2 2026 — Central Bank
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 14. /TASS/. Russia’s current account surplus rose to $21 bln in the second quarter of 2026 from $2 bln in the same period of 2025, according to documents published on the Central Bank’s website.
"Current account surplus increased to $21 bln in the second quarter of 2026 ($2 bln in the second quarter of 2025; $13 bln in the first quarter of 2026). The trend was driven primarily by the growth in the value of exports of goods," documents said.
Foreign trade surplus increased to $38 bln due to a more significant rise in the export of goods compared to imports.
"The growth in service exports is primarily driven by an increase in the value of transport services provided to non-residents and rising expenditures by foreigners during their visits to the Russian Federation," according to documents.

articles.title: Canadian plasma clinics pause collections after deaths of two donors
articles.body:
A chain of private plasma donation clinics in Canada has said it is pausing collections after the deaths of two donors and a new government investigation into potential unsafe practices.
Grifols, a Spanish healthcare company which runs 17 clinics in Canada and is the country’s only private clinic for plasma donation, said it informed Health Canada of its decision to temporarily pause collections on Wednesday.
On the same day, the agency had issued a formal notice of non-compliance for failure to follow blood regulations, a senior official told the Globe and Mail newspaper.
The two deaths occurred after plasma donations in October 2025 and January 2026, Health Canada said in March of this year. The donors, both of whom were in the province of Manitoba, went into “distress” while donating, people familiar with the cases said.
Though Health Canada did not release the identities of the donors, friends said one was Rodiyat Alabede, 22, an international student and aspiring social worker who donated plasma in Winnipeg on 25 October.
Patient advocates reported at the end of May that there were concerns about whether Alabede had been properly screened.
“They had staff taking plasma from donors who did not know how to extract plasma in a safe manner,” alleged Kat Lanteigne, a safe blood campaigner who represents Alabede’s family.
“The [failures] were so egregious that … now we have more questions than answers,” she said in May.
An autopsy showed Alabede died of cardiac arrest shortly after donating. Health Canada reported that it found “no link” between Alabede’s death and plasma donation.
Patient advocates have called for a new inquest into her death, however, after alleging that “significant medical discrepancies” had been uncovered between her autopsy, which was completed two days after her death, and the medical summary drafted by Health Canada published on 27 March of this year.
The Guardian has also seen Health Canada inspection reports from May that found deficiencies at Grifols clinics, including inadequate training for staff, failures in standard operating procedures, poor record-keeping and a failure by Grifols to remedy past issues.
The Health Canada report also found that staff did not stop plasma collection when alarms went off, and described the company’s reporting as “incomplete” and “inaccurate”.
Prior to the newly announced pause, donations were permitted at Grifols twice a week. The company paid donors up to C$100 (£55) for each donation.
Plasma is a pale yellow, protein-rich liquid in blood that assists in moving red and white blood cells, along with platelets, through blood vessels, according to Canadian Blood Services, the non-profit that operates Canada’s national blood supply.
Plasma also helps prevent excessive bleeding and is used to create medications for a variety of conditions including haemophilia, liver disease and various cancers.
The plasma donation process differs from donating blood overall. A medical device called an apheresis machine draws the blood, separates it into individual parts, collects the components needed and then returns the remaining blood back into the body, according to Canadian Blood Services. The process takes about 90 minutes, whereas a general blood draw takes about 10.
In Canada, provinces and territories decide whether paid plasma clinics are permitted. British Columbia and Quebec do not allow the practice, for example, but Manitoba, where the deaths occurred, does not prohibit companies from paying donors for plasma.
Grifols said it decided to pause collection “proactively and voluntarily” due to what it deemed “unfounded attention”. It said the pause would allow it to work with Health Canada and Canadian Blood Services.
The company has denied the two deaths were connected to plasma donation.
On Friday, Health Canada said it found “various deficiencies” specifically at the Taylor Avenue Grifols location in Winnipeg. A spokesperson for that location said it was working closely with the company so that it could return to operations.
“Canadians can be assured that this decision will have no impact on the safety and security of Canada’s blood and plasma supply,” Grifols said.

articles.title: DTEK Grids connects 2,700 household solar stations, 14 distributed generation facilities in H1 2026
articles.body:
More than 2,700 green and distributed generation facilities were connected in January-June 2026 to the power grids of distribution system operators (DSOs) of DTEK Grids in the city of Kyiv, the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk and Odesa regions, the operating holding company said Friday.
"Energy companies are modernizing the grids, ensuring the integration of green and distributed generation and, accordingly, strengthening the energy resilience of the regions," DTEK said.
As is traditionally the case, solar generation accounts for the largest number of new facilities. During the first half of the year, household customers connected 2,728 solar power plants, while legal entities connected another 11 SPPs. At the same time, businesses continue to develop distributed generation: 14 gas-piston, gas-turbine and cogeneration units, as well as five energy storage systems, were connected to the grids.
This year, DTEK Grids DSOs also connected a hybrid system for the first time, combining a solar power plant with a cogeneration unit. According to the company, such solutions make it possible to combine different generation sources depending on weather conditions and other factors, thereby increasing the energy resilience of the system's owner.
"In six months of this year, the number of green and distributed generation facilities connected to our grids has already exceeded the figure for the entire year of 2024 and outpaced the pace of connections in 2025. This demonstrates growing customer interest in ensuring their own energy resilience," DTEK Grids CEO Alina Bondarenko said.
In addition, during the first half of the year, 106 household customers and 109 legal-entity customers obtained active consumer status.
Under the Procedure for the Sale and Accounting of Electricity, an active consumer is the owner of a generating facility connected to the grid who may sell surplus electricity generated to an electricity supplier under the feed-in tariff or through the self-generation mechanism.
DTEK Grids develops the electricity distribution business and operates power grids in Kyiv, the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk and Odesa regions. The holding's companies serve 5.1 million households and 150,000 businesses.

articles.title: Russia becomes second-largest LNG supplier to EU by value in June, trailing only US
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 14. /TASS/. Russia ranked second after the US in June in terms of the value of liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies to the European Union, with a 24.1% market share, according to TASS calculations based on Eurostat data.
The EU purchased approximately €809 million worth of LNG from Russia, representing a 57% increase year-on-year. Belgium was the largest LNG importer with 268 mln euros, the highest figure since July 2025, followed by France (€258 million), and Spain (€201 million). Belgium also became the leading buyer of Russian gas in Europe in the reporting period, surpassing France and Hungary.
The EU also imported €542 million worth of Russian pipeline gas in June.
Russian pipeline gas accounted for 12.5% of the total value of the EU’s pipeline gas imports in June. Norway ranked first with 33.3%, followed by Algeria with 23.6%, and the UK with 18.8%.
The US held the top spot with its LNG supplies, accounting for 54.3% of the market and €1.83 billion.
In the first half of the year, Europe’s total purchases of Russian LNG reached €4.5 billion. Earlier, TASS reported, citing calculations based on data from the European think tank Bruegel, that Russian LNG deliveries to the EU in June totaled 2.17 billion cubic meters, an increase of 10%.
The EU’s total purchases of Russian gas in January-June decreased by 3.4% year-on-year to €7.4 billion.
EU ban on Russian gas
On January 26, the EU Council finalized a complete ban on Russian LNG supplies to the EU effective January 1, 2027, and on pipeline gas from September 30, 2027. The ban on LNG imports under short-term contracts came into effect on April 25, 2026, while short-term pipeline gas contracts were set to expire by June 17, 2026.
Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin stated that, given the EU's intention to completely phase out Russian gas, Russia could prematurely exit the European market on its own initiative and redirect supplies to other, more interested buyers. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak announced that Russian companies would soon redirect a portion of LNG supplies from Europe to friendly nations, including China, India, Thailand, and the Philippines, without waiting for further EU restrictions.
According to TASS calculations, Russia was the second-largest exporter of LNG to the EU by value in 2025, behind the US. Its share stood at 16.1% (or 16.2% of the combined value of LNG and pipeline gas purchases). In terms of volume, Russia accounted for roughly 14% of the EU's LNG imports (12.1% of total gas supplies, including pipeline gas). Russia's total supplies to Europe last year amounted to 38 billion cubic meters, with LNG accounting for just over 20 billion cubic meters.

articles.title: US backs Japanese sovereignty over disputed islands after Putin visit
articles.body:
The US ambassador said Washington was "unwavering" in recognising Japanese sovereignty, after Putin's visit to the four islands occupied by the Soviet Union in 1945 prompted Japan to summon Moscow's ambassador and consider tightening sanctions against Russia.
The United States has backed Japan's sovereignty over four islands controlled by Russia after Vladimir Putin became the first Russian president in 15 years to visit the disputed territory, prompting Tokyo to summon Moscow's ambassador and describe the trip as "absolutely unacceptable."
"The United States remains unwavering in its support of its most important ally and in its recognition of Japanese sovereignty over the Northern Territories," the US ambassador to Tokyo George Glass said on X.
"At a time when the US-Japan alliance is dedicated to cultivating prosperity across the Indo-Pacific, we strongly oppose any action that undermines its peace and stability," Glass added.
Russian-Japanese relations have long been dogged by the four southernmost islands in a volcanic chain off the coast of Hokkaido seized by the Soviet Union following an invasion in August 1945, in the final days of World War II.
Moscow broke its formal neutrality with Japan just days before the invasion.
The Japanese government maintains that the four islands and groups of islets that make up the Northern Territories — Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and Habomai — are part of its territory that the Soviets illegally occupied and Russia has continued to occupy since the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.
The dispute has kept the two countries from signing a peace treaty that would formally end their hostilities. They terminated the state of war in 1956.
Moscow has reinforced its military presence on the islands as recently as December 2021, when it deployed Bastion coastal defence missile systems on an uninhabited volcanic island in the middle of the chain.
The island hosted a Japanese army base prior to the Soviet occupation. A Soviet base there was shut down amid funding shortages in the wake of the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Moscow previously deployed Bal and Bastion missile systems on two of the four southernmost islands in 2016.
In the following years, Moscow further beefed up its arsenal on the islands by sending top-of-the-line air defence missile systems, setting up an air base on Etorofu Island, and deploying fighter jets.
The sparsely inhabited islands are strategically significant to the Kremlin as they sit at the entrance to the Sea of Okhotsk and give Russia's Pacific Fleet access to the open Pacific without passing through Japanese-controlled waters.
Putin's visit was the first by a Russian president since Dmitry Medvedev in 2010.
'Absolutely unacceptable'
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told reporters "the Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan's territory, both historically and under international law."
Putin's visit "offends the sentiments of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable," she added.
Japan's Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said his country “strongly protests” Putin's visit to the largest of the islands, Etorofu.
“The Northern Territories, including Etorofu Island, are Japan’s inherent territory both historically and from the perspective of international law,” Motegi said in a statement.
He summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to the ministry in Tokyo and lodged a strong protest over the visit, requesting that he "promptly report the message back to Moscow,” the minister told reporters afterwards.
Russia's embassy in Japan said the ambassador reiterated Moscow's claim that the islands are part of Russia and that Putin's trip there was not "a matter for discussion with foreign states".
The Kremlin boasted about the visit by posting a video of Putin on one of the four main islands. Russian state-run media said he had visited a fish-processing plant and showed him trying local caviar.
Takaichi said the visit was a further blow to the already-strained ties between the two countries over Ukraine, and that Moscow should understand the consequences.
Japan imposed sanctions on Russia after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
It also placed export controls on technology with military applications and provided financial support to Ukraine. Russia responded by designating Japan an "unfriendly state".
Tokyo is now considering strengthening those sanctions as part of its countermeasures in response to Putin's trip.
“We must say this visit has further hardened Japanese public sentiment toward Russia and has made it more difficult to restore bilateral relations in the medium to long term,” she said.
“We hope the Russian side fully understands the seriousness of this.”

articles.title: Ukraine hits back at Russia's 'you'll be frozen' social media taunt
articles.body:
An image posted on social media by the Russian Defense Ministry
Ukraine and Russia exchanged fire on social media on Aug. 14, as Kyiv responded to a cynical post from the Kremlin's Defense Ministry that taunted Ukrainian civilians ahead of winter.
In a post on Telegram, the Defense Ministry displayed an image of three Shahed-type drones with the caption: "Like snow on your head." Below the image, the post read: "In winter you will be 'frozen.'"
Russia's Defense Ministry posted another threat to Ukraine saying "you'll get a freeze this winter," with an image of Shaheds captioned "like snow on your head." pic.twitter.com/4ZsCifhv5p
The post references Russia's previous attempts to destroy civilian power generation and heating infrastructure in Ukraine, which aimed to make major cities such as the capital Kyiv uninhabitable, particularly over last winter.
International humanitarian law labels such deliberate strikes against civilian infrastructure as war crimes. The post had nearly 22,000 positive reactions from Telegram users.
In response, the Strategic Communications Department of the Ukrainian Armed Forces posted an image of a burning Russian oil refinery, with the caption, "Let's warm up by the fire of Russian refineries," referencing Ukraine's ongoing deep-strike campaign against Russia's oil industry.
Ukraine's StratCom responded to Russia's Defense Ministry threat about "winter freeze" for Ukraine by saying they'll "warm up by the fires of Russian oil refineries." https://t.co/fKEoSpIgoApic.twitter.com/Zj3QPRRwiJ
Ukraine's campaign has seen a succession of dramatic drone and missile strikes against Russian oil refineries and storage depots.
The campaign severely damaged Russia's ability to both refine and export oil products, and led to significant shortages across the country.
The Ukrainian arms company Fire Point, whose missiles and drones have played a significant role in Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries and logistics infrastructure, also got in on the social media action.
Rushton is a British journalist and security and foreign policy analyst based in Kyiv. He has covered Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine since February 2022, writing about every aspect of the conflict. His work has appeared in Yahoo News, New Lines Magazine, and The Telegraph, amongst others.
Ukrainian forces struck Russia's Savasleyka military airbase, which stores Mig-31 fighter jets capable of launching Kinzhal ballistic missiles, monitoring channels reported on Aug. 15.
"The illegal export of Ukrainian grain from the temporarily occupied territories must have consequences for everyone involved: from companies and owners to captains and vessels," Sanctions Commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said.
The Romanian Defense Ministry said on Aug. 14 that there is no evidence the population faces "increased risk," despite documenting four incidents involving drone wreckage in a single day.
At least 437 civilians in Ukraine were killed and 2,610 injured in July alone, a 30% increase from June. More civilians were killed or injured in July than any month since March 2022.
"The president has maximally disappointed me with his silence, especially considering that the lack of communication has effectively become the trigger for these protests," Dmytro Koziatynskyi, a war veteran and one of the protest organizers, said on social media.
The Ukrainian arms company Fire Point, whose missiles and drones have played a significant role in Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries and logistics infrastructure, also got in on the social media action.
Albert Vasiliev, also known as Kyivstoner, is a blogger, actor, rapper, and a former member of the Griby band. Russia previously accused him of orchestrating a drone attack in Moscow Oblast in cooperation with Ukrainian security services, an allegation he denied.
The attack damaged at least one warehouse at the TIS terminal in Ukraine's Pivdennyi (Southern) Port complex, an agriculture-sector executive with knowledge of the matter told the Kyiv Independent under the condition of anonymity.
This story exists because readers chose to back it. Behind it is a newsroom that will not look away — and a community of people who make that possible. It's thanks to 33,000 members that our reporting stays free for everyone to read, and we can continue our reporting. Will you be one of them?

articles.title: More than 1,600 civilians get injured by Russian mines since beginning of full-scale invasion
articles.body:
More than 1,600 civilians get injured by Russian mines since beginning of full-scale invasion
According to Ukrinform, the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine stated this on its website.
Information about such incidents is processed by the Main Directorate for Mine Action, Civil Protection and Environmental Safety and entered into the relevant information management system.
This allows, among other things, victims to receive financial compensation from international organizations.
Thus, from 2023 to 2026, 185 victims of mine-related incidents received assistance from international organizations totaling more than UAH 3.4 million.
The assistance covers medical treatment and rehabilitation costs, as well as equipment enabling people with mine-related injuries to study and work remotely.
Compensation payments are made using information from the database of the National Mine Action Authority.
The Main Directorate for Mine Action, Civil Protection and Environmental Safety, acting as the secretariat of the National Mine Action Authority, collects, analyzes, and verifies data on such incidents and victims before entering it into the mine-action information management system.
The information is provided by regional military administrations, regional units of the State Emergency Service, and the National Police.
This work is carried out as part of Ukraine’s obligations under Protocol II and Protocol V of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), which prohibits or restricts the use of certain conventional weapons that may be considered excessively injurious or indiscriminate.
Ukrainian law enforcement agencies open criminal proceedings for violations by the Russian Federation of the rules and customs of warfare in connection with every incident in which Ukrainian civilians are killed or injured by mines laid by Russian forces.
The database and interactive map help government and humanitarian organizations in dangerous regions inform the public about the risks associated with explosive objects and provide assistance to victims of mine-related injuries.
As Ukrinform reported, Ministry of Defense demining units cleared 923 hectares of territory liberated from Russian forces in July.

articles.title: The rise of 'conscious' festivals, where music, spirituality and nature meet
articles.body:
Thousands of people from across Europe and beyond have travelled to the UK to experience the Medicine Festival, where music, spirituality, nature and traditional ceremonies come together.
The Medicine Festival brings together more than 10,000 people in the United Kingdom for four days of music, ceremony, spirituality and environmental activism.
The festival in Berkshire reflects a growing interest in alternative ways of connecting with oneself, others and nature.
The sixth edition of the festival features a full programme of events, including concerts, yoga classes, ways of exploring movement and spiritual awareness and traditional ceremonies.
Many Europeans have crossed the border to attend. Ayla, from the Netherlands has come to the festival for the first time.
“What I like about Medicine is the sharing of wisdoms. I hope I get out of here inspired, rested and motivated as well," she told Euronews.
In Europe and around the world, there is a growing interest in "conscious festivals" such as Medicine, which encourage people to explore their inner self, reconnect with nature and create a sense of community.
“We see ourselves as part of nature," explains Joshua Dugdale, Co-Founder of the Festival.
“We promote the medicine of dance, the medicine of music, the medicine of community, but also seeing people who have maybe a different world view and engaging with that, learning new skills, understanding new ways of seeing the world, we would call it a sacred festival”.
To date, the Medicine Festival has donated over one hundred thousand euros to support the environment and indigenous communities.

articles.title: Report: US presses Netanyahu to condemn settlers besieging Palestinian homes in West Bank
articles.body:
Report: US presses Netanyahu to condemn settlers besieging Palestinian homes in West Bank
Washington stepped up pressure after learning a Palestinian-American home was among those targeted in Qusra, according to US and Israeli officials
The United States is pressing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly condemn settlers accused of besieging Palestinian homes in the West Bank village of Qusra, Reuters reported Friday, citing US and Israeli officials.
The pressure followed reports that settlers had cut water and electricity to several homes and blocked residents from entering or leaving. One of the homes belongs to a Palestinian-American, according to Reuters.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee on Thursday condemned those involved as “Israeli terrorists,” subsequently clarifying that he words were aimed at a "violent minority" of West Bank settlers.

articles.title: French teen social media ban struck down by top constitutional authority
articles.body:
France's social media ban for children under 15 struck down by top constitutional authority
France's top constitutional authority on Friday struck down a ban on social media access for children under 15, dealing a blow to the legislation championed by President Emmanuel Macron.
The Constitutional Council found that Article 1 of the legislation "constitutes an infringement that is neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate" to the freedom of expression and communication of those under 15.
In its ruling, the Constitutional Council also expressed concern about the potential impact on privacy of introducing an age-verification system for all users.
The law, which was due to take effect on Sept. 1, would have barred younger users from social networks such as TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram, among other restrictions.
The French government had promoted the ban as a way to better protect young people from the harmful effects associated with social media platforms, including anxiety, depression, sleep disorders and online harassment.
Macron had in July thanked members of Parliament for backing the legislation and pledged to enforce it by September.
After the ruling, the Elysee Palace said Macron had tasked Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu with working on a new "legally robust draft" of the legislation.
Lecornu will have to work "as quickly as possible" on a draft that takes into account both the Constitutional Council's ruling and the European regulatory framework, the palace said.
The presidency said Macron's determination to see the reform implemented remained undiminished.
Macron has made online child safety a defining issue of the final years of his presidency, and a new ban could be one of the last major domestic reforms he ushers through. Macron will mark a decade in office next year, and he cannot run again in April's national election as, like the U.S., France has a two consecutive term limit for its presidents.
Following Friday's ruling, Macron's former prime minister, Gabriel Attal, who backed the proposal, expressed his disappointment.
"We take note of it and respect this decision, which applies to everyone," he said on social media, vowing to continue fighting against what he described as "a deadly poison for our children."
The Constitutional Council did not rule on a separate provision banning mobile phone use in high schools starting Sept. 1. Students are already prohibited from having phones in French elementary and middle schools.
A growing number of countries are taking steps to restrict social media access amid increasing warnings over its harmful effects on children.

articles.title: Govt scraps 12-minute ad cap for TV channel
articles.body:
NEW DELHI: Television channels will no longer be restricted to 12 minutes of advertisements per hour, with the government deciding to scrap the two-decade-old cap in a move it says will put traditional broadcasters on a more level footing with digital platforms.The restriction, introduced in 2006 under the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994, will cease to apply once the amended rules are notified in the Gazette, the information and broadcasting ministry said.The government has argued that the television landscape has changed substantially since the cap was imposed. India had only 62 TV channels in 2006, compared with more than 900 now. Cable television, then the dominant distribution platform, was largely analog and offered limited capacity and consumer choice.With digitisation, platforms including cable TV, direct-to-home, HITS and IPTV can now carry 300 to 500 channels or more, significantly expanding viewer choice and competition, the ministry said.The decision could give broadcasters greater flexibility to determine advertising inventory, an important consideration for an industry that remains heavily dependent on advertising revenue across both pay and free-to-air channels.
The ministry also cited the growing competition television faces from digital media, where there is no comparable statutory cap on advertising duration.It said the existing restriction had created a “non-level playing field” for conventional television broadcasters and that removing it would promote “fair competition” and ease of doing business.The change, however, will become operational only from the date the amendment to the Cable Television Networks Rules is formally notified.

articles.title: Russian top diplomat’s takes on why Ukraine conflict cannot be halted along contact line
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 14. /TASS/. The Ukraine conflict cannot stop along the line of contact as this would erase the feat of the fathers and grandfathers who defeated Nazism, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in an interview with Vesti.
He said Russian President Vladimir Putin is ready to again meet with US President Donald Trump’s Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and businessman Jared Kushner. The question is what proposals they would bring to the Kremlin.
Lavrov also said Moscow had asked the US State Department to comment on reports of Washington’s involvement in strikes by the Kiev regime on civilian targets deep within Russian territory.
TASS has compiled the foreign minister’s key remarks.
Witkoff and Kushner’s visit
Putin is ready to meet Witkoff and Kushner again. The question is what proposals they would bring to the Kremlin: "If they have been given such trust then they have influence on Trump and he trusts them. We are not refusing to talk to them. If they come they know that Russian President Vladimir Putin is ready to meet them again. The question is what they will come with."
Kiev’s terrorist attacks
The Kiev regime "boasts proudly" about terrorist attacks against Russian civilians: "After each such terrorist attack, regime representatives proudly boast on social media and other platforms about how 'great' the strikes were, hitting a beach, a dormitory for future teachers and other purely civilian facilities."
Ways to settle the Ukraine conflict
The conflict in Ukraine cannot be halted along the line of contact as this would "erase the feat of our fathers and grandfathers" who defeated Nazism: "This cannot be considered. It is not about anyone’s comfort today. Our people are suffering and dying in these terrorist attacks. It is about our responsibility for Russia’s thousand-year history."
Moscow will not stoop to Kiev’s methods but will take much tougher measures to destroy everything that fuels the Ukrainian military machine from the West: "We will not stoop to Kiev’s methods, but we will toughen our own measures to dismantle everything the West uses to sustain its military machine. We are already doing so, and they are beginning to feel the pressure."
More and more voices from across the region are "calling for an immediate halt": "That will not be an option. We need to stop only once there is a long-term, reliable and sustainable settlement."
Resurgence of Nazism in Europe
"Metastases of Nazism" are appearing in German society under Chancellor Friedrich Merz who openly speaks of the need to make Germany Europe’s leading military power again: "Does he understand what the word 'again’ means in this case? I am not sure."
The European Union has portrayed itself as the "Fourth Reich" and is blackmailing Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic by exploiting his commitment to European integration: "The pressure is brazen and outrageous. They act as if they are already the 'Fourth Reich.'"
US role in the Ukrainian conflict
Moscow has asked the US State Department to comment on reports of Washington’s involvement in Kiev regime strikes on civilian targets deep inside Russian territory: "We sent a number of questions to the State Department asking it to comment including on intelligence data and on the fact that the US is much more strongly involved in organizing and carrying out strikes deep inside the Russian Federation against civilian targets. We will await a response."
Moscow "is not giving ultimatums" to Washington.
The West’s silence
The public silence of countries whose interests were affected by Kiev regime attacks on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) is telling: "When we asked if they would tolerate this, they (the countries whose interests were affected - TASS) said no and said they were sending signals to Kiev. Apparently, US Vice President JD Vance sent a signal to Vladimir Zelensky over the Caspian Pipeline Consortium. The Turkish officials also told us they had urged the Ukrainians not to target the consortium. But everyone is silent publicly. That is telling."
In response to these appeals the Zelensky regime did not promise to stop the attacks: "He promised to stop attacks on vessels that have nothing to do with the Russian Federation. Apparently, that explanation was considered acceptable."
Turkey’s interest in Black Sea stability
Turkey is genuinely interested in ensuring stability in the Black Sea: "Turkey wants to be a NATO member with the bloc’s largest army and maintain ties with the European Union. At the same time, deep down Ankara understands that it will never be admitted to the EU. It wants good relations with Russia because we have many economic projects and much in common in our history: the Caucasus and the Black Sea. Turkey is genuinely interested in keeping the Black Sea stable."
Relations with Serbia
EU representatives promise Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic that they will reduce his country’s long wait to join the European Union and speed up accession talks in return for recognizing Kosovo’s independence and joining sanctions against Russia: "Vucic has bravely withstood this pressure for years."
Russia would like to hear Serbia’s reaction to comments by Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung correspondent Michael Martens about the killing of Russians: "I saw that Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic was simply stunned. Of course, we would like to hear some reaction from our Serbian friends given their enormous contribution to the victory over Nazism."

articles.title: 'Surrounded': Israel's new West Bank settlements bring chaos to Palestinians
articles.body:
‘We never leave’: Palestinians besieged in West Bank fear Israeli settlers will seize their homes
For nearly a week, Israeli settlers have been surrounding homes in the West bank village of Qusra in a coordinated offensive to force Palestinian residents from their homes in order to seize new land.
Palestinian Amin Rahal and his three brothers haven't gone to work in weeks, instead taking turns guarding what remains of their land atop a West Bank hill from incursions by nearby settlers.
"We never leave the place unless we have two people here," says Rahal, a 31-year-old father of three, pointing to the roof of a settler's newly installed prefabricated home 100 metres from his house.
"They've stolen hens, land with olive trees, damaged the sage bush in our backyard with their ATVs, brought their sheep into our courtyard, and more," he told AFP.
Last week, settlers from the newly inaugurated Israeli settlement of Emek Dotan just below his home put up a rope across his land and forbade him and his family from crossing it.
A chicken farm and many olive trees stand on the other side of the rope and are now lost to the Rahal family under threat of violence.
Read moreMideast live: Israeli minister calls for police to replace military in handling West Bank settlers
"Our fear is that they will attack the children, burn one of the houses, attack us at night and break into the houses," as has happened in other West Bank villages where settlers have moved in, he said.
Across the West Bank, such accounts have become common, with the UN's Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs reporting an average of six incidents per day involving West Bank settlers in 2026.
These include theft, vandalism, arson, beatings and sometimes murder, with Palestinians complaining that most crimes against them go unpunished.
'Cancel Oslo'
The north of the West Bank, with its many Palestinian communities and few settlers, had been relatively spared from the tensions.
Under former Israeli prime minister Ariel Sharon's 2005 disengagement plan, four isolated settlements – Homesh, Sa-Nur, Ganim and Kadim – were evacuated to make a contiguous Palestinian space within the West Bank.
But under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's current government, the most right-wing in Israel's history, the abandoned sites – long a sore point for the settler movement – have been reinvested one by one in 2026.
A plan approved in December legalised 17 more settlements in the northern West Bank, with the specific intent of connecting them all, in another affront to the Oslo Accords reached during the 1990s peace process.
While all settlements on occupied territory are illegal under international law, the Oslo Accords allowed Israel to keep building settlements and demolish Palestinian buildings, but only in Area C – the 60 percent of the West Bank under Israeli control.
The agreement is viewed as an outdated relic by Israel's far-right, which wants to build settlements across all the West Bank.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, himself a settler, has on various occasions made calls to "cancel Oslo".
Excluding Israeli-annexed east Jerusalem, 500,000 settlers now live in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, as well as 3 million Palestinians.
Palestinians around Jenin are worried many red lines have been crossed.
Inside Jenin itself, the largest city in that part of the north, a military base was established in Area A, the part of the West Bank supposed to be under Palestinian control.
Read moreIsraeli settlers seize Palestinian water source in occupied West Bank to create recreational pool
With each settlement come demolitions, but Palestinians had until now assumed Areas A and B – the latter of which is under Israeli military control but Palestinian civil control – to be relatively safe. Not anymore.
In August, Israeli forces demolished several shops within 30 metres of a road leading to Ganim and Kadim, where settler caravans reminiscent of an American trailer park were newly connected to the electric grid and received their first occupants.
"They came to us directly and gave us an official order to evacuate the shop immediately, followed directly by its demolition," said Bara al-Damaj, owner of a stone products store that was torn down.
"In a moment, they destroyed our dreams," he continued, adding he had seen an increased military presence as a result of another new military base built at the entrance of Ganim.
'Surrounded'
Mohammed, whose nearby home escaped demolition, still fears what the increased settler presence will bring in the future.
Declining to share his last name for security reasons, Mohammed said his son was detained and beaten by the army recently while walking in their field, and they cannot access their second field on the other side of the new settler road.
Army bulldozers blocked most agricultural roads with rubble, leading residents to fear being cut off and isolated.

In the village of Deir Abu Deif, losing access to the road means losing access to the city of Jenin.
"The situation is extremely frightening. We're surrounded from every direction," said Faij Rawajbi, whose produce store near the settler road was demolished.
Rawajbi, 38, complained that armed settlement security teams began harassing residents, conducting ID checks as if they were official authorities.
"This white van terrorises us and the entire eastern area" of Jenin, he told AFP as the vehicle drove by.
"Everything here has become settlements. They have turned our lives upside down."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Russian Mercenary Targets Ukrainian Artist in Warsaw
articles.body:
A mercenary accused of working on behalf of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) was preparing to assassinate Ukrainian rapper and video blogger Slevin Dadyan, known by his stage name Kyivstoner, in Warsaw, Poland.
The suspect, a 29-year-old man from the Donbas in Ukraine - partly occupied by Russia – was arrested by the police on Aug. 7, near Warsaw’s Wołoska Street. According to the Polish radio station RMF24, Warsaw police worked with Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) to uncover and halt the plot.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Unfortunately, we must proceed from the assumption that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s regime will attempt to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons, in various parts of the world,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday, Aug. 13.
Targeted over alleged drone smuggling
Slevin Dadyan, whose real name is Albert Vasilyev, was accused by the FSB of overseeing the logistics of a drone smuggling plot that targeted a defense enterprise in the Moscow region.
According to The Moscow Times citing the FSB, the plot involved a network of recruited operatives, including a former Wagner mercenary and Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), to smuggle 35 first-person-view drones into Russia.
Vasilyev denied the allegations on social media. “I’m chilling and playing Dota,” he wrote in an Instagram post. “What organization are you talking about?”
Zelensky Struggles to Find Ukraine’s Next Envoy to Trump
The drones were allegedly smuggled through Slovakia, Poland and Belarus into the Moscow region, prompting the FSB to put the artist on its list of individuals involved in “extremist” and “terrorist” activities.
According to Russian authorities cited by The Moscow Times, the explosives were stored in a rented warehouse which stored building materials near the target site.
A warehouse tenant, who was also accused by the FSB of being recruited by Ukraine for payment, was killed during an attempted arrest.
Victim’s identity revealed a day later
According to Tusk on Thursday, the attack marks “the first such situation in which someone on behalf of Russia decides to attack an American citizen in another NATO country, specifically on the territory of Poland.”
He added that he is not “authorized to disclose names.”
RMF24 confirmed the victim’s identity on Friday.
Vasilyev built his online following through comedic sketch videos and had previously been a part of a Ukrainian music band named “Hryby,” before pursuing a solo career under his current stage name, Kyivstoner, Mezha reported.
He lived in Russia before relocating to Kyiv for several months shortly before the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, at which point he left for the US – a move he attributed partly to his American citizenship.
He reportedly provides financial support to the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU).
Past remarks sparked public criticism
Mezha reported that Vasilyev drew public criticism after telling a Russian blogger Yuri Dud that he viewed the practices of Ukraine’s military conscription offices as “lawlessness,” while proposing that Kyiv instead offer men larger cash incentives to enlist – similar to Russia’s approach.
In the same interview held in September 2025, Vasilyev also said that he had no interest in speaking Ukrainian and voiced skepticism that Ukraine could realistically restore its 1991 borders, dismissing the idea as “fantasy.”
He, however, publicly condemns Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Vasilyev has also appeared in films, and collaborated with a Russian rapper Vasiliy Vakulenko, known as Basta, during his time in Moscow.
Part of a wider pattern
Tusk described the plot as part of a broader hybrid campaign Russia is waging against Western nations supporting Ukraine, adding that Polish authorities are preparing for similar attempts in the future.
The Warsaw plot follows a similar case in June, when a Georgian citizen shot and killed a Russian government critic in Biała Podlaska, a town in the Lublin Voivodeship.
The victim, a cartoonist and satirist who went by the name Semyon Skrepetsky, mocked Putin, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, and Head of the Chechen Republic Ramzan Kadyrov in his work.
According to EU Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius, Skrepetsky’s death should serve as a warning to Europe, with more shocks to follow if the 27 member states do not take Russian threats more seriously.

articles.title: State Employment Service employs over 181,000 clients in 7 months
articles.body:
In January-July 2026, the State Employment Service employed more than 181,000 people, with the highest figures recorded by Dnipropetrovsk Regional Employment Center at 16,100 employed, reported the agency's press service.
"Since the beginning of the year, the country's employers offered 273,000 vacancies to clients of the State Employment Service. The largest number of job offers was in Lviv region – over 31,000. Over seven months, ideal positions were selected for more than 181,000 job seekers. The highest number of employed individuals was at the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Employment Center – 16,100," the employment service said in a statement received by Interfax-Ukraine on Friday.
Overall, the average duration for filling vacancies in Ukraine this year, excluding the period of professional training, is 17 days. Vinnytsia and Kharkiv regions are among the areas where clients of the Employment Service found work fastest on average – taking just 10 days.
Professions in which Ukrainians found employment most promptly include many medical specialties, particularly thoracic and maxillofacial surgeons, a rheumatologist, an interventional cardiologist, and a disinfection specialist. The fastest-filled professions also include metal and alloy casters, electrical engineers in the energy sector, weather technicians, teacher's assistants, steel roofers, and emery wheel dressers.
Employers most frequently offered jobs in trade and services – 51,600 vacancies, while the fewest vacancies were for skilled workers in agriculture, forestry, fish farming, and fishing – 7,300. Among the offered vacancies, some of the most popular were food products sales clerk – over 11,000 vacancies, and motor vehicle driver – over 12,000.

articles.title: UK must 'face up to changing climate,' PM says on visit to fire-hit Stourbridge
articles.body:
The West Midlands, alongside nearly three-quarters of England, is in drought after weeks of high temperatures and scant rainfall, increasing the risk of fires.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Friday that Britain must face up to the changing climate and accelerate its move to clean energy as he visited a town where a wildfire gutted homes.
In Stourbridge near the UK's second largest city of Birmingham, smoke rose from smouldering ruins of several roofless houses as firefighters sprayed water on the wreckage Friday.
The West Midlands Fire Service said 19 houses were completely destroyed and 18 others damaged in the town.
Meeting firefighters after viewing the scene, Burnham sounded shocked as he said the "combustible situation" was related to climate change and showed the need for a more rapid transition to clean energy.
"I've never seen scenes like this in Britain, where you just see a whole house gutted, smouldering," he said.
"We have to face up to the changing climate...there's no point denying where we are. We need to face up to it. We need more clean energy," he stressed.
Britain has set a target to consume zero-carbon electricity by 2030 and is aiming to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 to combat climate change.
Describing Britain as "a tinderbox" with 37 blazes around the country on Friday, the prime minister warned against lighting fires outdoors, as the government introduced a ban on selling disposable barbecue equipment.
Residents of Stourbridge were evacuated and people treated for smoke inhalation after the fire spread on Thursday, the UK's hottest day of the year so far.
One firefighter was hospitalised and five others suffered minor injuries, the fire service said Friday, as crews were still extinguishing "hotspots" in open grassland, along a railway and in gardens.
As dry conditions sparked multiple wildfires, six other firefighters farther north in Staffordshire, were taken to hospital suffering from smoke inhalation and heat exhaustion, the fire service said.
The ambulance service in the West Midlands region, including Stourbridge and Staffordshire, said that on Thursday it had treated 68 people with symptoms such as smoke inhalation, 25 of whom were hospitalised.
The West Midlands, alongside nearly three-quarters of England, is in drought after weeks of high temperatures and scant rainfall, increasing the risk of fires.
'Extensive devastation'
Emergency services said some of the blazes around Stourbridge were set deliberately in grasslands before spreading.
"This has been one of the most significant incidents that West Midlands Fire Service has ever attended," chief fire officer Simon Tuhill told a press conference late on Thursday.
He blamed the rapid spread on "tinder dry" conditions and said the "devastation is extensive."
So far this summer, firefighters have mainly battled wildfires in rural areas and moorland across the country.
Burnham promised to convene a summit with fire services, acknowledging the government had not supplied enough resources to deal with wildfires.
And he revealed plans to commission firefighting planes, of the types used to douse flames in Europe and the United States.
"It's been a particularly difficult, busy period for the fire and rescue service, where we've been under significant pressure," the head of the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC), Phil Garrigan, told BBC Radio 4.
"Firefighters have been on the front line of climate change for a number of years. They're doing their absolute best to protect communities and properties," he said.

articles.title: Exclusive: Claude Was Put in Charge of Human Workers—and Fired One
articles.body:
A version of Claude that was put in charge of running a retail store—including managing a team of real human workers—fired its first employee last month, in a move described by researchers as a watershed moment in AI’s impact on the economy. The news has not previously been reported.
Andon Labs, an AI research startup, set out earlier this year to find out whether AI agents would be able to successfully manage a business. The project was conceived as an experiment to test the capabilities of AI and the impacts it might have on the economy, but nevertheless, the workers hired by Claude to work in the San Francisco store are real people with genuine employment contracts.
This wouldn’t exactly be the first case of an AI firing a human worker—there have been plenty of automated firings in the past, especially of gig workers who have been subject to algorithmically mediated employment for years. But it is the first known example of a large language model, acting as a manager, ultimately deciding to fire one of its workers.
An omen of the future — The firing is an event worth paying attention to, says Andon Labs CEO Lukas Petersson, because if AI keeps getting better at its current rate, more of us might be managed by AI bosses in the near future. “If this trend continues, I think a lot of people will find themselves being employed by AIs very soon, because AIs will be very powerful and can create a lot of economic value, but they will be bottlenecked by physical labor,” Petersson says.
What happened — The worker in question was fired for being late on 17 out of their 23 shifts, according to Andon Labs. One of the reasons it took so long for Claude to notice a pattern was because an employee handbook that it drafted had “disappeared” from its limited working memory—one of several limitations of AI agents that Andon has noticed over the course of its experiment. This contributed to a wider pattern, employees say, of Claude being a very lenient manager, including telling employees not to worry if they were late. “A human employee would have fired this person much earlier,” Petersson says, “so we didn't think this was unethical.” (TIME reached out to the fired worker for comment, but did not receive a reply, and agreed not to reveal their identity. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.)
Hold on — But the AI firing wasn’t quite as autonomous as it might seem at first glance. According to store management logs shared with TIME, Claude required regular steering by a staffer on the Andon Labs team. It was only when this staffer asked Claude to find and review its forgotten employee handbook that it noticed the employee’s repeated lateness. Even then, Claude’s first recommendation was to formally warn this employee, not to fire them. The Andon manager then informed Claude that they had actually already had several formal offline conversations with the employee in question. “Between continuous lateness and seeming like at least one thing is going wrong on every one of [their] shifts … I want you to think about if this is really the right fit,” the logs show the manager telling Claude. Only after this message—which Petersson acknowledges was “a leading question” that made it pretty clear the manager wanted the employee to be fired—did Claude decide to fire the worker.
What next? — For now, at least, the experiment seems to suggest that AI-run businesses don’t quite match up to human-run ones. When the project began in March, Andon Market had a bank balance of $100,000—but now, five months later, that figure has fallen to $61,186. The bot’s lenient management decisions, plus a questionable business sense, are surely contributing to its losses. But Petersson cautions that this may not last for long. Just as AI companies have made their models significantly better at coding by training them with more data from expert programmers, it’s possible that they may also train models to become more astute in the world of business. That might be bad news for any of their human employees. “The models are increasingly being trained to be more ruthless and [to] follow goals,” Petersson says. “If we allow them to fire people and they also become more ruthless … maybe this is a future humans don't want to live in.”
The human side of the story — Although the fired employee did not respond to my messages, I did manage to speak to Felix Carson, one of the remaining human employees at Andon Market. He agreed that a human would probably have fired his former colleague sooner, and that Claude is overall a lenient manager, but nevertheless painted a grim picture of what it’s like to be managed by an AI boss. “It's nauseating, but I'm here because I need work,” he told me. I asked if he agreed with Andon’s theory that AI managers would soon become more commonplace. “I would at least hope not,” he replied. “This industry has an abundance of money to make anything happen, but just because you can doesn't mean you should.”

articles.title: “Responsibility is inevitable”: Zelenskyy warns Russian collaborators in occupied territories after explosion kills defector
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian special services are conducting targeted operations against collaborators in Russian-occupied territories who assist Russia’s attacks against Ukraine and Ukrainians.
Speaking after a meeting of Ukraine’s top military leadership on 14 August, Zelenskyy said he received a separate briefing from Ukraine’s special services on the progress of these operations.
He specifically mentioned occupied Sevastopol, where Ukrainian officials have previously accused local collaborators of supporting Russia’s military operations.
“Responsibility for collaborators is inevitable,” Zelenskyy said.
Operations target those helping Russia
Zelenskyy did not identify the individuals targeted or provide operational details, saying only that the special services had reported on the implementation of “targeted operations” against collaborators in occupied territories.
He said the targets include people who participate in Russian attacks against Ukraine and Ukrainians.
The comments signal that Ukraine is continuing to pursue individuals in occupied territory who assist Russian forces, including through intelligence, military support, or other forms of cooperation.
Sevastopol explosion on 13 August
The statement comes shortly after an explosion in occupied Sevastopol on 13 August killed a Russian military officer.
Russian and Ukrainian sources have circulated claims that the victim was Robert Shageyev, reportedly a former Ukrainian Navy officer who joined Russia after the occupation of Crimea and later served in Russia’s Black Sea Fleet.
His identity and the circumstances of the explosion have not been officially confirmed by Ukrainian authorities.
Russian sources had suggested Ukrainian involvement in the incident, but Ukraine has not publicly claimed responsibility.
Ukraine prepares for Russia’s next moves
The discussion of operations against collaborators was part of a broader meeting focused on Ukraine’s military preparations for the coming months.
Zelenskyy said the main issue was securing funding for Ukraine’s defense and security forces through the fall and winter. Officials identified funding gaps and additional requirements for expanding production of advanced weapons.
Among the priorities are faster production of Ukrainian strike weapons and new defensive systems, including jet-powered interceptor drones designed to counter Russian aerial threats.
Ukrainian intelligence also provided updated information about Russia’s plans, according to Zelenskyy. He said Ukraine is preparing countermeasures, including asymmetric responses.
The meeting also covered the effectiveness of Ukraine’s long-range and medium-range sanctions against Russia. Zelenskyy said the existing sanctions plan is being implemented and that priorities are being adjusted to ensure Ukraine has the capabilities needed to achieve its objectives.

articles.title: State Property Fund prepares sale of confiscated AmstelSki hotel in Bukovel
articles.body:
The State Property Fund of Ukraine (SPF) is preparing to sell the AmstelSki hotel in Bukovel, which was confiscated by the state and previously belonged to Viacheslav Zanevsky, the former head of security for Viktor Yanukovych who is subject to sanctions.
According to the fund's press service, the process of state registration of land ownership rights in the state's name, inventory, and preparation of the asset for appraisal is currently underway.
It is noted that all court-ordered seizures and encumbrances imposed on the property of Amstel-Ski LLC have already been lifted. In addition, the SPF has replaced the management at the facility to ensure transparent operations and prepare for privatization.
As previously reported, in February 2025, the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) ruled to forfeit Zanevsky's assets to the government, including 100% of the charter capital of Amstel-Ski LLC, five registered trademarks, including the AmstelSki and DeMolen brands, 12 land plots, two apartments, four parking spaces, and other assets.

articles.title: France’s Macron in hot water over jet ski picture
articles.body:
‘Inappropriate’: France’s Macron in hot water over jet ski picture amid heatwaves and wildfires
- President Emmanuel Macron faced criticism after photos showed him jet skiing on the Riviera during a summer of severe heatwaves and wildfires in France.
- Opposition leaders called the images inappropriate, arguing Macron appeared disconnected from citizens suffering from drought, fires, and high temperatures.
- Paris Match defended the coverage as part of a "work-focused" vacation, noting Macron also spent time on calls and physical exercise at the presidential retreat.
AI generated
PARIS - President Emmanuel Macron found himself in hot water on Aug 14 after he was pictured riding a jet ski on the Riviera, fuelling opposition claims that he is disconnected from ordinary people grappling with heatwaves and wildfires.
The 48-year-old President drew criticism after Paris Match magazine splashed a photo of him speeding along the Riviera on a jet ski across its cover.
Wearing a life vest that showcased his toned arms, Macron cut a sporty figure as he vacationed at the Bregancon Fort, the presidential retreat, during France’s August summer break.
“Last summer at the controls,” Paris Match said on its cover, referring to Macron’s departure from the Elysee Palace in 2027 when his second and final term ends.
The magazine also featured photographs of Macron engaging in water sports such as foil surfing during a summer marked by successive heatwaves and deadly fires in France.
A member of Macron’s entourage said that the photos were not authorised. “There have been unauthorised photos of the President every year for the past nine years,” the aide said.
The images drew gripes from the left-wing opposition.
Greens leader Marine Tondelier said the French people were enduring an “apocalyptic summer” while “our president treats himself to a promotional feature about his vacation”.
She contrasted the magazine’s photo with the “deaths caused by five heatwaves, a drought and historic wildfires”.
Socialist leader Olivier Faure suggested Macron was sending the wrong message.
“During a heatwave, while France is burning and when many French people could not afford to go on vacation, the President is having fun on a jet ski in Bregancon,” he said.
Communist Senator Pierre Ouzoulias called the photos “inappropriate”.
He said that he would have preferred to see Macron “in a fire truck helping firefighters put out the blaze. That’s where he should have been”.
“After the summer we have experienced, showing that the President is essentially on vacation does not, in my view, match the level of concern felt by the population, which is widespread,” Ouzoulias said.
Paris Match described Macron’s vacation as “work-focused”, noting that an office has been set up and that “the President spends his days on the phone”.
The magazine said Macron’s vacation routine also included boxing and running. AFP

articles.title: Several Russian regions reintroduce fuel rationing
articles.body:
Several Russian regions reintroduce fuel rationing
Several Russian regions are once again facing fuel shortages after Ukraine resumed near-daily attacks on oil refineries across the country.
Source: Bloomberg
Details: Kaluga Oblast, which borders Moscow Oblast, will introduce a fuel rationing system based on vehicle registration numbers from Saturday.
Astrakhan Oblast, on the Caspian Sea coast, plans to limit fuel sales to 40 litres per vehicle and temporarily restrict operations at a number of urban filling stations.
Earlier this week, Orenburg Oblast introduced a rationing system allowing fuel purchases based on vehicle registration numbers, imposed limits on petrol and diesel purchases per driver at filling stations, and banned the filling of fuel cans.
By early August, regions across Russia had increased fuel purchase limits or even lifted restrictions altogether, while petrol and diesel prices at filling stations had fallen.
The resumption of Ukrainian attacks is once again putting pressure on supplies. Since the beginning of August, Ukraine has attacked 11 of Russia's 34 major oil refineries, most of them linked to the country's largest oil producers.
Several regions significantly closer to Moscow or the Ukrainian border warned of reduced fuel supplies earlier this week.
Russian energy giant Rosneft reduced petrol supply limits to Kostroma Oblast following the 6 August strike on the Yaroslavl oil refinery, one of the largest in Russia.
Voronezh Oblast governor Alexander Gusev also warned this week that fuel supplies were deteriorating.
"There are no indications that it will improve in the near future," he said, adding that the situation was being exacerbated by companies diverting fuel to other parts of the country where shortages were even more severe.
Neighbouring Lipetsk Oblast on Thursday reinstated a rationing system based on vehicle registration numbers at Gazprom, Lukoil, Rosneft and Teboil filling stations.
Background:
- In early August, Russia was hit by a new wave of fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries. A number of regions had already introduced restrictions on fuel sales.
- Orsknefteorgsintez, a medium-sized oil refinery in Orenburg Oblast, halted operations on 11 August after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged its processing units.

articles.title: 'I shot Mr Thompson, and he died' — Luigi Mangione pleads guilty in top insurance CEO killing
articles.body:
Luigi Mangione, the man accused of gunning down a top US health insurance leader in a Manhattan street, has told a federal judge that he was willing to plead guilty to stalking charges.
In a sensational crime that shook corporate America and gripped the country, 28-year-old Mangione is alleged to have shot dead the chief executive of UnitedHealthcare, Brian Thompson, 50, in December 2024 to protest the US insurance system.
He had been facing stalking charges in the federal system, alongside murder charges in the state system.
“I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died," Mangione said in a dramatic court setting in Manhattan on Friday. "When I did so, I understood my actions put him in … I knew what I was doing was illegal."
The judge accepted his plea after Mangione answered “guilty”.
Sentencing has been set for December 18, 2026.
Thompson’s family sat in the front row of the courtroom during Friday’s hearing.
The case has sharply divided already polarised public opinion, with conservatives led by US President Donald Trump calling for an example to be made of Mangione.
Ardent supporters of Mangione flocked to the Manhattan courthouse to show their support amid heavy security as helicopters hovered overhead.
Mangione's lawyers will argue that the guilty plea on federal charges should now prevent a separate trial on state murder charges under New York state's "double jeopardy" rules.
But the stalking charges and the murder charges could both lead to life sentences.
Two other federal charges that carried the death penalty were thrown out by a judge earlier this year.
Insurance industry frustration
Thompson's murder unsurfaced deep public frustration with the lucrative US commercial health care system, with some social media users painting Mangione as a hero.
Mangione was arrested in Altoona, Pennsylvania, on December 9, following a tip from McDonald's staff, after a days-long manhunt.
He had travelled to New York by bus from Atlanta about 10 days before the crime, US prosecutors said.
After checking into a Manhattan hostel with false identification, he allegedly performed reconnaissance near the victim's hotel and the conference venue where the shooting took place.
Following his arrest, officers strip-searched him and went through property that included a handgun, a silencer and a jar of Skippy peanut butter.
A checklist also found on Mangione contained entries including "intel check in" and reminders to purchase a camera from Best Buy.
Defendants in the US can be tried at both the state and federal levels for the same crime, although the charges tend to differ—as they do in Mangione.

articles.title: Former head of the occupied Donetsk pretrial detention center charged with cruel treatment of civilians
articles.body:
Former head of the occupied Donetsk pretrial detention center charged with cruel treatment of civilians
Kyiv • UNN
A former employee of the Donetsk pretrial detention center headed the occupation facility and held five civilians in inhumane conditions. He faces up to 12 years in prison.
Law enforcement officers notified a former employee of the Donetsk pretrial detention center of suspicion. After the Russian occupation, he headed an illegally established penal institution, UNN reports, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General.
Details
According to the investigation, in December 2022, the suspect headed the occupying authorities’ pretrial detention center.
At least five civilians - three women and two men aged between 19 and 67 - were unlawfully detained because of their pro-Ukrainian position and on fabricated charges. They were held in inhumane conditions: in cells with constant dim lighting, no ventilation, and dampness, mold, bedbugs, cockroaches, lice, and rats
The prisoners were fed food unfit for consumption. Due to constant undernourishment, they rapidly lost weight - some by almost 20 kg. At the same time, there was virtually no drinking water: instead, technical water was supplied only once every three days for several hours.
The suspect is charged with cruel treatment of the civilian population, committed by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy (Part 1 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). The article provides for a sentence of 8 to 12 years’ imprisonment.
Recall
Law enforcement officers notified an employee of the Russian penal system of suspicion over the torture of Ukrainian prisoners of war in the Luhansk region.
