articles.title: Clean Arctic volunteers head for Eurasian northernmost point cleanup mission
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 14. /TASS/. Volunteers of the Clean Arctic public environmental project took a flight from Moscow heading for Cape Chelyuskin in the Arctic. They will be cleaning up the accumulated environmental damage and will participate in field scientific research and practical training, the project's press service said.
"This year, our project has received a grant from the Presidential Foundation for Nature. This allows us not only to organize the territory cleanup, but also to conduct in-depth scientific research. Clean Arctic has been preparing the ground for such expeditions for several years: we have repaired the volunteer campus, practiced the technology for cleaning and removing accumulated damage. In fact, this expedition to [Cape] Chelyuskin begins a big and comprehensive work to restore the cape's ecosystems and to develop the cape into an important center for scientific research," the press service quoted the Clean Arctic public environmental project's leader Andrey Nagibin as saying.
The expedition to Eurasia's northernmost mainland point is organized for the first time. The group of more than 20 people features volunteers as well as scientific specialists, museum experts, and Hero of Russia, Cosmonaut Alexander Gorbunov, plus winners of the Icebreaker of Knowledge international competition.
Cape Chelyuskin is a unique natural indicator where Arctic tundra and polar deserts alternate. It is home to the Red Data Book animals, including the polar bear. The cape's exclusive feature is that it is located on the watershed of the Kara Sea and the Laptev Sea, which makes it a key object for studying the global climate.
"We plan to try to assess the spatial picture of pollution: concentrations of pollutants, the degree of ecosystem disturbance. Pollutants get accumulated in organisms: mosses, lichens, and further - along the trophic chain. The highest concentrations are naturally observed in the polar bear, the highest predator. An additional factor is behavioral: animals demonstrate interest in abandoned structures, which creates a risk of direct contact with remnants of fuels and lubricants. The elimination and purification contribute to cutting these risk factors, and trigger the process of cleaning trophic chains," said Danila Bardashov, a researcher at the Dokuchaev Soil Institute, an expert of the Lomonosov Moscow State University's Geography Department.
The expedition will be different from other similar missions due to the plans to preserve historical artifacts. Cape Chelyuskin keeps a huge amount of Soviet-era machinery and equipment. Now, specialists have a chance to separate ordinary scrap metal from items having certain cultural and historical value. The group features specialists of the Arctic Museum Exhibition Center in St. Petersburg. Their task is to separate from a pile of scrap metal valuable exhibits of heavy machinery - the equipment that in the past was used in development of the Russian North.
About the project
The Clean Arctic Public Environmental Project has been cleaning the northern territories since 2021. The volunteers focus on objects, left since the USSR times. Waste removal is a complex technological work, where the movement teams work carefully minding the Arctic nature. Over all seasons, the project's almost 10,000 volunteers have collected 22,000 tons of waste and cleaned 1,100 hectares of land. The project's general partner is the Rosatom State Corporation, and TASS is the general information partner.

articles.title: Days until MoU deadline as US and Iran claim Hormuz control
articles.body:
The live blog is now over and will be back tomorrow at 9am BST. You can read more of The New Arab's coverage of the region here.
Breadcrumb
The live page is now closed.
Here were the key updates of the day:
And so we continue our live coverage of the day...
Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said early Saturday that Tehran would not be intimidated by threats or a show of force by Washington after US President Donald Trump said he would declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory.
Commenting on Trump's statements, Gharibabadi said in a post on X that the strategic waterway would only be opened or closed under Iran's authority.
UAE's Abu Dhabi National Oil Company said on Saturday that one of its vessels came under attack while transiting the Strait of Hormuz a day earlier.
The state oil company said no injuries were reported, with the situation now under control.
Britain on Friday hit back at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu derisively calling the country an "Islamic republic" in an interview, branding the remarks "completely unacceptable".
The diplomatic tit-for-tat came after the right-wing prime minister made the reference in an army radio podcast interview the previous day, in which he criticised the UK's stance on Israel.
It echoed the language of far-right politicians and commentators in the Western world who have made baseless claims that parts of Britain have come under Islamic law due to immigration, drawing accusations of Islamophobia.
"These comments are completely unacceptable and we have raised them with the Israeli Government," a UK government spokesman said Friday.
President Donald Trump on Friday said he would "soon" declare the Strait of Hormuz waterway part of US territory after defeating Iran.
"After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated -- pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," he said with a chuckle during a political rally at a police academy in New York state.
"It's true," he added.
Trump, together with Israel, launched a war against Iran on 28 February but remains locked in a stalemate with Iran over the strait, with Iran denying access to much of the civilian shipping and the US Navy mounting a blockade of Iranian ports in an attempt to cripple its economy.
"We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to," Trump the cheering crowd of supporters and police.
US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Friday that the United States will hit Iran hard economically as Washington and Tehran struggle to reach a deal to end a nearly six-month conflict.
His comments came a day after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US was going to apply measures that have "never been seen" on Tehran as soon as next week.
A military official from Yemen's internationally recognised government said a Houthi attack on Friday on the port city of Mokha killed six people, two of them security personnel.
The Iran-backed rebels "fired five missiles at commercial ships unloading at the port, and two ships are on fire", the official said.
Israeli settlers shot two Palestinians in the occupied West Bank town of Bani Na'im, east of Hebron, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa, citing the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.
Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem on Friday accused Lebanese authorities of subjecting the country's armed forces to undue pressure by implementing a framework deal agreed with Israel to end hostilities.
The June trilateral framework, to which the United States is also a party, involves the disarmament of the Lebanese militant group and a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon's south, where it has occupied several areas.
It also includes the deployment of the Lebanese army to areas where Israel's military has pulled out, starting in test areas known as "pilot zones".
"How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?" Qassem said in a speech.
In talks between Lebanon and Israel in Rome last week, both sides discussed which countries might participate in a committee tasked with verifying the Lebanese army's deployment in the pilot zones and clearance of Hezbollah weapons and infrastructure, a Lebanese presidency source told AFP.
"Israel is attempting to bind Lebanon to an inquiry committee that oversees the army's deployment, operations, and internal details. Where is the patriotism? Where is the dignity of the army that ought to be preserved?" said Qassem.
Yemen's Houthis said they targeted an Aramco facility in the Saudi city of Najran with a drone, the group-run SABA news agency reported on Friday, citing a military source.
The source said the attack was in response to what it described as Saudi military aircraft violating Yemen's sovereignty by entering airspace over the northeastern part of Saada governorate.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities or Aramco. It was not immediately clear from the report whether the facility was hit.
US President Donald Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner will visit Israel next week in hopes of bridging gaps on a Gaza plan rejected by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, officials said Friday.
Kushner and Nickolay Mladenov, the high representative for Gaza of Trump's so-called Board of Peace implementing the deal, will visit both Israel and key mediator Egypt.
The trip comes after Netanyahu publicly rejected a 15-point plan announced by Mladenov in which Hamas agreed to hand over its weapons to a new Palestinian governing committee in Gaza.
A Board of Peace official said Kushner and Mladenov hoped for "constructive conversations" on advancing Trump's overall peace plan that began with the October 2025 declaration of a ceasefire, which has reduced but not ended Israeli strikes in Gaza.
"The United States and Israel agree on the end state, which is a demilitarised Hamas," the official said on condition of anonymity.
"We will hear the concerns that have been raised and talk about next steps. What is critical is that we both agree on the desired outcome and are finding ways to accelerate progress."
The French embassy in Israel has called on the Israeli government to arrest and charge violent settlers in the occupied West Bank, saying in a post on X that the government must "take all necessary measures to protect the Palestinian civilian population, as required of them under international law," according to Haaretz.
The embassy added that it "call[s] on the Israeli authorities to arrest the perpetrators of these acts and bring them to justice."
Israeli forces and settlers continued their assault against Palestinian communities across the occupied West Bank on Friday despite mounting international condemnation over the siege of homes in Qusra and escalating attacks elsewhere.
In Qusra, south of Nablus, settlers remained near Palestinian homes for a sixth consecutive day, while Israeli forces prevented foreign and Israeli solidarity activists from reaching besieged families with water and other basic supplies.
The siege has drawn unusually sharp criticism from Washington, with White House officials pressing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly condemn the settlers after learning that one of the affected homes belongs to a Palestinian American.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee - a supporter of the settler movement - described those responsible as "Israeli terrorists" and their actions as "criminal", while France condemned what it called the "occupation" of Palestinian homes and called on Israeli authorities to arrest and prosecute those responsible.
Amid the criticism, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz ordered the military to prepare a plan to transfer civilian law enforcement in the occupied West Bank to the police.
Egypt is seriously considering joining the new joint defence agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said on Thursday.
Abdelatty made the remarks after talks with his Turkish counterpart, Hakan Fidan, in the northern coastal city of El Alamein.
Asked at a joint press conference whether Cairo would enter the agreement, Abdelatty said the pact was being examined by the relevant Egyptian authorities in accordance with the constitution and any legal obligations that membership could entail.
The agreement, known as the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, was signed last Friday by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
It includes a collective defence provision modelled on NATO’s Article 5, under which an attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all three.
Iraq's average daily oil exports since the beginning of August are the highest since the outbreak of the Middle East war between Iran and the United States choked off the Strait of Hormuz, the oil ministry said Friday.
Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair told a press conference that "exports since the beginning of the month have reached a rate of two million barrels" per day, for a total of around 26 million barrels.
He said the daily rate had been achieved "for the first time since the crisis began" on February 28 after US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which retaliated by blocking the waterway crucial for global oil and gas trade.
Before the war, Iraq produced around four million barrels per day, and exported an average of 105 million barrels per month, mostly from its Basra oil terminal via Hormuz.
Ali Nizar, the head of Iraq's State Organisation for Marketing of Oil (SOMO), said in a TV interview last week that Iraq exported in July "35.5 to 37 million barrels" via Hormuz.
Israel's defence minister called Friday for the police to take over law enforcement in the occupied West Bank from the military, which has come under fire from the right-wing for trying to remove settlers harassing Palestinians.
The measure, if implemented, would be a step towards Israeli annexation of the occupied Palestinian territory - something several ministers in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government openly call for.
Defence Minister Israel Katz's office announced he had "instructed the IDF to prepare a plan to transfer all enforcement powers regarding civil matters among Israeli communities and population in Judea and Samaria to the Israel Police," using the Biblical term for the illegally occupied West Bank.
The military would continue to exercise power over Palestinian residents of the West Bank.
"The IDF's role is to fight Palestinian terrorism, focus on defending borders and communities against threats... and not chase boys on the hilltops," Katz said, referring to the Hilltop Youth - a settler group regularly accused of violence towards Palestinians.

articles.title: Germany news: Car industry hemorrhaging jobs
articles.body:
Germany news: Car industry hemorrhaging jobs
Published August 14, 2026last updated August 14, 2026
What you need to know
This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Friday, August 14, 2026:
- A wildfire near the Belgian border has forced around 1,800 people to leave their homes
- Amid high temperatures, farmers say drought could badly damage grain, potato, vegetable and feed crop harvests
- Germany's car sector is losing jobs faster than any industrial sector in the economy
For coverage of the wildfire in western Germany click on our dedicated blog here
Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.
Extreme athlete arrives in Cologne after swimming from Frankfurt
Nathalie Pohl has completed her four-day swin down the Main and Rhine rivers from Frankfurt to Cologne.
The 31-year-old extreme swimmer started the aquatic journey of more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) on Tuesday morning, arriving on the banks of the Rhine in Cologne on Friday afternoon.
Her aim was to raise awareness on the importance of safe swimming among children, and to fund swimming projects. Her team says they managed to raise around €616,000 ($713,000) in total.
"Every child has the right to feel secure in the water," she said upon arrival. At the same time she was keen to point out that her challenge shouldn't be taken as a "false signal."
"Especially in the Rhine, far too many people still drown," she said. "It's not bathing water."
Germany sees rise in new business registrations
Germany saw a noticeable rise in new business registrations in the first half of this year. Around 352,400 new businesses were registered, up 8.3% compared with the same period last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office.
Of these, around 69,600 were considered businesses of greater economic significance — for example because of their legal form or because they planned to employ staff. That was 3.0% more than a year earlier.
At the same time, the number of complete business closures in this category fell by 3.8% to around 49,800.
Farmers fear drought will wipe out this year's harvest
German farmers fear they could see harvests wiped out entirely by ongoing drought and unseasonably high temperatures, says German Farmers' Association (DBV) President Joachim Ruckwied.
"We expect below-average grain harvests, especially when it comes to wheat and rapeseed," he said during an interview with Germany's Redaktionsnetzwerk media group.
"As far as fall crops are concerned, the trend suggests we must expect significant yield losses here as well."
Potatoes, vegetables and sugar beets, as well as grain maize and soy could be affected.
Ruckwied warned that although farmers in the north could hope for "acceptable" if "below-average" harvests thanks to occasional rains, farmers in drier southern Germany could be facing "total harvest loss."
"What's becoming a problem, especially in southern Germany, is that feed crops aren't coming in," he added, noting that this would force farmers to slaughter animals earlier than usual.
The threat adds to the financial pressure farmers already face when it comes to buying seed, fertilizer and pesticides, says Ruckwied.
"The economic situation is brutal… on the one hand high investment costs, and on the other, lower market prices for agricultural products."
Dramatic rescue in Berlin high-rise fire
Several people were injured Friday morning when fire broke out in a 21-story apartment complex in Berlin's Friedrichshain neighborhood, near the Ostbahnhof train station.
The blaze started on the 11th floor, say firefighters, and quickly spread to floors above.
A fire department spokesperson described the situation as "dramatic."
Witnesses say numerous residents stood at windows and balconies prepared to jump rather than be consumed by smoke and flames.
Although jump cushions were installed as a precaution below, these were not used and authorities say residents were retrieved from a stairwell with a rescue ladder.
Some 130 fire, police and emergency services personnel were in action before residents could be saved and the fire extinguished.
Smoke damage is said to have been extensive, causing at least five injuries, and leaving roughly 70 people to be cared for on site.
The cause of the fire is unclear, though police are treating it as a possible balcony fire.
German hiker injured in Alps fall
A 66-year old German hiker was seriously injured in a fall in the Austrian Alps on Friday according to authorities in Nesselwängle, Tyrol.
Emergency services say the man slipped and fell a few meters, losing consciousness before falling over a second, 40-meter-high (132-foot) cliff.
The man's daughter and others administered first-aid and contacted mountain rescue. He was airlifted to an Innsbruck hospital.
On Thursday, a 36-year-old German died in a fall in Zillertal, Tyrol. A few days earlier, a 74-year-old German similarly died from a fall in East Tyrol.
Almost half of Bundestag sign up to new 'opt-out' organ donor model
More than 200 lawmakers in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, have signed up to a cross-party initiative seeking to change Germany's organ donor rules.
The proposal seeks to move from an "opt-in" system to an "opt-out" one.
At present, people in Germany have to carry a donor card, register as an organ donor, or otherwise inform healthcare professionals of their willingness to donate in a legally binding manner before death. If they do not, and they are deemed potentially viable donors, sometimes their next of kin are asked to decide on their behalf — a traumatic and difficult decision in the midst of a bereavement.
With donor rates consistently failing to meet demand, some medical professionals have long advocated a system where instead of declaring your willingness to donate, you are assumed to be a potential donor unless you specifically say you are not a willing participant.
A draft law has been put forward in the Bundestag — not as a government initiative but as a cross party conscience vote, typically for causes with only a narrow chance of success but which politicians nevertheless wish to put in the spotlight.
In this case, however, 245 lawmakers have already signed the motion, in a chamber with 630 politicians. If the bill could gather some more support during the parliamentary process, it might have a chance of progressing.
Parliamentary debate on the bill is scheduled after lawmakers return from the summer break.
Around 8,000 people are currently on donor waiting lists in Germany.
Catamaran passenger ferry crashes into Lake Constance harbor wall
A catamaran passenger ferry has crashed on Lake Constance, colliding with the harbor wall.
Police said that 12 people were injured, and it was not immediately clear how seriously. They were receiving treatment on site.
Images showed that the ship had collided head-on with the harbor wall, sustaining quite considerable damage. It was still afloat, however.
Police said there was no fuel leak and no environmental hazard posed by the incident. What caused the early morning carsh was not immediately clear.
The hourly catamaran ferry brings people across Lake Constance, or the Bodensee in German, from Konstanz to Friedrichshafen.
Car industry hemorrhaging jobs
Germany's automotive branch is losing jobs faster than any industrial sector in the economy according to the Federal Statistical Office Destatis.
The car industry is second only to mechanical engineering when it comes to size, yet its employment numbers are now at their lowest since 2005.
At the end of the first half of 2026, 691,500 people were employed in Germany's leading industry, a drop of 42,300 workers, or 5.8%, within a single year.
Destatis said manufacturing employment fell by 2.7% overall but had fallen by 7.6% in the automobile sector. Smaller segments within the car sector fell by 10%, whereas manufacturers themselves registered a 6.1% drop in employment.
In May, Germany's Association of the Automobile Industry (VDA) warned that the sector stands to lose as many as 225,000 jobs by 2035.
Numerous German manufacturers, such as VW, Audi and Porsche, have all cut jobs in an effort to remain lean in the face of rising Chinese competition and punitive US tariffs.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

articles.title: Nenets Autonomous Region to develop oil production sector's personnel training — governor
articles.body:
ARKHANGELSK, August 14. /TASS/. The Nenets Autonomous Region will develop in the region a system of personnel training for the oil production sector, the region's Governor Irina Gekht said at the 4th Arctic - Regions Forum in Arkhangelsk.
"In my opinion, we need to develop first of all our strong aspects," she said at the forum's plenary session. "The Nenets Autonomous Region's strong side is precisely […] the growth of the oil and gas production sector, the increase in traffic and the associated development of transport and other infrastructures. One of our most important tasks is to attract to this work local specialists as much as possible. We have been solving this problem. This year, together with Lukoil, we are opening a specialized class. We will work with our colleges under the Professionalism program. We must clearly and consciously train young people so that they work within the region. This is one of the ways to keep young people here."
The oil and gas production sector is one of the most knowledge-intensive, industrially complex and rich in modern technologies areas, she continued. For the Nenets Autonomous Region, this is the main sector of the economy.
"I believe it is a weird situation when a young person born in the Nenets Autonomous Region, in the oil region, where ports, roads, and big infrastructure projects will be built, is forced to leave for Moscow or St. Petersburg to work there in the services market, for example. Why would a young man from Naryan-Mar prefer to leave to work as a waiter in a St. Petersburg cafe when here he has the opportunity to get involved in truly big, landmark projects," she added.
Noteworthy, the oil and gas industry is not just an enterprise that was built once and for good, and then it simply produces one and the same product, the governor continued. Work in this field requires a wide range of competencies.
Besides that, people working in the oil and gas sector need to be fed, transported, treated, their work needs to be ensured, and infrastructures and services need to be created. According to the governor, this will build up, among other things, the region's social base, like, for example, the Nenets Regional Hospital.
Attracting personnel
The region's another growth area is transportation along the Northern Sea Route, which requires land infrastructures, and their creation will attract people to the region. "In this case, our task as the government is to provide appropriate social infrastructures. At a certain point, one cultural and business center - the Arctic - will no longer be enough - and quite likely we would want to have a theater here. The Nenets Regional Hospital will require a thorough equipment upgrade. Importantly, we already have a good base of Arctic medicine and a strong team, and we have the base on which to build the further development. We will need new schools, new teachers, who we need to attract to the region from the mainland," the governor said.
People may go to the North also for higher incomes, the continued. The climate in the Nenets Autonomous Region is harsh, thus in addition to high incomes there should be other advantages, including a comfortable living environment. "Therefore, I believe that the development of oil and gas industrial projects, and further on - of others, including ore projects, is the natural way to develop the region. As we have the railway, the port, the option to transport ore cargoes, we will see a growth of container shipments. The current traffic along the Northern Sea Route is incomparable with the amounts planned for the future. This development requires infrastructures. And infrastructures mean first of all people," the governor said in conclusion.
TASS is the forum's general information partner.

articles.title: Housing investors say this is their worst market in at least 3 years
articles.body:
A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.
Investors in the single-family housing market are increasingly concerned about interest rates, rising insurance and home costs, and the ongoing war with Iran. As a result, they are less confident in their businesses than they have been in at least three years.
Investor sentiment at the end of June fell for the second straight quarter to an all-time low on the quarterly RCN Capital/CJ Patrick Company Investor Sentiment Index, or ISI. The index surveys more than 300 investors in the fix-and-flip and rental businesses.
Just 26% of respondents said they believe market conditions are better than they were a year ago, the lowest share since the survey began in 2023 and down from 35% in the first quarter. Fully 45% said the market has gotten worse, the highest in the survey's history.
"In addition to the ongoing conflict in Iran, rising finance costs, limited inventory, escalating home and renovation costs and downward pressure on rental rates are all contributing factors for their increased pessimism," said Jeffrey Tesch, CEO of RCN Capital, a private lender to real estate investors, in a release.
The vast majority of investors surveyed in this report were small to mid-sized. That's in contrast to large institutional investors covered by the recently enacted 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which will generally prohibit investors with at least 350 single-family homes from acquiring additional single-family homes. Small- to mid-sized investors tend to use bridge loans, special investor loans for rental properties and conventional loans that are typically 30-year and fixed rate. Of those surveyed, 28% reported paying cash in their recent purchases.
Mortgage rates hit a recent low at the end of February but rose sharply at the start of the war with Iran. They are now at their highest level in over a year.
More than half of survey respondents said the high cost of financing is "one of the biggest problems in today's market," according to the report. Three-quarters of them said they do not expect to see any rate relief anytime soon, and some expect rates to rise.
All of this is impacting investor purchase activity.
"Real estate investors purchased 23% fewer homes in the first quarter of 2026 than they did in the previous quarter and in the first quarter of 2025. The survey also shows that 32% of the respondents don't plan to buy any properties at all this year, and only 9% plan to buy more than they did a year ago," said Rick Sharga, CEO of the CJ Patrick Company.
More than 60% of respondents expect home prices to rise over the next six months, up from just under 52% in the prior survey. Higher prices can raise investors' acquisition costs while increasing the potential value of properties they already own.

articles.title: At least people in 10 in intensive care and thousands flee intense wildfire in Croatia
articles.body:
During a visit to the area Prime Minister Andrej Plenković stressed the dangers of the fire and praised the efforts of the firefighters.
A wildfire on Croatia's coast has left at least 10 people in intensive care and dozens more injured after fire crews battled overnight with "one of the worst" blazes in the country's history, according to officials.
Around 2,000 had been evacuated from nearby villages as the fire ripped through the surrounding hills, damaging homes and destroying cars in the early hours of Friday.
As access reopened mid-morning, the AFP news agency saw the blackened remains of several burnt out cars along roads near Omiš, some ringed by silver puddles of metal that had melted under the intense heat of the fires.
Several buildings in the area had also been damaged by the blaze, with some structures nearby completely destroyed.
During a visit to the area Prime Minister Andrej Plenković stressed the dangers of the fire and praised the efforts of the firefighters.
"This fire spread at lightning speed," he told reporters. "What the firefighters managed to save is truly a miracle."
Plenković pointed out that this was a "very densely populated" region, with a township of 15,000, currently bolstered by 12,000 tourists.
Hospital officials said 40 people had been admitted to Split hospital so far, including a German and Polish tourist.
Nearly 300 firefighters were deployed overnight but were often outpaced by the blaze, according to the country's fire chief Slavko Tucaković, who described it as "one of the worst in Croatia's history."
"It was frightening even to watch. Many houses, cafes, restaurants, cars, and boats that were on dry land were damaged," he told national radio.
Tourists flee
Firefighters battled through the night, with local media broadcasting images of crews facing walls of flames.
Hundreds of tourists were among those evacuated to a shelter set up by the Red Cross, Ana Stejskal, the organisation's director in the town of Omiš, told national broadcaster HRT.
Several other shelters have been opened in nearby coastal towns of Split and Makarska, the Croatian Fire and Rescue Service said in a statement.
"People have a bed, a shower, a toilet and food, but it's difficult to predict how long this situation will last," said TOmišlav Gojo, director of the Red Cross in Split.
After four Canadair water bombers were deployed at dawn, authorities said the situation was calmer.
But as conditions eased in Omiš, the firefighting aircraft had already been sent to another blaze on the Pelješac Peninsula, about 70 kilometres south, where homes were under threat.
Blazes were also burning in other parts of the Balkans as a heatwave brings soaring temperatures and worsens drought conditions.
Emergency crews in Montenegro have been battling fires along the coast for several days, while fires were reported near Albania's capital on Thursday.
Temperature records, already broken this summer, were again beaten earlier this week when nearby Split, about 30 kilometres north of Omiš, hit 39.7C.

articles.title: US threatens EU over its green reporting rules
articles.body:
United States Ambassador to the European Union Andrew Puzder speaks during an interview in Brussels on April 9, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
The U.S. on Friday threatened action against the EU unless Brussels reins in its environmental and human rights rules, which Washington says unfairly burden American companies.
Acknowledging Brussels had made “some positive reforms,” Washington said the EU had “failed to fully address U.S. concerns,” and that it “will take any actions necessary to address unreasonable burdens on U.S. commerce.”
U.S. Ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder piled on the pressure Friday, writing on X that “now it’s time for the EU to deliver.” He pointed to commitments made under last year’s Turnberry trade deal to ensure U.S. businesses do not face “undue restrictions” on transatlantic trade due to Brussels' green regulations.
Advertisement
The dispute centers on two pillars of the EU’s corporate sustainability rulebook: the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, which requires large companies to address human rights and environmental harms linked to their operations and supply chains, and the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, which requires companies to disclose sustainability-related information.
Brussels has scaled back both laws in its drive to cut red tape, but has stopped short of Washington’s demand to shield U.S. companies from their reach.
Last week, Puzder similarly attacked the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism as a tariff on U.S. exporters. On Thursday, the White House also accused the EU and more than 40 countries of enabling Chinese goods to skirt U.S. tariffs by rerouting them through their markets.
A European Commission spokesperson told POLITICO that Brussels had made “considerable efforts” to explain its rules and highlight "its willingness to cooperate with the US to increase trade where possible," but drew a line at changing its regulatory regime in response to U.S. pressure.
“We have been very clear and consistent on the fact that neither our rules framework nor our regulatory autonomy are up for negotiation,” said the spokesperson.

articles.title: US failed to achieve its goals in war on Iran: senior cleric
articles.body:
Speaking during Friday sermons in Tehran earlier today, Ayatollah Seyed Ahmad Khatemi said that Iranian missile power has brought humiliation to the U.S. and will continue to do so.
Khatemi noted that over more than 160 days of resistance since the aggression began on February 28, the Iranian nation has experienced numerous divine blessings.
He remarked that while the enemy sought to destroy the Islamic Republic, Iran has instead emerged as a major global power.
The senior cleric pointed to the anniversary of the 1953 CIA-led coup in Iran which toppled democratically elected government of Iran, saying that sicne 1953, Washington has not stopped plotting against Iran.
MNA

articles.title: Exclusive: Russia strikes Odesa port terminal recently acquired by Swiss investor
articles.body:
Russia strikes Ukraine's largest private port operator as Moscow rejects grain truce
Editor's note: An earlier version of this article incorrectly reported that the attack targeted a container terminal that was recently purchased by the by the Swiss-headquartered Mediterranean Shipping Company in March.
A Russian missile strike damaged a key Ukrainian port terminal on Aug. 14, as Russia continues to terrorize Ukraine's seaports.
The attack damaged at least one warehouse at the TIS terminal in Ukraine's Pivdennyi (Southern) Port complex, an agriculture-sector executive with knowledge of the matter told the Kyiv Independent under the condition of anonymity. 
TIS's press service declined to comment on the attack. 
The strike comes the same day as Russia rejected the idea of reinstating the 2022-2023 Black Sea grain initiative. Kyiv and Moscow have exchanged strikes on ports and vessels recently, leading to growing concern of a global food crisis. 
Turkey has attempted to mediate negotiations, having helped broker the original grain initiative, although Moscow has said Ankara has yet to send an official ceasefire proposal. 
Reviving the framework of the grain initiative would be "ill-advised," Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakaharova told reporters on Aug. 14, accusing "the West" of using the deal to attack Russia.
She also claimed that Ukraine was currently conducting maritime terrorism and "escalating" the situation. Meanwhile, Moscow relentlessly attacks Odesa Oblast, particularly port infrastructure.
TIS is co-owned by Andriy Stavnitser, a Ukrainian businessman who also owns the Superhumans Center, a specialist clinic for war veterans.
In March, the world's largest container shipping company, the Swiss-headquartered Mediterranean Shipping Company, took a majority stake in a TIS container terminal in Ukraine's Pivdennyi (Southern) Port, marking a rare high-profile foreign investment into the country. The container terminal was not hit in the Aug. 14 attack.
Over the last two months, Russia has stepped up its attacks on Odesa's seaports and civilian vessels in a bid to choke Ukraine's key trade route. Some 90% of the country's agricultural goods are exported via the Black Sea, accounting for 20% of the country's gross domestic product (GDP) before the full-scale invasion.
With Russia striking vessels 35 times in port waters and 22 times in the Black Sea during last month alone, ships are avoiding docking at Ukraine's ports, preventing agriculture and metallurgy businesses from exporting and importing goods.
The fallout of the attacks is already dire. Ukraine's exports fell to just 30% of its target in the first two weeks of August, Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky said at a briefing on Aug. 14. By November, the country could lose 10.8 billion euros ($12.5 billion) in blocked agricultural exports, according to the Agriculture Ministry.

articles.title: Across the world authoritarians want to tell us what a ‘good life’ looks like. Here’s how liberals must respond | Alexandre Lefebvre
articles.body:
Those of us who live in liberal democracies carry an image of what a decent state should do. It should protect rights, grow the economy, maintain order, uphold fairness and arbitrate disputes. But on life’s deepest questions – what makes a life worth living, and what sort of person one ought to become – it is meant to show restraint. The state should not privilege one vision of human flourishing, let alone promote it. That is for individuals, families and communities to decide. To borrow the Minnesota governor Tim Walz’s golden rule of politics: “Mind your own damn business!”
Consider birthrates. Across much of the wealthy world, they have fallen below replacement level. Fewer children mean fewer future workers, taxpayers and carers, and more pressure on pensions, health systems and aged care. Yet when liberal democracies encourage larger families, through baby bonuses or affordable childcare, they generally describe the goal as removing obstacles and expanding choice. Crucially, everyone should benefit: gay parents, straight parents, adoptive parents, biological parents, married parents, divorced parents – come one, come all.
Earlier this year, I saw a different approach in Hungary. Hosted by a thinktank aligned with Viktor Orbán, I interviewed leading figures from his Fidesz party before its defeat in April’s election. For them, demographic decline was existential, not technical. The family was where people learned to be Hungarian and acquired the virtues of love and fidelity – values so important that they are named in the constitution Fidesz enacted. The family also connects national survival to personal flourishing. One leading defender of Fidesz told me, with startling bluntness, that women without children tended to be miserable and unfulfilled. This was no random digression. What I call a “good life state” honours certain ways of living as superior and uses public power and money to promote them. A liberal state, by contrast, helps people pursue the lives they choose and refuses to rank them.
Fidesz lost the election, but the model it helped popularise has not disappeared. Politics is returning to its oldest – and for many, most fundamental – question: who decides what makes a life worth living? From Maga and Fidesz to Modi’s India, Xi’s China, Israel’s governing right and Iran’s theocracy, leaders and movements are treating the good life as a public affair. Law, education, welfare, incentives, penalties and national narratives advance particular ideals of human flourishing. Some are religious and others secular, but they are substantive, specific and impossible for an entire citizenry to share.
Liberals rightly find this abhorrent. Many of these regimes are already corrupt or repressive. Add the further mission of enforcing a vision of the good life and they become more frightening still.
Yet liberals should not be surprised or refuse to see what is happening. The liberal belief that decent states must avoid prescriptive visions of the good is historically exceptional. For most of human history, the good life state has been the norm. Aristotle’s claim that politics aims not merely at life but at the good life is only the most famous formulation. Confucian and Islamic political traditions likewise made moral formation a public task. Seen this way, post-liberals are self-consciously pre-liberal. They promise to return the state to a core task that liberals are supposedly too embarrassed, weak or polite to perform.
The mainstream liberal commentariat condemns these movements as simply bad. Their leaders want power, money and impunity, while their followers are ignorant, frightened or resentful – or so the thinking goes. Much of that may be true. But if liberals cannot see that these movements also hold out genuine human goods – belonging, purpose, family, faith and recognition, however cynically packaged – they will remain stunned by their appeal.
Has this wave reached Australia? We have been resistant, not immune. Pauline Hanson and One Nation are already learning to surf it. Hanson’s call for a “monocultural” Australia is not just an immigration proposal. It is a claim about which identities and loyalties deserve public honour, reinforced by positions on family, gender and religion. One Nation has yet to produce anything as coherent or ambitious as Fidesz’s program. But the direction is recognisable: government should do more than protect choice; it should tell us what a proper Australian life looks like.
What should the liberal answer be? Well, it can’t be to build a good life state of its own. That would sacrifice the freedom and pluralism it exists to protect. But neither can liberalism survive as a bloodless list of procedures and prohibitions. It needs an attractive moral and emotional vision of its own: fairness, freedom, irreverence and the adventure of living with difference. Those are not empty rules. They are elements of a common life worth loving. If liberals cannot say so – and make it credible in practice – authoritarians will make the good life state we hoped was past into our future.

articles.title: Abbas fought the Taliban alongside US and Australian troops. Now exiled in Iran, he feels abandoned
articles.body:
War is Abbas’s* earliest memory.
As a child, the first iteration of Taliban rule forced his family to flee – with nothing but the clothes on their backs and what food they could carry – for the relative safety of far-distant hills.
War became his profession. Joining republican Afghanistan’s fledgling army, Abbas fought alongside American, Australian and British troops, believing in the foreigners’ ultimately false promise that they could bring peace and prosperity to his homeland.
Conflict is his constant attendant now, over Afghanistan’s border in neighbouring Iran, as the US, the country he fought with, rains bombs on the land of his exile. Back home, the resurgent Taliban – unreformed, unrepentant and firmly in charge – seek him still.
The war – for all its varied complexions, it feels the same war – goes on.
In the five years since Kabul dramatically fell back into the hands of the Taliban, those who served Afghanistan’s republican government have found themselves the targets of violent retribution. Those who took up arms against the Taliban are particular targets.
Abandoned US military databases – containing Afghans’ personal and biometric data such as fingerprints, photographs, and home addresses – are being used to hunt former soldiers who served the “infidel” west.
Social media groups share information on the latest atrocities, videos of former soldiers being whipped in the street, shot in summary executions, or dragged away in night raids to be tortured in Taliban prisons.
Abbas joined the military – initially at least – for the money. For a poor boy from the provinces, the army represented a regular income and a full belly, a reliable way to support his family. That there was a war on was barely a consideration: there was always a war on.
After basic training, he passed a selection course to serve in the special forces.
“At first I joined for money but when I entered the commandos everything changed,” Abbas tells the Guardian. “There were foreign forces teaching us … they gave speeches about global terrorism.
“It was not about money any more. I became very committed; I just wanted to serve my country and fight Taliban and destroy the terrorist groups.”
He spent 12 years in the Afghan national army, most of those wearing the distinctive red badge of the special forces, “and we fought many hard battles”.
Abbas served alongside Australian troops in southern Afghanistan, night-time missions by helicopter in late 2011, in the restive and mountainous Khas Uruzgan district.
“There were many forces we served with: Germans in Kunduz, French in Kapisa, and especially we were with Americans. The Australian forces were in Uruzgan, and we went there. We took part in combat alongside them, especially in Khas Uruzgan, we … executed two missions with them by air.”
Abbas said he and his comrades “were always on the frontline”.
“We spent many days and nights with foreign forces. I performed combat duties in [approximately] 20 provinces of Afghanistan.”
He was wounded in a firefight in Laghman district, shot twice at close range. His bulletproof vest deflected the bullet that struck the left side of his chest, “but another hit my left arm, breaking the bone”. He was taken by US helicopter to Bagram hospital: “I still have a metal plate in my left arm.”
Abbas remembers the camaraderie of his days serving alongside western troops with fondness: “We risked our lives to help each other on and off the battlefield and to rescue one another. They always called us brothers.”
But he remembers too, the commitments that were made to him.
“They promised they wouldn’t abandon us. But in the end, when they withdrew, they simply left us. And they did it in such a way that we were left with our hands tied, the entire army was disarmed.
“Those who were high-ranking officials left, while the rest of us, sergeants like me, were left behind. No one even asked about us.”
When Kabul fell, Abbas was forced to burn most of his documents and destroy photographs: incriminating evidence in the eyes of the Taliban.
A bare handful remain secretly in his possession: pictures on patrol with western forces, certificates of appreciation from foreign militaries commending his “outstanding commitment, dedication and support” to their operations.
Life since the fall, with a wife and young son, has been precarious, often dangerous. His has been a shifting, uncertain existence in the shadows.
As the Taliban swept northwards across Afghanistan, expanding and consolidating its control from the major cities to smaller, more distant villages, there were fewer and fewer places to hide.
With his family, Abbas fled over Afghanistan’s arid, inhospitable border into Iran.
There, with no legal rights, he is vulnerable to exploitation and extortion: landlords demand thousands of dollars for tiny apartments that have been condemned as unfit for habitation; he has been forced to take dangerous, illegal work for far less than a living wage.
When US bombs started raining down on Tehran, Abbas and his family fled once again for the mountainous countryside.
“Our life in Iran is very difficult; refugees face a lot of problems. Especially for us former military personnel … we are still being threatened by Taliban groups even here. We also fear that we might be deported to Afghanistan.”
Abbas said his family’s future depends on being able to find a safe country, far from the reach of the Taliban, and the American war which has blighted his Iranian exile.
“I am waiting to see what will happen, but I am hopeful … I will build a better life for my family, a better future for my son.”
Many in Afghanistan feel as Abbas does – betrayed by the foreign forces in whom they placed their trust.
On the day of his second inauguration as US president, Donald Trump halted all Afghan refugee resettlement by executive order. The shutdown left more than 1,000 Afghan former interpreters and soldiers stranded in a US-run camp in Qatar, and hundreds of thousands more vetted applicants stuck in neighbouring countries like Pakistan.
In Germany, a new government sought to renege on a commitment to resettling hundreds of Afghan refugees it had identified as being at risk. The country’s highest court ruled it could not arbitrarily cancel hundreds of resettlement places it had already promised.
And in Britain, a House of Commons committee report this month reported that a massive data breach from within the UK government’s Afghan relocations and assistance policy exposed thousands of Afghans to potentially life-threatening danger. Afghans still trapped inside the country are being told by the UK government to “self-move” to safe third countries, a policy that “risks excluding people the UK has promised to help,” the committee chair, Tan Dhesi, said.
A spokesperson for Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said five years on from the fall of Kabul: “We stand firm in our pursuit to do all we can to protect the people of Afghanistan from the oppressive acts of the Taliban, particularly women and girls.
“We also remain committed to assisting those who helped Australia’s mission in Afghanistan.”
Until 2023, the Australian government ran a dedicated “locally engaged employee” (LEE) program for Afghans who worked for and with Australia “and are at risk of harm as a result of their work”.
The program certified 2,059 Afghans – but only 1,208 of those have reached Australia, according to the latest government figures (along with 4,493 immediate family members).
But hundreds of Afghans still living in hiding inside the country, or stranded in perilous situations elsewhere, say they were unable to apply before the LEE program closed, or had their applications rejected despite providing evidence of support for Australia, including fighting alongside Australian troops. A government review of the program found it was riven by “delays, double handling and confusion”, and it imposed an unreasonable administrative burden on those fleeing the Taliban seeking safety.
Abbas has family in Australia, and, having fought alongside Australian troops on their missions in Afghanistan, he applied for LEE protection from Australia.
He was rejected, the government ruling he had not been “in a direct employment relationship with defence”.
“While the applicant might have worked alongside the coalition forces, including members of the Australian Defence Force in partnership on operations in Afghanistan, it does not appear that the applicant was ‘employed with’ the ADF,” the government decision states.
Wong’s spokesperson said the current government had approved more LEE applications than any before it. “Since the Albanese government took office, Dfat has certified close to 650 applications from Afghan Locally Engaged Employees, more than the total approved under all previous foreign ministers combined since the program began in 2013.”
Australia, too, has provided broader support – more than $310m in humanitarian assistance, through established partners and UN agencies – “to ensure our aid supports those most in need – not the Taliban”.
Zaki Haidari, a former Afghan refugee who is now an Australian citizen, remains in close contact with dozens of former soldiers, interpreters and others who supported western nations in their failed two-decade mission in Afghanistan.
“Almost every conversation I have with people inside Afghanistan is filled with fear, uncertainty and hopelessness. Families tell me they struggle to afford food, many have lost their livelihoods, and parents worry constantly about the future of their children,” Haidari, Amnesty International’s Australian refugee rights advocate, says.
Haidari said women live under constant surveillance, fearing arrest for speaking out or failing to comply with the Taliban’s ever-tightening restrictions. Members of the Hazara ethnic and religious minority – for decades Taliban targets – are forcibly evicted from homes and face discrimination and violence.
Haidari said Australia’s LEE program “undoubtedly saved lives”, but there were still thousands endangered by their support and assistance for Australia.
Hopes that a Taliban desperate for international legitimacy would temper their more repressive instincts have proven illusory: with global attention shifted to other conflicts, the Taliban has further entrenched their brutality across Afghanistan.
Australia’s obligation to the people of Afghanistan “did not end with the military withdrawal”, Haidari says.
“Many people who supported Australia’s mission remain at risk and continue to wait for protection.
“Many fear for their lives every day.”
*Name/s have been changed

articles.title: Scientists hope to shed light on young universe by using far side of the moon
articles.body:
Little is known about what was happening shortly after the big bang, but now researchers are hoping to shed fresh light on the matter by harnessing the far side of the moon.
Scientists plan to put a suitcase-sized satellite into orbit around the moon, using the data it collects as it passes the far side to search for a radio frequency signal emitted by neutral hydrogen atoms in the early universe.
More specifically, the satellite, nicknamed CosmoCube, will be looking for what is known as the 21cm line. Crucially, the older the signal, the more its wavelength has been stretched, or redshifted, to longer wavelengths, providing a way for its strength to be tracked over time relative to the cosmic microwave background radiation.
“The main thing we track by looking at this signal is what’s the physical temperature of the gas during the early universe,” said Prof Eloy de Lera Acedo, the lead author from the University of Cambridge’s Cavendish Laboratory.
With the 21cm signal acting a bit like a thermometer, the team are hoping to study events from the start of the so-called “dark ages”, about 380,000 years after the big bang, through the cosmic dawn, when the first stars and galaxies emerged, to the end of what is known as the epoch of reionization, approximately 1bn years after the big bang.
“The temperature of the gas is affected by the things happening in the universe at the time,” said de Lera Acedo. In addition he noted the amplitude and shape of the 21cm signal was expected to be influenced by dark matter, offering a way for experts to investigate the nature of this mysterious component of the universe.
Researchers have attempted to detect the 21cm line before but it is difficult to do using Earth-based instruments. Not only is the signal weak but human-made technology – from FM radios to plane communication – can cause interference. Writing in the journal Nature Astronomy, de Lera Acedo and his colleagues said other challenges included disturbances created by the Earth’s ionosphere.
While experts at the Edges (Experiment to Detect the Global EoR Signature) radio telescope in Australia claim to have found the 21cm line, questions have been raised over the results.
The team behind the CosmoCube mission, which is expected to last two years, said taking observations from the far side of the moon should avoid many of the challenges faced by Earth-based instruments.
“The total cost is estimated to be just under £50m and the launching date – we expect it to be about five years from now,” said de Lera Acedo, adding that CosmoCube had already been granted more than £2m of funding by the UK Space Agency.
Phil Bull, a professor of cosmology at the Jodrell Bank Centre for Astrophysics who is not involved in the project, welcomed the mission.
“The CosmoCube measurements will help us understand the major ingredients of our cosmic origins – the processes that led to the formation of the first stars and galaxies, and lit up the Universe after a period called the cosmic dark ages,” he said.
But, Bull noted, CosmoCube was not the only mission trying to make these measurements, and others may get there first.
“More ominously, other planned lunar missions might bring with them exactly the type of human-generated radio noise that the mission is trying to escape,” he said, “making this a race against time.”

articles.title: ‘It opens up doors and minds’: inside Sydney’s tattoo convention
articles.body:
At the Sydney tattoo convention, the city’s historic town hall fills with the buzz of tattoo machines, the comforting aroma of hospital-grade sanitiser and the timeless tunes of Linkin Park.
The convention’s founder and managing director of Thirteen Feet Tattoo studios, Katie Bailey, says it wasn’t easy to secure the 137-year-old venue. When she pitched it to Sydney council for their first event four years ago: “at first they were nervous about it, they had people everywhere checking in on us, but after that first event, they thought it was amazing. Tattooing and town hall just go together.”
Roughly 700 artists applied for the convention, but only 180 were approved to display their work for a crowd of 5,000 visitors. Many artists have filled their weekend’s schedule well in advance while other stalls have left space for walk-ins. As well as seminars, documentaries, talks and a nail-biting, machete-juggling performance from the world’s most tattooed man, Lucky Diamond Rich, much of the event revolves around the competitions, held at the end of each day.
“It’s a platform to legitimise tattooing, which is becoming much more mainstream,” says co-organiser Rhys Gordon. “It opens up doors and minds,” making the world of tattooing more accessible to the uninitiated – like Sydney local Will, who is attending the convention to get his first tattoo.
As the stencil of a soaring American traditional eagle is placed across Will’s torso, he describes the situation as “a bit overwhelming … but I’ll get it done”. His artist, Ben Hastings from Sydney studio Tattoo Rosies supports his canvas – “he’s got this, he’s in the zone”. Not only did the piece get finished, Will’s inaugural ink won the tattoo of the day competition.
Organisers put a strong emphasis on diversity among the stalls, and sought tattooists from regional towns. Artist Duane James, from Higherground tattoo studio in Kurrajong, spends the day working on a marathon thigh piece for Dasha, a tattoo devotee from Sydney’s northern beaches. “Being fully tattooed, it’s nice being among people that all share a common interest, it’s like I’m among my people,” she says. “It’s been wonderful.”
“We’ll absolutely get it finished today,” James promises. The pair are committed.
Laura has travelled from Hobart to go under the needle of artist Anna Rose. Rose and fellow artist Twitch spend much of the weekend collaborating on a leg sleeve for Laura.
“Anna and I have built a bit of a rapport over the time that we’ve done a few tattoos together,” Laura says. “There’s a lot of trust involved in this now – from both directions. I have a lot of faith in Anna and I know her work. We were just throwing around ideas but I knew coming into this that I was going to love whatever she was going to do.”
Testament to fostering a close relationship between artist and canvas, Laura’s piece wins the best collaboration competition.
Shell, winner of perhaps the most-entered competition, best back piece, proudly displays a massive traditional American eagle entangled with a traditional Japanese dragon, “a duality that represents my own taste and style”, she says. Both a tattoo artist and canvas, Shell beams at the opportunities to fan out at the convention. “I’m wanting to see what the other back pieces look like! I wanted to see what I was up against, because I know a lot of people have amazing back pieces.”
But the convention is not all about competition.
Thirty-year veteran of the industry Ichi Hatano, visiting from Japan, and his canvas Hugh are slowly chipping away on a traditional Japanese back piece. “I’ve been going to Japan to see him since about 2022,” says Hugh. “I go over a couple of times a year”. They are in no rush to finish. “It’s a very slow process, but it’s always worth it,” he says.

articles.title: Civilian Casualties in Ukraine in July Hit Highest Monthly Toll Since March 2022, UN Says
articles.body:
Civilian casualties in Ukraine in July reached their highest level since the early months of Russia's full-scale invasion, as Russian forces intensified long-range missile and drone strikes on towns and cities far from the front line, the UN said in a report published Friday.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine confirmed that at least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured last month, the highest toll in any month since March 2022. The figures represent a 30% jump from June and a 70% increase compared to July 2025.
Long-range weapons, including cruise and ballistic missiles and drones, remained the primary cause of civilian casualties, accounting for 38% of all deaths and injuries in July.
"Most casualties from these weapons occurred far from the front line in urban centers," the UN report read.
In recent months, Russia has stepped up attacks using ballistic missiles, which fly at high speeds along steep trajectories that make them far harder to intercept than drones or cruise missiles.
Facing a critical shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky issued an urgent appeal to Washington this week for additional supplies.
In its report, the UN also noted a rise in the number of deaths from short-range drone attacks near the front line, which killed 111 people and wounded 710 in July, the highest monthly level since the war began in February 2022.
Overall, Kyiv was the hardest-hit city last month, with a total of 54 civilians killed, followed by the cities of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia.
More than 16,000 civilians have been killed since Russia's full-scale invasion, according to the UN, with the overwhelming majority of them Ukrainian.
Reuters contributed reporting.

articles.title: How a US crackdown is upending plans for Chinese ‘birth tourists’
articles.body:
How a US crackdown is upending plans for Chinese ‘birth tourists’
Prospective parents face growing uncertainty over whether their plans to secure broader education options for their children remain viable
Li, a woman in her late twenties from southwestern China, is anxious about her coming interview for a 10-year US visa.
She has big plans for her travels – a weeks-long stay next year that would be her first visit to the country – followed by a planned return trip in two years while pregnant so her child can attain American citizenship.
“I was speechless when I saw the news,” said Li, who preferred not to disclose her full name due to privacy reasons. “Trump is too unpredictable.”
With reports emerging on Chinese social media of pregnant women being turned away at US border checkpoints in the past week, prospective parents face growing uncertainty over whether their plans to secure broader international education options for their children remain viable.
A landlord based in Los Angeles – a popular entry port for expectant parents – said that four incoming tenants, who were Chinese and pregnant, were denied entry into the US over the past week.

articles.title: Tech Visionary Says the Big AI Labs Don’t Get What People Want
articles.body:
Tim O’Reilly’s yardstick for measuring the worth of a company, person, or society has long been create more value than you capture. It’s no surprise that O’Reilly—publisher, internet pioneer, VC, conference organizer, and dispenser of tech wisdom—is applying that metric to the way people design and use AI. Specifically, he’s pushing for a future where open-source AI is an elixir for the masses. He worries that, like Microsoft in the 1990s, today’s hyperscalers are trying to lock users into their products. So he is promoting efforts to open-source AI technology—not only making critical technical details such as neural-net weights accessible, but unlocking the whole stack of an AI system, giving control to designers and users.
O’Reilly sees AI as a new creative medium, which he uses extensively—and even has a blog about his chats with it. During our conversation, we discovered that we disagree about AI’s role in producing original content. Guess who took which side.
STEVEN LEVY: You are all in on open-source AI. Make your case.
TIM O'REILLY: First, let's make sure we're talking about the same thing. When most people talk about open-source AI, they're really just talking about open-weight models. It’s much bigger than that. In the ’90s, when everybody else was focused on open-source licenses, I was like, “No, no, it's about the architecture of the system. Does it enable participation?”
Why is that needed?
The big labs are reading the future wrong. They have told themselves a narrative where having the biggest, best model is the key to the future. Big models like Claude are optimizing for particular use cases, but they aren't necessarily the use cases that people want. I want to embed my own special sauce. The most important thing is having a clean separation between the model, the harness, and the application. And right now we're not getting that. They built an architecture of control rather than an architecture of freedom and participation, so they have the ability to track you.
Isn’t it against the interests of big companies to give up control?
Oh, it's totally against their interests. But that doesn't mean that they're making the right strategic decision. For a long time, the latest and greatest models were really better for everything. Now they’re better for some things and worse for others. People are talking a lot about how Fable and Sol are worse writers than the lower-level models. [Note: Anthropic and OpenAI would disagree.] The breakthroughs that we're getting in so-called frontier AI are actually pushing us further away from what ordinary people are going to need. We could win frontier AI here in the US, and China will kick our ass because they have lower-level models diffused widely through society. The goal is to give people the ability to innovate freely, to paint outside the lines.
People worry that open-source software can be a security risk, since bad actors will be able to jump the frontier model’s guardrails.
All of the cybersecurity incidents we’ve seen are from the frontier models. So risks like cybersecurity and the ability to develop pathogens are actually an argument for slowing down the frontier models more than an argument for restricting open-weight models.
So you feel that with open source the AI powers will no longer be dominant?
I don't predict the future. but I will say the world is proceeding the way that I hoped it would. What if the big frontier models end up like mainframes or supercomputers—aimed at really hard problems, which are not actually the thing that gets diffused throughout society? People are building things like Pi, an open-source [agentic] harness. One of the things we're working on at my nonprofit, the AI Disclosures Project, is the idea of an open-memory consortium. Mark Zuckerberg’s thesis is, he’s going to lock you in because Meta will give you the AI that knows you best. The open-source vision needs to say no to this. Open source can give you the ability to switch models, switch providers, and maintain all the context that it needs.
You recently wrote a piece in the Economist about how Elon Musk—as well as other tech leaders—have so much power in their companies that they are anti-capitalist, in the sense that their desires, rather than the marketplace, determine strategy.
In general, Silicon Valley has become anti-capitalist. They use the language of markets. But around 2010, the whole model came into play with Uber and Lyft. Funded by VCs, they literally spent billions of dollars to subsidize rides. The venture capitalists picked the winner rather than the market. That became the template. All the capital piles on and chokes out other possible paths.
In AI, all the money is funneling into a few companies, but none seem to have a lock.
Because it's a failed model. The real action is open source. Just like in the early 1990s, when everybody thought it was all a battle for who ruled the PC, and then the web came out of left field while nobody was paying attention. I think that the real AI future will be a ferment of innovation that's not being funded by venture capital—in the same way that the web wasn't funded by VCs.
One of those disruptions might be your own company, built on books and writing.
The book business has been in decline for 25 years. At our peak, our book business was maybe $70 million, and it's now $30 million. As books generated less revenue, we had to find a way to compensate people for sharing their knowledge, because that's our fundamental business. So now AI comes along and hoovers everything up. Can we build a set of tools that help people with that? Being able to invoke the knowledge of experts is a superpower, and we have to figure out what that looks like now.
When I edit this interview I will boil down our long conversation to a shorter one, but I won’t use AI to do it. And of course, the writing in the introduction will be all mine. It’s actually our policy.
I think that's a legacy thing that's going to go. My ability to have a thought partner in AI when I'm writing is very powerful.
AI does your writing for you?
No, no. I use it for brainstorming, and sort of just functional writing. When I interview somebody for an hour, I go to AI and say, “Turn it into something I can use.” I don't have the time to write up all those interviews.
Aren’t you worried that AI will eventually supplant human writing?
AI is literally a medium, in the same way that written words are a medium, or paint or music is a medium. When I talk to an AI or design art with it, I get something different out of it than you do, in the same way that Michelangelo and Van Gogh got completely different things out of paint. The idea that you can't write with AI will seem as curious as the idea that you can't make a good portrait or landscape with a camera. There will be people who are masters at expressing their ideas by summoning words from LLMs. People used to ride horses. Now, few do. We're in the early days.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

articles.title: Ahmed al-Sharaa: A New Vision for Syria
articles.body:
Al Jazeera World
Ahmed al-Sharaa: A New Vision for Syria
An exclusive Al Jazeera interview with the man who took over as president of Syria in January 2025 about his vision for the long-term future of his country.
From opposition figure to Head of State – how Ahmed al Sharaa plans to transform Syria into a modern Arab democracy. In this extended interview, Al Jazeera’s Ali Al Dafiri talks to al-Sharaa about his plans for Syria. In December 2024, the 53-year rule by the al-Assad dynasty crumbled in the face of overwhelming armed opposition, led by Abu Mohammed al-Julani, leader of Hayat Tahrir al-Sham. Bashar al-Assad was forced out of office and fled to Russia – and al-Julani took power to become President Ahmed al-Sharaa. In the months that followed, he re-established diplomatic relations between Syria and the regional and global community that had fractured over previous decades. Al Dafiri asks al-Sharaa about his plans to revitalise his country, where economic progress and social development had come to a standstill due to continued Western sanctions and increasing isolation. Al-Sharaa reveals a potential security agreement with Israel – and says he’ll play no part in military action in Lebanon or the disarmament of Hezbollah. He also celebrates his success in resolving Syria’s longstanding conflict with its Kurdish community. His vision is for Syrian democracy to be gradually restored after decades of authoritarian rule.
