articles.title: Sunil Amrith On 'The Burning Earth' And The Unequal Costs Of Environmental Destruction
articles.body:
Sunil Amrith is the Renu and Anand Dhawan Professor of History at Yale University with a secondary appointment as professor at the Yale School of the Environment. He serves as Director of the Macmillan Centre for International and Area Studies and Yale's Vice Provost for International Affairs.He has received the 2016 Infosys Prize in Humanities, a 2017 MacArthur Fellowship, and the 2025 Toynbee Prize in Global History, among others. He has authored five books that put Asia at the heart of global history. In this conversation, he discusses his book, 'The Burning Earth'.Excerpts from the interview.Q: Why did you feel this book needed to be written?
A: It was a coming together of my academic life and the rest of my life. For close to 20 years, I had been researching some of the themes that do make it into 'The Burning Earth'. I've particularly been interested in the relationship between migration, the movement of people and environmental change. So I wrote a book more than 10 years ago called 'Crossing the Bay of Bengal', which I think was my first foray into environmental history, in which I was really thinking about the enormous movement of people, particularly from Tamil Nadu, to southeast Asia in the 19th and 20th century, many of them to work on rubber plantations, but also to work in port cities, places like Singapore and Penang and Rangoon, and understanding that that was actually a moment of fundamental transformation in the environment.
.. At the same time, as a teacher, but also as a parent, as a citizen, the climate crisis became quite unavoidable in my own consciousness. And so for me, that prompted me to scale things up beyond my areas of specialisation towards perhaps the biggest question, which is how did we get to this point of planetary crisis? And that's really what's at the heart of 'The Burning Earth'.Q: You also bring in a kind of storytelling which positions itself in different geographies as if to say, the inherited narratives of Eurocentric histories are not what we're going to look at. A: If the question is what is it about my own perspective that may make this book a little bit different from some of the other books out there on this big theme of the environment, it is the fact that my own training is not in European and North American history. And I think most of what is called global history continues to take as its starting point and as its default, a kind of familiar North Atlantic history. And so by starting the book in China and ending it in Indonesia, I was really trying to write it anchored in Asia... Asia has always been home to the majority of humanity. It still is today. And so it seemed to me completely fitting to really think about the history of this planet with a firm anchor in the part of the world, the part of the planet which has been the most inhabited by most people throughout the longest period of time.Q: How do you bring in a methodology which ensures that what you're positioning and presenting can be as accurate as possible? A: That's the biggest challenge of a book like this. There's no possibility that I can have the primary expertise in all of these areas that I write about in the book. And so in some ways that was a leap that I took. Academia is a collective enterprise. And this is very much a book that builds on my own work in some areas. And in other areas, it's really sort of bringing together my reading in multiple fields of scholarship and different disciplines as well. So I'm a historian, but some of the most exciting new scholarship which I draw on and interpret is actually coming from the physical sciences.There's some phenomenally interesting work in paleoclimatology, for example, which is trying to reconstruct past climates using ice cores, using lake bed sediment, using tree rings. And of course, these disciplines traditionally and even still within the walls of the university barely meet. But what's been very interesting about recent work on climate and environment in particular, is you have this forcing together of completely different ideas of what the archive is.Q: You use the word 'elite' a few times when you're talking about social stratification for a very specific economic growth touted as well-being of a community, but usually you see it as exploitative. A: I don't use the word that many times, but when I do, I think it's doing a lot of work for me. 'The Burning Earth' is not an activist book, which is to say that it is just that bit muddier and less clear about the villains of the piece than activist writing necessarily has to be. And yet there is such a strong core in my own thinking of awareness of just how stark environmental inequalities are and just how much the scale of planetary destruction that has been achieved over the last two centuries has been disproportionately, not exclusively, but disproportionately driven by the elite pursuit of luxuries and of accumulation... There is a story of human need in this book and there's also a story of human greed... I think we need to think about desire, we need to think about states, we need to think about liberation, we need to think about the genuinely liberatory promises that led to some of this environmental destruction which can't be reduced to a question of greed or even of capitalism...There's no question that the social and economic system that has been a driving force in the climate crisis is the capitalist system. But the socialist system in some sense was even more environmentally profligate and wasteful. It was just less successful. And so in terms of its longevity, in terms of the scale on which it was operating, it kind of doesn't compare with what a particular capitalist mode of production does to our ability to treat all of nature as commodity and to lead to this kind of constantly expanding frontier of production.
But my question is really a different one, which is, where were the alternatives? Who was thinking differently?Q: You point out that there are these rather horrific incidents which are almost genocidal. A: I think that's one of the key narratives in the book to show that the moments of the most intensive and accelerated environmental destruction over the last several hundred years have almost always gone together with moments of intense violence. And violence is at the core of 'The Burning Earth'. Not just violence against the earth or against nature, but against other people... Wars that are going on all around us in the world today are part of a very long pattern where armed violence and militarism and military destruction have been inextricably bound with massive environmental destruction.

articles.title: Iberian orca known for ramming boats seen with suspected gunshot wounds
articles.body:
Spanish officials have launched an investigation after the matriarch of an orca pod known for jostling and ramming boats off the Iberian Peninsula was spotted with wounds suggesting she had been shot by a pellet gun.
On Friday, Spain’s environment ministry said Toñi, the oldest living member of the pod, had been seen swimming in the Strait of Gibraltar with markings on her dorsal fin that were “consistent with shots from a pellet gun”.
A source from the ministry told El País that some of the projectiles remained lodged in her fin, posing a risk of infection. The ministry was in touch with officials in Portugal, the source added, as the markings were detected after the orcas had travelled from the waters off the Portuguese city of Faro.
The orcas of the Iberian Peninsula burst into headlines in 2020 after sailors shared stories of rudders that had been rammed and boats that had been spun 180 degrees or tipped sideways. Since then, a small group of orcas from the pod have been blamed for damaging scores of vessels and sinking at least four boats, leaving scientists scrambling to explain the baffling behaviour.
Scientists have long pushed back against the assertion that the orcas are attacking vessels, instead suggesting that the behaviour could be a form of play or a means of practising their hunting skills.
In the days since Toñi’s injuries came to light, the WeWhale and Iberian Orca Guardians (IOG) association have been closely tracking the animal for any sign of weakness. “We know Toñi. We were with her a few weeks ago and these wounds were not there,” the IOG co-founder Janek Andre said.
“Seeing Toñi, la abuela [the grandmother], like this is devastating,” he added. “If someone has deliberately fired a shotgun at her, this is not only an act of extreme cruelty against an individual animal. It is an attack on one of the last remaining members of a critically endangered population.”
Researchers have long sought to highlight the many stressors faced by this population of orcas as they navigate life in a major shipping route. Food scarcity, injuries and pollution have left the population on a knife’s edge, reduced to between 30 and 40 individuals.
In 2023, video emerged that appeared to show people launching firecrackers into the sea as orcas rammed the rudder of their vessel, hinting that the animals were now facing another threat as sailors push back against their actions.
“There has been enormous public discussion about Iberian orcas and their interactions with vessels,” said Andre. “Whatever someone’s opinion about those interactions may be, shooting at these animals can never be an acceptable response. These orcas need protection, not retaliation.”

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes NOVATEK Facilities in Ust-Luga
articles.body:
On August 14, Ukraine struck NOVATEK facilities in the Russian port of Ust-Luga, located in the Leningrad region.
The report comes from the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
NOVATEK, Ust-Luga is a production and transshipment complex designed for the fractionation and processing of stable gas condensate. Its capacity is nearly 8 million metric tons of raw materials per year.
This morning, news broke of a fire caused by an attack by Ukrainian drones, and preliminary assessments of the strikes have already emerged.
The attack damaged stable gas condensate fractionation units and the combined hydrocracking unit.
Ust-Luga is not merely a terminal for transshipping raw materials. Within the complex, stable gas condensate was processed into light and heavy crude oil, jet fuel, diesel, marine fuel components, and LPG.
A significant portion of the products obtained after refining was exported by sea. Thus, the complex allowed Russia not only to export raw materials but also to produce petroleum products with higher added value.
According to data for 2022, the complex produced approximately 6.8 million metric tons of commercial products. Of this total, about 4.2 million metric tons were light and heavy crude oil, and 1.05 million metric tons were jet fuel.
Another approximately 1.49 million metric tons consisted of diesel fuel and marine fuel components, while LPG production reached approximately 78,000 metric tons.
According to Militarnyi’s analysis, the cargo line of the port terminal located next to the complex was also damaged.
The combined hydrocracking unit is of particular importance. This process allows for the conversion of heavier oil fractions and residues into more valuable light petroleum products, notably kerosene and gasoil.
Therefore, damage to the fractionation and hydrocracking units affects not only individual production facilities but also the entire gas condensate processing chain.
Ust-Luga is one of the key elements of NOVATEK’s export infrastructure in the Baltic Sea, which ensured the processing of raw materials and the subsequent shipment of finished products by sea.

articles.title: RSF drone attacks, Somalia’s drought emergency, and WFP sticks with Palantir: The Cheat Sheet
articles.body:
Share & more
Our editors’ weekly take on humanitarian news, trends, and developments from around the globe.
On our radar
RSF targets major Sudanese cities with drone attacks
The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) – the paramilitary group battling the Sudanese army for control of the country – has used drones to target major cities across Sudan including Khartoum (the capital) and El Obeid, where the group has been attempting a full-scale invasion. Several people were killed as Sudanese army bases, a mosque, and electricity infrastructure were all hit. The attacks were some of the largest and most coordinated from the RSF in several months, and were likely designed to send a message after a string of military setbacks. Last month, the UAE-backed group lost control over a highway connecting El Obeid to Khartoum, and they have also suffered defeats in Blue Nile and West Darfur states. In a sign of possible desperation, RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo has renewed threats to retake Khartoum, which his forces brutally occupied earlier in the war. But SAF officials claiming they can win the war by the end of the year are surely overconfident too. They have made many similar claims before, only for the pendulum to swing back against them.
MSF sounds alarm over Somalia’s drought emergency
Exhausted by four failed rainy seasons, more than half a million rural Somalis have left their homes this year looking for help. Over 85% of those displaced are women and children. The sprawling settlements on the outskirts of Baidoa, in the southwest, are one destination. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has found that every second child screened in these camps was malnourished. And yet donors have provided only 30% of the cash needed to support Somalia’s $852 million humanitarian response plan. Across the country, 6.5 million people are facing acute hunger, nearly double last year’s figure. Two million of those are in an “emergency” category, their assets and livelihoods whittled away by drought. Among the hardest hit is the Burhakaba district in southern Bay region, where earlier this year there was a “credible risk of famine”. MSF is ringing the alarm that donors need to find money urgently for preventative action as Somalia’s woes multiply. A severe El Niño is expected from October-to-December, triggering floods and yet more destruction and displacement.
As the Board of Peace falters, a dangerous governance gap forms in Gaza
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has now publicly rejected a US-backed plan for the future of Gaza that he had previously thrown cold water on. The rejection only intensifies a shroud of uncertainty hanging around a series of moves taken by the Board of Peace since the middle of July aimed at signalling some sort of progress on the implementation of last October’s long-stalled ceasefire agreement. With no clarity on a path forward, a dangerous governance gap on the ground is being filled by Israeli-backed militias, criminal groups, and family clans while also leaving Palestinians in Gaza in an administrative limbo. Meanwhile, Israel is carrying out a large-scale operation to crush rubble and clear it from the nearly 70% of the enclave directly under its control. The NGO Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor raised concerns about the rubble containing bodies of Palestinians killed in Israel’s military campaign and evidence of war and atrocity crimes. To find out more about how public health data can support accountability for alleged Israeli war crimes, check out our Weekend read below.
As atrocities in Myanmar intensify, investigative capacity shrinks
War crimes and crimes against humanity are escalating in frequency and intensity in Myanmar, according to the eighth and latest annual report from the UN’s Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM). The mechanism has identified military units and command structures linked to airstrikes on civilians, and is probing killings of detainees, torture, sexual violence, and “double-tap” attacks targeting rescuers. In Rakhine State, investigators are examining alleged crimes by both the military and the Arakan Army, including attacks on schools and hospitals, obstruction of aid, forced displacement, rape, executions, and the destruction of Rohingya mosques and neighbourhoods. The IIMM has collected more than 28 million items of evidence and shared thousands with the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Court, and several national jurisdictions. However, severe UN funding cuts have shrunk the mechanism’s investigative capacity to protect witnesses, process open-source evidence, and investigate sexual violence and crimes against children. For more on the impact of funding cuts on the IIMM’s work, read this piece.
Aid access severely constrained in two thirds of crises
Humanitarian access is severely constrained in two thirds of the crises assessed in the latest Global Humanitarian Access Overview by ACAPS. Of 66 countries reviewed, 44 face high, very high, or extreme barriers to aid, with 13 – including Sudan, Myanmar, Afghanistan, Palestine, Ukraine, and South Sudan – rated at the worst level. In addition to insecurity, governments and armed groups are increasingly restricting movement, deregistering NGOs, detaining aid workers, imposing checkpoints and informal taxes, and obstructing people from reaching services. Access deteriorated in 26 countries between December 2025 and May 2026, including Iran, Lebanon, Colombia, Niger, Mozambique, Uganda, and the Philippines. Rather than retreat, humanitarians have responded to constraints by negotiating passage with whoever controls territory, making aid slower, less predictable, and uneven.
New Colombian president criticised for restricting international quake response
As Colombians continued racing to find survivors of the powerful earthquake that struck the country on 10 August, President Abelardo de la Espriella’s decision to limit the entry of foreign rescue teams sparked controversy. As of 14 August, at least 281 people had been reported dead, nearly 4,000 injured, and 379 missing. Despite receiving multiple offers of assistance, De la Espriella – a far-right lawyer, businessman, and Trump ally who had taken office just three days before the earthquake – initially said Colombia did not need foreign personnel. Instead, he requested that international humanitarian aid be limited to supplies and funding. Some attributed the decision to the tense political transition and the lack of a formal handover from his predecessor, while others pointed to ideological motives. On 12 August, authorities eventually allowed foreign rescue teams to enter, but only teams from the United States, Israel, El Salvador, and Ecuador, arguing that these were the only countries whose teams met “international search-and-rescue standards”. Colombia will also receive an estimated $1.3 billion in humanitarian aid from 12 countries. For more on how escalating conflict is making aid work in Colombia more challenging, read our report here.
Weekend read
And finally…
WFP sticks with Palantir despite data security warnings
The World Food Programme has renewed its five-year contract with the controversial US data analytics firm Palantir despite “key privacy concerns” raised in a 2025 internal audit obtained by PassBlue and FRANCE 24. WFP said Palantir supports its “data-informed decision-making” and tackles data-integration challenges. Under a partnership dating back to 2019, Palantir developed DOTS, a system WFP uses to track aid and manage supply-chain data. Scrutiny over the relationship has intensified since a 14 May cyber-attack against a separate WFP system exposed sensitive data belonging to 600,000 Gaza households, alongside existing concerns over Palantir’s military and surveillance work. On 30 June, the UN’s special rapporteur on the right to food, Sofía Monsalve Suárez, publicly questioned the undisclosed terms of WFP’s agreements with Palantir and warned of conflicts of interest involving companies serving both civilian and military clients. The leaked 2025 audit warned that WFP “lacks a unified and trusted system” for managing its data and has “no clearly defined exit strategy for DOTS”, while “reputational considerations surrounding the partnership [with Palantir] have led to institutional uncertainty”. WFP sources told PassBlue and FRANCE 24 there is an “unspoken rule not to communicate on Palantir”.

articles.title: NATO scrambles warplanes to shoot down drone over Latvia
articles.body:
NATO scrambles warplanes to shoot down drone over Latvia
A NATO fighter jet has destroyed a drone that entered Latvian airspace, the US-led bloc has said.
The announcement came as Ukraine carried out a major UAV attack against Russia’s northwestern Leningrad Region on Friday. A total of 54 drones were shot down or intercepted above the region overnight, local governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said. A fire broke out at the key Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga during the raid, but it was swiftly extinguished, according to the governor.
There have been multiple reports in recent months of Ukrainian drones violating the airspace of Latvia, Estonia, Lithuania, and Finland, or crashing inside those countries, while on their way to Russia.
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said on Friday that “this morning, we saw Italian Eurofighters based in Lithuania and Turkish F-16s out of Estonia scramble, with one Eurofighter downing a drone over Latvian airspace.”
The Latvian Defense Ministry also confirmed the incident, saying in a statement that “fighter jets participating in the NATO Baltic Air Policing mission successfully shot down a foreign unmanned aerial vehicle.”
The ministry claimed that the UAV “entered Latvia as a result of Russian electronic warfare activities.”
“Similar incidents involving foreign unmanned aerial vehicles entering or approaching Latvian airspace may occur” as long as the conflict between Russia and Ukraine continues, the statement added.
Last week, Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania issued a joint demarche after Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said Moscow had “verified data,” showing that Baltic states had provided air corridors for Ukrainian drones attacking Russian civilian infrastructure. The governments in Riga, Tallinn, and Vilnius denied Galuzin’s accusations as “completely unfounded.”
On Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Russian military and intelligence services “see where things fly from and how they fly,” referring to incoming UAVs.
“This is well-known to everyone, and we are not going to prove anything to anyone here,” Peskov stressed.
Moscow previously warned that if Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania knowingly help to facilitate Ukrainian drone strikes, Russia could consider them complicit in the attacks and would have the right to self-defense under the UN Charter.

articles.title: Moment €9m worth of art stolen from Italy museum
articles.body:
Moment €9m worth of art stolen from Italy museum
Police have recovered three paintings that were stolen from a museum in Italy earlier this year.
CCTV footage of the theft on the night of 22 March was released by authorities, showing two masked thieves breaking into the Magnani Rocca Museum, near the city of Parma.
It is estimated the paintings have a combined worth of €9m (£7.8m), making it one of the most significant art thefts in Italy in recent years.
Police confirmed in a statement that the paintings by Cézanne, Renoir, and Matisse were recovered during searches, but gave no further details.
The investigation is ongoing.

articles.title: Captured Akhmat fighter says he chose Ukraine and a drone guided him away from Russia’s ranks
articles.body:
A former fighter from the Akhmat forces, armed formations loyal to Chechnya’s Kremlin-backed ruler Ramzan Kadyrov, said he wants to fight for Ukraine after nearly a year in captivity.
Identified only as Magomed, he gave his account to Dmytro Karpenko, a Ukrainian journalist and blogger known for interviewing Russian prisoners of war, in a video published on 9 August 2026. Militarnyi, a Ukrainian military news outlet, reported on the interview on 13 August.
Magomed’s reported crossing reflects a divide that has placed Chechen fighters on both sides of Russia’s war. Since 2014, Kadyrov-loyal formations have fought for Moscow, while anti-Kremlin Chechens seeking independence from Russia have supported Kyiv.
Magomed’s account traces one fighter’s claimed passage from the first camp toward the second after Russians allegedly killed his brother. His account has not been independently verified.
The Chechen fighter said he had served near Svitlodarsk, Bakhmut, and Horlivka, including evacuating soldiers’ bodies.
Magomed also claimed two Chechens had crossed before him, prompting Russian commanders to check fighters’ phones and tighten surveillance.
According to Magomed, he later followed a Ukrainian drone toward Ukrainian positions with other Chechens. Ukrainian troops dropped medicine, water, and a radio to guide them. A Russian FPV drone attacked during the crossing and killed one Chechen, he alleged.
Ukrainian forces received the survivors and handed Magomed to the police brigade "Liut". His captivity began on 29 August 2025. Magomed also alleged that Russians killed his brother and called the death an epileptic seizure. Magomed said that drove him to fight Russia.
Militarnyi reported that Magomed had joined the International Legion, which is run by Ukraine's military intelligence. However, Karpenko’s video description says he wants to join the legion. Neither source explained the discrepancy.
What is Akhmat?
Akhmat, the unit Magomed belonged to, provides Russia with frontline troops and rear-area security. UK intelligence estimated in 2024 that around 9,000 personnel served in pro-Russian Chechen units in Ukraine.
Kadyrov’s reach has also expanded during the war. A later investigation found that his armed network had grown to 20 units across Russia’s military and security structures.
The Akhmat group's influence may extend beyond military operations. In January 2026, ATESH, a Ukrainian-Crimean Tatar partisan group, said Moscow planned to hand occupied Mariupol to Akhmat as a reward for Chechen leaders’ loyalty. The resistance organization claimed that arriving Chechen forces sought control of the city’s resources and industry.
Chechens also fight for Ukraine
On the other side, Chechens seeking an independent Ichkeria (the indigenous Chechen name for Chechnya) have fought for Ukraine since 2014.
In April 2026, Ukrainian intelligence said Shamanbat, a Ukrainian special unit that includes Free Ichkeria fighters, helped conduct drone and artillery strikes on Akhmat positions. The agency claimed the operation killed dozens of Akhmat personnel and wounded about 80.

articles.title: Woman charged over vandalism of Washington's World War Two Memorial
articles.body:
Woman charged over vandalism of Washington's World War Two Memorial
Aug 14 - A Kentucky woman has been taken into custody and charged with two felony counts in connection with the vandalism at the World War Two Memorial in Washington, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, said on Friday.
Pirro said on social media that Melissa Farris faces charges each carrying penalties of up to 10 years in prison.
The World War Two Memorial was vandalized with bubbly soap and graffiti on Thursday. The fountain bubbled over with suds and the words "Clean hands Dirty $" were painted on one surface, splattering the area with red and green paint.
In videos posted to her Facebook account, Farris records herself spray painting the memorial and asking why she has not been arrested. She describes herself on the social media platform as a "pirate captain" who is "panhandling for America."
The criminal complaint filed on Friday quotes Farris as saying,
“Someone has to make choices that are different and I am accountable for my actions,” she said. “I am going to make these choices today and I will step foot into the courtroom and I will wait to be arrested …. Our government needs to be accountable for their choices too.”
In later videos posted after the incident, she appears disheveled and crying, saying she knows she upset people by her actions but was trying to get help for herself.
According to the complaint, a witness took a photo of Farris spray painting the memorial, an image that was circulated among U.S. Park Police.
An officer recognized Farris as someone they had arrested three days earlier for unlawfully camping on federal property a few blocks from the memorial.
Law enforcement found a white sign with painted letters in a nearby trash can. The paint on the sign appeared to match the paint used on the memorial.
Along with her statement on X, Pirro posted photos of a woman who appears to be Farris holding a can close to the red paint on the memorial.
In recent Facebook posts, Farris said she was planning the August 13 action to draw attention to U.S. tax dollars not being spent on ordinary Americans and to what she alleged were corporate racketeering, embezzlement and slave labor practices, among other issues. She had also contacted state and federal elected officials about her concerns, according to a person who knows her.
"She's not crazy, not at all," said the person, who asked to remain anonymous due the legal process surrounding Farris' arrest. "She's been trying to get attention."
TRUMP CONDEMNS INCIDENT
U.S. attorney Pirro has recently drawn President Donald Trump's anger for dropping charges against four people accused of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool after Trump oversaw renovations of the pool.
The pool's condition soon deteriorated, with a peeling liner and algae blooms. When dropping the vandalism charges, Pirro blamed the deterioration on faulty installation.
Trump said in response that Pirro had "folded like an umbrella."
Trump appeared to link the Reflecting Pool damage to the World War Two Memorial in a post on social media on Friday, calling it an insult to Americans who had died in the conflict.
"First the Reflecting Pool, now this," he wrote. "We are on their trail! Where do these animals come from???” REUTERS

articles.title: Konovalets' remains brought to UGCC Patriarchal Cathedral in Kyiv for farewell ceremony
articles.body:
The ashes of Yevhen Konovalets, the first head of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), have been brought to the Patriarchal Cathedral of the Resurrection of Christ of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church (UGCC) in Kyiv for a farewell ceremony, photographer Yan Dobronosov said.
"Yevhen Konovalets’ remains have already been brought to Kyiv. They were delivered to the main cathedral of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church in the capital, where people can pay their respects," he said on Facebook and posted corresponding photos.
Officials at the Patriarchal Cathedral of the UGCC said that clergy from the Patriarchal Cathedral, led by Bishop Joseph Milian, protosyncellus of Kyiv Archdiocese of the UGCC, participated in the gathering and prayer service.
In particular, the clergy performed a memorial service for the repose of Colonel Konovalets’ soul, praying for "the eternal rest of his soul and thanking God for the gift of his life and service to the Ukrainian people."
It is noted that memorial services will continue at the Patriarchal Cathedral, during which the faithful will have the opportunity to honor the memory of the colonel in prayer and bid him farewell.
"The return of Yevhen Konovalets’ remains is not merely the return of the remains of an outstanding Ukrainian. It is the return of historical memory that unites generations," the UGCC said.
On August 13, Konovalets’ coffin was received in Ukraine with full military honors.
As previously reported, on August 11 in Rotterdam (the Netherlands), a ceremony was held to exhume the remains of the prominent Ukrainian military and political figure, Colonel Yevhen Konovalets. His remains will be reburied at the National Military Memorial Cemetery.
The monument from Konovalets’ grave in Rotterdam (the Netherlands) will be brought to Ukraine as a memorial object and preserved at his family estate in Lviv region, while the burial site itself will be turned into a memorial.
Yevhen Konovalets (1891-1938) was a Ukrainian military and political figure, a colonel in the Army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic, commander of the Sich Riflemen Corps, founder of the Ukrainian Military Organization, and first head of the Leadership of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN).
Konovalets was assassinated on May 23, 1938, by Pavel Sudoplatov, an agent of the Soviet Foreign Intelligence Service, and was buried at the Crossways Cemetery in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.

articles.title: Israel's policing plan entrenches West Bank annexation: Palestine
articles.body:
Palestinian Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh has condemned an Israeli plan to transfer law enforcement powers over illegal Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank to the Israeli police, calling it another step towards imposing Israeli sovereignty and entrenching annexation.
Al-Sheikh said on Friday that the move announced by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz violates international law, UN resolutions and agreements signed between the two sides.
“It represents a new attempt to impose Israeli law and sovereignty on the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and to entrench the illegal annexation of Palestinian land,” he said.
He urged the international community, particularly the UN Security Council, to intervene and press Israel to comply with international law and relevant UN resolutions.
Israel plans new police force for illegal settlers
Katz on Friday instructed the Israeli military to prepare a plan to transfer forces' responsibilities over illegal settlers in the occupied West Bank to Israeli police, which operates under National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Katz’s office said a special police force would be established and given the necessary authority and funding.
The decision comes as the Israeli military provides security for illegal settlers during attacks on Palestinians, according to Palestinian officials.
Hamas also rejected the plan, describing it as a dangerous move towards de facto annexation and saying the transfer of authority to a police force under Ben-Gvir would further entrench illegal Israeli settlement policies.
UN warns of surge in occupied West Bank violence
The dispute comes amid growing international concern over violence and displacement in the occupied West Bank.
The UN said on Wednesday that settler violence had reached unprecedented levels, documenting more than 1,430 attacks since the beginning of 2026 across around 260 Palestinian communities.
The attacks, together with demolitions and evictions, have displaced about 3,800 Palestinians, roughly half of them children, according to the UN.
Al-Sheikh said Israeli settlements in territory occupied since 1967 are illegal and stressed that Israel has no sovereignty over any part of the occupied Palestinian territories.

articles.title: Pilot dies after helicopter crash in German forest
articles.body:
Pilot dies after helicopter crash in German forest
No one else was on the helicopter, which was carrying out liming work on the forest
A helicopter pilot has died after crashing in a forest in eastern Germany while carrying out liming work, the police directorate in the city of Chemnitz said on Friday.
Workers managed to pull the man from the helicopter after the impact, police said. Despite immediate first aid administered at the scene, the man died from his injuries.
The helicopter had no other people on board. Police did not provide information on the identity of the pilot or the cause of the accident near the small town of Sehmatal in the Ore mountains.
A police spokesman said they had been notified of the crash at around 9.55am local time.
More than 85 firefighters were deployed to the scene after the helicopter caught fire. The fire brigade was able to extinguish the blaze quickly, before the flames could spread.
District fire chief Falko Auerswald said one fire engine remained at the scene to complete safety measures.

articles.title: Ukrnafta CEO calls 3D seismic key after covering 1,210 sq km in 2024–2025
articles.body:
Ukrnafta JSC, the first company in Ukraine to use wireless 3D seismic surveying, carried out such surveys over an area of more than 1,210 square kilometers in 2024-2025, which, together with previous surveys, covers about 10% of its special permits, and considers the technology one of the key tools in oil and gas production, the company’s Chairman of the Board Bohdan Kukura said.
"In 2024-2025, Ukrnafta carried out 3D seismic surveys over an area of more than 1,210 square kilometers, which, together with previous surveys, covered nine fields and two prospective areas. This is approximately 10% of all our special permits. And this is a very much-needed process for the company to understand what is deep underground, what formations are there and at what depths. Without seismic surveying, it is very difficult to move forward with drilling," Kukura said in an exclusive interview with Interfax-Ukraine.
He stressed that the company’s task is to continue 3D seismic surveys, although due to the security situation it does not disclose the specific areas where the work is being carried out or the locations of new wells.
"But I can say that 3D seismic surveying has already become one of the key tools for making investment decisions in the exploration and development of our fields," the Ukrnafta CEO emphasized.
As reported, in this interview Kukura said that after JSC Ukrnafta came under state control, it introduced more than 100 American Petroleum Institute (API) standards into its production operations, which makes it possible to significantly improve operations and, for certain types of equipment, triple the interval between repairs. According to him, for example, two years ago the operating interval between repairs for electric submersible pumps used in oil wells was 200 days, which was not very efficient by global standards. Currently, the company-wide average is approximately 500-600 days, while for foreign-made equipment it is more than 700 days. Kukura explained that this allows the equipment to operate for a year or two without repairs or replacement, which clearly has a positive impact on production performance and offsets all additional costs associated with its acquisition.
The company’s plans for 2026 call for completing the drilling of 15 wells, but Kukura suggested that a balanced drilling program could make it possible to increase this figure (last year, the company set a drilling record, reaching 25 wells).
He added that, overall, 11 wells have already been drilled since the beginning of the year, including wells drilled jointly with Ukrgazvydobuvannia.

articles.title: Security issues shaped Estonian foreign policy last year  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
TALLINN - According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' 2025 activity report, last year's most significant foreign policy achievements included the agreement among NATO allies to raise the defense spending target to 5 percent of GDP, NATO Article 4 consultations and a UN Security Council meeting following the violation of Estonia's airspace, the strengthening of sanctions against Russia and measures against its shadow fleet, Estonia's election to the UN Human Rights Council, and the support of over a thousand Estonian companies in foreign markets.
According to Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna, 2025 demonstrated that in an increasingly complex security environment, Estonia must be even more active and proactive in its foreign policy, and has so far successfully influenced decisions that directly affect Estonia's security and well-being.
"In 2025, several topics championed by Estonia entered the European mainstream. As a significant step, the European Union agreed to keep Russia's frozen assets frozen until Russia ends its aggression and compensates Ukraine for the damage caused. The EU adopted four sanctions packages against Russia, strengthened measures against its shadow fleet, and reached a political agreement to end the import of Russian natural gas," Tsahkna said.
One of the most important security policy decisions of the year was the agreement reached at the NATO summit in The Hague, requiring all allies to invest 5 percent of their GDP in defense.
The reaction of the allies after Russian fighter jets violated Estonian airspace on September 19 last year was also important for Estonia. On Estonia's initiative, NATO Article 4 consultations were convened, and for the first time at Estonia's request, a UN Security Council meeting was held. Estonia received strong and clear support from allies and partners, and NATO strengthened its defense and deterrence posture in the region.
Last year, Estonian foreign policy was primarily shaped by Russia's continued aggression against Ukraine, changes in transatlantic relations, and Europe's need to take greater responsibility for its own security. Estonia focused on supporting Ukraine, raising the cost of aggression for Russia, strengthening NATO's deterrence and defense posture, increasing Estonia's international influence, and creating new opportunities for its companies in foreign markets.
"The task of Estonian foreign policy is to ensure Estonia's freedom and security. By supporting Ukraine's fight for its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independence, we are directly contributing to Estonia's own existence," the foreign minister said.
For this reason, Estonia's priority in 2025 was the political, economic, and military support of Ukraine and raising the cost of aggression for Russia. Estonia also actively participated in the work of the coalition of the willing developing security guarantees for Ukraine and supported Ukraine's path toward EU membership.
In 2025, Estonia took steps to expand its international reach. Estonia was elected to the UN Human Rights Council for the 2026-2028 term, and the government decided to expand Estonia's network of foreign missions with five new embassies in Yerevan, Chișinău, Baku, Brasília, and Nairobi.
"Opening new embassies allows us to increase Estonia's visibility, strengthen our security, build new partnerships, and open up opportunities for Estonian companies," the foreign minister said.
Promoting Estonia's economic interests and supporting its companies in foreign markets were also significant priorities last year. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs' business diplomacy activities supported 1,006 Estonian companies throughout the year, and new Estonian business hubs were opened in four cities.
"In today's world, security and the economy are increasingly intertwined. Helping Estonian companies enter new markets, find new partners, and reduce economic dependencies are also part of foreign policy and security," Tsahkna said.
In 2025, Estonia also strengthened its international position in digital and cyber diplomacy by participating in shaping the global dialogue on artificial intelligence, developing the GovStack initiative, and organizing the Tallinn Cyber Diplomacy Summer School. Alongside its partners, Estonia also resisted Russia's attempts to weaken international cyber norms. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs also played a significant role in organizing the Tallinn Digital Summit.
In cultural diplomacy, highlights included Arvo Pärt's 90th birthday, the ESTO cultural festival, and the 500th anniversary of the first printed text in the Estonian language. Throughout the year, dozens of events promoting Estonian culture were organized or supported by Estonia's foreign missions.
The full overview of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' 2025 activities is available on the ministry's website.

articles.title: Government to ask Saeima for authorization to participate in raising up to EUR 30 million in additional funding for airBaltic  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
RIGA - The government will ask Saeima for authorization to participate in raising up to EUR 30 million in additional funding for national airline airBaltic, Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis (New Unity) told reporters following an emergency government meeting on Friday.
This does not constitute state aid, and the government will ask Saeima for authorization to participate in securing temporary financing if necessary, Kozlovskis emphasized. The amount could range "from zero to EUR 30 million."
He also said that the repayment deadline for a EUR 30 million state loan granted to airBaltic was to be extended until December 31.
Originally, the loan's maturity date was set for August 31. Saeima will also have to decide on extending the loan repayment deadline.
As reported, on April 16 Saeima approved issuing a EUR 30 million short-term state loan to airBaltic. The deadline for repayment of the principal and interest on the short-term state loan is August 31. The loan was issued without collateral.
By July 24, airBaltic had repaid the principal sum of the state loan and the interest payments stipulated in the agreement in the amount of EUR 12.9 million.
Earlier this week, airBaltic supervisory council approved a business plan that calls for raising EUR 225 million in temporary financing to improve liquidity, using the existing collateral package for the 2029 senior bonds, as well as reducing the planned aircraft fleet from 100 to approximately 40 aircraft by 2031, airBaltic informed LETA.
airBaltic expects to operate approximately 36 Airbus A220-300 aircraft by the end of 2026, compared to 54 aircraft currently, with the fleet gradually expanding to approximately 40 aircraft by 2031.
LETA also reported, airBaltic group’s revenue last year increased by 4.2 percent compared to 2024, reaching EUR 779.344 million. Meanwhile, the airBaltic group’s losses last year totaled EUR 44.337 million, which is 2.7 times less than in 2024.
The airline carried a total of 5.2 million passengers in 2025, which is 1 percent more than in 2024.
Last summer, Germany’s national airline, Lufthansa, became a shareholder in airBaltic. Currently, the Latvian government owns 88.37 percent of airBaltic’s shares, Lufthansa holds 10 percent, the company Aircraft Leasing 1, owned by Danish businessman Lars Thuesen, a financial investor, holds 1.62 percent, and 0.01 percent is held by others. The company’s share capital is EUR 41.819 million.
Given the 2025 financial results and market conditions, airBaltic has suspended its planned initial public offering and does not currently view it as a potential source of capital for 2026, according to airBaltic’s annual report.

articles.title: Valga to Host the Largest Military History Festival in the Baltics  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
VALGA - The border town of Valga will host the largest military history event in the Baltic States on Friday and Saturday - the 18th International Military History Festival, or MilFest.
This year's main event focuses on large-scale reenactments of battles from the War of 1812 and the 1941 Summer War, a high-level historical conference, and the presentation of a significant work on the Forest Brothers, bringing together history enthusiasts and military history clubs from Estonia, Latvia, and Poland.
On the festival's opening day, a history conference will be held at the Valga Military Museum, featuring former Minister of Culture Anneli Ott, Senior Researcher at the Estonian Institute of Historical Memory Peeter Kaasik, and Commander of the Kuperjanov Infantry Battalion, Lieutenant Colonel Lauri Teppo, who will discuss the application of lessons learned from the war in Ukraine. The conference will be moderated by Erkki Koort, Director of the Institute of Internal Security. This will be followed by the presentation of the major work on the Estonian Forest Brothers, "Between War and Peace," and a panel discussion with its authors: Meelis Saueauk, Meelis Maripuu, Peeter Kaasik, and Martin Andreller.
On Saturday, spectacular staged battle reenactments will unfold in Valga's city park. The events will be preceded by a lecture on the War of 1812 by Siim Õismaa, a senior researcher at the Estonian War Museum, and a lecture on the 1941 Summer War by Peeter Kaasik and Meelis Maripuu. The Summer War-themed reenactment is directed by Merili Viks, and the battle will be conducted by the NGO Front-Line Estonia, led by Reimo Leoli, along with military history clubs from Estonia, Latvia, and Poland.
In addition to the historical spectacle, the city park will feature equipment and gear from the Estonian Defence Forces, allies, and various organizations, including the Rescue Board, the police, the Defence League, the Women's Home Defence, and the Valga Ukrainian Society "Kalyna." A traditional antiques and crafts fair will take place on the grounds of the Military Museum on Saturday, featuring a performance by the group Shukar Roma and a screening of the feature film "Tired," about Ukrainian war veterans.
"Valga MilFest is not merely a spectacle, but a living history lesson that helps us understand and value the story of the survival of the Estonian state and people," said Mart Kase, Mayor of Valga Municipality, who will also be hosting the Saturday program in the city park. "This year's large-scale battle reenactments and the in-depth events dedicated to the Forest Brothers confirm Valga's role as an important guardian of patriotic education and historical heritage."
Musical entertainment for the festival will include a major open-air concert on Friday evening with performances by Justament and Terminaator, and a commemorative event on Saturday evening at St. John's Church in Valga featuring an evening of 'Ave Maria' film music.
The Valga Military Museum, or the Foundation Valga Permanent Exhibition of Patriotic Education, is the most important center for patriotic education and military history on Estonia's southern border. The museum preserves, researches, and exhibits the history related to Estonia's national defense, internal security, and struggle for freedom, serving as a bridge between different generations. The annual international MilFest is the most prominent event of the museum's activities, supporting the population's will to defend, national defense awareness, and the region's sense of security.

articles.title: Bankrupt E-Piim factories receive 135 million euro bid at auction  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
TALLINN - A bid of 135 million euros has been made for the Paide and Põltsamaa factories of bankrupt dairy company E-Piim, which were put up for auction with a starting price of 80 million euros, reports the daily Postimees.
Bankruptcy trustee Indrek Lepsoo told the business daily Äripäev that the winner's name can be disclosed after the deadline for submitting potential objections has passed and the transaction is complete.
The court declared AS E-Piim Tootmine bankrupt on March 11 and appointed Indrek Lepsoo and Olev Kuklase as the company's bankruptcy trustees.
Creditors decided that the company's business operations should continue during the bankruptcy proceedings, as this would be the best way to preserve its assets. Following this directive, AS E-Piim Tootmine's production units have been operating at up to 30 percent capacity, while the Põltsamaa packaging unit has been running at full capacity, with serving retail customers being the priority. The company has made timely payments to dairy producers and other partners throughout the bankruptcy period.
"Functioning factories, a capable team, and a continuous milk supply system create the best conditions for the new owner to put the assets to use more quickly," commented bankruptcy trustee Olev Kuklase.
According to Anti Orav, CEO of E-Piim Tootmine, the auction's final result proved that the decision to keep the factories operational was the right one. "I was not particularly surprised by the price, as I had expected it to be significantly higher than the starting bid; you cannot build a factory like this for 80 million euros. The price offered also demonstrated that the decision to keep the plant running during the bankruptcy proceedings was correct," he said.
The new AS E-Piim Tootmine cheese factory in Paide is one of the most modern in Europe, capable of processing up to 1,200 tons of raw milk daily. In 2025, the company exported over 90 percent of its output. The company currently employs 180 people, 80 of whom are in Paide. In addition to the cheese factory in Paide, the company has production units in Põltsamaa and Järva-Jaani.

articles.title: NATO jet based in Lithuania shoots down drone over Latvia, official says  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
VILNIUS - A NATO air policing jet based in Lithuania intercepted and shot down a foreign drone in Latvia on Friday, Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre head Vilmantas Vitkauskas said.
Vitkauskas said the fighter jets were scrambled shortly after 4 a.m. to identify an object that had entered Latvian territory. The drone was identified and successfully destroyed within minutes.
According to Vitkauskas, the incident closely resembled a previous occurrence in May. Lithuanian radars did not detect any threat within the country's own borders at the time.
"This is a very similar episode to the one in May, where operations against legitimate targets in Russia were being conducted and Russian electronic warfare measures diverted this object, which then entered NATO territory," the National Crisis Management Centre head said.
"So far, only that single object was recorded (in Latvia), which changed direction and was diverted toward NATO territory instead of its legitimate target in the Leningrad region," Vitkauskas added.
Later on Friday, Vitkauskas, speaking to reporters, said the object likely entered Latvian airspace from Belarus.
"No other objects entering from Russia or Belarus were detected this morning. (...) According to our information, the object has not yet been located on Latvian territory. It crashed approximately 150 kilometres from the Lithuanian border. We hope that once the wreckage is found, we will be able to determine more about the object itself, its flight path and similar details," Vitkauskas said.
Asked whether Lithuania had observed the incoming drone or its trajectory, Vitkauskas said the radar system used to detect such incidents was integrated. He added that the decision to scramble fighter jets from Siauliai was based on the shared radar data.
Latvian authorities said the drone's position was tracked, although its exact location was not disclosed. An airspace threat alert was issued for five Latvian municipalities at approximately 4 a.m. and ended at 4:50 a.m.
Last week, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Russia was considering attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltic region using Ukrainian drones.

articles.title: Decision to shoot down drone was made to prevent it from harming Latvian residents - defense minister  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
RIGA - "The decision to shoot down the drone was made to prevent it from harming Latvian residents," Defense Minister Raivis Melnis told LETA.
"The decision to shoot down the drone was made in light of the danger it posed. Drones entering Latvian territory can endanger our residents, so they must be destroyed," the minister emphasized, noting that it is impossible to guarantee that an unmanned aerial vehicle will simply crash somewhere in a swamp or forest.
He also dismissed concerns raised by residents that several drones had allegedly been spotted today.
Melnis explained that only one drone had been detected, but residents may have heard the noise of the fighter jets accelerating.
As the Communications Directorate of the Information Analysis and Management Department of the Joint Staff of the National Armed Forces informed LETA, the National Armed Forces is currently unable to provide precise information on the type of drone or its country of origin. Such drones enter Latvian airspace as a result of targeted Russian electromagnetic warfare.
Early Friday morning, allied fighter jets shot down a drone entering Latvian airspace near Lake Bozeva, which is located about five kilometers from the center of Rugaji village in Balvi Municipality, Sandra Kapteine, head of the Rugaji Municipal Administration, told LETA.
She emphasized that the drone was shot down in a forested area and that no residents or property were harmed. The responsible services are currently working at the scene, Kapteine said.
As reported, according to currently available information, the drone entered Latvian airspace as a result of electromagnetic warfare conducted by Russia.
NBS soldiers, National Guard members, and State Police officers are involved in surveying the scene of the incident.
Since the drone was shot down at a high altitude, its debris could be scattered over a wide area, Iveta Berzina, a spokesperson for the Joint Staff of the National Armed Forces, said this morning.
Foreign media reported Friday morning that a fire broke out at the port of Ust-Luga overnight following a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia’s Leningrad region. According to Leningrad Region Governor Alexander Drozdenko, a total of 54 drones were shot down over the region.
On Thursday night, Ukrainian drones also attacked a warehouse belonging to the online retailer Wildberries in the Tver region.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces announced that over the past 24 hours, they had struck 29 power transmission substations in Russian-occupied territories, and 240 substations between August 1 and 13.
The Russian Ministry of Defense claims that a total of 553 Ukrainian drones were shot down overnight on Friday over 18 Russian regions and the occupied Crimea.
As usual, Russian authorities have not reported how many drones they failed to shoot down, but experts estimate that between 10 percent and 15 percent of the drones reached their targets.

articles.title: Eamets: Labor market indicators are a source of both optimism and concern  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
TALLINN - According to Raul Eamets, chief economist at Bigbank, labor market indicators are a source of both optimism and concern.
"The big picture is positive - the unemployment rate in the second quarter was 6.6 percent, and the decline is noticeable compared to a year ago, when the unemployment rate was 7.8 percent," Eamets said.
According to him, the significant increase in economic inactivity is a cause for concern. "A year ago, there were 255,000 people who were not working and not looking for work; in the second quarter of this year, that number was 13,000 higher. Yet, summer is a time when there are opportunities to find seasonal work. It's also true that the total number of people covered by the survey has decreased by 3,000," Eamets pointed out.
The number of employed people was also 5,700 lower than a year ago, bringing the employment rate slightly down. At the same time, Estonia's employment rate remains one of the highest in the European Union.
The decrease in unemployment is also confirmed by registered unemployment data. In July, there were 39,860 registered unemployed people in Estonia. A year ago at the same time, there were 5,851 more.
The number of registered unemployed has decreased the most in Rapla and Järva counties, by 27 percent and 24.5 percent, respectively.
"At the municipal level, the largest decreases were seen in Saarde municipality (a 46 percent drop), Märjamaa municipality (39 percent), and Rapla municipality (31 percent), and in the towns of Loksa (33 percent) and Paide (30 percent). In twenty municipalities, unemployment fell by more than 20 percent," Eamets said.
At the same time, there were also local governments where unemployment grew, for example, in Räpina (24 percent), Jõhvi (21 percent), Antsla (11 percent), and Muhu (9 percent) municipalities. In total, unemployment grew in 10 municipalities and in Põlva county as a whole (by 5 percent).
"Although Estonia is small and compact, the large disparities in regional unemployment figures prove once again that our population has low mobility, meaning people do not really move from one county or municipality to another in search of work. When they do move, it's only from rural areas to cities, i.e., to major hubs, especially the capital," Eamets added.

articles.title: Fighter jets shoot down drone that entered Latvian airspace; threat has ended  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
RIGA - Early Friday morning, allied fighter jets successfully shot down an unmanned aerial vehicle that had entered Latvian airspace, thereby ending the threat posed by the drone, according to the National Armed Forces (NBS).
The drone was shot down at high altitude over Rugaji village in Balvu Municipality, Iveta Berzina, a spokesperson for the Joint Staff of the National Armed Forces (NBS), said in an interview on the Latvian Television.
According to currently available information, the drone entered Latvian airspace as a result of electromagnetic warfare conducted by Russia.
NBS soldiers, National Guard members, and State Police officers are involved in surveying the scene of the incident.
Since the drone was shot down at a high altitude, its debris could be scattered over a wide area, Berzina noted.
As reported, residents of the Augadaugava, Preili, Rezekne, Balvi, and Aluksne municipalities were warned early Friday morning about the threat to airspace.
The NBS noted that fighter jets from NATO’s Baltic airspace patrol mission were activated.
LETA previously reported, early this summer, residents in Latgale and Vidzeme received multiple cell phone alerts about a potential airspace threat; in addition, several drones crashed and exploded in Latvia.
These drone incidents were most likely related to drones involved in the Russia-Ukraine war approaching or entering Latvian airspace.

- The Estonian state will celebrate the 35th anniversary of the restoration of its independence on August 20. On this occasion, President Alar Karis and Sirje Karis have invited guests to a reception in the rose garden of the presidential office.
- According to the Environment Agency's weather forecast, temperatures will reach up to 26 degrees Celsius in the coming days.

– A total of 62 members of the Riigikogu have signed their support for nominating Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise as a presidential candidate.

– Poland has arrested a Russian citizen who was planning to assassinate a person with dual Ukrainian and US citizenship in Warsaw on Moscow's orders, Prime Minister Donald Tusk told the AFP news agency on Thursday.

– A Ukrainian long-range drone attack on a major oil refinery in Orsk, Russia, has halted its operations for about six months, the governor of the Orenburg region announced on Thursday.

articles.title: Nauseda welcomes DEMZ plans for ammunition facilities in Lithuania  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
VILNIUS - Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda welcomed plans by Ukrainian defence company Dnipro Electromechanical Plant (DEMZ) to invest in Lithuania and establish production and assembly facilities for defence ammunition components.
"By actively supporting Ukraine, Lithuania is strengthening their defence as well as our own country and the entire eastern flank. Today we see that our support for Ukraine is also yielding clear economic dividends," the president said in a statement issued by his office.
Nauseda said the major investment agreement, signed on Friday in Vilnius between the Lithuanian government and DEMZ, would boost economic activity and expertise in Alytus and the Prienai district and create numerous new jobs.
Under the agreement, the Ukrainian company will produce ammunition and ordnance components in Lithuania. The investment is expected to create up to 450 new jobs in the region. The total value of the DEMZ investment has not been disclosed.
Construction of the plant in the Prienai district is scheduled to begin this autumn, with production expected to start by the end of next year.
The facility will be built near Balbieriskis, on a 30.6-hectare plot in the village of Azuolai. The site is the only one in the Prienai district included in the National Land Service's list of state plots reserved for investment.
DEMZ is a major supplier of defence goods to the Ukrainian military. Since the outbreak of the full-scale war in Ukraine, the company has shifted its operations from civilian to military production. The company has branches across Ukraine and employs approximately 4,000 people.

articles.title: French embassy thanks Lithuania for help fighting wildfires  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
VILNIUS - France’s embassy in Lithuania thanked Lithuania for its assistance in fighting wildfires in the Bordeaux and Marseille regions.
"France sincerely thanks Lithuania for its solidarity and assistance in extinguishing the fires. We are very grateful to the firefighters who risked their lives to protect ours," the embassy said.
The embassy said that in the face of natural disasters and the challenges posed by global warming, such mutual assistance demonstrates the importance of international and European cooperation through the European Union Civil Protection Mechanism.
Lithuania deployed 40 officers from the State Fire and Rescue Service and nine specialised vehicles to France. The Lithuanian firefighters worked alongside French rescue services for 13 days in the Bordeaux and Marseille regions. Their efforts contributed to protecting residents and the environment and supported the work of French agencies.
The Lithuanian rescue team was dispatched to France through the European Union Civil Protection Mechanism.
According to Saulius Tamulevicius, deputy director of the Fire and Rescue Department, this was the sixth international aid mission involving Lithuanian firefighters since 2010.
Some of the officers deployed to France had recently participated in missions to Venezuela and Turkey following devastating earthquakes in those countries.
As French firefighters battled forest fires in the Gironde region that forced the evacuation of 220,000 people, the blazes destroyed more than 200 homes and devastated 42,000 hectares of land.

articles.title: Estonia to Participate in European Culture Ministers' Meeting in Oulu  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
TALLINN – An informal meeting of European Union culture ministers will take place in Oulu, the European Capital of Culture, on Friday and Saturday. Discussions will focus on the directions for the next Cultural Work Plan (2027–2030) and the future role of culture—specifically, the impact of artificial intelligence on the cultural and creative sectors and the protection of creative freedom.
Estonia will be represented at the meeting by Eili Lepik, Undersecretary for Cultural Heritage at the Ministry of Culture.
"Culture plays a significant role in shaping social cohesion, the economy, and the future of Europe. In developing the next European Cultural Work Plan, it is important for Estonia to emphasize the role of culture in society's crisis preparedness and to highlight aspects of the cultural sector in the digital age, whether it be digital solutions for protecting cultural heritage or considering the specificities of small languages and cultures in the context of artificial intelligence," said Eili Lepik, who added that long-term resilience is built through culture, language, identity, and shared memory.
For Estonia, it is important to emphasize at the meeting the role of culture as the foundation of societal resilience, both in supporting Ukraine and in strengthening European democratic societies. Additionally, focus topics include the strategic cultural partnership between Estonia and Finland; culture as a driver of regional development and the creative economy; and the impact of artificial intelligence on culture, creators, and the visibility of small languages. The digital environment must also keep small languages and cultural spaces visible and ensure the protection of creators' rights, fair remuneration, and transparency.
The event provides an excellent opportunity to reaffirm our strong strategic partnership with Finland, which extends beyond one-off projects. Our cultural relationship with our neighboring country is broadly linked to international cooperation and increasing joint regional visibility, as well as to societal development and heritage preservation.
The informal meeting of culture ministers in Oulu also serves as a good prelude for Estonia to the NB8+Ukraine culture ministers' summit taking place in Tallinn this autumn, and the global conference on the reconstruction of Ukraine, also to be held in Tallinn in January 2027.

articles.title: airBaltic's business plan may mean significant reduction in number of employees - trade union  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
RIGA - The new business plan of national airline airBaltic, which envisages significant restructuring of airBaltic fleet and network, will directly affect employment guarantees for hundreds of employees, according to the Latvian Aviation Trade Union.
The union believes that during the work on the business plan, the company should have assessed various aspects of reducing the number of employees, as this is what would happen after a significant reduction in airBaltic fleet and operations, the Aviation Trade Union's President Dace Kavasa told LETA. Given such a significant impact, consultations with employee representatives should have been conducted, which did not happen, Kavasa notes.
The union says that in 2025, airBaltic's maximum number of aircraft was 54. According to the latest business plan of the airline, the number of aircraft will be reduced from 51 to 36 by the end of 2026. Furthermore, the long-term strategy calls for operating with only about 40 aircraft by 2031, which is a radical departure from the previously projected fleet of 100 aircraft.
Based on the Latvian Aviation Trade Union's calculations, which assessed the planned fleet reduction by approximately 30 percent and also considered other criteria related to the airline's operations, the union believes that scenarios involving a 20 percent to 30 percent reduction in the number of employees were also assessed during the development of the business plan.
In the union's assessment, even under the most optimistic scenario, the fleet reduction cannot be offset without a significant reduction in the number of employees. The union concludes that the company management's statements regarding the launch of an assessment of its impact only now are misleading, as such scenarios must have already been known during the planning process.
The Latvian Aviation Trade Union claims that airBaltic management has therefore failed to comply with regulatory requirements regarding timely notification and consultations prior to making decisions on its business plan that, by its very nature, has a significant impact on employees.
The Latvian Aviation Trade Union points out that no consultations with the union have taken place, and that the union was not provided with any information about the business plan at all - the union learned about it from the media.
Likewise, the Latvian Aviation Trade Union was not allowed to attend the August 11 online presentation of the business plan to airBaltic employees. The response to the union's request to join the online presentation was an invitation to meet on August 14. No other information regarding the business plan has been provided to the union at all.
The Latvian Aviation Trade Union points out that the obligation to consult is also stipulated by the European Union regulations, and the EU Court of Justice states in Case C-188/03 that the obligation to consult with employee representatives arises as soon as a strategic decision is made that requires the employer to anticipate or plan for termination of employment contracts or collective redundancies.
In the Latvian Aviation Trade Union's opinion, a business plan that already sets out specific, quantified targets for the airline's fleet and route network constitutes precisely such a strategic decision, and consultations with the union should have begun during the development of the plan, not during the plan's approval or implementation stage.
The Latvian Aviation Trade Union's is calling on airBaltic management and supervisory boards to commence discussions regarding the business plan's impact on the airline's employees, in accordance with the legal requirements to negotiate and consult with labor unions.
The Latvian Aviation Trade Union is currently the largest trade labor union in the aviation sector, representing employees from six aviation companies.

articles.title: From bivouacs to clothing, Cortina cracks down on 'loutish' tourism
articles.body:
Cortina d'Ampezzo is cracking down on
"loutish" tourism by banning bivouacs, packed lunches on steps,
and inappropriate clothing.
                                    
                                       
				As reported by Il Messaggero, Il Gazzettino, and Corriere del
Veneto, until October 15th, in the center of the Jewel of the
Dolomites, it will be forbidden to lie down on the steps of
monuments, in parking lots, on the street, or on the doorsteps
of buildings, according to an ordinance issued by Mayor Gianlua
Lorenzi Thursday.
                                    
                                       
				Sleeping bags are prohibited, even on benches, and food and
drinks are prohibited on public streets or under porticoes, and
washing on the streets will also be prohibited.
                                    
                                       
				Visitors will also have to be careful about how they dress, and
avoid attire deemed contrary to public decorum.
                                    
                                       
				For those who violate the rules, fines range from €25 to €500.
                                    
                                       
				Mayor Lorenzi observed in an interview with the Gazzettino that
residents "find themselves embarrassed, at certain times, in
certain situations. They are already inundated with a heavy
influx of tourists: at least the rules should be respected."
The mayor said he thought an ordinance shouldn't have been
necessary to "prevent camping in the city center, bivouacking in
front of the cemetery, or eating on church steps.
                                    
                                       
				Instead," he stated, "we were forced to take this action, so as
to allow our local police and other law enforcement agencies to
intervene."
The same battle against rough-and-ready tourists continues in
Venice, where Mayor Simone Venturini says he is ready "to
further tighten controls on decorum, commerce, and anything that
could compromise the quality and image of the city."
This was reported by the Corriere del Veneto.
                                    
                                       
				Diving, picnicking, and napping on towels and lilos in St.
                                    
                                       
				Mark's Square will no longer be tolerated.
                                    
                                       
				"Venice cannot be used as a stage for those seeking a few
minutes of visibility by displaying irresponsible,
disrespectful, or stupid behavior," Venturini adds.
                                    
                                       
				"The local administration and police are fully committed, and
the sanctions are being enforced."

articles.title: World Bank says it disbursed $200 million to Colombia for quake response
articles.body:
World Bank says it disbursed $200 million to Colombia for quake response
WASHINGTON, Aug 14 - The World Bank on Friday said it had disbursed $200 million to Colombia for its emergency response to a deadly August 10 earthquake that left hundreds dead.
The multilateral development bank said it was working with the Colombian government and development partners, financial institutions and the private sector to address immediate needs, while laying the foundations for recovery.
The bank said it had also launched a Global Rapid Assessment of Damages from Earthquakes (GRADE) to provide the Colombian government with an early assessment of damages and economic losses to help Bogota prioritize aid and reconstruction efforts.
Efforts were underway to channel financing to affected communities and businesses, including support for public health, housing, and small and medium-sized enterprises, the bank said.
The 7.4-magnitude quake struck shortly after 7:30 a.m. on Monday, toppling apartment blocks and damaging homes, schools and hospitals across western Colombia.
Authorities on Friday said that 285 people had been killed and nearly 4,000 injured. Nearly 400 others were still missing. REUTERS

articles.title: Kushner to visit Israel after Netanyahu rejects Gaza Board of Peace plan
articles.body:
Kushner to visit Israel after Netanyahu rejects Gaza Board of Peace plan
Visit to address Israeli opposition to plan for Hamas to disarm, Israel to withdraw from Gaza, board official says.
United States President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and aide, Jared Kushner, is set to travel to Israel and Egypt next week to support a US-backed Board of Peace plan for a permanent end to Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.
The visit, which was confirmed to Al Jazeera by a Board of Peace official, comes shortly after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected a Trump-backed 15-point plan for a lasting peace in the Palestinian enclave.
