articles.title: Health officials urge strong investment to end preventable maternal deaths in Africa
articles.body:
KIGALI, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Health officials and partners have called for stronger investment in women's and girls' health, improved quality of care, and stronger partnerships to accelerate the reduction of preventable maternal deaths and address challenges affecting reproductive health in Africa.
The call was made during the 12th Annual Scientific Conference of the Rwanda Society of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, held under the theme "Healthy Girls, Healthy Women: The Foundation of a Thriving Nation."
The conference, which runs through Friday, gathered health professionals, researchers, academics, residents, nurses, midwives, and partners from Africa and beyond.
Speaking at the forum, United Nations Population Fund Country Representative in Rwanda Olugbemiga Adelakin said the health, rights, and empowerment of women and girls should be treated as foundations for human capital, economic transformation, and sustainable development.
He called for strong and more resilient health systems capable of providing quality sexual and reproductive health services to every woman and girl, while highlighting the need to accelerate the reduction of preventable maternal deaths through improved quality of care.
Jean Marie Vianney Ndayizigiye, permanent secretary in the Rwandan Ministry of Health, emphasized that investment in women's healthcare is an investment in the country's future.
"Through the 4x4 reform (quadruple the current workforce in 4 years) led by our ministry and supported by development partners, we are doing a lot to increase the skills and capacity of our health workers. We have been able to increase the enrollment of obstetrics and gynecology residents from 25 to more than 160," Ndayizigiye said.
Nirite, a member of the 26th Chinese medical team in Rwanda, presented on the diagnosis, treatment, and home-based healthcare of common gynecological conditions from the perspective of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM).
The presentation highlighted several TCM approaches to menstrual pain and related gynecological conditions, including herbal medicines, acupuncture, and moxibustion. For conditions described in the presentation as involving cold-related abdominal pain and blood stasis, Nirite discussed approaches including Shaofu Zhuyu Capsules, warm-needle acupuncture, and moxibustion.
From adolescent menstrual regulation and reproductive-age fertility support to perimenopausal health management, TCM addresses gynecological conditions not as isolated symptoms, but as reflections of overall bodily balance, integrating herbal medicine, acupuncture, moxibustion, dietary therapy and lifestyle guidance into cohesive, personalized care plans, Nirite said.
The conference also featured practical training in obstetric ultrasound, contraceptive counseling, long-acting reversible contraceptives, uterine evacuation techniques, pain management, and post-abortion care. ■

articles.title: 2 HKSAR gov't teams win Chief Executive Award for Exemplary Performance
articles.body:
HONG KONG, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Two inter-departmental teams of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government handling wartime bomb disposal and light public housing respectively were presented with the Chief Executive's Award for Exemplary Performance on Friday.
Addressing the presentation ceremony, HKSAR Chief Executive John Lee praised the two award-winning teams for effectively fulfilling their different missions with steadfast determination and exceptional competence, winning public trust through tangible results.
Lee said that the teams demonstrated the HKSAR government's people-oriented, responsible and results-driven governance philosophy, and manifested the professional spirit of civil servants in rising to challenges and pursuing excellence, setting an example for the entire civil service.
In September 2025, a World War II-era bomb weighing about 1,000 pounds was discovered at a construction site in Quarry Bay of Hong Kong. With a super typhoon approaching, the operation time was severely compressed. The Emergency Monitoring and Support Center of the Security Bureau immediately activated the interdepartmental emergency mechanism. Under high pressure and high risk, the team evacuated residents and successfully defused the bomb.
The other award-winning team was the Light Public Housing team comprising the Housing Bureau and the Architectural Services Department. To address urgent housing needs, the government proposed building 30,000 units in a short time. By adopting innovative technologies and standardized designs, the team significantly boosted construction efficiency and helped reduce the composite waiting time for subsidized rental housing by 1.3 years.
Lee announced the launch of the Chief Executive's Award for Exemplary Performance in the 2022 Policy Address to give recognition to meritorious and exemplary teams or individuals in the civil service on a regular basis, with a view to encouraging civil servants to constantly strive for excellence. It also aimed to allow the public to have a better understanding of the HKSAR government's work and the excellence of the civil service. ■

articles.title: Chad's president pardons 9 political leaders, including former PM Masra
articles.body:
YAOUNDE, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Chadian President Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno has signed two decrees granting presidential pardons to nine political leaders and partial sentence reductions to other convicts across the country, the presidency said Friday morning.
Former Prime Minister Succes Masra, who was sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to pay 1 billion CFA francs (about 1.76 U.S. dollars) in damages, is among the beneficiaries of the pardon. Eight leaders of the Consultation Group of Political Actors, including party presidents and secretaries-general, have also been pardoned following requests submitted to the head of state.
The nine political figures will be released once the Ministry of Justice completes the required formalities. While the decision, initially announced by Mahamat Deby on Aug. 10 on the eve of Chad's Independence Day, lifts the prison sentences, authorities said it does not cancel civil penalties, which remain enforceable.
Masra, president of Chad's opposition political party The Transformers, served as prime minister of the transitional government from January to May 2024. He was arrested in May 2025 and sentenced in August 2025 for "inciting hatred and revolt" and complicity in murder. ■

articles.title: Africa CDC backs urgent vaccine deployment to contain expanding Ebola in DR Congo
articles.body:
ADDIS ABABA, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has called for support for the immediate implementation of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) government's decision to deploy the Ervebo vaccine to help contain the "rapidly escalating" Ebola outbreak in the country.
Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya, during an online briefing on Thursday, described the move as "a big step" in the ongoing response against the rare Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, highlighting that the Central African country has already submitted a request for 100,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine to the International Coordinating Group on Vaccine Provision.
Warning that the current emergency "risks becoming the deadliest the country has faced, and we cannot allow that trajectory to continue," Kaseya said the requested vaccine doses will support clinical trials, the vaccination of front-line responders, and those in urgent need of the vaccine.
The lack of licensed vaccines or targeted medical countermeasures against the rare Bundibugyo strain is further driving the disease's rapid transmission across parts of the DRC. According to the latest Africa CDC data, the country has recorded a total of 4,449 confirmed cases and 2,061 deaths, representing a case fatality rate of about 46.3 percent.
The Ervebo vaccine is a World Health Organization (WHO) pre-qualified, single-dose vaccine for the disease caused by the Zaire Ebola virus strain and has an extensive safety and deployment record.
Highlighting Ervebo's potential cross-protection and the current emergency context, Kaseya stressed that deployment of this vaccine is a strategic approach to reduce severe illness and deaths. He said this approach will simultaneously generate the rigorous evidence needed to guide the wider response.
The expanded use of the Ervebo vaccine is planned to begin with eligible contacts, healthcare responders, community health workers, burial teams, religious and village leaders, and people in high-transmission hotspots with repeated occupational exposure, it was noted.
The launch of the expanded use of the licensed Ervebo vaccine is one of the immediate measures agreed upon during a high-level crisis meeting convened by DRC President Felix Tshisekedi, alongside the Africa CDC chief and WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, last week in Kinshasa, the capital of the DRC.
The Africa CDC chief, however, stressed that vaccination must reinforce, not replace, other outbreak response efforts. These include active case finding, rapid diagnostics, isolation and supportive care, infection prevention and control, safe burials, contact management, and trusted community engagement.
The Ebola virus is highly contagious and causes symptoms such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea, generalized pain, and malaise. In severe cases, it can cause internal and external bleeding. ■

articles.title: China Focus: New materials on Japan's wartime "comfort women" system added to Nanjing museum
articles.body:
Photojournalist Yan Meihua displays a photo she took of Mao Yinmei, a Korea-born survivor of the Japanese army's World War II-era "comfort women" system, in Nanjing, capital of east China's Jiangsu Province, Aug. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Qiu Bingqing)
NANJING, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Inside the Nanjing Museum of the Site of the Lijixiang Comfort Stations in Nanjing, capital of east China's Jiangsu Province, a wall of portraits bears the weathered faces of more than 60 survivors of the Japanese army's World War II-era "comfort women" system.
On Friday, that visual record grew as a new batch of artifacts, photographs and video materials documenting the victims' experiences was added to the museum's collection.
The materials were donated mainly by two Chinese photographers after years of documentary work and field investigation.
One of them is Li Xiaofang, a member of the China Photographers Association, who spent more than two decades gathering the stories of survivors of the Japanese military's "comfort women" system. Traveling across China, Japan, and the Republic of Korea (ROK), he visited, interviewed and photographed more than 100 survivors.
Li donated more than 200 photographs of over 70 survivors, along with 43 replicas of their handprints. The photographs are now on display at the museum.
The stories behind the images remain vivid in his memory. Li recalled visiting survivor Zhou Fenying on a chilly autumn day. Despite the cold, the elderly woman insisted on taking a bath.
"After escaping from the comfort station, I had to take a bath every day, hoping to wash away the humiliation and pain from my body," Li recalled Zhou telling him.
"It was a psychological trauma she could never erase in her lifetime," Li said.
Another donor, photojournalist Yan Meihua from Xiaogan City in central China's Hubei Province, spent two years documenting the testimony and daily life of Mao Yinmei, a Korea-born survivor.
Yan eventually compiled more than 7,000 photographs and 10 videos, preserving a detailed visual record of Mao's life and experiences.
Born in what is now Jeonbuk State of the ROK, Mao was deceived by the Japanese military in the 1940s and taken to a "comfort station" in Hubei's Wuhan, where she endured inhumane abuse. After Japan's surrender, she fled to Xiaogan and settled there for the rest of her life.
"She often sat alone in silence. Whenever the Japanese were mentioned, her face would turn pale, and she would quietly shed tears," Yan recalled.
"You could truly feel that the harm caused by the atrocities of the Japanese military stayed with her throughout her life, like a shadow that never faded," she said.
Liu Guangjian, a researcher at the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders, said the newly donated materials will provide a stronger historical basis for future academic research and museum exhibitions.
"Li's more than two decades of field investigation have created a collective portrait of survivors, while Yan's two years of documentation have preserved a precious visual archive of an individual survivor," Liu said.
Affiliated with the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders, the museum preserves one of the former "comfort station" sites on the Chinese mainland that have been personally identified by survivors.
According to research, only six registered survivors of the Japanese military's "comfort women" system remain alive on the Chinese mainland. ■

articles.title: Ebola outbreak reaches 6th province in DR Congo as cases top 4,600: official
articles.body:
KINSHASA, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- The ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has spread to a sixth province, with confirmed cases rising to 4,665, the government said Friday.
The health zone of Buta in the northern province of Bas-Uele has been added to the list of affected areas, bringing the number of affected health zones nationwide to 54, according to the latest update released by the country's public health authorities.
The outbreak is now affecting six provinces -- Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu and Tshopo -- with the northeastern province of Ituri remaining the main epicenter.
A total of 2,184 deaths have been recorded among confirmed cases, putting the overall case fatality rate at 46.8 percent. Meanwhile, 965 people have recovered since the start of the outbreak.
On May 15, the DRC declared the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo ebolavirus. ■

articles.title: China's inclusive loans to small firms rise 8 pct
articles.body:
BEIJING, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's inclusive loans to small and micro enterprises maintained steady growth in the second quarter, official data showed Friday.
Outstanding inclusive loans to small and micro enterprises reached 38.9 trillion yuan (about 5.73 trillion U.S. dollars) at the end of the second quarter, up 8 percent year on year, according to the National Financial Regulatory Administration.
Outstanding inclusive loans related to agriculture stood at 15 trillion yuan, up 7.5 percent year on year.
Friday's data also showed China's banking institutions held 498 trillion yuan in renminbi and foreign-currency assets, up 6.6 percent year on year, while the total assets of insurance companies and insurance asset management companies reached 43.9 trillion yuan, up 6.2 percent from the beginning of the year.
Commercial banks maintained strong risk buffers, with their provision coverage ratio standing at 202.87 percent at the end of the second quarter. The capital adequacy ratio of commercial banks, excluding branches of foreign banks, stood at 15.26 percent. ■

articles.title: Slovenia's Q2 GDP up 5 pct, strongest in four years
articles.body:
LJUBLJANA, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Slovenia's gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 5 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, the strongest growth since the first quarter of 2022, the country's Statistical Office said Friday.
The growth accelerated from the first quarter, when it stood at 3.2 percent according to revised figures.
According to the office, domestic expenditure grew by 5.9 percent in the second quarter, driven by final consumption and gross capital formation which rose by 4 percent and 12.3 percent, respectively.
Expenditure for purchases on the domestic market went up in all product groups, the most in durable goods, by 10.1 percent, followed by services, by 3.7 percent, the office said.
The increase in external trade was the largest in the last two years, with exports growing by 6.4 percent and imports by 7.6 percent.
The Bank of Slovenia, which in June forecast annual GDP growth of 1.9 percent in 2026, said on Friday that the growth in the second quarter was above expectations.
It added, however, that prospects for the rest of the year are uncertain due to challenging international conditions, particularly the war in the Middle East and severe drought in Europe. ■

articles.title: Body found after massive wildfire injures 40 in Croatia
articles.body:
Photo taken on Aug. 14, 2026 shows the aftermath of a wildfire near the southern Croatian town of Omis. A body has been found at the site of a massive wildfire that swept through wooded and residential areas in Omis, Croatia overnight, and the number of people injured in the fire rose to 40, police confirmed on Friday. (Ivo Cagalj/PIXSELL via Xinhua)
ZAGREB, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- A body has been found at the site of a massive wildfire that swept through wooded and residential areas in Omis, Croatia overnight, and the number of people injured in the fire rose to 40, police confirmed on Friday.
The fire broke out around 8:15 p.m. (1815 GMT) Thursday in Lokva Rogoznica, near Omis, and quickly spread through grass, low vegetation and pine forest, fanned by strong winds. The blaze rapidly reached nearby settlements and destroyed houses.
Those injured in the fire were treated at Split hospital overnight and on Friday, hospital officials said at a press conference. Of these patients, 14 were hospitalized, and seven were on ventilators, including six adults and a 17-year-old minor.
Around 1,000 people were evacuated from the affected areas overnight, local authorities said.
"This was one of the worst fires we have encountered in recent years," Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said when visiting the burned area on Friday. He said it was a serious, large-scale fire that had spread extremely quickly due to drought and wind conditions, adding that the work of firefighters and emergency services had been exemplary.
Firefighters continued working to contain the blaze on Friday as strong winds hampered aerial firefighting efforts. ■

articles.title: At least 16 killed in Cameroon bus crash
articles.body:
YAOUNDE, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- At least 16 people died early Friday in a crash on the Yaounde-Bafoussam highway in Cameroon, police and witnesses said.
The accident happened in Nomale in the Ndikinimeki subdivision of the Mbam-et-Inoubou division, Centre region.
A passenger bus slammed into a truck loaded with planks that was parked on the road. Among the victims were seven members of the same family who were traveling to a funeral, witnesses said.
State broadcaster CRTV reported that about 40 people were injured in the collision.
Local police said formal investigations are underway to determine the exact cause of the crash.
Road accidents are common in Cameroon and are frequently blamed on poor road conditions and reckless driving. Data from the Cameroonian Ministry of Transport shows that about 1,500 people die each year in road accidents across the central African country. ■

articles.title: Residents in S. Africa's Gauteng call for stronger SADC economic integration to address migration pressure
articles.body:
by Ntandoyenkosi Ncube
JOHANNESBURG, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- As Southern African leaders prepare to meet in South Africa's coastal city Durban, residents and migrants in Gauteng Province are calling for greater regional economic integration, saying more jobs, trade and investment opportunities could help ease pressures driving migration across the region.
The Southern African Development Community (SADC) will hold its 46th Ordinary Summit of Heads of State and Government on Aug. 17.
In interviews with Xinhua in South Africa's economic hub Johannesburg, the administrative capital Pretoria, Ekurhuleni Metropolitan Municipality and the surrounding areas, people said the summit should focus not only on border management but also on addressing the economic factors behind migration.
"People leave home because they are looking for something better. If there are jobs and businesses doing well back home, fewer people will have to leave their families to look for work elsewhere," said Jorasimo Musanjeya, a Zimbabwean national living in Johannesburg.
He expected easier cross-border movement of goods, workers and businesses, saying regional integration should bring tangible benefits to ordinary people.
South African business owner Thabo Mokoena said stronger regional trade could help businesses expand and create jobs, particularly if barriers facing small enterprises were reduced.
"We need to see more business within the regional countries. If companies can buy, sell and invest more easily across the region, that creates opportunities," Mokoena, who is based in Pretoria, told Xinhua.
For migrants, clearer and more affordable legal pathways were also seen as important. Claudia Nhantumbo, a Mozambican migrant in Ekurhuleni, said SADC should make it easier for people to understand and comply with immigration requirements when moving for work.
"People will continue moving. That is a reality. What leaders can do is make the process clear and affordable so that people can come here legally," she said.
Fiston Kalala, a migrant from the Democratic Republic of the Congo living in Johannesburg, said migrants who meet legal requirements should be able to contribute to their host economies.
Better coordination among SADC countries could allow governments to manage migration while benefiting from the movement of workers and skills, he said.
For those interviewed by Xinhua, the expectation is that the summit will produce practical measures on jobs, trade, investment, skills mobility and legal migration, turning regional integration from a policy concept into tangible opportunities for ordinary people.
Kagiso Maseko, a community leader in Johannesburg, said the summit should result in practical commitments rather than broad statements.
"People want to see something that changes their lives. We hear a lot about regional integration, but ordinary people want jobs and better services. That is what leaders should be talking about," he said.
Echoing Maseko, Palesa Ndlovu, a migrant-rights advocate in Johannesburg, said regional integration needed to become more meaningful to ordinary citizens.
"SADC must make regional integration something people can feel in their daily lives. It should be easier to travel, trade, work and do business legally across the region," she said. ■

articles.title: World Snooker China Open: China's Zhou Yuelong advances to semifinals
articles.body:
TAIYUAN, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Chinese player Zhou Yuelong and Thailand's Noppon Saengkham defeated their opponents respectively to advance to the 2026 World Snooker Tour China Open semifinals here on Friday.
In the afternoon session, England's David Gilbert raced to a 3-0 lead, before Zhou seized an opportunity in the fourth frame to pull one back.
The two players shifted to a safety battle midway through the fifth frame. Zhou made several consecutive mistakes, while Gilbert later missed a crucial shot when attempting to secure the frame. Zhou failed to capitalize on the opportunity to mount a comeback, and Gilbert took the frame.
Gilbert's form then began to dip, allowing Zhou to seize the initiative. Zhou compiled a century break of 100 points in the eighth frame to win three frames in a row and level the match at 4-4.
Both players made mistakes in the ninth frame, but Gilbert quickly regained his composure to move 5-4 ahead. The 10th frame again developed into a tense battle, but Zhou was the first to seize his chance and level the score.
With the match going down to a deciding 11th frame, both players began to show signs of fatigue. Zhou capitalized on several errors from Gilbert to take the final frame and secure a 6-5 victory, booking his place in the semifinals.
"Today's match was extremely tight. I was well behind in the first half, but that didn't disrupt my rhythm. I kept waiting for my opportunities and eventually fought my way back to win the match," Zhou said after the match.
The other afternoon quarterfinal saw Saengkham take on English star Shaun Murphy. The two players were locked at 3-3 after the opening six frames.
Saengkham then won two consecutive frames to extend his lead. Murphy fought back with a frame win to cut the deficit to 4-5.
Saengkham maintained his strong form in the 10th frame, producing two decisive breaks to seal a 6-4 victory over Murphy.
Currently ranked No. 45 in the world, Saengkham has emerged as the tournament's dark horse after defeating world No. 1 Judd Trump and snooker star Ronnie O'Sullivan in the first and second rounds.
"I'm very happy to have beaten three great players in this tournament. It's the reward for all the hard work I've put into training," Saengkham said after the match.
The evening session features a quarterfinal clash between England's Stuart Bingham and China's Zhang Anda, with the winner advancing to Saturday's semifinals. ■

articles.title: Estonian swimmers advance and break record at Euro championships in Paris
articles.body:
Estonian swimmers advance and break record at Euro championships in Paris
Estonian swimmer Kregor Zirk comfortably advanced to the 200m butterfly semifinals at the ongoing European Championships in Paris, finishing sixth in the heats with a time of 1:55.96.
Zirk admitted he had been nervous before the start but was satisfied with his morning swim. "It went fine. It wasn't easy, but it wasn't very difficult either. I've competed less this season, so there were some nerves and jitters before the start," Zirk told ERR.
The Estonian said he had not yet shown everything he had in the heats and could improve in the evening semifinal. "Morning and evening swims are so different. The whole approach, the mental side. It's very different. I didn't use all my tricks in the morning," he said.
Zirk had no specific target time before the start, admitting he did not know exactly what kind of shape he was currently in. "I didn't really have any expectations; it was difficult to expect anything. I didn't know myself where I was at the moment. The realistic goal was to advance, and I managed that comfortably," he said.
Italy's Alberto Razzetti was fastest in 1:54.64.
Zirk's PB in the 200m butterfly is 1:54.22, set at the semifinals of the 2024 Paris Olympics.
Christopher Palvadre sets new domestic record
Of other Estonian competitors, Christopher Palvadre set a new Estonian record in the men's 50m breaststroke with a time of 27.70, finishing 29th overall though missing the semifinals. Kristjan Reivart placed 41st in 27.91 and Ralf Roose 45th in 28.04. Italy's Simone Cerasuolo was fastest in 26.20.
In the women's 50m freestyle, Egle Salu finished 46th in 26.79, with the Netherlands' Milou van Wijk fastest in 24.13. In the women's 100m backstroke, Maari Randväli placed 25th in 1:02.13 and Margaret Markvardt 36th in 1:03.73.
Zirk's 200m butterfly semifinal takes place at 8:25 p.m. Estonian time Friday. The European Championships continue through August 16.

articles.title: Ash clouds, lava flows and fertile soil: What are the effects of Mount Etna’s eruptions?
articles.body:
Human activities produce 100 times the carbon dioxide of the planet’s volcanic eruptions, according to NASA.
Europe’s most active volcano has been putting on a fiery show, and experts predict that this is just the beginning.
Tourists have flocked en masse to see molten lava spewing out of Mount Etna, a stratovolcano located on the east coast of Sicily.
As the eruption enters its seventh consecutive day, plumes of thick black smoke have continued to trigger travel chaos in the region, grounding dozens of flights at Catania–Fontanarossa Airport and temporarily suspending arrivals.
And yet, for all the fiery force Etna is displaying, the environmental consequences of its eruptions are not necessarily as far-reaching or devastating as they appear.
Etna is almost always erupting
For one, this kind of activity is not unusual for Etna. The volcano erupts several times a year, and sometimes multiple times a month. In fact, it erupted in late July.
The Sicilian landmark is one of the world’s most active volcanoes and has produced more than 70 paroxysmal eruptions in the past six years, Giorgio Costa, a PhD student at the University of Catania’s Department of Biological, Geological and Environmental Sciences, tells Euronews Earth.
These intense bursts of activity can send lava fountains hundreds of metres into the air and ash clouds several kilometres high. They typically last several hours.
“In reality, the volcano’s activity is currently perfectly normal,” says Costa.
Is Mount Etna an environmental disaster waiting?
Volcanic eruptions send a cocktail of debris and emissions into the air. The most obvious is ash, but volcanoes also emit carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide, as well as small amounts of hydrogen sulfide, hydrogen chloride and hydrogen fluoride.
That might make Etna’s regular eruptions seem like potential environmental catastrophes, but the truth is more complex.
The US Geological Survey explains that gases such as sulfur dioxide can cause global cooling while carbon dioxide has the potential to promote global warming.
The impact is minimal, however. NASA says that human activities generate 100 times the carbon dioxide of the planet’s volcanic eruptions.
And climate change itself doesn’t influence eruptions. “There is no correlation between meteorological events, including climate change, and the Earth's volcanic or tectonic activity,” Costa tells Euronews Earth.
Ash is a bigger – but still small – concern
“The main issue currently associated with the eruptions of Etna concerns the fallout of pyroclastic material, mostly ash and small lapilli, which can be carried by the wind to the slopes,” says Costa.
Lapilli are small fragments of rock, which typically range from two to 64 millimetres.
Costa explains that while ash and small lapilli are not dangerous to human health, they can become so when fine particles produced by the ash are lifted into the air.
“Inhaling large amounts of this material is certainly not healthy for the respiratory system, so wearing a mask is recommended,” he adds.
It can also pose a serious problem for aircraft.
If a plane flies through an ash cloud, the particles can enter its engines, where they can melt and damage components and, in some cases, cause engines to lose power. This is why ash in the airspace around Etna can force Catania Airport to close.
The airport is currently closed until 2am on Saturday, and hundreds of flights have been cancelled or diverted over the past week.
Why Etna’s ash is also a boon for human life
They may have a negative impact on aeroplanes, but these same materials can benefit the planet.
Etna’s ash acts as a mineral-rich fertiliser and can improve soil drainage and water retention, helping farmers produce Sicily’s renowned wines, pistachios and citrus fruit.
Research from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography in San Diego found that volcanic ash can do morethan simply add nutrients to soil, too.
In experiments, ash helped revive microbial communities in degraded soil, increasing the activity of organisms that play a key role in breaking down organic matter and making nutrients available to plants.
The researchers also found that plants grown in ash-rich soil developed larger root systems and produced more biomass.
Volcanic ash can also improve soil drainage and water retention.
Etna’s frequent eruptions mean it repeatedly deposits fresh layers of ash, creating a long-term cycle of destruction, enrichment and renewal. Even if ash causes problems when it falls, it eventually becomes part of the soil supporting new life, if not important crops for Sicilian farmers.
The dangers of getting too close
While some might be worried about Etna’s impact on the environment, the biggest immediate risk may come from people getting too close to the action.
“The greatest risk factor is the presence of large numbers of onlookers who set out along Mount Etna’s most rugged trails to watch the ongoing eruption, completely lacking in mountain gear,” says Mirko Messina, the co-founder of Bùum, a specialised tour service that leads excursions of Italian volcanoes, including Etna.
“The Alpine Rescue Service has already carried out numerous rescues, especially at night when law enforcement checks are not in place.”
Messina adds that Etna’s northeast slope – which has just one small, uphill road – has become “gridlocked with hundreds of cars, preventing normal traffic flow and hindering rescue efforts”.
While Etna erupting might be business as usual, Messina says, it should be anything but that for those looking to witness it up close.
“It is impossible to predict in advance how the eruption will evolve in the coming days,” he explains, “but it will be constantly monitored.”

articles.title: 'Greatest threat': How India, Pakistan view each other; data lays bare deep animosity
articles.body:
'Greatest threat': How India, Pakistan view each other; data lays bare deep animosity
Aashish Saxena / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 14, 2026, 19:53 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
A survey has revealed that a majority of adults in Pakistan and India view the other as their single greatest threat.
Nearly eight decades after the 1947 Partition of British India gave birth to two independent nations, deep-seated historical trauma, and territorial disputes that have led to multiple military confrontations continue to shape the mindset of citizens on both sides of the border.As the two countries celebrate their independence, a major survey by the Pew Research Center reveals that an overwhelming majority of adults in both nuclear-armed rivals view the other as their single greatest geopolitical threat.
Conducted across South Asia between February and May 2026, the findings highlight a persistent, deep-rooted mutual hostility that shows little sign of thawing. These sentiments reflect not merely political disagreements, but deeply entrenched unfavourable opinions among general populations, extending into perceptions of global superpowers, regional allies, and the long-term prospects for bilateral peace.
'Greatest threat': India and Pakistan point at each other
The data paints a stark picture of two neighbours frozen in mutual distrust.In India, 54% of respondents named Pakistan as the greatest threat to their country.Conversely, 43% of Pakistanis identified India as their primary security threat.
The data paints a stark picture of two neighbours frozen in mutual distrust.
For Indians, China is the next most cited threat at 21%. For Pakistanis, Israel and the US each register at 24% as major threats — though still far below India.These threat perceptions align closely with how each public judges the other’s commitment to peace.
Most Indians believe their own government and people are committed to good bilateral relations, but a majority say Pakistan’s government and people are not.Pakistanis mirror this: they express confidence in their own side’s commitment but doubt India’s.
Mutual hostility runs deep
The numbers on bilateral perceptions are stark.Nearly nine in 10 Pakistanis have an unfavourable view of India, with 73% describing their opinion as 'very unfavourable'. The sentiment cuts across demographic groups, suggesting that hostility toward India is not confined to any particular section of Pakistani society.The picture in India is similarly bleak. As many as 78% of Indians have an unfavourable view of Pakistan, including 65% who hold a very unfavourable opinion. There is, however, a notable internal divide in India. Indian Muslims are somewhat more favorable toward Pakistan (21%) than Indian Hindus (6%), and they are also less likely to name Pakistan as their top threat (34% vs 57% among Hindus).
The numbers on bilateral perceptions are stark.
Pew's polling also shows that this is not a temporary shift in sentiment.Indian views of Pakistan have remained overwhelmingly negative for more than a decade, with the share expressing a favourable opinion never rising above 20% since 2013.Historical Pew surveys also show that Pakistanis have long held predominantly negative views of India. Pakistani respondents expressing favourable views of India have generally ranged from single digits to around one-third.
Lack of trust
The survey further suggests that hostility is not simply about how Indians and Pakistanis perceive each other. It also extends to whether they believe the other side genuinely wants better relations.A clear pattern emerges: people tend to believe that their own government and population are committed to good bilateral relations, while doubting the intentions of the other side.
When asked whether the Indian and Pakistani governments and people are committed to good relations with each other, the clear pattern is that people only have faith in their own country
Pew Research report
A majority of Indians believe both the Indian government and Indian people are committed to maintaining good relations with Pakistan. But a majority of Pakistanis reject that assessment, saying the Indian government and people are not committed to good relations.The mirror image appears in Pakistan.
Beneath the geopolitical differences lies a more fundamental problem: the absence of trust.
A majority of Pakistanis say their government and people want good relations with India.Most Indians, however, believe Pakistan's government and people are not committed to improving ties. About a quarter of Indian respondents were unsure.This mutual lack of trust creates a difficult cycle: each side sees itself as willing to improve relations while viewing the other as unwilling to reciprocate.Indian Muslims again stand apart to some degree. Around a third say the Pakistani government and people are committed to good relations, significantly higher than the corresponding share among Indian Hindus.
How Bangladesh, Sri Lanka view the rivals
The Pew findings become even more revealing when India and Pakistan are placed alongside Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.Of the four South Asian countries surveyed, Sri Lanka is the only country that receives more positive than negative ratings from respondents in all three of the others.
The India-Pakistan divide extends beyond bilateral relations.
India, meanwhile, has the widest range of perceptions.Sri Lankans are overwhelmingly positive toward India, with 79% expressing a favourable opinion. In Bangladesh, 42% view India favourably. In Pakistan, however, the figure plunges to just 7%.India is also seen as Sri Lanka's most important ally by a clear majority: 63% of Sri Lankan respondents name India.The picture is very different in Bangladesh and Pakistan, where India is most often identified as the greatest threat.Views of Prime Minister Narendra Modi follow a broadly similar pattern. Seventy percent of Sri Lankans express confidence in PM Modi to do the right thing in world affairs, compared with 42% in Bangladesh and 4% in Pakistan.The survey also finds that Pakistan is not universally viewed negatively across South Asia.Fifty-seven percent of Sri Lankans and 54% of Bangladeshis have a favourable opinion of Pakistan, compared with only 8% of Indians.Bangladesh itself receives broadly positive views in Pakistan and Sri Lanka: 66% of Pakistanis and 56% of Sri Lankans express favourable opinions of Bangladesh. Only about a quarter of Indians do so.Sri Lanka emerges as the region's relative outlier. Around half or more of respondents in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh view the island nation positively, while significantly fewer hold negative views.
Divergent worldviews
The India-Pakistan divide extends beyond bilateral relations to the way each country views the global order.For Indians, Russia remains a particularly important and popular partner. Thirty-six percent identify Russia as India's most important ally, while 16% name the United States.Russia's favourable image in India is particularly striking. Fifty-eight percent of Indians have a favourable opinion of Russia, while 51% express confidence in Russian President Vladimir Putin.Pakistanis are considerably less positive: 39% have a favourable view of Russia and only 32% express confidence in Putin.India's relationship with the United States is also reflected in public opinion. Indians are substantially more favourable toward the US than Pakistanis are and are more likely to express confidence in US President Donald Trump.The picture is almost completely reversed when it comes to China.An overwhelming 90% of Pakistanis have a favourable view of China, while 83% express confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping. Three-quarters of Pakistanis identify China as their country's most important ally.Saudi Arabia is a distant second, named by 12%.In India, however, only around a quarter of respondents view China or Xi positively. Even Indian Muslims, who are more favourable toward China than Indian Hindus, remain negative toward both China and its president on balance.
Nearly 80 years after Partition, the survey suggests that the India-Pakistan rivalry remains deeply embedded not only in government policy and military strategy, but also in public perceptions.The most striking finding may therefore not be that Indians and Pakistanis dislike each other. It is that both overwhelmingly believe the other side sees them as the problem.That mutual conviction — reinforced by decades of conflict, competing national narratives and geopolitical rivalry — remains one of the biggest barriers to changing the relationship between the two nuclear-armed neighbours.Yet beneath these geopolitical differences lies a more fundamental problem: the absence of trust.Both populations believe their own side is committed to better relations, while doubting the intentions of the other.
Aashish Saxena is an Assistant News Editor at the Times of India. He has 14 years of editing and reporting experience in both print and digital media. He writes extensively on geopolitics, Indian politics, defence tech, and current affairs in South Asia and Middle East.

articles.title: The livin’ is no longer so easy: How carefree dreams of ‘summertime’ are fading in 2026’s swelter
articles.body:
The livin’ is no longer so easy: How carefree dreams of ‘summertime’ are fading in 2026’s swelter
LONDON (AP) — Dearly beloved, we are gathered here today to consider the death of the summertime state of mind.
The season itself is in no danger; climate change, mainly caused by the burning of oil, gas and coal, is warming the weather year-round. Viewed this way, summer-like weather is ascendant. It’s setting records across the globe — melting Arctic ice, driving droughts, intensifyingwildfires, spinning up storms and endangering millions of people who can’t affordair conditioning, time off work or “coolcations.” The heat is so extreme in Asia that Japan has coined a new meteorological category for the danger: kokusho-bi — or “cruelly hot day.”
What seems as dead as the grass in England this year is the summertime ideal — lazy days, warm nights and escape, however temporary, from classes or parents or work or rules. During the Summer of ’26, people are grieving that freedom. And perhaps, the versions of ourselves we become when our senses tell us that we are safe.
“I mourn for the way summer used to be,” author Debra Denker, who writes “cli-fi,” or climate fiction, wrote in an essay last month recalling leisurely days and July Fourth block parties of the 1960s. “Unless we change the trajectory we’re on, today’s children will never know the gentle and balmy summers of my childhood ... I feel sad that they may never know the truly carefree summers that the more privileged among us enjoyed.”
In 2026, summertime is a different kind of blast
No one needs meteorologists to confirm that this summer is different and our rituals are changing. Downwind from wildfires in North AmericaandEurope, the sky turns orange and the air tastes gritty. Life under Paris’ famous gray rooftops can be deadly. Nights can be a sullen cycle of sleep, showering and opening a window — only to close it later to block out the urban noise.
Everywhere, life-giving sun hurts during much of the day. Checking the air quality index has become part of the act of stepping outside. We get things done earlier in the day and stay up later at night. And a full day at the beach — or an August holiday in Europe — is more a matter of risk management than it used to be.
A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that Americans are more likely to say extreme heat has had either a “major impact” or “minor impact” on their travel or vacation plans, electricity bills, their sleep, their family’s outdoor activities and more parts of their day-to-day life than in July 2024. Research at Oxford University published in July found that the intense heat influences daily behavior globally, with such “everyday adaptations” to daily activities occurring across seven of the countries most at risk of heat waves: Brazil, France, India, Nigeria, Turkey, the U.S. and China.
For some, it’s a summer of discontent
Amber Risebrow, a teacher in Britain’s Channel Islands, said she yearned for England’s idyllic warm season — that period when the sunlight lingers.
“I wanted the long light evenings and the sunshine and the not-dark-at-4pm of it all,” she posted recently on Instagram. “What I did not want was to feel like a rotisserie chicken every single time I stepped outside. Slowly rotating. Gently basting. Questioning my life choices by 10am.”
For those who care to look, the data is plentiful and the weight of it is moving toward hotter and stormier summers. This week alone, intense heat hammered the U.K. and France as temperatures soared toward 40 Celsius (104 Fahrenheit). It was the fifth heat wave of the year in a region where air conditioning is sporadic at best. And the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration reported that the contiguous United States sizzled to its hottest month ever in July.
Globally so far, this is the third-hottest year, behind 2024 and 2025, climate statistics show.
But 2026 still has time to catch up. Thanks to the one-two punch of accelerated human-caused global warming and a supersized El Nino — a periodic warming of parts of the Pacific that leads to temperature variations around the globe — there’s an increasing chance that by the end of the year, 2026 could become the hottest year on record, scientists said.
“And it’s not just extreme heat,” the World Meteorological Organization’s Clare Nullis told reporters in Geneva. “We’re also seeing extreme rainfall, tropical cyclones. So we’re not in holiday mode at all.”
Is summer an ‘outdated sham’?
Somewhere deep, there’s a sense of acceptance that life-threatening, trip-canceling heat waves and their rippling effects aren’t a one-off fluke. So management has ensued, with the hope that escaping hot weather might somehow allow the return of that summertime feeling — for now.
Advisories urging tourists to limit outdoor activity during peak heat hours have become a standard part of trip planning from Cambodia to Cambridge, England. Dog walking is becoming a dawn-or-dusk activity, with governments in high heat zones advising owners against midday walks. Employers and workers are adapting, with work hours especially for agricultural and construction workers shifting to the morning, and policies in some places allowing employees to work from home when the heat becomes extreme.
But home doesn’t offer much solace for workers with no air conditioning. Only about 4% of British homes have “air-con,” compared to about 90% of American homes, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.
So achieving old-fashioned summertime bliss is, and perhaps always has been, mostly a matter of privilege.
In “An Open Letter to the Person Who Asked Me What I’m Doing For The Summer As If I Didn’t Have to Work,” comedy writer Elizabeth Simone addressed the issue in the Weekly Humorist last year.
“You do know that summer vacation is an outdated sham, right?” she wrote. “Obviously it’s because of what summer meant back when we were kids.”
___
Associated Press writer Mari Yamaguchi contributed from Tokyo.

articles.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to let White House ballroom construction continue during appeal
articles.body:
Trump asks Supreme Court to let White House ballroom construction continue during appeal
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s administration on Friday asked the U.S. Supreme Court to allow the White House to continue construction on its $400 million ballroom project while it appeals a lower court’s order to halt the work.
Trump’s solicitor general petitioned the high court to suspend last week’s decision by a three-judge panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. Chief Justice John Roberts set a deadline of Tuesday for a response by plaintiffs challenging the ballroom project.
The divided appeals court panel ruled last week Trump must stop the White House ballroom’s construction because Congress has not approved the project. The panel’s majority said Trump doesn’t have the unilateral authority to build a 90,000-square-foot (8,400-square-meter) ballroom where the White House’s East Wing stood before he ordered its demolition last fall.
The lower court suspended its own ruling for two weeks to give Trump’s Republican administration time to appeal to the Supreme Court. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the Supreme Court to rule on its stay petition before the appeals court panel’s decision takes effect on Aug. 21.
“This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security,” Sauer wrote.
Friday’s court filing includes the administration’s first confirmation that a threatened missile attack on Air Force One prompted the Secret Service to secretly fly Trump out of Turkey last month on an alternate military aircraft. In arguing for the need for a secure ballroom space, the filing cites “the threat of a missile attack against Air Force One on July 8” in a list of recent assassination attempts against Trump.
The filing also asserts that the project is “on time and under budget” with approximately $400 million in private donations obviating the need for any taxpayer dollars to be spent. However, Democrats in Congress have said it appears that funds from Trump’s “ big, beautiful ” tax cuts bill appear to be paying for ballroom work. The administration also has requested additional funding from Congress for the project, but lawmakers haven’t approved it.
In April, a district court judge ordered a stop to aboveground construction of the planned ballroom. But the judge stressed that the White House was free to proceed with underground work, including the construction of any bunkers, military installations and medical facilities.
The D.C. Circuit panel’s 2-1 decision upheld an order to pause aboveground construction on the project, siding with historic preservationists who sued to stop construction of the ballroom.
“Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help,” wrote the majority’s two judges, both appointed by Democratic presidents.
A third judge disagreed, finding that the preservationist group that challenged the project had no legal right to sue.
“The district court elevated the aesthetic displeasure of a single passerby over the government’s security interests in the ballroom,” wrote Judge Neomi Rao, who was appointed by Trump.
The Trump administration argues that the president, not Congress or the courts, has unimpeded authority to renovate the White House. The current state of the project, essentially an open construction site, makes it harder to protect the White House, the Justice Department contends.
The administration also says the National Trust for Historic Preservation does not have the legal right, or standing, to sue over the ballroom, which is part of Trump’s plans to quickly remake Washington. The solicitor general said the ballroom project “should be a matter for the President and the political process, not construction-by-injunction.”
In response to the petition, the trust accused the White House of trying to “outrun the courts” by accelerating construction work, pointing to the administration’s plans to install 1 million pounds of rebar and pour another 3,000 cubic yards of concrete in the next week alone.
“The Administration’s transparent efforts to evade the rule of law, frustrate judicial review, and limit the availability of meaningful relief in the courts must stop here,” the plaintiffs said in a statement.
During an appeals court hearing in early June, an administration lawyer defended a broad view of presidential control over iconic public facilities. The government could bulldoze the Statue of Liberty and the White House, Justice Department lawyer Yaakov Roth said in response to a hypothetical question, and the descendants of immigrants who came through Ellis Island and the enslaved people who built the White House would not have standing to sue.
The D.C. Circuit panel upheld a ruling by U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, who was nominated by Republican President George W. Bush. Leon concluded that a pause wouldn’t jeopardize national security. He also exempted any construction work that is necessary for the safety and security of the White House.
The ballroom has been under construction for 10 months. The administration says the work is roughly 65% finished.
“Given those developments, the injunction promises chaos in service of nothing,” Sauer wrote.

articles.title: Laufey created a ‘third space’ with her annual fan event, ‘A Very Laufey Day.’ Then it exploded
articles.body:
Laufey created a ‘third space’ with her annual fan event, ‘A Very Laufey Day.’ Then it exploded
NEW YORK (AP) — It was 2023 when Laufey, the Icelandic singer-songwriter known for her neoclassical jazz-pop, decided to create a global fan event. Her second album, “Bewitched,” was soon to be released and she wanted to do something big to celebrate it. But more than that, she says, she “wanted to find a way to get my fans out of their homes, and to really follow an itinerary of my perfect idea of a day and have the music from ‘Bewitched’ follow it.”
And thus, “A Very Laufey Day” was born. Each year, the Grammy-winning singer curates itineraries for different locations across the globe for her listeners to follow. It’s “anywhere I have been and loved,” she says. It allows them to live what she refers to as “a perfect day,” but also to connect with their community offline and in person. And as she approaches its fourth edition, it has only grown larger.
“It became much bigger than I anticipated, really,” she says. She sought to inspire her audience to find “third spaces,” and explore some of her favorite locales: museums, bookstores, cafes, concerts and the like, and foster community in the process. And each year, it has only grown bigger, with fans dressing up in their favorite Laufey-themed vintage fashions to celebrate the unofficial holiday.
And Aug. 23 will mark the fourth annual “A Very Laufey Day.”
“It is a fun puzzle every year,” she says.
‘A Very Laufey Day’ 2026
This year, “A Very Laufey Day” will include experiences in 75 cities across 25 countries, centering on the theme of “A Celebration of the Arts.”
Those include performances spanning symphony orchestras, ballet, jazz, opera and theater as well as events with libraries, bookstores, coffee shops, yogurt/ice cream shops and more. Her concert film “A Night at the Symphony: Hollywood Bowl” will be screened at select theaters. And she’s partnered with many museums around the world, including New York City’s Guggenheim, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago, London’s Tate Modern and National Gallery, Chile’s Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes, Seoul’s Daelim Museum and more. At some participating businesses, fans will be able to acquire limited edition merchandise and Laufey-themed specialty drinks.
“This year it was really about focusing on the arts and culture and finding ways to bring this barrier of entry down between my audience — which is mostly Gen Z and Gen A — and these kind of so-called high cultural experiences,” she says. “Whether it’s going to see an orchestra show … museums or galleries, we really want to find ways to connect with those institutions.”
Some of these spaces can be intimidating for younger fans, and Laufey says this year was all about making these rooms, some of her favorites, inviting to her audience.
“It doesn’t have to be this scary thing. And so, I’ve kind of made it my life’s mission to make spaces like that fun and accessible,” she says.

articles.title: Palestinians besieged in West Bank village fear Israeli settlers will seize their homes
articles.body:
Palestinians besieged in West Bank village fear Israeli settlers will seize their homes
QUSRA, West Bank (AP) — From inside his home in the West Bank town of Qusra, Qusai Abu Rida watched on Friday as Israeli settlers moved from where they had erected a tent in front of his house to the valley below, rather than returning to the nearby outpost where they live.
Even as the Israeli army took positions around him and the homes of two other Palestinian families that settlers had blockaded for most of this week, the settlers remained close enough that Abu Rida feared they would again return after the army left and try to take over the home owned by his Palestinian American brother in Ohio.
“I just don’t know when this will end,” he said.
The standoff in Qusra between Palestinian families and Israeli settlers who apparently want to push them out entered a new stage Friday as activists supporting the Palestinians marched toward the besieged homes to replenish their dwindling food and water supply. But Abu Rida said he was growing tired of the pattern, with Israeli forces removing the settlers, only for them to return and reestablish their positions after the troops withdrew.
“It’s like a kids’ game, like cat and mouse,” Ziv Stahl, the executive director of the Israeli rights group Yesh Din, said. “It’s clearly not a matter of capability but a matter of will.”
The siege of the homes is the latest episode in a wave of settler violence convulsing the occupied West Bank, which Israel seized in the 1967 Mideast war and which would make up the main part of a future Palestinian state. Israel’s military said the village — roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) from the Palestinian city of Nablus — was a closed military zone.
More than 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the occupied West Bank and east Jerusalem. The international community overwhelmingly considers Israeli settlements to be illegal and obstacles to peace.
Both Israel’s military and Israel’s police referred questions about the situation in Qusra to the other.
The West Bank has become more dangerous for Palestinians as Israel, under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has approved more than 100 new settlements. Extremist settlers routinely enter Palestinian towns, clashing with villagers, burning homes, mosques and cars.
Netanyahu is courting blocs of ultranationalist voters ahead of what’s expected to be a difficult reelection campaign in October. He and members of his cabinet have largely dismissed concerns about settler violence as overblown and attributed it to fringe groups of a few hundred youths. Yet rights groups and Palestinians say the government’s policies have made it more difficult to restrain settlers, who are rarely punished for attacks.
Qusra siege reflects broader violence
The standoff in Qusra began on Sunday when dozens of settlers arrived and blocked the doors to the three houses, preventing occupants from leaving, according to the families inside.
Israeli troops intervened multiple times and arrived in large numbers Thursday.
Abu Rida and his teenage son were temporarily moved by the army on Thursday but allowed to return hours later. He told his brother in Toledo, Ohio, that he planned on staying to defend the home.
Loui Ridi, the home’s owner who spells the family name differently, has been in constant contact with his brother and watching the siege unfold on security cameras until they went offline Thursday.
He plans to travel to the West Bank next week in hopes of delivering more food and “to do whatever I can to protect my brother and my house,” Ridi told The Associated Press on Friday.
“We want it to be resolved and permanent, not just for a couple of days,” he said.
For many, the scene unfolding in Qusra — now in its sixth day — reflected broader failures by Israeli authorities to curb the violence in the West Bank.
Itamar Weil, an Israeli human rights activist from the group Bnei Avraham, said the army had threatened to use tear gas against the activists and forced them to leave, even as settlers remained in the valley below Qusra.
“The army used to prevent settlers from carrying out this kind of violence,” he said. “Now, with a government that fully supports them, they’re not doing their job. They should be protecting both sides from violence, but instead they’re removing activists while barely doing anything about the settlers.”
Palestinian officials have reported 1,476 attacks by Israeli settlers in 2026, including several earlier instances in which settlers staged takeovers of Palestinian homes on the outskirts of other West Bank towns.
A total of 87 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli settlers and soldiers in the West Bank this year, according to the Palestinian Authority’s Health Ministry. Israel says some were involved in terrorism, which it defines broadly to include militancy and rock-throwing. Three Israelis were killed by Palestinians, including two in a July clash during which four Palestinians were also killed.
Katz strips army of enforcement power against settlers
Before calm was restored in Qusra, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz announced on Friday that he would transfer all enforcement powers against Israeli civilians in the West Bank from the army to Israel’s police.
“The (Israeli military’s) role is to fight Palestinian terrorism, focus on protecting the borders and settlements against threats, deal with the borders and the territory itself and security threats to the settlements and the State of Israel, and not chase after boys on the hills,” Katz said in a statement.
Historically, the army has been able to arrest Palestinians and bring those accused of crimes before military courts. But when it comes to Israeli civilians, in most circumstances it can only use temporary detention for those suspected of crimes, leaving arrests, investigations and prosecutions to police and civilian courts.
Katz’s move comes after he ended the use of administrative detention against Israeli civilians in November 2024. The military had used the policy as a tool to contain settler violence, allowing it to detain suspects without charge and remove them from the West Bank.
Much like with that move, rights groups said transferring all powers to the police was unlikely to restore order or ensure Palestinian safety.
Some 2.8 million Palestinians live under Israeli military rule in the West Bank alongside more than 560,000 Israeli civilians who live in settlements that the international community largely considers illegal and an obstacle to peace.
Though the Palestinian Authority exercises limited autonomy and policing power in the territory’s largest cities, agreements that date back to the 1990s give Israel security control over large swaths of the territory, including agricultural areas and communities such as Qusra.
Stahl, Yesh Din’s executive director, said Katz’s announcement wouldn’t change or help stem the violence because police will still require army escorts to operate in Palestinian areas.
“Unless (Katz) means he’s going to apply Israeli law and have the police control the West Bank, the military is still the main body in charge,” she said.
___
Associated Press reporter John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits the Control Network Behind Russia’s Geran and Gerbera Drones
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits the Control Network Behind Russia’s Geran and Gerbera Drones
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck two ground-based relay stations used to control Russian Geran and Gerbera strike drones, as well as five UAV command posts, on August 13 and overnight into August 14, Ukraine’s General Staff reported.
The two ground-based relay stations were targeted near Zaliiznyi Port in Ukraine’s Kherson region. Such systems transmit control and communications signals between drone operators and unmanned aerial vehicles, extending their operational range and improving the stability of their connection.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian forces also struck five Russian UAV command posts located in areas including Chasiv Yar in Donetsk region and Zaliiznyi Port in Kherson region.
Three additional UAV command posts were targeted in Russia’s Kursk and Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia regions, specifically near Volfinsky and Hordiyivka in Kursk region and Luhove in Zaporizhzhia region, according to the General Staff.
The strikes come as Russia continues to expand its production of attack drones. Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) estimates that Russia’s defense industry plans to manufacture 11,000 strike UAVs in August.
In an interview with RBC-Ukraine, HUR Deputy Chief Vadym Skibitskyi said the planned output includes Geran-1, Geran-2, Geran-3, Geran-4, and Geran-5 drones, as well as Harpy and several Gerbera variants, including strike and seeker versions.
According to Skibitskyi, Russia reduced both the intensity of its drone attacks and production volumes in July while restructuring its manufacturing capacity. The reconfiguration was aimed at increasing output of the turbojet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones.
Against this backdrop, Ukraine is also targeting the infrastructure that supports Russia’s drone operations. On August 13, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces struck 29 energy infrastructure facilities in Russian-occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, and Zaporizhzhia regions and Crimea.

articles.title: Ukraine Secretly Built a Shahed-Like Drone for SBU—Now Thousands Are Flying Deep Into Russia
articles.body:
- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Secretly Built a Shahed-Like Drone for SBU—Now Thousands Are Flying Deep Into Russia
Ukrainian engineers turned a Chinese civilian drone design into a domestically produced 2,000-kilometer deep-strike weapon now used exclusively by the Security Service of Ukraine’s (SBU) Alfa special operations center, according to Ukrainian defense outlet Oboronka, whose journalists visited the MICH 2000 production facility on August 12.
The drone, known as MICH 2000, can carry up to 60 kilograms of explosives and has already been used against targets deep inside Russia and temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
One of its most recent reported appearances came in early August, when Ukrainian forces struck the cargo ship Nadezhda near Novorossiysk with a drone that looked more like an Iranian-designed Shahed than Ukraine’s better-known Lyutyi or FP-1 long-range weapons.
According to Oboronka, that aircraft was a MICH 2000.
From Chinese drone to Ukrainian deep-strike weapon
Its story began before Ukraine had developed the large domestic deep-strike drone industry it operates today.
Beginning in 2022, Ukrainian teams converted Chinese-made Mugin-5 PRO civilian aircraft into attack drones, fitting them with explosive payloads for strikes against targets in the Russian rear. Each platform cost around $15,000, carried approximately 25 kilograms of explosives, and could fly roughly 500 kilometers.
China tightened restrictions on direct civilian drone exports in the summer of 2023, forcing Ukrainian developers to search for another approach.
In December that year, a Ukrainian engineering team traveled to China hoping to purchase complete airframes directly from manufacturers. According to Oboronka, they eventually found a factory producing dozens of ZTK-150 drones, aircraft closely resembling the Shahed configuration but identifiable by small forward canards.
“We were at a very large production facility and saw all the processes. Then we negotiated for several days with Chinese intermediaries until they came up with the idea to sell us the technology so we could make everything ourselves. That’s when they planted the idea that we could really build drones in Ukraine instead of buying and shipping them,” a member of the team told Oboronka.
Ukraine’s military leadership reportedly backed the proposal.
Ukraine couldn’t buy the tech—so engineers learned how to build it
But when the developers returned prepared to purchase the technology, management at the Chinese factory refused the deal.
The intermediaries offered another solution: drones could be assembled at a location outside the reach of China’s export restrictions, while Ukrainian personnel would receive training on how to operate them.
That training apparently provided much more than piloting experience.
“We went there to train pilots to fly the Chinese drones. And while training, we photographed everything there was, from the production process to the layout of the shelves and cabinets,” the team told Oboronka.
The Ukrainians returned home with eight Chinese-built aircraft, trained pilots, and a detailed picture of how the drones were manufactured.
The first prototypes barely flew
Testing began in the summer of 2024—and initially went badly.
The first prototype traveled only about one kilometer before crashing because of incorrect weight distribution. The second remained airborne for roughly an hour before vibration caused its propeller to break away. A third failed after losing its control signal under electronic warfare, exposing the original aircraft’s inability to operate reliably in a heavily jammed environment.
Building a Ukrainian version from scratch brought another wave of problems.
“When we started making our own fuselages, we made a lot of mistakes, aerodynamic and structural, that caused us constant problems. For about a month and a half to two months we were crashing planes at the range until our customer told us: ‘You’ve worn out your welcome, it’s time for combat.’ We said we hadn’t started flying properly yet. But Alfa wasn’t interested in that. They needed results,” the company’s owner told Oboronka.
The MICH’s first combat mission came in October 2024.
From three combat drones to eight MICH variants
Three drones were launched. One was shot down, while the other two reportedly missed their designated targets by approximately 10 meters.
The unit approved the platform for production, and the aircraft began evolving rapidly from an experimental adaptation into a family of deep-strike weapons.
The MICH uses a flying-wing design, meaning much of the aircraft body itself generates lift. Finished fuselages are weighed as part of a broader quality-control process intended to keep every airframe as close as possible to the same specifications.
“Repeatability of the technology matters to me. The lighter the airframe, the more fuel it can carry, and the fewer problems can occur in flight. Any millimeter, or a misplaced comma in the code, can cause an error,” the owner said.
According to Oboronka, the manufacturer now offers eight configurations for what it describes as “deep strike” and “middle strike” missions.
Depending on the version, the drones can fly up to 2,000 kilometers and carry between 25 and 60 kilograms of explosives.
Customers can select analog, digital, or Starlink communications, different warhead types, terminal-guidance systems, and CRPA antenna configurations intended to make satellite navigation more resistant to Russian jamming.
The original Chinese aircraft reportedly cost about $50,000.
Ukraine’s domestically produced version starts at approximately $48,000, although the final price rises depending on guidance, communications, and electronic-warfare-resistant navigation equipment.
Over the past two years, the manufacturer has built a network of dozens of Ukrainian subcontractors producing components including engines, warheads, fuselages, ignition boards, and rocket-assisted launch boosters.
One major foreign dependency remains: CRPA anti-jamming antennas.
Only a small number of manufacturers produce them, according to Oboronka, and individual systems can cost between $20,000 and $25,000 depending on the number of antenna modules.
A MICH 2000 without a CRPA system is approximately 85% localized in Ukraine by cost. Adding the imported antenna reduces that figure to about 55%.
The company has also learned the cost of relying on outside suppliers the hard way.
“We had an unpleasant incident where third-party boosters burned about a million dollars’ worth of our equipment. After that we were banned from launching on those boosters … We went to the range, launched the first aircraft, and the booster misfired, producing more impulse than it should have. Chemists and engineers worked all night reworking the rockets right there at the range. The next day three drones flew. After that we started scaling up and switching to our own boosters,” the owner told Oboronka.
6,000 drones a year—and one customer
The manufacturer currently produces roughly 6,000 drones annually and plans to increase output to 10,000.
That remains far below the 100,000-drone annual production target announced by Ukrainian manufacturer Fire Point for its own long-range systems, but MICH follows a very different model.
Unlike Fire Point’s FP-1, which is distributed across multiple Ukrainian units, MICH 2000 has one customer: SBU Alfa.
“We know our drones won’t just fly off somewhere into the swamps. They’ll fly to a specific target, because Alfa is about analytics and results,” the company told Oboronka.
Where MICH 2000 already struck
According to the outlet, Alfa has already launched thousands of MICH drones and struck hundreds of targets.
Oboronka identified at least eight publicly available videos showing the aircraft either in flight or striking targets.
The company says MICH 2000 has been involved in attacks on Moscow, Russian military infrastructure in occupied Ukrainian territory, and several high-value targets deep inside Russia.
Among the most notable reported operations was the destruction of a Tu-95MS strategic bomber at Engels airfield. Satellite imagery later showed that the rear section of the aircraft had been destroyed beyond repair.
The drone has also reportedly struck a Wildberries logistics hub in Russia’s Ryazan region, an electronic warfare system near Vladimir Putin’s residence in Gelendzhik, and a Russian Baltic Fleet naval facility.
The platform’s largest reported single operation targeted the Russian port of Ust-Luga, where more than 20 MICH drones reportedly reached their targets.
In another attack, according to the manufacturer, so many guided MICH drones successfully entered the target area that the operators began running out of designated objects to strike.
“During one attack with guided MICH drones, so many reached the target area that there weren’t enough targets left for them. They ended up chasing a Pantsir air defense system down the road after it had fired off all its ammunition,” the company’s head said, laughing.
The next MICH will carry a bigger warhead
Development has not stopped with the 2,000-kilometer version.
The company is now working on MICH+, a shorter-range “middle strike” variant without the front canards seen on the original design.
The new version is expected to carry a larger 70-kilogram warhead, include terminal guidance, and reach targets at distances of up to 600 kilometers. Its expected price is around $40,000.
The manufacturer is hiring additional workers, opening new production sites, and reinvesting approximately $1 million every month into research and development as it works toward the 10,000-drone annual production target.
But having only SBU Alfa as a customer also limits how quickly the company can finance further expansion.
According to Oboronka, the manufacturer is therefore exploring joint production with Baltic countries through the Build with Ukraine initiative, potentially opening access to European financing and additional manufacturing capacity.
What began with eight Chinese-built drones and a Ukrainian team photographing a foreign production line has evolved into a domestically manufactured family of strike weapons capable of reaching targets up to 2,000 kilometers away.
“Honestly, I don’t want to guess anymore what happens after 10,000. I just want the war to end. But if we need to keep working, we’ll keep working,” the company’s head said.
Earlier, Ukraine’s F-Drones delivered the first 2,000 F10 FPV drones to the US military under the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance Program, making the F10 the first Ukrainian drone authorized for export to the United States under the initiative.
