articles.title: Estonian pork industry squeezed as cheap imports fill production gap
articles.body:
Estonian pork industry squeezed as cheap imports fill production gap
A year after a major African swine fever (ASF) outbreak, Estonia's pork industry is struggling again as cheap European imports push local prices below production costs.
Although pig farms have disinfected facilities and rebuilt production since last year's outbreak, many producers are operating at a loss, forcing some smaller farms to close.
"If we stop production and ever want to restart, this isn't a case where you can say today you will, tomorrow you won't," said Saime Agro Group CEO Valmar Haava. "Restarting [pork production] isn't cheap, and it's a very, very lengthy process."
Farmers are having little trouble selling their pork, he added, but are doing so below cost.
Some of the effects of last year's ASF outbreak are only just hitting the meat processing industry, as farms emptied during the outbreak left months-long gaps in pork supplies.
"The farms that were hit were ones whose pigs would normally have reached the market just at the beginning or during the first half of this year, which is why recovery has taken quite a while," said Nõo Meat Factory CEO Ragnar Loova.
Lower pig numbers are also hurting businesses that supply the industry, including feed producers, said Atria Farms board member Meelis Laande.
"Volumes have fallen quite low, and that in turn has meant feed producers no longer have enough work either," Laande explained, adding that those resulting rising costs ultimately show up in pork prices as well.
Price wins over preference
Domestic pork now covers about 60 percent of Estonia's consumption, down from roughly 70–80 percent last year, Laande said. That leaves the market increasingly dependent on imports.
The Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture is seeking ways to ease producers' losses, while the government has already approved €14 million to help rebuild and expand domestic pork production, including sow farms.
"It's also important to continue discussions with the European Commission, because this isn't just Estonia's problem," said ministry deputy secretary general Madis Pärtel.
Despite consumers' preference for domestic pork, cheaper imported meat often wins at the grocery store.
--
Editor: Johanna Alvin, Aili Vahtla

articles.title: A blackout occurred simultaneously in four Central Asian countries
articles.body:
A blackout occurred simultaneously in four Central Asian countries
Kyiv • UNN
On August 14, an emergency shutdown of KEGOC JSC's 500 kV lines left Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan without power. Electricity has already begun to be restored, and power supplies have been fully restored.
A power outage occurred in four Central Asian countries at once—Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan—Tengrinews.kz reports, writes UNN.
Details
As reported, on the afternoon of August 14, residents of various districts of Almaty, Kazakhstan, began reporting disruptions to the power supply.
The cause was an emergency shutdown of 500 kV overhead power transmission lines belonging to JSC "KEGOC".
It later emerged that there was also no electricity in Almaty Region, Turkistan Region, the Zhetisu Region, and even in other Central Asian countries: Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.
According to reports, power has now begun to be restored.
Electricity has begun to be restored in some districts of Almaty. The Ministry of Energy of Kazakhstan had previously stated that power supplies in Almaty and other regions of Kazakhstan would be fully restored shortly.
The agency reported that power supply via the JSC "KEGOC" line had been fully restored. The situation is being monitored.

articles.title: 'Terrorists will face consequences': President Murmu addresses nation on eve of 80th I-Day - key quotes
articles.body:
NEW DELHI: President Droupadi Murmu on Friday addressed the nation and extended her greetings ahead of the 80th Independence day. On the eve of Independence Day, Murmu praised India's growth and said that "every citizen is contributing to nation building".
Here's are some of the key quotes from President Murmu's national address:
- Duty of every person associated with judicial system to ensure that no one is deprived of justice due to lack of resources.
- Citizens across all walks of life are making valuable contributions to nation-building, with the Armed Forces, CAPFs, police personnel, sanitation workers and the Indian diaspora playing a special role. India remains committed to building a Viksit Bharat by 2047 through inclusive development, while drawing inspiration from its rich heritage and the ideals of the freedom struggle.
- Operation Sindoor demonstrated Indian Armed Forces' capability for precision strikes against terror networks.
- People from different ideological streams shared one common goal, India’s independence. During the Swadeshi Movement, Vande Mataram became the song of the masses. Under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi, countless Indians joined the freedom struggle, while Dr BR Ambedkar set high ideals of social reform and national commitment.
- Suspension of Indus Waters Treaty with country harbouring terrorism a decisive step in national interest, particularly for farmers.
- Terrorists and those supporting them will have to face consequences no matter where they hide.
- Making India Naxal-free is a major national achievement.
- Due to communal violence, millions of people had to become refugees and endure the horrors of Partition. Yet, they did not abandon their identity. When our country became independent, along with the serious consequences of Partition, integrating more than 550 princely states with the newly independent India was also an extraordinary challenge. Sardar Patel integrated the princely states into our independent republic.
- Over 25 cr people lifted out of poverty in past decade through inclusive development initiatives.
- Free ration programme ensuring food security for more than 80 cr beneficiaries.
- We are moving forward with a balance between heritage and development. The world's largest and most advanced digital infrastructure has been developed in our country. Digital payments are being made even at small shops in villages and on roadside stalls. More than half of the world's real-time digital transactions are taking place in India. Our citizens and the government, working together, have presented an example of a digital revolution to the global community.

articles.title: Türkiye secures 245 extraditions in 2026: Minister
articles.body:
Türkiye has secured the extradition of 245 people from abroad so far this year, including 48 since July 1, Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said on Aug. 14.
Of the 48 people extradited from 12 countries over the past six weeks, 24 came from Georgia, eight from Germany and six from Greece, Gürlek said.
Türkiye had secured 197 extraditions from 31 countries in the first half of the year.
Gürlek said authorities would continue pursuing people wanted in Türkiye who had fled abroad, working in coordination with the Interior and Foreign ministries and their international counterparts.
His remarks came hours after the Interior Ministry announced that Serkan Kurtuluş, who had been sought under an Interpol Red Notice, was extradited from Argentina.
The ministry describes Kurtuluş as the leader of an organized crime group and said he was wanted on allegations including premeditated and intentional homicide, establishing a criminal organization, armed robbery and repeated armed threats.

articles.title: How the Iran war is taking a growing toll on the US military
articles.body:
When US President Donald Trump launched military operations against Iran, he promised the war would end “pretty quickly”. Nearly six months later, there is little sign of that happening.
While diplomatic efforts to end the fighting continue, the prolonged conflict is increasingly revealing the cost of an extended military campaign. Beyond the economic fallout from Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, signs of strain are emerging within the US armed forces, from exhausted troops and extended deployments to growing concerns over morale aboard frontline naval vessels.
USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72) was sent to the Arabian Sea in January, near Iranian shores, as tensions between the US and Iran increased earlier this year.
Although the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier can remain at sea for up to 20 years without refuelling, its crew faced fatigue and mental health issues after over 200 days without visiting a port.
In recent weeks, reports in US media have highlighted growing concern among military families over conditions aboard the carrier, citing allegations of exhaustion, food shortages, water contamination, disruptions to mail deliveries and multiple suicide attempts.
“My son is currently on that ship and listening to him say that he and his shipmates constantly think about jumping off the ship just for relief is so hard to listen to,” wrote one of the parents to a deployed troop to Stars and Stripes in July.
“We are all tucked in at night in our beds at night meanwhile our loved ones are out there fighting with no understanding as to what they’re defending,” she continued.
The Pentagon and the US Navy denied reports claiming the ship is running low on supplies and that soldiers are experiencing rising suicidal tendencies.
Three US officials, speaking anonymously to CNN, confirmed that a sailor aboard USS Abraham Lincoln went overboard earlier this month. The sailor was rescued by an air wing search and rescue helicopter about an hour after the incident, according to sources.
During a town hall in San Diego, the home city of the aircraft carrier, a sailor's spouse informed top Navy officials that her husband had written a note saying he hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow.
Depleting missiles and munitions
The US military faces issues beyond troop morale, as Tehran has shown no signs of yielding under Trump’s pressure, instead suggesting new conditions for a potential settlement.
The Iran conflict has caused a substantial reduction in American missile systems, including Patriots and THAADs, and the military has also lost 25 percent of its Reaper drones, raising concerns about the direction the war is taking.
Recent estimates indicate that the US military has significantly depleted its Patriot interceptors and THAAD missiles.
The situation is even more critical for the long-range precision missiles, including Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrCM), which sources familiar with military data say have been almost entirely used up.
Before the war, the US possessed 2,330 Patriots and 452 THAAD missiles. By late July, this number dropped to fewer than 1,000 Patriot interceptors and between 234 and 278 THAAD units, based on a recent report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
The Washington Post recently reported that depleted missile stocks sparked a heated dispute between Trump and Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth at Camp David, Maryland, where the President accused him of failing to properly inform the White House about the military's arsenal.
The White House, however, denied the report.
Analysts also caution that restoring US missile inventories will be challenging, potentially costing American taxpayers significant payloads and taking years.
Another CSIS report indicated that the US military would not be able to restore its pre-war levels for Patriots and THAADs before at least mid-2029.
Some estimates are even more pessimistic. Analysing the Pentagon's request for 857 THAAD interceptors—used to defend against ballistic missiles—the conservative American Enterprise Institute estimated that, at current production rates, it would take about 27 years to meet Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's request.
For analysts, the implications extend well beyond the conflict's financial cost. Months of sustained operations have depleted munitions, strained military resources and exposed the limits of America's defence industrial base at a time when Washington is also trying to deter rivals such as Russia and China.
Hegseth has already asked Congress for an emergency $87.6 billion supplemental defence package, saying the United States has spent $37.5 billion on the war with Iran so far and warning that additional funding may still be needed.

articles.title: Russian agent who set fires in Kyiv receives 15-year prison sentence
articles.body:
A Kyiv court has sentenced an unemployed man to 15 years in prison with confiscation of his property for carrying out arson attacks on behalf of Russian intelligence, Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) said on 13 August. The man was recruited while looking for "easy money" on Telegram channels and carried out two arson attacks in Kyiv before fleeing to Odesa, the SBU reported.
Russian intelligence increasingly recruits Ukrainians through Telegram for arson and sabotage. It targets people seeking quick money and treats them as disposable operatives, paying small sums for a single task and discarding them once they are caught.
The Russian agent carried out two arson attacks
According to the SBU, the man first set fire to a relay cabinet belonging to a railway signaling system. Russia intended the attack to disrupt freight logistics, including supplies to areas near the front.
The agent later burned a volunteer’s SUV used to deliver humanitarian aid and evacuate civilians from areas affected by Russia’s war. He carried out the attacks at night, using a flammable mixture and filming each incident on his smartphone before sending the footage to his Russian handler.
The SBU arrested him in Odesa in July 2025, where he had attempted to hide after carrying out the attacks. Investigators seized his phone, which contained evidence of his cooperation with Russia.
A court found him guilty on two counts — sabotage committed under martial law, and intentional destruction of property by arson — both carried out as part of a group acting on prior conspiracy. He was sentenced to 15 years in prison with confiscation of his property.
From “easy money” to murder: Russia escalates recruitment of Ukrainians for terrorist attacks inside Ukraine, police warn
Easy money, hard time: other Telegram recruits jailed too
The case follows several similar convictions. In a May case, an agent received 15 years for burning a railway relay cabinet near a Dnipro station in an attempt to disrupt frontline logistics. The SBU said the unemployed local, recruited through Telegram, filmed the arson and reported it to his handler, then was caught before he could carry out a planned series of attacks on the city's critical infrastructure.
In June 2026, another agent was sentenced to 15 years for preparing to burn an electrical substation in Kropyvnytskyi.
In July, SBU investigators reported that a GRU agent in Zaporizhzhia received 15 years for preparing explosives for Russian-organized attacks.

articles.title: ‘The fear keeps building’: Residents of Russia’s Nizhnekamsk on life after a deadly Ukrainian drone attack
articles.body:
‘The fear keeps building’: Residents of Russia’s Nizhnekamsk on life after a deadly Ukrainian drone attack
A Ukrainian drone attack on Nizhnekamsk, a city in Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan, on August 10 killed 13 people, including citizens of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. Residents quickly erected a makeshift memorial with flowers and candles, authorities canceled the city’s anniversary celebrations, and Tatarstan declared a period of mourning. The independent journalist cooperative Bereg reports on what residents of Nizhnekamsk saw and heard that day. Meduza is publishing the text in full.
Nizhnekamsk, a city on the Kama River 220 kilometers (137 miles) from Kazan, grew up around the Nizhnekamsk petrochemical plant, once one of the largest in the Soviet Union. Two oil refineries now operate there, Taneko and TAIF, and both have become regular targets for Ukrainian drones, with strikes recorded both in June and in July. But the attack on August 10 stood out.
The oil refineries were the intended targets, according to the General Staff of Ukraine’s Armed Forces, but the drones also struck residential buildings in the city and a hostel in the industrial zone. Russian officials said 13 people were killed, including citizens of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan and a 5-year-old girl who was sleeping on the balcony of a building on Shkolny Boulevard when a drone hit a tree and exploded, shattering a window. Another 78 people were injured.
The apartment building on Shkolny Boulevard, where the girl had lived, took the worst damage of any building in the strike: windows were blown out in 60 of its 132 apartments. Ninety-three residents applied to the Nizhnekamsk city administration for temporary housing, and 25 of the injured were hospitalized.
Here is how local residents reacted to the attack.
‘I’m an adult man, I’ve seen a lot, but I couldn’t hold back here’
Ruslan (name changed), a 53-year-old lawyer, was at home during the attack. He heard the sirens, since the balcony and windows in his apartment were open. He said he was among the first to reach the apartment building on Shkolny Boulevard.
“I stood near that building with tears in my eyes. I’m ashamed to admit it. I’m an adult man, I’ve seen a lot, but I couldn’t hold back here,” Ruslan said in a conversation with Bereg.
He didn’t know anyone among the dead or injured and learned about the victims from official reports, though what he saw on Shkolny Boulevard hit him harder than any report could. “It’s one thing to read about it in the news, and quite another to see the aftermath with your own eyes,” he said. “My first reaction was, of course, shock. It’s still very hard psychologically.”
A makeshift memorial appeared outside the city museum on August 10. Ruslan said people brought flowers, candles, icons, and children’s toys until evening. Many came as families, and local bikers arrived to lay carnations, he added.
“I stayed there for about 40 minutes, there were a lot of people. It’s amazing how close-knit our city is, how good our people are,” he told Bereg. He added that he worries most about the children: “At moments like this, you still end up thinking about the children rather than yourself.”
Olga (name changed) works on art projects in collaboration with a large local company. She doesn’t live in Nizhnekamsk full time but regularly travels there for work. “I don’t think it’s gotten more alarming, because I’ve already gotten used to everything that’s happening. It’s unsafe everywhere, really,” she said.
Olga said the attacks and restrictions have mostly disrupted her work schedule. Airport closures and rescheduled flights often force her to change plans and cancel meetings, which she said “affects her productivity overall.”
“There were times when we couldn’t get food [during business trips] because many cafes closed due to the drone threat,” she said. “But people there [in Nizhnekamsk] are calm. There’s no noticeable panic among residents.”
Despite the drones striking more often, her team has no plans to scale back its work in Nizhnekamsk. “People need this [the art projects] to cope somehow,” Olga said.
Unlike her, 44-year-old Alina (name changed) has lived in Nizhnekamsk her entire life. She told Bereg that in “recent months” she has often heard the sounds of drones at night. “It usually happens around four in the morning,” Alina added. She said that, over time, she has come to find these nights “harder and harder” to bear.
Alina was home during the August 10 attack, and this time, she recalled, the sound lasted longer than usual and seemed especially close:
The sound was long and happened not once but two or three times. The window was open, and the sound was very close, but nothing could be seen in the dark. I was very scared.
She said also heard “strange sounds” on August 12, even though authorities reported no drone attacks that day; other residents also wrote about the sounds in local community groups on social media.
Alina learned about the aftermath of the August 10 attack from her husband. “My anxiety kept growing, and I had to see a doctor. I’m afraid for my children and want to leave the city. The fear keeps building up because the strikes have become more frequent and more destructive,” the Nizhnekamsk resident said.
She’s especially worried about the start of the school year. Alina said parents in Nizhnekamsk school chat groups are already debating the September 1 assemblies. “Opinions are split 50-50. Some aren’t afraid, while others worry that large gatherings of people could be a reason for another drone attack. The school administration left the decision up to the parents,” she said. She plans to keep her own children home on September 1.
The children see things differently, she said. “They still don’t fully understand the danger,” Alina said with a sigh, adding that they don’t want to leave Nizhnekamsk, where they have friends, school, and their “familiar life.”
“But my husband and I are considering moving to a rural settlement where we have a plot of land. We don’t have enough money yet to fully build a house, [so we can’t leave right away],” Olga explained to Bereg.
‘These people should have been in shelters, but they weren’t’
Seven of the 13 people killed were citizens of Uzbekistan and two were citizens of Tajikistan. Their names were never published, and Bereg was unable to locate their relatives or friends. According to media reports, they were eating breakfast in a cafeteria when the strike hit Nizhnekamsk.
“We simply failed to meet the standards that are required by regulation. These people should have been in shelters, but they weren’t,” the head of Tatarstan, Rustam Minnikhanov, said after visiting the hostel.
A few days later, authorities announced the bodies of the dead had been sent to Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.
After the attack, Nizhnekamsk residents began petitioning the city administration to cancel the celebration of the city’s 60th anniversary, scheduled for August 15, writing on social media that holding a mass celebration so soon after people were killed would be inappropriate.
“They want to spend 60-80 million [rubles] on the city’s anniversary, that’s what was reported. Who needs this bravado when this kind of thing is happening. That money would be better spent on defending the city,” one person wrote on the social media site VK.
“All the celebrations should be canceled! The money would be better spent on strengthening the city’s defenses! How can there be any festivities while innocent civilians are dying!” another Nizhnekamsk resident wrote on social media.
In the end, authorities in Tatarstan declared a period of mourning and canceled City Day along with all other entertainment events. Nizhnekamsk Mayor Radmir Belyaev said City Day had been postponed indefinitely and would likely be held “in a different format.”
Ruslan, the lawyer, wants to see a permanent memorial built on Shkolny Boulevard in Nizhnekamsk to honor those killed on August 10. He has seen many people on social media express the same view and believes most residents of the city would support the idea.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: ‘We’ll Warm Ourselves With the Fire of Russian Oil Refineries’: Ukraine Hits Back at Russia
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Armed Forces responded to a Russian defense ministry post that appeared to threaten intensified attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure this winter with a warning about strikes on Russian oil refineries.
On Friday, the Strategic Communications Department of the Armed Forces of Ukraine published an image on Telegram showing a fire at an industrial facility with the caption: “We’ll warm ourselves with the fire of Russian oil refineries.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The post appeared to be a response to a message published earlier by Russia’s defense ministry featuring Shahed attack drones and the caption: “Like snow on your head.”
The Russian message appeared to hint at further attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure during the winter, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted power generation and heating infrastructure.
The reference to “freezing” also comes amid renewed discussions about a possible halt to hostilities. However, the Russian post appeared to suggest that Moscow could instead continue or intensify attacks on Ukraine’s energy system.
However, Ukraine’s Armed Forces responded with a direct warning aimed at Russia’s oil industry.
The image posted by the Strategic Communications Department showed a large fire at what appears to be an industrial facility, alongside the message about “warming” with the fire of Russian oil refineries.
The Ukrainian military did not provide details about any planned strikes or identify specific potential targets.
‘Only a Madman’ Would Say Sending Patriots to Ukraine Weakens Poland, Polish Minister Says
Russia rejects ceasefire efforts
The exchange came amid renewed discussions about possible limited ceasefires and restrictions on attacks against civilian infrastructure.
Reuters recently reported that Ukraine had proposed to Russia, through a third party, a mutual halt to attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea. Russian officials said they had not received any formal proposal.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has also called on Ukraine and Russia to develop a mechanism for a moratorium on attacks against ships in the Black Sea, according to Ukraine’s FM Andrii Sybiha.
However, on Friday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejected a halt to fighting along the current line of contact. Lavrov also threatened to make Russia’s approach “harsher,” saying Moscow would seek to destroy what he described as everything supporting Ukraine’s military machine from the West.
The latest statements from both sides come as Ukraine and Russia continue to signal that energy and other critical infrastructure could remain central targets as the war enters another winter.

articles.title: Wife of US soldier is removed from deportation flight and released from federal immigration custody
articles.body:
Wife of US soldier is removed from deportation flight and released from federal immigration custody
A U.S. soldier’s wife who spent more than a month in federal immigration detention said she is back home after officers removed her from a deportation flight to Brazil.
Earlier this month, The Associated Press highlighted Maisa Lopes Eliaser as one of dozens of spouses or parents of U.S. troops who had been detained after President Donald Trump’s administration rolled back protections for military families amid its push for mass deportations. Following the AP’s reporting, a group of Congressional Democrats launched an investigation into deportations of military service members and their families.
Eliaser was placed on a deportation flight Wednesday to her native Brazil when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers on the plane received a phone call about her midflight, she told the AP. She said she was then asked by an ICE officer whether she wanted to continue on to Brazil or go back to the U.S.
“Who made the call? We don’t know,” said Eliaser’s husband, Army Staff Sgt. Alexis Jaramillo. “But someone made the phone call, and then she came back.”
While other detainees were led off the plane in Brazil, Eliaser stayed on board and returned to Louisiana. ICE officers told her that she was “famous” because there were videos about her case, she said.
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, a former Navy officer, directly contacted the ICE field office involved in Eliaser’s detention, according to his spokesperson. He has also spoken out on behalf of two other detained military family members in the past year.
In a statement to the AP, Kelly said the policy of detaining military family members is “wrong and makes no sense at all.”
“We need real solutions to fix our broken immigration system,” Kelly wrote in a statement. “Going after military families instead of real criminals doesn’t solve anything.”
DHS previously told AP that Eliaser, 32, had been issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on April 15, after overstaying the tourist visa she used to enter the U.S. in 2019.
Jaramillo, a 43-year-old aviation operations specialist who has served in the Army for more than a decade, took leave of his duties training soldiers in Fort Polk, Louisiana, to care for Eliaser’s 5-year-old son after she was detained on July 8.
“This family’s reunion is proof of what’s possible when people set politics aside and do right by those who serve,” Danitza James, who heads Repatriate Our Patriots, a nonprofit that supports military families facing deportation and helped with Eliaser’s case, said at a news conference. “We won’t stop until every military family facing detention gets the same chance at justice.”
Eliaser, who was detained in July while at an immigration appointment, has another appointment scheduled for Monday in an effort to reopen her case and advance her green card application. Jaramillo is a U.S. citizen and the couple have been married since 2024.
Jaramillo said he has been told that there will be no further issues with Eliaser’s case, but the couple is still concerned.
“We are really, really, really scared about it, but you know, we have to go,” Jaramillo said. “I told the person who gave me the appointment, ‘Hey sir, don’t play with me, I’ve been through a lot.’”
Eliaser said she is still struggling to sleep and is afraid she will be sent back to the detention facility, where she said she was treated like “an animal.”
“It felt like I was in a nightmare,” Eliaser said. “I could not believe what was happening until I returned to my house. Day by day, I’m trying to recover from this trauma.”
There have been similar interventions in other high-profile cases over the past year. Annie Ramos, 22, was detained by immigration authorities as her husband, an Army staff sergeant, was preparing to deploy. She was released after a public outcry. Around the same time, U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, a Democrat and combat veteran, told the AP that she personally contacted DHS to call for the release of Deisy Rivera Ortega, the immigrant wife of an Army sergeant who did three tours in Afghanistan, after learning about her case from advocacy groups. She was eventually released from custody.
___
Brook is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

articles.title: Search for witnesses 'still active' over fire at Romanian embassy, Swiss police say
articles.body:
An employee from the embassy managed to put out the fire, before the Bern fire brigade deployed as a precaution and set up a fire watch at the scene.
Swiss police said on Friday they were still appealing for witnesses to come forward in connection with a fire they believe was deliberately started outside the Romanian embassy in Bern.
The blaze broke out on Monday and according to initial findings, "the fire was started deliberately," the Bern cantonal police said in a statement earlier this week.
"An unidentified perpetrator placed a burning object near the fence of the Romanian embassy in Bern. The fire subsequently spread to the surrounding vegetation."
An employee from the embassy managed to put out the fire, before the Bern fire brigade deployed as a precaution and set up a fire watch at the scene.
"No-one was injured, though property damage occurred," the police said.
The police have launched an investigation into the incident and are asking "anyone who may have observed anything suspicious in the vicinity of the Romanian embassy or who has any relevant information" to come forward.
"The appeal for witnesses is still active," a Bern cantonal police spokeswoman told the AFP news agency on Friday.
The Romanian embassy, a neo-Baroque villa built in 1904, is very close to those of other countries, including Canada, Austria, the Philippines, Ireland, Tunisia and Saudi Arabia.
"The Swiss authorities consider the incident to be a minor one, but because it occurred near an embassy, an investigation has been launched. Romania is cooperating with the Swiss authorities in this regard," the mission said in a statement on Wednesday.

articles.title: How England’s brutal summer heat is affecting farm animals and crops
articles.body:
As parts of the UK swelter through a fifth successive climate crisis-driven heatwave and nearly three-quarters of England remains in drought, how are six homegrown products faring?
Livestock
On her farm in Durham on Monday where she was vaccinating sheep, Clare Wise stopped and stood still. For the first time in weeks, it had begun to rain. “We didn’t think of taking cover, we just stayed out and enjoyed it!” she says.
Farmers farther south were less lucky, and the continuing drought, as well as causing distress for animals in danger of overheating, is storing up problems for livestock farmers this winter. Grass growth has been about half of what it should be by this time of year and mowing excess grass in summer is where most get their winter feed.
“This would be the peak season for collecting winter forage, but we have not been able to do that,” says Wise, who is also the acting livestock board chief for the National Farmers’ Union. “Grass growth has completely stalled.”
Some farmers have been forced to dip into their winter feed stores; others will need to supplement their scant supplies with bought-in feed.
Milk production is down, but so far only slightly – by about 1%, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), as cows have less to eat and are discouraged by the heat. Sheep shearers have been in short supply, making it difficult for farmers to make their flocks comfortable.
For future years, farmers can grow trees and higher hedges to provide shade for their beasts, says Tom Cantillon, an analyst at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank. Some with bigger herds might consider air conditioning in their sheds and milking parlours.
But for many livestock farmers, the fear is that this year is just the beginning.
Fruit
For aficionados of soft fruit, this is turning out to be a glorious summer. Berries are smaller but sweeter as the sunniest July on record in the UK has concentrated flavours. Strawberries and raspberries have done particularly well; stone fruit such as peaches, greengages and plums have ripened quickly, and cherries and blueberries have been cheap and plentiful.
Cider drinkers can also rejoice at the smaller and sweeter apples. Supermarkets tend to choose apples based on size, notes Cantillon, so if fewer of them make the grade, shoppers may be disappointed but drinkers will see the benefits. “It could be a bumper year for cider-making,” he says.
The picture is “genuinely mixed” for other produce, says Martin Emmett, the horticulture and potatoes board chair at the NFU.
Most fruit in the UK is grown covered on substrate, so a lack of rainfall in the fields has been less of an issue. But horticulturalists are worried about their water supplies. About half of the UK’s potato crop, for instance, is irrigated, often using groundwater from boreholes or abstracted from rivers. Many farmers would find it easier to store more of their own water on the farm, but constructing on-farm reservoirs requires complex planning permission.
Cereals
Britain could be in for its worst cereal harvest in four decades, with wheat, spring barley and oats all substantially down on their 10-year average, according to estimates from the AHDB analysed by the ECIU. This year’s cereal and oilseed harvest is forecast to be 18.5m tonnes, which would make 2026 the worst since detailed records began in 1984.
After a wet start to the year that affected late planting for spring wheat, a dry April hit winter wheat at a crucial growing stage. The record heatwave in May also deprived grains of the moisture they need to plump out.
Further heatwaves in June and July added heat stress, while the drought continued to stunt the grains. Since mid-June, there has been no rainfall or none of significance across much of England. July was the driest month ever recorded in southern England.
Yields on wheat are normally about 7.9 tonnes per hectare in the UK; that is forecast to be down by more than a tonne per hectare, at about 6.7 tonnes this year.
Estimates taken in early August, with about half the harvest gathered, showed that the loss of about 2.5m tonnes compared to early estimates would amount to about £390m in lost revenue for farmers.
Tom Lancaster, an analyst for land, food and farming at ECIU, says: “From the wettest winter on record in 2024, to the hottest summer in 2025, and now unprecedented heat and drought this year, we are in danger of UK farming entering a climate doom loop, as repeated impacts undermine the capacity of farmers to drill next year’s crop.”
Martin Lines, the chief executive of the Nature Friendly Farming Network, who farms in Cambridgeshire, says this year has been “brutal”, especially coming on top of two previous consecutive poor harvests. “Harvest this year has been a real kick in the teeth,” he says. “I’ve never known it this dry and hot on our farm. Even farmers I know who were sceptical of climate change are now saying they’re really worried.”
Europe is not faring much better, with heatwaves and fires contributing to a forecast of €2bn (£1.7bn) in lost revenue.
Wine
While traditional British crops are suffering, many vineyards are thriving. WineGB, the trade association representing the UK’s wine producers, says it is optimistic about the size and quality of the 2026 harvest. Producers are reporting healthy vineyards, clean fruit and encouraging ripening after stable summer conditions.
Nicola Bates, the chief executive of the trade body WineGB, said: “Whilst it’s too early to definitively say the overall impact on this year’s UK harvest – and what happens over the next few weeks will be crucial – the vineyards look strong and we’re optimistic.
“That said, seasonal conditions remain variable and producers continue to adapt, so building long-term resilience plans is essential for protecting our vineyards and to future-proof English and Welsh wine.”
Although some growers in Kent, the heartland of the British wine industry, suffered from late frosts most have managed to maintain fruit health.
Tim Spakouskas, a grower with 7 hectares (17.5 acres) of vineyard in North Yorkshire, says his farm has had very little rain for at least two months but his long-established vines are doing well as they have deep roots able to tap into moisture well below the sun-baked surface.
He is acutely aware that his wider family, who farm a variety of other crops, are “struggling a bit” in the hot dry weather which is not Yorkshire’s usual fare. Spakouskas says some of his newer vines planted last year are also showing signs of stress and he fears he may lose some if the weather does not change.
Salad
We may like to eat salad in the heat but lettuce is not a big fan of very hot weather. Its ideal growing temperature is about 20C, according to farmers, and it starts to get stressed at 24C. Over 35C, it won’t be suitable for sale, so the recent bouts of hot weather have been tricky for growers.
Ben Andrews, a salad farmer based in Herefordshire, posted on Instagram on Thursday: “There is still no rain and the veg is really struggling.” He said lettuce heads were likely to be smaller and it would probably take two to make up a portion, hitting takings.
Other leafy vegetables such as spinach and pak choi have also entered “thermal dormancy”, where they stop growing in the intense heat, according to Oddbox, which sells boxes of imperfect or surplus fruit and vegetables.
Even those growing in the controlled environments of greenhouses and polytunnels are struggling with the heat which topped 30C in parts of the UK again on Thursday.
Jan Bentley, the managing director of WS Bentley, which supplies salad cress, microgreens and pea shoots to restaurants and supermarkets grown in hydroponic systems, said yields had been reduced by “heat stress and some poor germination and crops destroyed when extremely hot”.
Oddbox also said the quality of cucumbers had been affected as “plants are stressed in the extreme heat, which causes them to misshape”.
Fish
It is not just people, animals and crops that have sweltered this summer: the water around Britain’s coast is also hotter.
Cornwall’s coastal waters are experiencing marine heatwave conditions for the third consecutive year, registering temperatures 3-4C warmer than at this time of year a decade ago, bringing challenges and opportunities for Britain’s fishers as Mediterranean species of fish and shellfish move into UK waters, while cod and haddock are migrating farther north.
Britain’s southernmost county is experiencing its largest octopus bloom in 75 years, according to the Marine Biological Association, thought to be linked to the warming seas.
As the octopus population has exploded, a record 130,000 tonnes has landed at Newlyn’s fish market so far this year. In previous years, less than 100 tonnes of octopus would have been brought ashore at the market, says Chris Ranford, the chief executive of the Cornish Fish Producers’ Organisation.
The fishing industry is “split down the middle whether it’s an opportunity or a problem”, says Ranford. “The volume has got to the level where it is a really solid export market, and the price has held up fairly well.”
Octopus is popular in countries including Spain, but there is little domestic appetite. UK fishers are also finding octopus have broken into their shellfish pots and eaten the crab and lobster inside, reducing catches of these species that are more popular with British diners.
Ranford, who is also the current chair of the National Organisation of Fishermen’s Federations, says there are concerns that a very cold winter or drop in water quality could suddenly cut octopus numbers, leaving fishers with little to catch as crab, lobster and scallop populations take time to recover.

articles.title: Türkiye’s defense industry undergoes strategic transformation over 25 years
articles.body:
The Turkish defense industry has evolved from a foreign-reliant structure based on licensed production and grown into a sector with significant transformations in scale, capability, domestically produced content, exports and product diversity over nearly a quarter-century.
Turkish defense has turned into a sector that develops original platforms and systems, invests in critical technologies and exports high-value-added products across the globe.
In 2002, Türkiye had only 56 defense firms and some 62 projects underway.
The number of defense companies surged to more than 4,500, and the number of projects surpassed 1,400 in 2024-2026.
The total project volume skyrocketed from $5.5 billion in 2002 to over $100 billion today.
Defense and aerospace exports surged from $248 million to $10.05 billion in 2025, while totaling $5.79 billion in the first six months of 2026 and $11.2 billion over the past 12 months as of July.
Research and development spending increased from $49 million to over $3.5 billion, while the domestically produced content ratio increased from 20% to more than 85%.
The Turkish defense sector provides direct employment to over 100,000 people, and the average age of a defense industry worker is 34.
Türkiye significantly shifted its approach to procurement, which drove the evolution of its defense industry.
Turkish defense was dominated by off-the-shelf purchases, licensed production and technology transfer in the early 2000s. This trend gradually shifted to promote domestic development, homegrown original design and the localization of critical subsystems.
The sector’s scope of operations expanded as project scales grew, with a broad range of products and technologies emerging, such as armored vehicles, conventional platforms, unmanned systems, warships, jet aircraft, air defense systems, radar and electronic warfare systems, smart munitions, engines, space technology and advanced electronics.
The Turkish defense and aerospace industry made around $1.1 billion in revenue in 2002, while this figure exceeded $20 billion by 2026.
Unmanned aerial vehicles have been one of the most significant areas of transformation over the past 25 years.
Defense firm Baykar’s Bayraktar TB2 unmanned combat aerial vehicle became one of the most symbolic breakthroughs in Turkish defense, recording significant export success and hence elevating Türkiye’s global standing in unmanned aerial vehicles.
Baykar’s multirole Bayraktar Akinci unmanned combat aerial vehicle further improved Türkiye’s drone capabilities with its high payload capacity, long range, advanced sensors and heavy munitions integration.
Baykar’s Bayraktar Kizilelma carried Türkiye’s drone expertise into the jet-powered unmanned combat aerial vehicle area by combining high speed, air-to-air and air-to-ground capabilities, and the ability to operate from short-runway ships.
Turkish Aerospace Industries’ Anka and Aksungur unmanned combat aerial vehicles contributed to the development of high-altitude, long-endurance and strategic reconnaissance and surveillance capabilities of Turkish drones by integrating satellite communications, homegrown electro-optical systems, munitions and engines.
The Turkish Aerospace Industries Kaan twin-engine stealth fighter and the Hurjet jet trainer also marked major milestones in Türkiye’s manned aviation.
The Kaan was one of the most technologically ambitious programs in Turkish aviation with its low observability, advanced avionics, mission computer, radar and system integration, while the Hurjet was developed to provide a homegrown trainer platform to advance the country’s capability to develop manned military aircraft.
The Turkish Aerospace Industries T129 Atak helicopter’s product and system integration experience translated into the homegrown T625 Gokbey helicopter, marking a giant leap in rotary-wing technologies.
Beyond aerial systems, Türkiye’s national ship project, called MILGEM, laid the foundation for domestic naval platform design, ranging from corvettes to frigates. Advancements in combat management systems, sensors and weapon integration became key to ensuring independence and export capacity in naval defense.
The TF-2000 anti-air warfare guided-missile destroyer extended the Turkish Navy’s air defense capabilities to the high seas through its long-range air defense and advanced radar and weapon-sensor integration.
The unique naval engineering capabilities Turkish defense gained through the MILGEM project enabled the development of the country’s domestic submarine project, called MILDEN, to develop underwater platforms.
The partnership between the TCG Anadolu drone carrier assault ship and the Bayraktar TB3 combat drone introduced a new sea-air operations concept to the Turkish defense industry, integrating amphibious capabilities with a UAV capable of operating from short runways.
Meanwhile, Türkiye’s air defense architecture also grew with Roketsan and Aselsan’s Hisar and Siper missile systems, which contributed to a layered air defense architecture combining integrated sensors, command-and-control systems and missile systems within a single domestic architecture against various threats at low, medium and high altitudes.
Türkiye’s multilayered air defense system, Steel Dome, was developed by bringing together radars, electro-optical sensors, electronic warfare components, command-and-control infrastructure and air defense weapons of various ranges under a common network.
Roketsan’s Som, Atmaca and Kara Atmaca developed long-range precision strike capabilities for air, sea and land platforms, while the same firm’s Tayfun missile introduced the ability to engage long-range and precision land targets, boosting Türkiye’s strategic deterrence.
Turkish defense also evolved in surface vehicles, with the main battle tank Altay establishing a broad industrial ecosystem around critical technologies, such as armor, active protection, fire control and power packs, while also highlighting the strategic importance of reducing foreign dependence on engines and power packs.
Aselsan’s Koral electronic warfare system and other homegrown radar systems enhanced the effectiveness of air, land and sea platforms in modern warfare through radar detection, electronic jamming, early warning and sensor superiority.
Meanwhile, the PD170, TF6000 and KTJ engine projects brought power system developments for UAV engines, turbofans, cruise missile engines and more. These projects have been key to ensuring platform independence in defense through indigenous engine technologies.
At the same time, Turkish defense transformed its export model from direct product sales to a broader approach that includes training, maintenance and sustainment, system integration, co-production and technology cooperation.
Turkish defense products are exported to some 185 countries, and around 230 different product types are actively used worldwide.
The sector’s primary goal this year is to further independence efforts in critical technologies, establish high-volume mass production capacity and permanently expand its share in the global market.

articles.title: Lebanese PM, speaker urge clear timetable for Israeli withdrawal
articles.body:
Lina Altawell
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri discussed the military track of the negotiation framework and developments in southern Lebanon with US officials on Friday.
The Lebanese Presidency of the Council of Ministers said in a statement that Salam received US Ambassador to Beirut Michel Issa and Gen. Joseph Clearfield, head of the military coordination group for Lebanon.
The meeting addressed the military track of the negotiation framework, along with the latest developments in southern Lebanon, the presidency added.
“Salam stressed the need for Israel to stop destruction operations, expand the scope of pilot areas, and set a clear timetable for Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory,” the statement said.
In a related development, Berri met in Beirut with the US ambassador and Clearfield, his office said.
According to a statement from Berri’s office, the meeting discussed conditions in southern Lebanon and the group’s work following the start of identifying “pilot areas,” as well as the mechanism for verifying an Israeli withdrawal and deploying the Lebanese army.
“Israel has not stopped its violations and attacks on Lebanon,” Berri said, pointing to the continued destruction of villages, bulldozing of fields and agricultural areas, burning of forested areas, and targeting of heritage sites.
“The key to stability remains forcing Israel to stop its war and withdraw to the international border,” Berri added.
After the meeting, the US ambassador described the atmosphere as “positive.”
Issa told reporters that negotiations between Lebanon and Israel “will continue,” without specifying a date for the next round, according to the statement.
Discussions on expanding the “pilot areas” would follow an evaluation of the current areas, while consultations were still ongoing on countries that would participate in the monitoring mechanism, he added.
On Thursday, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said Tel Aviv would not withdraw from Lebanon unless Hezbollah is disarmed.
Speaking at a ceremony, Katz said the Israeli army currently controls 700 square kilometers of Lebanese territory, about 7% of Lebanon’s total area, according to Israel’s Channel 7.
On Wednesday, a US State Department official said a permanent Israeli military presence in southern Lebanon would contradict commitments included in the framework agreement and would not serve peace.
Israel has continued its assault on Lebanon since March 2, killing 4,335 people and injuring 12,277 others, while displacing more than 1 million, according to Lebanese authorities.
Israel occupies areas in southern Lebanon, some for decades and others since the previous war between 2023 and 2024. During the current assault, it has advanced more than 10 kilometers into Lebanese territory.

articles.title: Over 2,000 humanoid robots to compete in Beijing games
articles.body:
Beril Canakci
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
More than 2,000 humanoid robots from 16 countries are set to compete in Beijing this month, quadrupling participation from last year's inaugural event, according to state-run Xinhua news agency.
The second edition of the World Humanoid Robot Games, scheduled for Aug. 22-26, has attracted 666 teams and 2,056 robots, it said.
Participants include teams from the US, Germany, Japan and Brazil, Xinhua reported, citing Jiang Guangzhi, director of the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology.
Chinese teams account for 641 of the registered teams.
The event will feature more than 30 competitions, including running and football, as well as newly added long jump, weightlifting, tug-of-war and table tennis.
Other contests will move beyond sports, testing robots on tasks such as assembly, housekeeping, emergency response and sorting books in settings designed to resemble factories, hotels, homes and logistics facilities.
The games are designed to test how well humanoid robots can move, maintain balance and manipulate objects, according to the report.
Organizers said some competition rules could eventually contribute to technical standards for industrial use.
The event gained international attention last year when the first games featured more than 500 robots from 280 teams representing 16 countries.
China's robotics push
Humanoid robots have since become a prominent part of China's technology push.
Videos of Chinese humanoid robots performing martial arts and gymnastic routines at the country's Spring Festival Gala on Feb. 16 went viral worldwide.
A Chinese government official said in July that the country's humanoid robot output is expected to exceed 100,000 units this year as the sector moves toward wider commercial use.
The games also serve as a showcase for an industry China now dominates commercially.
Chinese manufacturers accounted for more than 97% of global humanoid robot shipments in the first half of 2026, according to California-based market research firm Smart Analytics Global.
The industry's rise has also strained ties with Washington.
The US Federal Communications Commission on July 29 restricted new foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots from receiving the authorization generally required for import, marketing or sale in the US, citing cybersecurity and national security risks.
The restrictions do not affect robots already authorized for use in the US but could limit Chinese manufacturers' access to a key prospective market as they expand overseas.

articles.title: Committee chair says threat level unchanged despite warnings of Russia’s possible attacks
articles.body:
Lithuania’s security threat level remains largely unchanged despite warnings that Russia may be considering attacks on critical infrastructure in the region using Ukrainian-origin drones, the chairman of the parliamentary Committee on National Security and Defence said Friday.
“I want to reassure the public that the information presented in this manner has caused unnecessary anxiety. The threat level remains similar,” Rimantas Sinkevičius said after a closed-door committee meeting at the Second Investigation Department, Lithuania’s military intelligence service.
Sinkevičius said intelligence agencies had already warned in June of the possibility of various types of incidents, noting that the potential threats were not limited to Lithuania but also concerned other countries in the region.
He said Lithuania was strengthening its preparedness by acquiring defensive equipment and improving coordination among state institutions. However, he added that it was impossible to be fully prepared for every possible incident.
Reports emerged last week citing Lithuanian military intelligence that Russia might be considering sabotage operations against critical infrastructure in the Baltic region using drones of Ukrainian origin, so called “false flag” operations. The intelligence did not identify specific targets or provide a timeline for any potential attacks.
Since June 18, the Lithuanian military has been assisting in the protection of key infrastructure, including the liquefied natural gas terminal in Klaipėda, the LitPol Link electricity interconnection in Alytus and the Kruonis pumped-storage hydroelectric plant.

articles.title: Mount Etna continues to erupt in Italy
articles.body:
Flights at Catania airport in Sicily remain suspended because of ongoing volcanic activity from Mount Etna. But for those already on the island, the spectacular lava flows have become a major attraction, drawing crowds of tourists to safe viewing points. Companies organising guided nighttime hikes say they have been flooded with calls from visitors hoping to see the eruption up close. Etna is Europe’s largest active volcano, and the latest activity has been unusual for its persistence and sustained ash emissions. Emily Boyle reports.

articles.title: Taliban pressured by insurgents after 5 years in power
articles.body:
Taliban pressured by insurgents after 5 years in power
August 14, 2026
Less than a month before the five-year anniversary of the Taliban retaking power in Afghanistan, the Islamist regime lost control of the Yaftal-e Payeen district capital in the northeastern province of Badakhshan. The disruption was temporary, but it nevertheless marked the first time the Taliban lost control of a district center since returning to power in August 2021.
Reports from Badakhshan also indicated internal clashes among Taliban fighters and fatal attacks on high-ranking Taliban officials.
On August 2, some two weeks after the brief loss of the district center, former Afghan army general Sami Sadat ordered his forces to launch attacks against the Taliban across the country.
"Today at 5:00 AM, I ordered all military members of the United Front to begin military operations," General Sadat said in a video message released from the US, where he has lived since the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban.
Other armed groups, including the National Resistance Front led by the son of the late commander Ahmad Shah Massoud, have been engaged in a continuous armed struggle against the Taliban since 2021. While armed insurgents have not been able to pose a major threat to the Taliban's overall grip on power, experts are questioning whether the clashes in Badakhshan could pave the way for more impactful resistance.
"In these five years, this opposition existed in two forms: political and military... As the five-year mark approaches, both forms of opposition have taken shape," former Afghan Interior Minister Mohammad Umer Daudzai told DW.
Fear of new proxy wars in Afghanistan
The Taliban have reigned with an iron fist since the collapse of the US-backed Afghan government five years ago. The Islamist regime denied basic human rights and imposed strict restrictions on women, banning them from work and education beyond the sixth grade. Women are mostly banned from public life in Afghanistan as well, and have few rights at all.
Most former government officials are in exile. While the Taliban maintain that all Afghans are free to return and lead ordinary lives, opponents counter that return is only viable if political activity is permitted.
While the regime managed to cultivate some contacts internationally, they are still viewed as illegitimate by most of the world's governments. To date, only Russia has acknowledged the Taliban as the official government of Afghanistan.
Facing pressures both within and outside of the country, the Taliban repeatedly pointed to the restoration of nationwide security as their primary claim to legitimacy. However, experts warn that their governing style could in fact enable armed rebels to challenge them in various parts of Afghanistan.
"If this policy of the Taliban continues, armed forces will emerge against them, opposition will emerge, interference from neighbors will arise, and ultimately the ground will be prepared for proxy wars," former Acting Minister of Defense Shahmohammad Miakhel told DW.
Beyond political opposition, the regional branch of the "Islamic State" (IS) remains active in Afghanistan. The group has claimed responsibility for several high-profile attacks against Taliban officials, including a January explosion at a Chinese restaurant in central Kabul that killed at least seven people, and a December 2024 suicide bombing in Kabul that killed the regime's Minister of Refugees Khalil Ur-Rahman Haqqani.
Taliban claim Pakistan supports insurgents in Afghanistan
The strongest challenge to Taliban control could originate from outside Afghanistan's borders. Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan — once considered one of the Taliban's closest allies — have been fraught with tension since 2021, erupting in full on clashes this year. According to a United Nations report from May, cross-border hostilities during the first three months of 2026 resulted in at least 372 Afghan civilian deaths and nearly 400 injuries.
"When Mr. Sami Sadat issues such an order from America to those who must fight the Taliban, he has certainly seen a green light. And remember that in Afghanistan, no group and no one can carry out any activity without the support of one or more foreign countries," former defense ministry spokesperson Mohammad Radmanish told DW.
While the Taliban publicly downplay the threat posed by rebel groups, they also allege that external support for armed resistance is rising.
"We are aware that lame ducks were invited to Pakistan [...] A large group has been invited to Islamabad who are now discussing where they can have an office and center and refuge," Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid told DW in an interview.
When pressed by DW to provide evidence for these claims, Mujahid offered no proof.
'Islamabad has used all its options'
Pakistan accuses the Taliban of providing safe havens to militants executing attacks inside Pakistani territory, particularly the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). The Taliban deny these charges, in turn accusing Pakistan of harboring hostile elements and violating Afghan sovereignty.
Qamar Cheema, an Islamabad-based security expert, told DW in February that it is Pakistan that is targeting the militant groups.
"Pakistan wants the Afghan people to understand that the Taliban are harboring terrorists. Therefore, Pakistan will continue targeting military sites associated with the Taliban, TTP and ISIS-K hideouts," Cheema said.
"Islamabad has used all its options, including regional diplomacy and direct communication, but nothing has been honored," he added. "As a neighboring Muslim country, Pakistan appears to inflict damage in an attempt to alter Taliban behavior."
Edited by: Darko Janjevic

articles.title: Chadian President Déby pardons jailed main rival and 8 opposition leaders
articles.body:
Chadian President Déby pardons jailed main rival and 8 opposition leaders
Chad’s President Mahamat Idriss Déby on Friday pardoned the jailed ex-prime minister and leader of Chad’s main opposition party Succès Masra, along with eight other party leaders. Masra had been serving a 20-year sentence, convicted of hate speech, xenophobia and inciting a massacre, in what Human Rights Watch called a politically motivated trial.
Chadian President Mahamat Idriss Déby on Friday pardoned jailed ex-prime minister and leader of the main opposition party Succès Masra and eight other opposition leaders.
Déby has led Chad since 2021 after taking charge of a military transition following the death of his father, Idriss Déby Itno, who was killed by rebels after 30 years leading the central African country.

Analysts and the opposition had said that long jail terms imposed on opposition figures showed Chad was sliding further from democratic principles under Déby.
Masra, one of the president's fiercest critics, was sentenced to 20 years in prison a year ago, convicted of hate speech, xenophobia and inciting a massacre, in what Human Rights Watch called a politically motivated trial.
The eight other party leaders all belonged to the Political Actors' Consultation Group (GCAP), the main opposition coalition, which was dissolved by the Supreme Court in April.
They were arrested while organising a demonstration banned by the authorities and jailed in May for eight years after being found guilty of inciting an insurrection.
The presidential pardon entails a "full remission of custodial sentences for the convicted", according to a decree published on the presidency's Facebook page.
With a pardon rather than an amnesty, detained opponents regain their freedom but the conviction remains: they keep their criminal record, their civil and financial penalties and they become ineligible to stand in elections.
'Democratic regression'
Hissein Abdoulaye, GCAP spokesman, hit out at what he called "democratic regression" in the country.
"Arbitrarily arresting political leaders, hauling them before the courts, convicting them on fabricated charges and pardoning them a few months later while stripping them of their civil and political rights. It is simply abject and a very serious democratic regression," he told AFP.
Ndolembai Sade Njesada, vice president of Masra's The Transformers party, said the president had "braved the obstacles and chosen to move forward in the spirit of national unity that is now coming into being".
"We hope at last to sit down around a table to move peace forward," he added.
Déby's Patriotic Salvation Movement (MPS) also welcomed the "beneficial" development which allows the political leaders to return to their families, a spokesman said.
Like other opposition figures, Masra, 42, an economist, had fled Chad after the army and police opened fire on demonstrators protesting an extension of the political transition under the Déby-led ruling junta in October 2022.
Masra returned from exile and signed a reconciliation deal with Déby before being named prime minister five months ahead of the 2024 presidential election.
Déby was elected head of state with just over 60 percent of the vote, in a contested ballot boycotted by a majority of opposition parties.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Masra faced off against Déby in that vote, coming second with nearly a fifth of the vote, but claimed victory.
He was arrested in May 2025 and sentenced three months later to 20 years in prison on charges of inciting inter-communal violence in Mandakao, southwestern Chad, where 42 people were killed, most of them women and children.
Masra, originally from Chad's south, comes from the Ngambaye ethnic group and enjoys wide popularity among the predominantly Christian and animist populations of the south.
Those groups feel marginalised by the largely Muslim regime in the capital N'Djamena.
In October, parliament passed by a landslide a constitutional revision allowing the president unlimited seven-year terms.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: 'Unprecedented transformation': Rajnath hails fourfold rise in defence production in message to soldiers
articles.body:
'Unprecedented transformation': Rajnath hails fourfold rise in defence production in message to soldiers
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 14, 2026, 19:17 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Modernisation of the defence forces, driven by a self-reliant and future-ready defence sector is the first and foremost priority of government, Rajnath Singh told the Armed Forces on the eve of 80th Independence Day.
NEW DELHI: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Friday said India's defence sector had undergone an “unprecedented transformation” over the past 12 years, with domestic defence production rising nearly fourfold to a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26.In his message to soldiers on the eve of Independence Day, Rajnath said India had reduced its dependence on defence imports while strengthening indigenous manufacturing under the Aatmanirbhar Bharat and Make in India initiatives.
""You all know that under the leadership of the Hon'ble Prime Minister, our government has always accorded the highest priority to self-reliance in the defence sector. Over the past 12 years, you have witnessed unprecedented transformation in the defence sector through Aatmanirbhar Bharat and Make in India," he said.“Our domestic defence production, which stood at around Rs 46,000 crore in 2014, reached a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in FY 2025-26. This means that over the past decade, our domestic defence production has increased nearly fourfold. This is proof of the structural changes that have taken place over the past decade," the defence minister added.
The union minister further highlighted recent tests and developments in indigenous defence technology, including the MIRV-equipped Advanced Agni missile, Rudram-II air-to-surface missile, Long Range Land Attack Cruise Missile and Pinaka Long Range Guided Rocket.
“We have also made major advances in hypersonic technology. The successful demonstration of Solid Fuel Ducted Ramjet technology is equally significant,” he said.He also said the first successful test of the indigenous Kusha Long Range Surface-to-Air Missile had strengthened India's air-defence capabilities.
91% indegenisation in Army ammunitions
As Rajnath hailed the growth in defence sector, the ministry of defence said India's defence production reached a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26, nearly four times the level of 2014. The government said defence exports have grown 56-fold, from Rs 686 crore in 2013-14 to Rs 38,424 crore in 2025-26, with Indian defence products now reaching more than 80 countries.The defence budget has increased 3.1-fold, from Rs 2.53 lakh crore in 2013-14 to Rs 7.85 lakh crore in 2026-27, while capital expenditure has risen 2.3-fold to Rs 2.19 lakh crore. Defence R&D spending has more than doubled to Rs 29,100 crore in 2026-27 from Rs 13,716 crore in 2014-15.
The ministry said the Indian Army has achieved roughly 91% self-sufficiency in ammunition, having indigenised 159 of 175 ammunition variants.The government is targeting Rs 3 lakh crore in annual defence production and Rs 50,000 crore in defence exports by 2029.
