articles.title: Romania shuts down its only nuclear power plant
articles.body:
Romania shuts down its only nuclear power plant
The only nuclear power plant in Romania has been completely shut down due to record-low Danube River levels, state-owned energy company Nuclearelectrica announced on Thursday.
River water is essential for cooling many European nuclear plants, making low levels an increasing constraint on power generation. The severe heatwave and drought across Europe have pushed the Danube and Rhine, two of the region’s most vital rivers, to historic lows, disrupting stable electricity generation in several countries while hampering industrial output and major trade routes.
Cernavoda, which accounts for about 20% of Romania’s power output, has two reactors, each with a capacity of 706 MW. In late July, Nuclearelectrica shut down one of them as water levels in the drought-hit river fell dramatically.
Last week, Romanian authorities sank four rock-filled barges near the Danube’s Bala Canal in an unprecedented effort to redirect water toward the Cernavoda plant after the military blasted a channel through the riverbed. Water levels, however, ultimately fell below the threshold needed to keep the reactor operating, forcing the management to disconnect it from the power grid.
At the same time, Bucharest declared a state of energy emergency for August, urging businesses and households to voluntarily reduce consumption during peak evening hours. The government has prepared a system to cut power for industrial consumers in stages and with prior notice if needed.
The Cernavoda shutdown has also raised concerns in neighboring Moldova, which is facing low water levels on the Dniester and relies on Romanian power to cover up to 60% of its electricity shortfall.
The energy strain has been felt across the region, with Hungary’s Paks nuclear plant forced to sharply cut output as the Danube fell to record lows.
France has also reduced nuclear generation amid high river temperatures and low water levels. Earlier this week, French state-run energy group EDF said a massive swarm of jellyfish had forced the operator to shut down three reactors at Gravelines, one of the largest nuclear power plants in the country.
The severe drought has hit hydropower generation in Italy, while Norway’s reservoirs have fallen to their lowest level in three decades.
Analysts warn the reactor cuts and outages could increase electricity import dependence among the bloc’s most vulnerable countries and drive up power prices across the EU. The disruption could further deepen the bloc’s energy crunch, which began with the loss of cheap Russian gas following Ukraine-related sanctions on Moscow. The strain has worsened this year amid the US war on Iran and the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key global energy shipping route.

articles.title: Mulla Sadra house in Qom to become hub for astronomy and philosophy tourism
articles.body:
Mulla Sadra house in Qom to become hub for astronomy and philosophy tourism
TEHRAN – Local officials plan to turn the historic house of philosopher Mulla Sadra in Kahak, Qom province, into a hub for astronomy and philosophy tourism, under a cooperation agreement aimed at promoting the city’s cultural attractions and strengthening its tourism economy.
Behnam Ahmadi-Farsani, director general of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts of Qom province, announced the plan on Wednesday, following the signing of a memorandum of understanding among the provincial department, Kahak governorate and Kahak municipality.
The agreement is intended to promote Mulla Sadra house and develop the value chain of religious, literary and philosophical tourism in the city, according to the provincial cultural heritage department, Miras Aria reported.
Under the agreement, the historic house and its associated structures will be used more extensively for astronomy-related tourism and cultural and artistic events.
Ahmadi-Farsani said astronomy-related equipment has been installed at the centuries-old house and that the property will be made available to a knowledge-based company as a venue for astronomy and philosophy tourism events.
The official added that the initiative would also seek to connect tourism, handicrafts and cultural events. Plans include establishing a handicrafts bazaar at the historic house and organizing philosophical tourism events focusing on Mulla Sadra and his intellectual legacy.
The events will be incorporated into Qom province’s tourism calendar, which has been approved by the provincial department’s technical council, he said.
“The aim is to introduce the capacities of Kahak to pilgrims and tourism enthusiasts,” Ahmadi-Farsani said, adding that the province hoped to better promote Kahak’s cultural heritage, tourism and handicrafts potential.
Located in Kahak, about 30 kilometers from Qom, the provincial capital, the house is associated with Sadr al-Din Muhammad Shirazi, better known as Mulla Sadra, who lived in Kahak during a period of withdrawal from public life. Sources describing the monument identify it as a Safavid-era building constructed from adobe, mud mortar and timber. Its plan follows a cross-shaped layout, with a central domed space and surrounding rooms.
The house is an Iranian national heritage property registered under No. 1821. Its architecture includes a domed roof and simple plasterwork, while historical descriptions of the building note the use of raw mud brick, clay mortar and wooden structural elements.
The proposed tourism program would add a contemporary cultural and educational function to the historic property while retaining its role as a monument associated with one of Iran’s most influential philosophers.
Mulla Sadra was born in Shiraz around 1571–1572 and died in Basra around 1635–1640, although scholarly sources differ on the exact year of his death. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy gives his dates as approximately 1571–1636 and describes him as one of the most significant Islamic philosophers after Avicenna.
He developed al-hikmah al-muta‘aliyah, commonly translated as the “Transcendent Theosophy” or “Transcendent Wisdom,” a philosophical approach that brought together elements of Islamic philosophy, theology and mysticism. His work drew on earlier traditions including Avicennian philosophy, Illuminationism and Islamic mystical thought.
AM

articles.title: Beyond the headlines: Daniel Malikyar on capturing the unseen beauty of Afghanistan
articles.body:
Beyond the headlines: Daniel Malikyar on capturing the unseen beauty of Afghanistan
Photographer Daniel Malikyar is using his project titled Afghanistan to counter the way the country is typically seen through headlines of war, conflict and the Taliban's takeover.
For decades, the world's image of Afghanistan has been shaped almost exclusively by conflict, crisis and the headlines. In his ambitious new book, Afghanistan, photographer Daniel Malikyar hopes to change that.
The son of Afghan refugees who grew up in the United States, Malikyar travelled independently across the country before the Taliban's return to power, five years ago on 15 August 2021. He documented remote communities, everyday rituals and landscapes rarely seen by international audiences.
As he told Euronews Culture, his goal was simple: "When people think of Afghanistan, they just think of the headlines. But there's so much beyond that."
Malikyar's images celebrate the country's beauty, culture and resilience - from balloon sellers drifting through the streets of Kabul at sunrise, children flying kites above the city's rooftops, to Kyrgyz families herding yaks in the Pamir Mountains and intimate portraits of women and elders in some of Afghanistan's most remote regions.
Ahead of the book's publication, Euronews Culture spoke to Malikyar about the journey of reconnecting with his ancestral homeland and the stories behind some of his most striking images from the series.
Euronews Culture: For people who may not know your work, could you start by telling us about your relationship with Afghanistan and how this project first began?
Daniel Malikyar: Definitely. My family is originally from Afghanistan, and my parents immigrated to the United States in 1979, just before the Soviet invasion. Growing up, I had this dual experience where, at home, I was always shown and got to experience the beauty of our culture through the food, the music, and all of the different stories that my family would tell me about our homeland.
But then, when I'd step outside, the experience was entirely different. It was driven by the narratives you saw in the headlines. I always had this longing to bridge that gap and gain a deeper understanding of both where I come from and myself. It felt like a piece of me was missing.
Subconsciously, the stories my parents told me about their childhood - flying kites, their gardens, and all these beautiful little moments they experienced - I never really got to see what those looked like because there wasn't any documentation of them. The only visuals I saw were largely the things you saw on the news.
I believe this project was my way of trying to gain a deeper understanding of my roots and almost search for and document the missing pieces of those stories. A lot of these photographs were subconsciously inspired by those conversations around the dinner table when I was a kid. Seeing those moments unfold in front of me felt like a full-circle, homecoming experience.
How has making this project changed your own relationship with your Afghan identity? And what has it meant for your family to see these photographs?
I think this project gave my family a chance to reconnect with our homeland and with places they themselves had never been able to visit as children. Afghanistan is still developing, and after decades of conflict, travelling through certain regions hasn't always been easy.
They had heard stories about places like Nuristan - a province that almost felt mythical, with its lush forests and rivers. Seeing those places through my photographs, along with so many others across the country, was incredibly meaningful. I could see their faces light up when they saw everyday life. Sharing the photographs with my grandmother and watching the documentary come together with my parents was one of the most gratifying and full-circle moments of the entire project.
Personally, that sense of something missing has disappeared. The gap has been bridged. I feel more whole, and the way I see both Afghanistan and myself has shifted in a really positive way. Being able to relive those experiences through the photographs, the book, and the documentary series has been the most fulfilling experience of my life so far.
One of your biggest inspirations was your grandfather, Omar, who documented your family through photographs and home videos. What has stayed with you from that archive, and how has it influenced your own work?
As a kid, my grandfather Omar was somebody I really looked up to and had a very close relationship with. I only got to see him once a year because he lived in Virginia while I grew up in Los Angeles. He documented those visits, and I got to relive them through his perspective - through the tapes he sent us and the developed film. That subconsciously inspired me to pick up a camera and document the world around me.
This project is something I know he's looking down on, and it was deeply inspired by what he instilled in me simply by being himself.
One thing I love about these photographs is how intimate they feel. How do you build that trust with people you've often only just met?
For me, anywhere in the world, whether I'm photographing a fleeting encounter or someone who becomes a lifelong friend, everything is built on trust. And trust has to be earned.
A lot of the time I don't even take my camera out until I've sat with people, shared tea, explained my intentions, and told them that I'm Afghan, that I speak the language, and that I'm there as someone connected to them rather than as an outsider. That allows people to simply be themselves. There's no agenda, no posing. Many of these photographs were taken in remote villages where people were simply going about their day. I think that honesty comes through in both the big and the small details.
Often, when you see photographs from Afghanistan or other remote places, people can look uncertain about why they're being photographed. That wasn't the case here.
I photographed children at eye level because I wanted to meet them exactly where they were, rather than looking down at them. Through those decisions and intentions, I wanted to portray Afghan people with dignity, and I think that comes across throughout the project.
You've photographed people all over the world. What made photographing Afghanistan different from anywhere else?
Afghanistan is a country made up of many different ethnic backgrounds and thousands of years of history and culture. Today it's increasingly difficult to discover places and stories that genuinely feel unseen because of how connected the world has become through technology and globalization.
Afghanistan is one of the few places where there are still so many untold human stories and communities that deserve to be seen. It was an incredible privilege to visit communities that, in many cases, had never even seen a camera before, and to share the beauty of their traditions, culture, and everyday lives through this project.
Could we talk through a few of the photographs? I love the image of the two cyclists with the huge bunch of balloons trailing behind them. What's the story behind that shot?
That photograph is called Omid, which translates to "hope" in English. It's also my little brother's name.
The photograph was entirely serendipitous, as was much of this body of work. I was in a taxi very early in the morning, leaving Kabul on my way to a rural village to photograph a fashion subculture I'd discovered. The sun had just risen and, as we were leaving the city, I noticed these massive globs of colour dancing in the distance. It almost felt surreal, and I immediately knew they were balloon sellers.
The reason I named the piece Omid is because I believe balloon sellers spread hope. They make children happy. Balloons are nostalgic, and they were simply on their way to work that morning. You see them scattered throughout the city from time to time, but it's very rare to see them carrying all of their balloons because they gradually sell them throughout the day. I was very fortunate to capture that brief moment.
Oftentimes, I feel like the most special photographs are presented to you rather than taken. These beautiful moments appear, and if you're ready to witness and document them, they're gone just as quickly. It's one of my favourite images from the project because it represents exactly what I was hoping to witness while travelling through Afghanistan.
I'd also love to ask about the photograph of the young girl milking a yak. How did that come about?
That photograph of this beautiful Kyrgyz girl milking a yak was taken in the Pamir Mountains of Afghanistan, one of the highest inhabited regions in the world at around 4,000 metres above sea level.
The Kyrgyz people there are nomadic, travelling three or four times a year in search of the best grazing land for their cattle. They've preserved a way of life that stretches back generations and is very different from what most of us experience day to day.
Milking the yaks is a daily ritual, carried out every morning and evening. Much of their livelihood revolves around them. The milk is used to make yoghurt and qurut, a traditional food that's commonly eaten throughout the region and across Afghanistan.
I was very fortunate to document this moment of Shargha milking the yak that afternoon before the animals were tied down for the evening.
In what formats are you presenting this project?
Rather than telling the story through a single medium, I've created a storytelling blueprint that brings together several different formats. The project includes a coffee table book, a documentary series - where each episode corresponds with a chapter in the book - and a fine art exhibition featuring limited-edition framed photographs, projected films from the project, and handcrafted ancient artefacts from Afghanistan to create a fully immersive experience.
I wanted people to truly feel what it was like to step into my world while creating this project, which is why I chose to tell the story through multiple forms of storytelling.
A percentage of all proceeds will also go towards developing a new generation of visual storytellers within Afghanistan, so Afghans can continue telling their own stories through their own eyes.

articles.title: How EU research can help respond to heatwaves
articles.body:
This summer, we are facing unprecedented droughts and wildfires leading to casualties and devastation across the continent. While the immediate focus is on responding to the emergencies with firefighting helicopters, electric fans and shallow water vessels, EU-funded research and innovation is also essential for addressing the longer-term challenge of a changing climate. Initiatives such as the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change and research projects develop the knowledge and solutions needed to strengthen society’s resilience in the years and decades ahead.
This article illustrates in a few examples how Horizon Europe helps tackling extreme summer events.
Improving forecasting and early warning at the local level
Advances in climate science make it possible to forecast extreme events such as heatwaves earlier and with greater accuracy. This allows authorities to issue warnings, activate health services, and advise the public before temperatures peak to dangerous levels.
Among other objectives, the HealthRiskADAPT project helps cities and regions prepare for higher temperatures by mapping heat at a very local level, linking it to health risks in terms of illnesses and mortality, and providing early warning and planning tools.
The MountResilience project has created a platform that brings together observational tools and an AI prediction algorithm for early warnings against floods, forest fires, and other types of extreme weather in Bulgaria. Informed by the tool’s output, project partners installed forest fire detection equipment (e.g. a thermal vision camera) that detects heat before smoke becomes visible, facilitating an early reaction.
The AURORA project tackles extreme‑heat risks in the European Union’s Boreal Region by building high‑resolution Urban Heat Island models and embedding them in a climate‑health decision‑support system. In the Tampere, Finland, a machine‑learning model produces detailed, 1km maps of urban heat island, which are fed into a heat‑stroke risk‑assessment tool that combines hazard, exposure and vulnerability data to pinpoint the neighbourhoods most at risk.
Supporting cities and local authorities in designing tailored climate adaptation plans
EU-funded research on climate adaptation and resilience contributes to identifying which areas and population groups are most at risk, utilising these insights to develop effective adaptation plans and measures together with the public.
The work of Impetus4Change and MULTICLIMACT supports cities and local authorities in developing and implementing their own climate adaptation pathways. The projects are testing innovative solutions in Barcelona, Paris and Prague to reduce heat stress and improve urban resilience, e.g. by informing urban planning and house retrofitting policies.
Similarly, the NEVERMORE project assists regional authorities with tools to assess climate risks and plan adaptation strategies, with demonstrations in climate change hotspots. Its case study in Murcia focuses on drought and water scarcity, while its work in Sitia examines combined impacts of heat and drought.
The MIRACA project focuses on protecting critical infrastructure from climate impacts. Its case study in Spain examines how transport networks can adapt to the combined effects of heatwaves, droughts, and wildfires, ensuring continuity and safety under extreme conditions. Such cross-sectoral approaches are essential for maintaining resilience in interconnected systems that are increasingly exposed to climate stress.
The CARMINE project is deepening the knowledge of urban heat dynamics, including research on nocturnal heat patterns using crowd-sourced weather data. Its case studies in Athens and Barcelona provide valuable insights into how heat accumulates and persists in urban environments, informing more effective mitigation strategies.
Fighting heat and wildfires through conserving or restoring ecosystems and nature based solutions
Climate action-related research is informing and showing how ecosystems and nature-based adaptation can have a lasting effect in reducing impacts of extreme heat and forest fires.
The Trees4Adapt project explores post-fire recovery in Portugal, demonstrating how restoring forest ecosystems can enhance resilience to future heat and wildfire events while contributing to long-term climate adaptation.
The projects DRYAD, MED-IREN and DesirMED are testing and implementing nature-based solutions designed to reduce the combined risks of droughts and wildfires, which are often intensified during heatwaves. Measures such as reforestation and soil restoration help retain moisture and regulate local temperatures.
Identifying and testing adaptation measures that tackle the adverse effects of heatwaves on health
As heatwaves are becoming a public health risk, climate adaptation research and innovation projects are developing and implementing measures that protect people’s health and wellbeing from extreme heat.
ISMED-CLIM helps Mediterranean countries protect citizens from climate-related health risks, with a strong focus on extreme heat, by testing practical tools such as early warning systems, personalised advice and healthcare emergency plans for vulnerable groups based on clinical trials. For example, in Greece and Spain it supports outdoor workers with heat alerts and recommendations to reduce heat stress, while in Cyprus and Italy it tests measures to help pregnant women lower heat exposure and improve sleep.
In the mountainous Tirol region, the MOUNTADAPT project is looking at how heatwaves are affecting people’s health and how to help local health systems better prepare. Researchers are using data and artificial intelligence to understand how extreme heat can contribute to mental health problems and cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, and to estimate how these health risks could change as the climate warms. This will deliver the evidence that can help mountain health systems adapt to more frequent and intense heat.
Last year, the EU invested a further EUR 30 million in projects helping cities adapt to extreme heat and protect people’s health and wellbeing, placing local authorities and vulnerable residents at the centre. Three new projects CLIMACARE, EUROASIS and PROTECT will soon be putting into practice another set of innovative ideas, showing not only what works to cool our cities, but also how these measures can be scaled up and financed allowing more municipalities across Europe to benefit.
As these examples show, research and innovation in the EU is equipping communities across Europe with the knowledge, tools and effective solutions to adapt to the increasing occurrence of heatwaves, as part of the rapidly changing climate.

articles.title: $168,000 worth of handicrafts sold along Arbaeen pilgrimage routes
articles.body:
$168,000 worth of handicrafts sold along Arbaeen pilgrimage routes
TEHRAN - Handicrafts worth 31 billion tomans, equivalent to about $168,000 at the prevailing open-market exchange rate, were sold at stalls set up along the Arbaeen pilgrimage routes in six Iranian provinces, an official said.
Farzad Ojani, director general of marketing and commercialization at the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts’ Deputy for Handicrafts and Traditional Arts, said 453 stalls were established at 37 strategic locations in Khuzestan, Kermanshah, West Azarbaijan, Kordestan, Ilam and Hamadan provinces.
A variety of traditional handicrafts, including kilims, gemstone cutting, traditional embroidery, fine woodwork, wooden products, Ehrami weaving, mat weaving, pottery and ceramics, were displayed at the stalls, Ojani said.
The official added that products were selected based on factors including consumer preferences, ease of transportation and resistance to damage, in an effort to improve their sales potential.
Ojani estimated that around two million pilgrims visited the stalls, particularly visitors from Pakistan, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Türkiye and Iraq.
He said the presence of pilgrims from different countries could help Iranian handicraft producers and officials identify consumer preferences in those markets and explore export opportunities.
Arbaeen, observed 40 days after Ashura, commemorates the martyrdom of Imam Hussein (A.S.), the third Imam of Shia Muslims and grandson of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH). Millions of pilgrims travel to Karbala each year for the religious gathering, one of the world’s largest.
The US dollar was trading at around 185,000 tomans on Tehran’s open market at the time of writing.
AM

Nordic–Baltic hydrogen corridor project still in early stages
At the beginning of this year, the government launched a special national planning process to identify a suitable route in Estonia for hydrogen pipelines as part of a six‑country project. A consultant is still being sought; once selected, the planning and location assessment can begin.
According to Monika Korolkov, project manager for the national special plan at the Ministry of Economic Affairs, the project is extensive but important, and planning requires thorough studies, analyses and close cooperation with various stakeholders. She added that the project involves 24 municipalities, all of whom must be consulted during the planning process.
"We hope that if the procedure proceeds as planned, we can continue preparing the project according to the intended schedule," Korolkov said. The aim is to outline potential routes by next year so the ministry can present them to landowners.
There is also an idea on the table to build the corridor along the bottom of the Baltic Sea, creating a direct connection between Finland and Germany. Korolkov said work is being done to ensure the route also passes through Estonia.
"If the route comes over land, Estonia can serve as a link between the Nordic and Central European energy networks," Korolkov said. She added that this would strengthen energy security, bring new investments to Estonia and create conditions for developing a hydrogen economy. "If Finland decides it is more beneficial to build the route along the seabed, we will miss out on a great deal," she noted.
Siim Iimre, head of research and development at Elering, said the preferred approach is to use existing gas and electricity infrastructure to minimize the amount of new land needed.
"It is certainly a challenge that Estonia has dispersed settlement and many scenic areas and nature reserves," Iimre said. Because of this, it is difficult to find a corridor that would have minimal environmental impact or cause minimal disturbance.
Both Korolkov and Iimre stressed that building a hydrogen pipeline does not pose a danger to people or the environment. Iimre added that the main impact of an underground pipeline occurs only during construction. "As with building a natural‑gas pipeline, construction machinery will move around and excavation work will take place," he explained.
According to Elering, the project's progress depends both on the successful completion of Estonia's special planning process and on other countries staying on schedule.
Iimre said an investment decision could be made in early 2030, at which point it will be decided whether the infrastructure will be built. If approved, it could be completed by 2035.
He added that the project is necessary because around 80 companies have already expressed interest in producing or using hydrogen.
This week, the tender period for cooperation on the hydrogen corridor's national special plan concluded. The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications will now review the bids, and a contract with the successful bidder will be signed no later than October.
--
Editor: Merilin Leetna, Argo Ideon

articles.title: France urges Israel to act against illegal settlers as Italy monitors Qusra siege
articles.body:
France has called on Israel to arrest and prosecute rogue illegal settlers blockading Palestinian homes at Qusra in the occupied West Bank and to protect the civilian population, as Italy was also closely monitoring the situation, with at least five Italians reported to be under the settler siege.
"France condemns in the strongest possible terms the occupation of several Palestinian homes in the village of Qusra in the West Bank by Israeli settlers, as well as the acts of violence committed against Palestinian civilians," the French foreign ministry said on Friday.
"It calls on the Israeli authorities to arrest and bring to justice those responsible for these acts."
Italy is closely monitoring the situation in Qusra, which has been under siege by Israeli illegal settlers for five consecutive days, while five Italians were also reported to be under siege, ANSA news agency reported.
The Italian foreign ministry confirmed that five Italian nationals were also in Qusra.
The five Italians, four women and one man, were reportedly inside isolated homes.
Illegal Israeli settlers at Qusra near Nablus began blockading Palestinian homes on Sunday and have defied attempts to remove them, with residents saying they have been cut off from food and other supplies.
The siege has also drawn unusually sharp criticism from Israel’s ally the US.
France, on its part, stressed that acts of violence committed by settlers kept increasing in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.
"France reiterates its condemnation of Israel's settlement policy, which threatens the two-state solution and fuels tensions on the ground," the foreign ministry said.
The ministry is in coordination with its embassy in Tel Aviv as well as its crisis unit.
Attacks by Israeli illegal settlers against Palestinians and their property have intensified across the occupied West Bank since Israel’s Gaza genocide, prompting Palestinian and international warnings over the growing seizure of land and homes and the displacement of residents.

articles.title: David Charles (1947-2026)
articles.body:
David Charles (1947-2026)
David Charles, professor emeritus of philosophy at Yale University, has died.
Professor Charles was well-known for his work in ancient philosophy, and especially on Aristotle. He is the author of The Undivided Self (2021), Aristotle on Meaning and Essence (2000), Aristotle’s Philosophy of Action (1984), among other works, which you can learn more about here.
Professor Charles joined the faculty at Yale in 2014. Before that, he was at the University of Oxford. After retiring from Yale he was a visiting professor at Stanford University. He earned his D.Phil. from Oxford.
He died on August 12th.
(via Victor Caston)

articles.title: Le Conseil constitutionnel censure la loi interdisant les réseaux sociaux aux mineurs
articles.body:
Emmanuel Macron s'adresse à la presse à l'issue d'une visite au Centre Opérationnel Départemental d'Incendie et de Secours (CODIS) de Bordeaux le 27 juillet 2026. | Pool photo par Kenzo Tribouillard via AFP/Getty Images
PARIS — Le Conseil constitutionnel a rendu ce vendredi sa décision sur la loi interdisant les réseaux sociaux aux mineurs et a annoncé censurer son article 1er, qui acte ladite interdiction pour les moins de 15 ans.
De fait, la décision rend caduque le principal objet de cette loi portée depuis plusieurs années par le président de la République.
Dans sa décision, les Sages estiment en effet que cet article, en instituant une interdiction "de portée générale" des réseaux sociaux aux moins de 15 ans, porte “une atteinte disproportionnée à la liberté d’expression et de communication” qui n’est pas “adaptée, nécessaire et proportionnée à l’objectif poursuivi” : celui de protéger les mineurs en ligne.
Advertisement
“L’interdiction instituée par la loi est susceptible de s’appliquer à des services de communication en ligne dont les risques pour la santé et la sécurité des mineurs ne sont pas établis”, estime encore le Conseil constitutionnel, insistant sur l’imprécision autour du champ d’application de l’article.
Le risque avait été soulevé au moment de l’examen du texte au Sénat, certains élus de la Chambre haute ayant tenté d’imposer l’établissement d’une “liste noire” qui définirait plus précisément les plateformes concernées par cette limitation d’accès aux mois de 15 ans – et éviterait ainsi le risque de censure par le Conseil constitutionnel.
Un élément du texte retiré au moment de son examen en Commission mixte paritaire pour assurer sa conformité avec le droit européen.
Le Conseil constitutionnel estime par ailleurs que le texte ne définit pas les garanties légales propres à assurer le droit au respect de la vie privée des utilisateurs qui seront contraints de faire vérifier leur âge par les plateformes pour prouver leur majorité.
“Le gouvernement n’a pas assez écouté le Sénat et le risque d’inconstitutionnalité que nous pointions depuis des mois. Désormais, le risque, c’est que le texte soit vidé de sa substance”, a réagi, sur ce point, la rapporteure du texte au Sénat, Catherine Morin-Desailly, auprès de POLITICO.
Un constat partagé par le député socialiste Arthur Delaporte, à l’origine de l’une des saisines du Conseil constitutionnel. L'autre émanait du groupe de la France Insoumise (LFI).
Advertisement
“Dans notre recours, nous dénoncions un dispositif disproportionné passant à côté de son objectif”, a-t-il commenté sur X. “L’obstination présidentielle a été mauvaise conseillère”.
Le président du groupe EPR, Gabriel Attal, a déclaré sur X prendre acte de la décision de la juridiction concernant ce texte porté par son groupe : “Avec Laure Miller et les députés Ensemble nous poursuivons le travail pour atteindre notre seul objectif : protéger nos enfants et notre jeunesse”, a-t-il promis.
“Le Président de la République a chargé le Premier ministre de travailler, dans les meilleurs délais, à une rédaction juridiquement robuste tenant compte de la décision du Conseil constitutionnel ainsi que du cadre européen”, a assuré de son côté l’Elysée dans un communiqué publié peu après. Et de poursuivre : “la détermination du Président de la République à faire aboutir cette réforme d’ici au printemps 2027 demeure totale”.
Cet article a été mis à jour pour ajouter les réactions à la décision du Conseil constitutionnel.

articles.title: Ukraine has updated the rules for portfolio-based state guarantees for small businesses
articles.body:
Ukraine has updated the rules for portfolio-based state guarantees for small businesses
Kyiv • UNN
The Cabinet of Ministers has updated the terms of state guarantees for small and medium-sized businesses. The changes increase borrowers’ responsibility and clarify mechanisms for the return of funds.
The Cabinet of Ministers has updated the rules for providing state guarantees on a portfolio basis for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. This was reported by UNN, citing the Ministry of Finance of Ukraine
The changes are intended to make lending more reliable for banks and businesses, as well as strengthen the protection of state budget funds.
Details
As reported by the Ministry of Finance, the ministry analyzed the operation of the state guarantee program from 2020–2025 and, based on the results, revised a number of its terms.
In particular, the requirements for loans and the criteria that a loan agreement must meet when it is first included in a portfolio secured by a state guarantee have been updated.
Ukraine will also introduce additional liability for borrowers. If a guarantee event occurred under an entrepreneur's previous loan and the state fulfilled its obligations under the guarantee, the borrower will temporarily lose the right to receive new state guarantees.
In addition, the government detailed the algorithms for banks operating under the 50/70 and 80/80 risk-sharing programs and simplified the list of required documents.
Some changes concern the return of funds to the state budget. In particular, government officials defined a mechanism for conducting settlements in cases where a bank collects a debt from a borrower or restructures it.
What the program provides
State guarantees on a portfolio basis enable micro, small and medium-sized enterprises to obtain bank loans without having to fully secure them with collateral.
Under the program, the state may guarantee up to 80% of a loan. This mechanism is intended to facilitate businesses' access to financing, while part of the credit risk remains with the banks issuing the loans.
The Ministry of Finance expects that the updated rules will improve the operation of the program, reduce risks to the state budget, and make the lending mechanism more predictable for banks and entrepreneurs.

articles.title: Iran says it downed US-made MQ-9 drone over southern Hormozgan province
articles.body:
Rania Abushamala
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
Iran said Friday that its forces had intercepted and destroyed a US-made MQ-9 drone over the southern province of Hormozgan.
“An MQ-9 drone was intercepted and shot down over Iran’s Hormozgan Province by the IRGC’s new advanced air defense system,” state broadcaster Press TV reported.
Citing three officials, The Washington Post reported Thursday that the US military has lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones, or roughly 25% of its fleet, during its war with Iran.
The losses involve an aircraft used for surveillance and targeted strikes that can cost between $30 million and $50 million depending on its equipment, according to the report.
The newspaper said the potential cost of the lost Reapers exceeds $1.3 billion.
The drones have been heavily used around the Strait of Hormuz but are "relatively easy targets" for Iran and its proxies because they fly slowly and often at low altitudes, it said.
Hormozgan province overlooks the Strait of Hormuz and includes the port city of Bandar Abbas.
The US and Iran agreed to a Pakistan-brokered ceasefire in April and later signed a deal on June 17, launching negotiations toward a final agreement. But the talks later stalled over disagreements on security guarantees and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategic routes for global energy supplies and trade.
On July 8-24, the US and Iran exchanged more military strikes, with Washington launching attacks on targets inside Iran. Tehran responded by striking what it described as US military facilities and equipment in several Arab countries, including Jordan, Bahrain, and Kuwait.

Pakistan on Friday urged the US to implement the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in letter and spirit to end the ongoing tension in the Middle East.
During a meeting with US Charge d’Affaires Natalie A. Baker in Islamabad, Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar told her that full implementation of the MoU is the “only way forward” for addressing regional issues through dialogue and diplomacy, according to a Foreign Ministry statement.

Dar also held talks with British High Commissioner to Pakistan Jane Marriott, discussing bilateral relations, high-level contacts and regional and international developments.
He stressed that the MoU should be implemented fully and reaffirmed Pakistan’s position that dialogue and diplomacy remain the only viable means of resolving outstanding issues.
The US and Iran agreed to a Pakistan-brokered ceasefire in April and later signed a memorandum of understanding on June 17, launching negotiations toward a final agreement.
However, the talks later stalled over disagreements on security guarantees and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategic routes for global energy supplies and trade.
Between July 8 and July 24, the US and Iran exchanged military strikes, with Washington launching attacks on targets inside Iran and Tehran responding by striking what it described as US military facilities and equipment in several Arab countries, including Jordan, Bahrain and Kuwait.

articles.title: Ukraine’s grain exports have collapsed due to the situation in the Black Sea: what happened to the maritime corridor
articles.body:
Ukraine’s grain exports have collapsed due to the situation in the Black Sea: what happened to the maritime corridor
Kyiv • UNN
Due to Russian strikes on ports and vessels, Ukraine’s grain exports fell to 30% of the required volume at the beginning of August. Minister Vysotskyi said that without restoring the operation of the Black Sea ports, exports would not exceed 50%.
Due to Russian attacks on port infrastructure and civilian vessels, Ukrainian grain exports came under threat in early August. Minister of Agrarian Policy Taras Vysotskyi said this during a briefing in Kyiv on August 14, UNN reports.
Details
Between August 1 and 12, Ukraine exported approximately 590,000 tonnes of grain, which represents about 30% of the required volume.
There are opportunities to partially increase exports, but even so, without the resumption of operations at the Black Sea ports, they will amount to up to 50% of the required level
The decline in exports occurred amid the de facto temporary suspension of commercial vessels' entry into Ukrainian seaports due to an intensification of Russian attacks.
According to the Ministry for Communities, Territories and Infrastructure Development of Ukraine, at the end of July, the latest massive attacks by the russian federation on civilian port infrastructure, commercial vessels and crews effectively led to a temporary suspension of vessels' entry into Ukrainian ports. At the same time, no official decision to close the Ukrainian Maritime Corridor was announced, and the ports continued operating.
In July 2026 alone, russia carried out 67 attacks on Ukrainian seaport facilities. In addition, 35 attacks on civilian vessels directly in the ports and another 22 attacks on vessels in the Ukrainian Maritime Corridor were recorded.
The attacks continued in August. According to the relevant ministry, in the first days of the month russia attacked seaport facilities five times, civilian vessels in the ports three times, and vessels in the maritime corridor twice.
The ministry emphasized that the Russian strikes are aimed, in particular, at disrupting the operation of Ukrainian ports, intimidating international shipowners, and undermining the safety of civilian shipping.
Seaports handled about 90% of agricultural exports
The situation with maritime connections is critically important for Ukraine's agricultural sector, since the ports of Greater Odesa handled about 90% of Ukraine's agricultural exports. Ukrainian food products were supplied through them to more than 55 countries worldwide.
From the start of operations of the Ukrainian Maritime Corridor in September 2023 through the end of July 2026, approximately 209.3 million tonnes of cargo were transported through it. Of this, 124.1 million tonnes consisted of grain. During this period, more than 8,200 vessels used the corridor.
Ukraine's dependence on the ports of Greater Odesa is also demonstrated by cargo turnover figures. From the beginning of 2026 through the end of July, Ukrainian seaports handled approximately 46 million tonnes of cargo. Of this, 42.2 million tonnes accounted for the ports of Greater Odesa, and only 3.8 million tonnes for the ports of the Danube region.
Ukraine is expanding alternative routes
Against the backdrop of threats to maritime exports, Ukraine, together with the European Commission, Moldova and Romania, is working to increase the capacity of alternative routes.
In particular, the parties are discussing expanding the capacity of ports in the Danube region, railway and road infrastructure, speeding up customs and border procedures, and eliminating bottlenecks on transport routes.
A separate area of focus is increasing opportunities for the transit of Ukrainian agricultural products through Moldova and Romania and attracting European funding for the development of the relevant infrastructure.
At the same time, current cargo turnover figures indicate that alternative routes are not yet capable of fully replacing the capacity of the ports of Greater Odesa. This problem becomes particularly acute during the harvest season and the formation of grain export consignments.
The Ministry for Communities, Territories and Infrastructure Development warned that systematic attacks by the russian federation on Ukrainian ports and civilian shipping pose risks not only to Ukraine's economy, but also to international trade and global food security.
Context
The Ukrainian maritime corridor began operating in September 2023 after Russia withdrew from the Black Sea Grain Initiative and the previous mechanism for exporting food through the Black Sea effectively ceased to operate. Ukraine organized its own route for civilian vessels to the ports of Greater Odesa, which gradually became the country's main channel for maritime exports.
From the beginning of the new corridor's operation through the end of July 2026, it transported approximately 209.3 million tonnes of cargo, including 124.1 million tonnes of grain. During this period, more than 8,200 vessels used the route. Ukrainian agricultural products were supplied through the seaports to more than 55 countries.
The ports of Greater Odesa play a key role in Ukraine's agricultural logistics and handle approximately 90% of the country's agricultural exports by sea. Therefore, disruptions to vessels entering the ports directly affect the pace of grain and other agricultural product exports.
The situation sharply deteriorated in the summer of 2026 due to an intensification of Russian attacks on port infrastructure and civilian shipping. According to official data, in July alone, Russia attacked Ukrainian seaport facilities 67 times, civilian vessels directly in the ports 35 times, and vessels in the Ukrainian maritime corridor another 22 times.
At the end of July, the Ministry for Communities, Territories and Infrastructure Development reported that the latest massive attacks had effectively led to a temporary suspension of vessels entering Ukrainian ports. At the same time, Ukraine did not make an official decision to close the Ukrainian maritime corridor, and port infrastructure continued to operate.
Because of the situation in the Black Sea, Ukraine, together with the European Commission, Romania and Moldova, began working on increasing the capacity of alternative routes, including through Danube ports, railways and road crossings. However, their current capacity is significantly lower than that of the ports of Greater Odesa: of the 46 million tonnes of cargo handled by Ukrainian seaports from the beginning of 2026 through the end of July, 42.2 million tonnes were handled by Greater Odesa and only 3.8 million tonnes by the Danube region ports.
The decline in maritime exports is taking place against the backdrop of the new harvest, when Ukraine needs to increase grain shipments. Prolonged disruptions to shipping could place additional pressure on grain storage facilities and overland logistics, complicate exports and affect foreign-currency earnings from the agricultural sector.
We remind you
Earlier, it became known that Ukraine proposed a truce to Russia in the Black Sea but has not yet received a response.

articles.title: Fact check: False claims target US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed
articles.body:
Fact check: False claims target El-Sayed after primary win
August 14, 2026
On August 4, Abdul El-Sayed, a leading progressive candidate, won Michigan's Democratic primary for the US Senate.
The 41-year-old will face Republican Mike Rogers in the November 3 midterm elections. The winner will succeed retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.
Michigan is a battleground or so-called "swing" state, where both parties have a strong chance of winning. The large Arab American and Muslim population plays a key role.
If El-Sayed wins in November, he would become the first Muslim US senator in history.
Soon after his primary victory, several false claims about El-Sayed were spread online, including claims promoted by prominent political figures.
According to Lawrence Pintak, a journalism professor at Washington State University and author of America & Islam, El-Sayed is an ideal target for political disinformation.
"He checks off all the boxes: He's a Muslim, he's a progressive, and he is vocally critical of Israel," Pintak said in a written statement to DW.
DW Fact check examined claims about voting irregularities during the primaries, El-Sayed's political ideology and whether he said the US deserved the 9/11 attacks.
Alleged ghost votes
Claim: "Of course they cheated. Nobody actually votes for communists," a Facebook post claimed, linking to an article headlined: "Abdul El-Sayed got three times as many votes in Detroit as there are registered voters."
The article states that El-Sayed "received 1.4 million votes in Detroit alone — a city with approximately 480,000 registered voters."
DW Fact check: False
The Facebook account that shared the claim, "America's Last Line of Defense," states that "nothing on this page is real." The page has around 748,000 followers and is linked to a website run by Christopher Blair, a well-known creator of fabricated political content. The BBC once described him as the "godfather of fake news."
However, this disclaimer is often lost when the content is reposted on other pages, allowing the false claim to spread without context.
The invented story echoes a claim shared by US President Donald Trump days earlier about a county in Michigan: "Miracles happen in Wayne County, including more votes being cast than there are voters, by a lot."
Trump did not provide any evidence to support his claim of alleged voter fraud.
According to the Michigan Voter Information Center, Michigan has approximately 7.3 million active registered voters, while El-Sayed received 743,455 votes statewide in the Democratic Senate primary, not 1.4 million votes in Detroit alone.
Michael Hameleers, an associate professor of political communication at the University of Amsterdam who researches misinformation and disinformation, warned about the impact of such allegations.
"It is a prominent delegitimization technique to put democratic institutions and the fairness of elections in question," he said.
"Especially in a context where people perceive disinformation and fraud as highly likely, it may be a fruitful strategy to cast doubt on elections."
A 2023 US study found that exposure to unfounded claims of voter fraud can significantly undermine confidence in elections, particularly among Republicans and Trump supporters.
Claims about political ideology
Claim: US President Donald Trump has repeatedly described Abdul El-Sayed as a communist, most recently in a Truth Social post published shortly after El-Sayed's primary victory.
DW Fact check: False
El-Sayed's campaign has focused on government-sponsored health insurance, taxing billionaires and reducing the influence of corporate money in politics.
In the past, he has rejected claims that he is a socialist or a communist by stating he is a capitalist. "I'm not a socialist. I'm just a capitalist who understands how capitalism works," he said.
El-Sayed emphasized his views on capitalism as a point of difference from self-described democratic socialist Bernie Sanders.
In a recent interview with The New York Times, he responded to Trump's claims that he is a communist by saying: "The man is so clearly a joker."
In a comment to DW, Lawrence Pintak also called the claims historically bizarre. He sees it as part of systematic attempts by the Republican Party "to spin 'progressive' and 'democratic socialist' to be synonyms for 'Communist.'"
An analysis by Reuters found that Trump has significantly increased his use of the term in recent weeks.
Pintak told DW that the loaded term works well on social media.
Misattributing views on 9/11
Claim: After El-Sayed secured the Democratic nomination, his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, posted a statement on X, calling him "someone who believes America deserved 9/11."
DW Fact check: False
9/11 refers to the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, in which planes hijacked by militant al-Qaeda Islamists struck the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon near Washington, killing nearly 3,000 people.
The allegation has come up repeatedly but conflates previous remarks made by El-Sayed supporter Hasan Piker with El-Sayed's own views.
Piker has supported El-Sayed during his 2026 US Senate campaign, appearing with him at rallies and in livestreams.
During a 2019 livestream, Piker said America had "deserved" 9/11, a remark that generated widespread criticism. Since then, however, he has walked back this statement.
When asked by US-based fact checkers PolitiFactfor evidence to support his claim, the Rogers campaign pointed to a video clip of El-Sayed refusing to disavow Piker's 2019 comments.
Pintak, who researches Islamophobia, described "guilt by association" as one of the disinformation tactics used against El-Sayed.
He points out that El-Sayed has become a target of disinformation at a time when the Republican Party has shifted from an anti-immigrant focus back to an anti-Muslim narrative.
"Attacks on Muslim candidates, and El-Sayed himself, are nothing new," Pintak said, pointing to Islamophobic reporting during El-Sayed's 2018 campaign for Michigan governor and false claims portraying New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as an extremist.
During the 2018 midterms, Pintak led a research team that found Muslim candidates, from local school boards to Congress, were systematically targeted by "a social media narrative of manufactured outrage [that] was disproportionately Islamophobic, xenophobic, racist, and misogynistic."
The researchers concluded that such attacks were often aimed at undermining candidates' legitimacy and reducing trust among voters.

articles.title: Fuel prices: study says there is no "profiteering by operators"
articles.body:
An ERSE study found that in the first seven months of 2026 domestic prices broadly followed international costs, with no "evidence of profiteering by operators". Fuel prices are set to soar again next week.
Fuel prices shoot up rapidly but take much longer to come down. At least, that is the perception of many Portuguese drivers when they fill up, even if this view is not backed up by the relevant authorities.
The volatility of fuel prices has been increasingly evident, as a result of the current conflict in the Middle East and restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Faced with this situation, the Minister for the Environment and Energy, Maria da Graça Carvalho, requested a detailed study from the Energy Services Regulatory Authority (ERSE) (source in Portuguese), which found no irregularities or "profiteering" by the operators.
Published this Friday, the study on the evolution of road fuel prices, covering the period from 1 January 2023 to 27 July 2026, concludes that pump prices are based on international quotations for refined petrol and diesel, rather than directly on the price of crude oil (Brent). As a result, "the evolution of fuel prices in Portugal was explained above all by the evolution of those quotations".
"Rockets and Feathers" effect
Beyond understanding price volatility, the main aim of the study was to test whether increases in international prices are passed through to domestic prices faster than falls of the same magnitude.
An asymmetry dubbed "Rockets and Feathers", describing how prices "rise like a rocket" when international costs increase but "fall like a feather" when costs decrease, which, according to ERSE's study (source in Portuguese), was not observed.
"The results therefore do not support the existence of a persistent 'Rockets and Feathers' effect: increases and decreases start to be passed through in the same period, although in the case of diesel the estimated drop is initially slightly less pronounced," the document explains.
"For diesel, a small difference was observed in the first few weeks, which ceased to be statistically significant after four weeks. The results therefore do not support the idea that decreases are passed through persistently more slowly or less fully than increases".
The same report further states that it "found no evidence of operators taking advantage of the situation".
"These results are aggregated and do not allow an assessment of the behaviour or profits of each company individually. They do not, therefore, rule out isolated situations, but they also do not support the conclusion that fuel companies have taken advantage of the situation to increase their margins across the board."
How are the price differences with Spain explained?
Given the proximity of the border, many Portuguese have opted to refuel on the Spanish side because of the price difference, which has also been questioned by Portuguese consumers. According to ERSE, the reason is simple: taxes.
"In the second quarter of 2026, the difference was essentially the result of taxation," the authority said. "Without taxes, prices in Spain were higher than in Portugal by 5.9 c/l for petrol and 10.6 c/l for diesel. After taxes, however, prices in Portugal were 41.8 c/l higher for petrol and 25.1 c/l higher for diesel than in Spain".
According to ERSE, price movements should always be viewed together with taxation, "which plays an important role in the evolution of the final price borne by consumers. In 2026, the temporary mechanism for adjusting ISP mitigated part of the rise in final prices during the period of greatest market tension".
In addition to the direct comparison with Spain, the study also compares prices with those of other member states, indicating that "in Portugal prices, with and without taxes, evolved in line with the European Union and euro area average".
"In Portugal, in line with most countries in the European Union and the euro area, the tax burden over the period under review remained constant in €/l, unlike what happened in Spain," the document explains.
Fuel prices set to rise again next week
Next week, fuel prices are set to rise again.
According to projections by the Automóvel Club de Portugal (ACP (source in Portuguese), diesel prices are expected to rise by 10 cents, while petrol will go up by 9 cents.
If these forecasts are confirmed, the average price of diesel will rise to 2.068 euros per litre from Monday, while petrol will climb to 1.977 euros per litre, cancelling out the drop recorded last week. Fuel prices may vary between operators and filling stations.
These changes are not definitive, depending on the closing of the markets and also on a possible change to ISP by the government, which is applying an extraordinary discount on ISP whenever the increase exceeds 10 cents per litre.

articles.title: New Zealand joins the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children — Sybiha
articles.body:
New Zealand joins the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children — Sybiha
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha welcomed New Zealand's joining the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children, which now comprises 51 countries. He stressed that this increases international pressure on Russia to return the illegally deported children.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha welcomed New Zealand’s accession to the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children, which now has 51 member countries. He wrote about this on the social network X, reports UNN.
New Zealand has become the 51st member of the Coalition, strengthening our joint international efforts to bring home Ukrainian children illegally deported and forcibly transferred by Russia
He noted that with each new country joining the Coalition, international pressure on Russia grows, and the joint appeal becomes increasingly difficult to ignore – Ukrainian children must return home.
Sybiha added that their abduction and forced transfer cannot become yet another long-term consequence of Russia’s war.
The Ukrainian Foreign Minister also thanked New Zealand Deputy Foreign Minister Winston Peters and New Zealand for this important decision and unwavering solidarity with Ukraine.
He also stressed that Ukraine will continue to increase pressure on the Russian Federation until every Ukrainian child returns home.

articles.title: French court blocks social media ban for under 15s
articles.body:
Emmanuel Macron speaks to the press after a visit to the departmental fire and rescue operational center (CODIS) in Bordeaux on July 27, 2026. | Pool photo by Kenzo Tribouillard via AFP/Getty Images
A court in France on Friday shot downa bill seeking to ban access to social media for under-15s from September — a major blow to President Emmanuel Macron that raises fundamental questions about efforts to protect kids on the internet.
The Constitutional Council, which reviews the constitutionality of French legislation, said the restrictions in the bill disproportionately infringe on minors’ right to freedom of expression and communication.
Europe’s would-be first social media ban, which sought to prohibit access to anyone in France under the age of 15 from next month, had been a flagship policy of Macron's second and final term.
Advertisement
The French president has also pushed restrictions to the top of the EU agenda, with an expected announcement of bloc-wide measures by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in September.
In a statement late Friday, the French presidential office said the government would not be giving up on the bill. It has set a new target date for spring 2027, which coincides with when Macron will leave office.
The statement said Macron “has instructed the Prime Minister to work, as quickly as possible, on a legally sound draft that takes into account” the court's decision. The ruling hinted at what would make the age restriction align with fundamental rights: giving parents more flexibility.
Peter Craddock, a senior Brussels-based attorney advising social media firms, said the French court decision could have far-reaching implications.
"What they're basically saying here is: 'Listen, government, if you want to get this to succeed, you can't just work on the basis of a general ban. There have to be limitations," said Craddock, a partner at Keller & Heckman. "There have to be ways for people to say, 'well, actually, in my case, my son, my daughter is of a certain degree of maturity and is able to use this properly.'"
The government bill had passed through the French legislative procedure after a lengthy back-and-forth earlier this summer. It was set to bring forward Europe's first social media age restrictions, with Greece and Denmark planning to follow suit.
Advertisement
But Article 1 of the French bill essentially rendered it a blanket ban, without sufficiently distinguishing between the risks of each social media platform or the varying levels of vulnerability among minors themselves, said the court. The ban would also apply to online platforms that have not been proven to have risks to the health and safety of minors.
Craddock warned the court's judgment may not bode well for other national bans or restrictions coming from the European Commission, since the decision is framed around fundamental rights, which are harmonized across the bloc.
"The reasoning is actually equally relevant internationally, throughout the EU, because this fundamental freedom is not specific to France," he said.

articles.title: BNN IN FOCUS | airBaltic’s dilemmas and the difficult decisions facing the state
articles.body:
The fate of Latvia’s national airline airBaltic could very well be decided as early as this Monday. The company has a business plan in place; now it remains to be seen what its bondholders will say on Monday. BNN asked Filips Rajevskis, political scientist and co-owner of the company Mediju tilts, what is really happening with airBaltic.
“The priority of the new business plan is to restore the company’s ability to make a profit, cut costs, reduce the number of aircraft and make a range of other changes. In any case, this currently requires government involvement. The business plan indicated that around 225 million euros would be needed in borrowing for the transition period, followed by another 100 million euros in additional capital. For the business plan to start working, they will have to approach the government,” Rajevskis says.
BNN noted that the airline’s core group of major creditors consists of international airBaltic bondholders, banks, leasing companies and others with whom the company will have to reach an agreement. Rajevskis says this is always a dilemma for lenders.
“In restructuring situations like this, lenders face a choice. They can take a hard line and say: give us our money back. But if the company cannot pay, they have to join the queue with all the other creditors, and there is no telling how much they will ultimately recover. The other option is to make concessions in some areas while still remaining in a fairly comfortable position in terms of returns. Moreover, they have already earned well from bonds carrying very high interest rates. Reaching an agreement with lenders in a situation like this is the highest form of negotiation.
It requires experience and an understanding of how lenders think.”
The airline’s business plan paints an attractive revenue trajectory – from 800 million euros in 2027 to 1 billion euros in 2031. Asked whether this is realistically achievable, Rajevskis replies:
“The prime minister has said in his videos that we need to look at things realistically. We cannot see which passengers they are talking about or which destinations they intend to serve. That makes it difficult to assess. But these are very impressive figures and very ambitious projections.”
Asked by BNN whether airBaltic can actually deliver on this plan, Rajevskis says several factors must be taken into account. “If, for example, airBaltic were to go bankrupt, it would be an enormous loss for the Latvian state. Looking at the worst-case scenario, it would be a huge blow to our economy and to the country’s image. That would be a very bad outcome. On the other hand, continuously supporting the company financially is not easy either. These are complicated decisions. We also have to look at how much airBaltic’s own management and the state as shareholder are prepared to contribute.
All of this comes down to negotiations.”
The airline’s plan also envisages reducing its fleet from the current 54 aircraft to around 36 by the end of the year and returning surplus aircraft to their owners – the lessors. This, too, is likely to involve additional costs.
According to Rajevskis, this creates an extremely difficult dilemma not only for airBaltic’s management and supervisory board, but also for its shareholder – the Latvian state. These are difficult questions, he says, particularly given how challenging such decisions can be to push through the political process.
Asked at what point airBaltic’s business actually went wrong, Rajevskis argues that part of the problem lies with the state itself. As shareholder, it failed to exercise sufficient care and oversight both during the era of Bertolt Flick and under Martin Gauss.
“Now we are reaping the consequences of that carelessness.
Being a shareholder and participating in the governance of a company like airBaltic requires knowledge and understanding. It appears that the state has treated its own company rather casually.”
Asked to comment on the airline’s new business plan, Rajevskis says the situation has both objective and subjective elements. “The objective part is that the business model of flying from Latvia to Western Europe in one direction and to Russia, Belarus and various Eastern countries in the other was a good idea. Who could have imagined that Russia would start a war? The risk existed, and it materialised. You cannot say it was completely unforeseeable, but the approach was to try to live with that risk. The same applies to Covid. Nobody could have predicted that a pandemic would begin, airlines would be unable to fly anywhere for a long period and would simply keep spending money. Those are objective problems.
The question is what happened after those major changes had already taken place, particularly regarding the eastern market. As a shareholder, I would have demanded a revised business plan: what do we do when there is a war and we can no longer fly east? Should we reduce the scale of operations and avoid acquiring so many aircraft? I am not an aviation expert, but there is a sense that these questions were not asked in time.”
Read also: airBaltic to cancel flights from Tallinn to Gatwick during winter season

articles.title: Court reporter looks back on Marc Dutroux case that shook Belgium 30 years ago
articles.body:
Legal affairs journalist Caroline Van den Berghe looks back on the Marc Dutroux case, 30 years after the horrific summer of 1996. She was there at the trial of the kidnapper, rapist and murderer. “The site visit to the cellar in Marcinelle will stay with me forever,” she says.
Court reporter looks back on Marc Dutroux case that shook Belgium 30 years ago
Marc Dutroux was arrested 30 years ago, on 13 August 1996. He was found to be responsible for the abduction, captivity and rape of six girls: Julie Lejeune and Mélissa Russo, both eight, An Marchal, 17, Eefje Lambrecks, 19, Sabine Dardenne, 12, and Laetitia Delhez, 14. Julie, Mélissa, An and Eefje were killed. Only Laetitia and Sabine were rescued.
Dutroux was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2004. The case prompted outrage across the country and led to fundamental reform of the police and judiciary.
Those who grew up in the years before the Marc Dutroux case may well have had a different childhood to those who came after. “In that respect, there’s certainly a ‘before Dutroux’ and an ‘after Dutroux’,” journalist Caroline Van den Berghe says in the VRT podcast Onder ons, which looks back at the summer of 1996 and the horrific events that emerged.
“Most people didn’t have mobile phones back then, and apps that let you share your location didn’t exist at all,” she continues. “So you weren’t reachable and you just had to trust that everything would be all right. It wasn’t unusual for young children like Julie Lejeune and Mélissa Russo to go for a walk on their own in the neighbourhood.”
But when Julie and Mélissa failed to return to their homes in Grace-Hollogne at the agreed time on 24 June 1995, their parents panicked. They searched with friends and neighbours, and alerted the gendarmerie. There was no trace of the eight-year-old friends.
Search operations as we know them today, led by the Missing Persons Unit and involving Child Focus, did not exist at the time.
The parents of Julie and Mélissa, and later those of teenagers An and Eefje – who went missing on 23 August 1995 in Ostend – felt the police were not taking the cases seriously. “They’ve probably just spent the night at a boyfriend’s,” police told friends when they reported their disappearance.
“We now know that those first few hours are crucial for finding witnesses or clues, but at the time the police didn’t consider the disappearance of An and Eefje to be cause for concern,” Van den Berghe says.
By the time Sabine and Laetitia were kidnapped, the Missing Persons Unit had been set up. “I remember founder Alain Remue saying at the time that something wasn’t right: it simply wasn’t possible that those children hadn’t been found. That’s when large-scale search operations were launched, involving a great deal of manpower and resources.”
Even though it was 30 years ago, some images remain etched in her memory. “Sabine Dardenne and Laetitia Delhez being rescued from Dutroux’s cellar – that really is such an iconic image,” says Van den Berghe.
“And the moment those girls were brought home, the crowd standing there applauding, the girls throwing themselves into their families’ arms, and Sabine saying, ‘I’ve missed you all so much’. The joy and euphoria were immense; I still get goosebumps when I watch it.”
That joy would soon turn to sorrow. First, for the parents of Julie, Mélissa, An and Eefje. Dutroux had abducted them too, but they did not survive. Julie and Mélissa died of hunger and thirst; An and Eefje were buried alive.
I cannot imagine what it must be like as a parent to receive this news. It’s so heart-wrenching
“I cannot imagine what it must be like as a parent to receive this news,” says Van den Berghe. “It’s so heart-wrenching. All the time they were searching for their children, they hoped they were still alive. Then comes the harsh reality that they are dead.”
It emerged that the Charleroi gendarmerie had for some time been in possession of information pointing to Dutroux as a possible child abductor. He had previously been convicted, along with his wife, Michelle Martin, of the abduction and rape of minors. Despite this, he had been released following a decision by the then Justice minister, Melchior Wathelet.
The public outrage was immense. When Dutroux, Martin and his accomplice Michel Lelièvre were arrested on 13 August 1996, crowds protested outside the small courthouse in Neufchâteau.
“Those, too, are iconic images of the suspects being led out of the courthouse by police officers,” says Van den Berghe. “Barricades had been erected to keep the crowd at bay. There was shouting and shoving. The officers rushed down the stairs with the suspects, fearing they might be lynched.”
The Neufchâteau public prosecutor, Michel Bourlet, and investigating judge Jean-Marc Connerotte were held in high esteem by the parents and the community. Under their leadership, a breakthrough had been made in the disappearances and the feeling was that they were the only ones who would get to the bottom of the case. There were rumours of paedophile networks surrounding Dutroux who were said to be abducting children to order for high-ranking figures.
But Connerotte was taken off the case after he and Bourlet attended a fundraising evening organised by a charity to raise money for Laetitia’s defence; she was also present, along with Sabine.
When a photograph of the event appeared in a French-language newspaper, Dutroux’s lawyer went to the court to have the investigating judge removed. The court ruled in his favour, finding that Connerotte had been biased.
“And then all hell broke loose,” says Van den Berghe. “Spontaneous demonstrations and strikes broke out all over the country. Students took to the streets; workers downed tools. Eggs and spaghetti were thrown at courthouses. People were furious. At times, things turned very violent. It was as if a revolution were about to break out.”
At times, things turned very violent. It was as if a revolution were about to break out
A month later, on 20 October 1996, 300,000 people took part in the White March, a huge protest event in central Brussels. The march sent a signal to the police, the judiciary and political leaders that thorough reforms were needed. It would take until 1998, following a brief escape by Dutroux, for those reforms to actually be implemented.
It was only in 2004 – eight years after Dutroux’s arrest – that his trial for the abductions, rapes and murders began in Arlon. It attracted enormous media attention both at home and abroad.
The four Belgian broadcasters – VRT, VTM, RTBF and RTL – had containers installed with a view of the courthouse. “They were small newsrooms from which we could produce reports every day and provide live coverage of the trial,” Van den Berghe explains. “The small criminal court room had space for all the parties involved, but not for all the media. It was agreed that there would be a rota system to determine who could sit in the courtroom and who would have to follow the trial on a screen in another room.”
What has stayed with her most from the trial is the visit to the cellar and cage at Dutroux’s house in Marcinelle, where the girls were held.
“A site visit is quite exceptional in a criminal trial, but this was to show the jury what that cage looked like. How small it was. It was considered important for the jury to see this with their own eyes. When you enter that cellar and see the cage, you realise how inhumanly horrific it must have been to be locked up in there. Sabine Dardenne was held there for 81 days.”
Sabine’s courageous testimony has also stayed with her. “Her story made it very clear how Dutroux manipulated the abducted girls,” she says. “Sabine said Dutroux had led her to believe he was her protector against a big boss who would come to take her away and murder her.”
Sabine’s account was crucial to the investigation and clearly showed what the other girls had also gone through. There was no evidence found of a network or major ringleader. “Although many people found it hard to believe that a single man, with his wife and an accomplice, was capable of such acts, Sabine’s account showed it was indeed possible.”
