articles.title: Xi Focus: Charting a green path to development
articles.body:
BEIJING, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's landmark Ecological and Environmental Code, which for the first time enshrines Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization in law, will take effect on Saturday.
The core idea of the thought traces back to a concept first expressed 21 years ago by Chinese President Xi Jinping, then Party chief of east China's Zhejiang Province, during a visit to a small mountain village: "Lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets."
Over the past two decades, the concept has evolved into a national development strategy, helping shape the country's efforts to reconcile ecological conservation with economic development.
GREEN PATH
In August 2005, Xi visited Yucun Village. After learning that the village had shut down polluting mines to pursue a greener path, he called their choice a "wise move" and introduced the now-famous idea that "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets."
In the following years, residents of Yucun have developed rural tourism and carbon-sink projects, which helped them raise incomes and create better lives.
"Your achievements prove that green development is the right path. Having chosen it, we must press ahead," Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, said during a return visit to the village in March 2020.
Yucun offers a glimpse into China's approach to green development: economic growth must not come at the expense of the environment, and environmental protection itself can become a source of development.
China should maintain green and low-carbon development as the fundamental solution to ecological and environmental issues, accelerate the formation of green production modes and lifestyles, Xi said at a conference in 2023.
In June 2022, Xi made an inspection tour to Yibin, a city along the Yangtze River in southwest China's Sichuan Province.
Yibin once suffered from severe pollution as chemical factories lined the riverfront, discharging pollutants rampantly. To address the problem, the city cleared out energy-intensive and high-pollution factories, shut down small paper mills, banned river sand mining, and curbed sewage discharges, gradually restoring the ecological environment along its riverbanks.
Xi praised the progress and called for efforts to prioritize conservation and pursue high-quality development in the Yangtze River Economic Belt.
That green approach has taken root across the region. Traditional industries have been transformed and upgraded, and new sectors including automobiles and electronic information have emerged and thrived. While water quality has improved, the economic belt's GDP has more than doubled over the past decade, demonstrating how ecological protection and economic development can reinforce each other.
The Yangtze River has become a vivid example of China's broader efforts to advance ecological progress.
Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, China has waged a sweeping campaign against pollution while transforming its development model, significantly improving its ecological environment and fostering new, higher-quality and more sustainable growth drivers.
Today, China leads the world in expanding green coverage and has built the largest and fastest-growing renewable energy system anywhere. In the first half of 2026, emerging growth drivers such as advanced manufacturing, the digital economy and modern services, which are more energy-efficient and environmentally friendly than traditional industries, contributed more than 40 percent of economic growth.
Environmental protection and economic development are not contradictory but dialectically unified, Xi has said, noting that only by protecting the ecology and tapping its strengths can high-quality development be realized.
CONCRETE ACTION
Effective on Saturday, the Ecological and Environmental Code brings together years of legislative and regulatory progress, further strengthening the legal framework for ecological conservation.
China must have the strictest possible institutions and legislation in place in order to guarantee ecological progress, Xi has said.
Over the past decade and beyond, China has ramped up environmental legislation, strengthened enforcement, and made major strides in putting environmental regulations into practice.
The country enshrined ecological civilization in its Constitution, implemented what was described as the country's "toughest-ever" environmental protection law, tackled pressing environmental problems from air and water pollution to noise, and strengthened protection of key areas and fragile ecosystems, including the Yangtze River, the Yellow River, the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and China's black soil region.
At a symposium in 2018, Xi recalled how environmental authorities had taken tough action against violations, citing what was described at the time as the largest environmental fine ever imposed in the Yangtze River basin, exceeding 27 million yuan (about 4 million U.S. dollars).
The chemical company involved had been both a major taxpayer and major polluter in central China's Hubei Province. Faced with a huge fine for illegal emissions, it overhauled its operations and set out on a greener path. Now, the company has become a local model for green practices.
Another tough environmental mechanism is China's central environmental inspection system, which has strengthened accountability for local environmental protection and helped address long-standing problems in different regions.
Thanks to effective central inspections, the Lianjiang River in south China's Guangdong Province, once heavily polluted by industrial wastewater, has seen its water quality steadily improve. Ulan Suhai Lake, the biggest lake wetland of the Yellow River basin, once plagued by ecological degradation, has restored its ecological functions and become a haven for birds. The Qilian Mountains, where mining and other development activities had caused vegetation damage and ecological degradation, have begun to experience ecosystem recovery thanks to targeted restoration efforts.
These environmental improvements have translated into tangible benefits for local people, making a better environment part of a better life.
Highlighting the people-centered approach, Xi said ecological progress delivers the strongest sense of gain to the people, who feel its benefits most acutely when the environment improves.
The Ecological and Environmental Code stresses that a sound ecological environment is the most universal form of public welfare. Specifically, its pollution prevention provisions cover not only traditional concerns such as air pollution and black, foul-smelling water, but also emerging pollutants and newer forms of environmental risks, including light pollution and electromagnetic radiation.
GLOBAL CONTRIBUTION
The Ecological and Environmental Code is significant not only for China's efforts to protect its own natural environment, but also for global ecological progress.
According to the Ministry of Ecology and Environment, the code contains provisions on international cooperation and China's fulfillment of obligations under international environmental treaties. "It reflects the vision of a community with a shared future for humanity and contributes Chinese wisdom and solutions to global ecological and environmental governance," an official of the ministry said.
China has long been an active participant and major contributor to global green development.
While delivering video remarks at the UN Climate Summit in September 2025, Xi announced China's new Nationally Determined Contributions, including a 7 to 10 percent reduction in economy-wide net greenhouse gas emissions from peak levels and increasing the share of non-fossil fuels in total energy consumption to over 30 percent by 2035.
"These targets represent China's best efforts based on the requirements of the Paris Agreement," Xi said.
In addition to advancing its own green transition, China has been actively helping other countries pursue sustainable development.
Since 2016, China has provided and mobilized more than 177 billion yuan in funding for developing countries to address climate change and signed more than 50 memorandums of understanding on South-South cooperation on climate change with more than 40 developing countries.
During the past five years, Chinese exports of wind power and photovoltaic products helped other countries reduce carbon emissions by about 4.1 billion tonnes.
While speaking at the first phase of the 15th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, known as COP15, in 2021, Xi highlighted the significance of international cooperation, calling for building a homeland of harmonious coexistence between man and nature, of coordinated advancement of economy and the environment, and of common development of all countries.
Many such cooperation projects have already delivered tangible results in different parts of the world.
In Mauritania, a livestock technology demonstration center built with Chinese assistance has helped local communities improve their livelihoods while also guaranteeing environmental protection.
The "Africa Solar Belt" project, supported by China, is expected to bring electricity to tens of thousands of households without access to power in countries including Chad and Burundi, helping advance a green and low-carbon development path.
The integration of economic development and ecology championed by President Xi has offered valuable ideas for the world, former UN Under-Secretary-General Erik Solheim said. ■

articles.title: Slovakia's GDP grows 0.7 pct in Q2
articles.body:
BRATISLAVA, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Slovakia's gross domestic product (GDP) in fixed prices grew by 0.7 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, the slowest growth rate in the past four quarters, according to a preliminary estimate released by Slovak Statistics Office on Friday.
Seasonally adjusted, Slovakia's GDP rose by 0.8 percent in yearly terms, while it increased by 0.2 percent quarter-on-quarter.
GDP volume in current prices rose by 1.7 billion euros (1.9 billion U.S. dollars) year-on-year to reach 35.9 billion euros (41.4 billion dollars). When calculated in fixed prices, GDP amounted to 26.4 billion euros (30.5 billion dollars), which is an increase of nearly 187.5 million euros (216.6 million dollars) year-on-year.
The GDP growth in fixed prices in the second quarter was mainly driven by higher final consumption, according to the estimate. ■

articles.title: Chinese animated hit "All Wishes Come True" makes North American premiere
articles.body:
The North American premiere of the Chinese animated film "All Wishes Come True" is held in Los Angeles, California, the United States, on Aug. 13, 2026. Chinese animated fantasy-comedy "All Wishes Come True" held its North American premiere Thursday night in Los Angeles, ahead of its theatrical release across the United States and Canada on Friday. (Photo by Zeng Hui/Xinhua)
LOS ANGELES, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Chinese animated fantasy-comedy "All Wishes Come True" held its North American premiere Thursday night in Los Angeles, ahead of its theatrical release across the United States and Canada on Friday.
The film, inspired by the classic Taoist tale of the Eight Immortals crossing the sea, has emerged as a box-office hit in China this summer, winning both critical acclaim and commercial success. It has grossed more than 1.51 billion yuan (224 million U.S. dollars) at China's domestic box office as of Friday, according to Maoyan, a Chinese movie-ticketing and film data platform.
The film was written and directed by Mou Zhengyang, with voice direction by Chen Hao, whose credits include "Ne Zha" and "Ne Zha 2."
"All Wishes Come True" has received strong feedback from Chinese moviegoers, earning a rating of 9.7 out of 10 from more than 241,000 viewers on Maoyan.
Hannah Avison, a songwriter and content creator, gave the film a perfect 10 out of 10 after attending its premiere, praising it as a universal story about people coming together.
"The animation was beautiful. It was a beautiful story," Avison told Xinhua. "There were so many twists and turns, and the plot was really incredible. I never knew what to expect. I was constantly on the edge of my seat."
"I'm not usually a fan of long movies, but I was engaged the entire time," said Hollywood actor and producer John Kyle Sutton. "There was an incredible amount of Eastern mythology."
"I do think movies like this can attract U.S. audiences and inspire them to learn more about Chinese culture," he added. "I was really impressed by the artistry, the writing, and the animation style. The voice actors were all top-notch. Hats off to all the creators, everyone who worked on it, and the director. They were fantastic."
"All Wishes Come True" is being released by CMC Pictures in Mandarin with English subtitles in more than 100 selected theaters across Los Angeles, San Francisco, New York, Las Vegas, Seattle, Chicago, Dallas, Atlanta, Toronto, Vancouver, and dozens of other North American cities with large Chinese communities. ■

articles.title: NATO fighter jet shoots down unidentified drone over Latvia
articles.body:
RIGA, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Latvian armed forces confirmed on Friday that a NATO fighter jet operating under the Baltic Air Policing mission shot down an unidentified foreign drone that had violated the country's airspace in the northeastern region of Balvi.
According to a statement released by the Latvian National Armed Forces on social media, the interception occurred early Friday morning, and the incident prompted local authorities to issue temporary air raid alerts in the eastern municipalities of Rezekne, Balvi, and Aluksne, and were later lifted.
This marked at least the third violation of Latvian airspace this year. ■

articles.title: Lebanese PM urges clear timetable for Israeli withdrawal from south
articles.body:
BEIRUT, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam on Friday called for an expansion of pilot areas in southern Lebanon and a clear timetable for Israel's withdrawal from Lebanese territory, local media reported.
Salam made the remarks during a meeting with U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon Michel Issa and U.S. General Joseph Clearfield, head of the Military Coordination Group for Lebanon, and an accompanying military delegation, according to Lebanon's official National News Agency (NNA).
The meeting focused on the military aspect of the negotiating framework and the latest developments in southern Lebanon. Salam stressed the need for Israel to halt its destructive operations, expand the scope of the pilot areas and set a clear timetable for its withdrawal from Lebanese territory.
In a separate meeting with Clearfield, Lebanese Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri discussed the situation on the ground, the group's work following the identification of pilot areas, and mechanisms for verifying an Israeli withdrawal and the deployment of the Lebanese army, the NNA said.
Earlier this month, Israeli and Lebanese officials finished three days of negotiations in Rome aimed at advancing security arrangements along their border and implementing a framework agreement reached in Washington in late June, local media reported. The talks, opposed by Hezbollah, are the seventh round of negotiations between the two governments. ■

articles.title: Feature: Ancient Chinese astronomical instruments draw museum-goers to cosmic quest
articles.body:
A guide speaks to visitors at an exhibition titled "Heavenly Questions: The Cosmological Vision of Chinese Civilization" at the Anhui Museum in Hefei, east China's Anhui Province, July 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhou Mu)
HEFEI, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's museums are often defined by their porcelain, calligraphy and ritual vessels. But a new exhibition in east China's Anhui Province is turning the spotlight away from traditional treasures and toward scientific endeavors of the past, showcasing jade cosmograms, celestial star charts and bronze globes crafted by astronomers centuries ago.
Titled "Heavenly Questions: The Cosmological Vision of Chinese Civilization," the exhibition at the Anhui Museum brings together nearly 300 artifacts from 48 institutions nationwide. It is a rare exhibition in China focused specifically on presenting the country's "understanding of the universe" through cultural relics.
Since its launch in July, the show has drawn some 350,000 visitors, fascinated by the instruments ancient Chinese used to observe, measure and pay homage to the universe.
One of the star attractions is a jade slab, roughly the size of a smartphone, dating back 5,800 to 5,300 years. The eight arrows at the center of the slab map out the eight directions of space, and the arrows at the four corners appear to align with the positions of sunrise and sunset on the winter and summer solstices. The Chinese cosmological diagram is possibly older than Stonehenge in Britain.
Other highlights include the China's oldest equatorial instrument, a disk with 28-star mansions from a 165 BC marquis' tomb, a bronze water clock of the Western Han Dynasty (202 BC-25 AD), which is the earliest-dated water clock ever found, and a rubbing of a stone-carved astronomical chart in the Southern Song Dynasty (1127-1279) engraved with over 1,400 stars, which remains the oldest all-sky map based on actual observation.
"These 'hardcore creations' in ancient astronomy laid the technological foundation for studying the laws of celestial motion," said Meng Qian, director of the museum's research department.
The exhibition saves its best for last. In the final section, ancient instruments like globes and gnomons sit face-to-face with models of modern Chinese spacecraft, such as the lunar rover Yutu, and lunar soil sample collected by Chang'e-6 mission in 2024.
Interestingly, many of China's major space missions draw their names from ancient myths. Its moon mission is called "Chang'e," the goddess who lives there, while the Mars rover "Zhurong" is named after a fire god, and the sky-surveying telescope "Mozi" is the name of a philosopher, who was credited with conducting the earliest optical experiments.
The exhibition itself takes its title from patriotic poet Qu Yuan's epic poem "Tianwen," or Heavenly Questions, written more than 2,000 years ago. China's Mars exploration mission also shares the same name.
"This exhibition lets ancient astronomy and modern space exploration illuminate and interpret each other," said Shi Yunli, a professor at University of Science and Technology of China and advisor to the show.
"When visitors stand between the folded bronze gnomon and the Yutu rover, they see not just two objects on display, but they see a 5,000-year chain of quest," Shi added.
The exhibition runs through mid-October. And China's space explorations are expected to reach new heights.
"We hope this exhibition will let visitors look back at the early lights of our culture, and also see the way forward," Meng said. ■
A visitor takes photos of an ancient astronomical instrument at an exhibition titled "Heavenly Questions: The Cosmological Vision of Chinese Civilization" at the Anhui Museum in Hefei, east China's Anhui Province, July 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhou Mu)

articles.title: Hong Kong H1 GDP up 5.1 pct, strongest in nearly 5 years
articles.body:
HONG KONG, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- For the first half of 2026, Hong Kong's real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 5.1 percent over a year earlier, the strongest half-yearly performance in nearly five years, official data showed on Friday.
Hong Kong's real GDP grew by 4.3 percent in the second quarter over a year earlier, following 5.9 percent growth in the preceding quarter, according to the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government.
The data further showed that total exports of goods surged by 28.9 percent year-on-year in real terms in the second quarter, driven by robust trade flows fueled by strong global demand for artificial intelligence (AI)-related electronic products. Exports of services expanded solidly by 3.4 percent in real terms over a year earlier, with all major service groups continuing to expand.
Looking ahead, the Hong Kong economy should see solid growth in the second half of 2026, the HKSAR government's economist Irina Fan said, adding that the vibrant global demand for AI-related electronic products is expected to continue supporting Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance, and related logistics services should benefit from this momentum as well.
Taking into account the stronger-than-expected actual outturn in the first half of the year and the near-term outlook, the real GDP growth forecast for 2026 as a whole is revised up to 3.5 percent to 4.5 percent, from 2.5 percent to 3.5 percent in the May round of review. ■

articles.title: China to mark 4th National Ecology Day amid green modernization drive
articles.body:
BEIJING, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- China will hold a series of activities to celebrate the fourth National Ecology Day on Saturday, as the country accelerates its green modernization drive, the country's top economic planner said Friday.
This year's National Ecology Day, themed "Building a green foundation for Chinese modernization," will feature a main event in Hulunbuir, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, according to the National Development and Reform Commission.
A range of public-oriented activities will also be organized to help the public better understand the concept that "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets," as well as the key tasks and measures for advancing ecological civilization during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
China's top legislature designated Aug. 15 as National Ecology Day in 2023 to raise public awareness of ecological conservation and encourage action to protect the environment.
The country has maintained a strategic focus on strengthening ecological conservation. The landmark Ecological and Environmental Code, set to take effect on Saturday, marks another major step in these efforts, providing stronger legal support for sustainable and environmentally friendly development. ■

articles.title: China's yuan loans increase by 10.38 trln yuan in Jan.-July period
articles.body:
BEIJING, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 10.38 trillion yuan (about 1.53 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first seven months of 2026, central bank data showed Friday.
Outstanding yuan loans stood at 282.29 trillion yuan at the end of July, up 5.1 percent year on year, according to the People's Bank of China.
M2, a broad measure of money supply that covers cash in circulation and all deposits, increased by 7.7 percent year on year to 355.51 trillion yuan by the end of last month.
M1, which covers currency in circulation, corporate demand deposits, personal demand deposits and provisions received by non-bank payment institutions, reached 115.46 trillion yuan at the end of July, up 4 percent from a year earlier.
China's outstanding aggregate financing to the real economy stood at 463.27 trillion yuan at the end of July, up 7.4 percent year on year, according to the central bank.
"Outstanding aggregate financing to the real economy, M2 and other broad financial aggregates have all maintained reasonable growth, with their year-on-year growth rates continuing to exceed nominal GDP growth. This indicates that overall financing conditions remain relatively accommodative," said Tian Xuan, dean of Peking University's Guanghua School of Management.
China's credit structure has also improved. At the end of June, loans to technology, green development, inclusive finance, elderly care and the digital economy all posted year-on-year growth rates higher than that of overall loans.
Going forward, monetary and credit policies should play a stronger guiding role in channeling funds to the real economy, said Dong Qingma, deputy head of the Institute of Chinese Financial Studies at Southwestern University of Finance and Economics.
Alongside targeted credit support, overall financing costs have continued to decline. China's loan interest rates have stayed at low levels since the start of this year, and that trend persisted into July.
"Interest rates are price signals reflecting the supply-demand balance of funds. The downward trend in lending rates points to relatively ample credit provision," said Zhang Xu, an analyst at Everbright Securities.
Zhang added that greater transparency in corporate financing costs, as disclosure requirements advance, will help further reduce the funding burden on businesses and keep overall social financing costs low. ■

articles.title: China denounces accusations, smears by Philippines, Australia concerning CCG operations at Ren'ai Jiao
articles.body:
BEIJING, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese military spokesperson has voiced firm opposition against the unfounded accusations and smears made by the Philippines and Australia against China.
Chen Xi, a spokesperson for the Ministry of National Defense, made the remarks at a press briefing on Friday in response to a query about the recent Philippine-Australian joint statement from a defense ministers' meeting, which expressed "serious concern" over recent actions taken by the China Coast Guard (CCG) at Ren'ai Jiao.
The Chinese side took necessary countermeasures, which were professional, restrained and beyond reproach, regarding the Philippine side's deliberate provocations and attacks on the Chinese personnel at Ren'ai Jiao, about which the CCG has issued a statement and released evidence, Chen said.
Ren'ai Jiao is part of China's Nansha Qundao and an inherent territory of China, and whatever the Philippine side says or does cannot change this fact, the spokesperson noted.
"What the Philippine side should do is to remove the illegally grounded warship BRP Sierra Madre (LT-57) as soon as possible," Chen said.
The Chinese side will continue to conduct rights-protection and law enforcement activities to thwart any violations or provocations and safeguard national sovereignty and maritime rights and interests, he said.
"We urge relevant countries to stop peddling false narratives, provoking confrontation and undermining regional peace and stability," Chen said. ■

articles.title: Explainer: Unity doesn't mean uniformity: The true value of China's new ethnic law
articles.body:
BEIJING, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- As a multi-ethnic country with a long history, China is offering a new perspective on addressing common challenges in modern state governance through its recently enacted law on promoting ethnic unity and progress -- one that seeks unity without imposing uniformity.
The Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, China's fundamental law governing ethnic affairs, took effect on July 1 to strengthen law-based governance and promote unity and common prosperity among the country's 56 ethnic groups.
China has been ethnically diverse since ancient times, with many groups developing their own unique customs and cultural traditions. For thousands of years, governing such a vast and varied land has presented complex challenges, some of which have even continued into the modern era.
While countries may follow different institutional paths, safeguarding national unity, countering separatism, and protecting the equal rights of all members of society remain common challenges in modern state governance, said Hu Haifeng, director of the Institute of Ethnology at the Xinjiang Academy of Social Sciences.
Through the new law, China is incorporating its historical experiences and contemporary practices in governing ethnic affairs into a legal framework, with the aim of balancing national unity, regional stability and development, ethnic relations and public security, Hu said.
Drawing on years of field research in Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Hu views the legislation as a codification of the country's experience in combating separatism, countering terrorism and extremism, and promoting ethnic unity and progress.
The law expounds on the idea of building a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. It also sets up institutional safeguards to promote the common national language among different ethnic groups, while respecting and protecting the right to study and use ethnic minority languages.
The law's provisions on equality, ethnic unity and the protection of the rights of ethnic groups are broadly consistent with the core principles of international human rights law. This includes the principles of equality and non-discrimination enshrined in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, experts noted.
This "unity with diversity" approach stands in stark contrast to Western models of ethnic governance rooted in nationalism and colonial expansion, as well as a discourse that often views other civilizations through a self-centered, hierarchical lens, said Tian Feilong, vice dean of the law school at Minzu University of China.
According to experts, China's language policies seek to avoid the rigid either-or thinking found in some Western discourse, aiming to find a balance between promoting a common national language and protecting ethnic minority languages and cultures.
Throughout history, countries around the world, including the United States, Britain, France and Japan, have widely adopted policies and institutions to promote a common language, said Zhu Yafeng, a professor at Xinjiang University.
While promoting the use of standard Chinese, China also explicitly stipulates in its Constitution and laws that the rights of ethnic minority groups to learn and use their own languages and scripts shall be respected and protected.
The ethnic unity law stipulates that the state promotes the standardization and digitalization of ethnic languages and scripts, and supports the preservation, collation, research and utilization of ancient books in ethnic minority languages. It also encourages the innovative development of the fine traditional cultures of all ethnic groups.
China's promotion of the national common language in ethnic regions is aimed at better safeguarding the fundamental rights of ethnic minority citizens, including their rights to education, employment, and cultural development, said Hu.
Nyima Phentok, a middle school administrator in Lhasa, capital of Xizang Autonomous Region, said the school's students come from all seven prefecture-level regions of Xizang and speak different Tibetan dialects, making a common language essential for effective communication. The school specifically offers courses of Tibetan language, Tibetan calligraphy and traditional cultural activities such as playing Tibetan musical instruments.
Padma Choszom, a recent college graduate, said she felt confident speaking standard Chinese during a job interview for an automobile-related position in Xigaze, Xizang. "I was able to communicate smoothly with the HR staff and technical team. I also read materials in standard Chinese about the new energy vehicle industry," said the young woman, who also communicates effortlessly with local colleagues and customers in the Tibetan language.
Promoting a common language need not come at the expense of ethnic languages and cultures, said Penpa Lhamo, a national political advisor and deputy director of the Xizang Academy of Social Sciences.
Greater linguistic connectivity creates more opportunities for education, employment and cultural exchange while ethnic traditions and cultural practices continue to be preserved and passed down.
Local Tibetans observe a rich array of religious and folk traditions throughout the year, including the Shoton Festival, Butter Lamp Festival, Saga Dawa Festival, as well as pilgrimages around sacred lakes and mountains.
Tibetan Buddhist monasteries regularly hold traditional religious activities, including scripture study, debate, empowerment ceremonies and spiritual practice.
To Penpa Lhamo, the protection and preservation of Tibetan and other ethnic minority languages and cultures should go hand in hand with socioeconomic development.
Over one-third of China's ethnic minority population lives in urban areas and ethnically mixed communities. "Every ethnic group can thrive only by opening up to the outside world," said Cheng Yue, who also works for the Xizang Academy of Social Sciences.
The Tibetan people, for example, have never been self-isolated, nor has Xizang ever been an isolated region. The Tibetan script developed under the influence of writing systems outside the region, while numerous Tibetan words were borrowed from standard Chinese, Cheng said. ■

articles.title: Shell and Philips hit by Russian ransomware attack
articles.body:
Shell and Philips hit by Russian ransomware attack
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Russia-linked ransomware group Cl0p claims to have hacked global corporations Shell and Philips. The two are among nearly 50 companies Cl0p has listed on its website, alongside General Electric and payments firm Fiserv.
From the oil giant, the group says it has taken some 89 gigabytes of material, including technical drawings, facility images, scans of test reports and project plans. They claimed to have stolen another 13.5 gigabytes from health technology company Philips, mostly diagrams and blueprints.
Both companies are investigating, with Shell saying it is “aware of a possible incident”.
Philips said it had “identified and contained an attempted cybersecurity compromise of a specific enterprise server related to internal data”. A spokesperson told NOS that the incident is now under control and has no impact on its customers.
Russian hackers
Cl0p, which has been active since 2019, is a Russia-linked ransomware group that has likely already extorted $500 million from other victims.
It operates by stealing files and other sensitive data from companies and then threatens to publish them online unless a ransom is paid.
There’s no word yet on how much money the hackers are asking for in exchange for not selling or releasing the stolen data.
Security researchers have linked the campaign to a flaw in Windchill, engineering software made by American firm PTC, which was patched on June 17. Neither Shell nor Philips has said how it was breached.
Writing about the attacks, TNW editor-in-chief Ana-Maria Stanciuc said the pattern carried an uncomfortable lesson: “When enough of the corporate world standardises on the same enterprise platform, one shared supplier quietly becomes everyone’s single point of failure, and no amount of internal security spending can fully patch a hole in someone else’s code.”

articles.title: Tallinn Fringe Festival gets underway next week with biggest program yet
articles.body:
Tallinn Fringe Festival gets underway next week with biggest program yet
The annual Tallinn Fringe Festival (TFF) turns 10 next week and will mark it by bringing its biggest program yet.
The festival, featuring international comedians, cabaret, burlesque and theater across venues in Tallinn, mostly in the cultural quarters of Telliskivi and Kalamaja, starts next Tuesday.
What began as a street art festival a decade ago has grown into a key stop on the Nordic-Baltic fringe circuit, drawing performers from as far afield as Iceland and the U.S. and bringing the inevitable comparisons with the famous Edinburgh Fringe Festival.
TFF is Estonia's only open-access, multi-genre performing arts festival, and this year runs from August 18 to September 18. The events bring together local and international artists and will feature more than 80 shows across genres including circus, dance, music, burlesque, visual arts and theater, and organizers note that as artists work directly with venues rather than being selected by a committee, this leads to a diverse lineup.
Organizer and blues and cabaret performer Kaisa Ling says the festival has come a long way from its street art origins. "It is the 10th anniversary of fringe in different incarnations. It started out as a street art festival more than anything, but now it has grown organically, and the 10th anniversary is the biggest. If we go with the same tempo, it will become bigger and bigger – I'm not going to say Edinburgh look out! But…" said Ling, who was herself heading off to the Scottish capital for a few days before returning for the Tallinn event's start.
That growth has also put Tallinn on the international fringe map. "Some people are actually touring – this is part of the Nordic-Baltic touring circuit. Tallinn is on the map strongly at fringe festivals, and people find it nice to come off the Edinburgh hard work, take it a bit easier here, enjoy the beautiful town, and then continue to other Baltic-Nordic fringes in Sweden, Finland, Iceland," Ling went on.
For the performers, TFF is as much about the audience as the shows. "I'm seeing more and more international artists coming in, and this is my favorite time of the year because I get to visit a lot of shows of people who are not performing in Estonia the other 11 months of the year," said blues pianist and raconteur Rene Paul.
"The Estonian audience is not expecting a show in a cellar to have a touring comedian who is the real deal. This is not some kind of open mic – these are people who are doing it all night every night," Paul went on.
Both Paul and noted comic Sille-Kadri Simer highlighted the festival's growing audience and international flavor.
"New audiences, new faces, new artists, more people coming in. We have so many great acts – each year there's surprises, somebody coming from Iceland, the United States. It's so lovely to see that Tallinn is such a vibrant city for performing arts," said Simer, known as the Estonian Comedy Barbie.
"I've done Edinburgh twice. It went pretty well – I have done over 40 shows there and someone shows up every time. Same with Tallinn – so many shows, but all the shows have people," Paul added.
"I hope people can come and see multiple shows – the fringe is all about seeing different genres," Simer noted.
Burlesque is also a major part of the fringe festival's itinerary. Performer Katarina von Schatz told ERR News she brings a different kind of energy to the stage.
"The burlesque community is so safe. Men are afraid of us, because they see we have the power. What I want to bring on stage is that there will be all different sexes, all different bodies – you don't have to be fit, you can look however. Everything is good on the burlesque stage," von Schatz explained.
"We have our own stories – not like in theater where you have to tell other people's stories. We decide how we tell them and we make our own costumes. Sometimes the audience also affects how we tell it – if it's a different room, different vibe, different people, we just get inspiration from that."
"Daytime I'm home with my three cats and I make costumes (laughs). I love being a full-time artist, I've done it for three years now, I would never go back to work in a bank," von Schatz said of being a full-time performer.
The festival will see stand-up from Estonian and international comedians alike, with shows in both Estonian and English, a mix of Estonian and visiting companies across venues in the Telliskivi creative quarter and Old Town, while the Heldeke! venue in Kalamaja hosts English-language late-night cabarets throughout the month, as it does at other times of the year.
Retaining its street art roots, the festival includes outdoor performances and live music too.
Tickets to fringe festival events are available online and at the door and the full program is here.

articles.title: Family was asleep: mother and 9-year-old son killed in Russian strike on Sumy Oblast, father and grandmother suffer severe burns
articles.body:
Family was asleep: mother and 9-year-old son killed in Russian strike on Sumy Oblast, father and grandmother suffer severe burns
In the village of Stepanivka in Sumy Oblast, nine-year-old Hlib Kovtunenko and his mother, 29-year-old Olha, were killed on the morning of 14 August when Russia struck their home with two jet-powered drones.
Details: The boy attended Buryn City Lyceum No. 1, a specialised secondary school, and his mother had graduated from the same institution, according to a post on the school's page.
"War takes the most precious thing – the lives of our children and of those who shape our community's future. This terrible tragedy has been a heavy blow for the entire teaching staff, the student body and the parent community," the post said.
According to Oleh Hryhorov, Head of Odesa Oblast Military Administration, the child and the woman were killed at the scene. The house has been left in ruins by extensive destruction and fire.
Ukraine's national public broadcaster Suspilne reported that Russian forces began attacking the village after 05:00. The family was asleep at the time.
Olha's father-in-law said his son and wife sustained severe burns and are being taken to Kyiv for surgery. The boy who was killed had celebrated his birthday in July.
Besides the Kovtunenko family, two more people were injured.
Background:
- On the night of 13-14 August, the Russians launched more than a hundred drones at Ukraine. Air defence destroyed most of them.
- However, hits were recorded at 11 locations. Russian forces struck a residential building in the town of Smila, Cherkasy Oblast, with a drone, injuring five people.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia announces start of Red Sea defence alliance: Will it work?
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia announces start of Red Sea defence alliance: Will it work?
Thirteen countries have become members of the Saudi-led maritime alliance.
Saudi Arabia and 13 other countries have confirmed the creation of a maritime military coalition to safeguard freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, with more nations expected to join.
Bahrain, Bangladesh, the Comoros, Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Sudan, Turkiye and Yemen are the first to sign up.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Oman says massive oil spill reaches coastline: What damage could it do?
- list 2 of 3Will all-out war in Yemen reignite as the Houthis escalate attacks?
- list 3 of 3Yemen faces highest risk of returning to war since 2022 truce, UN warns
How significant is this alliance to the region?
Here’s what we know:
What has Saudi Arabia announced?
On Thursday, the Saudi Ministry of Defence announced that 15 countries have signed a declaration, 13 of which have fully joined the coalition so far.
On July 30, the ministry had announced the creation of the Multinational Maritime Defense Alliance as a framework to strengthen collective maritime defence cooperation.
The ministry described the coalition as “an open international coalition that welcomes the accession of all countries that align with its goals and principles”, adding that it continues to receive new membership applications.
On August 13, it posted on X: “The number of countries that signed the joint statement reached 15 countries, while 13 countries completed their national procedures, signed the coalition charter, and officially announced their accession.”
The statement came after the third meeting of the alliance, which was held on August 13 in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.
“This represents the actual launch of the coalition towards the stage of institutional and operational activation, while the rest of the countries continue to complete the necessary national procedures to join the coalition,” the Saudi Defence Ministry added.
Details of how the alliance would work are still being formulated, but, according to the ministry, member states will exchange information and intelligence, develop operational planning, and conduct joint naval exercises and drills, in addition to building military capabilities and carrying out joint naval operations.
The ministry earlier announced that Rear Admiral Abdullah bin Salem Al-Shehri has been appointed as the commander of the coalition. He will oversee joint naval defence, coordinate with member states and other maritime coalitions, and carry out missions under the coalition’s charter.
How significant is this coalition?
The announcement of the coalition comes as the United States-Israel war on Iran continues to upend the energy and civil infrastructure of the Gulf region.
It also comes as the war increases its focus on the Strait of Hormuz. The virtual closure of the route, which formerly carried about 20 percent of global oil and natural gas exports, is weighing heavily on the global economy.
In a recent escalation, Saudi-flagged ships in the Bab al-Mandeb-Red Sea-Gulf of Aden route have come under repeated attack from Iran-backed Houthi fighters in Yemen.
Ahmed Nagi, International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Yemen, told Al Jazeera that the new maritime alliance could be significant, but its importance will depend on how effective it is in practice.
“We have seen several maritime security initiatives before, including those established during the piracy crisis in the Gulf of Aden. While some of these initiatives had political significance, many struggled to translate their objectives into tangible results on the ground,” he said.
“The same applies to this alliance. It could become important if it is able to turn agreements and political commitments into concrete action that addresses the threats to maritime security and freedom of navigation,” he added.
What does this alliance aim to achieve?
Nagi, however, highlighted that the alliance is an attempt from Saudi Arabia not only to deter the Houthis but also to frame the Houthi attacks on shipping in the Red Sea as a global issue, rather than just a Saudi one.
The Iran-backed Houthis took control of Yemen’s capital Sanaa in 2014. Since then, they have been fighting the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government located in the port city of Aden.
These tensions have only worsened since the US-Israel war on Iran began with strikes on Tehran on February 28, with the Tehran-backed Houthis launching strikes against Saudi-flagged vessels and oil facilities in the Red Sea.
The escalating conflict has led to fears that the Houthis could fully block Bab al-Mandeb, a vital waterway which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a major supply route.
“From Riyadh’s perspective, the response to these attacks should not fall on Saudi Arabia alone. Instead, there should be a broader international effort to deal with the Houthis and the disruption they are causing in the Red Sea,” Nagi said.
He noted that so far, the alliance is “a largely defensive alliance”.
“There has been no indication that it is intended to launch offensive operations against the Houthis. But that does not mean the Saudis will remain silent if the attacks continue,” he said.
“At some point, Riyadh may decide that it needs to respond more directly,” he noted, explaining that if that happens, the alliance could provide a framework for Saudi Arabia to act with broader international backing.
“Ultimately, the goal is to raise the cost of Houthi attacks and create a stronger deterrent,” he added.
“The message Saudi Arabia is trying to send is that these attacks are not just targeting Saudi interests. They affect international shipping and global trade, so they should be seen as a concern for the wider international community as well.”

articles.title: Berlin theatre scraps pool event for black children citing ‘racist agitation’
articles.body:
Berlin theatre scraps pool event for black children citing ‘racist agitation’
- A Berlin theatre cancelled a special swimming event for black children due to racist threats and security concerns following far-right backlash.
- The event aimed to support structurally disadvantaged black and African diaspora youth through free pool access.
- Organisers condemned the racist agitation and pledged to continue positive initiatives against racism despite the cancellation.
AI generated
BERLIN – A Berlin theatre that has set up an outdoor swimming pool scrapped plans on Aug 14 to reserve it for black children and young people for one afternoon, citing a backlash and security fears sparked by “racist agitation”.
The Volksbuehne theatre and the anti-racism organisation Each One Teach One (EOTO) had intended the event, for black “children, young people and their relatives”, as “a positive measure to support structurally disadvantaged groups”.
However, they said this had sparked inflammatory media coverage as well as racist emails and threats of violence that had raised safety concerns.
The theatre’s new artistic director Matthias Lilienthal recently launched the pool project for eight weeks this summer, in which people can book free time slots online, with some days reserved for partner organisations.
One of the groups, EOTO, is a publicly funded group that runs programmes for people of black and African diaspora backgrounds.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) was among those who strongly objected to the special programme at the “Volksbad” pool set up by the state-funded theatre.
The party’s co-leader Alice Weidel wrote in an X post: “Apartheid as a model for Germany? In the tax-funded art project ‘Volksbad’, white people are temporarily denied access.
“What is this supposed to mean? Tax funds for such events should be cut immediately!”
One local conservative politician, Aileen Weibeler, on Instagram spoke of “a really strange and discriminatory feeling”.
“Berlin is a liveable, diverse, colourful and free city,” she said, “so why do we need safe spaces?... To be honest, I don’t quite get it.”
The theatre and EOTO said they cancelled the event because of safety concerns after it “became a target of right-wing and racist agitation”.
Lilienthal said that, despite Friday’s cancellation, “we will, of course, continue to offer positive initiatives for structurally disadvantaged people.
“We stand in solidarity – today and every day – with all those subjected to racism and right-wing hostility.”
Berlin’s anti-discrimination official Cansel Kiziltepe decried the “heated campaign of hostility and threats” sparked by the one-time project and stressed that “racism and exclusion are part of the everyday reality for black people”. AFP

articles.title: FIA lifts restrictions on Russian, Belarusian drivers
articles.body:
Halis Sunnetci
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
The International Automobile Federation (FIA) on Friday announced that it has lifted restrictions on Russian and Belarusian motorsport participants, allowing them to compete with their national flags, symbols and anthems.
"After consultation, the WMSC (World Motor Sport Council) decided that the FIA emergency measures shall be revised to lift the restrictions on the participation of Russian and Belarusian drivers, national teams, individual competitors and officials," the federation said in a statement.
The decision also lifted restrictions on "the display of their national symbols, colours, flags and anthems," it added.
The World Motor Sport Council had imposed the restrictions after Russia launched its war on Ukraine in February 2022.
Under the measures, Russian and Belarusian competitors were barred from displaying national symbols or playing their national anthems and were required to sign a commitment to neutrality.
The new decision reverses those measures.
"Russian and Belarusian drivers, national teams, individual competitors and officials are allowed to participate in international/zone competitions without any restrictions. The requirement of signing a commitment to neutrality no longer applies," the federation said.
"The display of Russian and Belarusian national symbols, colours, flags (uniform, equipment and car), and the playing of their anthems are permitted at international/zone competitions," it added.
The governing body said participation would remain subject to laws and regulations in host countries.
"For the avoidance of doubt, the participation of Russian and Belarusian drivers, competitors and officials in a given country remains subject to compliance with any applicable transnational, national and local laws," it said.
The federation said it would continue to monitor events in Ukraine and reserved the right to take further action, including measures needed to comply with applicable sanctions or contractual obligations.
The changes do not lift the ban on holding international motorsport events in Russia or Belarus.
Formula 1 terminated its contract with the Russian Grand Prix promoter in March 2022, ending plans for future races in Russia.
Sochi Autodrom hosted the event from 2014 to 2021, while Igora Drive outside St. Petersburg had been due to take over in 2023.

articles.title: Ranked: These are the world’s best countries for retirees to travel to
articles.body:
Europe dominates the list of the best countries for retirees to travel to for offering transport discounts available to visitors, lots of age-rewarding experiences and Michelin-backed spots to dine at.
Retirement may mean leaving behind the 9-to-5, but it doesn't mean having to abandon travel, too.
In fact, as the world’s population of 65 year olds is forecast to reach 1.5 billion by 2050, research shows that seniors don't disregard their travel bucket lists with at least 65% seeing travel as the perfect way to enjoy later life, according to a study by Booking.com.
For those with more time on their hands to explore the world, some destinations are more suited than others – and that’s where Firebird Tours latest findings from the Where Being 60 Beats Being 20: The Best Countries for Retirees in 2026 survey come in.
With the mature voyager in mind, the Swiss-based travel specialists analysed 100 countries across the globe and assessed them across seven categories: the over-65 population density, availability of senior discounts, walkability, healthcare, safety, and age-rewarding cultural experiences.
Europe is clearly doing something right – claiming eight of the top 10 best countries in the ranking, while 18 feature in the top 25.
Which are the best countries for retirees?
Crowned the best place for retirees to travel to, thanks to its museum discounts, public transport discounts, and a walkability score of five, Japan ranks as number one.
Firebird Tours also found the east Asian nation to have the highest instance of people aged 65 or over at 29.5% – as such, “Japan doesn't just have the world's oldest population – it's built a society around it,” the travel specialists said.
“The result is a destination that rewards older travellers at every turn. Entry to the Tokyo National Museum, one of the most visited in Asia, is free for over 70s year-round,” it added.
However, the remaining four countries in the top five all hail from Europe: Germany ranked second, Spain third, Slovenia fourth and Switzerland rounding off the top five.
Germany leads Europe with 23.7% of its population aged 65 or over. It also offers up to 70% senior discount on public transport through the BahnCar scheme that visitors can also benefit from. The country is also home to 54 UNESCO World Heritage Sites and 336 Michelin-starred restaurants for mature travellers to immerse themselves in local culture and cuisine.
In Spain, the capital Madrid earned a perfect walkability score and the country’s healthcare ranks 15th in the world. Mature travellers are also treated to a 50% discount at the Prado Museum, alongside there also being 50 UNESCO World Heritage Sites to explore. However, one of the downsides is that Spain’s senior transport discount is reserved for residents only.
According to Firebird Tours, Slovenia’s entry was “the result nobody predicted – and the most interesting story in the index,” beating countries like Switzerland, France and Italy. Despite being low-profile as a travel destination in English-language media, it ranks third on the Global Peace Index – making it one of the safest countries to visit. Mature travellers are also treated to a 50% EU visitor-accessible senior transport discount and almost 27% museum discount at the country’s National Museum of Contemporary History.
Switzerland made the ranking thanks to its 50% discount on public transport for visitors through the GA TravelCard. For older travellers with a sweet tooth, The Lindt Chocolate Museum in Zurich offers a discount for seniors year-round and the country's perfect walkability score means all those choco-calories can easily be walked off.
When it comes to the top countries for transport discounts for visitors, Firebird’s top eight ranking is almost exclusively dominated by European countries. The only exception was Canada in seventh place.
While France ranked 24 overall in the study, the country leads in the most Michelin-backed restaurants at 641 eateries for travellers to choose from.

articles.title: Gandhi's letter to India, as told through TOI
articles.body:
After returning to India, he continued to write about the poor conditions of Indians legally settled in South Africa. In an Aug 29, 1919 letter, Gandhi blamed the “greedy Europeans of Natal” for importing Indian indentured labour
A fast unto death announced by Mahatma Gandhi in Pune’s Yerawada jail in 1932 was to change the course of India’s political history. Imprisoned for the Civil Disobedience Movement, Gandhi announced the fast in a Sept 13 letter to British PM Ramsay MacDonald that was shared with the press. His aim was to oppose a separate electorate for Dalits, proposed under the Communal Award of August 1932.“I have to resist your decision with my life,” Gandhi wrote, saying his fast would begin on Sept 20. “As a man of religion that I hold myself to be, I have no other course left open to me.”The award classified Dalits as a minority whose representatives would be elected only by Dalit voters, just as Muslims, Christians and Sikhs would elect their own representatives. Gandhi believed this would divide Hindu society; BR Ambedkar supported it as a safeguard for Dalit political representationGandhi acknowledged that he might be wrong. If his judgement was “warped”, he wrote, his death would be “a penance for my error” and would lift the burden from those who had “child-like faith” in his wisdom.His week-long fast led to the Poona Pact, negotiated by Madan Mohan Malaviya and Ambedkar and accepted by Gandhi. It abandoned a separate electorate but reserved seats for Dalits within the general electorate, becoming a milestone in Dalit representation and a precursor to reservations for SCs and STs in independent India.
Suspending Satyagraha
Gandhi also used a letter to the press to announce the suspension of Satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act.
Writing on July 21, 1919, he asked satyagrahis to “swallow the bitter pill” and halt their campaign after protests had turned violent.The act allowed the colonial government to detain political prisoners for two years without trial. Gandhi’s campaign against it, launched in March 1919, was his first nationwide political mobilisation after returning from South Africa. Despite his appeals for peaceful hartals, fasts and prayers, violence erupted in several places. Gandhi was prevented from entering Punjab and arrested; the Jallianwala Bagh massacre on April 13 made the situation explosive. Attacks on police stations and railway property, and deadly clashes between protesters and authorities, led him to pause civil disobedience.
For Gandhi, non-violence was not merely tactical. Amid divisions within Congress and Subhas Chandra Bose’s different course, he wrote from Sevagram on July 21, 1941
In the July letter, published under the headline “SATYAGRAHA. Civil Resistance Suspended”, Gandhi disclosed that the governor of Bombay had conveyed “a grave warning” from the Government of India that renewed civil disobedience could threaten public security.Writing from Mani Bhavan in Bombay, Gandhi conceded that the suspension was painful. Yet he remained unyielding on the law: “Satyagrahi will pay for its removal with their lives if it cannot be removed by lesser means.” He also warned the Raj: “If my occasional Civil Resistance be a lighted match, Rowlatt legislation…is a thousand matches scattered throughout India.”For Gandhi, non-violence was not merely tactical. Amid divisions within Congress and Subhas Chandra Bose’s different course, he wrote from Sevagram on July 21, 1941: “With me, no doubt non-violence is an end in itself, though it is also a means for the attainment of the freedom of the country.” A year earlier, he had underlined its voluntary nature: “Non-violence cannot be imposed upon anyone. It has to come from within.”
The South Africa Years
Gandhi’s letters to the editor predated his emergence as a leader of India’s freedom struggle. During his 21 years in South Africa, where he first used Satyagraha as a method of resistance, he repeatedly drew attention to discriminatory laws against IndiansIn a Dec 19, 1901 letter, he described the restrictions in the Transvaal, where Indians could not hold land, were required to live and trade only in designated areas, and were barred from footpaths. In the Orange River Colony, he wrote, an Indian could not even enter without special permission, except as a domestic servant or labourer.After returning to India, he continued to write about the poor conditions of Indians legally settled in South Africa. In an Aug 29, 1919 letter, he blamed the “greedy Europeans of Natal” for importing Indian indentured labour at miserably low wages while ignoring local Zulu workers, all in pursuit of “enormous profits”.
Cow Slaughter And Eid
Gandhi’s correspondence also addressed social fractures, particularly Hindu-Muslim relations. In a 1919 letter written around Bakrid, he recounted a conversation with Maulana Abdul Bari of Lucknow’s Firangi Mahal, a prominent supporter of the Khilafat Movement.
Gandhi quoted the Maulana as saying: “Islam will fall to pieces if it ever takes and never gives…. If we take from you, we must give to you.” Abdul Bari had urged his followers to abstain from cow slaughter. On Bakrid, he sent Gandhi a telegram: “In celebration of Hindu-Muslim unity, no cow sacrifices in Firangi-Mahal this Bakri-Id.”More than a century later, these letters are more than historical records. They reveal Gandhi not only as a politician confronting colonial power but as a public figure wrestling with representation, violence, communal division and moral responsibility. Through TOI’s pages, his words travelled beyond the immediate battles of the freedom struggle, leaving an intimate record of how he tried to shape public opinion — and India itself.

articles.title: Luigi Mangione expected to plead guilty to federal charges over killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO: Reports
articles.body:
Beril Canakci
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
Luigi Mangione, accused of killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York in 2024, is expected to plead guilty in his federal case Friday, according to several US media reports.
Mangione, 28, is due to appear at 11 am local time (1500GMT) before US District Judge Margaret M. Garnett in Manhattan for a hearing jointly requested this week by federal prosecutors and his defense lawyers, according to reports.
Thompson, 50, was the chief executive of UnitedHealthcare, the insurance arm of UnitedHealth Group, the largest health insurer in the US. He was shot from behind on a Manhattan sidewalk on Dec. 4, 2024, as he walked to the company's investor conference.
Mangione was arrested five days later at a fast-food restaurant in Pennsylvania.
The killing sparked widespread debate in the US over health insurance practices, while Mangione drew an unusual wave of online sympathy from people frustrated with the country's healthcare system, alongside condemnation from officials and Thompson's family.
Mangione faces separate state and federal prosecutions stemming from the shooting.
In New York state court, he pleaded not guilty to murder and terrorism-related charges. Jury selection is scheduled to begin Sept. 8. If convicted, he could face 25 years to life in prison, though the state judge dismissed the terrorism charges last September. 
In the federal case, Mangione faces two counts of stalking resulting in death, each carrying a maximum sentence of life in prison without parole. Garnett earlier dismissed a federal murder charge against Mangione, the only count against him that could have carried the death penalty.
Mangione's federal trial had been tentatively scheduled for January 2027.

articles.title: Ilu-hack, pop-up pood: Estonian-English mixing thrives in compound nouns
articles.body:
Ilu-hack, pop-up pood: Estonian-English mixing thrives in compound nouns
In recent years, English is finding its way into everyday Estonian mainly through compound nouns, with video bloggers leading the trend, a new study finds.
Tallinn University (TLÜ) linguists Anna Verschik and Helin Kask analyzed texts from more than 40 blogs, 10 video blogs and eight podcasts, examining hundreds of thousands of words to see how younger adults in Estonia mix English into Estonian.
The researchers found clear differences across platforms: video bloggers, or vloggers, mixed languages about twice as often as bloggers in written content and podcast hosts.
Compound nouns accounted for 85 percent of all mixed-language expressions, including terms such as "bomber-jakk" ("bomber jacket") and "trummi-set" ("drumset"). English verbs and longer phrases such as "ära friikima" ("freak out") or "must-have asjad" ("must-have items") were much less common.
English-derived terms also often outcompete their official Estonian equivalents online.
Google searches returned about 3.5 million results for "foto-shoot," ("photoshoot") compared with 173,000 for the recommended Estonian term "fotosessioon." "Auto-trip" ("roadtrip") appeared nearly five times more often than the Estonian "autoretk."
The researchers say speakers may turn to English because it can better convey a particular meaning or emotional tone more naturally. For example, "üli-happy" ("incredibly happy") can sound more casual and expressive in everyday speech than the formal Estonian "üliõnnelik."
Original grammar still intact
Despite the influx of English vocabulary, the researchers found no evidence that language mixing is disrupting the mechanics of Estonian grammar, with English elements generally being adapted to fit within Estonian sentence structure and inflection rules.
The two languages also share a tendency to create new words by combining existing ones, making it relatively easy for native speakers to seamlessly slot English word stems into their Estonian.
The findings were published in the International Journal of Bilingualism.
--
Editor: Airika Harrik, Aili Vahtla

articles.title: As Wildberries Burns, Russia Launches Military Marketplace “Roy.Market” for Drones and Defense Equipment
articles.body:
- Category
- World
As Wildberries Burns, Russia Launches Military Marketplace “Roy.Market” for Drones and Defense Equipment
Russia has taken its military-focused marketplace “Roy.Market” out of pilot operation, allowing suppliers to independently list and manage products for drones and other military equipment, RBC-Ukraine reported on August 14, citing Russian outlet Kommersant.
“Roy.Market” was initially launched in early 2025, but remained in a pilot phase as Russia’s Center for Unmanned Systems and Technologies (CBST) developed its logistics infrastructure and tested the specialized procurement model.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the updated system, suppliers can now independently add products, manage inventories and prices, and process orders through personal accounts. Previously, much of this work was handled by the marketplace’s own staff, according to CBST Chairman Andrei Bezrukov.
The platform’s catalog extends beyond drone components. It includes 3D printers, fiber-optic spools, antennas, chargers, and other equipment intended for field laboratories and unmanned systems operations, according to RBC-Ukraine.
CBST plans to further expand the marketplace by adding suppliers of field uniforms, personal protective equipment, and body armor. The organization also intends to attract vendors that previously operated on civilian e-commerce platforms such as Wildberries and Ozon.
The marketplace is designed around a lower commission than major civilian platforms, according to CBST representatives, although sellers will remain responsible for logistics costs, the outlet reported.
To handle deliveries, “Roy.Market” is shifting to a distributed 4PL logistics model. Under the system, products can remain with suppliers or within existing logistics networks until an order is placed, after which several logistics operators can be involved in completing the delivery. CBST expects the model to expand the platform’s delivery coverage without requiring it to build its own warehouse network.
Access for buyers remains restricted. The marketplace operates as a closed platform requiring authentication and different levels of user access.
CBST also plans to connect other Russian security agencies to the system beyond the Russian Defense Ministry and develop its business-to-business operations.
The organization aims to expand the catalog to more than 10,000 products by 2027.
The push to expand Russia’s military-oriented e-commerce infrastructure comes as Ukrainian strikes have increasingly affected the country’s civilian logistics networks. Ukrainian drone attacks on Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, have destroyed around one-third of the company’s total warehouse capacity.
The retailer generates roughly 6 trillion rubles ($74 billion) in annual sales through nearly 100,000 pickup locations.

articles.title: Japan Weighs New Russia Sanctions After Putin’s First Visit to Disputed Kuril Islands
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Japan Weighs New Russia Sanctions After Putin’s First Visit to Disputed Kuril Islands
Japan is weighing additional sanctions on Russia after the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, traveled to the disputed Kuril Islands on August 13, his first visit as the leader.
A senior Japanese Foreign Ministry official told reporters that Tokyo is "considering what step to take going forward," Kyodo News reported on August 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Putin traveled to Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu and the largest of the four Russian-held islands Tokyo claims, days after overseeing Russian Pacific Fleet exercises in the Far East. According to the Russian government, he visited a fish-processing plant, a hospital and a school and met with local residents.
Tokyo summoned Russia's ambassador, Nikolay Nozdrev, and lodged a formal protest, calling the visit "totally unacceptable." Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi declared the islands "an inherent part of Japanese territory both historically and under international law."
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed that the Kremlin is likely using the visit to deter Japan from adopting a more assertive defense posture. The move also aims to discourage EU seizures of Russian shadow-fleet vessels, tying the island dispute to the pressure campaign around Moscow's war against Ukraine.
Russia and Japan have never signed a peace treaty to end World War II, a stalemate entirely rooted in the Kurils. Soviet forces seized the four southernmost islands—Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai islets—in the war's final weeks, expelling the Japanese residents. Japan calls them the Northern Territories and has never dropped the claim.
The visit lands as Tokyo's posture toward Moscow hardens. Japan's 2026 Defense White Paper, published earlier this month, named Russia among the country's principal threats. Putin criticized the paper on Wednesday, asserting the islands became Russian territory "as a result of World War II" and accusing Japan of imposing "unprovoked sanctions" over the war in Ukraine.
The trip closes even the pretense of a diplomatic thaw. Under former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, Takaichi's political mentor, Japan met Putin 27 times in pursuit of a peace treaty. In 2018, the two sides agreed to accelerate talks on a 1956 declaration that envisaged returning Shikotan and the Habomai islets after a treaty was signed. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine froze those negotiations in 2022.
The visit is not without precedent. In 2010, then-President Dmitry Medvedev became the first Russian head of state to visit the islands, traveling to Kunashir, a move that drew a formal protest without severing bilateral contact. Putin's trip arrives as a harder marker, set against Russia's sustained war footing rather than a peacetime dispute.
Ukraine has staked out its own position in the row, aligning with Tokyo against Moscow. Kyiv's parliament recognized the islands as Japanese territory in 2022, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree affirming Japan's sovereignty over its Northern Territories.
The protest has drawn a combative response from Moscow, where Security Council deputy chairman Dmitry Medvedev warned that Tokyo's insistence on its historical claim would change nothing and threatened grave consequences should Japan continue to press it. He dismissed Takaichi's position outright, asserting the islands had always been and would remain Russian territory.

articles.title: Japan Scrambles Fighter Jets as Chinese Y-9 Recon Aircraft Approaches Okinawa
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Japan Scrambles Fighter Jets as Chinese Y-9 Recon Aircraft Approaches Okinawa
Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter jets on August 12 after a Chinese Y-9 reconnaissance aircraft flew through the East China Sea near southern Japanese territory, Defence Blog reported on August 13.
These airspace intercepts come against a backdrop of escalating regional tensions with Moscow. Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev had recently threatened Tokyo with “monstrous consequences” over its territorial claims to the disputed South Kuril Islands, responding to an official Japanese protest sparked by Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s first-ever visit to the contested archipelago.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Joint Staff Office reported that the Chinese intelligence-gathering aircraft flew from mainland China, crossing the East China Sea south of Nagasaki Prefecture’s Danjo Islands.
The plane then turned southwest and flew northwest of Okinawa’s main island before changing course again to head back toward the mainland.
In response, Japan’s Western Air Defense Force launched its fighter jets. While the exact number of scrambled interceptors was not specified, the published flight track shows that the Chinese aircraft remained over international waters throughout the incident, Defence Blog wrote.
The Y-9, a Chinese-built military transport aircraft adapted for signals and imagery intelligence collection, has become a routine presence in the region. The incident adds to a rapidly growing pace of Japanese fighter launches, which have averaged roughly two per day in recent months.
Between April and June alone, Japan conducted 181 scrambles, with 139 responding to Chinese aircraft and drones, and 42 to Russian aircraft, according to Defence Blog.
Japan’s Ministry of Defense attributes this elevated tempo to the expansion of Chinese and Russian military activity near the Nansei Islands chain, which stretches from Kyushu toward Taiwan and includes Okinawa.
A spokesman for Japan’s Joint Staff described the regional operations as “certainly expanding and intensifying,” citing previous incidents involving Chinese aircraft carrier deployments, joint Russian-Chinese bomber patrols, and a December 2025 incident in which a Chinese J-15 fighter intermittently illuminated its radar on a Japanese F-15 interceptor.
Defence Blog notes that, to counter these frequent approaches, Japan relies on F-15J, F-2, and F-35A stealth fighters, which sit on high-readiness alert and can take to the air within minutes of detecting an incoming track.
This growing tempo of airspace intercepts aligns with Japan’s annual Defense Ministry White Paper, which recently warned that expanding military coordination between China, Russia, and North Korea is creating escalating regional security risks.
The report highlighted that joint flights by Chinese and Russian strategic bombers have occurred annually since 2019, with recent patrols in December and June turning directly toward Tokyo for the first time.
